authors.name: Abbo of Fleury
authors.identity: hagiographer, grammarian, computist; Latin prose writer
authors.biography: Born c. 945 near Orléans, oblate of Fleury, and trained there in grammar, dialectic, and computus. At the invitation of Oswald of Worcester he taught at Ramsey Abbey in the Fenland from 985 to 987, where he wrote the Passio Sancti Eadmundi at the request of the Ramsey monks and dedicated it to Dunstan. Returning to Fleury, he became abbot in 988 and defended his monastery against episcopal encroachment; he died in 1004 in a brawl at La Réole while attempting to reform the priory of La Réole.
authors.profile: One of the leading scholars of tenth-century Europe. At Ramsey he composed the Passio Sancti Eadmundi (985-987), the earliest Latin life of King Edmund of East Anglia and the basis of Ælfric's Old English life; his other works include the Quaestiones grammaticales (dedicated to his English students), computistical treatises, and the Collectio canonum.
authors.style: Clear, correct Latin prose with the polish of the Fleury school; the Passio builds its narrative through dramatic dialogue and carefully staged scenes of Edmund's martyrdom and the discovery of his incorrupt body.
authors.concerns: The union of grammar, computus, and exegesis in monastic learning; royal sanctity and the cult of St Edmund; the reform of monastic discipline.
authors.significance: The principal conduit of continental monastic learning into the English Benedictine Reform; his teaching at Ramsey raised the standard of Latin scholarship in England, and his Passio Eadmundi founded the literary cult of St Edmund, patron saint of the English kingdom.
authors.uncertainty: None significant for the works recorded here; the Passio's dedication to Dunstan and composition at Ramsey (985-987) are established.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography

authors.name: Abraham Cowley
authors.identity: Poet, essayist, and royalist secretary; the most celebrated English poet of the mid-seventeenth century, who adapted metaphysical wit, introduced the 'Pindaric' ode to English, and championed the new science and the plain prose style.
authors.biography: Born 1618 in London, a posthumous son of a grocer; a child prodigy educated at Westminster and Trinity College, Cambridge, publishing Poetical Blossoms at fifteen (1633). A royalist, he served Queen Henrietta Maria in Paris (1646–56) as secretary and cipher-clerk, was imprisoned briefly on returning to England, and published his Poems (1656), including the Pindarique Odes, The Mistress, and Davideis. At the Restoration he was rewarded with the lease of Chertsey Abbey and a modest sinecure, wrote essays on retirement and the Royal Society (Of Plants, 1668), and died 28 July 1667. He was buried in Westminster Abbey near Chaucer and Spenser.
authors.profile: The transitional figure between the metaphysicals and the Augustans, whose graceful verse, essays, and advocacy of the Royal Society made him the model of the cultivated Restoration man of letters.
authors.style: Metaphysical conceit gradually disciplined toward neoclassical clarity; the irregular 'Pindaric' ode; fluent essayistic prose; and a witty, learned, but increasingly plain idiom.
authors.concerns: The value of retirement and the country life; the new experimental philosophy and Baconianism; biblical epic; love and poetic wit; the reform of prose style toward clarity.
authors.significance: Cowley's reputation stood above all his contemporaries' at the Restoration; his Pindaric odes created a major English form, his essays shaped the periodical and the plain style, and his advocacy of the Royal Society linked literature to the new science.
authors.uncertainty: Cowley's life is well documented; the value of his poetry declined sharply after Johnson's Life exposed the 'violence' of his conceits, though modern criticism has revived interest.
sources: The Prose Writings of William Cullen Bryant (2 volumes)

authors.name: Adam Ferguson
authors.identity: Minister, army chaplain and professor at Edinburgh, whose Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767) made commercial progress and the loss of civic spirit a single problem.
authors.biography: Born at Leith in 1723, the son of the town's minister, he was educated at Edinburgh, was licensed as a preacher and served as a regimental chaplain abroad during the Seven Years' War. In 1764 he supplied the Glasgow lectures left uncovered when Adam Smith went abroad with the Duke of Buccleuch, and in the same year was appointed to the Edinburgh chair of moral philosophy, which he held until his resignation. His Essay on the History of Civil Society (1767) and the four-volume History of the Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic (1769) won him a wide reading in Britain and France, and he helped found the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1783. His Principles of Moral and Political Science, from his lectures, appeared in 1792 and his Institutes of Moral Science posthumously in 1823. He was a friend of Hume, Smith, Robertson and Carlyle, and a frequent visitor to Paris and Geneva. He died in 1816.
authors.profile: The moral historian of civil society, who read history as the unintended product of human action and warned that commerce could purchase comfort at the cost of citizenship.
authors.style: Large-swinging historical prose, sententious and rhetorical; generalisation from ancient and modern instances; a preacher's cadence and a stadial theorist's confidence in periods and stages.
authors.concerns: Stages of society from savage to commercial life; the unintended consequences of action; corruption, arms and civic participation; the psychological costs of the division of labour; the Roman republic as a mirror of modern politics.
authors.significance: His Essay founded the sociological reading of history and supplied the republican critique of commercial modernity that later political theory, from Marx to Arendt, has reused.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of his lecture courses and the relationship between his published works and his teaching manuscripts remain matters of scholarly argument.

works.title: An Essay on the History of Civil Society

authors.name: Adam Smith
authors.identity: Moral philosopher and political economist of Glasgow and Kirkcaldy, author of The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776).
authors.biography: Born at Kirkcaldy in 1723 and educated at Glasgow and at Balliol College, Oxford, where he found the place intellectually barren, he returned to Scotland and began public lectures in Edinburgh in 1748 with the encouragement of Lord Kames. He was appointed successively to the chairs of logic and of moral philosophy at Glasgow, where his teaching on jurisprudence, rhetoric and police shaped a generation. The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), built on sympathy and the impartial spectator, made his reputation. As tutor to the young Duke of Buccleuch he spent nearly two years in France, meeting philosophes and physiocrats, and then retired to Kirkcaldy to write, publishing the Wealth of Nations in 1776 with Strahan and Cadell. He took office as a commissioner of customs in Edinburgh in 1778, became a fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh and was elected lord rector of Glasgow. He died in Edinburgh on 17 July 1790, having asked that his unpublished manuscripts be destroyed; the Essays on Philosophical Subjects, a posthumous volume, appeared in 1795.
authors.profile: A moral philosopher of commercial society who joined the analysis of sympathy to the analysis of exchange, and wrote economic reasoning as part of ethics.
authors.style: Long, periodic, expository prose built from illustration and qualification; a lecturer's plainness and abundance of example; irony directed at merchants, ministers and monopolists.
authors.concerns: Sympathy, propriety and the impartial spectator; the division of labour, self-interest and the invisible hand of adjustment; the history of civil society and the effects of commerce; justice, utility and the proper limits of government.
authors.significance: He founded political economy as a systematic discipline and remains the reference point of liberal arguments about markets, while his moral philosophy has been recovered as the indispensable half of his work.
authors.uncertainty: His lecture notes survive only in student reports and later copies, so the chronology and content of his teaching on jurisprudence are disputed.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations

authors.name: Aemilia Lanyer
authors.identity: poet
authors.biography: Baptized 27 January 1569 in London, daughter of Baptist Bassano, a court musician of Italian origin. After her father's death she became the mistress of Henry Carey, Lord Hunsdon, the Lord Chamberlain; later she married the court musician Alfonso Lanyer. In 1611 she published Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum, making her one of the first Englishwomen to issue a volume of poetry in her own name. She died on 3 April 1645.
authors.profile: Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum (1611) — a long poem on Christ's Passion with a proto-feminist 'Eve's Apology' and the defence of women's learning, prefaced by dedicatory poems to a roll-call of great ladies and followed by 'The Description of Cooke-ham', the first country-house poem in English.
authors.style: Devotional narrative in rhyme royal with a distinctively woman-centred exegesis; a grave, ornate, occasionally magnificent handling of biblical story.
authors.concerns: Women's virtue, learning, and agency; the Passion and its female witnesses; patronage among women.
authors.significance: A founding voice of English women's poetry; 'Eve's Apology' is the first sustained feminist argument in English verse, and Cooke-ham precedes Jonson's Penshurst in the country-house genre.
authors.uncertainty: Her relationship with Shakespeare, if any, is the stuff of speculation, not record; the Forman casebooks document her consultations but their readings are contested.
sources: The Letters of Robert Bloomfield and His Circle

authors.name: Alcuin of York
authors.identity: teacher; poet; letter writer; theologian
authors.biography: Pupil and then master of the school of York under Ælberht; visited Rome in 781 and joined the court of Charlemagne, becoming the leading intellectual of the Carolingian Renaissance; abbot of Tours from 796 until his death.
authors.profile: A large corpus of letters (including the famous letter of 793 on the sack of Lindisfarne), poems (notably on York and its library), educational dialogues on grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic, biblical commentaries, and liturgical and polemical writings against adoptionism.
authors.style: Elegant, courtly Latin; epistolary warmth and learning; verse of wide metrical range.
authors.concerns: The reform of learning and the correction of texts; pastoral care of rulers; orthodoxy; the preservation of the Northumbrian scholarly tradition abroad.
authors.significance: The chief transmitter of Anglo-Saxon learning to the Continent; architect of the educational program of Charlemagne's court.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate (c. 735, sometimes given 732–735).
themes: The transience of earthly glory (ubi sunt)
sources: The Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records: A Collective Edition

authors.name: Aldhelm
authors.identity: poet; prose writer; churchman
authors.biography: West Saxon nobleman educated at Canterbury under the archbishop Theodore and the abbot Hadrian; abbot of Malmesbury and, from c. 705, first bishop of Sherborne. The first major Anglo-Latin author, he composed in an elaborate 'hermeneutic' style that set the standard for insular Latinity for centuries.
authors.profile: Principal works: the prose and verse De virginitate (in praise of virginity, with a catalogue of exemplars), the Epistola ad Acircium (a treatise on Latin metre addressed to King Aldfrith of Northumbria), the Aenigmata (one hundred Latin riddles), the Carmen rhythmicum, and a small corpus of letters.
authors.style: Learned, allusive 'hermeneutic' Latin rich in Grecisms, archaisms, and rare vocabulary; metrical virtuosity in both hexameters and rhythmic verse.
authors.concerns: Monastic virtue, especially virginity; Latin learning and prosody; the unity of the English church.
authors.significance: Founder of the Anglo-Latin literary tradition; his works were models for Bede, Boniface, Alcuin, and the tenth-century Benedictine reformers.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate (from later sources, principally William of Malmesbury).
movements: Early Anglo-Latin Learning and the Northumbrian Golden Age
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Old English Literature, 2nd edition

authors.name: Alexander Barclay
authors.nationality: English (writing in England); Scottish by birth
authors.identity: poet; translator; priest
authors.biography: Born about 1484, probably in Scotland; educated perhaps at Oxford, he became a priest, chaplain at the college of St Mary Ottery in Devon, then a Benedictine monk of Ely and finally rector of All Hallows, Lombard Street. He died at Croydon in June 1552. His Ship of Fools (1509) adapted Sebastian Brant's Narrenschiff through Locher's Latin, and his five Eclogues (c. 1514) introduced pastoral to England.
authors.profile: The first English pastoralist and the translator of the most widely read satire of the age. The Ship of Fools is a comprehensive estates satire — a gallery of fools from the scholar to the bishop — written in fluent rhyme royal and five-line stanzas, and the Eclogues, based on Mantuan, moralize the shepherd's life and the corruption of courts and clergy.
authors.style: Smooth, competent stanzaic verse; moral satire without Skeltonic fury; a translator's fidelity to his Latin sources over originality.
authors.concerns: The folly of the estates; clerical reform; the moral uses of pastoral; the dignity of English as a literary language.
authors.significance: Introduced both the estates satire of the continental Renaissance and the pastoral eclogue into English; a principal channel by which humanist satire reached the Tudor reading public.
authors.uncertainty: Birthplace and early life uncertain; the date of the Eclogues is approximate.
sources: William Wordsworth: The Major Works

authors.name: Alexander Pope
authors.identity: English poet, satirist, and translator, the dominant verse mind of Augustan England and a leading figure of the heroic-couplet tradition.
authors.biography: Born in London into a Roman Catholic family, Pope was largely self-educated because his faith barred him from the universities, and lifelong ill health confined him much to the countryside at Windsor and later Twickenham. An early Essay on Criticism (1711) established his reputation, followed by the mock-heroic Rape of the Lock (1712, expanded 1714). Between 1715 and 1720 he published a celebrated verse translation of the Iliad, financed by subscription. His political and personal satires culminated in the Dunciad (1728, revised 1743), and his philosophical poem An Essay on Man appeared in 1733-1734. He died at Twickenham in 1744.
authors.profile: A poet of satire, epistle, and translation who perfected the closed heroic couplet and made verse the instrument of social and intellectual criticism; his work ranges from elegant ridicule to sustained moral philosophy.
authors.style: Epigrammatic compression and antithesis in the heroic couplet; balanced syntax, precise rhyme, and pointed wit; a commanding satiric voice; and a neoclassical polish that subordinates invention to judgement.
authors.concerns: Order amid social and literary chaos; the limits and uses of reason; self-knowledge and self-interest in society; the corruption of taste and learning; and the poet's relation to patronage and the market.
authors.significance: The central English poet of the early eighteenth century and the standard-bearer of the neoclassical heroic couplet; his satires and criticism defined Augustan literary culture and influenced prose style for decades.
authors.uncertainty: A frail, deformed body and his Roman Catholicism shaped his life; some details of his schooling and the dating of his early poems are reconstructed from family and manuscript evidence rather than firm records.

works.title: Peri Bathous, the Art of Sinking in Poetry
The Works of Mr. Martinus Scriblerus
Verses to the Memory of an Unfortunate Lady

sources: The Literature of Political Economy: A Classified Catalogue of Select Publications in the Different Departments of That Science, with Historical, Critical and Biographical Notices (Cambridge Library Collection)

authors.name: Alfred the Great
authors.identity: king; translator; lawgiver; patron of letters
authors.biography: King of Wessex 871–899. After the near-collapse of his kingdom before the Viking army, his victory at Edington (878) and the treaty with Guthrum secured a period of reconstruction in which he pursued a deliberate program of educational revival, gathering scholars at his court and translating into English the books 'most necessary for all men to know'. Died 26 October 899.
authors.profile: Personally translated (or directed the translation of) Gregory's Pastoral Care with his famous Preface (c. 890), Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Augustine's Soliloquies, and the first fifty prose Psalms; commissioned the Old English Orosius, the Old English Bede, Werferth's translation of Gregory's Dialogues, his own law code (the Domboc), and the Common Stock of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (c. 892).
authors.style: Clear, idiomatic prose that adapts rather than slavishly renders its Latin sources; the Preface to the Pastoral Care is a classic statement of vernacular purpose.
authors.concerns: The restoration of wisdom and literacy as the foundation of just rule; the defense of the kingdom and the Christian people.
authors.significance: Founder of the English prose tradition; his translations preserved classical and patristic texts in the vernacular and set the model for all later Old English prose.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of his personal authorship is debated: the Preface is certainly his, but the translations were produced by his circle under his direction.

works.title: Old English Boethius (with the Meters of Boethius)
Old English Pastoral Care (with Alfred's Preface)

sources: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: A Revised Translation

authors.name: Amelia Opie
authors.identity: Novelist, poet, and abolitionist
authors.biography: Amelia Opie was born Amelia Alderson in Norwich, daughter of the physician and author John Alderson. Educated in a wide range of languages and literature by her father, she moved to London in the 1780s and entered literary and dissenting circles. She married the painter John Opie in 1782 (her first marriage, to John James Opie, had been annulled on grounds of his prior marriage) and hosted a celebrated literary salon. Her first novel, The Tricks of Innocence, appeared in 1794, followed by The Father and Daughter (1801). After her husband's death in 1807 she retreated from the literary world, becoming a Quaker and devoting herself to abolitionism and religious writing. She died in Norwich in 1853.
authors.profile: Opie's fiction of the Romantic period, especially The Father and Daughter, is a distinctive form of sentimental moral realism that treats the seduced woman with compassion. Her early novels explore the condition of women in patriarchal society and the moral failings of men with a directness unusual for their date; her later writing abandoned fiction for verse and religious tract.
authors.style: Sentimental prose of moral directness; domestic realism; sympathetic interiority focused on women's vulnerability; narrative address to the reader's moral feeling; the seduction plot used as a vehicle for moral argument rather than titillation.
authors.concerns: The condition of women in a patriarchal marriage market; the moral responsibility of fathers and men; the abolition of slavery; Quaker testimony and pacifism; the education of women's sensibility.
authors.significance: Opie's The Father and Daughter is one of the most important sentimental novels of the 1790s and a key text in the genealogy of the 'fallen woman' novel; her later activism and Quaker life make her a distinctive figure in the transition from Romantic fiction to Victorian moral campaigning.
authors.uncertainty: Her birth year is sometimes given as 1769 and sometimes as 1768.

authors.name: Andrew Bell
authors.nationality: Scottish and British; Anglican evangelical educational reform and the monitorial-school tradition
authors.identity: Church of Scotland-trained clergyman and school superintendent, author of the Madras System of Education and founder-figure of the National (Church of England) school movement
authors.biography: Andrew Bell was born at St Andrews on 27 March 1753, the son of a local magistrate and wig-maker of the burgh, and was educated at the grammar school and from 1769 at the University of St Andrews, where he studied mathematics and natural philosophy and supported himself by teaching, later adding medical study. Ordained in the Church of England after taking orders, he went to India in 1787 as an East India Company chaplain attached to a European regiment, and in 1789 was appointed superintendent of the Madras Male Orphan Asylum, the school for fatherless soldiers' children at Egmore. There, watching an Indian boy teach letters to his companions on a board of sand, he devised and applied what he called the Madras System of Education: the school taught itself through pupil monitors, graded classes, sand and slate instead of paper and pens, and rewards and emulation administered by the children themselves. He returned to England in 1796 and published the account as An Experiment in Education, Made at the Male Asylum of Madras; Suggesting a System by which a School or Family may teach itself, under the Superintendence of the Master (1797), reissued and enlarged in 1805 with a full exposition of the system, followed by his System of Education (1808) and a long series of reports, extracts and defences. In 1798 he placed his pamphlet in the hands of Joseph Lancaster, whose London school for the poor adopted and publicised the method under the name "British" or "Lancasterian" system; the resulting priority quarrel, pursued through prefaces, replies, evidence before the parliamentary committees on education of 1816-18 and the rival societies, embittered the cause of mass elementary schooling. The Church of England party, seeking a denominational alternative to Lancaster's undenominational and nonconformant patronage, formed the National Society for Promoting the Education of the Poor in the Principles of the Established Church in 1811 with Bell as its superintendent and organizer, and by his death it had founded thousands of schools. Made a prebendary of Westminster and honoured with the degree of D.D., Bell remained a bachelor of imperious manner and enormous savings; in 1831 he settled some £120,000 on trustees, half destined for his native town, funding Madras College and other schools. He died at Cheltenham on 27 January 1832.
authors.profile: Bell's writings are practical and polemical: the school report and manual (An Experiment in Education, 1797; the enlarged Experimental Education / exposition of the system, 1805; System of Education, 1808), the edited series of Asylum and National Society reports, and the Extracts, Remarks, Facts and Documents assembled to vindicate his claim. They are prose of instruction and litigation - instruction sheets, tables of rewards, testimonial letters, and argument.
authors.style: Clear, dry, exemplum-driven and relentlessly concrete: the writing moves from observed detail (the sand, the slate, the monitor's cue) to general rule. Its rhetoric is that of the testimonial and the specification, with numbers, prices and school returns used as proof. In controversy it becomes curt and accusatory, dense with documents and dates rather than with theory.
authors.concerns: How to educate great numbers of poor children at almost no cost; order, emulation and self-government in the classroom; the religious character of national education and the rights of the established Church; the moral uses of military orphanage; priority and authorship as property; education as a defence of empire and social stability.
authors.significance: Bell, with Lancaster, invented the monitorial system that first made mass elementary education practically imaginable in the English-speaking world; his Madras experiment travelled to Britain, Ireland, the United States and the colonies, and the National Society he organised built the Church-school network that preceded the great elementary acts of 1870. His bequest created Madras College at St Andrews, one of the largest public schools in Scotland.
authors.uncertainty: The year in which Bell actually began the monitorial "experiment" at the Asylum is variously given (1787, 1789, or the early 1790s); the first edition of An Experiment in Education is catalogued in 1797 and re-issued enlarged in 1805. The brief's "controversy before the Privy Council in 1818" could not be verified: the sources checked place the Bell-Lancaster priority fight before the parliamentary committees on education of 1816-18, while the Committee of Council on Education belongs to 1839. Some older notices give his death as 24 January 1832.

authors.name: Andrew Boorde
authors.identity: physician; traveller; writer
authors.biography: Born about 1490 in Sussex; educated at Oxford and a Carthusian monk before leaving the order to practise medicine. He travelled widely in Europe and the Mediterranean, and his books — The Dyetary of Health (1542) and The First Book of the Introduction of Knowledge (1547) — made him the first English writer of popular medicine and travel. He died in the Fleet prison in April 1549.
authors.profile: The first English popular medical writer and the father of the English travel book. The Dyetary prescribes diet and regimen in plain English for the common reader, and The Introduction of Knowledge — the first English book of travels written from personal observation — describes the peoples of Europe in prose and verse, with specimens of their languages.
authors.style: Homely, practical prose; the physician's plain advice; travellers' tales told with a journalist's eye for the odd and useful.
authors.concerns: Popular health and regimen; the description of foreign nations; the usefulness of knowledge to the commonwealth.
authors.significance: Founded the English traditions of popular medicine and of the travel book; his writings document the widening world of the Tudor reader.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; parts of the biography rest on late testimony.
themes: The supernatural ballad and willed belief
sources: The Cambridge Companion to British Romanticism

authors.name: Andrew Marvell
authors.identity: Metaphysical and political poet, satirist, and long-serving Member of Parliament for Hull; author of 'To His Coy Mistress', 'Upon Appleton House', and the Horatian Ode, and of fierce Restoration prose satires against popery and arbitrary government.
authors.biography: Born 31 March 1621 at Winestead, son of a Puritan clergyman; educated at Hull Grammar School and Trinity College, Cambridge (BA 1639). He travelled abroad (1642–46), served as tutor to Mary Fairfax at Nun Appleton (1651–52), where he wrote several major poems, and to Lord Dutton's ward (1653–57). Elected MP for Hull in 1659, he held the post through the Restoration until his death, serving on the Council of State and defending religious toleration and the City of London's liberties. He wrote the prose satire The Rehearsal Transpros'd (1672–73) and An Account of the Growth of Popery (1677), and died suddenly on 16 August 1678. His Miscellaneous Poems were published posthumously in 1681.
authors.profile: The poet of balance and irony, who combined metaphysical wit with public conscience, writing equally as a lover, a country-house observer, a republican sympathiser, and a champion of toleration.
authors.style: Tightly argued conceits and dramatic irony; the Horatian ode; satiric bite and wit; the country-house poem's topographical detail; and a prose of urbane, devastating irony and plain argument.
authors.concerns: Time, mortality, and desire; liberty of conscience and resistance to tyranny; the ethics of the estate and the country house; the corruption of court and clergy; the balance of wit and judgment.
authors.significance: Long valued only for a few lyrics, Marvell was re-established by T. S. Eliot as a major metaphysical poet and is now recognised as one of the greatest English lyric and political satirists, bridging the Interregnum and the Restoration.
authors.uncertainty: Marvell's politics and even his religion were ambiguous in his lifetime and remain debated; most of his poems were published posthumously, so their dating is often inferential.

works.title: An Account of the Growth of Popery and Arbitrary Government in England
An Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland

sources: Joel Barlow's Columbiad: A Bicentennial Reading

authors.name: Ann Radcliffe
authors.nationality: English; the Romantic period and the Gothic novel
authors.identity: Novelist, travel writer and the most widely read English prose fiction writer of the 1790s; the defining practitioner of the Gothic romance of terror.
authors.biography: Ann Radcliffe was born in London in 1764, the daughter of George Ward, and was educated in a Quaker school before her first writings appeared. She married William Radcliffe, a journalist and bookseller, in 1787, and he remained the manager of her publishing affairs throughout her career. Her early romances established a readership that her third prose romance, The Romance of the Forest (1791), made large, and The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794) made her famous; a tour of Holland and the Rhineland in the summer of 1794 produced A Journey Made in the Summer of 1794 (1795), and a longer stay in Italy, undertaken with her husband and her father, supplied the scenery of The Italian (1797). After 1797 she published no further fiction in her lifetime, and contemporaries reported that her later years were given to travel and to a retirement from the reading public. She died in London on 7 February 1823, within weeks of her father's death. Walter Scott's account of her, written for his series of lives of the novelists published in 1821, is the earliest substantive memoir and shaped the biographical tradition; the posthumous volume of 1826, which gathered Gaston de Blondeville with her Italian journal, was published after her death and carries the memoir compiled from the journals she kept.
authors.profile: Radcliffe's mature romances work from a single, disciplined pattern: a sensitive young woman, usually orphaned or separated from protection, is pursued through an environment of ruined castles, monasteries and Alpine solitudes by an authoritarian male figure, and the terrors that appear supernatural are resolved at the end by rational explanation. Her prose is organised around landscape and light, and songs and ballads are interspersed at intervals in the narrative. She claimed for her writing the distinction that terror, proceeding from the sources of sympathy and astonishment, expands the mind, whereas horror, produced by physical distress, contracts it; that distinction, stated in an essay attributed to her in the New Monthly Magazine after her death, is the most quoted account of her method.
authors.style: Long periodic descriptive sentences built on scenery, colour and architectural decay; explained supernaturalism, in which an apparent marvel receives a natural cause in the closing volumes; interspersed songs and ballads; picturesque and sublime landscape derived from contemporary aesthetic theory and from her own travel journals; heroines whose sensibility is both the means of perception and the site of danger.
authors.concerns: The limits of rational explanation; the authority of the past and of Catholic institutions as figures of tyranny; the pursuit of female autonomy within patriarchy; the aesthetics of the sublime and the picturesque as they were debated in the 1790s; sensibility as a mode of knowledge and as a vulnerability.
authors.significance: Her novels set the template for the Gothic romance of terror and fixed the vocabulary and settings that later writers inherited and reacted against. The Mysteries of Udolpho became a cultural touchstone, read and quoted by characters and writers of the next generation, and Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey (1817) parodies its influence while acknowledging it. Sir Walter Scott's memoir and the posthumous publication of her journal in 1826 made her example available to the nineteenth-century Gothic, and her theory of terror versus horror remains a standard term in the criticism of the genre.
authors.uncertainty: Radcliffe's private life is thinly documented and much of the detail in Scott's memoir and in later accounts rests on family recollection reported long after the events. The date of her marriage, the extent of her early education, and the precise itinerary of her Italian journey are known mainly from her own journals as published in 1826 and from Scott's account. The essay on the supernatural in fiction, printed in the New Monthly Magazine in 1826 and attributed to her, is of uncertain authorship and is best read as a contemporary summary of her practice rather than as a work she published. Some attributions of early juvenile and translation work to her remain unsettled in modern scholarship and are not asserted here.

authors.name: Anna Laetitia Barbauld
authors.identity: English poet, essayist, children's writer, and editor, a leading literary and political voice between the Augustan and the Romantic ages.
authors.biography: Barbauld was born into a literary Dissenting family, the daughter of the teacher and historian John Aikin, and was partly educated through her family and the circle of the Warrington Academy. She married the Unitarian minister John Barbauld in 1773 and was involved in running a school kept by him. Her Poems (1773) established her reputation as a polished neoclassical writer. She became a celebrated author of children's literature with Hymns in Prose for Children and the influential Early Lessons (1778-1779), and she wrote political prose, including the pamphlet Sins of Government, Sins of the Nation (1793). She edited the anthology The British Novelists (1810) with an important prefatory essay. A long poem, Eighteen Hundred and Eleven (1812), drew hostile reviews, and she died at Stoke Newington in 1825.
authors.profile: A versatile writer of polished Augustan poetry, moral and political prose, and pioneering children's literature, whose work links the neoclassical and the Romantic, the rational and the sentimental.
authors.style: A clear, correct, often elevated couplet in her verse, marked by Pope-like balance and moral seriousness; a lucid, persuasive, and at times passionate prose; and an intimate, instructive address adapted to children.
authors.concerns: Liberty, dissent, and the ethics of government and war; the education and moral formation of the young; the proper objects of poetry and taste; and the relation of feeling, reason, and public duty.
authors.significance: A major woman of letters who shaped late-Augustan poetry, helped found children's educational literature in English, and influenced contemporaries; her critical and editorial work made her a central figure of her age.
authors.uncertainty: Her exact birthplace is given variously; details of her schoolwork with her husband's academy and the full extent of her editorial series are known only partly and require careful reconstruction.

authors.name: Anne Askew
authors.identity: religious writer; Protestant martyr
authors.biography: Born about 1521 into a Lincolnshire gentry family; married against her will to Thomas Kyme. Her refusal to accept the doctrine of transubstantiation brought her before the authorities in 1545 and 1546; racked in the Tower — reportedly by the Lord Chancellor himself — she was burned at Smithfield on 16 July 1546. Her accounts of her two examinations were printed with John Bale's commentary in 1546–47.
authors.profile: Author of the first English autobiography of a Protestant martyr and the most important woman's voice of the Henrician Reformation. The Examinations record her interrogations in her own words — scriptural, witty, and unyielding — and made her the exemplary female witness of the English church, read and reprinted through the sixteenth century and canonized by Foxe.
authors.style: First-person testimony in the plain style; scriptural riposte reported as dialogue; a cool exactness under the shadow of the stake.
authors.concerns: The right of the laity, and of women, to read and interpret scripture; the sacrament debated as doctrine; the witness of the body against the bishops.
authors.significance: The founding text of English women's religious autobiography and a landmark of the martyrological tradition; her voice resounds in Foxe and in the later women writers of the Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of the racking rest on Foxe and Bale.
themes: Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
sources: The Letters of John Keats, 1814-1821 (2 volumes)

authors.name: Anne Bradstreet
authors.identity: The first published poet of the English colonies in America; a Puritan woman whose verse — 'The Tenth Muse' (1650) and later the intimate family and religious poems published from her manuscript — expresses both learned ambition and the domestic piety of New England.
authors.biography: Born c. 1612 at Northampton, daughter of Thomas Dudley, steward to the Earl of Lincoln; exceptionally well educated. She married Simon Bradstreet (1628) and emigrated with him and her father to Massachusetts Bay on the Arbella (1630), where both husband and father served as governors. She bore eight children and wrote poetry amid the hardships of colonial life. Her brother-in-law published The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America (London, 1650) without her knowledge; a second, more personal collection appeared posthumously (Several Poems, 1678). She died on 16 September 1672 at Andover, Massachusetts.
authors.profile: The Puritan poet who reconciled learned ambition with humility, writing public 'quaternions' on the elements and the ages as well as tender poems to her husband, children, and house, all framed within a faith that submits worldly loss to God's will.
authors.style: Formal 'quaternions' and duologues in the Du Bartas tradition; the intimate domestic lyric; self-deprecating prefaces that assert a woman's right to write; and a plain, heartfelt Puritan piety.
authors.concerns: Faith and submission to Providence; marriage, family, and motherhood; the place of the woman writer; loss, mortality, and the vanity of the world; and the New England experiment.
authors.significance: Bradstreet is the founding figure of American poetry and the first Englishwoman to publish a volume in the New World; her work documents Puritan inner life and women's experience and has been central to the recovery of early American and women's literature.
authors.uncertainty: Bradstreet's exact birth year is uncertain (c. 1612); the dating of her manuscript poems and the authorship of some attributed pieces remain matters of scholarship.

works.title: The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America

sources: Sketches of American Character

authors.name: Anne Conway
authors.identity: Philosopher; her posthumous The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy (1690, Latin 1692) advanced an original metaphysical monism of living spirit and influenced Henry More, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and later thinkers.
authors.biography: Born 14 December 1631 in London, daughter of Sir Heneage Finch; she was educated at home, corresponded in philosophy with Henry More (her brother's Cambridge tutor) from her teens, and married Edward Conway (later Viscount and Earl of Conway) in 1651. Suffering lifelong, disabling headaches, she sought cures across Europe, and in her later years was drawn to Quakerism (she received Quaker visitors including George Fox's circle). She wrote her philosophical treatise in the 1670s; it was published posthumously in Amsterdam (1690, English; 1692, Latin) and circulated among European philosophers. She died on 18 February 1679.
authors.profile: The original metaphysician who argued against the dualism of Descartes and the materialism of Hobbes for a universe of spiritual, mutable substance, anticipating Leibniz's monads in a work admired across Europe.
authors.style: Systematic philosophical argument; a treatise of propositions and demonstrations; metaphysical reasoning about substance, spirit, and creation; and a clear, technical prose.
authors.concerns: The nature of substance, spirit, and body; the critique of Descartes and Hobbes; the goodness and unity of creation; free will and theodicy; and religion and philosophy.
authors.significance: Conway's Principles is a major, original work of early modern philosophy by a woman, influencing the Cambridge Platonists and Leibniz, and her recovery has established her as a significant figure in the history of philosophy.
authors.uncertainty: Conway's life is documented through letters and family records; her single major work was published posthumously and its reception history is partly reconstructed.

works.title: The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy

sources: Maria Edgeworth: A Literary Biography

authors.name: Anne Finch, Countess of Winchilsea
authors.identity: Poet and courtier; one of the finest women writers of the late seventeenth century, whose posthumously celebrated verse ranges from nature lyrics and the celebrated 'Nocturnal Reverie' to witty social poems and meditations on melancholy and her own precarious standing as a woman author.
authors.biography: Born April 1661 at Sywell, educated and appointed maid of honour to Mary of Modena (wife of the Duke of York, later James II). She married Colonel Heneage Finch (1684); after James II's fall in 1688 the Finches were Jacobite exiles, and her husband's death (1689) plunged her into depression, which she wrote about candidly. When her brother-in-law became Earl of Winchilsea she became Countess of Winchilsea (1712). Her poems circulated in manuscript among a literary circle that included Pope and Swift; a collected Poems on Several Occasions appeared in 1713. She died on 5 August 1720.
authors.profile: The poet of sensuous nature, melancholy, and female authorship, whose 'Nocturnal Reverie' Wordsworth singled out as the finest nature poem between Milton and himself.
authors.style: Mellifluous couplets and Pindaric forms; precise, sensuous nature description; candid treatments of depression ('The Spleen'); self-aware wit about being a woman writer; and translations from the French.
authors.concerns: Nature and contemplation; melancholy and the 'spleen'; the constraints on women's writing; Jacobite politics and exile; friendship; and religious resignation.
authors.significance: Long neglected, Finch was recovered by feminist criticism and is now recognised as a major poet of the period; her nature poetry influenced the Romantics and her verse on women's authorship ('The Introduction') is a key early feminist text.
authors.uncertainty: Much of Finch's verse circulated in manuscript and its dating is often uncertain; her canon was substantially expanded by modern editions of her manuscripts.
sources: The Geography Made Easy: Being a New Abridgement of the American Universal Geography

authors.name: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
authors.identity: English peer and moralist whose Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times (1711) made politeness, wit and ridicule the tests of virtue and of religious sincerity.
authors.biography: Born in London on 26 February 1671 and named for his grandfather, the First Earl of Shaftesbury, he was educated privately under the supervision of John Locke and kept only a brief residence at Oxford. He sat in the Commons for Christchurch from 1695 until he succeeded to the earldom in 1699. A failing chest ended any political career, and from 1704 he travelled for his health in the Netherlands and in Italy, corresponding with Dutch and French heterodox writers. He revised the essays, letters and dialogues of those years into Characteristics (1711), which he superintended through the press himself and introduced with a Design'd Letter satirising bookmaking. He died at Consendula in Calabria on 4 February 1713, leaving a daughter; the earldom passed to a nephew.
authors.profile: A philosopher of polite conversation who wrote in genres - letter, dialogue, soliloquy, rhapsody - and treated the inspection of one's own heart as a moral exercise.
authors.style: Aphoristic, urbane and deliberately witty; sustained irony and theatrical self-examination; long periodic sentences pointed by sententious tags; argument conducted as banter.
authors.concerns: An innate moral sense and self-approval; enthusiasm, superstition and the ridicule of fanatics; the fitness of religion to common sense; politeness, reputation and the love of one's country.
authors.significance: He set the terms of eighteenth-century moral-sense theory and of the age's debate about enthusiasm, influencing Hutcheson, Hume, Adam Smith, Chesterfield, Voltaire and Kant, and making ridicule a standard weapon against priestcraft.
authors.uncertainty: Several pieces in Characteristics circulated in manuscript and in unauthorized copies, so the order of composition is still debated.
influencedBy: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury

works.title: Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times
Sensus Communis: An Essay on Wit and Humour

authors.name: Anthony Collins
authors.identity: Barrister and freethinker whose Essay Concerning the Use of Reason (1707) and inquiry on human liberty (1717) made him the boldest English deist before Hume.
authors.biography: Born at Heston in Middlesex in 1676, he was educated at Eton and at King's College, Cambridge, and was called to the bar. He became the close friend and literary executor of John Locke, lived on a property in Lincolnshire, divided his years between Heston and Pall Mall, and gathered a club of free inquirers. His Essay Concerning the Use of Reason (1707) and the Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion (1707) drew a barrage of replies from churchmen, and the published correspondence with the Bishop of Winchester on the evidences of Christianity ran through 1708 and 1709. A Philosophical Inquiry Concerning Human Liberty (1717) denied the liberty of indifference, and The Scheme of Literal Prophecy Considered (1727) denied that Old Testament prophecy proved the gospel. He died in London on 13 December 1729, and a servant's tale that he defied the priests on his deathbed was long printed as a model of infidel constancy.
authors.profile: A lawyer's deism: courteous, relentlessly procedural argument that demands of revelation the same evidence it would require in court.
authors.style: Clear, dry and forensic; scholastic distinctions and long chains of consequence; courteous invective; a fondness for published correspondence and formal rejoinder.
authors.concerns: The boundaries of reason in religion; liberty, necessity and the will; the evidential value of miracle and prophecy; priestly authority and the rights of private judgement; tolerance as a civil necessity.
authors.significance: He moved deism from a defence of natural religion into a historical and philosophical critique of revelation, and defined the freethinking tradition that Bentley, Clarke and Butler were recruited to answer.
authors.uncertainty: The celebrated deathbed declaration is reported by a hostile servant and is generally doubted by modern scholars.

works.title: An Essay Concerning the Use of Reason

authors.name: Aphra Behn
authors.identity: The first English woman to earn a living as a professional writer; a prolific playwright, poet, novelist, and (she claimed) secret agent, whose The Rover (1677) and the novella Oroonoko (1688) are landmarks of Restoration drama and of the early English novel.
authors.biography: Born c. 1640, probably at Canterbury; she claimed (in Oroonoko) to have lived as a girl in Surinam, though this is disputed. She may have served as a royalist intelligence agent in Antwerp (as 'Astrea') during the Second Dutch War, was imprisoned for debt in 1668, and from the 1670s supported herself by writing for the stage. She produced some nineteen plays — comedies including The Rover (1677, 1681), The Feign'd Curtizans (1679), and The Lucky Chance (1686), and the tragicomedies Oroonoko (adapted) and The Widow Ranter (1689) — as well as poetry, translations (from Fontenelle and La Rochefoucauld), and the prose fiction Oroonoko; or, The Royal Slave (1688), Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister, and The Fair Jilt. A staunch royalist and Tory, she wrote for James II's cause and died on 16 April 1689, buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The professional woman of letters who wrote with energy and commercial acumen across every genre, defending a woman's right to write and to pleasure while exposing the sexual and colonial politics of her age.
authors.style: Vigorous comic prose and verse; the rake and the resourceful heroine; bawdy wit and sexual frankness; narrative prose blending travel, romance, and reportage; and political and amorous verse.
authors.concerns: Women's authorship, sexuality, and economic independence; libertinism and the double standard; slavery, colonialism, and the 'noble slave'; royalist and Tory politics; and the professional writer's life.
authors.significance: Behn is the first Englishwoman to have lived by her pen and a founding figure of the English novel; Oroonoko is an early anti-slavery narrative, and her recovery by Virginia Woolf and feminist criticism has made her central to women's literary history.
authors.uncertainty: Behn's early life, her Surinam voyage, her marriage, and her espionage are all disputed or thinly documented; she freely fictionalised her own biography, making the factual record uncertain.

The Widow Ranter; or, The History of Bacon in Virginia

authors.name: Arthur Golding
authors.identity: translator; Puritan gentleman
authors.biography: Born about 1536, half-brother of Margaret Golding, mother of the Earl of Oxford. Educated perhaps at Jesus College, Cambridge, he served in the household of Sir William Cecil and translated steadily through the 1560s and 1570s, chiefly from the classics and from Calvin. He died in May 1606.
authors.profile: The translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses — the first four books in 1565, the complete fifteen in 1567 — together with versions of Caesar, Justin, Seneca, and Calvin's sermons and treatises; his Ovid is 'Shakespeare's Ovid' and the Renaissance Englishman's classic.
authors.style: Energetic fourteeners (rhymed seven-stress couplets) that render Ovid with moralizing commentary and a homespun vividness; Puritan in gloss, pagan in gusto.
authors.concerns: The reconciliation of classical myth with Protestant morality; the edification of the common reader.
authors.significance: His Metamorphoses made Ovid an English book and fed Shakespeare, Spenser, and the entire mythological vocabulary of the Elizabethans.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his education are uncertain.
sources: The Monk (Oxford World's Classics)

authors.name: Asser
authors.nationality: Welsh (writing in Latin for the West Saxon court)
authors.identity: biographer; bishop
authors.biography: Monk of St David's in Wales, recruited by Alfred c. 885 as one of the scholars of his court; bishop of Sherborne from c. 895. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records his death in 909 (or 908).
authors.profile: Author of the Life of King Alfred (893), the principal contemporary biography of an English king: a vivid, partly annalistic portrait of Alfred's wars, piety, illnesses, and program of learning.
authors.style: Latin biography blending Welsh and Carolingian conventions (Einhard's Charlemagne is a model) with annals of the years 849–887.
authors.concerns: The justification and celebration of Alfred's kingship; the union of learning with rule.
authors.significance: The main primary source for Alfred's reign and character.
authors.uncertainty: The Life's authenticity was long debated (the 'Leofric interpolation' question); modern scholarship accepts it as substantially genuine. Dates approximate.
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry

authors.name: Bede
authors.identity: historian; theologian; poet; scholar
authors.biography: Entered the monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow as a child and remained there all his life, becoming priest and teacher; he never travelled beyond Northumbria yet became the most learned man of his age in western Europe. Died on Ascension Day, 26 May 735, dictating his last work.
authors.profile: Author of the Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (completed 731), the foundational history of the English people; De temporum ratione (725), which fixed the practice of dating from the Incarnation (AD); biblical commentaries on nearly every book of scripture; the metrical and prose lives of St Cuthbert; De natura rerum; the letter to Egbert (734); and school texts on orthography and metre.
authors.style: Clear, economical, carefully sourced Latin; narrative skill in the miracle stories of the Historia; scholarly exactitude in computus and chronology.
authors.concerns: The unity and orthodoxy of the English church; chronology and computus; the transmission of patristic exegesis; the moral formation of clergy.
authors.significance: 'The father of English history'; the Historia preserves the Cædmon story, the earliest extended Old English verse, and much else besides; his computus standardized European chronology.
authors.uncertainty: Little uncertainty: the Historia's autobiographical colophon and Cuthbert's account of his death are reliable; birth year inferred from his own statements.

works.title: Vita Sancti Cuthberti (metrical and prose lives)

sources: A Guide to Old English, 8th edition

authors.name: Ben Jonson
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and critic; the first great English literary professional and the presiding classicist of the Jacobean stage, author of the comedies of humours, the masques, and 'To Penshurst'.
authors.biography: Born June 1572 in Westminster (posthumous son of a clergyman), educated at Westminster School under William Camden, and briefly a bricklayer (his stepfather's trade) before soldiering in Flanders. By 1597 he was acting and writing for Henslowe (imprisoned in 1598 for killing the actor Gabriel Spencer in a duel, escaping hanging by benefit of clergy); Every Man in His Humour (1598, with Shakespeare in the cast) made his name. The comedies Volpone (1606), Epicene (1609), The Alchemist (1610), and Bartholomew Fair (1614) and the tragedies Sejanus (1603) and Catiline (1611) followed, together with the masques written with Inigo Jones for the Jacobean court (1605–31). He published his Works in folio in 1616 — the first English playwright to do so — and died on 6 August 1637, buried upright in Westminster Abbey ('O rare Ben Jonson').
authors.profile: The laureate of the Stuart court and the legislator of classical taste: his comedies anatomize human folly through the theory of humours, his poems ('Drink to me only', the Cary–Morison ode, the epitaphs) set the standard of English neoclassical lyric, and his Timber is the period's major critical commonplace book.
authors.style: Classical discipline and satirical vigour; the humours theory of character; erudite, plain-style verse of great metrical skill; the masque's fusion of poetry, spectacle, and antimasque.
authors.concerns: The moral function of poetry and satire; the correction of folly and vice; classical imitation and the English claim to Augustan standing; patronage, fame, and the writer's craft.
authors.significance: The first English author to treat writing as a profession and the canon as a curated Works; his comedies and critical authority shaped English drama and letters for a century, and his 'tribe of Ben' founded the Cavalier lyric.
authors.uncertainty: The year of birth (1572 or 1573) is inferred; the canon of his collaborations (with Chapman, Marston, and others) and the lost plays are matters of scholarly reconstruction.

works.title: The Magnetic Lady; or, Humours Reconciled

sources: The Poetical Works of Barry Cornwall

authors.name: Benjamin Lundy
altNames: Benjamin Lundy of Mount Pleasant and Baltimore
authors.nationality: American; the Quaker frontier abolitionism of the old Northwest and the border states; editor and journalist of the formative periodical stage of American antislavery, between the gradualism of the 1820s and the immediatism of the 1830s
authors.identity: An editor, conducting 62 numbers and then hundreds more of a single sustained abolitionist sheet, and therefore chiefly a writer of leading articles, extracts, statistical tables, petitions, correspondence and prospectuses. His independent literary productions are a tract on the colonisation and emancipation questions, his circulars and annual registers of the manumitted, and an enormous body of letters. He invented the American abolitionist periodical as an institution: a monthly carried by agents, sustained by female subscribers, and dependent on the reprinting of British and foreign material.
authors.biography: He was born on 4 January 1789 at Hardwick in Sussex County, New Jersey, the son of Joseph and Eliza Lundy, and was raised in the plain speech and circuit ministry of the Society of Friends on the western frontier. He served an apprenticeship, learned the saddler's trade, and for many years financed his presswork with his own hands and with the proceeds of a small shop. He became an emancipationist through familiarity with the slave country of the border regions, began to contribute to the antislavery press about 1817, and in January 1821 established at Mount Pleasant in Jefferson County, Ohio, on the bank of the Ohio River and immediately opposite slave territory, the Genius of Universal Emancipation. Long afterwards held to have been the first American newspaper wholly devoted to emancipation, it was in fact preceded by Elisha Bates's short-lived Emancipator of Ohio, whose name and subscription lists Lundy bought and merged into his own sheet. He carried the paper to Jonesboro in Tennessee and then in 1824 to Baltimore, where it found its largest circulation and its most dangerous readership, and where for a decade he edited it, appointed agents, and supplied it with reprinted British parliamentary returns, slave-code extracts and accounts of manumission by will. In 1829 he engaged the young William Lloyd Garrison as a corresponding agent and contributor, gave him charge of the memoranda of the department called Plain Fact, and so provided the apprenticeship from which The Liberator issued in the following year. The two men parted over Garrison's immediatism and unconditional refusal of colonisation, Lundy holding to gradual measures, to emancipation financed by the sale of western land, and to the counsel of the Maryland Colonisation interest. He continued the Genius through the crisis years of the 1830s, travelling and publishing to the last, and died at Lowell, Illinois, on 22 August 1839.
authors.profile: His writing is the prose of an editor obliged to fill a sheet monthly at almost no cost: sober, argumentative, heavily indebted to quotation and to table. He worked by accumulation, re-printing British debates, legislative enactments, wills of manumission and Methodist and Quaker resolutions, and framing them with a leading article that stated the case for compensated and staged emancipation. The tone is exhortatory rather than prophetic, and it is characteristically addressed to slaveholders as erring neighbours rather than to the nation as a whole. His most effective prose is in the short factual paragraph, where a single returned fugitive, a shipload of the newly kidnapped or a price-current from a southern market carries its own argument.
authors.style: Plain unadorned Quaker diction; heavy use of extract, quotation and tabulated statement; a modest first-person editorial voice that reports his own journeys and receipts; moral argument conducted by enumeration of cases; long running titles and departmental headings; earnest, repetitive address to the conscience of the border-state reader; little irony except in the Plain Fact memoranda compiled by his sub-editor.
authors.concerns: The extension of slavery into the western states and its effect upon free labour; the education and moral elevation of the free coloured population; gradual emancipation, compensated manumission by will and the purchase of land for the settled freedom of the manumitted; the danger of the slave trade's renewal after the abolition of importation; the use of periodical publicity and female subscription as the engine of reform; the kinship of American and British emancipation, and the example of the West Indian apprenticeship debate.
authors.significance: He made American abolition a continuing organised press enterprise rather than an occasional address. For a dozen years the Genius was the movement's record and its correspondence network, and through it Lundy trained and launched William Lloyd Garrison, whose first abolitionist editorship was in Lundy's Baltimore office. His papers document the transition from the founding generation's gradualism to the immediatism of 1831 and later, and the disputes in which he was defeated, over colonisation, over the union of the churches and over the sinfulness of slaveholding, defined the programme of the movement that succeeded him. He is justly called the father of American organized abolition.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is disputed in popular account: the weight of authority places it at Hardwick or in Sussex County, New Jersey, while a minority of local and school tradition gives a Pennsylvania birth, and the family's settlement on the upper Ohio is variously dated. The exact chronology of the Genius is complicated by changes of title, place and frequency, and surviving runs are incomplete, so that particular numbers and their contents cannot always be tied to a fixed date. His share in the authorship of material printed under his editors name, as distinct from that contributed by Garrison and by corresponding agents, is not separable in every case.

authors.name: Bernard Mandeville
authors.identity: London physician and satirist whose Fable of the Bees (1714) argued that private vices, worked through vanity and emulation, produce public benefits.
authors.biography: Born at Rotterdam about 1670 into a medical family, he trained in medicine in the Dutch Republic, spent time in France, and from the 1690s practised as a physician in London. His Grumbling Hive (1705) was reissued in 1714 as The Fable of the Bees: or, Private Vices, Publick Benefits, with prose remarks on the paradox. A medical treatise on the hypochondriacal and hysterick passions (1715) and Free Thoughts on Religion, the Church and National Happiness (1720) established him as a sceptical physician-philosopher. The enlarged Fable of 1723, with its Essay on Charity and Charity-Schools, was presented by the Middlesex grand jury as a public nuisance and denounced from pulpits. He added a second part in 1729 and an anonymous enquiry into the original of honour in 1732, which broke with the moral-sense creed of the late Earl of Shaftesbury. He died at Hackney on 21 January 1733.
authors.profile: A clinical satirist of commercial society who turned the maxim tradition of the French moralists into an unsentimental analysis of appetite, flattery and trade.
authors.style: Tight Augustan couplets and deadpan prose paradox; fable, dialogue and case history; medical and commercial vocabulary; a sardonic refusal to moralise.
authors.concerns: Vice as the motor of prosperity; vanity, luxury and emulation; the hypocrisy of public benevolence; the origin of honour and shame; the self-deception of the virtuous.
authors.significance: The Fable became the century's most provocative thesis about commercial society, censured in its own day and recovered later by writers from Adam Smith to Keynes as a forerunner of the economics of unintended consequences.
authors.uncertainty: His birth is only fixed approximately, about 1670; his early training and the details of his practice are thinly documented, and the dating of some tracts varies.

works.title: A Modest Defence of Publick Stews

authors.name: Blind Hary
authors.identity: poet; minstrel
authors.biography: A blind poet or minstrel ('Blind Hary') who composed the Wallace c. 1477, reciting it before James IV for payment; royal treasury records note payments to him in the 1470s and 1490s. Almost nothing else is known of his life.
authors.profile: Author of The Wallace (c. 1477), an epic verse life of William Wallace in heroic couplets, drawing on the lost biography by John Blair and on oral tradition.
authors.style: Robust, declamatory couplets; fierce anti-English sentiment and graphic battle scenes; the folk-heroic exaggeration of Wallace's deeds.
authors.concerns: Scottish freedom and the cult of Wallace; loyalty and betrayal; national memory.
authors.significance: The Wallace was for centuries the most popular book in Scotland after the Bible (Burns acknowledged its inspiration) and fixed the popular image of Wallace for posterity.
authors.uncertainty: Nearly everything about him is conjectural; dates approximate.
sources: Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse

authors.name: Boniface
authors.identity: missionary; letter writer; grammarian; poet
authors.biography: Monk of Nursling (Hampshire); missionary to Frisia and Germany from 716, organizing the church in Hesse and Thuringia; archbishop of Mainz from c. 745; reformed the Frankish church in councils; martyred with his companions at Dokkum in Frisia on 5 June 754.
authors.profile: His correspondence — with popes, kings, and English correspondents such as Eadburga, Bugga, and Egbert of York — is the richest epistolary record of the eighth century; he also wrote an Ars grammatica, an Ars metrica, and a collection of Latin riddles and poems.
authors.style: Plain, forceful epistolary Latin; pedagogic clarity in the grammatical works.
authors.concerns: Mission; church discipline and reform; the pastoral and intellectual nurture of his English network.
authors.significance: The greatest of the Anglo-Saxon missionaries; his letters document the cultural links between England and the Carolingian world.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the Crediton birthplace rests on late tradition.
sources: The Blackwell Encyclopaedia of Anglo-Saxon England, 2nd edition

authors.name: Bryan Waller Procter
authors.nationality: English; poet and essayist of the Romantic period writing under a pseudonym, and a lawyer who served as a metropolitan Commissioner in Lunacy
authors.identity: Lyric and dramatic poet of the Hunt school, who published as 'Barry Cornwall' to keep his professional reputation as a lawyer clear of his verse, and who became one of the most reprinted short-poem writers of mid-Victorian anthologies.
authors.biography: Born at Leeds on 21 November 1787, the only son of the circuit barrister and public orator Bryan Procter, he was educated in the north and in London, entered a solicitor's office, and was called to the bar, where he practised as a special pleader. He began to publish verses about 1815 and came under the notice of Leigh Hunt, whose papers gave him a first public; in 1819 he issued 'Dramatic Scenes, and Other Poems', and the volumes that followed established him as a writer of simple, musical lyric and of dramatic verse for the closet. He was on terms of close friendship with Charles Lamb, whose letters to him are among the happiest documents of Regency letters, and with Hunt, Hazlitt, and the circle about the Indicator and the London Journal. From 1832 to 1861 he served as a metropolitan Commissioner in Lunacy, an office which gave his career its public shape and which he held while continuing to publish poems, essays, and literary-critical prose. His collected poetical works were reissued repeatedly, his lyrics entered the school and gift-book canon, and his songs and dramatic monologues were praised by Robert Browning and by the editors of household anthologies. He died on 5 October 1874.
authors.profile: His work is mostly short: songs and lyrics of quiet domestic or melancholy turn, dramatic scenes and monologues in the Elizabethan manner, metrical tales and legends of Italy and of the Cavalier period, and a few closet tragedies and sacred dramas. He wrote also prose essays and literary reminiscence, including papers on the old drama and on his friends, and his volumes of 1819-23 gathered the pieces by which Hunt's circle hoped to be read next after Byron.
authors.style: Verse of deliberate plainness and song-like regularity: short lines, recurring refrains, and an affectation of old English and Cavalier music ('Cavalier Tones' is his best-known experiment in the manner). His dramatic poems take the monologue or the dialogue of two, with a prose-like directness of speech, and his prose is garrulous, affectionate, and anecdotal after Lamb.
authors.concerns: The persistence of the past in song and in domestic feeling; the pathos of private life and of the abandoned or betrayed woman; Elizabethan and Cavalier culture as an alternative to the high Romantic manner; the claims of professional respectability upon the literary life; madness, confinement, and the institutions charged with their care, which his official duties brought before him daily.
authors.significance: He marks the transmission of Hunt's 'new poets' programme into the mid-Victorian recital tradition: his lyrics and songs were staples of anthologies and of the household recitation that gave Romantic verse a popular afterlife. His friendships with Lamb, Hunt, and the Indicator circle make his work and papers a useful record of Regency literary society, and his career in the lunacy commission is a document of the professional Victorian man of letters.

works.title: English Songs, and Other Small Poems

authors.name: Byrhtferth of Ramsey
authors.identity: scholar; computist; hagiographer
authors.biography: Monk of Ramsey Abbey, pupil of Abbo of Fleury during Abbo's stay there (985–987); the most learned English computist of his generation.
authors.profile: Author of the Enchiridion (c. 1011), a bilingual manual of computus and related sciences in Latin and Old English; probably the author of the Life of St Oswald and possibly of annals in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the late tenth century.
authors.style: Learned, allusive Latin (in the hermeneutic tradition) alternating with clear expository Old English.
authors.concerns: Computus, number symbolism, and the sciences of the quadrivium as handmaids of the liturgical year.
authors.significance: The chief witness to the scientific culture of the Benedictine Reform in England.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; attributions partly conjectural.
sources: British Library Digitised Manuscripts

authors.name: Caroline Norton
authors.birthplace: London, into the Sheridan theatrical and Whig-political family; her father was Thomas Sheridan, actor, soldier and later colonial secretary at the Cape of Good Hope, and her grandfather the playwright Richard Brinsley Sheridan
authors.nationality: English; the Byronic lyric and the literary-annual and periodical writing of the closing Romantic decades, together with the sentimental legal-reform pamphlet literature generated by the agitation over the civil disabilities of married women
authors.identity: Poet, novelist and annual-writer who became the most publicised campaigner in England for reform of the law of infant custody and of the property and divorce rights of married women
authors.biography: Caroline Elizabeth Sarah Sheridan was born in London on 22 March 1808, the second of three daughters of Thomas Sheridan and Caroline Henrietta Callander, herself a novelist; her grandfather was Richard Brinsley Sheridan. Thomas Sheridan died at the Cape of Good Hope in 1817 in the public service, leaving his widow nearly penniless, and the Duke of York obtained grace-and-favour apartments for the family at Hampton Court Palace. Caroline and her sisters Helen, afterwards Lady Dufferin, and Georgiana, afterwards Duchess of Somerset, were famous for beauty and wit, and she turned to writing to escape her feelings and because her family depended on her pen. On 30 June 1827 she married the Honourable George Chapple Norton, barrister and Member of Parliament for Guildford. The marriage was embittered by his violence and debts; she left him in 1836, and his criminal-conversation action against Melbourne, tried on 23 June 1836, collapsed but ruined her reputation. Under the law she lost all access to her three sons and the proceeds of her own books, and her second son William was killed by a fall from his pony in 1842. Out of that private catastrophe she made a public campaign, publishing the factory poem 'A Voice from the Factories' (1836), 'The Separation of Mother and Child by the Law of "Custody of Infants" Considered' (1838) and her 'Plain Letter to the Lord Chancellor on the Infant Custody Bill' (1839), which helped carry the Custody of Infants Act of that year. She petitioned unsuccessfully for the laureateship after Southey's death in 1843, wrote socially purposeful verse in 'The Child of the Islands' (1845), and renewed her agitation in 'English Laws for Women in the Nineteenth Century' (1854) and her 'Letter to the Queen' (1855) before the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857. After George Norton's death in 1875 she married, on 1 March 1877, Sir William Stirling-Maxwell, an old friend; she died at her London home on 15 June 1877 and was buried in the Stirling-Maxwell vault at Lecropt church near Keir; she is now remembered as a founding figure of English marriage-law reform.
authors.profile: Norton's reputation rests on three bodies of writing. Her verse begins with 'The Sorrows of Rosalie: a Tale, with other Poems' (1829), warmly praised in 'Noctes Ambrosianae', continues with 'The Undying One and Other Poems' (1830), a romance on the Wandering Jew legend, 'The Dream and Other Poems' (1840), 'The Child of the Islands' (1845), 'Aunt Carry's Ballads for Children' (1847) and 'The Lady of La Garaye' (1862), the last thought her best by contemporaries; lyrics, ballads and metrical tales supplied the literary annuals in seasons when she is said to have earned fourteen hundred pounds. Her fiction includes 'The Wife, and Woman's Reward' (1835), 'Stuart of Dunleath' (1851), 'Lost and Saved' (1863) and 'Old Sir Douglas' (1867), the last appearing in Macmillan's Magazine. Third, and historically the most consequential, the reform prose: 'A Voice from the Factories' (1836), the custody pamphlets of 1838-9, 'English Laws for Women in the Nineteenth Century' (1854) and the letters to the Queen and on Cranworth's divorce bill of 1855-7, with much anonymous literary and artistic criticism in her later years.
authors.style: Her manner is the Byronic one of the 1820s and 1830s: emphatic first-person remonstrance, pathos, passion, sonorous blank verse and closed couplets, and strong simple ballad stanzas for popular recitation. The Dictionary of National Biography recorded the judgement that 'she follows Byron as the dominant poet of her day', with sincere emotion but conventional expression, and that her best effects are passages of impassioned rhetoric embedded in the longer poems; 'The Lady of La Garaye' was thought to temper the Byronic note toward something like Thomas Campbell's dignity. Two lyrics, 'Joe Steel' and 'The Faded Beauty', show an arch Irish humour quite unlike her usual manner. The pamphlets are argumentative, autobiographical, pointedly domestic in their appeal to motherhood, and written to be quoted in Parliament.
authors.concerns: The legal non-existence of a married woman: the custody of children, the confiscation of a wife's earnings by her husband, the expense and sex-bias of the divorce court, and the exposure of a woman who defended herself in public. Her writing also holds the condition-of-England questions of the 1840s - factory labour, the education of the poor, the Prince of Wales as a national emblem - and shows her reading of Carlyle and Disraeli, while her famous refusal of the 'doctrine of equality' in 1838 marks her reform as maternal and sentimental rather than proto-feminist in the later sense. Personal grievance, evidence and petition are treated as literary instruments.
authors.significance: She converted a private scandal into a legislative campaign, and the Custody of Infants Act of 1839 gave married women for the first time a legally enforceable right to their children; her later pamphlets fed the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, and she is often claimed for the Married Women's Property Act of 1870, though her part in that measure is disputed. Lord Melbourne's trial and her notoriety touched the politics of the early Victorian premiership, she supplied hints for Dickens's 'Bardell v. Pickwick', she modelled for Daniel Maclise's House of Lords fresco of 'Justice', and George Meredith used her as the basis of Diana of the Crossways (1885). Modern scholarship and legal history treat her as the emblematic case of the personal made political in Victorian reform agitation.
authors.uncertainty: Her own later assertions are sometimes unverifiable - including her claim to have taken part in the Tolpuddle Martyrs demonstration of 1834 - and biographers differ over how far her pamphlets caused the Acts of 1839 and 1857 and over any share in the Act of 1870; no fully satisfactory portrait of her survives.

works.title: The Sorrows of Rosalie: A Tale, with Other Poems
The Undying One, and Other Poems

authors.name: Catharine Maria Sedgwick
authors.nationality: American; novelist and writer of the domestic and historical tale of New England, the most considerable American woman fiction-writer of the 1820s and 1830s and a chief practitioner of the Protestant moral tale
authors.identity: A writer of prose fiction, chiefly domestic, moral and historical novels and shorter tales, together with a body of religious and educational narrative, a memoir of a friend and occasional biographical and editorial work. She published her first two novels without her own name and wrote in the manner of the novel of character and conscience rather than of romance or sensation.
authors.biography: She was born at Stockbridge, Massachusetts, on 28 December 1789, the daughter of Theodore Sedgwick, a Federalist member of Congress from Massachusetts and later chief justice of the state, and of Pamela Dwight Sedgwick of the Stockbridge Dwight family. She grew up in the Stockbridge household, where a woman formerly held in slavery who had obtained her freedom by suit in the courts of the state served the family, and an early religious experience attached her to the Unitarian sympathy rather than to the strict Calvinism of her parents' world.
