Her own illness and convalescence in 1816, when she was nursed by a physician of the new school and read the novels she had been forbidden, decided her upon fiction as her work. A New-England Tale appeared anonymously in 1822, Redwood followed in the same concealment in 1824, and with Hope Leslie in 1827 her name first stood upon a title-page and her reputation as a writer of the national tale was made. Through the 1830s she published tales of New England and of colonial history, wrote for the annuals and for her friend's magazine, and supported her family by her pen; Elm Park, the Stockbridge house, became her home and a centre of the country's literary visiting. She remained unmarried by choice, corresponded widely with the men of letters of her generation, and after her brother's death wrote a memoir and an account of the household which had formed her. She died in 1867 at the age of seventy-seven, and by the end of her life was beginning to be read as the representative woman novelist of the early republic.
authors.profile: Her novels fall into a domestic and moral group, treating conscience, prejudice and the discipline of a young woman's judgment, and a historical group, treating the colonial and Indian border of New England; between them are shorter tales, religious and educational narratives and contributions to the literary annuals. Her habit is the novel of opinion and character, argued through a heroine's errors of judgment, with the sect, the party and the treatment of the Indian brought into the moral account. The memoir and the family narrative show the same concern with testimony, character and the reliability of a community's memory.
authors.style: A clear, straightforward and consciously unadorned narrative prose, with a firm control of the middle-length sentence and an economy of description; her force lies in the analysis of motive and in the dialogue of household and country society. She is careful of probability, dislikes the machinery of sensation, and closes her argument with a moral reckoning which she declines to dress up as providence.
authors.concerns: The duty and the right of private judgment against priest, party and neighbour; the education of a woman's mind and the claims of an unmarried woman's independence; the treatment of the Indian and the justice of the settlement; sectarian bitterness and the possibility of a reasonable religion; slavery, freedom and the memory of service in the household; the authority of prejudice in a small community; the obligations of the powerful to the dependent.
authors.significance: She established the woman's American novel on grounds of conscience and social argument rather than sentiment, and Hope Leslie gave the colonial and Indian material a critical treatment unmatched before her. For half a century she was the example by which the professional woman fiction-writer of the republic was understood, and recent scholarship has returned her to the history of the American novel and of the argument over removal.
authors.uncertainty: Accounts differ as to the place of her death, some putting it at Stockbridge and others at a relative's house in the neighbourhood of Boston; the exact share of the physician who superintended her convalescence in determining her career rests chiefly on her own autobiographical papers.

authors.name: Catherine Parr
authors.identity: queen consort; devotional writer
authors.biography: Born about 1512; the sixth wife of Henry VIII, whom she married in 1543. A learned woman of reformist sympathies, she narrowly escaped arrest for heresy in 1546. Her Prayers or Meditations appeared in 1545, the first book printed under the name of an English queen, and The Lamentation of a Sinner in 1547 after the king's death. She died on 5 September 1548, shortly after marrying Thomas Seymour.
authors.profile: The first English queen in print. Prayers or Meditations (1545) adapts the Imitatio Christi into a personal devotional idiom, and The Lamentation of a Sinner (1547) is a conversion narrative and confession in the new evangelical mode, declaring the futility of works and the sufficiency of faith in Christ.
authors.style: Warm, first-person devotion; the language of interiority and the afflicted conscience; scriptural quotation woven into prayer.
authors.concerns: Personal faith and justification; the education of women (she oversaw the schooling of the young Elizabeth); the reform of devotion from within the court.
authors.significance: A pioneer of English women's devotional writing and a patron of the reformed cause; her example licensed the religious authorship of later English women.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (1512); the extent of her direct influence on Elizabeth's education is documented but partly inferential.
sources: The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake

authors.name: Charles Brockden Brown
authors.nationality: American; novelist, tale-writer and editor of the early republic, working in Philadelphia and New York; the first American writer of prose fiction to attempt a professional literary career
authors.identity: A writer of prose fiction and of periodical and editorial work: four gothic narratives published in 1798 and 1799, a domestic romance of 1801, tales and sketches for the magazines he edited, and moral, political and historical argument in essays, prefaces and reviews. He wrote no verse of consequence and no drama; his criticism lives in advertisements and periodical matter rather than in a treatise.
authors.biography: He was born in Philadelphia on 7 January 1771, the son of Elijah Brown, a Quaker merchant of English descent, and grew up within the discipline of the Society of Friends. The prosperity of his father's house broke up in the early 1790s, and the loss of a commercial fortune of his own while still in his twenties decided him upon the pen. He had already left the Friends after a religious crisis of opinion, and turned instead to the rational dissent he found in Godwin and in the English moralists. In 1796 he began Brown's Weekly Political Intelligencer and in 1797 the American Monthly Magazine, the first of several editorial ventures by which he tried to live by periodical writing in the United States. During 1798 and 1799 the Philadelphia publisher Mathew Carey issued his four novels in quick succession, and their reception, hostile at home and warmer in Britain, encouraged him to believe that an American romance of ideas was possible. He tried briefly and unsuccessfully to practise law after being admitted to practice, and for a season kept a country place in the New Jersey shore and in the Genesee region with no better result. From 1806 to 1811 he edited The American Register at New York and Philadelphia, a miscellany which reprinted British review criticism and American news and gave him the largest reading public he ever commanded. He died in Philadelphia in 1810, at the age of thirty-nine, leaving editorial and historical projects unfinished.
authors.profile: His fiction divides into the four gothic narratives of 1798 and 1799 and the later domestic romance of 1801, with tales and sketches scattered through the magazines he controlled. His non-fictional work is larger than his surviving novels and consists of prefaces, reviews, political intelligence, historical and biographical compilation and editorial matter of every kind. The whole of it is prose, and its most distinctive feature is the argumentative narrative: a plot of evidence, rumour and mistaken testimony carried by speakers who reason about their own case. He also wrote on the abolition of slavery and on the condition of the Indian countries, and his western tale draws upon captive narratives as well as upon romance.
authors.style: A plain, unadorned and deliberately rational diction applied to scenes of terror; long first-person confessions, letters within letters, and a preference for memoir and journal forms over the plot of the ordinary romance. Explanation is pushed so hard that it becomes an engine of doubt, and the tales end in contentions about what the evidence proves. Topographical and medical detail is used to give the marvellous an air of report, and the prefaces argue the moral purpose of the fiction before the fiction is allowed to speak.
authors.concerns: Godwinian inquiry into the power of opinion over conduct; enthusiasm as a disease of the imagination and its relation to religious and political credulity; the pathology of solitude and sleep; the credibility of testimony and the limits of evidence; the condition of women without fortune or protection; slavery, manumission and the meaning of republican equality; the interior frontier as a moral as well as a geographical zone; the education of a republic and the uses of periodical literature.
authors.significance: He created the American gothic and with it the first American prose fiction taken seriously by British reviewers, so that the history of the American novel cannot be written beginning anywhere else. His treatment of belief, sleep and pursued virtue opened lines of development that run through later American romance, and his editorial labours showed what a man of letters in the republic could actually do for a living. Twentieth-century scholarship, which at first set him aside as an oddity, restored the four novels to the canonical history of gothic and early American fiction.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his legal studies and his admission to practice is imperfectly settled; the religious crisis which ended his connection with the Friends is known only from his own allusions and from those of his family; and the cause of his death at thirty-nine, variously reported as consumption and as an acute fever, cannot be determined from the surviving accounts.

works.title: Arthur Mervyn; or, Memoirs of the Year 1793
Edgar Huntly; or, Memoirs of a Sleep-Walker

authors.name: Charles Lamb
authors.nationality: English; the familiar prose of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Essayist and letter-writer, a London clerk by profession, who wrote as Elia and became the most admired practitioner of familiar prose between the spectatorial essay and the Victorian essay.
authors.biography: Lamb was born in London into a family long in the service of the Inner Temple, the elder brother of Mary Lamb. He was educated at Christ's Hospital, where Samuel Taylor Coleridge was a schoolfellow and remained a friend for life, and in 1792 he was placed in the East India Company's accounts office at India House, where he worked as a clerk until his retirement in 1825. His early ambition was the stage, and the plays and verses of those years are lost. On 18 March 1796 Mary, in an attack of insanity, killed their mother, and Lamb thenceforward lived with her as her guardian and companion through recurring illness, quarrels and reconciliation. He contributed occasional verse, essays and theatrical criticism to the morning papers from the 1790s, published a selection of the old dramatists with observations in 1808, and worked with his sister on books for children. From 1820 the Elia papers began to appear in periodicals and were collected in 1823 and again in 1833; his letters, much imitated in the century after his death, were published in full only after him. He died at Edmonton in December 1842 of erysipelas and was buried in the churchyard there.
authors.profile: His work is almost wholly prose of a personal kind: the Elia essays and their sequel, a book of old-play specimens with commentary, an editorial and collaborative share in children's books, and a body of letters that he treated as a form of essay. He wrote occasional verse and dramatic criticism, and projected histories and scholarship that he never completed. The characteristic piece is a short meditative essay on a London or a country scene, on the theatre, on books, or on the poor, which wanders from anecdote to reflection and returns to the writer's own life. His subject is memory, friendship, the pleasures of the town, the ruined eighteenth-century house of his childhood, and the tender treatment of the failings of the mind.
authors.style: A colloquial yet elaborately allusive prose, full of half-quoted phrases from the old drama and from the Bible, with Latinate inversions, parenthetical self-correction, sudden tenderness under irony, and a persona that admits its own fictions. The sentences imitate the rhythms of talk and of the seventeenth-century writers together; the humour is self-deprecatory and the pathos is never separated from it.
authors.concerns: The essayist's persona as a moral and social mask; sympathy with the poor, the servants, the outcast and the insane; the value of the old plays as a school of imagination; the lost haunts and houses of childhood; the claims of duty and dependence within a family; the place of literature in an ordinary working life.
authors.significance: With Hazlitt he defined the Romantic prose essay, and Elia supplied the model of the familiar essayist that the Victorians inherited, most obviously in the essayists of the 1840s and in Stevenson's treatment of the essay voice. His edition and commentary helped establish the modern serious reading of the Jacobean and Caroline dramatists, and his letters form one of the principal records of London literary society between the 1790s and the 1840s.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of Mary Lamb's share in the children's books and in some of the papers printed over his name is debated; the plays and most of the early writings are lost and can only be dated approximately; and the part of the Elia voice that is a self-portrait and the part that is invention cannot be separated.

authors.name: Charles Robert Maturin
authors.identity: Gothic novelist, Anglican clergyman, and dramatist
authors.biography: Charles Robert Maturin was born in Dublin of French Huguenot descent; his grandfather was the distinguished mathematician Lord Chief Baron Maturin. Educated at Trinity College Dublin, he took Anglican orders and served as rector of St Peter's, Dublin, attracting audiences with sermons that advanced controversial Calvinist doctrines. He published Gothic novels from 1812 to 1820, including The Milesian Chief, Bertram, Women, and Melmoth the Wanderer. He left the ministry under some cloud and turned to theatre management and ultimately emigrated to England, where he died in poverty in 1824. He was the maternal grandfather of Oscar Wilde.
authors.profile: Maturin is the pre-eminent Irish Gothic novelist of the Romantic period. His fiction explores theological terror — damnation, guilt, and the impossibility of redemption — through labyrinthine narrative structures. Melmoth the Wanderer is the last great Gothic novel of the 1790s tradition. His verse drama Bertram drew Byron's public praise.
authors.style: Elaborate recursive frame structures; prose of rhetorical intensity and theological solemnity; sustained Gothic imagery; embedded narratives across multiple centuries and nations; the double and the pursued self as recurring psychological motifs.
authors.concerns: Calvinist theology and the anxiety of election; Catholic-Protestant conflict in Ireland; colonial subjectivity and the politics of dispossession; the Gothic as spiritual allegory; narrative form as psychological and theological entrapment.
authors.significance: Maturin represents the Irish Gothic as a distinct tradition: the colonial subject's terror turned into theological drama. Melmoth influenced Balzac and Baudelaire; his work was central to the recovery of Gothic fiction by Victorian and modernist writers.
authors.uncertainty: His exact birth year (1780 or 1782) is uncertain; the circumstances of his departure from the Anglican ministry remain obscure.

works.title: Bertram; or, The Castle of St. Aldobrand

authors.name: Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
altNames: Charles Sackville, Sixth Earl of Dorset
authors.identity: Courtier, patron, and occasional poet; as Lord Buckhurst he was a leading Restoration wit and rake, famed for his songs and satires, and later as Earl of Dorset a generous patron of Dryden, Prior, and the writers of the 1690s.
authors.biography: Born c. 1643 (baptised 24 January 1638 — the commonly cited birth year is 1643; records vary), styled Lord Buckhurst, educated at Westminster. He served at sea against the Dutch (reportedly writing the song 'To all you ladies now at land' the night before the Battle of Lowestoft, 1665), was a boon companion of Rochester and the court wits, and succeeded as Earl of Dorset and Middlesex in 1675. After the Revolution of 1688 he became Lord Chamberlain to William III and a key literary patron, supporting Dryden after his fall, and Prior, and Montagu. He died 19 January 1706.
authors.profile: The elegant, careless court versifier whose few surviving songs and satires were praised by contemporaries (Prior, Dryden) for their natural wit and ease, and whose chief literary role was patronage.
authors.style: Light, graceful songs and satires; an easy, natural wit; libertine and amorous subjects; and the occasional political satire.
authors.concerns: Love, pleasure, and court life; the passing of youth; loyalty and the politics of the Revolution; and the patronage of letters.
authors.significance: Dorset is remembered more as the ideal Restoration patron — Dryden dedicated works to him and mourned his circle — than for his slender but admired verse, which exemplifies Cavalier wit surviving into the 1690s.
authors.uncertainty: Dorset's birth year is variously given (1637–38 or 1643); his poetic canon is small and some attributions are uncertain, and much of his reputation rests on testimony rather than surviving verse.

works.title: Songs and Poems of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset

sources: An Appeal in Favor of That Class of Americans Called Africans

authors.name: Charles Wesley
authors.identity: Anglican clergyman and the finest hymn-writer of the English revival, whose lyrics gave Methodism its voice and much of its theology.
authors.biography: Born at Epworth in 1707, one of the numerous children of Samuel and Susanna Wesley, he was sent on a scholarship to Westminster School and from there to Christ Church, Oxford, where he kept a journal of his religious progress and joined with his brother John and a few friends in the small society later mocked as methodists. Ordained and briefly in Georgia with John, he returned to an assured conversion recorded in his journal in 1738, and thereafter preached as an assistant revival preacher while labouring chiefly in verse. He married Sarah Gwynne in 1749, lived for years near the Methodist work at Bristol, where the Wesleyan school at Kingswood was founded, and settled in London later, remaining an Anglican priest who disliked several of his brother's concessions. His collections of hymns, published singly and with John, begin with Hymns and Sacred Poems of 1739 and run through the following decades. He died in London in March 1788.
authors.profile: The lyric theologian of the revival, who put doctrine, penitence and joy into metres that congregations could carry away.
authors.style: Dense, tuneful, ecstatic lyrics in common and ballad measures; first-person plural address; paradox, tenderness and bodily feeling; a gift for the repeating clause that binds a singing congregation.
authors.concerns: Assurance, atonement and the witness of the Spirit; the praise of God by redeemed creatures; the holy year of nativity, passion and resurrection; the communion of the faithful and the terrors of judgement.
authors.significance: He is the century's most sung religious poet in English and the founder of Methodist hymnody; his texts still stand in most English-speaking hymnals and shaped the devotional language of revival Christianity.
authors.uncertainty: The number of hymns credited to him varies widely between early accounts and modern scholarship, and some of his texts were revised by others in transmission.

works.title: A Collection of Psalms and Hymns

authors.name: Charlotte Dacre
authors.identity: Gothic novelist, poet, and dramatist
authors.biography: Charlotte Dacre was born Charlotte Robinson, daughter of Lieutenant-Colonel George Augustus Robinson, known as the 'Chinese Officer' after years in India, and Anne Remee, said to be of part-African descent — a family history that gave rise to Dacre's persistent preoccupation with racial otherness and belonging. She began writing in the 1790s and published her first collection of poems, The Choice of the World, in 1797. Her novel Zofloya; or, The Moor (1806) made her reputation in the Gothic. She continued publishing fiction and verse into the 1820s; her exact date of death is not recorded.
authors.profile: Dacre's Gothic combines the sensational traditions of Lewis and Radcliffe with exploration of female agency, racial otherness, and the destructive power of desire. Zofloya is the great Gothic femme fatale novel of the period; her later verse and prose continued to examine fantasy, transgression, and the limits of sensibility.
authors.style: Lush, ornate prose; saturated Gothic imagery; psychological interiority from the perspective of transgressive women; embedded tales; dramatic dialogue in the verse works.
authors.concerns: Female desire and agency within the Gothic; the social construction of racial and cultural otherness; imagination and delusion; the dangers of unchecked sensibility; the subversion of patriarchal authority.
authors.significance: Dacre's Gothic represents the female appropriation of the sensational mode; Zofloya is a key text in the genealogy of the femme fatale. Her recovery as a major contribution to 1790s–1820s Gothic fiction is well established in modern criticism.
authors.uncertainty: Her exact birth year is debated — candidates include 1771, 1772, and 1777; the date and circumstances of her death are not precisely recorded.

works.title: Zofloisca; or, The Rose of Fantasy: A Romance

authors.name: Charlotte Lennox
authors.identity: Novelist, dramatist, and editor, a writer of Scottish parentage born in Gibraltar whose The Female Quixote made her one of the leading novelists of the mid-eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born Charlotte Ramsay around 1729 or 1730, probably in Gibraltar, the daughter of a Scottish army officer, she came to London after family losses and made her way as a writer. Her novel The Female Quixote (1752), a parody of romance-reading, was admired by Samuel Johnson, who befriended her and contributed to the periodical The Adventurer, with which she was associated; a tale in that periodical concerning a romantic heroine has often been linked to her. She later published Henrietta (1758), the novel Shirley (1760), and edited the periodical The Lady's Museum (1760-61). She also wrote plays and historical and translated works. She died on 4 January 1804.
authors.profile: A writer of social and didactic fiction who critiqued the illusions of romance and the marriage market from a woman's perspective, and who moved comfortably among the literary circles of her age.
authors.style: Ironical, corrective realism; a light satirical touch on romance conventions; social comedy of manners; and an editorial, periodical-bred economy of narration; with a move toward more serious domestic plotting in later fiction.
authors.concerns: The dangers and pleasures of reading; female expectation and disillusion; romance versus reality; education and reason; and women's position in the marriage market.
authors.significance: A prominent woman novelist and editor of the Augustan and Johnsonian age, whose The Female Quixote is now studied as a key text in the debate over fiction and female readers and in the rise of women's writing.
authors.uncertainty: Her exact year of birth (1729 or 1730) and place (Gibraltar is probable but not certain) are uncertain, and the precise extent of her authorship of the periodical The Adventurer and of related tales remains a matter of scholarly debate.

works.title: The Female Quixote; or, The Adventures of Arabella

sources: Mason Locke Weems, His Works and Ways (3 volumes)

authors.name: Charlotte Smith
altNames: Charlotte Smith, of Bignor Park, in Sussex
authors.birthplace: London, King Street, off St James's Square, born on 4 May 1749, the eldest daughter of Nicholas Turner of Stoke House, Surrey, and Anna (Towers) Turner
authors.nationality: English; the pre-Romantic and Romantic lyric tradition of the sensibility and the sonnet revival, joined to the radical and domestic novel of the 1790s and to the educational literature for young women produced by the London and provincial presses between the French Revolution and her death
authors.identity: Poet and novelist who revived the regular English sonnet in the 1780s and, from 1789 to 1806, supported herself by her pen through a series of epistolary and domestic novels, juvenile letters, a blank-verse poem on the French Revolution and a topographical poem of the Sussex coast
authors.biography: Charlotte Turner was born in King Street, off St James's Square, London, on 4 May 1749, the eldest daughter of Nicholas Turner of Stoke House, Surrey, a country gentleman, and Anna Turner. Her mother died early and, after her father's reckless speculation dissolved the family fortune, she was largely raised by an aunt and put to girls' schools at Chichester. On 23 February 1765, aged fifteen, she was given by her father in marriage to Benjamin Smith, a much older man of violent temper and ruinous debts whom she afterwards described as a species of sale; the marriage produced a large family, twelve children being counted, of whom six survived her. The couple lived successively on the Isle of Wight and in Hampshire and Sussex, and Smith filled her years of marriage with the duties of a gentleman's wife, French and Italian reading, drawing, music and the care of her children's education. Benjamin Smith squandered a considerable legacy and was committed to the King's Bench prison for debt in December 1783, where his wife stayed with him, and it was during these years of confinement and disgrace that she assembled Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Poems (1784), the little volume which made her name and went through nine or more enlarged editions in her lifetime. On her separation from her husband she became, in effect, the first English woman of letters to live by professional authorship under the modern meaning of the word: she wrote a novel, a juvenile work or a volume of verse almost annually for the rest of her life, and her later title pages describe her as 'Charlotte Smith, of Bignor Park, in Sussex'. From 1776 the disposition of a family inheritance worth nearly £36,000, settled on her by her uncle James Turner in preference to her brother George, was tied up in Chancery for almost forty years; the litigation, its costs and the failures of her solicitors absorbed her income and her attention until her death and long afterwards, and she dedicated much of her preface-writing to telling the story of it. She lived in consequence at Chichester, Brighton, Storrington, Bath, Exmouth, Weymouth, Oxford, London, Frant and Elstead, moving whenever her creditors or her health required it; at Brighton in 1791-3 she was in the company of English radicals, and her sympathy with the Revolution in France, openly declared in Desmond (1792) and The Banished Man (1794), cost her subscribers and publishers in the reaction of the late 1790s. She corresponded with Joseph Cooper Walker, with the Cadells and with Samuel Harper, and in her last years her health failed, one eye being lost and her chest disease advancing. Charlotte Smith died at Tilford in Surrey on 28 October 1806 and was buried at Stoke Church, Stoke Park, near Guildford, within sight of the downs she had celebrated; she was widely lamented, especially by other women writers, and left unfinished manuscripts which her daughter published afterwards.
authors.profile: Her poetry begins with Elegiac Sonnets, and Other Poems (London, 1784), enlarged in successive editions (third edition 1786; fifth 1789; seventh 1795; eighth 1797; ninth 1800) by new sonnets, by translations and imitations from Petrarch and other originals, and by an increasingly explicit advertisement of the poet's own injuries. To it she appended the two-book blank-verse poem The Emigrants (1793), on the French royalist exiles of the Revolution, and her last and most assured volume, Beachy Head, and Other Poems (1807), published after her death and including shorter pieces such as 'Flora' and 'Studies by the Sea' which had first appeared in her juvenile books. Her fiction, when she resumed it after 1788, is at the centre of her modern reputation: Ethelinde, or, The Recluse of the Lake (1789), Celestina (1791), Desmond (1792), The Old Manor House (1793), The Wanderings of Warwick (1794), The Banished Man (1794), Montalbert (1795), Marchmont (1796) and The Young Philosopher (1798), with the tale-series The Letters of a Solitary Wanderer (1800). She also made a permanent parallel reputation as an educational writer, in The Rural Walks (1795), Rambles Farther (1796), Minor Morals (1798) and Conversations, Introducing Poetry to the Young (1804), and she printed A Narrative of the Loss of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont Transports (1796) for the benefit of a survivor of the wreck. Her earlier books, the translation The Romance of Real Life (1787) and the revised edition of her first novel Emmeline (Cadell, 1788), belong to the eighteenth century; the collections and the comedy got up after 1806, including the Commonplace Book and the novel attributed to her as the Literary Don Quixote, extend the record but not the lifetime's work. Modern scholarship is served by Stuart Curran's edition of her Poems (Oxford University Press, 1993), by Judith Phillips Stanton's Collected Letters (Indiana University Press, 2003), by the Pickering and Chatto collected edition of her Works in a numbered series of volumes, and by the essay collection Charlotte Smith in British Romanticism edited by Jacqueline Labbe (2008).
authors.style: Her sonnets are written in the regular fourteen-line form she preferred, with an attention to turn and closure that she set against what she thought the license of the Pindaric and Della Cruscan modes; the diction is that of sensibility - elegiac, personal, topographically exact, frequently addressed to a river, a headland, an old tree or a remembered haunt, and closing on a pointed couplet or a turned sentence. She introduced into the lyric a documentary force, the poet's own history of injury and dependence appearing in prefatory prose beside the verses. Her novels are mostly epistolary and self-consciously empirical, opening with an advertisement or prefatory letter claiming that the events are drawn from real life and from her own observation, and dividing sympathy between an impoverished heroine, a disputed heir and an oppressive relative; Gothic machinery - the abbey, the castle, the secret of birth - is retained but explained by law, money and interest rather than by fate. The juvenile books put instruction into conversation and the familiar letter, with natural-history observation and short quoted poems as the method of teaching. Her late blank verse, in The Emigrants and Beachy Head, is descriptive and meditative, moving from panoramic landscape to local history and personal resignation in the same sentence.
authors.concerns: The condition of a woman compelled to make a living by writing, and the dependence, debt and litigation that governed her work; the justice of property, the rights of an disinherited heir and the operation of law and the equity courts upon families; the French Revolution followed at first hand and in its effects on exiles, on the poor and on the conscience of a sympathiser; the education of young women and the uses of conversation, natural history and poetry as teaching; the claims of sensibility and their limits; landscape as evidence of feeling and as a record of loss; the superstition and the suffering of Catholic and rural communities; and the dignity of the humble and the aged, especially women, in a poetry of place.
authors.significance: By reviving the legitimate sonnet in the 1780s and holding it open through nine editions she made the form available for the meditative and personal use that Wordsworth and his contemporaries afterwards made standard; Stuart Curran's judgement that she is 'the first poet in English whom in retrospect we would call Romantic' states the modern claim. Her novels supplied the model of empirical, socially realistic domestic fiction written by a woman for a professional living, and Desmond and The Old Manor House are now read as political fictions of the 1790s answering Godwin and arguing with the reaction; her juvenile books carried that realism into the education of girls. Her long Chancery suit and her prefaces made the economics of authorship part of her texts, and her recovery since the 1990s, through Curran's, Stanton's and the Pickering and Chatto editions, has made her the central case in scholarship on women's writing, the sonnet revival and Romantic print culture.
authors.uncertainty: Her birth is fixed at 4 May 1749 by the Dictionary of National Biography tradition and by modern accounts, but older reference works long hesitated over the year, and her own statements about her childhood differ; the day and year of several first editions remain disputed in the secondary literature, Desmond (1792 in the English Short Title Catalogue records inspected here) still often being cited as 1796, and the revised Emmeline as 1788 or 1789 according to the copy examined; the attribution of the anonymous comedy What Is She? (printed 1799) is accepted by some modern scholars and doubted by others; the number of her children and the details of her residence at Bignor Park are variously reported; and the date at which her Chancery suit ceased to be pending is usually given from her own letters rather than from the court records.

works.title: A Narrative of the Loss of the Catharine, Venus, and Piedmont Transports
Conversations, Introducing Poetry to the Young
The Emigrants, A Poem, in Two Books

authors.name: Christopher Marlowe
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and translator; the creator of the Elizabethan tragic stage and of the 'mighty line' of blank verse.
authors.biography: Baptized 26 February 1564 at Canterbury, son of a shoemaker; a King's Scholar at the King's School, Canterbury, and a Parker Scholar at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge (BA 1584, MA 1587, the latter after the Privy Council intervened over his absences, plausibly for government service). In London he wrote Tamburlaine (1587–88), Doctor Faustus (c. 1588–92), The Jew of Malta (c. 1589–90), Edward II (c. 1592), and The Massacre at Paris (c. 1592–93), and translated Ovid's Amores and Lucan's Pharsalia I. He was associated with Ralegh's circle and suspected of atheism (the 'Baines note'); on 30 May 1593 he was killed in a quarrel at a Deptford house by Ingram Frizer, the coroner recording the stabbing as self-defence in a dispute over the reckoning.
authors.profile: The founder of Elizabethan tragedy: Tamburlaine's conquering rhetoric, Faustus's aspiring intellect, Barabas's satanic wit, and Edward II's study of a king's fall created the overreacher and the tragic stage that Shakespeare inherited.
authors.style: The 'mighty line' — muscular, end-stopped blank verse of enormous rhetorical force; the set-piece oration; lyric interludes ('Come live with me'); ironic juxtaposition of grandeur and brutality.
authors.concerns: The limits of human aspiration — power, knowledge, wealth, desire; Machiavellian statecraft; religious scepticism and the fear of damnation; the collision of the individual will with the order of things.
authors.significance: The greatest dramatic innovator before Shakespeare: he made blank verse the language of the stage, created the Elizabethan history play and tragedy, and his life and death — poet, spy, atheist — became the legend of the Elizabethan imagination.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of the plays rest on publication and performance records (none of the plays was printed in his lifetime); the circumstances of his death, his alleged espionage, and the authorship of parts of his canon (Dido with Nashe, the Henry VI plays) remain debated.
sources: Robert Bloomfield: Selected Poems (revised and enlarged edition)

authors.name: Christopher Smart
authors.identity: English poet, scholar, and editor, a brilliant and erratic man of letters whose religious hymns, especially Song to David, make him a singular visionary voice.
authors.biography: Smart was born in Kent, educated at Cambridge, and took holy orders. A fine Hebrew and classical scholar, he lived in London as an editor, schoolmaster, and hack writer, and edited early plays and other texts. His great religious poem, Song to David (1763), was published amid a reputation for madness, and in 1763 he was confined in a private madhouse for some years, during which he wrote the wild private poem Jubilate Agno in a manuscript not printed until the twentieth century. Released in later life, he continued to write and edit and was eventually admitted to an institutional charity for the poor. He died in 1771 of exhaustion.
authors.profile: A poet of intense religious enthusiasm and metrical experiment, whose verse praises the created world and its Creator with an incantatory, cataloguing energy; he also edited, translated, and wrote in prose.
authors.style: Irregular, energetic metrical vitality; antiphonal and parallel religious praise; catalogues of creatures and things; Hebrew and liturgical influence; and a visionary, sometimes deranged sublimity of imagery.
authors.concerns: Divine praise through the natural world; enthusiasm, reason, and madness; the sanctity of language and naming; liberty and the animal creation; and the poet's suffering and consolation.
authors.significance: Long undervalued, Smart is now recognised as one of the most original religious and visionary poets of the century, a forerunner of Romantic interest in the irrational and a master of ecstatic hymnody.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is given as about 1722 from baptismal records; the chronology of his confinement and the survival and dating of the Jubilate Agno manuscript are complex and partly reconstructed.

works.title: Hymns for the Feasts of the Church

authors.name: Clara Reeve
authors.identity: English novelist and critic of the tale of romance, known for The Old English Baron and for the critical Progress of Romance.
authors.biography: Born on 23 January 1729 at Ipswich, the daughter of an attorney, she grew up in a literary household and turned to writing and translation. Her Gothic novel first appeared as The Champion of Virtue (1777) and was soon republished and long known as The Old English Baron (1778), modeled on Walpole's The Castle of Otranto but more probability-bound. She also published other fiction and, in 1785, the critical history The Progress of Romance, an early survey of prose fiction. She died on 3 December 1807.
authors.profile: A writer of Gothic and sentimental romance and a pioneering critic of the prose tale, who sought to defend and historicize romance while making it more rational and morally restrained.
authors.style: A moderated, realistic Gothic that tempers marvel with probability; plain, earnest prose; epistolary and moralizing passages; and a self-conscious critical awareness of the conventions of romance.
authors.concerns: The legitimacy and history of romance and fiction; the balance of wonder and probability; female virtue and sensibility; and the moral and social uses of the tale.
authors.significance: A key transitional figure in the development of Gothic fiction and one of the earliest historians of the prose romance, whose Progress of Romance is an important document of eighteenth-century critical thought about fiction.
authors.uncertainty: Her broad life is documented, though details of her education and early writings are imperfectly recorded, and the dating of the first appearance of her Gothic novel has often been confused between 1777 and 1778.
sources: Modern Chivalry (American Fiction Series)

authors.name: Colley Cibber
authors.identity: Actor-manager, playwright, poet laureate, and autobiographer; his comedy Love's Last Shift (1696) inaugurated 'sentimental comedy', and his flamboyant An Apology for the Life of Colley Cibber (1740) is a vivid memoir of the Restoration stage — though Pope made him the hero of The Dunciad.
authors.biography: Born 6 November 1671 in London, son of the sculptor Caius Gabriel Cibber; educated at the Free School, Grantham. He joined the stage as an actor and wrote some twenty-five plays, beginning with Love's Last Shift (1696), whose reformed rake launched sentimental comedy; his adaptations of Shakespeare and Molière and farces like The Non-Juror were commercially astute. He became a leading actor-manager (patentee of Drury Lane, 1710), poet laureate (1730, a deeply unpopular appointment), and wrote his celebrated Apology (1740). He died on 12 December 1757.
authors.profile: The shrewd, vain, and gifted man of the theatre whose sentimental comedies and lively memoir shaped eighteenth-century drama and whose laureateship made him the byword for poetic dullness.
authors.style: Sentimental, moralising comedy; theatrical savvy and adaptation; a lively, self-promoting prose in the Apology; and occasional verse of modest quality.
authors.concerns: Moral reform and sentimental virtue; the business and life of the theatre; vanity and self-justification; and the reform of comedy toward feeling.
authors.significance: Cibber founded sentimental comedy and left in his Apology one of the most valuable first-hand accounts of the Restoration and early Georgian stage; his laureateship and feud with Pope secured his immortality as the 'king of dunces'.
authors.uncertainty: Cibber's Apology is candid but self-serving; details are embellished for effect, and his reputation was distorted by Pope's satire.

works.title: Apology for the Life of Colley Cibber
Love's Last Shift; or, The Fool in Fashion

sources: Lydia Sigourney: Selected Poetry and Prose (Broadview Editions)

authors.name: Cynewulf
authors.identity: poet
authors.biography: Nothing is known of Cynewulf beyond his name, which he wove as a runic acrostic into the epilogues of four Old English poems: The Fates of the Apostles, Elene, Juliana, and Christ II. Candidates proposed for identification include a Cynewulf bishop of Lindisfarne (d. 783), but the question remains open.
authors.profile: The four signed poems form a coherent body of religious narrative and meditation; scholars have also attributed other poems (notably in the Exeter and Vercelli books) to his 'school' without consensus.
authors.style: Ornate, reflective religious narrative; typological reading of scripture and legend; runic signature passages that meditate on judgment and the last things.
authors.concerns: Salvation, judgment, and the vanity of the world; the apostolic and imperial foundations of the Church; the poet's own sinfulness.
authors.significance: The only named author of a substantial Old English poetic corpus besides Cædmon, and the first English poet to sign his work.
authors.uncertainty: Identity and dates entirely unknown; dating proposals range from the late eighth to the tenth century.
movements: The AB Language Group (West Midlands Devotional Prose)
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume I: c. 500–1042

authors.name: Cyril Tourneur
authors.identity: dramatist; soldier; diplomat
authors.biography: Born about 1575, of obscure family. He served in military and diplomatic posts — in the Low Countries, and as secretary to the council of war in the Cadiz expedition of 1625. On the return voyage he fell ill and was put ashore at Kinsale, Ireland, where he died on 28 February 1626.
authors.profile: Certainly his are the morality-influenced tragedy The Atheist's Tragedy (1611) and the elegy A Grief on the Death of Prince Henry (1613); The Revenger's Tragedy (1606–07) was long printed under his name but is now generally assigned to Middleton.
authors.style: Senecan rhetoric pressed toward allegory and emblem; a satiric, almost allegorical handling of revenge and atheism.
authors.concerns: The punishment of atheism; the workings of providence; revenge and its ironic reversals.
authors.significance: His name remains attached to one of the masterpieces of Jacobean tragedy, even as scholarship has transferred the play itself to Middleton.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and parentage unknown; the Revenger's Tragedy attribution is now disputed and generally given to Middleton.
themes: Puritan inheritance and the secret sin
sources: The North American Review

authors.name: Cædmon
authors.identity: poet
authors.biography: The first named English poet. According to Bede's account (Historia ecclesiastica IV.24), Cædmon was an illiterate cowherd at the monastery of Whitby under Abbess Hild who received the gift of song in a dream; thereafter he turned biblical narrative into vernacular verse, becoming a monk and composing a large body of religious poetry, of which only the nine-line 'Hymn' survives in Old English.
authors.profile: Cædmon's Hymn, a praise of God the Creator, survives in Northumbrian and West Saxon versions copied into manuscripts of Bede's Historia. It is the earliest datable poem in Old English and the foundation of the English vernacular religious tradition.
authors.style: Alliterative verse in the traditional Germanic style applied to Christian subject matter; simple, dignified praise of creation.
authors.concerns: The rendering of scripture into the vernacular; creation as the work of God.
authors.significance: As narrated by Bede, Cædmon exemplifies the consecration of native poetic form to Christian content; his Hymn is the starting point of the English poetic record.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from Bede's account, which has legendary elements; dates approximate; no poetry beyond the Hymn is securely attributed to him.
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume A: The Middle Ages

authors.name: Dan Michel of Northgate
authors.identity: translator; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: A Benedictine monk of St Augustine's Abbey, Canterbury, who in 1340 completed the Ayenbite of Inwyt (Remorse of Conscience), a Kentish translation of the French Somme le Roi of Frère Lorens. He is the first known translator of that influential manual of vices and virtues into English.
authors.profile: Translator of the Ayenbite of Inwyt (1340), the most extensive surviving Kentish prose text and a mine of early fourteenth-century English vocabulary.
authors.style: Faithful, word-for-word translation preserving the structure of the French original; conservative Kentish dialect with extensive learned vocabulary.
authors.concerns: The moral instruction of the laity through the doctrine of vices, virtues, and the sacrament of penance.
authors.significance: The Ayenbite is a unique record of the Kentish dialect and a major document of lay religious instruction on the eve of the Black Death.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from the colophon of his translation.
sources: The King's Reformation: Henry VIII and the Remaking of the English Church

authors.name: Daniel Defoe
authors.identity: English writer, journalist, and pamphleteer, long regarded as one of the founders of the English novel and among the most prolific and versatile prose authors of his age.
authors.biography: Born in London around 1660, the son of James Foe, a candlemaker and Dissenter, he was raised outside the Church of England and educated at a Dissenting academy. He engaged in trade, went bankrupt, and turned to political writing, publishing verse and hundreds of pamphlets, often courting danger from the authorities. He is best known for fiction written later in life, including Robinson Crusoe (1719), Moll Flanders (1722), and Roxana (1724). He was also associated with periodical and intelligence work under the government. He died in London on 24 April 1731.
authors.profile: A prolific author of fictional narrative, travel writing, conduct literature, and journalism, whose longest-lasting achievements are extended first-person fictions that treat crime, survival, and self-examination with realistic detail. His place as an early novelist rests on the vividness of that persona-based narration.
authors.style: Plain, direct, largely unornamented prose; an insistent first-person voice; accumulation of concrete and material detail; and a documentary, autobiographical surface that lends improbable stories an air of fact.
authors.concerns: Providence and self-preservation; sin, repentance, and material rising; credit, risk, and survival in a commercial world; political allegiance and religious nonconformity; and the fortunes of social outsiders.
authors.significance: One of the most widely read English prose writers of his generation and a central figure in the emergence of the novel, with Robinson Crusoe becoming one of the most influential narratives in English.
authors.uncertainty: His birth year (c. 1660) and exact birthplace are not firmly documented, and the authorship of a body of works attributed to him remains disputed.

works.title: A General History of the Pyrates
A Journal of the Plague Year
Serious Reflections During the Life and Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
The Political History of the Devil
The Shortest Way with the Dissenters

sources: William Harrison Ainsworth and His Friends (2 volumes)

authors.name: David Hartley
authors.identity: Physician and Dissenting philosopher whose Observations on Man (1749) built a complete system of mind, morals and religion on the doctrine of association of ideas.
authors.biography: Baptised at Luddenden near Halifax in 1705, the son of a poor clergyman, he lost both parents early and was brought up by an uncle. Educated at Jesus College, Cambridge, where he took his degrees and later his MD, he abandoned a clerical career, studied medicine in London and at Cambridge and practised successively in the provinces, in London and at Bath. His early medical studies prepared his larger scheme, which reduced mental life to vibration, sensation and the association of ideas as Locke had described them. Observations on Man, His Frame, His Duty, and His Anticipations (1749, two volumes) derived the whole of ethics, religion and hope from that mechanism, and its second part argued for a future state of universal happiness. He married and had several children, and died at Bath in 1757.
authors.profile: The architect of associationist psychology, who made the mechanical linking of ideas the explanation of character, virtue and religious expectation.
authors.style: Tight, numbered, propositional prose; long chains of deduction from a single principle; a physician's plainness and a dissenting divinity's earnestness of reference.
authors.concerns: Association as the law of mind; the physiological basis of thought; the derivation of moral sense from education and habit; the accumulation of desires and the scheme of future happiness; necessitation and prayer.
authors.significance: His Observations founded the associationist tradition that Priestley, Darwin, the Mills and the psychology of the next century developed, and made the link between mind and mechanism a standard explanatory programme.
authors.uncertainty: The date and exact place of his birth are uncertain; his son's memoir and later accounts disagree on the details.

works.title: Observations on Man, His Frame, His Duty, and His Expectations

authors.name: David Hume
authors.identity: Philosopher, essayist and historian of the Scottish Enlightenment, the most rigorous sceptic in English prose, whose Treatise and Enquiries remade the theory of knowledge, morals and politics.
authors.biography: Born in Edinburgh in April 1711 into a small landowning family, he was educated at home and at the university, tried a merchant's life in Bristol, and then withdrew to France to write. The Treatise of Human Nature (1739-40) appeared to little acclaim, and he confessed his distress at its neglect; the moral and political essays of 1741 and the Enquiries of 1748 and 1751 restated the same philosophy in a public style. He was blocked from an Edinburgh professorship in 1745 by clerical opposition and was summoned before the presbytery of that city in 1756 without being censured; he earned his living as a private tutor, as keeper of the Advocates' Library and, from 1754, as a historian, and his History of England made him wealthy. He served in the embassy in Paris from 1763, briefly at the foreign office, and accompanied Rousseau to England in 1766 before their quarrel. He died in Edinburgh on 25 August 1776, having written his own short account of a life he called so little interrupted.
authors.profile: A sceptical humanist who reduced causation, induction, the self and moral obligation to habit, sentiment and custom, yet wrote with an urbanity that made disbelief amiable.
authors.style: Lucid, measured, ironized prose; the clean paragraph of the Enquiries; examples drawn from common life; dry humour and a refusal of technical jargon; historical narrative of stately balance.
authors.concerns: Custom as the guide of life; the limits of reason in belief and in morals; the passions and the rules of justice; natural religion, miracle and the design argument; the principles of taste, party and commerce.
authors.significance: He set the agenda of post-Kantian philosophy in the problem of induction and personal identity, founded the empirical study of religion and of politics, and gave classical liberalism its sceptical defence of convention.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his father's estate, his Bristol period and his Parisian secretarial work are patchy; his posthumous Dialogues were published in 1779 under his brother's editorship against his own instructions on timing.

works.title: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals

authors.name: David Walker
authors.nationality: American; the abolitionist writing of the free Black communities of the northern seaports, of Black mutual-aid and Masonic civic life, and of the immediatist pamphlet agitation of the later 1820s
authors.identity: Boston clothes merchant, civic organizer and pamphleteer; the author of the first and most uncompromising American demand for immediate unconditional emancipation written by a Black American, and the founding polemicist of the immediatist agitation in the United States.
authors.biography: Walker was born in Wilmington, North Carolina, in or about 1796, and grew up free; his mother's condition and his father's status are reported differently in the sources, and under the law of the state his freedom or enslavement would have followed the condition of the mother. He appears in the record as a mariner's and then a merchant's man, with years in Charleston, South Carolina, before he settled in Boston by 1825. There he kept a clothing and second-hand goods business, joined the Prince Hall Masonic lodge and took an active part in the Black civic, mutual-aid, educational and religious networks of the city, whose print culture and subscription lists gave the abolitionist press its first readers and its earliest money. He was in sympathy with the colony scheme then advancing in the white press and became its most furious opponent, and his Appeal, issued in Boston on 28 September 1829, was printed at his own instance, smuggled into the Southern states through sailors and Black seaport channels, and reissued in three enlarged editions within a year. Its call to the enslaved to read, remember and act, and its prophecy of judgment on the republic, produced a legislative reaction in the Southern states, a bounty on his person announced in Georgia, and a permanent alarm in the slaveholding press. He died in Boston on 6 August 1830, at about thirty-four years of age, and was buried in what is now an unmarked grave; the cause of his death was never established, and from his own lifetime some suspected he had been murdered. The Liberator, founded the year after his death, printed his Appeal in full and treated it as the opening document of the movement.
authors.profile: His surviving literary work is a single pamphlet, and a work of sustained argument rather than narrative: Walker's Appeal, in four articles with a preamble, addressed in the first instance to the coloured citizens of the world and particularly of the United States. It mixes indictment, scriptural exegesis, historical parallel, statistical citation from encyclopaedias and the slave codes, and an appeal to the diaspora to educate, organise and remember itself; a supplementary appeal to the slaveholders follows in later editions. Its manner is sermon, courtroom remonstrance and open letter at once, and its four articles pass from the condition of free Black Americans, through the crimes of slavery and the rebuttal of racist pseudo-science, to a programme of self-help, schools and mutual inspection. He also wrote short public letters and minutes to the Black press of the later 1820s, and left a son of the same name who preserved the text.
authors.style: An amplified, prophetic and incantatory prose, built on apostrophe, anaphora, long cumulative sentences and repeated charges of hypocrisy; the irony of quotation turned against the quotations' authors, with the Declaration, the Bible and the language of Christianity cited to condemn the nation that uses them. The argument proceeds by indictment, evidence and threat rather than by politeness, and it deliberately abandons the petitioning manner of earlier reform writing.
authors.concerns: The standing of the enslaved as fully human and as citizens of the republic that professes their equality; the sin and political danger of slavery and of the colour line; the complicity of the churches and of the colonisation movement in American slavery; the duties of self-education, industry, temperance and organisation in the free Black community; the use of scripture and of founding documents as instruments of accusation; the right of the oppressed to speak for themselves and, under judgment, to act.
authors.significance: The Appeal marks the moment when American abolitionist writing turned from gradualist appeal and white benevolence to immediate unconditional demand voiced by the oppressed themselves, and it supplied the rhetorical model of the agitation of the 1830s. It was the first American pamphlet to make the condition of the enslaved a national rather than a charitable question in the language of self-assertion; it was read aloud, reprinted, smuggled and prosecuted, and the laws passed against Black literacy and importation of seditious press in the Southern states after 1829-30 were partly a reply to it. Garrison's paper made him its prophetic precursor, and later Black radical tradition has read him as its founding political writer.
authors.uncertainty: Almost all the facts of his life before Boston are uncertain. The year of his birth is given only approximately (c. 1796, sometimes 1797), and the date of 28 September in some accounts is borrowed from the anniversary of the Appeal's publication; the conditions of his parents, and therefore the basis of his own free status, are reported contradictorily, with one account making his mother free and his father enslaved and another the reverse. The story of his early life is derived largely from what he says of himself in the Appeal and from Southern newspaper reportage hostile to him. The cause of his death is unknown, and the poisoning theory belongs to contemporary suspicion and to later tradition rather than to evidence. No manuscript of the Appeal survives and the details of its printing and distribution are known from the editions themselves and from the reports of agents.

works.title: Walker's Appeal, in Four Articles; Together with a Preamble, to the Coloured Citizens of the World, but in Particular, and Very Expressly, to Those of the United States of America

authors.name: Delarivier Manley
authors.identity: English novelist, playwright, and political satirist, one of the most prominent and scandalous female writers of the early eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born on the island of Jersey, the daughter of Sir Roger Manley, a military governor, she was raised within an aristocratic milieu and later turned to literary work to support herself. She wrote fiction, plays, and political journalism, and her satirical key to court and party figures, The New Atalantis (1709), brought her fame and a prosecution for libel. Her fictionalized account of her own career, The Adventures of Rivella, appeared in 1714, and other prose romances circulated under her name. She died in London on 24 July 1724.
authors.profile: A writer of amatory and political fiction who blended scandal, party satire, and autobiography, and who helped to establish the commercially published prose romance and the politically engaged key-writing tradition of her period.
authors.style: Gossipy, satirical, and romance-inflected prose; use of the roman a clef; allegorical and disguised portraiture of real persons; and a self-conscious blend of fiction, memoir, and political invective.
authors.concerns: Party rivalry and court corruption; reputation, scandal, and the exposure of the powerful; the situation of the writing woman; and the interplay of sex, money, and political patronage.
authors.significance: A leading female author of early-eighteenth-century London letters and a key figure in the development of political satire and scandalous fiction, her work a central document of party-age writing.
authors.uncertainty: Her birth year is disputed (given variously as 1663 or c. 1670), and the authorship of several novels published under or attributed to her name, including Queen Zarah, is contested.
sources: William Harrison Ainsworth (Twayne's English Authors Series, no. 138)

authors.name: Dorothy Osborne
authors.identity: Letter-writer; her Letters to Sir William Temple (1652–54), written during their protracted courtship against her family's opposition, are among the finest and most natural prose works of the century and a rare surviving woman's voice of the Interregnum.
authors.biography: Born 1627 at Chicksands Priory, Bedfordshire, daughter of a royalist family; she nursed her father during the Civil Wars and lost most of her siblings. Between 1652 and 1654 she conducted a secret correspondence with William Temple (later the diplomat and essayist), whom she married in 1654 against strong family pressure and other suitors. Her letters — witty, tender, shrewd, and critical of the romances and poetry of the day — survive in some seventy-seven; Temple preserved them and they were published in 1888. She lived as Lady Temple, accompanying her husband's career, and died in 1695.
authors.profile: The natural, intelligent letter-writer whose prose, free of artifice, offers a woman's candid view of love, family duty, books, and society in the 1650s, and a remarkable literary self-portrait.
authors.style: Easy, colloquial, unforced prose; wit and psychological insight; literary criticism and quotation; and an intimate epistolary voice of great spontaneity.
authors.concerns: Love, marriage, and family obligation; the position and intelligence of women; reading, romances, and poetry; society and character; and the conduct of the inner life.
authors.significance: Osborne's Letters are a masterpiece of informal English prose and one of the most important documents by a seventeenth-century woman, valued for their literary quality and as a witness to women's intellectual life and to the early career of Temple.
authors.uncertainty: Only Osborne's side of the correspondence survives in full; her later life is documented mainly through Temple's papers, and the letters' publication was long delayed.

works.title: Letters from Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple

sources: Perdita: The Life of Mary Robinson

authors.name: Douglas William Jerrold
authors.nationality: English; the Regency and Victorian stage and the comic journalism of the metropolis
authors.identity: Dramatist, journalist and humorist; the most popular writer of domestic melodrama of the later 1820s and a defining voice of the metropolis's comic press
authors.biography: He was born in London into a poor family, was apprenticed as a boy, ran to sea in his early youth, and then took to the stage as an actor in the minor theatres. He turned to writing for those theatres, and his nautical domestic drama of a sailor's sweetheart, played south of the water in 1829, became the most performed and most pirated piece of the decade, acted with alterations all over the country and in America. He then lived by journalism, and his sketches of married life from a bedpost and his contributions to the great comic weekly made him one of the most widely read prose humorists of the 1840s. He edited a cheap daily paper of wide circulation, quarrelled with the managers of the patent theatres and campaigned publicly against their monopoly of legitimate drama, and wrote plays, essays and stories for the periodicals until his later years. His miscellaneous comic prose was collected in several series, and his after-dinner wit was reported throughout the period. He died in 1866, leaving a son who continued his father's theatrical and journalistic work.
authors.profile: A long list of dramas, melodramas and farces for the minor and patent theatres, of which the nautical domestic drama is the surviving piece; the bedpost sketches and the other collected humorous prose; essays, tales and journalistic writing on the metropolis and its poor. His characteristic method is the sentimental domestic situation treated with a comic, speech-reporting economy, in which the jokes of character and the pathos of the situation are delivered by the same lines.
authors.style: A plain, point-driven comic prose built on the epigram and on reported cockney and maritime speech; in the drama, workmanlike dialogue, effective stage business and a song placed exactly where the pathos of the situation needs relief. His humour is domestic and verbal rather than satirical in the philosophical manner.
authors.concerns: The virtue and the exposure of the poor. The sailor's condition, the press-gang and domestic waiting. The monopoly of the licensed theatres and the interests of the unlicensed stage. Marriage, its drudgery and its comedy, seen from the bedroom and the public house.
authors.significance: He is the central figure of the great decade of penny melodrama and of the agitation over theatrical monopoly which led to the patents reform of the 1840s; his comic journalism defined the voice of the mid-century metropolitan weekly. His best-known drama remains the standard example of nautical melodrama in criticism and theatre history.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his boyhood at sea and of his first acting engagements are given inconsistently in the memoirs written after his death.

works.title: Black-Eyed Susan; or, All in the Downs

authors.name: Edgar Allan Poe
authors.nationality: American; the Richmond, Baltimore and Philadelphia periodical world, and the Southern and Mid-Atlantic review and magazine culture of the 1830s and 1840s
authors.identity: Poet, tale-writer, reviewer and editor; the most exacting and most combative American critic of his generation, the maker of the analytical and the tales of horror, and the poet of the pure musical lyric, who attempted to live wholly by the pen in a country that had not yet a paying market for it.
authors.biography: Poe was born Edgar Poe at Boston, the second of three children of travelling actors, and was left fatherless and motherless in early childhood: David Poe deserted the family, and his mother Elizabeth, an actress of Richmond, died there in 1811, after which he was taken into the household of John Allan, a wealthy Richmond tobacco merchant, from whom he took his middle name but who never adopted him. He went with the Allan family to England in 1815, was schooled in London and its neighbourhood, and returned to Richmond a boy formed on the Byron models and on the German tale then reaching America in translation. At the University of Virginia, which he entered in 1826 on Allan's terms, he contracted gambling debts that Allan refused to discharge; he broke with his foster father, removed to Boston, where his first slim volume of verse appeared without his name in 1827, served a short time in the United States army under an assumed name, and obtained through Allan's interest an appointment to the Military Academy at West Point, which he was deliberately dismissed from in the spring of 1831. Comes of age and without a fortune, he resolved to live by his pen, and the early 1830s found him contributing poems, tales and reviews to the annuals and magazines of the Southern and Middle States, with the collected volume of 1831, printed by subscription and prefaced by an attack upon the current American poets, as his profession of faith. He became editor of the Southern Literary Messenger at Richmond in 1835, and by his tales, his poems and his reviews made it the most widely circulated American monthly of its day; there followed the New York and Philadelphia years, employment on the magazines of those cities, and in 1840 the two-volume collection of his tales, which established the prose reputation that then carried him far beyond his verse. In 1836 he had married at Richmond his cousin Virginia Clemm, a child of thirteen, whose mother kept house with them; her long consumption and her death in 1847 left him, in his own account, without any tie. He edited a short-lived journal at New York in 1845, lectured on poetry and on the material universe, printed his prosimetrical cosmology in 1848, and projected a magazine of his own that was never funded. He was found in a state of insensibility at Baltimore in the first days of October 1849, on his way to remove to the city where his father's family lived, and died there on 7 October, aged forty; the circumstances of those last days have never been settled, and the friend who printed his works at length after him did so with a malicious preface which governed his reputation for a generation.
authors.profile: Within the range of this installment his work is the verse of three pamphlets and volumes - the first anonymous booklet, the longer poem of the star-island and the collected volume of 1831 with its short lyrics of classical beauty and its vision of the doomed city; afterwards came the tales, the poems of the later magazines, the criticism, the essay on the principle of composition and the prose of the cosmic argument. He wrote the analytical tale of ratiocination and the tale of nervous horror, the hoaxes and the marginal criticism of his own review work, and he projected, in his criticism of contemporary American books, the first serious American account of the poetical principle. His career as an editor is part of his work: the monthly, the annual, the magazine and the projected review are the forms in which he wrote.
authors.style: In verse an intense and deliberate music, with internal rhyme, refrain, repetition of key words and an incantatory regularity of stanza, a command of the short lyric of address and of the long meditative or narrative poem; in prose an analytical first person, a nervous precision of detail, an art of suspense and anticlimax, and a criticism of bludgeon irony - abrupt, technical, and personal in attack, with a habit of defining his own practice against that of the traffic in magazines.
authors.concerns: Beauty as the sole province of the poem, and its exaltation into the supernal; the death of a beautiful woman as the most poetical of topics; the unity of effect and the economy of means by which a work of art should be constructed; the reach and the limits of analysis and of the calculating intellect; the isolation of the imaginative individual in a commercial letterscape; the material unity of the universe and the theological consequences of drawing it together.
authors.significance: He invented the analytical or detective tale and practised before anyone in English the short tale of single psychological effect; his theory of the poem, of the unity of impression and of the music of verse, passed by his French interpreters into the symbolist movement and so into the modern poetry of Europe, and his criticism created the model of the professional American reviewer. His tales of horror and of analysis founded durable native genres, and his career, cut short by a struggle with the economics of American periodical writing, became the standard case of the unhoused artist in a commercial republic.
authors.uncertainty: The identity of the woman addressed in the lyrics of beauty, and the chronology of his engagement to Sarah Helen Whitman, are variously stated; the quarrel and money history with John Allan is known largely from the Allans' side and from Poe's own complaints; the causes of the insensibility in which he was found at Baltimore, and the company he kept in the two or three days before his death, remain unexplained, and the evidence is disputed between intemperance, bodily disorder and the political violence of the election week. The printed obituary and the first collected edition were prepared by a literary enemy, and many anecdotes of the early life rest on his own jesting and on later reminiscence.

works.title: Al Aaraaf, Tamerlane, and Minor Poems

authors.name: Edmund Burke
authors.nationality: Irish-born British; Anglo-Irish, and the Whig parliamentary oratory and the political and aesthetic prose of the later eighteenth century
authors.identity: Statesman, political writer and philosophical critic of the passions; the Rockingham Whig parliamentarian and manager of the Hastings impeachment, whose Reflections on the Revolution in France became the classic English argument against the French Revolution, and whose Enquiry of 1757 supplied the period's standard analysis of the sublime and the beautiful.
authors.biography: Burke was born in Dublin in 1729, the son of a solicitor who conformed to the church of Ireland and of Mary Nagle of a Cork Catholic family; brought up in his father's communion but kept on friendly terms with his Catholic kindred, he entered Trinity College Dublin, and removed to London and the Middle Temple about 1750, where he abandoned the law for letters. His first books made his name: A Vindication of Natural Society (1756), a sceptical exposure of civil government which many readers mistook for a grave attack on revelation, and the Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757). Through the publisher Robert Dodsley he founded the Annual Register and wrote its historical and critical survey of Europe for many years. He entered the Commons in 1761 as member for Wendover, was private secretary to Rockingham in the administration of 1765-66, and in the Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770) turned party connexion into a doctrine of organised principled opposition. Member for Bristol from 1774, he argued in his address of that year and in the Speech on Conciliation with America of 1775 that a representative owes his unbiased judgement to his constituents, not his obedience. He bought the estate of Gregories near Beaconsfield in 1768 and lived thereafter in permanent tension between country propriety and heavy borrowing. Paymaster of the Forces in the Rockingham ministry of 1782, he became the manager of the impeachment of Warren Hastings, which he opened in Westminster Hall in 1788 and which filled the rest of his public life. The French Revolution broke his long alliance with Charles James Fox; the Reflections on the Revolution in France of November 1790, the Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs of 1791 and the Letters on a Regicide Peace of 1795-97 made him the most read and most attacked political writer of the war years. He retired from the Commons in 1794 and died at Beaconsfield in 1797, buried at Gerrards Cross. The death of his only son Richard in 1794 darkened his last years, and unfinished pieces on the revolution and on Shakespeare were published after his death.
authors.profile: His writings form three connected bodies: the early philosophical treatise, the parliamentary speech and printed letter, and the great state paper of the impeachment. The Philosophical Enquiry states a theory of the sublime and the beautiful as passions rooted in self-preservation and in society, and its divisions on the passions, on the sublime, on the beautiful and on the effect of general and obscure notions became the received framework of aesthetic discussion in the 1790s. The Annual Register's annual historical and critical articles made it the standard English chronicle of European affairs for two generations. The Reflections is a letter of remonstrance and prophecy that mixes constitutional argument with the elevated lament; the speeches on America and on the conduct of the East India manager are oratory revised into printed state papers; the Letters on a Regicide Peace argue publicly and at great length against a settlement with revolutionary France.
authors.style: A prose of sustained periodic sentence in which abstraction is embodied in image and in moral feeling, and argument advances by concession, by historical instance and by the accumulating weight of clause upon clause. He can be plainly businesslike in a minute or a resolution, ironical in definition, and torrential in the rhetorical burst, of which the passage on the queen of France in the Reflections is the most quoted and most imitated specimen in English. The characteristic movement is nevertheless the long qualification and the appeal to prescriptive usage, the concrete enumeration of institutions and orders. In the treatise the manner is analytic and deliberately dry; in the speeches judicial and cumulative; in the late pamphlets urgent, and occasionally uneven with anger.
authors.concerns: Liberty as an inherited and prescriptive estate rather than an abstract speculable right; the moral limits of empire and the duties and accountability of power; party, connexion and principled opposition as the conditions of constitutional freedom; the dangers of an armed metaphysics and of geometric abstraction in politics; the civilising uses of prejudice, of religious establishment and of the learned and gentle orders; the passions of the sublime and of beauty, and the effect of obscurity and sympathy; the prudence and historical consequence that should govern imperial and foreign policy.
authors.significance: The Reflections created the durable language of modern political conservatism and supplied the founding text of the anti-Jacobin answer to 1789, at which Paine's Rights of Man and Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Men were aimed; the Enquiry fixed the terms of the debate on the sublime for two generations of artists and writers. His speeches and letters are the central English documents on the American and Indian questions, and his management of the impeachment established the doctrine of public accountability in colonial government. His account of party and of the independence of the representative remains the standard statement of eighteenth-century Whig parliamentary practice.
