authors.uncertainty: His Dublin birthplace is not in question, though the street of his birth is variously identified and the day is usually given as 12 January 1729. The day of his death is reported now as the ninth and now as the end of July 1797 in different calendars, and his house is described sometimes at Beaconsfield and sometimes at Gregories in that parish. His matriculation and degree at Trinity College Dublin, the chronology of his removal to London and of his keeping in the Temple are set down with small variations in the biographies. The extent of his share in the earliest volumes of the Annual Register, and the responsibility for the anonymously printed pieces of the 1750s, remain matters of bibliographical inference rather than of documented fact.

works.title: A Letter to a Member of the National Assembly
A Letter to a Noble Lord
An Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs
Reflections on the Revolution in France

authors.name: Edmund Spenser
authors.identity: Poet; colonial administrator in Ireland; the self-fashioned 'new poet' of the English Renaissance and its greatest non-dramatic poet.
authors.biography: Born in London c. 1552, the son of a journeyman clothmaker; educated at Merchant Taylors' School under Richard Mulcaster and at Pembroke Hall, Cambridge (BA 1573, MA 1576), where he associated with Gabriel Harvey. He entered the household of the Earl of Leicester, met Sidney and Dyer in the 'Areopagus' circle, and published The Shepheardes Calender (1579) to immediate fame. In 1580 he went to Ireland as secretary to Lord Grey de Wilton and spent most of his remaining life there as a planter and official (Kilcolman Castle, Co. Cork), publishing The Faerie Queene (1590, 1596), Complaints (1591), Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595), Amoretti and Epithalamion (1595), and Prothalamion (1596). In 1598 Kilcolman was burned in Tyrone's rebellion; Spenser fled to London and died there on 13 January 1599, and was buried in Westminster Abbey near Chaucer.
authors.profile: The laureate of Elizabethan England, whose career was a deliberate imitation of Virgil's — from pastoral to epic — in the service of Protestant nationhood; he made the English language the vehicle of a full-scale national epic and a new poetic idiom (the Spenserian stanza).
authors.style: Archaizing diction ('the antique rolles'), the nine-line Spenserian stanza, elaborate allegory, musical fluency, and the fusion of Italian romance (Ariosto, Tasso), classical epic, and native English tradition (Chaucer, Langland).
authors.concerns: Protestant nationalism and the reform of the church; virtue and courtesy as the disciplines of the self; Ireland and the ethics of colonization; mutability, time, and the poet's immortal fame; love and marriage as sacramental.
authors.significance: The greatest non-dramatic poet of the English Renaissance: The Faerie Queene created the English national epic and shaped the language's poetic tradition from Milton to Keats ('the poet's poet'), while Amoretti and Epithalamion founded the English marriage poem.
authors.uncertainty: The year of birth rests on the sonnet 'Amoretti' 60's allusion and the records of his schooling; the exact circumstances of his final flight from Ireland and his poverty at death are reported by Ben Jonson and William Camden.

works.title: A View of the Present State of Ireland

sources: Jack Sheppard (Broadview Editions)

authors.name: Edmund Waller
authors.identity: Court poet and politician, credited with perfecting the smooth closed heroic couplet and the Cavalier lyric; a long-lived figure whose verse was admired for its polish, melody, and gallantry from Charles I's court to the Restoration.
authors.biography: Born 3 March 1606 at Coleshill, educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge. He entered Parliament and court society, celebrated Sacharissa (Lady Dorothy Sidney) in his lyrics, and was implicated in 'Waller's Plot' (1643) to secure London for the king, for which he was fined and banished. He returned under the Commonwealth, was elected to Parliament, and served through the Restoration with continued favour, revising his poems across a long career. He died 21 October 1687 at Beaconsfield.
authors.profile: The courtly lyricist whose 'smooth' verse and closed couplets became the model of elegant Restoration poetry; Dryden credited him with beginning 'the excellence of numbers' in English.
authors.style: Melodious, polished, and balanced verse; the closed heroic couplet; gallant compliment and Petrarchan conceit refined to ease; panegyric and occasional poetry of public grace.
authors.concerns: Love and courtly compliment; royalist loyalty; the praise of patrons and the nation; the value of poetic polish and decorum; and, in later poems, time and old age.
authors.significance: Waller's technical refinement of the couplet directly shaped Denham, Dryden, and the whole Augustan line; though his reputation declined after the seventeenth century, he was the acknowledged father of smooth Restoration verse.
authors.uncertainty: Waller's life is well recorded; the dating of individual lyrics and the identity of 'Sacharissa' are established, though many poems circulated in manuscript before print.
sources: William Ellery Channing: An Essay on the Liberal Spirit in America

authors.name: Edward Fairfax
authors.identity: translator; poet
authors.biography: Born at Leeds about 1580, younger son of Sir Thomas Fairfax of Denton. He lived as a scholarly country gentleman, devoted to translation, and died on 27 January 1635. His fame rests on a single book.
authors.profile: Godfrey of Bulloigne, or the Recovery of Jerusalem (1600) — his translation of Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata into English ottava rima — together with twelve eclogues printed in 1631 and a lost history of Edward the Black Prince.
authors.style: A grave, musical, deliberate verse that renders Tasso's romance-epic with fidelity and grace; Dryden judged him the equal of the best translators.
authors.concerns: The heroic ideal; the claims of romance against epic; English verse as a fit medium for Italian poetry.
authors.significance: His Tasso is the great English version of the Italian epic tradition and a landmark of translation as an art.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his lost works are known only by report.
sources: Selected Poems of Thomas Hood

authors.name: Edward Gibbon
authors.identity: Historian of the decline and fall of the Roman Empire, whose six volumes (1776-1788) made the fate of ancient civilisation and of Christianity the central narrative of the age.
authors.biography: Born at Putney in 1737, a delicate child largely left to his own reading, he went up to Oxford in 1752, was converted to Rome there and was removed from the university, and spent several formative years at Lausanne under a Calvinist pastor. He returned to Protestantism, read widely in French and Latin, and served in the Hampshire militia during the Seven Years' War without seeing action. In 1764 he reached Rome, and among the ruins of the Capitoline resolved to write the history of its decline. The first volume of the Decline and Fall appeared in 1776, the second and third in 1781 and the last three in 1788; between them he sat in Parliament, took office at the board of trade, and endured a hostile controversy over his fifteenth and sixteenth chapters, which he answered in 1779. He fell with the North ministry in 1782, settled for years at Lausanne with his friend Deyverdun, and completed his history there before returning to London, where he died in January 1794.
authors.profile: A philosophic historian who explained empires by manners, superstition and circumstance, and whose irony gave religious narrative the poise of an autumn evening.
authors.style: A grand periodic style of balanced clauses and weighted antithesis; sustained irony that never declares itself; narrative panache in collapse and battle; a footnotes apparatus of learning used as concealed argument.
authors.concerns: The causes of the fall of the western empire; the relation of Christianity to the decline of civic and military virtue; superstition, enthusiasm and ecclesiastical history; national character, barbarism and the progress of society.
authors.significance: The Decline and Fall set the modern standard of source-based secular history and remains the model of historical narrative in English; its account of the triumph of the church has been argued over ever since.
authors.uncertainty: The exact circumstances of his Oxford expulsion and conversion, and the dates of several of his own memoirs, remain imperfectly settled.

works.title: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

authors.name: Edward Hall
authors.identity: chronicler; lawyer
authors.biography: Born in London about 1497; educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, and at Gray's Inn. A lawyer and MP, he compiled his great chronicle of the Wars of the Roses, The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York, which Richard Grafton printed in 1548, the year after Hall's death.
authors.profile: Author of the chronicle that made the Tudor interpretation of history — the Wars of the Roses as God's judgement on rebellion, culminating in the providential union under the Tudors — the official story of England. Shakespeare drew the material of his English history plays, often nearly phrase by phrase, from Hall's Union through Holinshed.
authors.style: Ample, oratorical prose; set speeches composed for the great men of the action; the providential scheme applied to the narrative of faction and battle.
authors.concerns: The horror of civil war; the legitimacy and providence of the Tudor dynasty; history as the school of princes.
authors.significance: The principal historiographical source of Shakespeare's histories and of the Elizabethan understanding of the fifteenth century; his set speeches shaped the English historical imagination.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York

sources: The Collected Works of Samuel Taylor Coleridge (16 volumes)

authors.name: Edward Jenner
authors.nationality: English; the provincial medical and scientific writing of the Gloucestershire country practitioners, and the empirical pamphlet literature of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries
authors.identity: Country physician and naturalist, and the founder of vaccination; a writer of short, plain, evidence-driven medical pamphlets whose Inquiry of 1798 is one of the most consequential scientific books in English, and whose published work sits beside a large unpublished record of observation on birds, geology and the natural history of the Severn vale.
authors.biography: Jenner was born at Berkeley in Gloucestershire on 17 May 1749, the son of the vicar of Berkeley, the Rev. Stephen Jenner, and lost his parents while still a child. He was put out at about thirteen to a neighbouring surgeon-apothecary at Sodbury, and served his apprenticeship in that practice before removing to London, where he lodged and studied, attended the lectures and the house practice at St George's Hospital, and worked under John Hunter, whose experimental method he adopted. Admitted a member of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1773, he returned to Berkeley and settled there in practice, in a country partnership which gave him the range of cases, and the leisured observation, on which his later work was built; he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1788. His inquiry into the cowpox of the Gloucestershire dairies grew out of the common belief of the dairy women, that infection with the cow's distemper protected against smallpox. On 14 May 1796 he inoculated with cowpox matter taken from the hand of Sarah Nelmes, a dairymaid, James Phipps, the young son of his gardener, and afterwards tested the boy's immunity by variolous matter. The results were published in London in 1798 in a small self-printed volume, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, a Disease Discovered in Some of the Western Counties of England, Particularly Gloucestershire, and Known by the Name of the Cow Pox, which established the practice of vaccination and gave it its name. The book was attacked, ridiculed and answered in pamphlets, and was also adopted rapidly on the Continent and in the Americas; Jenner continued to publish the progress of the new practice, supplied vaccine matter gratuitously to inquirers and correspondents, and prosecuted his observations on the migration and habits of the swallow and on other natural-history questions. His wife Catherine died in 1815; his own health failed after a mild stroke in 1822, and he died at Berkeley on 26 January 1823, buried in the church there. The practice he founded became the basis of immunology and of the public vaccination programmes of the century.
authors.profile: His published medical writing is short, practical and cumulative rather than systematic: the Inquiry of 1798, a plain statement of cases arranged as evidence, with the history of the cow-pox, the account of the experiments on Phipps and on other persons, and the anatomical and clinical description of the vesicle; the Continuation of Facts and Observations relative to the Variolae Vaccinae of 1800; and The Origin of the Vaccine Inoculation of 1801, a summary of the case against variolation. To these belong his introductory letters to correspondents, his papers to the Royal Society, and his observations on the natural history of the rook and the swallow, published separately and in the philosophical transactions of the day. He wrote also an account of his own inoculations and a pamphlet of popular instruction, and left the manuscripts and notebooks of a lifelong naturalist.
authors.style: A spare, unornamented and avowedly diffident prose of case, date and outcome, in which the claim is carried by the enumeration of instances and by the repetition of the same experiment on different persons, with a deliberate refusal of theory. He writes plainly and even homely, names his informants and their parishes, dates each case, and reserves his judgement to the shortest possible conclusion; the polemic against his opponents, when it appears, is cool, factual and occasionally wry. His natural-history writing shares the same habits of close observation of particular creatures in a particular country.
authors.concerns: The relation of cattle disease to human infection, and the specific protection given by one disease against another; the trial of an hypothesis by a single designed experiment and its repetition; the immunity produced by cow-pox and its duration; the comparison of vaccination with the dangerous practice of inserting smallpox matter; the safety and public diffusion of a cheap remedy; the honest reporting of failed and anomalous cases; the natural history, habits and migration of the birds and animals of the Gloucestershire vale.
authors.significance: The Inquiry of 1798 founded vaccination and gave preventive medicine its first rational procedure; within a few years the practice spread through Europe and the Americas, was adopted by governments and public institutions, and displaced the older variolation, preparing the way for the eradication of smallpox announced in the twentieth century. His method, an hypothesis tested by inoculation and by subsequent challenge with the dangerous matter, became a model of experimental medicine, and the derivation of that method from John Hunter's practice is the best-known instance in English of the country physician changing the practice of a whole society. He is also a figure of literary history, since the controversy over vaccination filled the pamphlet and cartoon literature of the Regency years.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his apprenticeship and of the Sodbury years, and the chronology of his London study with Hunter at St George's, are given with small variations in the memoirs, which depend heavily on his own notebooks and on the family Life written by his early biographer John Baron. The order of the first cowpox experiments is sometimes told so as to make the 1796 Phipps case the sole decisive instance, whereas his earlier local observations and the trial on his own children are variously dated; and the exact priority of the dairymaid Sarah Nelmes's infection, and of the accounts of farmers and physicians who had practised something like vaccination before him, remains disputed. The day of his death is given as 26 January 1823.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae

authors.name: Edward Moore
authors.identity: English dramatist, poet, and periodical essayist, editor of the essay series The World and a writer of fables and plays.
authors.biography: Born on 22 March 1712 at Abingdon in Berkshire, the son of a Dissenting minister, he was educated at a Dissenting academy and turned to literary work in London. He wrote poems, including Fables for the Female Sex (1744), and stage works such as the tragedy The Trial of Selim the Persian (1748) and the adaptation Gil Blas (1751). He was editor of the periodical essay series The World (1753-56). He died on 1 March 1757.
authors.profile: A miscellaneous writer of the mid-century who moved between the stage, the periodical essay, and verse, best remembered as a compiler-editor of one of the more successful periodical collections of his decade.
authors.style: Polished didactic and satirical verse; the familiar essay and periodical manner; theatrical plotting in his dramas; and a conventional Augustan prose ease.
authors.concerns: Moral instruction through the fable; manners and the observation of society; the education and conduct of women; and the periodical's critique of public life.
authors.significance: A representative figure of mid-eighteenth-century periodical and theatrical writing, whose editorship of The World situates him within the age of the essay series that flourished after the Spectator.
authors.uncertainty: The outlines of his life are documented, though his minor plays and essays are unevenly dated and some occasional attributions are uncertain.
sources: Timothy Dwight (Twayne's United States Authors Series, No. 145)

authors.name: Edward Young
authors.identity: English poet and essayist, Regius Professor of Civil Law at Oxford, whose meditative Night Thoughts and critical Conjectures made him a precursor of Romantic sensibility.
authors.biography: Young was born in Hampshire, educated at Exeter College, Oxford, and became a fellow, later holding the Regius Professorship of Civil Law. His early verse included a poem on Parliament, and he wrote occasional and festival verse before settling into his characteristic meditative mode. After years of relative quiet he published The Complainture, or Night Thoughts on Life, Death, and Immortality (1742-1745), which made his name through its meditations on grief after family bereavements. Later nine additional nights followed, together with plays and the prose critical treatise Conjectures on Original Composition (1759). In his last years he was tied to the Welwyn living through family connections. He died at Welwyn in Hertfordshire in 1765.
authors.profile: A poet of melancholy, death, and immortality in blank verse, and a critic of genius and originality; his grave meditation and his theory of the creative self mark him as a bridge to Romanticism.
authors.style: Tumid, exclamatory blank verse of the night and the grave; rhetorical question, antithesis, and point; an introspective, brooding persona; and a taste for the sublime and the morbid.
authors.concerns: Death, grief, and the proof of immortality; the vanity of worldly ambition; the nature of poetic genius and originality; the self in solitude; and religious consolation against despair.
authors.significance: Night Thoughts dominated the graveyard and melancholy vogue of later eighteenth-century poetry, and his Conjectures shaped the Romantic cult of original genius and influenced writers abroad.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is disputed, commonly given as 1683 but sometimes earlier; the precise chronology of his Oxford preferment and family tragedies rests partly on his own partly fictionalised accounts.

works.title: A Paraphrase upon Part of the Book of Job
The Complaint, or, Night Thoughts on Life, Death and Immortality

authors.name: Eliza Haywood
authors.identity: English novelist, playwright, and actress, one of the most prolific and popular writers of amatory fiction in the early eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born around 1693 (her birthplace is disputed, with Ireland traditionally but uncertainly given), she married a Welsh gentleman and, after his early death, turned to the stage and to writing. She first achieved fame with the long romance Love in Excess (1719), followed by shorter amatory fictions such as Fantomina (1724). She acted, wrote plays, and later published the novel The History of Miss Betsy Thoughtless (1751), a more morally serious work. She also edited periodical and miscellaneous collections. She died in 1756.
authors.profile: A central author of the amatory-fiction vogue whose narratives explore desire, deception, and the vulnerability of women in a commercial marriage market, and whose range later extended toward conduct-adjacent domestic realism.
authors.style: Sensational, emotionally heightened prose; first-person and epistolary insertions within narrative; elaborate rhetoric of passion; tightly plotted intrigue centered on seduction; and a strong attention to the interior states of female characters.
authors.concerns: Desire and deception; the seduction and reputation of women; the economics of marriage; the perils and knowledge of the female heart; and the pleasures and dangers of reading romance.
authors.significance: A leading and widely read novelist of her day, once ranked alongside Richardson and Fielding, whose recovery by modern scholarship has made her central to the study of women's writing and the rise of the novel.
authors.uncertainty: Her birth year, birthplace, parentage, and the details of her marriage are all uncertain and variously reconstructed; the precise dating of some works also varies.

works.title: Fantomina; or, Love in a Maze
Love in Excess; or, The Fatal Enquiry
The History of Miss Betsy Thoughtless

sources: The Poetical Works of Thomas Lovell Beddoes (2 volumes)

authors.name: Elizabeth Carter
authors.identity: Scholar, poet, and translator, one of the most learned of the Bluestockings, famed for her Greek and her translation of Epictetus.
authors.biography: Born on 16 December 1717 at Deal in Kent, the daughter of the Reverend Nicholas Carter, a clergyman, she displayed an early aptitude for languages and largely educated herself in Greek and other tongues. She published poems in Gentleman's Magazine and other collections and moved in learned and Bluestocking circles, corresponding widely with Elizabeth Montagu. Her major work, a translation of the discourses of Epictetus, was published in 1758 and earned her high regard among scholars. She never married and continued literary work in later life. She died on 19 February 1806.
authors.profile: A classicist and writer whose translation of Epictetus and whose learned essays and poems made her a byword for female scholarship, and whose correspondence is a key document of Bluestocking culture.
authors.style: Learned, precise, and unadorned prose; measured, didactic verse; and a scholarly, self-effacing manner suited to translation, essay, and letter.
authors.concerns: Learning and the intellectual life of women; Stoic philosophy and virtue; religion and morality; and friendship and correspondence as a form of sociable culture.
authors.significance: One of the most accomplished of the eighteenth-century Bluestockings, celebrated as a female scholar of Greek and a moral writer, whose life expanded the accepted scope of women's learning.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is well recorded; the specific claim that she bore the name 'Cassandra' as a formal periodical or correspondence persona was not firmly verified here and is therefore not asserted.
sources: Freedom's Journal (New York, 1827-1829): Digitised Run, Chronicling America

authors.name: Elizabeth Hamilton
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish and Scottish; the anti-philosophical novel and educational writing of the 1790s
authors.identity: Novelist and educational writer; the sharpest woman satirist of rational philosophy applied to domestic life
authors.biography: She was born in the north of Ireland in the middle years of the century, of a Scottish family settled there, and was left early dependent on her own abilities; she spent much of her life in Scotland and in the north of England, supporting herself and her household by writing. Her first book, a satire in the form of translated letters from an Indian envoy observing England, appeared in 1796 and was an immediate success, establishing her name in the Edinburgh and London reviews. The following years brought the great anti-philosophical novel of a family ruined by a system-maker, published in 1800 and much the most effective of the conservative answers to the fashion for speculative fiction. She then turned to education, publishing a long series of letters on the principles of teaching children which was widely used and reissued, together with tales and tracts on the conduct and instruction of young people and a work on the preferences and prejudices of nations. Her later writings mixed educational theory with political and religious argument, and she corresponded with the reviewers and moralists of the day. She died in 1816, leaving a body of fiction and educational prose which her nineteenth-century readers remembered chiefly as a defence of orthodoxy against the schools.
authors.profile: An epistolary oriental satire, a five-volume novel of philosophical delusion, an educational correspondence in several volumes, tales and tracts for young readers, and a work on national prejudice. Her fiction argues by exposure of consequences: an idea is placed in a household and observed until the household is undone. Her educational writing belongs to the Scottish tradition of instruction by development rather than by rote.
authors.style: A clear, argumentative and deliberately unimpassioned prose, strong on the reported dialogue of doctrinal talk and on the comic exposure of a speaker's inconsistency. Her satirical voice is more directly polemical than that of the contemporary English comedy of manners, and her educational writing is orderly, examples-driven and addressed to parents.
authors.concerns: The domestic consequences of speculative philosophy. The education and judgement of children and of young women. National prejudice, the character of nations and the British empire in India. Religious orthodoxy against infidelity. The duties and dependencies of household life.
authors.significance: Her novel of 1800 is the most effective single piece of fiction in the campaign against the philosophical schools and helped end the fashion it attacked; her educational letters were a standard work of the first decades of the century. She is now studied as a central figure of the conservative woman's novel and of writing on the British rule in India before the 1820s.
authors.uncertainty: The year and place of her birth are not securely documented, and the chronology of her residence in Scotland and the north of England, and of her family's circumstances, is known mainly from the prefaces and letters she published.

works.title: Translations of the Letters of a Hindoo Rajah

authors.name: Elizabeth Heyrick
authors.nationality: English; the Quaker plain-style remonstrance, the women's anti-slavery agitation of the Midlands, and British immediatism
authors.identity: Leicester banker's wife, plain-style Quaker and pamphleteer; the writer of the tract which broke the British movement's long gradualism and supplied the slogan and the logic of immediate emancipation.
authors.biography: Heyrick was born Elizabeth Coltman at Leicester on 4 December 1769, the daughter of John Coltman, a surgeon and apothecary of the town, and was educated in a family of dissenting and then Quaker connection. She married John Heyrick, a Leicester banker and businessman whose affairs miscarried, and after his death and the failure of the house she maintained herself and her daughters in the town by keeping a shop and by her writings, living a life of plain-living, careful dressing of the poor and strenuous correspondence. She joined the Society of Friends, and her Quaker habits of remonstrance, of the plain style and of personal testimony shaped everything she printed. She had long written against the slave trade and the colonies, sending tracts on the subject to Zachary Macaulay and to the friends of gradual measure, and in 1824 she threw a printed circular, Immediate, Not Gradual Abolition, upon the members of the London society, following it with an Apologia and with the arguments addressed to the conscience of the slave-holder and to the West India interest. The pamphlet was passed from hand to hand, reprinted, and made the turning-point of the agitation, furnishing the demand for unconditional and immediate emancipation which the new society of 1831 adopted and which the abolition act of 1833 carried. She was one of the first to urge the women's anti-slavery societies, the boycott of slave-grown sugar and the apprenticeship scheme's rejection, and she corresponded with American friends on the colonisation enterprise, denouncing the American Colonization Society in letters published after her death. She died at Leicester on 18 October 1831, within a few months of the foundation of the society which took her programme, and her posthumous volume of essays and letters on the colonies appeared in 1832.
authors.profile: Her writing is the short reform tract and the printed circular, argumentative, urgent and addressed to a named society or to the reader's conscience: the 1824 pamphlet states the case for the shortest, safest and most effectual means of getting rid of colonial slavery, and the Apologia of 1825 defends the principle against the gradualists of her own party. Her later letters on the colonisation system and her essays on the condition of the people, published in a volume after her death, extend the same method of plain appeal, arithmetic and moral demonstration. She wrote also on war and nonresistance, on the treatment of animals and on the education and dress of the labouring poor, in a literature of remonstrance rather than of system.
authors.style: The plain Quaker style of remonstrance: direct address, short declarative sentences, the pointed question, the enumeration of instances and the arithmetic of compensation turned against the claim it supports; an absence of ornament and of classical allusion, and a moral pressure carried by repetition and by the refusal of euphemism. The tone is neither petitioning nor declamatory but adjuring, and it is frequently startling because it will not concede the premises of its opponents.
authors.concerns: The sin of holding the enslaved and the impossibility of a just gradual measure; immediate emancipation without compensation to the holder; the duty of the consumer, and the boycott of the product of slave labour; the claims of women to take a public part in moral agitation; nonresistance, the cruelty of war and the treatment of animals and of the poor as one question of justice; the colonisation of free Black Americans as a scheme of expulsion rather than of liberation.
authors.significance: Her pamphlet is the pivot text of British immediatism, the document that shifted the agitations demand from apprenticeship and gradual measure to unconditional emancipation, and it directly shaped the programme of the society founded in 1831 and the argument over compensation before the legislation of 1833. She is also a founding figure of women's organised anti-slavery work in England, since her circulars and her example supplied the logic of the female societies and of the sugar boycott, and her colonisation letters carried into the American debate.
authors.uncertainty: Her birth and death dates are given in the parish and family records of Leicester but are omitted altogether, or printed wrongly, in many standard histories of the movement and in most nineteenth-century notices, and her place of birth is sometimes stated only as the town, sometimes as a village near it. The extent of her authorship of anonymous tracts and letters in the abolitionist press is uncertain, and the part she played in the founding of the Leicester ladies society and in the national immediate-abolition organisation of 1830-31 is known chiefly from the proceedings and the correspondence of those bodies.

works.title: Immediate, Not Gradual Abolition; or, An Inquiry into the Shortest, Safest and Most Effectual Means of Getting Rid of West Indian Slavery

authors.name: Elizabeth Montagu
authors.identity: Writer, critic, and hostess, the most prominent of the Bluestockings, long called the 'Queen of the Blues.'
authors.biography: Born Elizabeth Robinson on 2 October 1718 in Yorkshire, she was largely self-educated through the library of her family's York home and moved to London, where she married her cousin Edward Montagu. A central figure in literary society, she hosted salons that gathered writers and scholars and corresponded with Elizabeth Carter, Hannah More, and others. Her critical work An Essay on the Genius and Writings of Shakespeare (1769) defended Shakespeare against neoclassical objections. Her many letters remain a major source for the period. She died on 25 September 1800.
authors.profile: A critic, essayist, and letter-writer whose defense of Shakespeare and whose conduct of Bluestocking conversation made her a defining arbiter of mid-eighteenth-century literary taste and sociability.
authors.style: Vigorous, assertive critical prose; lively, witty, and discursive letters; a sociable, argumentative tone; and an emphasis on nature and original genius against rigid classical rule.
authors.concerns: Shakespeare and original genius versus neoclassical rules; women's education and intellectual society; taste, criticism, and the republic of letters; and friendship and reputation.
authors.significance: The presiding figure of the Bluestocking movement and an influential critic, whose salon and correspondence shaped literary culture and whose Essay helped to advance the reputation of Shakespeare.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is well documented; her year of birth was once given inaccurately in older sources, and the precise dating of some unpublished writings and of correspondence remains a matter of editorial work.

works.title: An Essay on the Learning and Genius of Shakespeare

sources: The Rights of All (New York, 1829): Digitised Run, Chronicling America

authors.name: Elizabeth Rowe
authors.identity: Poet and prose writer, known as the 'Heavenly Singer,' a leading woman writer of pious verse and moral fiction in the early eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born Elizabeth Singer on 11 September 1674 at Ilchester in Somerset, the daughter of a Nonconformist minister, she was educated at home and began writing verses and answering the Athenian Mercury's queries as a young woman. Her early poems appeared as Poems on Several Occasions, written by Philomela (1696). She later married the minister Thomas Rowe, after whose death she continued to write devotional and moral works, including the biblical poem The History of Joseph (1736). Posthumous collections of her letters and writings were published and widely read. She died on 11 February 1737.
authors.profile: A writer of religious, moral, and sentimental verse and prose whose pious tone and defense of female learning made her one of the most admired women authors of her day, read across the eighteenth century.
authors.style: Devotional and moralizing verse and prose; elevated, earnest diction; a plain, reflective Augustan manner; and an epistolary and meditative tone in her prose works.
authors.concerns: Piety and the virtuous life; female education and learning; friendship and moral duty; and the consolation and exemplarity of Scripture.
authors.significance: A highly esteemed woman writer whose posthumous reputation lasted well into the century, influencing ideals of pious womanly letters and serving as a model for later women writers.
authors.uncertainty: The outlines of her life are documented, though the composition and dating of some early poems and the extent of her early manuscript circulation are imperfectly recorded.
sources: Dictionary of Irish Biography: From the Earliest Times to the Year 2002 (9 volumes)

authors.name: Erasmus Darwin
authors.identity: Physician, inventor and didactic poet of the Midlands Enlightenment, who put Linnaean botany, the chemistry of the senses and the transmutation of organs into heroic verse.
authors.biography: Born at Elston in Nottinghamshire in 1731, the seventh child of a small landowner, he was educated at a school in the neighbouring town and at St John's College, Cambridge, where he won a reputation as a Latin poet, and completed his medical training in the north. He settled as a physician at Nottingham and then at Derby from the mid-1750s, and built one of the widest provincial practices in England, visiting patients over the counties about him. At Derby he became the friend and neighbour of the manufacturers, potters and natural philosophers who met in the Lunar Society, helped to found the Derby Philosophical Society in 1783, and occupied himself with canals, drainage and agricultural machinery. His poems made the new science readable: the first published part of his projected Botanic Garden, The Loves of the Plants, appeared in 1789 with elaborate prose notes, and its companion The Economy of Vegetation followed in 1791. His prose speculations on life, Zoonomia (volume one in 1794), and the poem The Temple of Nature (1803), belong to the years after the period covered here; both scandalised the pious and anticipated debates about the derivation of species. He died at Derby in April 1802, the grandfather of Charles Darwin.
authors.profile: The poet of the senses and of machinery, who wrote physiology, botany and agriculture as a single animated system of pleasure and use.
authors.style: Couplet didactic verse of florid energy, with personified plants, sexual metaphor and an appeal to the five senses; long explanatory prose notes; exuberant, sometimes overreaching imagery.
authors.concerns: The Linnaean sexual system and the culture of plants; the chemistry of sensation, irritation and the motions of living bodies; the improvement of agriculture, machinery and public health; the derivation and progress of organic life; the rights of reason against priestcraft.
authors.significance: He carried the scientific Enlightenment into English verse and into provincial industry, and his speculations on life made him one of the ancestors of evolutionary biology as well as the grandfather of its founder.
authors.uncertainty: His early education and medical qualifications are imperfectly recorded, and the chronology of the parts of the Botanic Garden is complicated by pirated and revised printings.

authors.name: Felicia Hemans
authors.birthplace: 118 Duke Street, Liverpool, in a family of Welsh descent; raised from about the age of seven at Gwrych near Abergele in Denbighshire
authors.nationality: English by birth and Welsh by upbringing and self-identification; the popular lyric, metrical romance and devotional verse of the later Romantic period, and the literary annual and gift-book public that made it
authors.identity: The most extensively read and reprinted woman poet of the nineteenth century in Britain and America, and the first to build a complete professional authorship on the lyric of domestic affection; a contributor of verse and prose to every leading magazine and annual of her day, and the settled authority for a whole repertoire of women's feeling.
authors.biography: Hemans was born at Liverpool on 25 September 1793, the daughter of George Browne, a merchant whose affairs failed at the turn of the century, and of a mother whose father had held a foreign consular appointment in the same city; when the girl was about seven the family removed to Gwrych, near Abergele in the Welsh north, and the scenery and the Welsh claims of her childhood stay visible throughout her work and in her own account of herself. She was educated largely at home, an avid and early reader with an unusual memory for verse, and by about 1808 she was contributing poems to a popular monthly magazine; her first collected volume, declaring domestic affection as the durable ground of happiness, appeared in 1812. In that year she married an army officer of Welsh birth, Captain Hemans, a Peninsular-war survivor several years her senior, and within the next few years she bore him a family of sons; about 1818 her husband quitted England for the continent and did not return, and from her twenties until her death she maintained herself and her children wholly by her pen. The following decades made her the leading female poet of the day: volumes of lyric and occasional verse, translations and imitations from the Romance languages, metrical tales, and in 1825 the ambitious Spenserian romance of a child preserved within a monastic retreat. Records of Woman of 1828, whose title names a design rather than a poem, consolidated her authority over the history of women's feeling and drew a substantial notice in the Edinburgh review; Songs of the Affections followed in 1830, gathering the shorter manner of her last decade. Her homes moved from Wales to the neighbourhood of Liverpool, where she rented in the later years, and finally to Dublin, in which city she had lived at an earlier period of her married life; her income came from the annuals and the magazines, and from an American market which reprinted her faster than any copyright could follow. Her health, never robust, gave way under overwork, anxiety about her sons and private grief, and she died at her lodging in Dublin on 16 May 1835, in her forty-second year, and was buried in the vault of the Dublin church near her house. The collected editions, one of them with a memoir prepared by a member of her family, and the interminable reprints in gift-books, schoolbooks, hymnals and recitation collections, kept her lines before the English-speaking world for the rest of the century; her dismissal by high modernist taste as merely sentimental, and her recovery by later scholarship on women's writing, are both part of her recorded history.
authors.profile: Her canon runs to many separate volumes and includes the lyric meditation and song, the short dramatic address in a historical or imaginary woman's voice, the metrical tale and romance, the devotional hymn and sacred poem, the topographical and national piece, and translations or imitations from Spanish and Italian sources; her prose is slight beside her verse, and a great deal of that verse was made to order for the annuals, often written to accompany a specified engraving. Her characteristic single poem builds upon one emblem, one farewell or one grave, and develops it as a meditation; the longer narrative poems of the middle years, of which The Forest Sanctuary is the example, are her attempt to be read as a moral poet of sustained design. Posthumous collections gathered what the market had demanded, and the arrangement of her volumes by length and tone rather than by plan is itself evidence of her relation to her publishers.
authors.style: A deliberately vocal and singable smoothness, in common and short iambic measure with marked refrains, adapted to recitation and to musical setting; the closed heroic couplet used where feeling is to settle into maxim; personification, apostrophe and the address to an absent or dead beloved; an emblematic method in which a token, a lamp, a bracelet or a bird carries the whole argument; historical and Romance colouring softened to a domestic and moral use; and a pathos concentrated on a single situation, which contemporaries found overpowering and later critics found repetitive.
authors.concerns: Affection tried by separation, bereavement and time, and its survival as the ground of identity; the destinies, claims and education of women, and the mind set against the lot allowed it; constancy, forbearance and jealousy recorded as history; Providence, gratitude and vocation in the poem of preservation; consolation and the hope of reunion after death; exile and homelessness; Catholic and legendary Romance matter subdued to a plainly Protestant devotional temper; national memory, Wales and the scenery of childhood.
authors.significance: She made the woman poet a mass-market professional figure, and the idiom of her affectionate and mourning lyric became the ordinary language of Victorian domestic and devotional culture, quoted, paraphrased and set to music without attribution for generations. Her career is the clearest record of the economics of the literary annual before it reached its full height, and of the transatlantic circulation that could support a British writer's income. The design of Records of Woman gave the century a durable subject and a set of transferable female personae, and the sequence of her reputation - enormous fame, modernist dismissal, and recovery by feminist scholarship from the late twentieth century - is now a standard case in the history of canon formation and of the gendering of literary value.
authors.uncertainty: Her birthplace and her national identity are given variously in the authorities: the register evidence places her birth in Duke Street, Liverpool, in September 1793, while a strong Welsh tradition, resting on her upbringing and on her own identification, has claimed her as Welsh, and older handbook accounts sometimes misdate the month of her birth. The christian name of the officer she married is given by most modern sources as Alfred, though some catalogue traditions style her by the other name; the date and terms of the separation, and the number and survival of her sons, rest largely on family and later testimony; the nature of the illness that killed her is variously described; and how much editorial control she exercised over the posthumous collections, and what share her family's memoir has in shaping the record of her life, cannot be determined.

works.title: Songs of the Affections, with Other Poems
The Domestic Affections, and Other Poems

authors.name: Felix of Crowland
authors.identity: hagiographer; monk
authors.biography: Monk and hagiographer of the first half of the eighth century, associated by later tradition with the monastery of Crowland in the Fens; he wrote at the request of King Ælfwald of East Anglia (r. c. 713–749).
authors.profile: Author of the Vita Sancti Guthlaci (c. 730–740), the Latin life of the Mercian hermit Guthlac of Crowland, which became the source of the Old English poems Guthlac A and B and of later vernacular lives.
authors.style: Clear, careful Latin prose modeled on Evagrius's Life of Antony and Sulpicius Severus's Life of Martin; vivid accounts of Guthlac's battles with demons in the fens.
authors.concerns: The eremitic ideal; spiritual warfare; the sanctity of the Anglo-Saxon royal and monastic world.
authors.significance: His Life is among the earliest Latin hagiography composed in England and the starting point of a long vernacular tradition devoted to Guthlac.
authors.uncertainty: Almost nothing known of his life; the Crowland association is late.
sources: The Riverside Chaucer, 3rd edition

authors.name: Fitz-Greene Halleck
authors.nationality: American; New England and New York Knickerbocker letters
authors.identity: Poet and periodical essayist, the most widely read American verse-writer of the 1820s and 1830s and a mentor to the younger New York authors
authors.biography: Fitz-Greene Halleck was born at Guilford, Connecticut, on 8 July 1790, the son of a farmer of old New England stock, and was named after a family friend. His formal education was fragmentary: he attended Yale College as a teenager without taking a degree, and then earned his living for years as a clerk, working in a Virginia counting house before settling in New York City about 1811. There his friendship with Joseph Rodman Drake became a literary partnership. In 1819 the two contributed the "Croaker Papers", a series of Addisonian essays and satires on New York society, to the New York Evening Post and the National Advertiser; Drake's death in 1820 left Halleck the surviving partner and, later, the devoted compiler of Drake's Poetical Works (1835) with a memoir. Halleck's verse spread quickly through anthologies and newspapers: the humorous narrative "Fanny" appeared anonymously in December 1819, and his first collected volume, Alnwick Castle, with Other Poems (1827), made him nationally famous and, for a generation, the canonical American poet of the schoolroom recitation. Commercial failure of that volume and a large family kept him in salaried work; from 1832 he served in New York as private secretary and adviser to the philanthropist John Jacob Astor, a post that also involved him in the Astor family's quarrels and in the slanders that dogged his later reputation. He returned to Guilford, where he died on 19 November 1867, honoured in his lifetime as the "American Byron" and as the patron of emerging writers such as Junius Henri Wilson and the young Herman Melville's circle.
authors.profile: Halleck wrote occasional, descriptive and satirical verse in a deliberately polished public style: lyric and meditative poems on the American landscape ("Columbia", "The Western Worlds", "Robin Day"), humorous character sketches in verse ("Fanny"), and elegies and odes on national subjects. His essays in the Croaker series are urban comedy of manners. He published little fiction and no drama; his prose work is chiefly the biographical memoir prefixed to Drake's poems and a body of letters.
authors.style: Diction is elevated but plain, modelled on eighteenth-century sententiousness rather than on Romantic experiment. Blank verse and the eight-line stanza of Burns dominate; the couplet of Pope and the periodical essay of Addison shape his satirical voice. His effects rest on antithesis, apostrophe to America and nature, prosodic regularity designed for recitation, and a pathos that is sentimental rather than psychological. The humorous pieces rely on colloquial New England and New York speech and brisk narrative pacing.
authors.concerns: National identity and the possibility of an American literature; the poet's economic dependence on business employment; friendship, loss and posthumous reputation; the moral influence of landscape and home; Whig and Jacksonian-adjacent politics of the era; the education of a popular reading public through anthologised verse.
authors.significance: Halleck helped make professional authorship a visible American ambition and was the first United States poet to be read continuously in Britain after Byron's vogue. The Croaker Papers gave New York its first native periodical-essay school; Alnwick Castle circulated American themes in British editions for decades; his memoir of Drake fixed the enduring image of the two Knickerbocker poets. Long a staple of nineteenth-century elocution and school readers, his eclipse in the twentieth century is itself a document of changing American taste.
authors.uncertainty: The brief given for this project stated a 1777 birth and an 1819 Alnwick Castle volume; both are incorrect against the sources checked, which give 8 July 1790 for his Guilford birth and 1827 for Alnwick Castle, with the 1819 date belonging to the Croaker Papers and the anonymous "Fanny". The precise identity of his pre-Astor clerkships, including the stage-boat "hire office" employment recorded in older memoirs, is inconsistently reported.

authors.name: Frances Burney
authors.identity: Novelist and diarist, creator of the comedy of manners in early women's fiction and a keen observer of eighteenth-century society.
authors.biography: Born on 13 June 1752 at King's Lynn in Norfolk, the daughter of the music historian Charles Burney, she was raised in literary and musical circles and began writing early. Her first novel, Evelina (1778), published anonymously, was a success, followed by The Wanderer's precursor Cecilia (1782). She served at court as a lady of the bedchamber to Queen Charlotte and, after marriage to the French exile Alexandre d'Arblay, lived partly in France. Her diaries and letters, spanning decades, are a major social document, and she continued to write fiction and drama. She died in Bath on 6 January 1840.
authors.profile: The inventor of a graceful comedy of female sensibility and manners in Evelina, a precursor to Austen, and a memoirist whose diaries record the society and literary world of her age with wit and precision.
authors.style: Witty, observed comedy of manners in her fiction; epistolary and third-person narration; an acute ear for social speech; and lively, detailed, self-aware journal and letter prose.
authors.concerns: Female sensibility and the navigation of society; reputation and the marriage market; the manners of the court and the town; the position of the writing woman; and class and identity.
authors.significance: A pioneering woman novelist of manners whose Evelina shaped the school of social realism and proto-feminist comedy, and whose diaries and letters are indispensable to the history of late-eighteenth-century society and letters.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is abundantly documented through her own journals; the chief editorial question concerns the dating, abridgment, and revision of her diaries rather than any biographical crux.

works.title: Cecilia; or, Memoirs of an Heiress
Evelina; or, A Young Lady's Introduction to the World

sources: Landor's Cleanness: A Study of Walter Savage Landor

authors.name: Francis Bacon
authors.identity: philosopher; essayist; statesman; lawyer
authors.biography: Born 22 January 1561 at York House, London; son of Sir Nicholas Bacon, Lord Keeper. Educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn, he rose under James I to Attorney General (1613), Lord Keeper (1617), Lord Chancellor (1618), and Viscount St Alban (1621), then fell in 1621 on charges of corruption, was fined and briefly imprisoned, and spent his last five years in philosophical retirement at Gorhambury. He died on 9 April 1626 of bronchitis contracted while stuffing a chicken with snow to test refrigeration.
authors.profile: The Essays (1597; enlarged 1612 and 1625), The Advancement of Learning (1605), Novum Organum (1620), the utopian New Atlantis (1626, published 1627), and the History of the Reign of King Henry VII (1622), together with a mass of legal, scientific, and political writings.
authors.style: Aphoristic compression, balanced antithesis, and the deliberate plainness of a mind committed to lucid exposition; his Essays made the form an English genre.
authors.concerns: The reform of learning; induction and the interpretation of nature; the uses of knowledge for power and charity; the conduct of public life.
authors.significance: The chief English spokesman of the new science and the maker of the English essay; his vision of organized inquiry shaped the Royal Society and the Enlightenment that followed.
authors.uncertainty: The circumstances of his fall are still debated by historians; the 'Baconian' claims about Shakespeare's works are rejected by scholarship.
sources: The Examiner

authors.name: Francis Beaumont
authors.identity: dramatist; poet
authors.biography: Born in 1584 to a prominent Leicestershire legal family; his brother was the poet Sir John Beaumont. He entered Broadgates Hall, Oxford, in 1597 and the Inner Temple in 1600, but the law gave way to the theatre. From about 1606 to 1613 he collaborated with John Fletcher in one of the most celebrated partnerships in literary history, living with him in Bankside 'in the same house and bed'. He married an heiress in 1613, retired to Kent, and died on 6 March 1616; he is buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: With Fletcher he wrote Philaster (c. 1609–10), The Maid's Tragedy (c. 1610–11), A King and No King (1611), and The Knight of the Burning Pestle (c. 1607), the brilliant mock-romance that failed on its first production; his unaided works include the verse epistle to Jonson and the poems in the 1618 collection.
authors.style: Wit, metrical suppleness, and a taste for burlesque and self-conscious theatricality; the Beaumont–Fletcher canon is noted for its tragicomic design and its courtly polish.
authors.concerns: The ethics of honour and friendship; the conventions of romance and their parody; the relation of the stage to its audience.
authors.significance: Half of the partnership whose plays dominated the stage for fifty years after Shakespeare's death; Beaumont–Fletcher tragicomedy defined the Caroline and Restoration taste that followed.
authors.uncertainty: The exact division of labour between Beaumont and Fletcher in each play is unknown and much debated.

works.title: The Knight of the Burning Pestle

sources: The Collected Letters of Samuel Taylor Coleridge (6 volumes)

authors.name: Francis Hutcheson
authors.nationality: Anglo-Irish moral philosopher of the Scottish Presbyterian tradition
authors.identity: Seceding minister and first professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow, who founded the moral-sense school and taught the generation that carried natural rights into the Atlantic revolutions.
authors.biography: Born at Saintfield in County Down in 1694 into a Scottish Presbyterian family, he studied at Glasgow and was licensed by the Associate or Seceding ministry, though he soon gave up preaching for teaching. He kept a school in Dublin, and in 1730 was appointed to the newly founded chair of moral philosophy at Glasgow, which he held until his death. His Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue (1725), with its defence of a disinterested moral sense against Mandeville, and his Essay on the Passions (1728) established a new science of approval. His System of Moral Philosophy was published after his death in 1755 from his manuscripts and lectures. He died in Dublin on 8 August 1746.
authors.profile: The systematizer of sentiment as a moral faculty, who located virtue in benevolence toward the greatest number rather than in self-interest or in reason alone.
authors.style: Textbook plainness with a preacher's warmth; definitions, divisions and a running argument with opponents; a vocabulary of sense, taste, benevolence and approval.
authors.concerns: Moral sense and disinterested benevolence; the happiness of the greatest number; the distinction of natural and moral good; the right of resistance and limited government; the senses and the relish of beauty.
authors.significance: He founded the sentimental and utilitarian strands of eighteenth-century ethics, taught the generation that framed American natural-rights politics, and made benevolence a central term of moral philosophy.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of his Dublin academy years is uncertain; his Irish and Ulster origins are documented but his university career was cut short by his early death.

works.title: A Short Introduction to Moral Philosophy
An Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, with Illustrations on the Moral Sense
An Inquiry Concerning Virtue or Merit
An Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue

authors.name: Francis Jeffrey
authors.nationality: Scottish; the Whig criticism of the Edinburgh Review and the Scottish legal and literary culture of the early nineteenth century
authors.identity: Advocate, critic and judge; the founder and long editor of the Edinburgh Review, the maker of the modern review article as an instrument of literary and political power, and the most feared English-language critic of the Romantic generation.
authors.biography: Jeffrey was born in Charles Street in Edinburgh on 23 October 1773, the son of a depute-keeper of the signet, and was educated at the Royal High School and at the University of Edinburgh, from which he was withdrawn at fourteen and sent to complete his studies at home in the classics. He studied law, was admitted to the Scottish bar in 1794, and passed the 1790s in a literary Edinburgh society in which the terrors of the French Revolution and the trials of the Scottish radicals had made liberal opinion cautious. With Sydney Smith, Horner and Brougham he projected a quarterly journal, and the Edinburgh Review began in October 1802 with his article on the peerage, which he wrote at once as a defence of the new undertaking and as a statement of its principles. He edited the journal to 1829, wrote the critical and review articles in enormous number, and practised at the English bar after 1815, taking silk in 1821. His reputation for severe and elegant judgement made him the arbiter of Romantic poetry: his treatment of Wordsworth, of Byron and of the Lake school established the review as a power in letters, and his name gave the enterprise the credibility that a Scotch and Whig quarterly needed in a loyal and Tory reading public. In 1830 he went to the bench as a lord of session and justiciary under the title Lord Jeffrey, from which office his death at London on 26 January 1850 relieved a career that had long been more legal than critical. His contributions to the later numbers of the Review were collected and reprinted, and his correspondence and the memoirs of his brother-in-law Lord Cockburn remain the chief record of the circle that founded the journal.
authors.profile: His literary form is the review article, and he practised it as a genre of its own: a discursive essay that reviews books as occasions for argument on constitution, finance, education, religion and taste, written in the first person plural of the journal and closing with an assessment of a nation's condition. His critical papers on the poets and novelists of the day, on the Scottish law schools and on the Whig historians, and his contributions on the French revolutionary and post-revolutionary writers, make up a continuous commentary on the literature of the first third of the century; his editorial and political articles on the peerage, on Catholic emancipation and on reform are documents of Whig argument.
authors.style: A polished, urban and deliberately moderate irony, in which severity of judgement is carried in the language of good-breeding; long circumstantial periods, understatement, the concession that precedes the demolition, and a marked use of the collective editorial voice. The prose is rhetorical rather than technical, and its effects depend on balance, on the well-placed aside, and on a self-conscious elegance which his opponents read as the arrogance of the critic.
authors.concerns: The authority of criticism and its relation to party and to patronage; the freedom of the press and of review against the quarterlies and the publishers; the Whig account of liberty, of the peerage and of reform; the taste and the standing of the new Romantic poetry, and the charge of egotism and of deliberate vulgarity brought against it; the place of Scottish letters within a British public; the relation of religion, education and political temper in a commercial society.
authors.significance: He made the Edinburgh Review the model of the literary-quarterly as a political institution and gave the review article its modern authority and its modern weapon, and for a generation English Romantic writing was read, priced and judged in relation to his verdicts. His editorship established the practice of the unsigned but personally identified critic, and his career from bar to bench is the central case of the union of letters and public office in nineteenth-century Britain. He also fixed the shape of the anti-Romantic reception, since the famous quarrel over the Lake poets began with his pages.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of individual unsigned articles in the early numbers of the Edinburgh Review is still in part a matter of inference from diary, correspondence and the ledgers of the journal, and the standard tables of attribution are not unanimous. His birth is given in some earlier biographical accounts at the family place of Argaty near Doune in Perthshire rather than in Edinburgh, though the Edinburgh parochial and school records support the city.

authors.name: Francis Quarles
authors.identity: Emblem-book poet and devotional writer; author of Emblems (1635), the most popular book of verse in seventeenth-century England, whose combination of picture, biblical motto, and moral verse made religious meditation accessible to a vast readership.
authors.biography: Born 1592 at Romford, Essex, educated at Christ's College, Cambridge and Lincoln's Inn. He held minor offices under the crown, served as cupbearer to the Princess Elizabeth (the 'Winter Queen') at Heidelberg, and wrote a series of biblical paraphrases and religious poems (Esther, Job Militant, Divine Poems, 1620s–30s). His Emblems (1635) and Hieroglyphikes of the Life of Man (1638) were phenomenally popular. A royalist, he wrote pamphlets during the Civil Wars and died in London on 8 September 1644.
authors.profile: The master of the English emblem, whose illustrated moral verses blended Protestant devotion, common proverb, and baroque imagery for an enormous popular audience.
authors.style: Emblem structure (picture, motto, epigram, verse); biblical paraphrase; a plain, proverbial, sometimes homely wit; and a mixture of learned allusion and popular appeal.
authors.concerns: Protestant devotion and moral instruction; the vanity of the world and the soul's pilgrimage; scripture and its paraphrase; and the edification of a lay readership.
authors.significance: Quarles's Emblems was arguably the bestselling English poem-book of the century and shaped popular religious imagination; though later critics (and Pope's 'the mob of gentlemen who wrote with ease') mocked him, his influence on Bunyan, the emblem tradition, and devotional culture was profound.
authors.uncertainty: Quarles's life is documented in outline; his enormous popularity was later eclipsed by critical contempt, and the attribution of some anonymous emblem verses is uncertain.
sources: Modern Chivalry: Containing the Adventures of Captain John Farrago, and Teague O'Regan, His Servant

authors.name: Fulke Greville, Lord Brooke
authors.identity: Courtier, statesman, and poet; Sidney's closest friend and biographer, and the most philosophically austere of the Elizabethan sonneteers.
authors.biography: Born 3 October 1554 into a Warwickshire gentry family; educated at Shrewsbury (with Sidney) and Jesus College, Cambridge. He served Elizabeth as treasurer of the navy and of war, and James I as chancellor of the Exchequer (1614–21), being created Baron Brooke in 1621. His poetry — Caelica, the treatises on monarchy and religion, and Mustapha and Alaham — circulated in manuscript in his lifetime; he was murdered on 30 September 1628 by a servant he had omitted from his will, and was buried in St Mary's, Warwick. His Life of the Renowned Sir Philip Sidney (printed 1652) is the classic memoir of the period.
authors.profile: A philosophical poet of power and dark inwardness whose verse dramas and treatises anatomize the corruptions of monarchy and the vanity of earthly desire; his Caelica turns the sonnet sequence into a meditation on the failure of worldly love and the turn to God.
authors.style: Dense, aphoristic, and abstract diction; Senecan sententiae; a Calvinist suspicion of the world expressed in sinewy couplets and dramatic choruses.
authors.concerns: The corruption of power and the duties of counsel; the vanity of human wishes; predestination and divine grace; the memory and meaning of Sidney's life and death.
authors.significance: The intellectual centre of the Sidney circle after Sidney's death; his poems and treatises form the most searching Elizabethan anatomy of politics and the soul outside Shakespeare and Donne.
authors.uncertainty: His works were printed posthumously (1633, 1652) and the dating of Caelica's composition is approximate (c. 1580s–1610s).
sources: The Poetical Works of Thomas Moore

authors.name: Gavin Douglas
authors.identity: poet; translator; bishop of Dunkeld
authors.biography: Born about 1474, third son of the Earl of Angus; educated at St Andrews and provost of St Giles, Edinburgh. His Palice of Honour (c. 1501) and the allegories King Hart and Conscience followed; his Eneados, the translation of Virgil's Aeneid completed on 22 July 1513, is the first complete rendering of the poem in any British language. Bishop of Dunkeld from 1515, he died in London of the plague in September 1522.
authors.profile: The last great poet of the Scottish Chaucerians and the first British translator of the Aeneid. The Palice of Honour is a courtly dream vision of dazzling learning; King Hart an allegory of the heart's court; and the Eneados — in vigorous Scots couplets, with a prologue to each book describing the Scottish seasons — ranks with Surrey's as one of the two great Tudor translations of Virgil.
authors.style: Aureate Chaucerians diction in the allegories; in the Eneados, a plain, energetic Scots that renders Virgil's gravitas in northern idiom; the seasonal prologues are the finest nature poetry in Scots.
authors.concerns: The translation of classical epic into the vernacular; honour, fame, and the education of princes; the defence of poetry against its detractors.
authors.significance: Author of the first complete Aeneid in any form of English and the summit of the Scottish Chaucerians; his Eneados passed the classical inheritance to the northern Renaissance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the dating of King Hart is editorial.
themes: Rebellion, guilt, and the outcast hero
sources: The Complete Works of William Hazlitt (21 volumes)

authors.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
authors.identity: poet; courtier; civil servant; diplomat
authors.biography: Son of a London vintner; page in the household of the Countess of Ulster, soldier in France (captured 1359–60), and thereafter a royal servant — esquire of the king's household, controller of customs and of the wool subsidy, justice of the peace for Kent, clerk of the king's works, and member of parliament. His diplomatic missions took him to France and Italy (1372–73, 1378), where he encountered the poetry of Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio. He died on 25 October 1400 and was buried in Westminster Abbey, founding what became Poets' Corner.
authors.profile: Author of the Book of the Duchess (c. 1368–72), the House of Fame (c. 1378–80), the Parliament of Fowls (c. 1380–82), Troilus and Criseyde (c. 1382–86), the Legend of Good Women (c. 1386–88), the Treatise on the Astrolabe (1391), and the unfinished Canterbury Tales (c. 1387–1400), together with Boece, the Romaunt of the Rose (disputed), and the short poems.
authors.style: The perfection of the decasyllabic line and rhyme royal in English; mastery of frame narrative, ironic personae, and dramatic monologue; the synthesis of French courtly forms, Italian narrative, and native English comedy into a new poetic language.
authors.concerns: Love in its courtly, comic, and philosophical dimensions; the ethics of storytelling; fortune, free will, and providence; the estates of society in pilgrimage and satire.
authors.significance: Universally regarded as the father of English poetry: he fixed the London dialect as the literary standard, naturalized the decasyllabic line, and created a body of work — above all the Canterbury Tales and Troilus — of the first European rank.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the canon and chronology of some minor works are debated; the Romaunt of the Rose attribution is disputed.
themes: Reformation faith and the authority of scripture
sources: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton

authors.name: Geoffrey of Monmouth
authors.identity: historian; chronicler; bishop
authors.biography: Of Welsh or Breton descent and educated probably at Oxford, he spent most of his career as a canon of St George's chapel, Oxford; in 1152 he was consecrated bishop of St Asaph in Wales, a see he may never have visited, and he died c. 1155. His Historia Regum Britanniae made him one of the most influential writers of the European Middle Ages.
authors.profile: Author of the Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136–38), the Prophetiae Merlini (c. 1135), and the Vita Merlini (c. 1150), which together created the Matter of Britain.
authors.style: Elegant, deliberately classicizing Latin prose; the fabrication of a continuous British history from Trojan Brutus to the Saxon conquest; the vivid set-pieces of Arthur's reign and the prophecies of Merlin.
authors.concerns: The antiquity and dignity of the British (Welsh) past; the legitimation of Norman rule through Trojan descent; prophecy as political instrument.
authors.significance: The Historia created the Arthurian legend as a European literary possession and shaped British historiography for four centuries; without it there is no Brut, no Grail cycle, no Malory.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the sources of his 'British book' remain the central problem of Arthurian scholarship.
sources: The Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson (21 volumes)

authors.name: George Berkeley
authors.identity: Irish-born philosopher and Church of Ireland bishop whose immaterialism, theory of vision and Alciphron make him one of the two or three metaphysicians whom the century could not ignore.
authors.biography: Born at Thomastown in County Kilkenny in 1685, he went to Trinity College Dublin, where he became a fellow and a tutor, and in 1707 took his degree. In a single brilliant period of young manhood he published the Essay towards a New Theory of Vision (1709), the Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710) and the Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous (1713), which reduced sensible qualities to ideas in a mind and made the existence of matter depend on being perceived. Ordained in the Church of Ireland and appointed dean of Derry in 1724, he married Esther Vanhomrigh in 1723 and spent a decade in America trying to fund a college in Bermuda. The failure of that scheme ended his hopes of a transatlantic church; from 1734 he lived as bishop of Cloyne, where he wrote Siris (1744) on tar-water as a remedy, and he died at Oxford on 14 January 1753.
authors.profile: A philosopher of perception and language who argued that mind, not matter, is the ground of the visible world, and who wrote his hardest metaphysics as lively dialogue.
authors.style: Sparse, precise, almost aphoristic argument; numbered propositions and sharp objection-and-reply; a sceptic's ingenuity in the service of a pastor's conclusions.
authors.concerns: The nature of ideas, perception and the external world; abstraction and the misuse of signs in language; the absolute space and time of the Newtonians; the reality of spirit and active agency; religious language and the minute philosopher.
authors.significance: He carried early modern empiricism to its sceptical limit, anticipated later work on vision and on language, and supplied Hume, Reid and the whole tradition of idealism with the problems they inherited.
authors.uncertainty: The details of the Bermuda college scheme and of his American years survive unevenly, and his motives for the enterprise are still argued.

works.title: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge
An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision
Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous

authors.name: George Cavendish
authors.identity: biographer; gentleman usher to Cardinal Wolsey
authors.biography: Born in Suffolk about 1497; entered the service of Cardinal Wolsey as gentleman usher about 1522 and attended him through his fall and death in 1530. Retiring to Suffolk, he wrote The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey between about 1554 and 1558 from his intimate knowledge of the Cardinal's household. The work circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1641. He died about 1562.
authors.profile: Author, with Roper's Life of More, of the twin masterpiece of Tudor biography. The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey — the rise, magnificence, and fall of the butcher's son who ruled England — is the classic of Tudor life-writing: eyewitness, circumstantial, and tragic, with the great scenes (Wolsey's fall at Cawood, his death at Leicester) rendered as drama. Shakespeare drew on it for Henry VIII.
authors.style: Ample, plain narrative prose; the usher's exact memory for gesture, word, and scene; tragic structure imposed on recent history.
authors.concerns: The fall of princes as moral example; the memory of Wolsey against his detractors; loyalty to the great house he had served.
authors.significance: With Roper, founded English secular biography; his portrait of Wolsey — and through it of Henry VIII's court — shaped the English historical imagination from Shakespeare onward.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.

works.title: The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey

sources: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus: The 1818 Text

authors.name: George Chapman
authors.identity: poet; dramatist; translator of Homer
authors.biography: Born near Hitchin about 1559; studied at Oxford but left without a degree, then served in the Low Countries. He began writing for the theatre around 1594 and completed Marlowe's Hero and Leander in 1598. His great labour was the translation of Homer: the Iliad (1598–1611) and Odyssey (1614–15), which Keats would celebrate in the sonnet 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer'. He died in London on 12 May 1634.
authors.profile: Plays include The Blind Beggar of Alexandria (1596), the two-part Bussy D'Ambois (c. 1604), The Conspiracy and Tragedy of Charles, Duke of Byron (1608), Eastward Ho (1605, with Jonson and Marston, which landed its authors in prison for satire of the Scots), and The Widow's Tears (c. 1605); his verse includes the philosophical poem The Shadow of Night (1594) and Ovid's Banquet of Sense (1595).
authors.style: A dense, oracular style — packed conceits, stoic sententiae, a 'dark' obscurity his contemporaries mocked but which carries his tragedies of heroic aspiration.
authors.concerns: Stoic virtue; the heroic individual against the court; Neoplatonic theories of inspiration and learning.
authors.significance: His Homer fixed the English reading of the epics for two centuries, and his tragedies of Bussy D'Ambois and Byron are the fullest English expression of the heroic, Senecan mode.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; his claims of gentility and a university degree are unproven.
themes: Industry, enclosure, and the changed countryside
sources: The Collected Writings of Charles Brockden Brown

authors.name: George Etherege
authors.identity: Restoration wit and dramatist; the originator of the comedy of manners with The Comical Revenge (1664), She Would if She Could (1668), and especially The Man of Mode (1676), which created the ideal rake-hero Dorimant and set the pattern for Wycherley and Congreve.
authors.biography: Born c. 1635–36, probably in Berkshire; educated at Trinity Hall, Cambridge and the Middle Temple, with time in France.
