His first play, The Comical Revenge (1664), mixed verse and prose; She Would if She Could (1668) was less successful; but The Man of Mode (1676), with its rake Dorimant (thought to caricature Rochester) and the witty Harriet, was the triumph of the age. Etherege led a dissolute court life, was knighted (1679), and served as diplomat at Regensburg (1685–89), where he famously neglected business for pleasure. He returned after the Revolution and died c. 1691–92, possibly in Paris.
authors.profile: The elegant, careless founder of the comedy of manners, whose plays established the prose of witty gallantry, the rake-hero, and the social world of the town that the genre would perfect.
authors.style: Sparkling prose repartee; the rake and the witty heroine; intrigue and sexual politics; a light, ironic tone; and a deliberate 'careless' elegance.
authors.concerns: Wit, gallantry, and libertinism; courtship and marriage as social negotiation; fashion, affectation, and the town; and the amoral play of desire.
authors.significance: The Man of Mode is the first great comedy of manners and defined its conventions; Etherege's rake-hero and social comedy directly shaped Wycherley, Congreve, and the whole tradition of English wit comedy.
authors.uncertainty: Etherege's birth and death dates are approximate, his diplomatic correspondence survives but his private life is thinly documented, and he has been confused with a namesake.

works.title: The Comical Revenge; or, Love in a Tub
The Man of Mode; or, Sir Fopling Flutter

sources: The Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, Volume I: Poems

authors.name: George Farquhar
authors.identity: Anglo-Irish Restoration-early Augustan dramatist; author of the lively, humane comedies The Constant Couple (1699), The Inconstant (1702), and his masterpiece The Beaux' Stratagem (1707), which infused the comedy of manners with warmth, Irish vigour, and social observation.
authors.biography: Born c. 1677–78 at Londonderry, educated at Trinity College, Dublin. He became an actor (stabbing a fellow-player in a stage duel), then a playwright with Love and a Bottle (1698) and The Constant Couple (1699), whose Sir Harry Wildair was hugely popular. He served briefly as an army officer and recruiting agent (the material for The Recruiting Officer, 1706). Despite success he died poor and young on 29 April 1707, weeks after The Beaux' Stratagem. His plays' gaiety and humanity mark the transition from Restoration wit to the gentler comedy of the eighteenth century.
authors.profile: The comic dramatist who softened Restoration intrigue with warmth, humour, and social realism, creating breezy, well-constructed comedies of love, roguery, and provincial life.
authors.style: Lively, humorous prose; brisk plotting; roguish, charming heroes; Irish and provincial colour; and a humane, genial comic tone.
authors.concerns: Love, courtship, and roguery; money and marriage; the world of the provinces and the recruiting office; and the good humour of human frailty.
authors.significance: The Beaux' Stratagem and The Recruiting Officer are among the most enduring comedies of the period, continuously performed and admired for their vitality; Farquhar bridged Restoration and Augustan comedy and influenced Goldsmith and Sheridan.
authors.uncertainty: Farquhar's birth year is uncertain (1677 or 1678) and details of his life are thin; the anecdotes of his stage-duel and poverty are traditional.

works.title: The Constant Couple; or, A Trip to the Jubilee

sources: Travels in New England and New York (4 volumes)

authors.name: George Gascoigne
authors.identity: poet; dramatist; soldier; courtier
authors.biography: Born about 1539 at Cardington, Bedfordshire, into a landed family; educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. He sat in Parliament, served in the Low Countries campaigns, and was captured by the Spanish at Leiden in 1574. He died on 7 October 1577 at Stamford, having returned home to revise his works.
authors.profile: A Hundred Sundry Flowers (1573) — including the prose fiction The Adventures of Master F.J. — The Posies (1575), the satiric mirror poem The Steel Glass (1576), the plays Supposes (1566, from Ariosto) and Jocasta (1566, from Euripides via Italian), the hunting manual The Noble Art of Venery (1575), and the first English treatise on verse, Certain Notes of Instruction (1575).
authors.style: Experimentation across every available form — prose fiction, satire, drama, sonnet, blank verse — with a confessional, self-advertising wit.
authors.concerns: The reform of English versification; the moral uses of satire; the politics of courtly advancement.
authors.significance: The first great professional man of letters in English — innovator of the sonnet, the essay-like miscellany, and the English blank-verse drama from Italian models.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the autobiographical readings of Master F.J. remain contested.
sources: The Early Poems of John Clare, 1804-1822 (2 volumes)

authors.name: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
authors.nationality: English; British peer, poet of the Romantic period, and a central figure of the European Romantic movement
authors.identity: Poet above all: writer of narrative and lyric verse, of metrical romances and tales, of verse satire in couplet and ottava rima, and of tragic poems designed for the reader rather than the playhouse; also the first modern literary celebrity, whose life was read as commentary on his work.
authors.biography: Born 22 January 1788 in London, son of Captain 'Mad Jack' Byron (d. 1791) and Catherine Gordon of Aberdeen, he spent part of his childhood in Aberdeen before returning to England. In 1798 he inherited the barony and the embarrassed estate of Newstead Abbey, Nottinghamshire, from his great-uncle the fifth baron. He was at Harrow from 1801, where he wrote and circulated a great deal of school verse, and matriculated at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1805, withdrawing in 1808 without a degree. 'Hours of Idleness' was privately printed in 1807, and the hostile Edinburgh Review notice of its enlarged London issue drew from him the reply-satire 'English Bards and Scotch Reviewers' (1809). A journey to Portugal, Spain, Albania, and Greece with his companion John Cam Hobhouse (1809-11) supplied the matter of 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage', Cantos I-II, whose appearance in 1812 made his fame in a single season; he sat in the House of Lords, making his first speech against the Frame Bill in 1812. His marriage in January 1815 to Anneabella Milbanke ended in separation in January 1816 amid public scandal, and within months he left England for good, passing by Geneva and Lucerne to Venice (1816-19), Ravenna (1819-21), and Pisa and Genoa (1821-3), where he projected the monthly 'The Liberal' with Leigh Hunt and Percy Bysshe Shelley. In July 1823 he sailed to Greece for the war of independence, fell ill at Missolonghi in December, and died there on 19 April 1824 after repeated bloodletting; burial in Westminster Abbey being refused, he was laid in the Byron vault at Hucknall, Nottinghamshire.
authors.profile: His canon falls into three recognizable groups: the early satire and the romance tales in verse of 1813-16; the meditative-narrative 'Childe Harold' with the lyrics and short poems of the Italian exile; and the late work in which ottava rima and the tragic poem carry his most serious argument ('Beppo', 'Don Juan', 'Manfred', 'Cain', 'Heaven and Earth', the Venetian plays). He wrote no fiction of his own, no systematic criticism, and only prefatory and controversial prose, so his literary thought is best read in the poems, their advertisements and prefaces, and his letters and journals. His late verse tales and dramas in Greece and Italy were also the period's most spectacular commercial successes, and his letters and journals, edited after his death by Thomas Moore, became a foundational Romantic document.
authors.style: Two contrasting manners in one voice: a high, sonorous descriptive rhetoric (Alpine, Adriatic, and Trojan scenery, apostrophe, the proud solitary speaker) and an urban, colloquial, laughing irony learned from Pope and from Italian ottava rima. He rhymes with ease and often with designed anticlimax, interrupts his own narrative to address the reader or publisher, and blends autobiographical confession with romance plot. In the dramas he aimed at a plain, passion-driven declamation and famously refused the 'poetry of description' for the stage.
authors.concerns: Liberty against tyranny, political and domestic; the guilt and self-fashioning of the outlawed aristocrat; scepticism toward revealed religion and sympathy with Milton's rebellious intellect; fame measured against its machinery of publishers and reviewers; sexual love, constancy, and betrayal; the rise and fall of states and dynasties; the capacity of irony to speak truth in a corrupt public culture.
authors.significance: He made the Romantic poet a European public person: 'Byron mania' swept British fashion, imitative verse tales, and the stage, while his example governed the second generation (Shelley's 'Adonais' and 'Epipsychidion' answer him), Pushkin and Lermontov, Mickiewicz, and the French Romantics. 'Don Juan' is the last great English poem in the Augustan satirical line and one of the first modern irony-driven long poems; his tragic poems and the Greek cause for which he died made him a liberal icon deep into the nineteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: The precise grounds of the 1816 separation and the rumours of incest with his half-sister Augusta Leigh were suppressed in the family settlement and remain a matter of disputed interpretation; the paternity of his daughter Allegra was doubted in contemporary gossip and cannot be settled from the surviving evidence.

works.title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto the Fourth
Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto the Third
Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Cantos I and II

authors.name: George Herbert
authors.identity: Anglican priest and devotional poet; author of The Temple, the greatest work of English religious lyric, whose intricate forms enact the struggles and consolations of the soul in God's service.
authors.biography: Born 1593 at Montgomery into the distinguished Herbert family, brother of Lord Herbert of Cherbury; educated at Westminster and Trinity College, Cambridge (Fellow 1609, MA 1616), where he became Public Orator (1620). Patronized by James I, he hoped for court preferment, but on the king's death turned to the church, taking holy orders (1626) and the poor country rectory of Bemerton near Salisbury (1630). He served as a devoted parish priest ('the holy Mr Herbert') until his death from consumption on 1 March 1633, aged 39. The Temple was published posthumously in 1633 by his friend Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding.
authors.profile: The poet of the parish and the conscience, who made the plain country church the setting for a demanding, intimate, and formally inventive poetry of devotion, doubt, and surrender.
authors.style: Metaphysical wit turned to religious use; shaped and pattern poems ('Easter Wings', 'The Altar'); emblematic simplicity; dramatic colloquy with God; puns, scriptural allusion, and a musical variety of stanza forms.
authors.concerns: The soul's relation to God; obedience, affliction, and consolation; the priesthood and pastoral care; the conflict between worldly ambition and spiritual calling; the discipline of prayer.
authors.significance: The Temple is the supreme achievement of English devotional verse, influencing Vaughan, Crashaw, Coleridge, and the twentieth-century religious poets; Herbert's marriage of metaphysical wit to Anglican humility made him the model of the priest-poet.
authors.uncertainty: Herbert's life is documented by Izaak Walton's Life (1670); the dating of individual poems in The Temple is largely inferential.
sources: A Common Heritage: Noah Webster's Blue-Back Speller

authors.name: George Peele
authors.identity: dramatist; poet; pageant-maker
authors.biography: Baptized 25 July 1556; son of the clerk of Christ's Hospital. Educated at Christ's Hospital and Broadgates Hall (later Pembroke College), Oxford, where he took BA (1577) and MA (1579). He came to London in the early 1580s, wrote for the public stage and the City, and dissipated his talents and health; he was buried on 9 November 1596.
authors.profile: His pastoral-mythological court play The Arraignment of Paris (c. 1581–84) pleased Elizabeth; The Old Wives' Tale (c. 1591–93) is a folkloric comedy of enchantment; The Battle of Alcazar (c. 1588–89) and Edward I (c. 1590) are chronicle plays; he also wrote Lord Mayor's pageants and the biblical tragedy David and Bethsabe (c. 1594).
authors.style: Lyrical sweetness, Ovidian ornament, and a gift for pageantry and stage spectacle; the famous 'garden speech' in the anonymous play sometimes assigned to him shows his fluent, decorative blank verse.
authors.concerns: Court compliment and civic ceremony; classical myth reworked for English audiences.
authors.significance: A pioneer of the history play and of polished stage verse; traditionally credited with a share in Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus.
authors.uncertainty: The extent of his share in Titus Andronicus remains debated; his canon is the most unstable among the Wits.
themes: The annual, the keepsake, and the gift-book economy
sources: James Fenimore Cooper: The Leatherstocking Tales (2 volumes, Library of America)

authors.name: George Whitefield
authors.identity: Calvinistic Methodist preacher of the Great Awakening, the first true celebrity of the Atlantic religious world, whose open-air sermons and journals moved crowds on two continents.
authors.biography: Born at Gloucester in 1714, the son of an innkeeper who died while he was a child, he worked as a servant at the town grammar school and went up to Oxford in 1735 as a humble self-paying student, where he joined the small religious society and experienced the conversion he never ceased to describe. Ordained in the Church of England, he began to preach in the fields about Bristol in 1739 and in London's Moorfields, since the pulpits were closed to him, and crossed the Atlantic repeatedly, preaching through the colonies in 1739-40 and again on great touring circuits. His Calvinism separated him from John Wesley in the early 1740s, and he devoted much of his later energy to fundraising for the Georgia orphan house he called Bethesda and for the preaching houses his converts built. His journals and his Narrative of God's Dealings with Him (1740) made his inner life public property, and Benjamin Franklin, who printed them, left the most admired contemporary account of his command of crowds. He died at Newburyport in Massachusetts in September 1770 and was buried there beneath the pulpit he had used.
authors.profile: A declaimer of irresistible voice and posture who turned conversion narrative and printed publicity into an engine of revival.
authors.style: Vocal, theatrical, extempore sermon style preserved imperfectly in print; vivid personal narrative; plain scriptural address with an actor's gesture; prolific printed circulars and journals.
authors.concerns: Election, new birth and the immediate call of the Spirit; the ministry of the word out of doors; the unity of the revival across the denominations; the religious education and charity of converts, and the problem of slavery in the colonies he loved.
authors.significance: He created the model of the transatlantic evangelist and gave the Great Awakening its public form, influencing American preaching, revivalism and the culture of religious celebrity.
authors.uncertainty: His early years at Oxford and the chronology of his ordination are recorded unevenly, and his journals were edited by friends and by himself.

works.title: A Short Account of God's Dealings with the Reverend Mr. George Whitefield

authors.name: Gerald of Wales
authors.identity: chronicler; topographer; churchman
authors.biography: Grandson of Nest, the Welsh princess, and of a Norman baron; educated at Paris, he became archdeacon of Brecon and courtier of Henry II, accompanying Prince John to Ireland in 1185 and preaching the crusade through Wales with Archbishop Baldwin in 1188. He twice sought the see of St Davids and was twice refused; retired to Lincoln, he died c. 1223, still writing.
authors.profile: Author of the Topographia Hibernica (1188), Expugnatio Hibernica (1189), Itinerarium Cambriae (1191), Descriptio Cambriae (1194), and the autobiographical De Rebus a Se Gestis, among much else.
authors.style: Vivid, gossipy, self-promoting Latin; ethnography seasoned with marvel and prejudice; the love of a good story over strict accuracy; an unflagging attention to his own career.
authors.concerns: The Welsh church's independence; the conquest and description of Ireland; the character and customs of the Welsh and Irish peoples.
authors.significance: The Itinerarium and Descriptio are the classic medieval accounts of Wales, and the Expugnatio the principal narrative of the English conquest of Ireland; his works are foundational for both national historiographies.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his own writings, though copious, are self-serving.
themes: Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
sources: The Poems of Robert Burns, 3 volumes

authors.name: Gerrard Winstanley
authors.identity: Digger (True Leveller) leader and radical pamphleteer; his tracts — The New Law of Righteousness (1649) and The Law of Freedom in a Platform (1652) — argued for communal cultivation of the land and an agrarian communism grounded in reason and the inner light.
authors.biography: Born c. 1609 at Wigan, Lancashire, son of a merchant; he worked as a cloth merchant in London before being bankrupted by the Civil Wars. In 1649 he led the 'Diggers' in communally cultivating St George's Hill and other commons in Surrey, publishing pamphlets defending the action against landlords and the state. Suppressed by local opposition and the authorities, the movement collapsed by 1650. His fullest statement, The Law of Freedom in a Platform (1652), dedicated to Cromwell, set out a communist commonwealth governed by reason and law. Little is known of his later life; he may have become a Quaker and died c. 1676.
authors.profile: The visionary radical whose prophetic, plain-style pamphlets argued that true freedom requires common ownership of the earth and the abolition of wage labour, grounding communism in reason, scripture, and the 'inner light'.
authors.style: Urgent, prophetic, plain-style pamphlet prose; scriptural and rationalist argument; dialogue and declaration; and a direct, popular address.
authors.concerns: Common ownership and agrarian communism; the rights of the poor and the commons; reason, the inner light, and true religion; the critique of private property, law, and clergy; and popular sovereignty.
authors.significance: Winstanley is the foremost theorist of the Diggers and an early exponent of agrarian socialism and communism; his tracts are foundational documents of English radicalism and have been central to Marxist and libertarian-socialist readings of the English Revolution.
authors.uncertainty: Winstanley's life after 1652 is very poorly documented; his birth and death dates are approximate and his later Quakerism is conjectural.

works.title: The Law of Freedom in a Platform; or, True Magistracy Restored

sources: Thomas Chalmers and the Godly Commonwealth in Scotland

authors.name: Gilbert Burnet
authors.identity: Scottish-born Anglican bishop, historian, and memoirist; author of the History of the Reformation of the Church of England (1679–1715) and the posthumous History of His Own Time, whose vivid, opinionated accounts are primary sources for the politics and religion of the era.
authors.biography: Born 2 September 1643 in Edinburgh, educated at the University of Aberdeen and in Holland; ordained in the Scottish church, he travelled and preached widely, becoming a moderate latitudinarian and a chaplain to Charles II. He fell from favour, went into exile after the accession of James II (1685), and supported William of Orange, becoming Bishop of Salisbury (1689) and a leading Whig churchman. His History of the Reformation (in parts, 1679–1715) won him fame (and a doctorate from Oxford); his memoir, History of His Own Time, was published posthumously (1724–34). He had attended the deathbed of the Earl of Rochester (1680), which he recorded. He died on 17 March 1715.
authors.profile: The busy, partisan, and readable bishop-historian whose histories and memoir give a vivid, if biased, first-hand account of the Reformation, the Restoration, and the Revolution.
authors.style: Lively, discursive, opinionated historical prose; memoir and eyewitness reportage; a plain, energetic style; and polemical digression.
authors.concerns: Church history and the Reformation; the politics and religion of Restoration and Revolution England; latitudinarianism and toleration; and the defence of the Protestant succession.
authors.significance: Burnet's History of the Reformation and History of His Own Time are indispensable (if partisan) sources for the period; his memoirs of Rochester's conversion and of the Whig churchmen illuminate the religious politics of the age.
authors.uncertainty: Burnet's life is well documented through his own writings; his histories are avowedly partisan and require critical use, and the History of His Own Time was edited and published posthumously.

works.title: Bishop Burnet's History of His Own Time
The History of the Reformation of the Church of England

sources: Selected Prose of John Hamilton Reynolds

authors.name: Gilbert White
authors.identity: Selborne naturalist and clergyman whose Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne (1789), assembled from letters to correspondents, founded the English observation of the living world.
authors.biography: Born at Selborne in 1720 into a family of Hampshire clergymen and college men, he was educated at Winchester and at Oriel College, Oxford, took holy orders, and returned to the parish of his birth, of which he held the living. He never married and spent his income on his books and collections. For decades he kept registers of the weather and of the dates of flowering, bird arrival, nesting and hibernation, and he tested his questions by experiment, on the torpor of tortoises and bats, on the flight of swifts and swallows, on the insect world and on the habits of the field and the garden. His letters on these matters went to the Royal Society and to correspondents, above all to Daines Barrington and to the naturalist Thomas Pennant, whose questions and his own made the printed book. His book appeared at last in 1789, cast as a correspondence, and its two parts were quickly followed by a third volume of further letters. He died at Selborne in 1793.
authors.profile: The quiet observer of a single parish, whose method of numbered dates, experiment and plain statement made small facts carry weight.
authors.style: Epistolary, unhurried and exact prose; dated field entries and the language of experiment; a naturalist's precision joined to a countryman's affection and gentle humour.
authors.concerns: The seasonal movements and instincts of birds and beasts; the limits of the systems of the schools; local history, antiquities and the surface of an English parish; the evidence of patient observation against the authority of books.
authors.significance: His book became the most beloved of English natural histories and a model for field biology, phenology and the whole later literature of the countryside.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of his observations and the relation between the manuscript journals and the printed letters have been re-examined by later editors.

works.title: The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne, in the County of Hampshire

authors.name: Gildas
authors.identity: cleric; historian; polemicist
authors.biography: British cleric of the sixth century, traditionally associated with the north of Britain and later with Brittany; revered as 'Gildas the Wise' by the Anglo-Saxons, who drew on his work.
authors.profile: Author of De excidio et conquestu Britanniae (c. 540s), a fierce sermon-polemic against the sins of the British kings and clergy which opens with the only near-contemporary narrative of the Saxon settlement of Britain, including the battle of Mount Badon.
authors.style: Rhetorical Latin saturated with biblical allusion, in the tradition of the Old Testament prophets; denunciatory and elegiac by turns.
authors.concerns: Divine punishment and national sin; the ruin of Britain as a moral catastrophe.
authors.significance: The principal source for post-Roman Britain; heavily used by Bede, who made Gildas's providential scheme the backbone of early English history.
authors.uncertainty: Dates and career largely conjectural, reconstructed from later Welsh and Breton tradition and internal evidence.
sources: A Book of Middle English, 4th edition

authors.name: Granville Sharp
authors.identity: London merchant's apprentice turned jurist-divine, the first great legal strategist of British abolition, who made the condition of enslaved people in England a question of common law.
authors.biography: Born at Durham in 1735 into a large clerical family, he was apprenticed to a London draper at fifteen and, with the help of a legacy, kept himself free for study, mastering law, divinity, biblical languages, music and a remarkable range of authors. A beaten black servant, Jonathan Strong, whom his brother's hospital had discharged, drew him in the mid-1760s into the question of whether a man could be held as property in England, and he answered it by research and by litigation. He gave counsel and money to the test cases of the following years, and the cause of James Somerset, argued before Lord Mansfield in 1772, was pressed forward by his advice and reporting. He printed legal essays and letters maintaining that slavery had no footing in English law, corresponded with governors and colonists, promoted schemes for settling freed people in Africa, and was among the founders of the committee of 1787 for the abolition of the trade, in which Ottobah Cugoano lived and worked in his household. He wrote also on prophecy, on translation and on the affairs of the church, and died unmarried at Fulham on 6 July 1813, buried in the churchyard there.
authors.profile: A lay lawyer of immense industry who read texts, digested opinions and turned scholarship into an instrument for the deliverance of individuals.
authors.style: Dense, citational and dogged prose; folio-long footnotes of law, scripture and the fathers; argument built from authority pressed to a single conclusion; a devout and combative directness.
authors.concerns: The legal status of persons on English soil; the sin and the policy of the slave trade; the rights of the individual against magistrates and merchants; the interpretation of prophecy and of the languages of the Bible; the duty of public charity.
authors.significance: He made the Somerset judgment possible and founded the legal and organisational base of British abolition, standing beside Wilberforce and Equiano as an architect of the movement that ended the trade.
authors.uncertainty: The exact contribution of his advisers and of Cugoano to his papers and cases is difficult to separate, and his chronology of the earlier suits is debated.

works.title: A Representation of the Injustice and Dangerous Tendency of Tolerating Slavery; or, of Admitting the Least Claim of Private Property in the Persons of Men, in England

authors.name: Hannah Cowley
authors.identity: Dramatist and poet, one of the most successful female playwrights of the late eighteenth century.
authors.biography: Born Hannah Parkhouse on 14 March 1743 at Tiverton in Devon, the daughter of a bookseller, she married Thomas Cowley and moved to London, where she supported herself by writing. Her poems circulated widely under the name Anna Matilda. Beginning in the later 1770s she became the most performed woman dramatist of her generation, writing comedies and sentimental drama for Drury Lane and Covent Garden, of which the best known is The Belle's Stratagem, with later successes including Which Is the Wife?. She retired from the theatre in the 1780s, returned to Devon after her husband's death, and continued to publish verse. She died at Tiverton on 11 March 1809.
authors.profile: A writer of sentimental and witty comedy and verse who became the most frequently performed woman dramatist of her era, her plays championing female constancy and cleverness within the comic and sentimental modes.
authors.style: Neat comic dialogue in the manner of sentimental comedy; well-made plots of courtship and testing; virtuous, articulate heroines; and conventional, polished eighteenth-century verse.
authors.concerns: Female constancy and virtue; wit and the testing of character in marriage; reputation and delicacy; and the social position of women within sentimental comedy.
authors.significance: The most successful female playwright of the 1770s and 1780s in London, whose comedies held the repertory and whose career is a landmark in the history of women's professional authorship in the theatre.
authors.uncertainty: Her year of birth has sometimes been given as 1742 or 1743, and her death date was long misreported in some older sources; modern scholarship, following the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, fixes it as 1809.
sources: Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland, with a Short Memoir of the Author by His Son

authors.name: Hannah More
authors.identity: Writer, dramatist, and philanthropist, a Bluestocking and Evangelical who became one of the most influential moral and religious authors of her age.
authors.biography: Born on 2 February 1745 at Fishponds near Bristol, the daughter of a schoolmaster, she was educated partly at her father's schools and moved in Bath and London literary circles, where she was befriended by Joshua Reynolds and the Montagus and associated with the Bluestockings. She wrote plays and poems, including the popular tragedy Percy (1777), and conduct works. In later life she turned decisively to Evangelical and moral writing and philanthropy, becoming associated with abolition and popular religious tract work. She died at Clifton on 7 September 1833.
authors.profile: A versatile author of drama, conduct literature, and religious and moral writing who bridged the fashionable literary world of the 1770s and the Evangelical reform culture of the following decades.
authors.style: Polished sentimental drama and conduct prose in her early career; then a plain, persuasive, urgent moral and religious manner aimed at wide popular readership.
authors.concerns: Female education and conduct; religion, evangelism, and social duty; the abolition of slavery and moral reform; taste versus piety; and the responsibilities of the educated to the poor.
authors.significance: One of the most prolific and widely read women writers of her era, whose career traces the shift from Augustan literary society to Evangelical reform, and whose later tract work reshaped popular religious literature.
authors.uncertainty: Her life is extensively documented; some details of her early education and the precise dating of individual plays and tracts vary across sources.

works.title: Essays on Various Subjects, in Prose and Verse
Strictures on the Modern System of Female Education

sources: The Complete Works of Walter Savage Landor (16 volumes)

authors.name: Hartley Coleridge
authors.birthplace: On the Bristol side of the Severn at Kingsdown, Gloucestershire, according to modern authorities, though the Dictionary of National Biography gave Clevedon, Somerset; eldest child of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Sara Fricker Coleridge
authors.nationality: English; the Lakeland and Wordsworth-Coleridge circle of British Romanticism inherited by the second generation, and the province of the magazine essay, of old-dramatist scholarship and of northern biographical compilation
authors.identity: A poet of sonnets and short occasional lyrics, an essayist and biographer of the early English dramatists, and a schoolmaster who never held a steady post; the most celebrated instance in English letters of brilliant promise unfulfilled, and by inheritance and by friendship the closest surviving link between Wordsworth, his father and the Victorian man of letters.
authors.biography: Hartley Coleridge was born on 19 September 1796, the eldest child of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Sara Fricker Coleridge, and was named after David Hartley, the associationist philosopher of his father's early allegiance; he is the infant addressed in 'Frost at Midnight'. His childhood was passed mainly in the Lake District, where he was schooled at Ambleside and, after the Wordsworth family settled at Rydal Mount, enjoyed the unusual privilege of the use of Wordsworth's library; about the age of eight he and his brother Derwent invented the imaginary kingdom of Ejuxria, whose affairs he continued in later years to record and to regret. He went up to Oxford in 1815 and was elected to a fellowship at Oriel College, which he lost within a few years on the ground of intemperance; that loss determined the outline of the rest of his life. Two years in London as a journalistic writer were followed by a return to Ambleside, where an attempt to keep pupils was abandoned about 1830 and he was thrown upon the kindness of friends and of the publisher F. E. Bingley, under whose eye he compiled the Biographia Borealis of 1833 and printed the small volume of Poems of the same year. The Worthies of Yorkshire and Lancashire followed in 1836, and his scholarly work on the old drama issued in the memoirs and editing of Massinger and Ford of the late 1830s and about 1840, while he wrote at intervals for Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine and the London Magazine and in 1837 and 1838 helped to manage Sedbergh grammar school. Dependency on alcohol, embarrassment of money and a constitutional indolence defeated every plan of steady work; he died of bronchitis on 6 January 1849 and was buried in Grasmere churchyard within sight of Wordsworth's grave. His brother Derwent Coleridge edited his Poems and his Essays and Marginalia, four volumes in all, in 1851, and his letters, an indispensable record of the Coleridgean household, were edited in the twentieth century, as modern reassessment has established the sonnets and the dramatic criticism as a considerable minor body of work.
authors.profile: His verse is small in bulk and almost all occasional: the Poems of 1833, enlarged in the two volumes of 1851, consist of sonnets on friendship, on the Lakeland landscape, on books and on his own defeat, together with ballad-measure pieces, translations and fragments such as the Prometheus; the longer narrative and dramatic projects remained unfinished. His prose divides between biographical compilation, in the Biographia Borealis of 1833 and the Worthies of Yorkshire and Lancashire of 1836, and dramatic scholarship and criticism, in the memoirs and editing of Massinger and Ford and in the magazine essays which the posthumous Essays and Marginalia of 1851 gathered; his correspondence, published as Letters, is a third and perhaps the most valuable part of his work.
authors.style: A compressed, plain and deliberately unimpassioned manner of verse, in which the sonnet of ten or twelve lines carries the argument in a single sentence of argument and close with a sententious turn; a fondness for the abstract noun, for balance and antithesis, and for the colloquial idiom of cultivated speech, with an occasional Jonsonian point and an occasional Wordsworthian simplicity of diction. His prose is digressive, allusive and conversational, made of quotations, marginal notes and catalogues of names, and its virtue is rather its range of reading and its good sense than any sustained architecture.
authors.concerns: Associationist psychology and the formation of character, inherited from Hartley and argued over with his father; providence, prayer and the morality of a clergyman's family in an age of doubt; the claims of genius against indolence and appetite, and the ethics of self-knowledge; the dignity and the national use of the old English drama; the worthies tradition of regional biography, in which local fame is gathered as evidence of a nation's intellectual history; and the obligations of a son to a father's texts, which made him editor, witness and apologist.
authors.significance: He stands in the history of Romanticism as the living proof of its anxieties of inheritance, the child of the Lyrical Ballads generation whose failure was memorialised by his own father and by Wordsworth and afterwards read as the paradigm of unfulfilled promise. His essays and his edition of the old dramatists kept the Jacobean and Caroline stage before a Victorian public, his northern worthies volumes made regional biography an instrument of literary history, and his letters and conversations are a primary source for the Coleridge family and for Wordsworth at Rydal, giving him a durable, if subordinate, place in the documentation of the period.
authors.uncertainty: Reference works long antedating the modern calendars give his birth as 1791 and the Dictionary of National Biography gives Clevedon where later scholars give Kingsdown, while the year in which he held and lost the Oriel fellowship is reported variously as about 1819, 1820 and 1826; the long narrative poem 'Davysses', sometimes entered among his works in library catalogues, could not be traced in the printed bibliographies and should be treated as unverified.

authors.name: Henry Fielding
authors.identity: English novelist, dramatist, and magistrate, creator of the comic epic in prose and one of the most influential of the early English novelists.
authors.biography: Born on 22 April 1707 in Somerset into a gentry family, he was educated at Eton and studied briefly abroad and at law in London. He began as a playwright, producing political and theatrical satires in the early 1730s, and after the licensing censorship of 1737 turned to prose fiction. He published Joseph Andrews (1742), the burlesque Shamela in response to Pamela, the masterpiece The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling (1749), and Amelia (1751). He also served as a Westminster and Bow Street magistrate and wrote on law and social reform. He died in Lisbon on 27 June 1754.
authors.profile: A novelist who defined the picaresque comic epic in prose, combining broad social panorama, irony, and authorial commentary, and who responded critically to the sentimental and epistolary modes of his contemporaries.
authors.style: Omniscient, intrusive narration with discursive chapter prefaces; irony and good-humoured satire; a picaresque, episodic plot; robust and colloquial diction; and careful structural balancing of character and design.
authors.concerns: Human nature and motive; hypocrisy versus goodness; class and the social order; justice, law, and authority; and the education of the individual within society.
authors.significance: A central founder of the English novel, whose theoretical prefaces and Tom Jones set the terms for realist narrative, and whose dramatic and legal careers left a major imprint on eighteenth-century culture and on the reform of the theatre and the law.
authors.uncertainty: The outlines of Fielding's life are well documented, though some dates of early writings and details of his authorship of particular pamphlets remain matters of scholarly attribution.

works.title: A Journal of a Voyage to Lisbon
An Enquiry into the Causes of the Late Increase of Robbers
The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling
The Tragedy of Tragedies; or, The Life and Death of Tom Thumb the Great

sources: Early American Drama (Penguin Classics)

authors.name: Henry Home, Lord Kames
authors.identity: Judge of the Court of Session and polymath of Edinburgh, the patron and publisher of the Scottish Enlightenment, whose Sketches of the History of Man tried to write the whole of society as natural history.
authors.biography: Born about 1696 at Kames House in Berwickshire and educated largely at home, he became an advocate and built a leading practice at the Scottish bar. He rose to the bench of the Court of Session in 1752 as Lord Kames and sat there until his death, taking a prominent part in the political and cultural life of Edinburgh. His Historical Law-Tracts (1732) read early law as evidence of early society; his Essays on the Principles of Morality and Natural Religion (1751), which grounded morals in instinct rather than in revelation, were censured by the church courts. Elements of Criticism (1762) analysed the passions and the effects of the beautiful and the sublime, and the four-volume Sketches of the History of Man (1774) surveyed races, languages, government and agriculture as a single natural history. He encouraged and published the younger writers around him, and died in Edinburgh on 27 December 1782.
authors.profile: A lawyer-naturalist of society who treated customs, laws and tastes as specimens to be classified rather than as doctrines to be defended.
authors.style: Miscellaneous, encyclopaedic and aphoristic; numbered propositions, cases and historical instances; a judge's love of definition combined with an amateur's appetite for generalisation.
authors.concerns: The historical development of law and property; the instincts underlying morality and religion; the physiology of the passions and the analysis of aesthetic effect; the comparative history of races and of the stages of society.
authors.significance: He gave the Scottish Enlightenment its institutional encouragement and its model of conjectural history, and his criticism of the passions shaped the aesthetic theory of his century.
authors.uncertainty: The year of his birth is only approximately fixed, and his authorship of some tracts and his role in the patronage of others are difficult to separate.

works.title: Sketches of the History of Mankind

authors.name: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
authors.identity: nobleman; soldier; poet; translator
authors.biography: Born at Hunsdon about 1516, eldest son of the Duke of Norfolk; brought up with the Duke of Richmond (Henry VIII's illegitimate son) and educated in the humanist manner. A soldier and courtier — he served in the French wars of the 1540s and was wounded at the siege of Montreuil — he was arrested in December 1546 on largely fabricated charges of quartering the royal arms, and beheaded on Tower Hill on 19 January 1547, the last victim of Henry VIII's reign. His poems circulated in manuscript and were printed in Tottel's Miscellany (1557); his translation of Aeneid II and IV was published in 1554 and 1557.
authors.profile: The refiner of the English sonnet: he gave the form the rhyme scheme (abab cdcd efef gg) that became the 'English' or Shakespearean sonnet, and his smooth decasyllabic line pointed the way to the Elizabethan style. His translation of Virgil's Aeneid, Books II and IV — the first English blank verse — created the unrhymed iambic pentameter that Marlowe and Shakespeare made the language of English drama.
authors.style: Regular, musical decasyllables; elegant management of the Petrarchan materials; a grave, chivalric sensibility; in the Aeneid translation, a new plainness of diction answering Virgil's.
authors.concerns: Nobility and honour under tyranny; love, constancy, and the ruin of Troy as an image of English court politics; the translation of classical epic into English verse.
authors.significance: Inventor (with Wyatt) of the English sonnet form and of blank verse — the two technical foundations of Elizabethan poetry and drama; his life and death dramatized the fate of the old nobility under the Tudors.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year given as 1516 or 1517 in the records; some lyrics attributed to him in Tottel are of uncertain authorship.
themes: Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense

works.title: Aeneid, Books II and IV (Surrey's translation)

sources: The Works of Mary Wollstonecraft, 7 volumes

authors.name: Henry Medwall
authors.identity: playwright; chaplain to Cardinal Morton
authors.biography: Born about 1462; educated at Eton and King's College, Cambridge, and employed as chaplain and notary to Cardinal John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury. His Fulgens and Lucrece, played at Morton's household at Lambeth about 1497, is the earliest surviving secular English play, printed by John Rastell about 1512–16. He died about 1502.
authors.profile: Author of the first secular English drama. Fulgens and Lucrece dramatizes a humanist debate — whether nobility lies in birth or in virtue — as a Roman comedy of courtship, complete with a subplot in which two servants, A and B, compete for the audience's employment; his Nature is a full-scale morality play of man's fall and amendment. Both were played in Morton's great hall, the seedbed of the Tudor interlude.
authors.style: Debate framed as drama; the interweaving of serious argument and servant comedy; the morality convention put to secular and humanist use.
authors.concerns: True nobility and the claims of virtue over birth; the reform of manners; the education of the great household through play.
authors.significance: Bridging medieval morality and humanist comedy, Fulgens and Lucrece begins the secular English stage tradition that runs to the Elizabethan theatre.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate.
themes: Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
sources: The Complete Poetical Works of Lord Byron (7 volumes)

authors.name: Henry More
authors.identity: The leading Cambridge Platonist; a poet-philosopher who defended a rational, spiritual Christianity against materialism and atheism, and who corresponded with Descartes and Anne Conway while writing philosophical and mystical treatises in verse and prose.
authors.biography: Born 12 October 1614 at Grantham, educated at Christ's College, Cambridge, where he became a Fellow (1639) and remained for life, declining preferment. He corresponded with Descartes (1648–49) and was the philosophical mentor of Anne Conway. His works include the Philosophical Poems (1647, including the 'Psychozoia' and 'Antipsychopannychia'), An Antidote Against Atheism (1653), Enthusiasmus Triumphatus (1656), and the Enchiridion Metaphysicum (1671), which argued against Cartesian mechanism and for the reality of spirit, extension, and the 'boniform faculty'. He defended belief in spirits and apparitions and died on 1 September 1687.
authors.profile: The Platonic philosopher-theologian who sought to reconcile reason, religion, and the new philosophy, opposing Hobbesian and Cartesian materialism with a spiritual, emanative metaphysics expressed in both verse and prose.
authors.style: Philosophical verse (Spenserian stanzas) and prose; Platonic and mystical argument; a serene, speculative, sometimes visionary style; and polemic against atheism and 'enthusiasm'.
authors.concerns: The existence and nature of spirit and God; reason and religion; the critique of materialism and of religious 'enthusiasm'; the immortality of the soul; and the relation of Descartes to Platonism.
authors.significance: More was the central figure of Cambridge Platonism, influencing Conway, Glanvill, and later Latitudinarian and Romantic thought; his correspondence with Descartes is a key document of seventeenth-century philosophy.
authors.uncertainty: More's life is documented through his works, correspondence, and a contemporary biography; his philosophical positions evolved and some attributions of influence are interpretive.

works.title: Enthusiasmus Triumphatus; or, A Brief Account of the Nature, Causes, Kinds, and Cure of Enthusiasm

sources: The Life and Letters of Lord Macaulay (2 volumes)

authors.name: Henry of Huntingdon
authors.identity: historian; churchman; poet
authors.biography: Son of a Norman clerk and an English mother, and archdeacon of Huntingdon from c. 1110, he was commissioned by Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, to write a history of England; he travelled with the court, visited Rome (1139), and continued revising his Historia Anglorum until his death c. 1157.
authors.profile: Author of the Historia Anglorum (first version 1129, continued to 1154), the most widely read English chronicle of the twelfth century, and of verse epigrams including the satirical De contemptu mundi.
authors.style: Clear, vivid narrative with a moralist's relish for battles, plagues, and the falls of great men; the ubi sunt meditation and the contemptus mundi theme; patriotic celebration of the English past.
authors.concerns: The providential shape of English history; the transience of earthly power; the continuity of the English people through conquest.
authors.significance: The Historia Anglorum is a principal source for the Norman and Angevin periods and the classic expression of twelfth-century historical moralism.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; details of his career rest on his own book.
themes: Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
sources: The Poems of Thomas Gray, William Collins and Oliver Goldsmith

authors.name: Henry Vaughan
authors.identity: Anglo-Welsh physician, royalist, and metaphysical devotional poet; author of Silex Scintillans, whose mystical nature-poetry and longing for eternity distinguish him among Herbert's followers.
authors.biography: Born 1621 (baptised 16 April) at Newton St Bridget, twin brother of the alchemist Thomas Vaughan; educated privately and at Jesus College, Oxford, then trained in medicine. A royalist during the Civil Wars, he retired to his native Breconshire, practised medicine, and published Olor Iscanus (1651) and Silex Scintillans (1650, expanded 1655), influenced by Herbert. He also wrote prose devotional and hermetic works (The Mount of Olives, 1652) and translations of Nolle and Boece. He lived quietly through the Restoration at Newton and Alway, dying 23 April 1695.
authors.profile: The 'Silurist' whose verse seeks God through the natural world and childhood memory, marked by a mystic's sense of eternity glimpsed behind the material world ('intimations' later echoed by Wordsworth).
authors.style: Luminous nature imagery; a mystical, visionary quality; Herbert's influence tempered by a wilder, more personal imagination; emblematic structure; and Welsh landscape as the locus of spiritual experience.
authors.concerns: Eternity and the soul's pre-existence; nature as the book of God; childhood innocence; royalism and religious loyalty; hermetic and alchemical philosophy; death and resurrection.
authors.significance: Long neglected, Vaughan was recovered in the nineteenth century and prized by the Romantics and T. S. Eliot as a visionary metaphysical poet; 'The Retreat' and 'The World' are among the great English mystical lyrics.
authors.uncertainty: Much of Vaughan's life is obscure; his exact birth date and many details of his royalist activities and medical practice rest on inference and local records.
sources: A New-England Tale (Penguin Classics)

authors.name: Hester Chapone
authors.identity: Moralist and essayist, a Bluestocking associated writer best known for her conduct work Letters on the Improvement of the Mind.
authors.biography: Born Hester Mulso on 27 October 1727 at Twywell in Northamptonshire, the daughter of a clergyman, she was educated largely at home and became known in learned society, corresponding with Elizabeth Carter and moving in Bluestocking circles before marrying the lawyer John Chapone. Her Letters on the Improvement of the Mind (1773), addressed to young women, went through many editions, and she published further conduct and moral works, including Miscellanies in Verse and Prose (1775). She continued to write for the education of women into later life. She died at Hampton in 1801.
authors.profile: A writer of conduct and educational literature whose Letters shaped thinking about women's rational and moral improvement, making her one of the most widely read female didactic authors of her period.
authors.style: Clear, warm, rational didactic prose in the letter form; an accessible, moralizing tone; and an easy blend of religious seriousness with practical advice.
authors.concerns: The rational and moral education of women; conduct, religion, and duty; taste and the improvement of the mind; and friendship among the learned.
authors.significance: An important conduct writer and Bluestocking figure whose Letters on the Improvement of the Mind circulated widely and influenced ideas about female education in the late eighteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: Her broad life is documented; details of some minor writings and the precise chronology of her correspondence remain matters of editorial reconstruction.

works.title: Letters on the Improvement of the Mind

sources: The Struggles of John Brown Russwurm: The Life and Writings of a Pan-Africanist Pioneer, 1799-1851

authors.name: Horace Walpole
authors.identity: English man of letters, antiquary, and politician, creator of the first Gothic novel and one of the most celebrated letter-writers of the century.
authors.biography: Born on 24 September 1717 in London, the son of Sir Robert Walpole, the first Prime Minister, he was educated at Eton and Cambridge and entered Parliament as a Whig. A lifelong man of letters, he built the Gothic villa at Strawberry Hill and wrote on art and antiquities. He published the novel The Castle of Otranto (1764), at first presented as a translation, and later the tragedy The Mysterious Mother (1768). His extensive letters, on society, politics, and literature, are a major historical source. He died on 2 March 1797.
authors.profile: The author of the founding Gothic romance and a prolific writer of tales, plays, antiquarian histories, and correspondence, whose work fused taste, antiquarianism, and a cultivated horror of the medieval past.
authors.style: Elegant, urbane, witty prose; deliberate archaism and romance convention in Otranto; a gossipy, polished epistolary style; and an antiquarian's eye for the picturesque and the marvelous.
authors.concerns: The revival of interest in the Middle Ages and Gothic taste; ancestry, prophecy, and the supernatural; the interplay of romance and reason; sociability and political gossip; and the aesthetics of terror and the picturesque.
authors.significance: The originator of the Gothic novel with The Castle of Otranto and a defining figure of eighteenth-century taste, antiquarianism, and letter-writing, whose influence shaped Gothic fiction and the Gothic Revival.
authors.uncertainty: His life is well documented; the chief uncertainty concerns the framing and initial pseudonymous or 'translated' presentation of The Castle of Otranto rather than his biography.

works.title: A Description of the Villa of Mr. Horace Walpole
Historic Doubts on the Life and Reign of King Richard the Third

sources: The Life and Writings of Hugh Henry Brackenridge

authors.name: Hugh Blair
authors.identity: Scottish Presbyterian minister, rhetorician, and literary critic of the Scottish Enlightenment, the first professor of Rhetoric and Belles Lettres at Edinburgh.
authors.biography: Blair was born in Edinburgh, studied divinity there, and was ordained to a ministry in the Church of Scotland, rising to the leading Edinburgh congregations and becoming a prominent figure of the Moderate interest. He lectured on rhetoric and belles lettres and was appointed to the newly created chair of Rhetoric and Belles Lettres at the University of Edinburgh in 1762. His best-known work, Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres, was published in 1783, drawing on decades of teaching and becoming a standard text on taste, style, and criticism. He wrote influential sermons and critical essays, and his endorsements figured in the literary debates over Ossian and the ballad. He died in 1800.
authors.profile: A critic, rhetorician, and preacher who codified Enlightenment ideas of taste, style, and eloquence, defending polite letters, sensible religion, and the analysis of beautiful writing.
authors.style: A clear, measured, authoritative critical prose of definition, example, and classification of styles; a temperate homiletic voice in the sermons; and an emphasis on perspicuity, harmony, and decorum.
authors.concerns: The nature of taste, genius, and the sublime; rhetoric and the principles of eloquence; the history and criticism of style and genres; and the alliance of politeness with reasonable religion and morality.
authors.significance: A defining voice of the Moderate wing of the Scottish Enlightenment; his Lectures standardised rhetorical and literary-critical teaching for a century, and his judgments shaped taste in the Ossian and ballad debates.

works.title: Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres

authors.name: Hugh Henry Brackenridge
authors.nationality: American, born in Scotland; the letters of revolutionary Philadelphia and of the western Pennsylvania frontier, the first American writer of that interior
authors.identity: Novelist, poet, playwright, orator, lawyer, judge, schoolmaster and founder of colleges; the inventor of the American picaresque comic novel of politics and settlement, and the most considerable man of letters of the Pennsylvania west before the 1830s.
authors.biography: Brackenridge was born on the Kintyre peninsula near Campbeltown in Argyllshire, in the year 1748, of a Scottish family in straitened circumstances, and was carried by his parents to York County in Pennsylvania in the fifth year of his life. He grew up on the edge of the settlement, largely self-taught, herding cattle and picking up such learning as the country afforded until a neighbour recognized his capacity and helped him to books; he entered the college at Princeton, graduated in 1770, and gave himself afterwards to teaching, keeping a classical school and preparing young men for the college. He served the Revolutionary army as a chaplain, and about the same time began to publish verse, including a poem on the death of the general before Quebec which was recited and reprinted through the war years and gave him his first name in America. After the peace he removed to Philadelphia, read and practised law, wrote for the stage and the press, and about 1779 fixed himself in the western country, at first near Hannastown and afterwards about Pittsburgh, where the frontier supplied the society he satirized. There he founded an academy in 1787, the institution which became the university of the city, gave aid to the first newspaper of the west, and practised his profession before the county courts; he sat in the convention which framed the state constitution of the 1790s, and was made a judge of the courts of the western district. In the excise trouble of 1794 he rode with the militia, and tried at once to suppress the insurrection and to restrain the measures which had provoked it, and was reviled by the partisans of both sides; the controversy cost him his political standing and much of his professional business. His comic romance of Captain Farrago and his ragged Irish servant was put out in parts beginning in 1792, continued at intervals, and reissued in a revised and completed form shortly before his death; he wrote also a tragedy on the point of honour, sermons, orations and a quantity of controversial pamphlet matter, and he projected histories and plans of western education which he did not finish. His last years were clouded by the death of an elder son through intemperance, by his own increasing dependence on drink, by removed poverty and by quarrels with the neighbours among whom he had made his fortune, and he died on 25 June 1816 at Carlisle, whither he was journeying, and was buried there in the churchyard.
authors.profile: His central work is the long comic romance, begun in numbers and completed after more than twenty years, which follows a captain of militia and his servant through the elections, militias, speculations, sects and law circuits of the western republic, and which is the first American fiction to make popular politics and office-seeking its sustained subject. He wrote verse of the college and war occasion, including the funeral poem on the general at Quebec, a tragedy of honour and the duel, sermons and orations on education and on the diffusion of knowledge, and pamphlets on the insurrection and on the affairs of the west. Education was his lifelong scheme: the academy, the college, the school and the public library were for him the instruments by which a frontier country might be made a community, and his fiction is continuously an argument about learning, pretension and the uses of books.
authors.style: A robust and colloquially various prose, moving between the high-flown rhetoric of the speculators and politicians, the blunt sense of the servant and the ironied narration of the author, with proverbs, misquotations, Latin school phrases and the speech of the courts and the back settlements all set against one another; an episodic and unhurried picaresque structure, tolerant of digressions and of essays within the story; and in the verse and the orations a fluent eighteenth-century diction of couplet and periodic sentence.
authors.concerns: The dangers and the promise of a republic without ranks, which has only invented new ones; office-seeking, demagogy and the pretensions of the wilder democracy; education and learning as the only safe foundation of western settlement; sectarian zeal and enthusiasm measured against reason and decency; the law, the militia and the conduct of the frontier; the claims of chivalry, honour and duelling in a country of common men.
authors.significance: He is the founder of the literature of the American interior and the author of the first American comic novel of politics, a book which carries the eighteenth-century picaresque across the mountains and applies it to the elections, speculations and sects of the new settlements. His academy became a university and his fiction is the beginning of a native tradition of the frontier satirists; the modern recovery of his work has placed him at the head of the line which runs to the comic storytellers of the Mississippi, and his career documents the intellectual history of the American west in the generation after the Revolution.
authors.uncertainty: The year and place of his Scottish birth are given in the earliest memorials with small variations, the interval and conditions of his emigration rest on family narrative, and the chronology of the several parts and revised issues of his comic romance, and of the authorship of some pamphlets printed in his name, is still imperfectly settled.

authors.name: Hugh Kelly
authors.identity: Dramatist and poet, an Irish-born writer of sentimental comedy who became a prominent figure and government supporter on the London stage.
authors.biography: Born around 1739 in Ireland (his birthplace is given variously as Dublin or Killarney), the son of a publican, he worked as a staymaker and studied law before turning to the stage and journalism in London. Employed as a writer for government, he produced the successful sentimental comedy The False Delicacy (1768), followed by A Word to the Wise (1770), and wrote verse including the poem Thespis (1766). His rivalry with Oliver Goldsmith generated well-known theatrical and literary quarrels. He died in London on 3 February 1777.
authors.profile: A writer of sentimental and moral comedy and occasional verse, whose plays appealed to mid-century tastes for delicacy and virtue and who was a rival to Goldsmith in the competition for the comic stage.
authors.style: Sentimental comedy of delicate feeling and moral testing; neat comic plotting; conventional Augustan diction in his verse; and a polished, sometimes didactic tone.
authors.concerns: Virtue, delicacy, and moral feeling; the testing of character and reputation; the politics of the stage; and literary rivalry and patronage.
authors.significance: A leading comic dramatist of the 1760s and 1770s and a memorable rival of Goldsmith, whose career illustrates the intertwining of the stage, government propaganda, and literary politics in the period.
authors.uncertainty: His exact year and place of birth are uncertain, with Dublin and Killarney both claimed, and the full scope of his government-sponsored journalism is imperfectly recorded.
sources: Researches in the South of Ireland (CELT: Corpus of Electronic Texts)

authors.name: Hugh Latimer
authors.identity: preacher; bishop of Worcester; martyr
authors.biography: Born of a yeoman family at Thurcaston about 1485; educated at Cambridge, where he was converted from conservative orthodoxy to the reformed faith in the 1520s. A preacher of extraordinary popular power, he became bishop of Worcester in 1535, resigned in 1539 over the Six Articles, and preached through the Edwardian years, notably the Sermon of the Plough (1548) and the Lent sermons before Edward VI (1549). Under Mary he was imprisoned with Ridley and Cranmer and burned at Oxford on 16 October 1555, urging Ridley: 'we shall this day light such a candle, by God's grace, in England, as I trust shall never be put out.'
authors.profile: The greatest English preacher of the Reformation. His printed sermons — above all the Sermon of the Plough and the Sermons before King Edward VI — are the classics of Tudor homiletics: plain, concrete, homely in metaphor, and fearless in their attack on landlords, enclosers, and corrupt clergy.
authors.style: The plain style made dramatic: rural simile, proverb, anecdote, and direct address; a yeoman's concreteness yoked to scriptural authority.
authors.concerns: Preaching as the cure of the commonwealth; social justice against enclosure and greed; the duty of bishops and landlords; the Word before ceremony.
authors.significance: The model of English preaching for a century and a principal voice of the Reformation's social conscience; his sermons document the moral crisis of mid-Tudor England.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: The Sermons before King Edward VI

sources: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, 7 volumes (Bury edition)

authors.name: Humphry Davy
authors.nationality: English (Cornish); the Regency science and literary culture of Bristol and the metropolitan institution
authors.identity: Chemist, lecturer and poet; the most brilliant public expositor of the new chemistry, the founder of electro-chemical investigation in Britain, and a representative figure of the union of science, literature and celebrity in the Romantic period.
authors.biography: Davy was born at Penzance in Cornwall on 17 December 1778, the second of eight children of a carpenter and portrait-painter of modest means, and was put out as an apprentice to his brother John, a Penzance surgeon, where the pharmacy and a chance of chemistry first attracted him. Removed to Bristol in 1798 by Thomas Beddoes, he worked at the Pneumatic Institution founded for the trial of the new gases in disease, and the experiments on nitrous oxide and on other aeriform fluids recorded in the Researches, Chemical and Philosophical of 1800 made his name. He came to London as assistant lecturer at the metropolitan institution and from 1802 delivered the annual course that made him the most attended scientific speaker in the kingdom, lecturing on agriculture, on the chemistry of combustion and respiration, and, before a mixed fashionable audience, on the powers of the new science. In 1807 and 1808, with the great battery of the institution, he decomposed the fixed alkalis and the earths and isolated the metals of potash and soda, and he established the electro-chemical doctrine of affinity; he was knighted in 1812, and the Elements of Chemical Philosophy of that year, the first part only of a projected treatise, gathered the new chemistry into a philosophy. Returned to Parliament for the Devon borough of Ashburton in 1812, he also took the professional care of mining safety that produced the safety lamp of 1815, the instrument for which he refused a patent. He was president of the Royal Society from 1820 until ill health compelled his resignation in 1827; his marriage of 1812 had ended in separation, and after leaving the presidency he set out on a last tour of the Continent, dying at Geneva on 29 May 1829 at the age of fifty, a figure of celebrity whom the literary public remembered as a poet and a moralist of science as well as a chemist.
authors.profile: His scientific writing is at once an experimental record and a public performance: the Bristol volume of 1800 is a narrative of inquiry, with the history of the compound, the account of the inhalations made on his own body and on his friends, and the physiological speculation about respiration and animal heat, while the Elements of Chemical Philosophy of 1812 states the doctrines of the elements, of the atomic theory and of electro-chemical affinity as a complete system, and closes with a celebrated prospectus of the power of chemical discovery. He left also lectures on agricultural chemistry, papers to the Royal Society, a set of early poems and dramatic attempts preserved in his notebooks, and a large correspondence.
authors.style: A lecture prose of great rhetorical command, in which the experimental narrative is arranged as discovery, with the sentence of wonder, the apostrophe to nature and the elevated close on the uses of science; the technical writing is clear, generalising and ambitious of system, and it self-consciously claims the imagination for the chemist. His early verse and the manuscripts of his youth show an accomplished Romantic diction of the school he read, and the two manner, the poetical and the philosophical, are continuous in the public lectures.
authors.concerns: The chemical constitution of bodies and the electrical origin of affinity; the decomposition of the earths and alkalis and the nature of the elements; the chemistry of respiration, of animal heat and of the effects of gases upon living bodies; the safety of the miner and the duty of the scientist to useful invention; the relation of physical enquiry to poetry, to religion and to public improvement; the limits of the atomic and the electro-chemical explanations.
authors.significance: He founded electro-chemistry as a branch of the science, established the list of the elements as it stood before the periodic scheme, and gave the Royal Institution its public character, making the scientific lecture a fashionable and literary event for the first time in England. His safety lamp, adopted with modifications after the inquiry into coal mining, was the first great instrument of industrial humanity produced by scientific method, and his presidency of the Royal Society and his teaching of Michael Faraday place him at the origin of the professional scientific culture of Victorian Britain.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his Cornish apprenticeship and of the removal to Bristol is given with small variations in the biographies, and the dating of his earliest verse and dramatic manuscripts is uncertain. The full extent of his authorship of anonymous reviews and of contributions to the fashionable literary and scientific journals of the 1800s has never been settled, and the records of the inhalation experiments at Bristol survive only as he and Beddoes reported them.

authors.name: Hwætberht
authors.identity: Latin riddler; abbot and scholar
authors.biography: A monk of Wearmouth-Jarrow from boyhood who studied in Ireland in his youth and took the religious name Eusebius. He succeeded Ceolfrith as abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow c. 716 and remained abbot until his death c. 747. He was a friend and correspondent of Boniface and a close associate of Bede, who dedicated works to him.
authors.profile: Author of the Aenigmata Eusebii, forty Latin riddles on encyclopedic subjects ranging from the alphabet and the liberal arts to the natural world, composed in the tradition of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
authors.style: Hexameter riddles marked by learned wordplay and allusive density, modelled closely on Aldhelm; the subjects move from grammatical abstraction to cosmology and natural history.
authors.concerns: The encyclopedic ordering of knowledge; the riddling description of creation; the transmission of Aldhelmian learning in Northumbria.
authors.significance: His riddles, together with Tatwine's, carried the Aldhelmian riddle tradition into the Northumbrian Renaissance and stand behind the vernacular riddle collection of the Exeter Book.
authors.uncertainty: Death date approximate (c. 747); the riddles are securely attributed by manuscript tradition.
sources: The Oxford Handbook of Tudor Literature, 1485–1603

authors.name: Isaac Watts
authors.identity: Independent minister, logician and the father of English hymnody, who taught Dissent to sing its own composed songs and wrote a textbook of reasoning used on both sides of the Atlantic.
authors.biography: Born at Southampton in 1674, the eldest of the children of a Southampton Nonconformist family whose father suffered imprisonment for religious meetings, he showed a remarkable gift for Latin as a child and was educated for the ministry under Dissenting tutors. He preached early and reluctantly, held a small charge in the country, and settled in London, where from the early 1690s he led the Independent assembly in Mark Lane and built one of the largest and most cultivated congregations in Dissent. His hymns and songs of worship began with the Horae Lyricae and the Hymns and Spiritual Songs of 1707, followed by Divine and Moral Songs for Children and by his bold paraphrases of the psalms, which provoked long disputes about whether congregations might sing anything not taken from the biblical psalter. His Logic, or the Art of Reasoning, his Improvement of the Mind and his theological and homiletic works made him a standard author for schools and preachers. Suspected by some of abandoning the Trinity, he was honoured with a doctorate and spent his last decades an invalid, still writing and visiting, until his death in November 1748; he was buried at Bunhill Fields.
authors.profile: The scholar-preacher of hymns and rules of thinking, who joined catechetical plainness to a lyricist's sense of meter and of congregational feeling.
authors.style: Clear, taught, unhurried prose in his logic and divinity; hymn verse in simple common measures with strong doctrinal structure and affective immediacy; a psalm paraphrase of dignified warmth.
authors.concerns: The signs, ideas and method of right reasoning; human composition in worship and the education of a singing people; the doctrine of the atonement and the disputed Trinity; childhood, catechism and the piety of the common Christian.
authors.significance: He invented the English congregation hymn and made it the vehicle of doctrine, and his Logic was a chief instrument of education for a century, used by Dissenters, Anglicans and the American colleges alike.
authors.uncertainty: The precise sequence of his early pastoral settlements is uncertain, and the authorship of a few works printed under his name has been debated.

works.title: Divine and Moral Songs for the Use of Children
The Psalms of David Imitated in the Christian Stile

authors.name: Izaak Walton
authors.identity: Anglican biographer and author of The Compleat Angler (1653), the beloved pastoral dialogue of fishing whose serene celebration of the contemplative country life made it one of the most reprinted books in English.
authors.biography: Born 9 August 1593 at Stafford; apprenticed to a linen-draper, he prospered as a haberdasher in London (Fleet Street and later Chancery Lane) and moved in literary circles. A devout royalist Anglican, he served the cause during the Civil Wars and at the Restoration. He wrote gentle biographies of John Donne (1640), Sir Henry Wotton, Richard Hooker, George Herbert (1670), and Robert Sanderson, collected as Walton's Lives. His masterpiece The Compleat Angler (1653), enlarged over five editions to 1676 (with Charles Cotton's second part on fly-fishing), became a classic. He retired to the country and died on 15 December 1683 at Winchester, aged 90.
authors.profile: The biographer of the devout and the angler of the contemplative life, whose unhurried, genial prose celebrates friendship, piety, and the pleasures of riverside retirement.
authors.style: Gentle, pastoral, conversational prose; dialogue form (Piscator, Venator, Auceps); a serene, pious tone; digressive quotation of verse and lore; and unpretentious charm.
authors.concerns: The contemplative and retired life; friendship and piety; the natural world of rivers and fish; Anglican devotion and modest virtue; and the celebration of simple pleasures.
authors.significance: The Compleat Angler has been continuously in print and is one of the most beloved of English books; Walton's Lives established a tradition of affectionate biographical portraiture and shaped the ideal of the Anglican 'holy life'.
authors.uncertainty: Walton's life is documented; his Lives blend fact with hagiographic affection and are not always reliable as biography, and his dates for some subjects are traditional.

works.title: The Compleat Angler; or, The Contemplative Man's Recreation

sources: Hobomok: A Tale of Early Times (Broadview Edition)

authors.name: James Beattie
authors.identity: Aberdeen professor and poet, the most widely read assailant of Humean scepticism, whose Essay on Truth (1770) and The Minstrel (1771) made him a European name.
authors.biography: Born at Laurencekirk in 1735, the son of a shopkeeper and small farmer, he was educated at Marischal College, Aberdeen, took his MA in 1753 and served briefly as a schoolmaster. He was appointed in 1760 to the Marischal chair of moral philosophy and logic, which he held for four decades, and married Mary Dun in 1767. The Essay on Truth (1770), a robust defence of common sense against the ideal system, made his reputation and earned him a pension from George III; the didactic poem The Minstrel, with its sketch of a young genius, followed in 1771 and was enlarged in 1773. His essays on poetry and music were gathered with the rest of his later writing in the Dissertations Moral and Critical of 1796, after the period covered here. He corresponded with Johnson and Witherspoon and was widely praised, and for a generation his name stood in the American colleges for the Christian answer to scepticism. He died in Aberdeen on 16 February 1803.
authors.profile: A professor of common sense and of taste, who argued that scepticism refutes itself in the ordinary belief of mankind and versified the same appeal to feeling.
authors.style: Confident, declamatory argument and good-humoured invective; descriptive and personifying verse in a meditative, Thomson-like manner; a didactic plainness of diction.
authors.concerns: The instincts and the first principles of knowledge; the reality of the external world and of other minds; genius, taste and the psychology of poetry; the moral sentiments and their cultural conditions.
authors.significance: For a generation he was the standard answer to Hume in Britain and above all in the American colleges, and his career shows both the strength and the superficiality of the common-sense assault on scepticism.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his abolitionist writing and the extent of his debt to Reid's unpublished teaching are still debated.

works.title: The Minstrel; or, the Progress of Genius

authors.name: James Boswell
