authors.identity: Scottish lawyer and autobiographer, immortal as the biographer and companion of Samuel Johnson and as a diarist of his own life and times.
authors.biography: Boswell was born in Edinburgh, the son of a judge, Lord Auchinleck, and was called to the Scottish bar. A restless, self-analysing young man, he travelled widely and met David Hume and Jean-Jacques Rousseau before becoming, in 1763, Johnson's devoted friend and would-be biographer. He wrote essays for his own periodical The Hypochondriack and travelled to London and to Corsica, recording a Journal of a Tour to Corsica (1768) with admiration for its patriots, and later a Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides (1785) with Johnson. His masterpiece, The Life of Samuel Johnson, appeared in 1791. In later years he lived at the family estate of Auchinleck and died in London in 1795; his frank private journal was printed only in the twentieth century.
authors.profile: A biographer, diarist, and essayist whose genius was for recording speech, personality, and the texture of daily life; his journals and Life of Johnson founded modern biographical and autobiographical realism.
authors.style: Vivid, intimate, anecdotal prose; faithful reproduction of talk and character; a self-exposing, confessional diary manner; and a mixture of Scotticism with cultivated Augustan ease.
authors.concerns: The study of character and genius; friendship, emulation, and self-knowledge; nationality, law, and politics; and the value of the everyday and the documentary record.
authors.significance: His Life of Johnson and his rediscovered journals make him a founder of modern biography and autobiography and one of the most valuable witnesses to eighteenth-century literary and social life.

works.title: Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides

authors.name: James Fenimore Cooper
authors.nationality: American; novelist, romancer of forest and sea, satirist of society and naval historian, the first American writer of prose fiction to sustain a European reputation as a creator of a national romance
authors.identity: A novelist above all, and the founder of the American romance of the frontier and of the sea; he also wrote travel and social criticism, a naval history and a body of controversial prefatory and political prose. His fiction divides into the historical and Indian tales, the sea tales, the settlement and frontier tales and the later domestic and political romances; he wrote no verse of consequence.
authors.biography: He was born at Burlington, New Jersey, on 15 September 1789, the son of William Cooper, a member of the legislature who laid out the village of Cooperstown in the Otsego country, and he was bred from infancy in that new settlement on the edge of the western wilderness. Sent to Yale at thirteen, he withdrew without taking a degree and was placed in the merchant service, from which he passed into the navy as a midshipman, serving in the years before and during the war with Great Britain and resigning in 1811 on the eve of his marriage. He settled in the country of his youth, lived for a season in St. Louis territory and in Washington, and turned to fiction after a chance comparison with a popular English romance. Precaution appeared in 1820 and The Spy in 1821, and the frontier tales of the 1820s, ending with The Prairie of 1827, established his fame. From 1826 to 1833 he lived abroad chiefly in Paris and Italy, with a brief appointment as consul at Algiers which he did not use, and during those years wrote the sea romances, the Italian and Dutch historical tales and the travel book Notions of the Americans. His return brought a long quarrel with the American press and with the society he found waiting for him, and in his last decade he answered his critics in fiction, in political argument and in the history of the American navy. He died at his home in Cooperstown on 14 September 1851.
authors.profile: His career may be read as a series of groups: the society and historical tales of 1820 to 1823, the Indian and frontier romance of the Ottsego stories and the Prairie, the sea tales of the late 1820s, the Italian and European romances of the 1830s, and the home criticism of the last ten years. He is the only American writer of his generation whose work holds both the maritime and the wilderness subject at the same scale, and he prefaced and defended his own theory of romance in a large body of prefaces, letters and polemical pamphlets. The naval history and the travel books stand beside the fiction as deliberate contributions to the national record and to the argument about American institutions.
authors.style: A vigorous, spacious and often unequal narrative prose, capable of sustained description of forest, coast and sea and of an impressive rhetorical elevation in the speech of his chief personages. He uses the surveyor's eye and the chronicler's manner, interpolates document, ballad and legend, and lets his narrators moralise at length; dialogue is often stately and repetitive, and his satire of society is carried by a frank and indignant declamation rather than by irony.
authors.concerns: The wilderness as the moral scene of the republic and the fate of its original possessors; the relation of genuine to borrowed rank and of merit to privilege; the abuses of a corrupted press and of a party-democracy; the justifiable order of a settled community; the sea service as a school of heroism and of national character; the romance of the frontier, the capture, the scout and the boundary between civilisation and the wild; the Christian and republican answer to aristocratic travel.
authors.significance: He made the American frontier and the American sea service subjects of serious romance, and the Leather-stocking series gave the national literature its first continuous mythical cycle. His contemporaries in Europe read and imitated him, and his sea tales founded the tradition of American maritime fiction. At the same time his treatment of Indian removal and of the displaced possessor of the soil became the central instance in the later argument about what the American romance had been willing to see.
authors.uncertainty: The story of the wager or chance comparison that first set him to write a novel is anecdotal and variously told; the dating of some of the sea tales' composition rests on letters and on his own later statements rather than on manuscripts.

works.title: Notions of the Americans, Picked Up by a Travelling Bachelor

authors.name: James Harrington
authors.identity: Political philosopher; author of The Commonwealth of Oceana (1656), an influential republican utopia that argued government follows the distribution of property and prescribed a balanced constitution, shaping Whig and American republican thought.
authors.biography: Born 3 January 1611 at Upton, Northamptonshire, educated at Trinity College, Oxford and the Middle Temple, travelling widely in Europe. He served as a groom of the bedchamber to Charles I (1647), remaining loyal in person while arguing republican principles, and was much affected by the king's execution. Imprisoned briefly, he published Oceana (1656), dedicated — provocatively — to Cromwell, arguing that political power rests on the 'balance' of landed property and proposing an ideal mixed republic with rotation of office and a secret ballot. He wrote further republican tracts (The Prerogative of Popular Government, 1658) and, after the Restoration, was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy and died, broken in health, on 11 September 1677.
authors.profile: The republican theorist whose materialist analysis of power and property and whose constitutional utopia Oceana provided a durable vocabulary of republicanism for the English and American revolutions.
authors.style: Argumentative political prose and utopian fiction; historical and classical analogy; constitutional scheming; and a dense, sometimes obscure, learned style.
authors.concerns: Republicanism and the balance of property; constitutional design, rotation, and the ballot; the rise and fall of states; civic virtue; and the critique of monarchy and of Hobbes.
authors.significance: Oceana profoundly influenced later republican and Whig thought, the 'country' ideology of the eighteenth century, and the American founders (Jefferson and Adams drew on Harrington's ideas of property, rotation, and the balanced constitution).
authors.uncertainty: Harrington's life is documented but his later imprisonment and decline are partly anecdotal; the reception of Oceana was shaped by its dedication to Cromwell and its suppression.
sources: New Perspectives on Malthus: 250th Anniversary Essays

authors.name: James Hervey
authors.identity: Country clergyman and devotional writer, the most ornate of the meditative prose writers between Browne and the lake poets, author of Meditations among the Tombs (1746) and Theron and Aspasio (1755).
authors.biography: Born at Hardingstone in Northamptonshire in 1714 into a family of small means and many children, he was educated for the church at Oxford, where he sat at Lincoln College, and took holy orders. Delicate and retired by temperament, he served country parishes, chiefly in Suffolk, under the patronage of great neighbours, and passed his short life among books, correspondence and the composition of devotional essays. His Meditations among the Tombs (1746) made at once a new fashion for the graveyard reverie and a reputation for splendid, melancholy prose; other volumes of meditations, letters and dialogues followed, together with a psalmody and hymns. Theron and Aspasio (1755), a long set of dialogues on natural and revealed religion, was read by its author as a defence of scriptural Christianity against deism and by John Wesley as a masked enthusiasm, and the attack pursued him for the rest of his days. He died suddenly at the end of 1758, still in his forties, and his works were repeatedly reprinted and translated.
authors.profile: A rhetorician of devotion, who turned the cemetery, the grove and the fireside into stages for the meditation on death, providence and the soul.
authors.style: Richly ornamented, Latinate periodic prose; personification and apostrophe pressed to the edge of excess; dialogue and epistolary forms; a colour sense of leaves, twilight and marble that the next century would inherit.
authors.concerns: Death, immortality and the resurrection of the body; the evidences and the inward experience of revealed religion; the piety of natural scenery; taste, ornament and the uses of melancholy.
authors.significance: He fixed the graveyard meditation as a literary mode and supplied the ornate devotional prose that Johnson, the romantic naturists and the nineteenth-century tractarians all read; his controversy with Wesley sharpened the century's quarrel about enthusiasm and conversion.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his preferments and patronage are slight, and the chronology of his several volumes is confused by reissues and collected editions.

works.title: Theron and Aspasio; or, A Scriptural and Critical Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians

authors.name: James Hogg
authors.identity: Poet and novelist; the Ettrick Shepherd
authors.biography: James Hogg was born into extreme poverty in Ettrick Forest, Selkirkshire, the son of a tenant farmer. Largely self-educated, he worked as a shepherd from childhood and became a lifelong shepherd and farmer — hence his enduring epithet. He contributed ballads and essays to the Edinburgh Scots Magazine and was taken up by Sir Walter Scott, who helped publish The Poetical Works of James Hogg (1801). His major poetry, including Mador of the Moor and The Queen's Wake, appeared between 1813 and 1819; his great novel, The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner, followed in 1824. He was a central figure in Edinburgh's literary bohemian circles and a contributor to Blackwood's Magazine.
authors.profile: Hogg is the major Scottish poet of the ballad tradition after Burns and the most formally experimental Scottish novelist of his generation. His fiction and verse explore religious enthusiasm, the double, and the supernatural with a scepticism born of his Calvinist upbringing. His metafictional games in the Confessions anticipate modernist narrative.
authors.style: Scots and border dialect; ballad stanzas; Gothic psychological intensity in prose; self-conscious narrative games; a blend of high rhetoric and colloquial earthiness derived from oral performance.
authors.concerns: Calvinist election and religious mania; the supernatural as psychological projection; the divided self and the double; the oral ballad tradition and popular Scottish memory; the shepherd's relation to the literary market.
authors.significance: Hogg's Confessions was ignored in his lifetime and is now recognised as one of the supreme Scottish novels and a precursor of modernist and Gothic fiction; his poetry kept the ballad tradition alive between Burns and the later Victorians.

works.title: The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner
The Three Perils of Woman; or, Love, Jealousy, and Disobedience of Parents

authors.name: James I of Scotland
authors.identity: poet; king
authors.biography: Captured at sea by the English in 1406 at the age of eleven, he spent eighteen years as a prisoner at the English court, where he received a full education in the company of Henry V's courtiers and poets. Released in 1424, he returned to rule Scotland with reforming vigour until his murder by conspirators at Perth on 21 February 1437.
authors.profile: Traditionally credited with The Kingis Quair (c. 1424), the dream vision in which the captive narrator sees his beloved and is consoled by the goddesses of love and fortune; the attribution rests on the poem's own claims and manuscript tradition.
authors.style: Graceful Chaucerian rhyme royal with an autobiographical frame; the fusion of Boethian consolation with courtly love vision; precociously Renaissance delight in nature and architecture.
authors.concerns: Love, fortune, and providence; the education and duties of a prince; captivity and deliverance.
authors.significance: The Kingis Quair is the fountainhead of the Scottish Chaucerian tradition and one of the great prison poems of European literature.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of the Quair to James I is traditional and widely accepted but not absolutely certain.
movements: Charles Brockden Brown and the American Gothic
themes: Time, death, and immortality through verse
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Restoration Drama

authors.name: James Kirke Paulding
authors.nationality: American; essayist, tale-writer, poet of the frontier, dramatist and office-holder, the partner of Irving in the periodical that founded the Knickerbocker group and a defender of a plain native literature
authors.identity: A writer of periodical papers, character sketches, domestic and frontier tales, a poem of the backwoodsman's argument and a play of native comedy, joined to a long after-life in office and in public letter. His work is the democratic and contentious side of the New York school, and he wrote verse, prose fiction and drama without settling on either.
authors.biography: He was born in New York City on 22 August 1778 into a family of Dutch and English descent long settled about the Hudson, and he grew up in the country which supplied the legend of his later tales. He was a friend of Irving from boyhood and with him and a brother conducted in 1807 and 1808 the periodical papers which gave the American essay its first native school. He tried law and a commercial life in New York and in the southern cities without success, and after his return wrote The Backwoodsman, a two-canto argument for the western settler and against borrowed European taste, which appeared in 1818. In the same season he published a play of New York character and a volume of tales and sketches, and from the papers and sketches of these years the Dutchman's Fireside of 1831 was finally drawn. He held federal office in the 1830s and was Secretary of the Navy from 1838 to 1840, an appointment which ended his literary career in everything but pamphlet and preface. He retired to the family place at Fishkill on the Hudson, where he died on 6 April 1860.
authors.profile: His work is a mixture of the periodical essay, the descriptive poem of argument, the frontier and Hudson valley tale, and a comedy of native character; it is continuous in one design, the assertion of American plainness against aristocratic and foreign pretension. He is the least finished and most outspoken of the Knickerbocker writers, and his tales of the Dutch country and of the western settlement supplied material and argument which his friend's sketches did not touch.
authors.style: A blunt, polemical and homely prose, strongly accented, given to direct address and to invective against rank, and carrying the argument of the piece on its sleeve. His verse is in the descriptive and argumentative couplet of the earlier American school, robust and unpolished, and his character drawing proceeds by the outside stroke of custom and speech rather than by analysis.
authors.concerns: The republican objection to hereditary wealth and to the borrowed standards of Europe; the merits of the backwoods settler and of plain democratic character; the Dutch settlement of the Hudson valley as a vanished society; the claims of a native literature and of native subject; the corruption of office and of party in the republic; the hospitality, superstition and quietly treated custom of the old country.
authors.significance: As the joint author of the first Knickerbocker periodical he shares the founding of the American sketch and character tale, and his poem of 1818 is the earliest considerable statement of the claim to a national literature in American verse. His Dutch tale preserved one version of the Hudson valley legend on which later writing about the region drew, and his contentious defence of democratic plainness marks the political edge of the New York school.
authors.uncertainty: The division of the separate papers of the 1807 periodical between the three conductors has never been settled to general satisfaction, and the earlier state of the Dutch tale, as it existed before the recasting of 1831, is known only from its reprint and preface.

authors.name: James Mackintosh
authors.nationality: Scottish and British; Whig intellectual and legal-humanist tradition
authors.identity: Advocate, jurist, Whig parliamentarian and philosophical historian; the most influential British reply to Burke on the French Revolution and a leading liberal reformer of his generation
authors.biography: Sir James Mackintosh was born on 24 October 1765 at Aldourie, on the shores of Loch Ness in Inverness-shire, into a Highland Episcopalian family of Jacobite and Catholic sympathies; his father, Captain John Mackintosh, died while James was a boy. He was educated at the grammar school of Fortrose and at King's College, Aberdeen, and went to Edinburgh in October 1784 to study medicine, joining the Speculative Society and absorbing the moral philosophy of the Scottish Enlightenment. A visit to France in 1787-88 made him an admirer of the Revolution; he married Catherine Stuart in February 1789 and settled in London, where, abandoning medicine for law, he was called to the bar and earned his living as a reporter, reviser and contributor to biographical and encyclopaedal work. His Vindiciae Gallicae; A Defence of the French Revolution and its English Admirers (April 1791), written in a few weeks in reply to Burke's Reflections, made his reputation and remained the classic Whig argument that revolution could be a lawful, moral restoration of liberty; its author nonetheless fell silent on public questions for nearly two decades, during which he was taken up by Samuel Romilly, introduced to Charles James Fox and Richard Brinsley Sheridan, and wrote Fox's great obituary for the Gentleman's Magazine after 1806. Knighted on his appointment, he served in India as Recorder of Bombay from 1804 until he sailed for England in November 1811, where he earned the respect of Indian administrators for his learning, his defence of press freedom and his work on the digest of regulations. Returning to public life, he resumed writing, attacked Jeremy Bentham's Plan of Parliamentary Reform in the Edinburgh Review in 1818, became the philosophical historian of the Whig revival, sat on the committee on capital punishment, advocated Catholic emancipation, and entered the House of Commons for Newcastle's borough of Knaresborough, where he sat until his death. His last labours were literary: a Life of Sir Thomas More (1830) with its Dissertation on the Study of the Law of England, and the first volume of his History of England from the Revolution to the Treaty of Peace of 1748 (1830), continued after his death. He died at his house in Langham Place, London, on 30 May 1832 and was buried at Hampstead.
authors.profile: Mackintosh's writings are those of a lawyer-moralist: the controversial tract (Vindiciae Gallicae, the Whig speeches), encyclopaedal and biographical composition (his Dissertation on the Progress of Ethical Philosophy, contributions to general biography and to the family of British classic lives), and philosophical history, above all the History of England, which treats institutions, opinions and laws rather than court narrative. His speeches and reported arguments are a substantial part of his posthumous literary record.
authors.style: A Latinate, balanced and generously periodic prose, marked by candour, qualification and an urbanity of argument that concedes the opponent's strongest point before answering it. He writes in the manner of historical jurisprudence: long periods of classification, abstract nouns, moral elevation and an antipathy to epigram. Burke's vehemence is answered by cool enumeration of principles; the history is dignified, discursive and deliberately unhurried.
authors.concerns: The lawfulness and morality of revolution; prescription, progress and the rights of nations; the relation of religious belief to public order and to toleration; the correction of penal law and the abolition of capital punishment; national character, opinion and institution as the matter of history; the education of a lawyer and the study of English law as philosophy.
authors.significance: Vindiciae Gallicae fixed the Whig-liberal answer to Burke and shaped the trans-Atlantic debate about the French Revolution for a generation; his Edinburgh Review attack on Bentham's reform plan defined the moderate liberal position on parliamentary reform. As Recorder of Bombay he became a byword for learned, humane jurisdiction in British India; in Parliament he advanced criminal-law reform and Catholic emancipation; and his History of England and his More biography transmitted the Whig view of the eighteenth century to Victorian readers.
authors.uncertainty: The Dictionary of National Biography prints his birth as 24 October while its text has been read as 1766 by some cataloguers, and the standard modern date is 1765; the day of his death is given as 30 May 1832 in the sources checked (Wikipedia, DNB), though 30 April appears in some references. His Indian office is the Recorder of Bombay, 1804-11, in the accounts consulted here, not the Recorder of Madras, which is sometimes asserted; the year of his call to the bar (Michaelmas 1795 in DNB) is variously reported, as is the date of his knighthood (1803/1804).

authors.name: James Macpherson
authors.identity: Scottish scholar and literary forger, the Ossian, whose claimed ancient Gaelic epics won European fame and a long authenticity controversy.
authors.biography: Macpherson was born in Inverness-shire, educated briefly at Aberdeen and Edinburgh, and worked as a schoolmaster while collecting Highland ballads and Gaelic fragments. With the encouragement of Hugh Blair and other patrons he published Fragments of Ancient Poetry (1760), followed by Fingal (1761) and the epic Temora (1763), presented as translations of the ancient bard Ossian. The works were translated across Europe and admired by many, while critics, notably Samuel Johnson, charged him with forgery. He used the fame and a government pension to secure posts in colonial administration and later sat in the British Parliament. He died in 1796.
authors.profile: A maker of pseudo-primitive epic; his translations of Ossian offer a vast, dim, elegiac world of heroes, ghosts, and landscapes in a singularly hypnotic, rhythmic prose-poetry.
authors.style: High, cadenced, repetitive prose-verse; invocations, apostrophe, and broken parallelism; an intentionally archaic, primitive sublimity and melancholy.
authors.concerns: National and Celtic origins of poetry; primitive genius and the sublime of the elder world; memory, loss, and the passing of heroes; and the authenticity of literary tradition.
authors.significance: The Ossianic vogue was a European literary event that fed Romantic primitivism, melancholy, and nationalist epic; the ensuing forgery debate sharpened ideas of authenticity and folk-poetry collection.
authors.uncertainty: His exact date and place of birth are given as 1736 in Inverness-shire but only approximately; the degree to which he worked from genuine Gaelic tradition versus pure invention remains contested.

works.title: Fragments of Ancient Poetry, Collected from the Bards

authors.name: James Mill
altNames: The author of the History of British India
authors.nationality: Scottish; the philosophical radical and Utilitarian school, and the political economy of the Ricardian writers
authors.identity: Historian, economist and logician of the Utilitarian school; the writer who gave British rule in India its most influential English history, who first made Ricardian political economy teachable, and whose plan of education and whose controversial reviews shaped the radical thought of a generation.
authors.biography: Mill was born at Northwater Bridge in the parish of Logie Pert in Forfarshire on 6 April 1773, the son of a cobbler who held a small piece of land, and was named James Milne, the spelling of the family name being altered later in life. He was taught at the parish school and at the Montrose burgh school, took the M.A. at King's College Aberdeen in 1798, and was licensed by a Secession presbytery, serving for a time as a dissenting chaplain and schoolmaster before private tuition in Fife gave him leisure for scholarship. He came to London in 1810 with the intention of emigrating to America, and stayed, writing for the Encyclopaedia Britannica and the Critical Review and editing a short-lived journal. Through Joseph Hume he met Jeremy Bentham in 1808-1810 and became his disciple, friend and for a decade his most devoted public advocate. The three volumes of the History of British India, published in 1817 and written entirely from books, made his reputation and an opening in official opinion; he entered East India House as an examiner in 1823 and rose to be chief of the office, and from that position, and later through his son's influence, he acted on the appointments and educational policy of the company's service. The Elements of Political Economy of 1821 stated the Ricardian doctrine in the form of a textbook, and his contributions to the Edinburgh and Westminster Reviews made him the most feared controversialist of the philosophical radicals. He helped found the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge and University College London, and he educated his son John Stuart Mill under a documented and much-criticised plan of instruction. He died in London on 23 June 1836, having long been a figure of official influence and of party suspicion.
authors.profile: His literary work is argumentative and systematic rather than imaginative: a three-volume history that treats the civilisations of India as stages of improvement to be judged by European standards of science and law; a compact economic textbook built on a few rigorous definitions and on the doctrine that demand does not regulate production; and a vast body of review essay, pamphlet and encyclopaedia article on government, jurisprudence, colonies, education and the analysis of the human mind. His Fragment on Finance and his articles on the Law of Nations and on Colonies carry the same school of argument into the general literature of the period, and his Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind, published posthumously with his son's notes, closes the associationist tradition of Hartley and Locke.
authors.style: A dry, lucid and unrelenting prose of definition, division and deduction, in which a proposition is isolated, supported by enumeration and then applied without concession to feeling or authority; long sentences of parallel members, abstract terms handled as instruments, and a polemic that is severe rather than witty. In the history the manner becomes judicial and rhetorical, with the repeated verdict of stationary, despotic and childish upon whole civilisations.
authors.concerns: The application of the associationist psychology of Locke and Hartley to the whole of mind and society; the principle of utility as the measure of institutions, of punishment and of education; the government of India, its history and its reform; the laws of value, wages, profit and rent, and the division of wealth; the representative and educative function of a democratic institution; the relation of religion to priestcraft and to state; the proper ends and methods of instruction.
authors.significance: The History of British India was for a century the standard English account of the subcontinent and a decisive influence on the policy and the self-justification of the company's rule, as well as the textbook against which later Indian historians wrote. The Elements of Political Economy made Ricardian doctrine transmissible, and his official position at East India House gave Utilitarian principle an unusual direct effect on appointments, education and administration. As Bentham's chief public advocate and as the father and first teacher of John Stuart Mill he stands at the centre of the philosophical radicalism that links the Utilitarian school to Victorian thought.
authors.uncertainty: The family name was Milne, and Mill wrote of his own boyhood in the autobiographical material later used by his son, whose account is the principal source for the years before 1810 and is necessarily retrospective. The exact chronology of his chaplaincies, schoolmastering and tutoring in Scotland in the years 1798-1810 is variously set down in the biographies.

authors.name: James Montgomery
authors.nationality: Scottish-born English; the dissenting hymnody and the reform journalism of the northern manufacturing towns
authors.identity: Hymn-writer, poet and editor of a manufacturing-town newspaper; the most widely sung of the evangelical hymnists of his generation and a combative Whig and abolitionist journalist.
authors.biography: Montgomery was born at Irvine in Ayrshire on 4 November 1771, the second of the four children of a Moravian itinerant preacher of poor means, and at about six years of age was sent to board at the Moravian school and community at Fulneck near Leeds, where he was educated and from which, on the death of his parents in the West Indies, he was bound apprentice in 1787 to a Sheffield printer. His master Joseph Goforth, proprietor of the Sheffield Register, fled to America in 1792 to avoid prosecution, and the nineteen-year-old apprentice carried on the paper as the Sheffield Register and Independent Miscellany, and after a change of title and of politics established it in 1794 as the Sheffield Iris, of which he was proprietor and editor until 1825. He was imprisoned in 1795 for nine months for a seditious article on the arbitrary measures of the government, and again in 1810 for reporting in full a speech delivered at a public meeting in his town, and both commitments made him a recognised figure in the controversy about the liberty of the press. He removed from the Moravian to the Unitarian connection, preached and taught, and supported Catholic relief, the abolition of slavery, education for the labouring poor and factory reform, using the Iris as a register of the manufacturing district's agitations as well as a vehicle for his own verse. In 1825 he retired to London to conduct the Christian Observer, the evangelical monthly founded by the supporters of the Church Missionary Society, and he edited it until his death, publishing in the same years a volume of hymns and several longer poems, of which The World before the Flood and the songs and ballads of the Iris were the best known. He died at the Mount, near Sheffield, on 30 April 1854, and was buried in the General Cemetery there, having become the most frequently sung of the hymn-writers of his connection.
authors.profile: His work is divided between the hymn, the occasional and narrative poem and the newspaper. The hymns, written mostly for congregational singing and for the anniversaries of the evangelical connection, are compressed, strictly metrical and deliberately simple, and a large number of them passed into the standard hymnals. The verse of the Iris years includes songs, ballads and topographical and political lyrics, and the later volumes carry scriptural and oriental subjects treated in the long manner; his journalism, editorial, reported and correspondence, is the bulk of his printed remains, together with the speeches and tracts of the reform and missionary causes he served.
authors.style: A clear, tuneful and strictly metrical verse manner, built on short lines, on balanced stanzas and on the strong close of the hymn; an ear for the singable phrase, and a marked preference for concrete image over abstraction. The journalistic prose is brisk, indignant and personal, with the report, the editorial stroke and the appeal to the readership of a manufacturing town all fused in a single number.
authors.concerns: The duties and liberties of the press in a time of war and of domestic alarm; the service of the evangelical and dissenting communities by their own verse and their own news; the sin of the slave trade and of colonial oppression, and the obligations of the emancipation cause; the education of the labouring poor and the Sabbath and Sunday-school; the providential reading of public history and of national judgment.
authors.significance: He gave the English hymnody of the nineteenth century some of its most permanently sung tunes and texts, and his example helped to make the denominational hymn a recognised literary form; as editor of the Iris he created the model of the independent manufacturing-town newspaper, and his imprisonments were cited for a generation in the argument for the freedom of reporting. He is one of the clearest instances of the union of evangelical dissent, reform journalism and abolitionist publicity in the northern industrial counties.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his apprenticeship and of the transfer of the Sheffield Register to his hands in 1792 are recorded chiefly from his own prefaces and from the memoirs written after his death, and the two accounts differ on the dating of the first number under his management. The authorship of unsigned editorial matter in the Register and the Iris is not recoverable, and the list of his contributions to other journals has never been settled. His parents' year and place of death in the West Indies, and the length and the prison of his first commitment, are variously stated in the biographies.

works.title: The World before the Flood: A Poem, in Ten Cantos

authors.name: James Nelson Barker
authors.nationality: American, of the Philadelphia theatre; the republican historical drama and melo-drama of the early national stage, and the first significant American dramatist of the Pocahontas and Indian-captivity legend
authors.identity: A playwright of ten plays, comic and tragical, written for the stock companies of Philadelphia and afterwards produced in New York and London, together with adapted comedies, verses and civic odes. His forms are the afterpiece and the melo-drama, the domestic comedy of manners and the historical tragedy, and he works characteristically with the musical interlude, the tableau and the moral epilogue.
authors.biography: He was born on 17 June 1784 at Annapolis in Maryland, of a family of military standing, the son of the man whom the Philadelphia finding aid for his papers styles General John Barker, and he was brought up in Philadelphia, the city of the American stage. He held a commission in the artillery and served with the army through the second war with England, rising to the rank of major, and he carried into public life the reputation of an officer of the regular establishment. His first printed play, The Indian Princess; or, La Belle Sauvage, was published at Philadelphia by the firm of Palmer in 1808, the year of its first performance on the Philadelphia stage, and it made his name: it is the first American play upon an Indian theme and the first successful Pocahontas drama, and in December 1820 it was produced at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, the first play of an American author to reach that house in the nineteenth century. He followed it with comedy and melo-drama, a translated or adapted piece entitled How to Try a Lover issued in the dramatic repositories of 1817, and the domestic comedy Tears and Smiles, which is usually counted among the contributing forms of the stage Yankee. Superstition; or, the Fanatic Father, a tragedy of monastic guilt printed in 1824, was long accounted the best of his serious dramas and held the repertory in the United States. Public office succeeded the stage: he represented Philadelphia interests, and in the years 1819 and 1820 he served as mayor of the city, after which he continued to write occasional verse and prose for civic occasions. He died on 9 March 1858, having been remembered throughout his later life as the soldier, manager and magistrate who had first put the American Indian legend on the public stage.
authors.profile: His drama is constructed for effect and for the capabilities of a stock company, and his best scenes are those of spectacle, capture and deliverance, in which moral argument is carried by situation rather than by speech. The Indian Princess treats Pocahontas as a principle of natural generosity and of converted gentleness, and its plea for mercy between the strong and the weak is delivered in the verse and song proper to the afterpiece and in a diction of buoyant sentimental declaration. His comedy of Philadelphia life depends upon assumption, mistaken identity and the satire of manners, while his tragedy of Superstition attacks monastic fanaticism and priestly power with the plain Protestant vehemence proper to the popular stage. He prefixes prefaces to his printed plays in which he defends the treatment of historical character, an early instance of the American dramatist's claim to be read.
authors.style: Verse and song intermixed with prose dialogue; tableau, entrance and explosion as the units of structure; declarative sentiment in long moral period; heroic-couplet dignity for Indian and heroic characters; comic dialogue built on mistake, assumption and the manners of Philadelphia society; anti-Catholic polemic in the tragedy; an epilogue or moral gloss addressed directly to the audience.
authors.concerns: The treatment of the American Indian in legend and in history and the possibility of generosity between races; national subject matter for a national theatre, and the claim of American drama to the London stage; the tyranny of superstition, monastic power and the fanatic father; the ethics of capture, adoption and deliverance; gentility, manners and civic virtue in the early republic; the soldier's and the magistrate's duty to the republic.
authors.significance: He fixed the Pocahontas story in its American dramatic form and made the Indian Princess a stock piece of the nineteenth-century stage, on which the legend passed into pictorial, juvenile and later cinematic treatment. His production at Drury Lane in 1820 was a milestone in the transatlantic recognition of American drama, and his plays are the principal evidence that the early national theatre could treat colonial history as national myth. As a soldier and mayor of Philadelphia he also illustrates the union of letters, military service and civic office characteristic of the generation after the revolution.
authors.uncertainty: The Annapolis birthplace rests upon the standard biographical account, beginning with Musser's study of 1929 and repeated by the later encyclopaedias, and no registry record is cited for it; the identity and rank of his father are reported only in finding-aid style. The dates of first performance and of publication of several of his plays differ in the extant playbills and editions, and the order and attribution of his ten dramas, especially of the adaptations issued in the dramatic repositories, are unsettled. The precise offices he held in the artillery and the chronology of his mayoralty vary between civic memoirs.

works.title: The Indian Princess; or, La Belle Sauvage

authors.name: James Ramsay
authors.identity: Naval surgeon and West India clergyman whose Essay on the Treatment and Conversion of African Slaves (1784) supplied the abolitionist movement with its documentation and its moral case.
authors.biography: Born at Fraserburgh in Aberdeenshire in 1733 and educated for medicine, he served as a surgeon in the navy, was present in the West Indies, and after leaving the service settled as a planter's physician and then as a clergyman on the sugar islands, where he saw the working of the slave system at its worst and quarrelled with the island planters over it. Ordained and returned to England, he was given the living of Teston in Kent, where the Bouverie family became his friends and encouragement, and there he wrote his Essay on the Treatment and Conversion of African Slaves in the British Sugar Colonies (1784). Its companion volume, an Inquiry into the effects of stopping the African trade and opening a commerce with Africa, argued that emancipation and lawful trade would enrich the nation. The sugar interest answered him in a swarm of hostile pamphlets, attacked his conduct as a planter and as a clergyman, and pursued him over his account of the killing of mutinous ratings on a king's ship; he replied at length and lost certain friends by his stubbornness. He advised the committee formed in 1787 and instructed its members in the evidence of the colonies. He died in 1789, the year of Equiano's narrative, leaving the Teston circle to carry his arguments into Parliament.
authors.profile: The witness-clergyman, who made an accumulated case of particulars, dates and amounts out of twenty years of service in the slave-holding islands.
authors.style: Plain, accumulative, heavily evidenced prose; narrative of cases joined to statistical and scriptural argument; a surgeon's specification of wounds and punishments; occasional bitterness of reply.
authors.concerns: The treatment, conversion and education of enslaved people; the criminality of the trade and the duty of the nation; the economics of emancipation and of African commerce; the moral responsibility of the planter and the clergy.
authors.significance: His two books of 1784 converted a clerical protest into the printed evidence on which the organised abolition campaign of the following decade was built, and the circle he gathered at Teston became a nursery of the Clapham reformers.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of his island ministry and of his ordination are reported inconsistently, and the details of the controversy over the mutiny narrative are partisan on both sides.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Effects of Putting a Stop to the African Slave Trade, and of Granting Liberty to the Slaves in the British Sugar Colonies

authors.name: James Robinson Planché
authors.nationality: English; the Regency stage, burletta and extravaganza, and the antiquarian study of drama
authors.identity: Dramatist, antiquary and officer of arms; the reformer of the burletta and the historian of English costume and stage archaeology
authors.biography: He was born in London into a family of French Huguenot descent, and was bound apprentice in a City business before he began to write verse and then plays for the theatres. His supernatural melodrama of the corpse-bride, played at a secondary London theatre in the summer of 1820, was the sensation of the season and began a decade of vampiric competition between the houses, and he went on to write burletta, farce, historical drama and the short classical burlesque for which he is best remembered. He superintended stage costume with an antiquary's accuracy, took an active part in the reform of the theatre after the patents crisis of the 1840s, and wrote a notable tract on the condition of the drama. He was appointed to the heralds' college and rose to a king at arms' place, edited ancient romances and chronicles for the societies, and published a nine-volume collection of his plays with a history of the Irish stage and his autobiography. He died in 1880, having been one of the most durable of Victorian men of letters.
authors.profile: Melodrama, burletta, extravaganza, farce, historical play and classical burlesque in a long series running from the last years of the George III reign into the 1870s; a considerable body of antiquarian writing on costume, heraldry, monuments and the stage; editorial work on early English romance and chronicle; and an autobiography. He is credited with the deliberate reform of the burletta into a lighter, literary form and with introducing archaeological accuracy into stage costume.
authors.style: A neat, literate and often rhymed dialogue, with a fondness for the anapaestic and the short lyric measure used in the extravaganza. His stage writing is brisk and allusive, treating supernatural machinery with a knowing lightness, and his antiquarian prose is precise, descriptive and illustrative.
authors.concerns: The archaeology of the dress and appointment of the stage. The literary reform of the small musical drama. The monopoly, licensing and condition of the theatres. The transmission of early romance and chronicle, and the antiquities of the British islands.
authors.significance: His vampire melodrama fixed the stage iconography of the undead and is the pivot of the decade's supernatural drama; his antiquarian work on costume and the stage founded the modern archaeological study of the English theatre, and his extravaganza is the origin of the classical burlesque tradition of the mid-century.
authors.uncertainty: The date of his first printed verse and of his earliest unacted dramas is uncertain, and the extent of his alterations to his own texts in the collected edition makes the relation of print to performance difficult to fix.

works.title: The Vampire; or, The Bride of the Islands

authors.name: James Shirley
authors.identity: The leading Caroline dramatist; a prolific author of comedies of fashionable London manners and of tragedies and tragicomedies, whose work T. S. Eliot called the 'last of the Elizabethan playwrights' and whose verse lyric 'Death the Leveller' remains famous.
authors.biography: Born September 1596 in London, educated at Merchant Taylors' School, St John's College, Oxford, and St Catharine's, Cambridge. Converted to Catholicism, he taught school then turned to the stage, writing some thirty plays for the King's Men and Queen Henrietta's Men (1625–42), including The Wedding, Hyde Park, The Cardinal, and The Lady of Pleasure. During the Civil Wars he served as secretary to the royalist Earl of Newcastle; at the Restoration his old plays were revived with success. He died on 29 October 1666 in London, reportedly perishing with his wife in the Great Fire's aftermath.
authors.profile: The chronicler of Caroline fashionable society, whose comedies of intrigue, gallantry, and manners look forward to Restoration comedy, and whose tragedies show the late Jacobean taste for moral complexity and rhetorical set pieces.
authors.style: Polished verse and prose; witty, fashionable dialogue; intricate plots of courtship and intrigue; sententious moralising; and a lyric grace ('Only the actions of the just / Smell sweet and blossom in the dust').
authors.concerns: Manners, fashion, and the morals of the town; love, honour, and gallantry; political corruption and tyranny; death and the levelling of rank; and the fate of virtue.
authors.significance: Shirley was the principal dramatist of the Caroline theatre and the direct model for Restoration comedy; his plays kept the professional drama alive in style until the theatres closed in 1642.
authors.uncertainty: Shirley's life is documented in outline; the exact dates and authorship of some plays, and of his posthumous Six New Plays (1653), remain matters of scholarship.
sources: An Essay on the Principle of Population: The 1803 Edition (Rethinking the Western Tradition)

authors.name: James Thomson
authors.identity: Scottish-born poet, best known for the blank-verse landscape cycle The Seasons, who helped introduce descriptive and sensuous nature poetry to English verse.
authors.biography: Thomson was born in the Scottish borders, the son of a minister, and studied divinity at the University of Edinburgh before abandoning the church for letters in London. He supported himself by tutoring and writing, and published Winter in 1726, soon expanding his descriptive pieces into The Seasons in its four-part edition of 1730. He wrote political and patriotic dramas, including Sophonisba (1730), and the Liberty poems (1734-1736). He enjoyed patronage associated with the Prince of Wales's circle at Leicester. He died suddenly in London in 1748.
authors.profile: A poet of nature, sensation, and civic patriotism; his central work observes the changing seasons in rich descriptive blank verse and infuses landscape with emotional and moral reflection.
authors.style: Sensuous, pictorial blank verse in long descriptive passages; accumulation of visual and atmospheric detail; a meditative, sometimes rapturous tone; and Miltonic diction and inversion.
authors.concerns: Nature as spectacle and moral teacher; the senses and the passions; British liberty, trade, and empire; the pleasure of the sublime and the picturesque; and the relation of landscape to feeling.
authors.significance: The Seasons transformed English nature poetry and anticipated the Romantic sensibility and the picturesque; it was one of the most influential and often-set poetic works of the eighteenth century.

authors.name: Jane Austen
authors.nationality: English; the novel of manners of the Romantic decade
authors.identity: Novelist; the principal English prose satirist of manners between the 1790s and the 1810s
authors.biography: She was born at the rectory of Steventon, where her father was the incumbent, the eighth child of a large clerical family, and she grew up in a household of reading, translation, theatre and joke-telling. From childhood she wrote for family entertainment: the early notebook writings of the 1790s, including an epistolary novel and a burlesque history, were performed and circulated among her brothers and sisters. The family's moves to Bath, to Southampton and finally to Chawton interrupted and then resumed her revision of the three novels she had drafted in the 1790s. Her father negotiated the publication of Sense and Sensibility in 1811 and her remaining novels followed with little public fame; she had no income of her own and published anonymously throughout her life. She died at Winchester in 1817, soon after completing her last novel, and a posthumous pair of novels with a biographical notice appeared in 1818, after which she disappeared from the English novel for half a century. Her manuscripts, letters and family papers survived through her sisters and nephews and were edited in the later nineteenth century.
authors.profile: Six completed novels, an early fragmentary and burlesque juvenilia, a short epistolary novel and a juvenilia history, all written between the mid-1790s and 1817. Her subject is consistently the marriage market of the provincial gentry and the moral education of a young woman whose judgement is tested against flattery, family pressure and her own feelings. Her method is concentrated: few characters, one district, a short period, and a plot advanced almost wholly by conversation, letter and misinterpretation. Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published posthumously.
authors.style: Free indirect discourse used to shade irony and sympathy without comment. Epigrammatic sententious openings and closings. Dialogue so patterned that character is exposed by speech rhythm rather than description. A sparing narrative voice whose moral weight falls on the qualifications of a single word. And a prosody of ordinary English speech carried in balanced clauses.
authors.concerns: The morality of prudence and the cost of self-deception; the education of feeling and its exposure to flattery. The economics of marriage, entail, living and dependence; the authority of family, rank and place. The claims of constancy against first impressions; the limits of sympathy and the difficulty of self-knowledge. The suspicion of novels and of the Gothic as a model of mind.
authors.significance: She transformed the eighteenth-century comedy of manners into a modern analytic prose fiction, and her technical example - the use of a limited intelligence and of reported speech as the instrument of moral judgement - established the line of English realism that the later nineteenth century took as its beginning. Her rehabilitation from Victorian obscurity made her the most continuously critiqued English novelist, and her work is now central to study of the period's sexual, economic and literary history.
authors.uncertainty: Her working chronology is contested in detail: the first-draft dates of the early novels, the order of revision, and the extent of the 1809-1817 recasting are argued from the family memoranda and her own letters rather than fixed by external record.

authors.name: Jane Taylor
authors.birthplace: London (Red Lion Street, Holborn); removed in infancy to Lavenham, Suffolk
authors.nationality: English; the dissenting and evangelical nursery verse of the early nineteenth century, and the moral essay and tale written for children and domestic periodicals
authors.identity: Nursery poet, hymn-writer and moral essayist; the younger of the Miss Taylors, whose joint Original Poems for Infant Minds rebuilt the English verse addressed to very young children, and the author of the poem 'The Star', known ever afterwards as 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star'.
authors.biography: Jane Taylor was born in London on 23 September 1783, the second of the eleven children of Isaac Taylor, a portrait-engraver of some reputation who turned to the dissenting ministry, and whose family removed to Lavenham in Suffolk while she was an infant, her father being settled there over a congregation. She was educated at home in a household of engravers, ministers and writers, and her printed work began in close collaboration with her elder sister Ann, who was her companion in authorship all her life. In 1804 the London firm of Darton published Original Poems for Infant Minds by the two Miss Taylors; the book was taken up at once by the evangelical and dissenting nursery and went through many editions. Rhymes for the Nursery followed in 1806, and in it appeared 'The Star', the poem which, set afterwards to an air from a French collection of melodies, became the most widely reprinted and best-known nursery rhyme in English. Hymns for Infant Minds of 1810 continued the same joint work. The earlier volumes were issued anonymously or under initials, and were read for a long time as the utterance of a single nursery voice. From about 1810, when the family removed from Lavenham, Jane's life was that of a dependent unmarried woman among her relatives, with long stays at Colchester, at Marazion in Cornwall, and at Ongar in Essex, where a brother held a ministry; her health steadily failed under constant literary work. She wrote increasingly in prose as well as in verse: Display of 1814, a set of tales and illustrations on the power of truth which reached several editions; Essays in Rhyme, on Morals and Manners of 1816; and the papers contributed to the Youth's Magazine which were collected after her writing as Contributions of Q. Q. to a Periodical Work. She died at Ongar in Essex on 13 April 1824 and was buried there, and her Memoir and Letters were published by friends and kindred, while her sister Ann outlived her by more than forty years and became herself a familiar religious writer.
authors.profile: Her work is an infant and nursery literature made deliberately: short poems in the simplest metres, addressed to children of two to seven, on small animals, on servants and children, on the weather, sleep and the duties of the family, together with hymns, and with prose tales and essays in which children reason their way out of a false step. The joint volumes of Original Poems for Infant Minds and Rhymes for the Nursery are the core, the former more narrative and argumentative, the latter more purely rhyming; Hymns for Infant Minds adapts the same diction to devotional use. Display, the Essays in Rhyme and the magazine papers signed Q. Q. extend the method into the essay and the tale, with a constant didactic aim and an unusual attention to the mind of the reader addressed.
authors.style: An extremely plain, light and conversational verse of short lines, of nursery rhyming couplet and ballad stanza, with a fondness for the question addressed to the child, for the personified small creature, and for the easy moral turn in the closing couplet. Her compression, the perfect fit of sound to sense, and the absence of archaism and of ornament give the best of her poems their lasting hold on memory. Her prose is clear, domestic, quietly humorous and didactic without declamation, nearer to the familiar essay and the tale than to the sermon; in the hymns and the graver verse a cooler and more reflective manner appears.
authors.concerns: The infant mind as a thing to be studied and not merely governed; the moral training of pity, truthfulness and self-command through the smallest daily incidents; the place of religion, of the natural world and of the family in a child's first knowledge; the claims and dignity of servants and dependents; the danger of false feeling in children's books, and the duty of writing to the actual capacities of the reader addressed.
authors.significance: With her sister she created the standard English nursery book of the nineteenth century: the Original Poems and the Rhymes were the volumes from which generations of children learned to read, and 'The Star' passed into a global children's song and is the single most quoted poem of the period's writing for the young. Her method of addressing the child's own mind helped to move English children's literature from instruction toward observation, and her prose and magazine work belongs to the large dissenting literature of domestic education which links the Edgeworth circle to the Victorian nursery.
authors.uncertainty: Her birthplace is given in most popular accounts as Lavenham in Suffolk, and in the modern scholarly and family record as Red Lion Street, Holborn, London, the family having removed to Lavenham in her infancy; the day is recorded as 23 September 1783. The division of authorship between the two sisters in the joint volumes of 1804 to 1810, which were published anonymously or under initials, is still not settled piece by piece, and the constant attribution of 'The Star' to Jane rests on family tradition and publisher's records rather than on a signed first text. The order and dates of her later residences, and the year in which her share in the nursery volumes came to be distinguished from her sister's, vary in the memoirs written by relatives.

authors.name: Jared Sparks
authors.nationality: American; the Unitarian Boston review circle about the North American Review and the Harvard divinity and professoriate, and the New England editorial school of national records
authors.identity: Editor, biographer, historian, Unitarian minister and educator; the first American who made the documentary edition of the founding records a great national work, and the chief editor, teacher and institutional man of letters of the generation between the centennial and the Civil War.
authors.biography: Sparks was born at Willington in the upland of Tolland County in Connecticut, the first of a large family of small means, and was put to school and to such Latin as the country afforded before his parents removed to the Ohio country while he was still a boy. There he taught, learned a little medicine and practised it, and read with that extraordinary diligence which made him a scholar without a college; after some years he returned east, was fitted for the college at the academy in New Hampshire, entered Harvard, and after his graduation studied for the ministry, being ordained a Unitarian minister and serving congregations in Massachusetts and in the west. From the first he combined preaching with authorship and editing: he wrote articles of history and biography for the journals, became connected with the North American Review at Boston and for some years conducted it, and at the same time planned the great work which gave him his fame - a collection of the letters and papers of the American ministers abroad during the Revolution, printed from the state records and furnished with notes and biographical and historical dissertations, in twelve volumes beginning in 1829. This was the first considerable documentary edition of the founding period in America, and it made him the recognised master of the method: he travelled and corresponded to copy and to purchase manuscripts, drew the historical societies into systematic work, and was the first American to hold a professorship of history, which he filled at Harvard. His life of the governor Morris of the Constitutional Convention, his collection of the writings of Washington with a history of his presidency, and his Library of American Biography, with its many volumes of the short life, made the biography of the republic a proper literary work for a generation of American readers. Public office followed his letters: he was chosen governor of Massachusetts, served in the Senate of the United States, and was placed at the head of Harvard College in 1849, which he governed until his resignation in 1853 left him free to return to his collections of documents and his editing of the records of the Revolution. He died at Cambridge on 14 March 1866, and was buried in the suburban cemetery there, the most employed and most copied American editor of his day, and the man by whom the public records of the founding period were first made accessible to historians.
authors.profile: His works are editorial, biographical and historical rather than imaginative: the twelve volumes of the Diplomatic Correspondence of the Revolution, the writings and the correspondence of the first president with a history of his administration, the memoirs and correspondence of the diplomatist of the Convention, the national biographical library and its many Lives, his reports and addresses on the historical manuscripts in Europe and at home, the editions of the treaties and of the public records, and the discourses, reviews and addresses on American history which he delivered to societies and on public occasions. He wrote, too, histories and biographies for schools and kept a great correspondence on the collecting and the publication of records; his editorial method - the transcription, the collation, the note and the biographical preface - was for forty years the American standard.
authors.style: A plain, careful, circumstantial and entirely unadorned prose, whether in the editorial preface, the note on a document or the biographical narrative; a habit of arrangement and of chronological and documentary evidence in place of argument or colour; in the Lives a brief, respectable and fact-laden manner which supplies the dates and the papers rather than the character; and in the Addresses and reviews a formal and patriotic diction of the historical societies of the period.
authors.concerns: The preservation and right reading of national records as a public duty; the diplomacy, the institutions and the motive of the Revolution as documentary history; the education of a republican people through biography and through exact narrative; the relation of the scholar to the state and to the college; the religious and civic obligations of the Unitarian ministry and of the historical society; the character and the motives of the founders, studied in their own letters.
authors.significance: He created the American documentary edition and with it the modern American historical profession's apparatus: the Diplomatic Correspondence, the Washington and the Morris collections and the national biography set the standard of scholarly editing and of public provision for records, and his advocacy gave the historical societies their work and the state legislature its first appropriations. As the first professor of history in the United States, as the editor whose methods were imitated for half a century, and as the minister, governor, senator and president of Harvard who joined letters to office, he is the type of the man of letters as a national institution in the generation before the Civil War.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of his Harvard course and of his first settled ministry, and the order of his Ohio years, are stated variously in the memoirs and in the biographical dictionaries, the chronology of his share in the conduct of the review being complicated by the anonymous practice of the journal; some of the anecdotes of his poverty and of his western years depend upon the memoir written by himself and by his family.

works.title: The Diplomatic Correspondence of the American Revolution

authors.name: Jedidiah Morse
authors.nationality: American; New England Congregational (Orthodox standing order) and early-national scientific writing
authors.identity: Congregational minister, geographer and publicist; the "father of American geography" whose school textbooks defined geographic education for a generation, and the chief orthodox polemicist against Unitarianism
authors.biography: Jedidiah Morse was born at Woodstock, Connecticut, on 23 August 1761, the son of a Congregational minister of modest means, and was educated at home and in the local schools before entering Yale College, from which he graduated in 1783. He studied divinity, was licensed and ordained in 1785-86, held a brief pastorate at Norwich, and in 1789 began the long pastorate of the First Church at Charlestown, Massachusetts, which he served until ill health and the controversies he had stirred forced his retirement to New Haven about 1820. From his student years he wrote for the classroom: Geography Made Easy (1784), the two-volume American Geography (1789) with its maps, The American Universal Geography (first edition in the early 1790s, repeatedly revised and reissued through the 1820s), and The American Gazetteer (1796) - the first American gazetteer - together with atlases, a Universal Geography for schools, and a series of enlargements that made him the standard authority on the physical and political geography of the new nation and a supplier of maps to Congress and to state governments. A convinced Federalist and opponent of the French Revolution, he kept politics inside his religion: he helped found Andover Theological Seminary in 1808 as an orthodox alternative to Harvard, backed foreign missions and the missionary printing that flowed through the Missionary Herald, and served as corresponding secretary of Massachusetts mission societies. In September 1822 he preached the annual sermon before the Association of Ministers of Massachusetts at Cambridge, an explicit challenge to Unitarian teaching and an argument that associations should examine orthodoxy before ordination; its publication, requested by the Association, detonated the Unitarian controversy in the standing order, producing replies from William Ellery Channing and others and years of pamphlet war. He died at New Haven on 9 June 1826 and was buried in Grove Street Cemetery, leaving sons - among them Samuel Finley Breese Morse - who carried his public prominence into art and invention.
authors.profile: Morse's output is essentially informational and polemical rather than imaginative: school geography and gazetteers, maps and their explanatory keys, a compendious New England history, sermons, election and missionary discourses, tracts on political character, and the 1822 Cambridge sermon. He writes as a compiler-didact, arranging observation under moral and providential headings; his prose exists to be learnt, recited and believed.
authors.style: Expository prose of tremendous compression: enumerative, topographical, and laden with statistics, distances and tables, yet framed by homiletic reflection on climate, character and providence. The schoolbooks are deliberately plain and question-driven. In the sermons and tracts the same clarity turns adversarial - syllogistic argument, pointed biblical inference, and an insistence on definitions, tests and confessions of faith.
authors.concerns: How a young republic might know its own space and produce its own textbooks instead of importing British ones; the relation of climate, geography and national character; the authority of scripture and of confessional standards in a changing New England; the danger of theological liberalism to social order; education, missions and print as instruments of civic and religious unity.
authors.significance: Morse established American geography as a school subject and a publishing industry, and his gazetteers and maps were the reference works of the early republic; his 1822 Cambridge sermon is conventionally taken as the opening gun of the Unitarian-Congregational split that remapped New England religion and led directly to the founding of Harvard Divinity's rival, Andover, and to the institutional separation of Unitarianism. As a Federalist churchman he also links partisan politics, missions and education in a single career.
authors.uncertainty: The exact first-publication year of The American Universal Geography varies in the sources consulted (the early 1790s; commonly 1793, with a two-volume edition of 1792 also cited), as does the end-date of his Charlestown pastorate (given as 1819 or 1820). The precise day of the 1822 Cambridge sermon is not fixed by the accounts checked, though its place before the Association of Ministers and its 1822 date are standard. His role as an Indian-trades agent and the later Texas-colonization accusation against him belong after this period and remain disputed.

authors.name: Jeremy Bentham
authors.identity: Law reformer and moral philosopher, founder of classical utilitarianism, who measured institutions by pleasure and pain and subjected the common law, the church and the prison to the test of utility.
authors.biography: Born in London in 1748 into a wealthy family of attorneys, a child prodigy in Latin and French law books, he was educated at Queen's College, Oxford, and was called to the bar in 1769, though he never practised and soon abandoned the profession to write on legislation. He inherited property and leisure, attached himself to no party, and passed his life in lodgings and in correspondence, drafting codes, inspecting prisons, and corresponding with rulers and reformers across Europe and America. Two long stays at the estates of his brother Samuel, the engineer in Russia, sharpened his ideas about inspection and the organisation of labour. He wrote against Blackstone in the 1760s, published the Fragment on Government anonymously in 1776, the Defence of Usury in 1787 and the Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation in 1789. His Panopticon scheme and his writings on colonies and on judicial procedure belong to the 1790s; the coded works edited for him by Dumont appeared in the 1800s, and his attack on Blackstone's Commentaries remained in manuscript until the twentieth century. He died in London in 1832, having asked that his body be dissected and preserved as his auto-icon.
authors.profile: A jurist of facts and consequences, whose vocabulary of utility, felicity and the greatest number recast moral and legal argument as an arithmetic of interests.
authors.style: Technical, taxonomic, tireless prose; long definitions, enumerated situations and coined terms; polemic conducted through analysis rather than rhetoric; a satirist's dryness about lawyers and priests.
authors.concerns: The greatest happiness principle; the anatomy of law, sovereignty and obligation; punishment, deterrence and the inspection of the idle; the interests of women, of colonial subjects and of animals; the corruption of church, university and common law.
authors.significance: He founded utilitarian ethics and systematic law reform, shaped Victorian policing, education and welfare legislation, and made the critical test of institutions their consequences for the greatest number.
authors.uncertainty: The order of his vast unpublished manuscripts, much of it first printed by editors after his death, makes the dating of his ideas a continual problem.

works.title: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

authors.name: Jeremy Taylor
authors.identity: Anglican divine and devotional writer, called 'the Shakespeare of the divines'; his Holy Living (1650) and Holy Dying (1651) are the supreme prose achievements of Caroline Anglican piety, rich in imagery, learning, and moral casuistry.
authors.biography: Born August 1613 at Cambridge, son of a barber; educated at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge (BA 1630, MA 1634) and All Souls, Oxford. Patronised by William Laud and Charles I, he became a royalist chaplain, was twice imprisoned during the Civil Wars, and was deprived of his living. In seclusion in Wales he wrote his great devotional manuals Holy Living (1650) and Holy Dying (1651), and the casuistical Ductor Dubitantium (1660). At the Restoration he was consecrated Bishop of Down and Connor (1661) and Vice-Chancellor of Trinity College, Dublin; he died on 13 August 1667 at Lisburn.
authors.profile: The eloquent Caroline divine whose devotional prose combines baroque imagery, immense learning, and tender moral guidance, treating the whole of life as a preparation for a holy death.
authors.style: Lush, metaphorical, Latinate prose; abundant simile and classical and scriptural allusion; casuistical moral reasoning; and a rich, musical rhythm.
authors.concerns: Holy living and dying; Christian virtue, patience, and repentance; liberty of conscience and toleration (The Liberty of Prophesying, 1647); moral casuistry; and Anglican devotion.
authors.significance: Holy Living and Holy Dying shaped English devotional prose and the Anglican ideal of the good life and good death for centuries; Taylor's eloquence and advocacy of toleration mark him as one of the greatest prose writers and most liberal-minded of the Caroline divines.
authors.uncertainty: Taylor's life is documented; his imprisoned royalist years and some details of his preferment rest on tradition and ecclesiastical records.

works.title: The Rule and Exercises of Holy Dying
The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living

sources: The Poems of Charlotte Smith

authors.name: Joanna Baillie
authors.nationality: Scottish; the tragedy of the passions and the dramatic verse of the Romantic decade
authors.identity: Tragic dramatist and poet; the most serious English-language woman dramatist of the age and the theorist of the analysis of a single passion
authors.biography: She was the daughter of a Scottish university teacher of divinity and grew up in the Lanarkshire manse before the family removed to Glasgow and then to London, where her brother became one of the most distinguished physicians of the day. She was formed by a long private reading in the old drama and in Greek and modern tragedy rather than by the theatre itself, and she wrote from early womanhood with the plan of a series of plays each founded on one passion analysed in its progress. The first series appeared by subscription in 1798 and was praised by the most influential critic of the age as the work of a serious tragic mind; two further instalments of the series followed in the next fifteen years, and one tragedy of the number, of a man consumed by hatred, was acted at the patent theatre and held the stage with great success in the 1820s. She published a volume of dramatic and descriptive verse and a tragedy attempted at Drury Lane which failed in spite of management support, and she wrote much occasional and ballad verse for the annuals. She never married, lived with her brother and his family and afterwards in her own house in north London, and became the centre of a long literary circle of visitors and correspondents. She died in 1851 at Hampstead, leaving unpublished papers.
authors.profile: A planned series of plays on the passions, issued in several volumes over fourteen years, of which the tragedy of hatred is the enduring piece; a volume of metrical sketches and descriptive and occasional verse; a ballad and legend of the Scottish past; and an important preface and argument setting out the theory of the single-passion analysis. Her dramaturgy is analytic and rhetorical, built on soliloquy and on the progressive disclosure of one governing feeling rather than on incident.
authors.style: Correct and sustained blank verse, closer to the eighteenth-century school of tragedy than to the looser practice of her contemporaries, with a strong use of sententious generalisation and of the interrupted speech of self-examination. Her prose argument is plain and methodical, and her ballad and descriptive verse is quieter and more colloquial than her tragedy.
authors.concerns: The anatomy of the passions and their tyrannical progress. The obligations and injuries of family and benefaction. Revenge, hatred and their effect on the mind that harbours them. The responsibility of the dramatist to moral philosophy. Women's authority in the serious drama and the difficulty of the stage for a woman's writing.
authors.significance: She is the principal tragic poet of the Romantic period who was also a woman, and her series is the most systematic attempt of the age to unite the moral-philosophical analysis of the passions with regular drama. The successful revival of her best play by a famous actor of the 1820s gave her a place in the acting repertory, and her theoretical preface remains a key document of Romantic dramatic thought.
authors.uncertainty: The date at which the several plays of the series were composed is uncertain, since the published volumes were assembled from a much longer period of writing, and the extent of her brother's household's influence on her publication is imperfectly documented.

authors.name: Joel Barlow
authors.nationality: American; the New England letters of Hartford and New Haven in the 1780s, and the revolutionary and deist circle of Americans and French philosophes in the 1790s
