The volume 'Poems' appeared on 3 March 1817 and 'Endymion: A Poetic Romance' in 1818, and the attacks on both in Blackwood's Magazine and the Quarterly Review fixed the 'cockney' warfare that shadowed his career. In 1818 he walked in the Lake District and with Reynolds in Scotland, nursed his brother Tom, who died of consumption that December, and fell in love with Fanny Brawne at Hampstead. At Wentworth Place in 1819 he wrote 'Isabella', 'The Eve of St. Agnes', 'Lamia', the Hyperion poems, and the spring odes; with health failing and marriage impossible he sailed for Italy with Joseph Severn in September 1820 and died near the Piazza di Spagna in Rome on 23 February 1821, aged twenty-five. He lies in the Protestant Cemetery at Rome under the stone he dictated, recording only that here lies one whose name was writ in water.
authors.profile: His output is short and dense: the early Spenserian and Homeric exercises, the 1816-18 sonnets, epistles, and 'Sleep and Poetry'; the four-book romance 'Endymion'; the metrical tales 'Isabella' and 'Lamia' and the romance 'The Eve of St. Agnes'; the two Hyperion poems; the odes of 1819 with 'To Autumn' and the late lyrics; and two unfinished attempts in tragedy and dramatic sketch. His prose letters - to Reynolds, to Woodhouse, to Bailey, to the Dilkes and Woodleys, and to Severn from Rome - carry his most quoted critical statements on negative capability, the poetical character's want of self, and the world as a vale of soul-making.
authors.style: Sensation rendered as texture: heavy sensory concreteness, compound epithets, synaesthesia, and a slow, vowel-weighted music; an insistence on the palpable image that stays before the senses instead of resolving into argument. He rebuilt the English ode in stanzas of his own devising, handled the Spenserian and Elizabethan stanza and the Italian romance stanza with a romantic ear, and turned the sonnet into a vehicle of high statement about poetry, mortality, and the imagination.
authors.concerns: Identity and the dissolution of the self in other existences (negative capability); the agonistic love of the old poets - Chapman, Spenser, Shakespeare, Milton; beauty, truth, and the evidence of the imagination; early death, consumption, and the endurance of verse; the ethics of making in a reviewing market that punished ambition of humble origin; the Hellenic world as a school of form; the search for a theodicy without theology in the 'vale of Soul-making'.
authors.significance: Within a decade of his death he had become one of the most reprinted poets in English, and the 1819 ode sequence set the model for later aesthetic and sensualist traditions. His letters made him the Romantic period's most quoted theorist of imagination and selflessness; the 'cockney' attacks on him sharpened the class war in Romantic letters, and his death at twenty-five in Rome fixed the enduring myth of the early-martyred poet which Shelley's 'Adonais' first consecrated and which Hunt's and Woodhouse's papers afterwards preserved.
authors.uncertainty: The exact course of his last illness (consumption, with a fatal haemorrhage, aggravated by the treatment he received) and the weight of the hostile criticism in hastening his decline were argued from 1821 onward and remain matters of interpretation rather than record; the dates of his engagement to Fanny Brawne are better documented than the later legend that he died of a broken heart.

works.title: Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil
On First Looking into Chapman's Homer
The Fall of Hyperion: A Dream

authors.name: John Leland
authors.identity: antiquary; poet; King's Antiquary
authors.biography: Born in London about 1503; educated at St Paul's School under William Lily and at Cambridge, Oxford, and Paris. Commissioned in 1533 as King's Antiquary, he travelled England and Wales in the 1530s and 1540s recording libraries, monuments, and topography, planning a vast description of Britain he never completed. He went mad in the late 1540s and died on 18 April 1552. His Itinerary remained in manuscript until the eighteenth century.
authors.profile: The father of English antiquarianism. His Itinerary notes preserve the record of monastic libraries on the eve of the Dissolution and remain a primary source for English topography; his Cygnea Cantio (1545), a Latin poem on the Thames, and his other Latin verse earned him a European reputation in his lifetime.
authors.style: The note-taking style of the field antiquary: inventories, measurements, and reports jotted on the road, without literary finish.
authors.concerns: The recovery of British antiquity; the description of the realm; the preservation of manuscripts and monuments against the destruction of the Dissolution.
authors.significance: Founded the study of British antiquities and preserved irreplaceable evidence of medieval England; his collections were quarried by every later antiquary from Bale to Camden.
authors.uncertainty: None significant; the Itinerary's exact itinerary chronology is editorial.
genres: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
sources: The Complete Poetical Works of Samuel Taylor Coleridge (2 volumes)

authors.name: John Lilburne
authors.identity: Leveller leader and pamphleteer; 'Freeborn John', whose tracts and trials demanded popular sovereignty, extended suffrage, and the legal rights of the 'freeborn Englishman', making him a founding figure of English radical and constitutional argument.
authors.biography: Born c. 1614–15, probably at Greenwich, Kent; apprenticed to a London clothier and drawn to Puritan dissent. Imprisoned by Star Chamber (1638) for distributing unlicensed books, he was whipped and pilloried but defied the court, refusing to incriminate himself — a landmark for the right against self-incrimination. He fought for Parliament in the Civil Wars, then turned against the Grandees, co-authoring Leveller petitions and The Agreement of the People and repeatedly publishing tracts demanding legal rights and popular sovereignty. Repeatedly imprisoned by both Royalists and Parliament/Cromwell, he briefly became a Quaker before his death on 29 August 1657.
authors.profile: The tireless polemicist of the 'freeborn' rights of Englishmen, whose pamphlets and courtroom defiance advanced principles of due process, self-incrimination, and popular consent that echo in modern constitutional law.
authors.style: Forceful, plain, popular polemic; legal and scriptural argument; petitions, tracts, and declarations; and a combative, self-justifying, energetic prose.
authors.concerns: Popular sovereignty and suffrage; the rights of the freeborn Englishman; legal process, self-incrimination, and imprisonment; the Leveller programme; and resistance to arbitrary power.
authors.significance: Lilburne and the Levellers produced the earliest sustained English arguments for democracy and legal rights; his defence against self-incrimination influenced the development of due process and the Fifth Amendment, and his tracts are foundational to radical constitutionalism.
authors.uncertainty: Lilburne's birth year and birthplace are uncertain; his voluminous pamphlets and trials are well documented, though his shifting allegiances complicate his record.
sources: Memoirs of the Life and Writings of Thomas Chalmers, D.D., LL.D. (4 volumes)

authors.name: John Locke
authors.identity: Philosopher and political theorist; author of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), the foundational text of British empiricism, and the Two Treatises of Government (1689), whose defence of natural rights, consent, and toleration shaped the Enlightenment and modern liberalism.
authors.biography: Born 29 August 1632 at Wrington, Somerset, educated at Westminster and Christ Church, Oxford, where he turned from scholasticism to medicine and the new science, associating with Boyle and Sydenham and joining the Royal Society (1668). He became physician and close adviser to Anthony Ashley Cooper (later Earl of Shaftesbury), was drawn into Whig politics and the Exclusion Crisis, and fled to Holland (1683–89). Returning with William of Orange after the Revolution, he published in 1689 the Essay Concerning Human Understanding, the Two Treatises of Government, and A Letter Concerning Toleration, and later Some Thoughts Concerning Education (1693) and The Reasonableness of Christianity (1695). He spent his last years at Oates in Essex in the Masham household, dying on 28 October 1704.
authors.profile: The empiricist who argued that the mind at birth is a blank slate furnished only by experience, and the liberal who grounded government in consent, natural rights, and the pursuit of happiness — a prose of patient, plain, argumentative clarity.
authors.style: Clear, methodical, argumentative prose; plain style as an ideal; careful definition and example; and a moderate, reasonable, conversational tone addressed to the 'underlabourer's' task.
authors.concerns: Knowledge, ideas, and empiricism; personal identity and the limits of understanding; natural rights, consent, and government; religious toleration; property and money; and education.
authors.significance: Locke founded British empiricism and modern liberal political theory, profoundly influencing Berkeley, Hume, the American and French revolutions, and all subsequent Western political thought; his Essays and Treatises are also classics of English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Locke's life is thoroughly documented through his correspondence and journals; the authorship of the Two Treatises (published anonymously) was long uncertain but is now securely his.

works.title: The Reasonableness of Christianity, as Delivered in the Scriptures

sources: The Collected Letters of Sir Humphry Davy (4 volumes)

authors.name: John Lydgate
authors.identity: poet; translator; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: Benedictine monk of the abbey of Bury St Edmunds, ordained priest in 1397, and educated (perhaps at Gloucester College, Oxford) before a career as the most prolific English poet of the fifteenth century. He enjoyed the patronage of Henry V, Humphrey Duke of Gloucester, and the London civic elite; late in life he received a royal pension, and he died c. 1449, buried at Bury.
authors.profile: Author of the Troy Book (1412–20), the Siege of Thebes (c. 1420–22), the Fall of Princes (1431–38), the Temple of Glas (c. 1400–05), the Life of Our Lady, and an immense output of mummings, pageants, saints' lives, and devotional and occasional verse — over 140,000 lines attributed to him.
authors.style: Chaucerian forms (rhyme royal, couplets) with aureate diction and rhetorical amplification; copious moralizing; the 'Lydgate line' (often headless pentameter) that became the standard of mid-century verse.
authors.concerns: The moral exemplarity of history (the falls of princes); the honour of England and its rulers; devotional and civic piety.
authors.significance: The dominant English poet between Chaucer and Skelton, read and imitated throughout the fifteenth century (and printed by Caxton and de Worde); his Fall of Princes shaped the Tudor mirror-for-magistrates tradition.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the canon is so large that attributions remain in flux.
movements: The Graveyard School and Preromantic Meditation
themes: Tyranny and the abuse of power
sources: The English Poems of George Herbert

authors.name: John Lyly
authors.identity: prose writer; dramatist; courtier
authors.biography: Grandson of William Lily the grammarian; educated at Magdalen College, Oxford (BA 1573, MA 1575). His Euphues (1578) made him famous overnight. From 1583 he wrote court comedies for the Children of Paul's and the Children of the Chapel, and sat in Parliament four times. He spent years petitioning in vain for the post of Master of the Revels and died in relative poverty, buried 30 November 1606.
authors.profile: Inventor of Euphuism — the antithetical, allusion-laden prose style of Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit (1578) and Euphues and His England (1580) — and author of the elegant court comedies Campaspe (1584), Sapho and Phao (1584), Gallathea (c. 1588), Endymion (1588), Midas (1589), Mother Bombie (c. 1590), and Love's Metamorphosis (c. 1590).
authors.style: Euphuism: balanced antitheses, elaborate similes drawn from the natural histories of Pliny, proverbial wisdom, and a polished, self-conscious wit carried into his prose-like dramatic dialogue.
authors.concerns: The education and conduct of the courtier; the claims of love against the claims of state; the language of power and persuasion.
authors.significance: His prose style dominated fashionable writing for a decade and his court comedies laid the foundation of high English comedy; Shakespeare parodied and absorbed him in equal measure.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; some plays are dated conjecturally from performance records.
sources: Washington Irving: History, Tales, and Sketches (Library of America)

authors.name: John Marston
authors.identity: dramatist; satirist; clergyman
authors.biography: Baptized 7 October 1576; son of a lawyer of the Middle Temple, where he himself was admitted in 1592. He took his BA at Brasenose College, Oxford, in 1594. He wrote verse satires and plays for the boy companies, fought the war of the theatres with Jonson (who caricatured him in Poetaster), then abruptly left the stage in 1608, took holy orders in 1609, and spent his last years as rector of Christchurch, Hampshire. He resigned his living in 1631 and died in London on 25 June 1634.
authors.profile: Verse satires The Scourge of Villainy and The Metamorphosis of Pygmalion's Image (1598); plays include Antonio and Mellida (c. 1599–1600), Antonio's Revenge (c. 1600), The Malcontent (1604), The Dutch Courtesan (1605), and Eastward Ho (1605, with Chapman and Jonson).
authors.style: A deliberately harsh, snarling satiric style — neologism, paradox, and a bitter wit aimed at courtly vice and poetic affectation alike.
authors.concerns: The exposure of vice; malcontentedness as a moral stance; the corruption of the court and the law.
authors.significance: The malcontent he created in The Malcontent became one of the defining types of Jacobean drama and inspired Shakespeare's and Webster's handling of the figure.
authors.uncertainty: The reasons for his abrupt retirement from the theatre are unknown.
themes: The marriage market and the limited estate
sources: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson

authors.name: John Millar
authors.identity: Regius Professor of Civil Law at Glasgow, who turned the history of ranks and of property into an explanation of law, government and the condition of women.
authors.biography: Born at the manse of Kirk o'Shotts in 1735, the son of the parish minister, he was educated at Glasgow, where he sat under Adam Smith, and became an advocate. With the support of Adam Smith and of the Duke of Buccleuch he was appointed in 1761 to the Glasgow chair of civil law, which he held until his death. His Origin of the Distinction of Ranks (1771) explained subordination as the consequence of subsistence, marriage and property rather than of nature, and drew a friendly critique of its chapter on women from John Dalton, printed with later editions. His Historical View of the English Government from the Settlement of the Saxons to the Revolution of 1688 (1787) applied the same method to English liberty and to the growth of the commercial orders. A sympathiser with the French Revolution after 1789, he was harassed by the alarm of the 1790s. He died on 30 May 1801.
authors.profile: The most systematic of the Scottish historians of society, who wrote the equality of conditions as a question of law, labour and domestic authority.
authors.style: Clear, cumulative, lecture-hall prose; long historical sequences argued from causes; a lawyer's precision about ranks, tenures and rights; comparatively little ornament.
authors.concerns: The dependence of political authority on property; the origins of rank, servitude and gender subordination; the history of law as social history; the foundations of English liberty and of representative government.
authors.significance: He carried stadial conjectural history into the analysis of class and of the family, and became a chief source for later theories of social development, including the tradition that linked property to political power.
authors.uncertainty: His published works are only parts of a large lecture output, some of which survives in student notes of uncertain date.

works.title: Observations Concerning the Distinction of Ranks in Society

authors.name: John Milton
authors.identity: Poet, polemicist, and Latin secretary to the Commonwealth; the author of Paradise Lost and the greatest English epic poet after Chaucer, whose career moved from lyric and masque through two decades of political prose to the late biblical epics and tragedies written in blindness.
authors.biography: Born 9 December 1608 in London, son of a scrivener and composer; educated at St Paul's School and Christ's College, Cambridge (BA 1629, MA 1632), where he wrote his early odes and masques. After six years of private study at Horton (1632–38) producing 'L'Allegro', 'Il Penseroso', 'Comus', and 'Lycidas', he travelled in Italy (1638–39), meeting Galileo. From 1641 he threw himself into the Puritan cause, writing anti-prelatical tracts, the divorce pamphlets, Areopagitica (1644), and, after the regicide, The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates (1649) and Eikonoklastes; he served as Latin Secretary to the Commonwealth under Cromwell, defending the republic in Latin (Defensio Pro Populo Anglicano, 1651). Totally blind by 1652, widowed twice, and imprisoned briefly at the Restoration, he composed and dictated Paradise Lost (1667), Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes (1671). He died 8 November 1674 in London.
authors.profile: The poet who claimed to write with 'no middle flight' and to 'justify the ways of God to men'; his career is the most consciously ambitious in English literature, yoking classical and Hebrew learning, republican politics, and Protestant faith to a grand style of Latinate blank verse.
authors.style: Unrhymed blank verse of great sonority and extended periodic syntax; dense allusion to classical, biblical, and Renaissance sources; grand invocations and epic similes; a learned, muscular diction; and, in the prose, a fierce polemical vigour with sprawling, powerful sentences.
authors.concerns: Liberty of conscience, republicanism, and the defence of regicide; the problem of evil and free will; obedience and temptation; the fall and regeneration of mankind; the vocation of the poet as prophet and public teacher; marriage and divorce; the corruption of the church.
authors.significance: Paradise Lost is the supreme epic of the English language and reshaped English poetry and politics for three centuries; his prose tracts are foundational documents of free speech and republican theory, and his example defined the role of the poet as moral and political witness.
authors.uncertainty: Milton's life is exceptionally well documented (Edward Phillips's and John Aubrey's early lives); the dating of Paradise Lost's composition and the precise nature of his blindness remain matters of scholarship.

works.title: Comus (A Masque Presented at Ludlow Castle)
On the Morning of Christ's Nativity
The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce
The Ready and Easy Way to Establish a Free Commonwealth
The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates

sources: The Life of Washington (The John Harvard Library)

authors.name: John Mirk
authors.identity: homilist; Augustinian canon
authors.biography: An Augustinian canon and prior of Lilleshall Abbey, Shropshire, active in the 1380s and 1390s; he compiled the Festial, a cycle of English sermons for the feasts of the church year, with a companion instructional work for parish priests (Instructions for Parish Priests).
authors.profile: Author of the Festial (c. 1380s) and Instructions for Parish Priests, among the most widely copied English sermon collections of the later Middle Ages.
authors.style: Plain, lively English sermons built on exempla, miracles, and verse tags; the vivid storytelling of popular piety adapted for parish preaching.
authors.concerns: The instruction of the laity in the feasts, sacraments, and moral duties of the church year.
authors.significance: The Festial is the classic collection of the English late medieval sermon and a principal witness to orthodox vernacular preaching in the age of Lollardy.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; details come almost entirely from his own prefaces.
themes: Colonial enterprise and the New World
sources: The Poems of Alexander Pope, Twickenham Edition (11 volumes)

authors.name: John Neal
authors.nationality: American; the Baltimore and Philadelphia periodical world and the aggressive New England literary nationalism that preceded the Young America movement
authors.identity: Novelist, poet, critic, editor and lecturer, the most combative and most influential American reviewer of the 1810s and 1820s, the chief American champion of Byron and of the new British and German poetry, and the boldest early claimant of an American literature independent of English judgment.
authors.biography: Neal was born at Portland in the district of Maine, then part of Massachusetts, of a family of small means; his father was a schoolmaster, the household fell into difficulty early, and the boy was put behind a shop counter instead of being sent to a college. Largely self-taught, he was bound to learn law and read it, went to Baltimore in 1816, was admitted to the bar there but practised little, and gave himself to the newspapers and the weekly literary journals of the city. He edited at Baltimore a short-lived review of arts and books called The Portico in 1818, and for a season a political paper; his poems of 1819 and 1820, his frontier tale of 1822 and his novel of the revolutionary year followed fast, and made him the most forward and most quarrelsome of the young American men of letters. His survey of American writing, contributed to a Scottish monthly from the winter of 1824 into 1825, was the first attempt to take the whole of the native literature as a single history and made him the most quoted critic of the decade. He passed to England in 1823 and remained in London and on the continent until 1827, knew the painters, publishers, reformers and periodical writers of the London literary world, contributed at length to the Edinburgh magazine which had taken him up, and in those years made the acquaintance of the young American poet of the Baltimore and Richmond periodicals whose cause he afterwards pleaded against his own former friends. His novels of the later 1820s, which turned to colonial history and to social and religious doctrine, sold poorly and one of them provoked a scandal of its own; he married in 1828, and after a return to Portland he gradually reinvented himself as the respected man of letters of his native city, writing history and biography for young readers, reminiscence and domestic papers, lecturing on American society, and taking part in civic, temperance and charitable work. He died at Portland on 20 June 1876, having long abandoned the aggressive manner that had made his name notorious, and leaving a body of criticism which the twentieth century reprinted as the founding document of American literary nationalism.
authors.profile: His work covers almost every province of the letters of his generation: verse in the Byronic and the descriptive manner, tales and novels of border adventure, society and doctrine, a large body of critical and programmatic prose, editorial miscellany, lectures, reminiscence and autobiography. His critical papers are the first sustained American argument for literary nationalism and for a realism of language and character, and they attacked at once the caution of American letters and its deference to Edinburgh and London. His fiction is experimental in scale and in manner, opening the Revolution and the western settlements to a colloquial, sensational and digressive narrative voice; the later books on the founders of independence, on Catholicism and on social questions belong to the respectable Victorian career that succeeded the earlier warfare.
authors.style: A deliberate vehemence and abruptness of style, with short paragraphs, exclamations, coined words, Americanisms and colloquialisms forced upon the page, and an incessant personal challenge to reader and opponent alike; in the fiction an expansive, digressive and sensational manner, with direct address, self-quotation, unfinished plots and a roughness of execution that later critics reclaimed as a native modernism. The criticism is aphoristic and combative, the autobiography garrulous and self-justifying.
authors.concerns: The independence of American letters from English judgment and imitation; the originality of the individual genius and the cowardice of the deferential critic; realism of language and the dignity of common speech; the claims of the new poetry and of the romance; national character, the Puritan inheritance and the duties of the American writer to his own public; the condition of women, Roman Catholicism, slavery and temperance in their American forms.
authors.significance: He was the first American critic of sustained force and a principal transmitter of the new British and German poetry to American readers, and his demand for an American literature of the present shaped the generation that followed, from the Young America writers to the romancers of the 1840s and 1850s. His survey of American writing supplied the first history of the whole native field and helped make the phrase American literature current; his advocacy was decisive for the American recognition of Edgar Allan Poe, whom he introduced to the Richmond and Philadelphia journals, and his irregular, open-form novels are now read as part of the native origin of American prose fiction.
authors.uncertainty: Much of his periodical writing of the Baltimore years appeared over shifting names and is still imperfectly identified; the names sometimes proposed for him in general reference works cannot be confirmed, and only the Byronic and Scottish-magazine pen name recorded in his own bibliography is secure; part of his early career is known chiefly from his own later reminiscences, which are self-serving and variously dated.

authors.name: John Newton
authors.identity: Former slave-ship captain turned Anglican minister and hymn-writer, whose Authentic Narrative (1764) and Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (1788) made a converted trader the most searched witness against the trade.
authors.biography: Born in London in 1725, the son of a sea captain, and left largely to his own devices after the early death of his mother in his seventh year, he ran to sea as a lad, was pressed into the navy, flogged for desertion and then carried on the slave ships between West Africa and the Americas, where for a time he was in effect the property of an African owner. A violent storm in 1748 opened a religious conversion that he never forgot, although he continued in the trade and rose to be the master of a slave ship before illness and conscience ended his sea service in the mid-1750s. He left the sea in the mid-1750s, held a minor shore appointment, married and studied for the ministry, and published in 1764 An Authentic Narrative, an account of his mercy and of his former occupation that was widely read. About the same time he was appointed curate of Olney in Buckinghamshire, where he became the friend and guide of William Cowper and gave the village its hymn book of 1779. Presented in 1780 to St Mary Woolnoth in the City of London, he preached there for the rest of his life, consulted the parliamentary abolitionists and gave them Thoughts upon the African Slave Trade (1788), a belated and unsparing self-accusation. He died in London in December 1807, having written the inscription for his own grave.
authors.profile: A pastor of the converted sinner who wrote his own career as a case of grace and then pressed that case into public argument against the trade that had made him.
authors.style: Plain, nautical and self-examining narrative prose; homely, concrete hymn verse in familiar metres; sermons built of plain doctrine pressed home; a letter-writer's intimacy and candour.
authors.concerns: Grace, remorse and the reality of change; the guilt of the slave trade and the complicity of churches and nations; providence in the lives of sailors; assurance, obedience and comfort for the afflicted.
authors.significance: His narrative and his 1788 tract supplied the abolitionist movement with its most credible first-hand testimony, and his hymns, written with Cowper, remain part of the ordinary worship of English-speaking Christianity.
authors.uncertainty: His early years and the details of his service in Africa are known chiefly from his own narrative, which shapes the facts to a providential design.

authors.name: John of Salisbury
authors.identity: philosopher; political theorist; bishop
authors.biography: Educated at Paris under the greatest masters of the twelfth-century schools — Abelard, William of Conches, Gilbert of Poitiers — he returned to England as secretary to Archbishop Theobald and then to Thomas Becket, whose exile he shared and whose murder he witnessed (1170). He became bishop of Chartres in 1176 and died there on 25 October 1180.
authors.profile: Author of the Policraticus (1159), the first great medieval treatise on political theory; the Metalogicon (1159), a defence of the trivium; the Historia Pontificalis; and a celebrated correspondence.
authors.style: Classical learning worn lightly and worn for moral ends; the organic metaphor of the body politic; satiric portraits of courtiers; the first medieval theory of tyrannicide.
authors.concerns: The limits of royal power; the education of the prince and the clerk; the relation of church and state; the value of humane letters.
authors.significance: The Policraticus is the most important political treatise between Augustine and Aquinas and the fountainhead of medieval constitutionalism; its organic state theory shaped political thought for centuries.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his Paris studies is reconstructed from the Metalogicon.
movements: Austen and the Novel of Manners
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Eighteenth-Century Poetry

authors.name: John Ramsay McCulloch
authors.nationality: Scottish and British - a Romantic-period political economist, statistician and reviewer: an Edinburgh-trained Ricardian who made his career in London, and the genre-defining writer of the expository treatise, the review article and the statistical dictionary.
authors.identity: A publicist and systematiser of political economy rather than an original theorist - the man who made Ricardo a curriculum. His proper forms are the expository treatise, the review article, the pamphlet addressed to a parliamentary committee, and the statistical dictionary built from consular returns; his most lasting single performance is the Introductory Discourse prefixed to Adam Smith, where a science is given a history, a pedigree and a canon of texts.
authors.biography: John Ramsay McCulloch was born at Whithorn, Wigtownshire, on 1 March 1789, eldest son of Edward McCulloch, laird of Auchengool in the stewartry of Kirkcudbright, and Sarah Laing. His father died while he was a child and his grandfather taught him first; after his mother's remarriage he went to school at Kinross, then attended Edinburgh University without taking a degree, sitting with Sir John Leslie, who became his friend, and with Thomas Brown, from whom he learned to distrust metaphysics. He entered a writer to the signet's office and soon left it in disgust. His Essay on a Reduction of the Interest of the National Debt (1816) drew Ricardo's correspondence, and his Edinburgh Review essay on Ricardo's Principles of 1818 began twenty years of periodical writing, seventy-six articles in all by 1837. He helped to found The Scotsman in 1817, edited it from 1818 to 1820 and wrote its economic copy for a decade. In 1824 he delivered the Ricardo Memorial Lectures in London, which became A Discourse on the Rise, Progress, Peculiar Objects, and Importance of Political Economy (1824), the Britannica article on Political Economy, and The Principles of Political Economy with a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science (1825), the standard textbook until Mill's treatise of 1848. The Essay on the Circumstances which Determine the Rate of Wages (1826) gave the English-speaking world the wages-fund doctrine, and his edition of Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations with an Introductory Discourse appeared in 1828, the year he took the unendowed chair of political economy at the new University of London. Principles, Practice and History of Commerce (1831) and his Dictionary of Commerce and Commercial Navigation (1832) were followed by the Descriptive and Statistical Account of the British Empire (1837), the geographical dictionary of 1841, the Treatise on Taxation and the Funding System (1845), The Literature of Political Economy (1845), his edition of Ricardo's Works (1846) and the Political Economy Club's collections of scarce tracts (1856-59). Comptroller of the Stationery Office from 1838, he died there on 11 November 1864 and lies in Brompton Cemetery.
authors.profile: His work is systematic rather than imaginative, and divides into four bodies. Treatise and textbook: A Discourse on the Rise, Progress, Peculiar Objects, and Importance of Political Economy (1824) and The Principles of Political Economy, with a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science (1825; enlarged editions 1830, 1843, 1849), with the applied studies An Essay on the Circumstances which Determine the Rate of Wages (1826), the Principles, Practice and History of Commerce (1831) and the treatises on Taxation and the Funding System (1845) and on Succession to Property Vacant by Death (1848). Reference and statistics: the Dictionary, Practical, Theoretical and Historical, of Commerce and Commercial Navigation (1832), the Descriptive and Statistical Account of the British Empire (1837) and the geographical dictionary of 1841. Editing and bibliography: Smith's Wealth of Nations (1828), Ricardo's Works (1846), The Literature of Political Economy (1845) and the tract collections edited for the Political Economy Club and for Lord Overstone (1856-59). Periodical prose: seventy-six Edinburgh Review articles (1818-37) and a decade of economic leading in The Scotsman.
authors.style: Bald, emphatic and expository: a prose of definition, enumeration and example, written to be taught from. He repeats himself across book, review and pamphlet until a doctrine becomes a commonplace, and his habitual move is to dispute an opponent's terms rather than his facts. Abstractions are handled concretely - the cask of new wine that gains five pounds in the cellar carries the whole question of profit - and his tables of prices, rents, colonies and population are themselves the evidence. Caricature caught the manner with the accent: Carlyle's McGroudy, Peacock's MacFungus, Christopher North's Stot and the Mordecai Mullion parody of 1826 all satirise a dogmatic, repetitive, plain-spoken Scot.
authors.concerns: The labour theory of value and the impossibility of an invariable measure of value; rent and the corn laws; the wages-fund and the condition of the labouring classes; profit, interest and whether time can of itself produce value; taxation, the funding system and the national debt; free trade, colonization and emigration; the statistical knowledge of a commercial state as the ground of legislation; the history, literature and right boundaries of political economy as a science; and the diffusion of economic orthodoxy by textbook, review, professorial chair and discussion class.
authors.significance: He was the leader of the Ricardian school after 1823 and the man who turned it into a teachable public doctrine: his Principles was the orthodoxy that Mill superseded, was translated into French, German and Italian, and made him the most quoted and most abused of economists in his own generation. His editions of Smith and of Ricardo fixed the canon of classical political economy, and their prefaces, with The Literature of Political Economy, founded the history and bibliography of the subject. The Dictionary of Commerce and the Statistical Account of the British Empire set the model of the official factual compendium, and his appointment in 1828 made him the first professor of political economy in the University of London.
authors.uncertainty: The dates are firm and agreed (born 1 March 1789, died 11 November 1864). The birthplace is given as Whithorn, Wigtownshire, by the Dictionary of National Biography and repeated by modern encyclopedias and by Wikipedia, but the family's standing is reported differently: the Dictionary of National Biography calls his father laird of Auchengool, while social-science encyclopedias describe a small landowner who lost his fortune, so the economics of McCulloch's childhood cannot be stated precisely. The end of his University College professorship is disputed: the Dictionary of National Biography and the Macmillan Encyclopedia of Economic History say he resigned the unendowed chair in 1832, while the History of Economic Thought archive has him holding it until 1837. He is sometimes described as an editor of the Edinburgh Review; the succession from Francis Jeffrey in October 1829 belongs to MacVey Napier, and his relation to the Review should be stated as contributor and its principal writer on political economy. His Treatise on Taxation and the Funding System is dated 1845 by the Dictionary of National Biography and by first-edition imprints, but appears under 1863 in some modern lists, presumably a later issue. The surname is printed both McCulloch and M'Culloch, and the count of seventy-six Review articles is the Dictionary of National Biography's estimate rather than a census.

authors.name: John Rastell
authors.identity: printer; lawyer; playwright
authors.biography: Born in London about 1475; a lawyer of the Middle Temple and the brother-in-law of Thomas More, whose circle he printed. His press issued More's early works and his own plays — The Four Elements (c. 1520) and the translation Calisto and Melebea (c. 1530) — and his chronicle The Pastime of People (c. 1529). His opposition to the clergy's exactions brought him imprisonment, and he died in prison in June or July 1536.
authors.profile: The first English printer-playwright. The Four Elements is a didactic interlude teaching cosmology and geography through drama, and The Pastime of People compresses the history of Britain into a popular chronicle; his press was the vehicle of the More circle and of the earliest English humanist drama.
authors.style: Instruction through entertainment; the interlude as lecture hall and theatre at once; plain prose and functional verse.
authors.concerns: Popular education in the new learning; the reform of clerical exactions; law, printing, and the spread of knowledge.
authors.significance: A founder of the English printing trade in its humanist phase; his interludes and chronicles made the new learning available to a popular audience.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the date of his death (1536) is established by legal records.
themes: Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
sources: The Edinburgh Edition of Walter Scott's 'Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border' (3 volumes)

authors.name: John Redford
authors.identity: playwright; composer; master of the choristers at St Paul's
authors.biography: Born about 1486; almoner and master of the choristers at St Paul's Cathedral, where he trained the boys who performed his play Wit and Science (c. 1539). He was a noted composer and organist — John Heywood married his daughter — and died in 1547.
authors.profile: Author of Wit and Science, the most accomplished of the school moralities: the allegory of Wit's wooing of Lady Science, with the giant Tediousness, the Vice Idleness, and the comic conversion of the booby Ingnorance, written for boy actors with songs and dances. The play survives in a single manuscript with its music cues.
authors.style: The morality convention refreshed with music, dance, and schoolroom comedy; allegorical personification handled with theatrical tact.
authors.concerns: The marriage of wit and learning; the discipline of the school; the education of boys through play and music.
authors.significance: The finest of the school interludes and a direct ancestor of the academic drama and the court masque; his St Paul's boys became one of the great Elizabethan playing companies.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the play's date (c. 1539) is editorial.
themes: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
sources: The Works of Thomas De Quincey (21 volumes)

authors.name: John Skelton
authors.identity: poet; satirist; orator regius; tutor to Prince Henry
authors.biography: Educated at Cambridge and Oxford, where he was laureated (1488), and at Louvain (1492); he styled himself 'poet laureate'. Tutor to Prince Henry (the future Henry VIII) from about 1496 to 1502, he became rector of Diss in Norfolk (c. 1504) and 'orator regius' at court. His later career was a running satirical war with Cardinal Wolsey, whom he attacked in verse so freely that he took sanctuary at Westminster in 1523, where he died on 21 June 1529.
authors.profile: The dominant English poet of the early Tudor period and the inventor of the 'Skeltonic' line — short, breathless, rhymed couplets of irregular length. His canon runs from the dream-satire The Bowge of Courte (c. 1499) through the mock-elegy Philip Sparrow (c. 1505), the low-life tour de force The Tunning of Elinour Rumming (c. 1517), the morality play Magnificence (c. 1515–23), and the great anti-Wolsey satires Speke Parrot (1521), Colin Clout (c. 1522), and Why Come Ye Nat to Courte? (c. 1522–23), to the self-crowning dream vision The Garland of Laurel (1523).
authors.style: The Skeltonic: tumbling short lines, obsessive rhyme, macaronic Latin, colloquial diction, and a satirical voice that moves between learned allusion and street abuse; also a master of the aureate, 'laureate' high style.
authors.concerns: The corruption of the clergy and the court; the duties of kingship; the poet's laureate authority; the defence of the English language against Latinate pretension.
authors.significance: The first great English satirist of the print era and the bridge between the medieval and Renaissance poetries; his Skeltonics were imitated for a century and admired by the Elizabethans, who read him as the scourge of Wolsey.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace uncertain; some Skeltonic attributions among minor poems remain debated.

works.title: Why Come Ye Nat to Courte?

sources: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, 2 volumes

authors.name: John Stow
authors.identity: antiquarian; chronicler; tailor
authors.biography: Born in the parish of St Michael Cornhill, London, about 1525, son of a tallow-chandler. A tailor by trade, he gave up the craft for antiquarian study, publishing chronicles and surveys on which he spent his modest means. In old age he was licensed to beg, and he died in poverty on 6 April 1605; his monument stands in St Andrew Undershaft.
authors.profile: The Survey of London (1598; enlarged 1603), the loving topographical description of the city, and A Summary of English Chronicles (1565), the basis of his larger Annales (1580, 1592).
authors.style: Plain, affectionate, accumulative prose — the voice of a man walking his city street by street, ward by ward, remembering what was there before.
authors.concerns: The preservation of civic memory against Reformation destruction and urban change; the antiquity and honour of London.
authors.significance: The Survey is the foundation of London historiography and an irreplaceable record of the pre-Fire city.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.
sources: Adeline Mowbray: or, The Mother and Daughter (Broadview Editions)

authors.name: John Tillotson
authors.identity: Latitudinarian divine and Archbishop of Canterbury; the most influential preacher of the late seventeenth century, whose clear, reasonable, moral sermons defined Anglican pulpit prose and the ideal of a tolerant, rational Christianity.
authors.biography: Born 1630 at Sowerby, Yorkshire, educated at Clare Hall, Cambridge (Fellow). A Puritan by upbringing, he conformed at the Restoration, held preferment, and became Dean of St Paul's (1664) and a leading latitudinarian preacher. He supported the Revolution of 1688, was made Archbishop of Canterbury (1691) under William III, and worked for comprehension and toleration. His sermons — reasonable, moral, and elegantly plain — were immensely popular and widely published (posthumous collected volumes 1695–1704). He died on 22 November 1694.
authors.profile: The model Latitudinarian preacher, whose sermons argued for a reasonable, benevolent, practical Christianity in a lucid, classical prose that set the standard for Augustan pulpit and essay style.
authors.style: Clear, plain, elegant, well-reasoned prose; the moral sermon of practical divinity; classical balance and lucidity; and an irenic, moderate tone.
authors.concerns: Reasonable religion and natural theology; morality and practical Christianity; toleration and comprehension; the relation of reason and revelation; and the church's public role.
authors.significance: Tillotson's sermons were among the most read prose of the age, shaping Anglican latitudinarianism, the plain prose style, and eighteenth-century moral and religious writing (admired by Addison, Swift, and Johnson).
authors.uncertainty: Tillotson's birth year is approximate; his life and sermons are well documented, and his posthumous publications were edited by others.
sources: Mrs. Sherwood and Her Books for Children

authors.name: John Toland
authors.identity: Ulster-born freethinker, heterodox scholar and hard-line Whig pamphleteer, a founding figure of English deism after Christianity Not Mysterious (1696).
authors.biography: Born in 1670 on the Inishowen peninsula, of a Gaelic family whose name was anglicised from O'Tolian, he studied at Glasgow, at Edinburgh, where he took his MA, and at Leiden, acquiring an extraordinary range of languages. Christianity Not Mysterious (1696), arguing that the gospel holds nothing properly above reason, was ordered burned by civil and ecclesiastical authority and made him the most attacked writer of his generation. He moved in London Whig and commonwealth circles, edited Milton's prose, defended Lucan against his classical detractors, and wrote on party management, the Hanoverian succession and the Bible as history: Nazarenus (1718) recovered apocryphal gospel fragments, and Tetradymus (1720) gathered four sceptical treatises. His political work carried him between Dublin, London and the Hague, where he cultivated Leibniz and Berkeley; he died at Putney on 11 March 1722.
authors.profile: A combative polymath of letters, party and scripture, who treated the history of religion as a history of power and of priestly imposture.
authors.style: Dense, allusive and polemic; scholarly footnotes used as weapons; blunt deistical reasoning dressed in commonwealth rhetoric; a restless, digressive pamphlet energy.
authors.concerns: The reduction of mystery to evidence; tolerance and its clerical enemies; the political history of the biblical canon; pantheistic materialism and the eternity of matter; the management of parties and the secret history of states.
authors.significance: He fixed the agenda of deism and of the historical criticism of Scripture, gave the commonwealth Whigs a model of scholarship in the service of liberty, and provoked the century's long rearguard action of Christian apologetics.
authors.uncertainty: His degrees, employments and embassies are imperfectly documented and rest partly on his own claims; several works appeared anonymously.

works.title: A Philosophical Inquiry Concerning Human Liberty

authors.name: John Trevisa
authors.identity: translator; scholar; priest
authors.biography: Cornish-born scholar of Exeter College and Queen's College, Oxford, fellow of Queen's and later vicar of Berkeley, Gloucestershire, in the household of Thomas, Lord Berkeley, for whom he translated major Latin works into English prose.
authors.profile: Translator of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon (completed 1387, with his famous Dialogue on Translation between a Lord and a Clerk) and of Bartholomaeus Anglicus's De proprietatibus rerum (1398); also translated works of religious instruction and political theory.
authors.style: Vigorous, expansive English prose; the confident handling of learned Latin vocabulary and its rendering into idiomatic English; a stated program of translation for the benefit of English readers.
authors.concerns: The provision of learning in English; the dignity of the vernacular; the duties of lordship and clergy.
authors.significance: With the Wycliffite translators, Trevisa helped create the learned English prose of the late fourteenth century; his Dialogue on Translation is a classic statement of vernacular self-consciousness.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the extent of his role in the Wycliffite Bible translation is debated.
sources: Poetry and Politics in the English Renaissance, revised edition

authors.name: John Vanbrugh
authors.identity: Restoration playwright and, later, the great baroque architect of Blenheim Palace and Castle Howard; his bawdy, energetic comedies The Relapse (1696) and The Provoked Wife (1697) revived the Restoration comedy of manners at the turn of the century.
authors.biography: Born January 1664 (baptised 24 January) in London, of a Flemish merchant family; educated at Chester and briefly a soldier and an officer in the East India Company. Imprisoned in the Bastille (1690–92) on suspicion of espionage, he turned to the stage on his release, producing The Relapse; or, Virtue in Danger (1696) and The Provoked Wife (1697), huge successes that scandalised the reformers. He also wrote The False Friend (1702) and farces. From about 1702 he became, astonishingly, a leading architect (Knighted 1714), designing Blenheim Palace and Castle Howard in the English baroque. He died on 26 March 1726.
authors.profile: The robust, good-humoured comic writer whose plays are broad, bawdy, and structurally bold, contrasting with Congreve's polish; his Lord Foppington and his treatment of marital misery are Restoration comedy at its most energetic.
authors.style: Broad farce and bawdy wit; energetic, colloquial prose; bold double plots; memorable comic types (Lord Foppington); and a genial, unsentimental view of vice.
authors.concerns: Sexual appetite and marriage; social pretension and foppery; virtue and its dangers; and the comedy of manners under moral attack.
authors.significance: Vanbrugh's comedies are the last great works of Restoration comic drama and a bridge to eighteenth-century comedy; his subsequent career as England's foremost baroque architect makes him a unique figure in the arts.
authors.uncertainty: Vanbrugh's early life (soldiering, Bastille) is documented but partly legendary; his birth date is approximate, and the transition to architecture is remarkable but well recorded.

works.title: The Relapse; or, Virtue in Danger

sources: The Letters of William Lloyd Garrison, Volume I: I Will Be Heard!, 1822-1835

authors.name: John Webster
authors.identity: dramatist
authors.biography: Son of a prosperous London coachmaker and member of the Merchant Taylors' Company; born about 1580. He entered the Middle Temple about 1598 and began collaborating with Dekker and others (Westward Ho, 1604; Northward Ho, 1605) before the independent tragedies that made his name. Nothing is known of his last years; he was dead by about 1634, when Heywood called him 'that worthy poet' in the past tense.
authors.profile: The White Devil (1612), The Duchess of Malfi (c. 1614), The Devil's Law Case (c. 1619), and Appius and Virginia (c. 1626, with Heywood); his famous character essays were appended to the 1615 Overbury collection.
authors.style: A poetry of darkness: lurid emblems, macabre wit, great set-piece dirges, and a sombre moral seriousness beneath the sensational surface.
authors.concerns: Corruption of courts; the abuse of women by rank and power; the gulf between appearance and worth; death as the great leveller.
authors.significance: With The Duchess of Malfi he wrote what many rank the greatest non-Shakespearean tragedy of the English stage; his heroines and villains shaped the Jacobean imagination.
authors.uncertainty: Both birth and death dates approximate; almost all personal details are inferred from records of the Coachmakers' Company and the Middle Temple.
genres: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse
themes: Natural history, science, and the poetic eye
sources: The Works of Maria Edgeworth (12 volumes)

authors.name: John Wesley
authors.identity: Anglican priest, evangelist and organiser of the Methodists, whose sermons, journals, hymnals and rules of society made a religious revival into a permanent connection.
authors.biography: Born at Epworth in 1703, the fifteenth of the children of Samuel Wesley, a country rector, and of Susanna Wesley, who governed the household and its education, he was sent to the Charterhouse and then to Christ Church, Oxford, where he was elected a fellow and took his degrees. Ordained in the Church of England, he went with his brother Charles to Georgia as a missionary in the mid-1730s and came home a failure in his own judgement. At a meeting in Aldersgate Street in May 1738 he described the assurance of his pardon, and in the following year he began to preach out of doors in Bristol at Whitefield's example, since the churches would not open to him. For fifty years he travelled through Britain and Ireland on horseback, organising societies, classes and bands, training lay preachers and holding annual conferences, and he wrote and printed for the movement with tireless industry: sermons on several occasions, Notes upon the New Testament, a Journal, a Christian Library and the Collection of Hymns of 1780. He defended the salvation of slaves in Thoughts upon Slavery (1775) and in his last years encouraged the parliamentary agitation against the trade. He died in London in March 1791, having preached almost to the end, and was buried beside his chapel in City Road.
authors.profile: A preacher-writer of enormous practical energy, whose plain prose and vigorous verse carried a revived religion to colliers, miners and farm servants.
authors.style: Direct, urgent, colloquial sermon prose; rules, minutes and class lists shaped for use; a journal kept for the public; hymn and paraphrase verse of muscular, repetitive simplicity.
authors.concerns: Original sin and universal redemption; justification by faith and the witness of the Spirit; Christian perfection and the means of grace; free grace against Calvinist decree; Methodist discipline, education and the duty of saving souls.
authors.significance: He made Methodism, the largest religious movement of the century in the English-speaking world, and shaped the hymnody, revival practice and later social history of Britain and America.
authors.uncertainty: The tallies of his sermons and mileage are traditional estimates rather than records, and the editing of his Journal for publication was a work of self-presentation.

works.title: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists
A Collection of Psalms and Hymns
Explanatory Notes Upon the New Testament

authors.name: John Wilkins
authors.identity: Clergyman, natural philosopher, and organizer of science; the central figure of the 'invisible college' that became the Royal Society, whose works on a universal philosophical language and on the plurality of worlds made him a pioneer of scientific communication.
authors.biography: Born 1614 (baptised 1 January 1614/15), probably at Fawsley, Northamptonshire; educated at New Inn Hall and Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served as chaplain and, under the Commonwealth, as Warden of Wadham College, Oxford (1648), where he gathered the circle of experimental philosophers (including Boyle, Wren, and Hooke) that formed the nucleus of the Royal Society. He married Robina, sister of Oliver Cromwell (1656), was deprived at the Restoration but reconciled, became vicar of Polebrook and then Dean of Exeter. His works include The Discovery of a World in the Moone (1638) and An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language (1668), a scheme for a universal language. He died on 19 November 1672.
authors.profile: The genial organizer and populariser of the new science, whose speculative works on the moon, cryptography, and a philosophical 'real character' promoted experimental learning and clear communication.
authors.style: Clear, expository, speculative prose; scientific and linguistic schemes; popularisation of the new philosophy; and an irenic, moderate clerical tone.
authors.concerns: The new experimental philosophy and its institutions; a universal philosophical language; the plurality of worlds and astronomy; cryptography and communication; and religious latitude and toleration.
authors.significance: Wilkins was the practical founder of the Royal Society's collaborative ethos and a pioneer of the search for a universal language and of scientific popularisation; his Essay influenced later philosophers of language and utopian writers.
authors.uncertainty: Wilkins's birthplace and early life are uncertain; his career is documented through university, church, and Royal Society records.

works.title: An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language
The Discovery of a World in the Moone; or, A Discourse Tending to Prove That 'Tis Probable There May Be Another Habitable World in That Planet

sources: The Whole Disgraceful Truth: Selected Letters of Lady Caroline Lamb

authors.name: John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester
altNames: John Wilmot, Second Earl of Rochester
authors.identity: Libertine poet, courtier, and wit of Charles II's court; the greatest of the Restoration rakish versifiers, whose savage satires, bawdy lyrics, and bleak 'Satyr against Reason and Mankind' combine intellectual rigour with scandalous candour.
authors.biography: Born 1 April 1647 at Ditchley, Oxfordshire; educated at Burford and Wadham College, Oxford, then travelling in France and Italy. He became a favourite of Charles II, distinguished himself in the Second Dutch War (1665–66), and lived a notorious life of debauchery, abduction (of the heiress Elizabeth Malet, whom he married), imprisonment, and wit. His verse circulated largely in manuscript among the court wits; he wrote for the stage (a version of Valentinian, 1685) and translated Lucretius and Seneca. After a profound deathbed conversion under the bishop Gilbert Burnet, he died at Woodstock on 26 July 1680, aged 33. His Poems on Several Occasions appeared posthumously (1680).
authors.profile: The libertine philosopher-poet whose work interrogates reason, appetite, and human pretension with a cynical honesty and formal skill that modern critics rank among the finest of the age.
authors.style: Biting satiric verse; the bawdy and obscene lyric; a philosophic bleakness and intellectual paradox; vigorous colloquial energy; and skilful use of the couplet and the song.
authors.concerns: Reason and appetite; the hypocrisy of civilization and court life; sexual libertinism; mortality and the vanity of human pride; and, at the last, repentance and faith.
authors.significance: Once dismissed as merely obscene, Rochester is now recognised as a serious and original satirist whose 'Satyr against Reason and Mankind' is a major philosophic poem and whose influence extends to the modern revival of interest in Restoration libertinism.
authors.uncertainty: Rochester's canon is unstable because most poems circulated anonymously in manuscript; attribution of individual verses is often uncertain and disputed.

works.title: A Satire Against Reason and Mankind

sources: Early American Drama

authors.name: John Wyclif
authors.identity: theologian; philosopher; reformer
authors.biography: Fellow and master of Balliol College, Oxford, and the dominant figure in the university's theological debates from the 1360s; doctor of theology c. 1372. From c. 1376 he developed the doctrines — dominion founded on grace, the primacy of scripture, and the rejection of transubstantiation — that were condemned by the Blackfriars council of 1382. Retired to his living at Lutterworth, Leicestershire, where he died on 31 December 1384; his remains were exhumed and burned as a heretic in 1428.
authors.profile: Author of an immense Latin corpus — De Civili Dominio (1375–76), De Veritate Sacrae Scripturae, De Officio Regis, the Trialogus, the Postilla, and many sermons — and traditionally credited (though modern scholarship dissents) with inspiring the English Wycliffite Bible.
authors.style: Relentlessly logical scholastic argument deployed for radical ends; a plain, urgent English style in the sermons attributed to him.
authors.concerns: The poverty of the church and the renunciation of temporal lordship; scripture as sole authority; the eucharist; the rights of kings against the papacy.
authors.significance: The intellectual founder of Lollardy and the most consequential English heretic: his movement produced the first English Bible and permanently altered the terms of English religious debate.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the extent of his personal role in the English Bible translation is disputed.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Ben Jonson

authors.name: Jonathan Swift
authors.identity: Anglo-Irish satirist, pamphleteer, and cleric, Dean of St Patrick's Dublin, widely regarded as the greatest prose satirist in English.
authors.biography: Born in Dublin, Swift was educated at Trinity College Dublin and took holy orders in the Church of Ireland. He worked in London as secretary to Sir William Temple and later sought Anglican preferment, aligning with the Tories as editor of the Examiner. His political and literary writings include the Battle of the Books (1704), the Bickerstaff pamphlets, and A Tale of a Tub (1704). The Drapier's Letters (1724) made him a popular hero in Ireland for resisting Wood's halfpence. His masterpiece, Gulliver's Travels, appeared in 1726, followed by the Modest Proposal (1729). In his last years a probable illness impaired his speech and memory; he died in Dublin in 1745.
authors.profile: A prose satirist and moralist whose range runs from savage irony to learned parody and invective; he wrote fiction, pamphlets, sermons, journals, and verse, always in service of unmasking pride, folly, and abuse of power.
authors.style: The plain, concrete style he prized, with short clauses and deadpan seriousness; sustained irony and personation; grotesque and anatomical imagery; and a harsh, uncompromising satiric logic.
authors.concerns: The pride and rationalisation of humankind; the abuse of learning, religion, and language; English domination of Ireland and political corruption; and the tension between reason and the passions.
authors.significance: The foremost English-language satirist and a defining prose stylist; Gulliver's Travels and the Modest Proposal became touchstones of satire, and his Irish writings shaped modern Irish political consciousness.
authors.uncertainty: The diagnosis of his later mental and physical decline is uncertain and retrospectively labelled by modern physicians; his parentage and early years in Dublin are partly known only from contested accounts.

works.title: A Project for the Advancement of Learning
A Proposal for Correcting, Improving and Ascertaining the English Tongue
Peri Bathous, the Art of Sinking in Poetry
The Predictions for the Year 1708 (Isaac Bickerstaff Esq.)
The Works of Mr. Martinus Scriblerus
Verses on the Death of Dr. Swift

authors.name: Joseph Addison
authors.identity: English essayist, poet, dramatist, and Whig politician who, with Richard Steele, created the periodical essay and shaped Augustan letters.
authors.biography: Born at Milston in Wiltshire, the son of a clergyman, Addison was educated at the Charterhouse and at Queen's College, Oxford, where he became a fellow. Early Latin and English verse won him patronage, and he travelled on the Continent before returning to public life. With Richard Steele he wrote for the Tatler and then founded the Spectator, which established the modern periodical essay. His blank-verse tragedy Cato (1713) was widely performed and admired. He held government posts, including a secretaryship of state, as a prominent Whig, and edited the Whig journal the Guardian. He died in London in 1719.
authors.profile: Best remembered as a moral essayist and critic of taste whose Spectator papers observe manners, commerce, reading, and sociability with urbanity and restraint. He also wrote neoclassical tragedy and didactic and occasional verse.
authors.style: Clear, balanced, conversational prose in the middle style; a temperate, courteous humour; aphoristic moral reflection; and a preference for good sense, decorum, and polished plainness over extravagance.
authors.concerns: Cultivation of polite sociability and taste; the moral duties of commercial and leisure classes; religion regulated by reason; classical learning made accessible; and the refinement of public manners through letters.
authors.significance: Co-creator of the periodical essay, a form that influenced eighteenth-century prose, journalism, and the idea of a reading public; Cato was a model of neoclassical English tragedy and a lasting political emblem.
authors.uncertainty: His birth date is recorded, though the precise circumstances of his Oxford fellowship and his share of authorship in the joint periodicals with Steele remain debated by scholars.

works.title: Remarks on Several Parts of Paradise Lost

sources: William Cobbett: The Politics of Style (Cambridge Studies in Romanticism)

authors.name: Joseph Butler
authors.identity: Anglican bishop and the most formidable Christian apologist of the century, author of the Analogy of Religion (1736) and of the sermons on human nature.
authors.biography: Born at Wantage in Berkshire in 1692 into a Presbyterian family, he was designed for the Dissent and educated under Dissenting tutors in London before turning to the Church of England and entering Oriel College, Oxford. His published correspondence with Samuel Clarke on the foundation of virtue and moral government (1716) gave him an early philosophical reputation, and he was chosen a fellow of his college. As preacher at the Rolls Chapel he delivered the sermons on human nature, conscience and self-love printed in 1726. The Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed, to the Constitution and Course of Nature (1736), answering the deists of his day by arguing that the course of nature is as full of mystery and difficulty as revelation, made him the acknowledged champion of his church. Preferred by Queen Caroline, he was clerk of the closet, then bishop of Bristol, dean of St Paul's and, from 1750, bishop of Durham. He died at Bath on 16 June 1752.
authors.profile: A casuist of common sense who argued from probability, analogy and the structure of the mind rather than from demonstration.
authors.style: Balanced, deliberate, heavily qualified prose; a preacher's plainness sharpened by philosopher's distinctions; patient enumeration of cases and the famous weight given to probability.
authors.concerns: Conscience as supreme authority within the mind; selfishness and benevolence; the analogies between nature and revelation; theodicy and future punishment; the historical evidences of Christianity.
authors.significance: His Analogy set the terms of British natural theology for a century, and his account of conscience and of the plurality of motives shaped British moral philosophy and theology alike.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his academy years and his Oxford degrees is imperfectly documented.

works.title: Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
The Analogy of Religion, Natural and Revealed, to the Constitution and Course of Nature

authors.name: Joseph Glanvill
authors.identity: Latitudinarian clergyman, philosopher, and apologist for the new science; his Scepsis Scientifica (1665) argued a constructive scepticism and the value of experimental enquiry, and his writings on witchcraft defended the reality of spirits against atheism.
authors.biography: Born c. 1636 at Plymouth, educated at Exeter College and Lincoln College, Oxford (MA 1658), where he came under the influence of the Platonic and latitudinarian circle. A Fellow of the Royal Society (1664), he published The Vanity of Dogmatizing (1661), revised as Scepsis Scientifica (1665), advocating a modest, probabilist scepticism and the new experimental philosophy, and Essays on Several Important Subjects (1670). As a clergyman (vicar of Frome and later a prebendary of Worcester) he wrote latitudinarian sermons and, famously, defended belief in witchcraft and spirits (Saducismus Triumphatus, 1681, posthumous) as a bulwark against atheism. He died on 4 November 1680.
authors.profile: The 'sceptical' apologist who turned doubt to the service of the new science and of religion, arguing for a plain, probabilist, experimental approach to knowledge in an influential, readable prose.
authors.style: Clear, persuasive, latitudinarian prose; philosophical scepticism turned constructive; advocacy of the Royal Society's plain style; and a reasoned, moderate argumentative manner.
authors.concerns: Scepticism and the limits of dogmatism; the new experimental philosophy; the defence of religion and of spirits against atheism; the reform of prose style; and religious toleration and latitude.
authors.significance: Glanvill was a leading populariser of the Royal Society's ideals and of latitudinarian theology; his Scepsis Scientifica influenced Locke and the plain-style movement, and his witchcraft writings reflect the period's contested boundary between science and superstition.
authors.uncertainty: Glanvill's birth year is approximate and his life documented mainly through his works and Royal Society records; his witchcraft defence has been much debated by historians.

works.title: The Vanity of Dogmatizing; or, Confidence in Philosophy

sources: Monk Lewis: A Critical Biography

authors.name: Joseph Lancaster
authors.nationality: English (Quaker); British and trans-Atlantic monitorial / Lancasterian education movement
authors.identity: Educational pioneer and popular writer on mass schooling; the demonstrator-organizer whose name attached to the undenominational "Lancasterian" system of mutual instruction
authors.biography: Joseph Lancaster, a Friend by birth and breeding, was born on 25 November 1778 in the Borough side of Southwark, London, the son of a working Quaker family; he was educated at a Friends' school and served twice as an assistant teacher before, in 1798 and at about nineteen, he gathered a handful of poor neighbourhood children into a borrowed room to teach them reading, writing and arithmetic on a plan of his own. His method - the school divided into classes each governed by a pupil monitor, taught from cards and slates, drilled by signals, rewarded by badges and regulated by emulation, so that one master might superintend hundreds at trivial cost - filled his room and then, in 1801, larger premises in Borough Road, where his Free School became the most visited educational spectacle in Europe. Merchants, Whigs and dissenters subscribed; the Prince of Wales and King George III were shown the school, and royal and parliamentary money followed. In 1803 he published Improvements in Education, as it Respects the Industrious Classes of the Community, a plain, boastful, persuasive tract that ran through many editions and translations and made "Lancasterian" schooling a movement in Britain, Ireland and the United States. From 1805 he was embroiled in the priority quarrel with Andrew Bell, whose Madras monitorial plan he had learned of and adopted, and whose supporters accused him of borrowing the system while his own patrons quarrelled over the money he raised; a Royal Lancasterian Institution was formed in 1808 with royal patronage, and after his dismissal in 1814 its rivals merged their efforts into the British and Foreign School Society of 1814, which carried the Lancasterian schools forward. His public career was ruined by the mismanagement of funds and by prosecution in 1813, and he spent his last two decades promoting his system abroad: invited to New York in 1815 by De Witt Clinton and the city's friends of education, where Lancasterian schools were established and he was paid for superintendence; then to Venezuela and New Granada, where Bolívar's government employed him to organize schooling; and later in British North America, where he continued to found schools. Returning to New York, he was killed in a street accident on 23 October 1838, trampled by a horse, still lecturing and planning schools. His writings are practical - the 1803 Improvements, its enlarged editions with instructions, lessons and accounts of the school, and a stream of letters, replies and appeals - a literature of demonstration rather than of argument.
authors.profile: Lancaster was an author of one sustained subject: how to teach numbers of poor children cheaply. Improvements in Education (1803, enlarged 1805 and 1807) mixes rules, lesson plans, prices, class returns and testimonials; his later pamphlets, letters and reports are appeals to subscription and to government, and his American writings adapt the plan to public schooling. Nothing in his output is imaginative, and the rhetorical power of the books comes from the visible school.
authors.style: Direct, unlearned and urgent, in the plain Quaker idiom of fact and testimony; long enumerations of apparatus, method and cost, punctuated by personal narrative and by effusive appeals to patrons and to the reader's philanthropy. The prose is procedural - rule following rule - but the argumentative move is always demonstration: the school itself as evidence.
authors.concerns: Cheap mass instruction as the remedy for poverty and ignorance; religious neutrality in state-supported schooling and the quarrel it provoked with the established Church; emulation, order and self-government as pedagogy; the education of the poor as a public and imperial duty; the management of charitable funds and the accountability of the reformer.
authors.significance: Lancaster made universal elementary schooling seem technically and financially possible and created the first international school movement: Lancasterian societies and schools spread through Britain, Ireland, the United States, Canada and Latin America, and the British and Foreign School Society descended from his work. His visit to New York in 1815 helped prepare the American public-school idea; his fall in 1813-14 and the Bell controversy also defined the denominational politics of English education for half a century.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is given in the sources checked as Southwark, while some biographies place his family's origin at Rokeby in Westmorland; the day and month of his death are variously reported (23 October and 23 December 1838), with the Dictionary of Canadian Biography giving 23 October. The name of the 1798 premises ("Borstret House" in some accounts) could not be confirmed, and the details of his 1813 prosecution, conviction and sentence are reported inconsistently.

works.title: An Experiment in Education, Made at the Male Asylum of Madras
Improvements in Education, as it Respects the Industrious Classes of the Community

authors.name: Joseph Priestley
authors.identity: Unitarian minister, chemist and controversialist who isolated the gas he called dephlogisticated air and who argued that the same free enquiry applied to matter, to government and to Christian doctrine.
authors.biography: Born at Birstfield in Yorkshire in 1733, the son of a clothier and a dissenting mother, he was intended for the ministry, studied under Dissenting tutors, learned several languages and began to preach. He held small charges in Suffolk, taught for years at the academy in Warrington, and in the early 1760s began the electrical and chemical experiments that won him election to the Royal Society in 1766. Abandoning the doctrine of the Trinity, he served at Mill Hill in Leeds, acted as librarian and companion to the Earl of Shelburne on a continental tour, and settled in Birmingham in 1780 as minister of New Meeting, in the company of the natural philosophers and manufacturers of the Lunar Society circle. His Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air (1774-1777) made him famous; his Institutes of Natural and Revealed Religion, his Essay on a Doctrine of Scriptural Necessity and his histories of early Christian opinion attacked corruptions he believed priests had introduced. His defence of the French Revolution, printed in 1791, brought a mob to Birmingham, and he emigrated to Pennsylvania, where he died in 1804.
authors.profile: An investigator who refused the distinction between laboratory and pulpit, and whose prose kept the plain, earnest manner of the practical dissenting preacher.
authors.style: Clear, unadorned, accumulative expository prose; experiment described in reproducible detail; polemic conducted as historical evidence and close reading of texts; a controversialist's appetite for reply.
authors.concerns: The chemistry of the air and the phlogiston question; electricity, optics and the materialism of mind; the historical corruptions of Christianity and the rejection of the Trinity; political liberty, toleration and the progress of society.
authors.significance: He was a central figure of the Enlightenment's unite of science with radical religion and politics, a founder of modern gas chemistry, and the most feared Unitarian apologist of his day.
authors.uncertainty: Priority in the discovery of oxygen, and the chronology of his religious conversion, are still argued between his partisans and historians of chemistry.

works.title: Disquisitions relating to Matter and Spirit
Experiments and Observations on Different Kinds of Air
The Doctrine of Philosophical Necessity Illustrated
The History and Present State of Electricity

authors.name: Joshua Sylvester
authors.identity: translator; poet; merchant
authors.biography: Born in Kent in 1563, son of a clothier. He was educated at King's School, Southampton, and worked as a merchant and secretary, spending much of his life on the Continent in the service of the Merchant Adventurers. He died at Middelburg in the Netherlands on 28 September 1618.
authors.profile: Du Bartas His Divine Weeks and Works — his translation of Guillaume de Saluste du Bartas's biblical epic La Sepmaine, published piecemeal from 1592 and complete in 1608 — the most widely read religious poem of its generation after the Bible.
authors.style: Copious, inventive, heavily figured verse that renders du Bartas's cosmological baroque with gusto; a diction of striking coinages that fed Milton's word-hoard.
authors.concerns: The creation and providential order of the world; sacred poetry as the highest calling; Protestant piety in verse.
