authors.uncertainty: The dating of the Fairy Legends is unsettled - the Dictionary of National Biography gives 1825, 1827 and 1834 for the successive issues while modern accounts speak of three series from 1825 to 1828, and the year of the German translation is given as 1826 by the Dictionary of Irish Biography and variously elsewhere. Authorship is disputed at several points: the first series went out anonymously because Croker had lost his manuscripts and let Maginn and other friends rewrite parts; 'The Adventures of Barney Mahoney' is dated 1832 by Ricorso and 1852 by the Dictionary of National Biography, and Ricorso and his son's testimony would give it to his wife Marianne Nicholson Croker; and 'The Talisman' (1820) rests on the Dictionary of National Biography alone. His mother's name and fortunes, and the share in his collections of Richard Sainthill and of the manuscripts of R. Adolphus Lynch, are variously reported. No influence relationship could be verified strongly enough to record, so major_influences is left empty: Scott's praise and Moore's acquaintance are relations of reception and friendship, not documented influence.

works.title: Researches in the South of Ireland
The Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland

authors.name: Thomas De Quincey
authors.nationality: English; the confessional and analytical prose of the later Romantic period
authors.identity: Essayist, confessor and magazine writer, the most deliberate artist of prose rhythm among the Romantics and the first English writer to make the opium habit and the divided mind the sustained subject of a book.
authors.biography: De Quincey was born at Manchester, the son of a merchant, and was educated at Manchester Grammar School, at boarding schools near London and at Bristol Grammar School. A rebellious adolescence took him away from his guardians and, by his own later account, into a period of wandering and destitution; he entered the University of Oxford in 1803 and left without a degree. Reading the poetry of the day led him to the Lake District, where in the years after 1808 he lived near the poets he admired, at one time in the cottage their family had quitted, and where he began the habit of opium that he described as governing his life. He settled in London as a contributor to the magazines, and his narrative of an opium eater, printed in a metropolitan periodical in 1821 and in book form the following year, made his name. From the middle of the decade he was a steady contributor to a leading Edinburgh magazine, publishing essays on literature, on German writing, on logic, on postage and on murder as a subject of taste, together with a long autobiographical sequel and a narrative of the mail-coach mail service. His later years were spent largely in Scotland, and he died at Edinburgh in December 1859, shortly after a fire at his lodgings had destroyed his papers and the stores of opium that had long been in his keeping.
authors.profile: His proper field is prose of a highly elaborated kind: the autobiographical confession and its sequel, the literary and political essay, the tale of murder and its parody of forensic reasoning, and a large body of periodical writing on books, on German literature and on the questions of the day. He published no volume of poetry and planned a vast history of literature and a learned dictionary that were never executed; his output was chiefly written for magazines and collected, often revised and often incompletely, after publication. His characteristic manner is the digressive essay that returns upon itself, with a passionate elaboration of the periodic sentence and a fondness for the nightmare image.
authors.style: Prose built on long cadenced periods, balanced clauses, repeated keywords and sudden shifts from the ironic to the terrible, self-consciously modelled on the rhythms of Latin and English biblical prose; a irony that is carried by elaborate courtesy of tone; and a imagery of dreams, palaces, seas and pursuers that he himself discussed as the rhetoric of the opium vision.
authors.concerns: The divided and self-observing mind under stimulation; guilt, pursuit and the logic of crime as a pleasure of the intellect; literature as a power of expansion rather than of instruction; the machinery of the mind as studied by the metaphysicians; the social economy of letters and the condition of the magazine writer; the sublime and the pathetic as the two modes of great writing.
authors.significance: He created the modern literary confession of addiction and the literature of dream psychology, and his analytic tale of murder invented a form that the detective story later inherited; his essays on prose style, on the literature of knowledge and on the laws of rhetorical composition were among the most influential statements of the nineteenth century, and through them his work reaches the symbolists and the twentieth-century prose imaginations.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology and quantity of his opium use rest almost entirely on his own statements, which he allowed to be rhetorical; the dates and incidents of his wanderings in Wales as a boy, and of his first residence in the Lake District, cannot be verified independently and are differently reported in the biographies.

authors.name: Thomas Dekker
authors.identity: dramatist; pamphleteer
authors.biography: Born in London about 1572, probably of Dutch descent. He began writing for Henslowe's companies in 1598 and was imprisoned for debt in the Poultry Counter (1598–99). He collaborated with nearly every dramatist of the age — Jonson, Marston, Webster, Middleton, Ford, Massinger — and wrote some of the period's most vivid plague pamphlets. He died on 25 August 1632, still in debt.
authors.profile: Plays include The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599), Old Fortunatus (1599), Satiromastix (1601, with Marston, in the war of the theatres against Jonson), The Honest Whore (1604–05, with Middleton), and The Witch of Edmonton (1621, with Ford and Rowley); prose includes The Wonderful Year (1603) and The Gull's Hornbook (1609).
authors.style: Warmth, sentiment, and a Londoner's ear for the trades and cries of the city; his best scenes have a lyrical realism unmatched by his contemporaries.
authors.concerns: The dignity of citizens and craftsmen; plague and providence; the cheerful endurance of poverty.
authors.significance: The great celebrant of London's citizens; The Shoemaker's Holiday remains the most performed city comedy of its generation, and his pamphlets are major documents of urban life.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; little is known of his family and education.
themes: Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
sources: The Letters of William Cullen Bryant (6 volumes)

authors.name: Thomas Deloney
authors.identity: balladeer; prose fiction writer; silk weaver
authors.biography: A silk weaver by trade, probably born in Norwich about 1560. He became the most popular ballad-maker of his generation; several of his broadsides offended the authorities, and he was briefly in trouble over a ballad on the scarcity of grain in 1596. He died in 1600, apparently in poverty, leaving the fiction on which his later fame rests.
authors.profile: The prose narratives Jack of Newbury (1597), The Gentle Craft (c. 1597–98), and Thomas of Reading (c. 1600), which turned the lives of English craftsmen and merchants into popular fiction, together with hundreds of ballads of which a handful survive.
authors.style: Plain, vigorous, humorous prose full of proverbs, workman's lore, and the speech of shop and street; a bourgeois realism new to English fiction.
authors.concerns: The dignity and prosperity of trade; the pleasures of the middling sort; charity, industry, and honest dealing.
authors.significance: The first English novelist of the working people; his fictions reached a readership far below the court and founded the tradition of popular prose romance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate; his surviving ballad canon is a fraction of a much larger lost output.
sources: Zofloya: or, The Moor (Oxford World's Classics)

authors.name: Thomas Fuller
authors.identity: Anglican clergyman, historian, and wit; author of The Holy State and the Profane State (1642), a compendium of characters and maxims, and The History of the Worthies of England (1662), a pioneering biographical-topographical survey written in an energetic, proverbial style.
authors.biography: Born 1608 at Aldwincle, Northamptonshire (the same parish as Dryden); a prodigy educated at Queens' College, Cambridge (BA 1624/25) and Sidney Sussex College. He held various livings, served as a royalist chaplain during the Civil Wars, and was known for his preaching, memory, and wit. His major works include The Holy State (1642), Good Thoughts in Bad Times (1645), The Church-History of Britain (1655), and the posthumous Worthies of England (1662). A moderate during the Interregnum, he was restored at the Restoration and died on 16 August 1661 in London.
authors.profile: The learned, witty compiler and historian whose pithy, proverbial, digressive style and love of anecdotes and characters made him one of the most readable prose writers of the century.
authors.style: Terse, epigrammatic, proverbial prose; the 'character' sketch; abundant anecdote, pun, and quotation; a genial, learned wit; and a digressive, associative method.
authors.concerns: Moral and religious instruction; English history, biography, and topography; the virtues of the 'holy state' and the vices of the 'profane'; wit and wisdom; and moderation in the church.
authors.significance: Fuller's Worthies is a foundational work of English local history and biography, and his Church-History a pioneering ecclesiastical history; his prose style, full of quotable maxims, was widely admired and influential.
authors.uncertainty: Fuller's life is documented; the accuracy of some of his historical and biographical anecdotes was questioned even in his day and he himself admitted a love of a good story.

works.title: The History of the Worthies of England
The Holy State and the Profane State

sources: Charlotte Smith in British Romanticism

authors.name: Thomas Gray
authors.identity: English poet and scholar, Professor of Modern History at Cambridge, whose Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard is among the most quoted poems in the language.
authors.biography: Gray was born in London and educated at Eton and at Peterhouse, Cambridge, where he later returned as a scholar and, from 1768, held the Professorship of Modern History. A careful, slow writer of small output, he published little in his lifetime, including the Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College and the Hymn to Adversity. His finest Pindaric odes, The Progress of Poesy and The Bard, appeared in 1757. His Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard (1751) brought him fame. He declined the laureateship and lived a studious, largely private life, close to a circle that included Horace Walpole. He died at Cambridge in 1771.
authors.profile: A poet of the graveyard, the meditative ode, and antiquarian romance; he combined neoclassical polish with a new interest in melancholy, the common dead, and the music and history of earlier English and Welsh verse.
authors.style: Exquisite diction and sonorous, Latinate word order; a restrained, melancholy dignity; Pindaric and Norse-influenced ode experiments; and an antiquarian taste for the ballad and the picturesque.
authors.concerns: Unfulfilled potential and the fate of obscure lives; death, memory, and the moral lesson of the grave; the history and progress of poetry; and the aesthetics of melancholy and the sublime.
authors.significance: The Elegy became the landmark of the graveyard school and a touchstone of sensibility, while his odes and editorial interests in old poetry helped open the way to Romantic and antiquarian taste.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is usually given as 1716, but some records support 1717; the dating of the Elegy's composition, long associated with the churchyard at Stoke Poges, is debated.

works.title: Elegy Written in a Country Church-Yard
Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College

authors.name: Thomas Heywood
authors.identity: dramatist; poet; prose writer
authors.biography: Born in Lincolnshire about 1573; studied at Emmanuel College, Cambridge. He was acting and writing for Henslowe's companies by 1598 and claimed to have had 'an entire hand, or at least a main finger' in 220 plays. He wrote pageants, translations, and compendious works of history and mythology, and died in Clerkenwell on 16 August 1641, one of the last survivors of the great Jacobean generation.
authors.profile: A Woman Killed with Kindness (1603), the domestic tragedy The English Traveller (c. 1627), the four-part Ages cycle (1611–32), The Fair Maid of the West (c. 1600), and the prose An Apology for Actors (1612), the period's chief defence of the stage.
authors.style: Plain, humane, middle-style verse; domestic settings; moral plots of patience and repentance that avoid the lurid excesses of his rivals.
authors.concerns: The dignity of the ordinary household; marital betrayal and forgiveness; the moral legitimacy of the theatre.
authors.significance: His domestic tragedy founded a genre that runs through Lillo to Ibsen; An Apology for Actors is the classic defence of the English stage.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the vast collaborative canon makes his exact share in many plays uncertain.
sources: The Quarterly Review

authors.name: Thomas Hobbes
authors.identity: Philosopher and political theorist; author of Leviathan (1649), the founding text of modern political philosophy, whose materialist, mechanistic system and prose of austere clarity transformed English thought and letters.
authors.biography: Born 5 April 1588 at Westport, Wiltshire (the year of the Armada — 'fear and I were born twins', he joked); educated at Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served for decades as tutor and secretary to the Cavendish family (Earls of Devonshire), travelling Europe and meeting Mersenne, Gassendi, Descartes, and Galileo. Alarmed by the political crisis, he went into exile in Paris (1640–51), publishing De Cive (1642) and, in 1651, Leviathan, whose defence of absolute sovereignty and its Erastianism offended both royalists and Parliamentarians. He returned to England, was distrusted by the restored court, and, after the Clarendon attack and the 1666 parliamentary scrutiny of 'atheism', published little more political philosophy. His later works include Behemoth (1668–70) and an autobiography in verse. He died on 4 December 1679 at Hardwick.
authors.profile: The philosopher who derived the state from a contract among self-interested individuals in a 'war of every man against every man', and who wrote with a logical, powerful, and lucid prose that made philosophy English literature.
authors.style: Rigorous, deductive argument; a clear, forceful, sometimes ironic prose; striking metaphors (the state as 'Leviathan', life as 'nasty, brutish, and short'); and a materialist, mechanistic vocabulary.
authors.concerns: Sovereignty, the social contract, and the state of nature; materialism and mechanism; human nature, appetite, and reason; religion and its political control; and the philosophy of language and knowledge.
authors.significance: Leviathan founded modern political philosophy and social contract theory, profoundly influencing Locke, Rousseau, and all subsequent thought; Hobbes's materialism and prose style also made him a central, if feared, figure in English intellectual and literary history.
authors.uncertainty: Hobbes's life is well documented (including his own prose and verse autobiographies and Aubrey's Life); the sincerity of his religious professions remains debated.

works.title: Leviathan; or, The Matter, Forme, and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill
The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic

sources: The Selected Works of Robert Owen (4 volumes)

authors.name: Thomas Hoccleve
authors.identity: poet; clerk
authors.biography: A clerk of the Privy Seal office in Westminster from c. 1387 for some thirty-five years, he knew Chaucer personally and called himself his disciple; his poems — above all the autobiographical passages of the Series — record his anxiety, his 'maladie' of 1416, and the precarious life of a married office-holder. He died in 1426.
authors.profile: Author of the Regiment of Princes (1411), the classic English mirror-for-princes addressed to the future Henry V; the Series (c. 1419–21), a linked set of tales and complaints containing the first English poetic autobiography; and shorter poems including the Male Regle.
authors.style: Correct Chaucerian verse with a plain, personal voice; rueful self-portraiture; the adaptation of courtly and didactic forms to the experience of bureaucracy and illness.
authors.concerns: Good governance and the duties of princes; poverty, patronage, and the ethics of office; his own mental suffering and its consolation.
authors.significance: The first English poet to write extensively about his own life and illness; the Regiment is a principal document of Lancastrian political literature and of the Chaucerian inheritance.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the cause of his 1416 'maladie' remains debated.
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling
themes: The English vernacular and national letters
sources: The Diary of Samuel Pepys

authors.name: Thomas Hood
authors.identity: Comic verse-maker, essayist, and magazine and annual editor of the London periodical trade, with an unsuccessful ambition to be a serious poet; the founding figure of the English punning comic verse tradition and one of the most reprinted poets of the mid-Victorian anthologies.
authors.biography: Thomas Hood was born on 23 May 1799 in London, in the Poultry in Cheapside, the son of a bookseller and publisher of Scottish Presbyterian origin whose death in 1811 left the family in straits. Withdrawn from school for a merchant's counting house and then bound to learn engraving in his maternal uncle's London workshop, he ran away northward as an apprentice and passed some years in Scotland, working as a journalist and schoolmaster before returning to London. From 1821 he was attached to the London Magazine as sub-editor and contributor after the death of its first editor, and for the next twenty-four years he was engaged, as writer or editor, with most of the leading London periodicals, among them the Athenaeum, the New Monthly, and the keepsake annuals. In 1825 he married Caroline Reynolds, sister of the poet John Hamilton Reynolds, with whom he had already collaborated in burlesque verse, and the burden of a growing household and of chronic ill health fixed his subsequent career in the market. Whims and Oddities, first series, appeared in 1826 and the second series in 1827, the two volumes making his name with the public; National Tales, two volumes of novella imitation, and The Plea of the Midsummer Fairies, his one book of serious verse, followed in 1827. He edited the annual The Gem from 1829, giving early pages to Tennyson, and founded and conducted The Comic Annual from 1830 into the 1840s, while his ballad of the murderer's dream was reprinted separately in 1831 from the annual pages. Speculative ventures in publishing and on the stage, a novel of 1834, and a long residence abroad for his health, recorded in a travel book of 1840, left him in debt and in permanent overwork, and he wrote for the magazines and for Punch into the last years of his life. He died at his home at Finchley Road, London, on 3 May 1845, was buried on 10 May at Kensal Green cemetery, and was memorialised there in 1854 by a monument paid for by public subscription, an unusual testament to a writer of comic verse.
authors.profile: His work divides between a serious poetry of fairy legend, melancholy ballad, and seasonal meditation, represented by The Plea of the Midsummer Fairies, Hero and Leander, and the ballad-poem on Eugene Aram, and an enormous comic output of punning song, parody, and sketch in prose and verse. He also wrote prose tales, a novel, editorial and reviewing matter for magazines and annuals, and the account of his continental exile. The social lyrics of his last years, on the seamstress, the lost child, and the bridge of sighs, converted his command of the popular stave into the most quoted humanitarian verse of the 1840s and held his place in the school anthology for a century.
authors.style: In the comedy, an accumulating engine of homonym, internal rhyme, refrain, and mock-earnest rhetoric driven to the point of collapse, with the argument of a sketch abandoned to the pursuit of the joke. In the serious and sentimental verse, a measured descriptive line of the eighteenth-century school above a ballad stave, with a fondness for the dying child, the drowned bride, and the vanished fairy. The two manners coexist in the same volumes, and the pun survives even into the elegy.
authors.concerns: The psychology of guilt and of concealed crime; the decay of popular fairy belief under tillage and improvement; the poverty, debt, and dependence of the professional hack; the relation of comic verbal play to genuine feeling; the labour and distress of paid workers in a factory town; the uses and the failures of the annual and the periodical as a literary economy.
authors.significance: He is the source of the nineteenth century's punning comic verse tradition, inherited by the joke-book, the music hall song, and the magazine wit, and one of the most reprinted poets of the mid-Victorian period. His double career measures the gap between Romantic ambition and its commercial reward, and his editorial work in the annual and the comic keepsake is a document of the gift-book economy at its height, while the later labour lyrics supplied a lasting model for verse on industrial poverty.
authors.uncertainty: His birth year is occasionally given as 1798 in older reference works, but 23 May 1799 is the received entry date. The year in which he took up work at the London Magazine, whether early or late in 1821, and the exact share of his editorial responsibility are variously reported. The publisher of the first series of Whims and Oddities is given differently in modern bibliographies, and the imprint requires checking against the copy; his contributions to Blackwood's Magazine, often asserted, were not confirmed during this review. The standard Victorian memoir written by his daughter compresses the chronology of his debts and of his Scottish years.

works.title: Odes and Addresses to Great People
The Plea of the Midsummer Fairies

authors.name: Thomas Kyd
authors.identity: dramatist; scrivener's son
authors.biography: Son of Francis Kyd, a London scrivener; baptized 6 November 1558. Probably attended Merchant Taylors' School. Little is known of his life before The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587), which made his name. In May 1593 he was arrested after papers denying the deity of Christ were found in his lodgings; he claimed they belonged to Christopher Marlowe, his former room-mate, and was tortured in Bridewell. He died in August 1594, buried on 15 August, in debt and obscurity.
authors.profile: Author of the most influential revenge tragedy of the age, The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587), with its play-within-the-play, its ghost of Don Andrea, and its hero Hieronimo; also wrote the tragedy Soliman and Perseda (c. 1592) and Cornelia (1594), a translation of Robert Garnier's Senecan tragedy, and is the probable author of the lost ur-Hamlet.
authors.style: Senecan rhetoric, ghosts and revenge choruses, dramatic irony, the device of the play within the play, and a blank verse line of strong end-stops that Marlowe and Shakespeare both learned from.
authors.concerns: Justice and its frustration; the morality of private revenge; the theatre's power to reveal concealed crime.
authors.significance: The founding figure of English revenge tragedy; The Spanish Tragedy was the most popular play of its generation and shaped Hamlet and a hundred imitations.
authors.uncertainty: Almost nothing certain about his education; the ur-Hamlet attribution is probable but not proven; several minor plays have been conjecturally assigned to him.
themes: Dream, intoxication, and the divided mind
sources: The Norton Anthology of American Literature (9th edition)

authors.name: Thomas Linacre
authors.identity: physician; humanist; founder of the Royal College of Physicians
authors.biography: Born about 1460, probably at Canterbury; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek from Politian and took a medical degree at Padua. Physician to Henry VIII, tutor of the young Thomas More, and founder of the Royal College of Physicians (1518), he translated Galen into Latin with unprecedented accuracy and wrote De Emendata Structura Latini Sermonis (1524), the first scientific Latin grammar by an Englishman. He died on 20 October 1524.
authors.profile: The English pioneer of Greek medicine and philology. His Galen translations (1517–23) restored the texts of ancient medicine to the West, and his Latin grammar, applying the new philology to the classical language, is a landmark of English humanism.
authors.style: The philologist's precision; translation as recovery of the original; grammar as science rather than schoolroom drill.
authors.concerns: The restoration of Greek learning; the reform of medicine on Galenic foundations; the accurate use of Latin among physicians and scholars.
authors.significance: Founded the scientific study of medicine in England and the College of Physicians; his translations and grammar made him, with Colet and Grocyn, one of the three pillars of the Oxford reform.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and birthplace approximate.
themes: Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
sources: The Edinburgh Edition of the Waverley Novels

authors.name: Thomas Lodge
authors.identity: prose romancer; poet; dramatist; physician
authors.biography: Born in London in 1558, son of a Lord Mayor of London. Educated at Merchant Taylors' School and Trinity College, Oxford, he turned to literature, travelled to the Canaries and South America, then converted to Catholicism and took up medicine, graduating MD at Avignon in 1600. He practised in London until his death of the plague in September 1625.
authors.profile: The romance Rosalynde (1590) — the direct source of Shakespeare's As You Like It — the euphuistic romance Euphues' Shadow (1592), the mythological poem Scilla's Metamorphosis (1589), the satires A Fig for Momus (1595), the play The Wounds of Civil War (c. 1588), and the translation of Josephus (1602).
authors.style: Euphuism softened into pastoral lyricism; a fluent, musical prose of courtship, disguise, and greenwood virtue.
authors.concerns: Pastoral retreat and its therapeutic power; love and loyalty; the quarrel between poetry and the professions.
authors.significance: Through Rosalynde he gave Shakespeare one of his richest sources and helped fix the English pastoral romance as a form.
authors.uncertainty: The dates and details of his travels are reconstructed from allusions in his own works.
sources: Melmoth the Wanderer (Oxford World's Classics)

authors.name: Thomas Love Peacock
authors.birthplace: Widdicombe Gate, near Plymouth, Devon (raised in London and Southampton)
authors.identity: Comic novelist and satirist of Romantic intellectual culture
authors.biography: Thomas Love Peacock was born near Plymouth and raised in London and Southampton; his father was a lawyer who fled to the Continent to escape debt. apprenticed to the East India Company, he spent most of his working life there, rising to be Chief Officer of the India Office. He was an intimate friend of Percy Bysshe Shelley, with whom he shared radical and literary enthusiasms; Shelley dedicated The Revolt of Islam to him and used Peacock as the model for the idealist in the novel. His first novel Headlong Hall (1816) began a sequence of short comic dialogues; Nightmare Abbey (1818) was his most successful. He married into the Loved family and his daughters married the novelist George Meredith. He stopped publishing fiction after Crotchet Castle (1831) and continued in the East India Company until retirement. He died in 1866 at Lower Heyford.
authors.profile: Peacock is the century's great comic satirist of ideas; his novels are sequences of witty dialogue among intellectual types — the phrenologist, the reformer, the Byronic melancholic — whose absurd positions are made to clash in country-house settings. He is the direct heir of the Augustan novel of ideas and the ancestor of Huxley's and Wells's intellectual comedy.
authors.style: Dialogue-driven comedy without conventional plot; satirical caricature through speech; compressed, urbane prose; use of named types whose theories are the object of the joke; occasional lyric verse in Maid Marian.
authors.concerns: The absurdities of specialist intellectual languages; the Romantic cult of melancholy; the politics of reform in 1830s England; the commercial book trade and the condition of the professional writer; German metaphysics and British Utilitarianism.
authors.significance: Peacock's novels are the principal comic record of Romantic intellectual fashion; Nightmare Abbey's satire of Byronic melancholy and Mr. Listless's enervation from reading are among the defining images of the period's self-awareness. His influence on Victorian and modern comic fiction is extensive.

authors.name: Thomas Lovell Beddoes
authors.birthplace: Clifton, then in Gloucestershire and now part of Bristol, son of Dr Thomas Beddoes the physician and chemist and of Anna Maria Beddoes (née Edgeworth), sister of Maria Edgeworth
authors.nationality: English; the morbid and neo-Jacobean wing of British Romanticism, a Catholic-Emigre tradition of unread closet tragedy which took Elizabethan and Jacobean drama as its working model and was formed in the German universities
authors.identity: A physician who wrote plays and poems, and the most considerable English dramatist in the closet between Byron and Swinburne: the author of one early revenge tragedy and of one great tragedy, Death's Jest-Book, which he rebuilt and unbuilt for twenty years and never lived to publish.
authors.biography: Thomas Lovell Beddoes was born at Clifton in the summer of 1803 (30 June is the date now usually given; the eleventh Encyclopaedia Britannica printed 20 July), the son of Dr Thomas Beddoes, physician, chemist and projector of the Pneumatic Institution at Bristol, and of Anna Maria Beddoes, sister of Maria Edgeworth, so that he was bred inside the most argued and most experimental household of late Georgian England. He was educated at Charterhouse and at Pembroke College, Oxford, where he was in residence from about 1820 to 1824, and he began to print while still under age: The Improvisatore appeared in 1821 and The Bride's Tragedy, the revenge drama of his eighteenth year, in 1822. He then took up medicine as his father had done, studying at Göttingen from 1824 and afterwards at Würzburg, where he proceeded to the doctor's degree, and he spent the rest of his life as a practising physician in the German-speaking towns, in poverty, in quarrels with his lodgers, and under the notice of the police for the democratic and republican opinions he vented in verse and prose for German and Swiss periodicals. Behind the medical work went on the unceasing revision of Death's Jest-Book, drafted in the later 1820s, since the text of 1829 survives in manuscript, while The Second Brother, Torrismond and much occasional verse were left in fragment. Illness, debt and disappointment ended in self-destruction: he took poison at Basel on 26 January 1849, usually reported as prussic acid, after surgery on a diseased limb. His friend and executor Thomas Forbes Kelsall printed Death's Jest-Book in 1850 and the posthumous Poems in 1851 with a memoir, and their circulation among the generation of the Pre-Raphaelites secured his survival; Lytton Strachey named him 'the last Elizabethan', H. W. Donner's Oxford edition of the Works of 1935 fixed the canon, and the recovery of the 1829 text of Jest-Book confirmed the estimate of a dramatist who wrote for a theatre he never saw.
authors.profile: His printed work in his lifetime was two thin volumes of narrative and dramatic verse, The Improvisatore (1821) and The Bride's Tragedy (1822); almost everything else appeared after his death, above all the five-act Death's Jest-Book, privately printed in 1850, and the posthumous Poems of 1851, which gather The Second Brother, Torrismond, dramatic scenes and fragments, miscellaneous lyrics, sonnets and versions from the Greek anthology. He is therefore a dramatist first and a lyric poet second: two completed plays in verse, a body of short reflective and occasional lyrics, and a critical and polemical margin of German journalism, of scholarship on Greek tragedy and of correspondence, none of which he reduced himself into a book.
authors.style: A deliberate archaism of diction and syntax learnt from the Jacobeans: compounds, reduplications and obsessions of phrase, an anatomical and clinical vocabulary turned to metaphor, and imagery of corpses, drugs, dissection and sleep. His verse moves in long, musical, heavily alliterating lines broken by asides and stage business, and his later drama interplots comedy, philosophy and ghostcraft so fiercely that plot is sacrificed to verbal and intellectual energy. The lyrics are more controlled than the plays, and the whole work is marked by a self-quoting, revisionary habit of mind, since he reworked the same scenes and the same images for two decades.
authors.concerns: Death as an object of knowledge rather than of piety; the identity of the person across dissolution and resurrection; the credibility of ghosts, dreams and the post-mortem senses; suicide and the will to die, considered with a physician's exactness and a dramatist's self-interest; the ethics of experiment on living bodies, in his father's line; Greek tragedy, its machinery and its civic religion; and republican liberty, which he attached to his medical practice and paid for with his livelihood.
authors.significance: He carries on into the nineteenth century the old English tragedy of revenge and of the grave, and makes it the vehicle of a specifically modern morbidity; through the 1850 volumes he passed into the inheritance of the Pre-Raphaelites, of the decadent poets and of the twentieth-century revivals of verse drama, and he is the standing example of the 'closet drama' that is unread because unperformable. His case is also a document of Romantic medical culture, of the intellectual exile of a British radical in the German states, and of the transmission of Coleridgean and Wedgwood-Edgeworth family networks into a generation that knew its own inheritance as a debt.
authors.uncertainty: His birth is unsettled and the older catalogues and this project's list of installments give 1813 and Cannon Street, London, whereas modern authorities give 30 June 1803 at Clifton, with the 1911 Encyclopaedia printing 20 July; his birthplace has also been reported as Clifton in Shropshire; the place of his death is variously given as Basel and as Frankfort-on-the-Main, and the poison as prussic acid or as curare, and the dating of his drafts of Death's Jest-Book and the extent of Kelsall's editorial reconstruction remain matters of argument.

works.title: Death's Jest-Book; or, The Fool's Tragedy

authors.name: Thomas Malory
authors.identity: prose writer; knight
authors.biography: Commonly identified with Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel, Warwickshire, a War of the Roses knight with a long record of violence and imprisonment, who describes himself in the colophon of his book as 'knight prisoner' and prays for his deliverance. He completed Le Morte Darthur in prison in the ninth year of Edward IV (1469–70) and died on 14 March 1471; Caxton printed the work in 1485.
authors.profile: Author of Le Morte Darthur, the great prose compilation of the Arthurian legend in English, from the sword in the stone through the Grail quest to the death of Arthur and the ruin of the Round Table.
authors.style: A spare, rhythmic prose of paratactic clauses and ritual dialogue; the reduction of the French prose cycles to a single tragic arc; scenes of chivalry, combat, and pathos of enduring power.
authors.concerns: The ideals and contradictions of chivalry — loyalty, love, and treason; the costs of the Grail quest; the fall of a fellowship through sin.
authors.significance: Le Morte Darthur is the definitive English Arthurian book and the first great prose romance in the language; through Caxton's edition it fixed the Arthurian story for all subsequent English literature.
authors.uncertainty: The identification of the author with the Warwickshire knight is probable but not certain; the circumstances of composition are known only from the colophon.
sources: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden

authors.name: Thomas Middleton
authors.identity: dramatist; city chronologer; poet
authors.biography: Baptized 18 April 1580 in London; son of a bricklayer who left a comfortable estate. He matriculated at Queen's College, Oxford, in 1598 but left without a degree to write for the theatre. From 1613 he wrote the annual Lord Mayor's pageants, and in 1620 was appointed City Chronologer. His political allegory A Game at Chess (1624) — a satire on the Spanish match — became the greatest box-office success of the age and provoked a diplomatic uproar. He died at Newington Butts and was buried 4 July 1627.
authors.profile: The most versatile of the Jacobean professionals: city comedies (A Mad World, My Masters, 1605; A Trick to Catch the Old One, c. 1605; A Chaste Maid in Cheapside, 1613), tragedies (Women Beware Women, c. 1621; The Changeling, 1622, with Rowley; and — by the current consensus of attribution — The Revenger's Tragedy, 1606), and the political satire A Game at Chess (1624).
authors.style: Swift, sardonic wit; a fascination with money, appetite, and the mechanics of deceit; ferocious tragic irony; and a moral disgust that never blunts his comic energy.
authors.concerns: The corruptions of City and court; marriage as property transaction; the ethics of revenge; political and religious controversy.
authors.significance: The second great dramatist of the Jacobean age after Shakespeare and Jonson; A Game at Chess is a landmark of political theatre.
authors.uncertainty: The attribution of The Revenger's Tragedy has shifted from Tourneur to Middleton on stylistic evidence; much of his output was collaborative and shares are sometimes disputed.
themes: The wilderness, settlement, and Indian removal
sources: An American Dictionary of the English Language (2 volumes)

authors.name: Thomas Moore
authors.birthplace: 12 Aungier Street, Dublin, only son of a grocer and wine merchant of the city who later held office as a magistrate there
authors.nationality: Irish, working for a metropolitan British public; the Irish national lyric and song tradition, the Whig-liberal and emancipation cause, and the fashionable Oriental and satirical verse of the Regency
authors.identity: Poet, lyricist, satirist, editor and biographer: in his own lifetime the most widely known and most lucratively published of the Romantic poets, the maker of the national air set to modern words, and the assumed national bard of Ireland who ended his life in an English country cottage.
authors.biography: Moore was born in Dublin on 28 May 1779, the only son of a grocer and wine merchant who rose to municipal office in the city, and he showed such early facility in verse that his college years at Trinity, to which he entered in 1794, were remembered for his printed attempts rather than for his reading. He quitted Ireland for London about the turn of the century, established himself by his pen, and published in those first years translations of the Anacreontic poems and a small collection put out under the name of a fictitious deceased author. He was received in society and in the drawing rooms, moved in the theatre and publishing world, and became the most sought-after lyric writer of the Regency, supplying words to recovered Irish airs in a serial publication that grew through more than two decades into a national monument in song; his satires on the London society he lived in, a sequence of intercepted verse epistles of 1813 and the comic tourist letters of 1818, were issued under the name of a young Irish correspondent, a disguise that answered the risk of libel and sharpened the outsider's eye on English vanity. Lalla Rookh of 1817, with its framed Oriental romances, brought him a publisher's fee of three thousand guineas and a European fame that no poem of his second decade exceeded, and the religious narrative of the angel lovers which followed in 1822 drew upon him the loudest borrowing controversy of his career. His friendship with the greater poet of the generation, begun in London, cooled and revived, was renewed in Italy, where Moore visited him in the last years at Venice and at the towns of the Adriatic and the Ligurian coast, and it ended in the office of literary executor which he accepted and in the suppression and burning of the dead man's memoirs in the publisher's rooms in May 1824, a transaction in which the sums exchanged and the shares of the parties were reported differently by each of them. He printed a defence of Byron's poetry against clerical attack and, after long delay, the Letters and Journals with Notices of his Life in 1830, the book on which the century's knowledge of its subject chiefly rested. He had married in 1811 a woman whose family connections gave him entry to the professional gentry, and from 1818 his home was Sloperton Cottage near Bromham in Wiltshire, where he lived, honoured at home and abroad but reproached by a younger school of Irish writers for the moderation of his lyrics, until his death; his later labour was largely prose, a life of the Irish dramatist of the previous generation, a history of Ireland carried through several volumes, and a vast correspondence, and his own papers were edited and published after his death by the statesman who had been his friend. He outlived the children of his marriage, several of whom died in youth, and that grief darkens the record of his last years; he died at Sloperton on 25 February 1852 and was buried in the churchyard of the next village, a long way from Dublin.
authors.profile: His work has five distinct departments: the serial national lyrics and songs written to airs; the Oriental and romantic narrative in verse, of which Lalla Rookh is the centre; the light satirical verse epistle and comic poem; the devotional and religious narrative and hymn; and the editorial, biographical and historical prose, including the Byron correspondence and memoirs, the life of the dramatist, the history of his country and his own posthumous autobiography. He was also a performing musician who sang and accompanied his own songs, and much of his verse was made for the voice rather than for the page. The habitual form is the short dramatic lyric or the ornamental narrative divided into easily detached pieces, and his prose is the same gift of easy narration carried into biography.
authors.style: Lyric measures of exceptional fluency, often in triple time and built on refrains and on the requirements of a pre-existing air, with a vocabulary of tenderness and national regret; in the romances a richly coloured and sensuous descriptive style, anapestic and musical, depending on scenery and on effect rather than on analysis; in the satire an easy decasyllabic and octosyllabic couplet of the Augustan familiar school, carried by gossip, insinuation and feigned simplicity; in the religious poem an unction of address and apostrophe which contemporary critics found either affecting or mercenary. Facility, finish and a constant attention to the ear are his permanent characteristics, and the same qualities, to later judges, are his limitation.
authors.concerns: The survival of a conquered nation in its music, its memory and its lost causes; religious zeal, imposture and fanaticism as the motives of history, and the possibility of a holiness preserved through temptation; emancipation, toleration and the civic claims of Irish Catholics; the ethics of editorial discretion, friendship and the keeping of dead men's secrets; exile, travel and the southern sojourn; the commerce between cultural nationalism and the metropolitan market that pays for it; the relations of words to music, and of song to poetry.
authors.significance: He made the recovered national air a European form and gave Ireland the song repertory by which the nineteenth century imagined it, at the cost of a lasting argument about compromise and authenticity. As the best-paid and most translated poet of his generation he demonstrates the commercial possibilities open to Romantic verse before the annuals reached their height, and his Fudge Family letters long remained the template of tourists' satire. His edition and memoir of the greater poet of the generation founded the serious editing of literary correspondence and, in the suppression of the memoirs, supplied the canonical case in the history of editorial ethics and of literary reputation. His late eclipse, while a dozen of his lyrics stayed in the recital and schoolbook repertory, is a standard illustration of the severance between popular Romantic fame and modern canon.
authors.uncertainty: The family's religious history and Moore's own communion are variously represented in the biographies, which reflect his Catholic Irish origins and his Anglican connections; the exact sums paid and received over the suppression of the memoirs, and how much of that manuscript he had seen, copied or destroyed, are still argued from party statements; the chronology of his Italian journeys of the later 1810s and early 1820s is given differently in the standard accounts; and the authenticity of several airs and of his own share in their arrangements remains a matter of musicological dispute.

works.title: Intercepted Letters; or, the Two-Penny Post-Bag
Letters and Journals of Lord Byron

authors.name: Thomas Nashe
authors.identity: pamphleteer; satirist; dramatist; poet
authors.biography: Baptized November 1567 at Lowestoft; son of a curate. BA from St John's College, Cambridge (1586). He came to London about 1588 and earned a living by the pen, often in hardship. He fought the pamphlet war with Gabriel Harvey in the 1590s, fled London after the scandal of The Isle of Dogs (1597), and died in or about 1601, aged thirty-three.
authors.profile: Pierce Penniless His Supplication to the Devil (1592), The Unfortunate Traveller (1594) — the first picaresque novel in English — the anti-Puritan satire Christ's Tears over Jerusalem (1593), the play Summer's Last Will and Testament (1592, printed 1600), the erotic poem The Choice of Valentines, and the lost Isle of Dogs (1597), co-written with Ben Jonson, which closed the London theatres by order of the Privy Council.
authors.style: Furious verbal energy: colloquialism mixed with learned allusion, compound coinages, mock-heroic rhetoric, and the fastest, funniest prose of the decade.
authors.concerns: The condition of authorship without patronage; the hypocrisy of Puritans and pedants; urban poverty and plague; the grotesque body.
authors.significance: The great prose satirist of the 1590s and a pioneer of English fiction; his prose style was absorbed by Jonson, Dekker, and the pamphleteers who followed.
authors.uncertainty: Death date approximate; the circumstances of his last years are obscure.
themes: Exile, travel, and the southern sojourn

works.title: Pierce Penniless His Supplication to the Devil

sources: The Novels and Related Works of Charles Brockden Brown: Bicentennial Edition

authors.name: Thomas Otway
authors.identity: Restoration tragedian; the master of pathetic, sentimental tragedy in blank verse, whose The Orphan (1680) and above all Venice Preserv'd (1682) were the most performed serious plays of the eighteenth century until superseded by later taste.
authors.biography: Born 3 March 1652 at Trotton, Sussex, educated at Winchester and Christ Church, Oxford, then briefly a soldier in Flanders. Turning to the stage, he wrote comedies (Alcibiades, 1675; Friendship in Fashion, 1678), the tragicomedies Titus and Berenice and Cheats of Scapin (1676–77), and his great tragedies The Orphan (1680) and Venice Preserv'd (1682), the latter inspired by the Popish Plot and starring the actors Thomas Betterton and Elizabeth Barry, with whom he was infatuated. He also wrote the verse tragedy Caius Marius (1679). He died in poverty on 14 April 1685, supposedly choking on bread after a long fast.
authors.profile: The poet of 'pathetic' tragedy, whose heroines and heroes of overwhelming, tender passion moved audiences to tears and created the sentimental mode that dominated the serious stage for a century.
authors.style: Passionate, tender blank verse; the tragedy of suffering innocence; scenes of heightened pathetic emotion; and a rhetoric designed to elicit tears and pity.
authors.concerns: Love, friendship, and betrayal; suffering innocence and female distress; political conspiracy and loyalty; the passions and their tragic cost; and sentimental virtue.
authors.significance: Venice Preserv'd held the stage continuously until the 1830s and was admired by Dryden, Pope, and Johnson; Otway's pathetic tragedy shaped the sentimental drama of the eighteenth century and the acting careers of Betterton and Barry.
authors.uncertainty: Otway's life is documented but romanticised; the story of his death by choking is traditional, and details of his military and amorous life are partly anecdotal.

works.title: The Orphan; or, The Unhappy Marriage
Venice Preserv'd; or, A Plot Discover'd

sources: David Walker's Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World

authors.name: Thomas Paine
authors.identity: Artisan, excise officer and the most powerful political pamphleteer of the Atlantic revolutions, whose Common Sense (1776) turned revolt into ordinary language.
authors.biography: Born at Thetford in 1737, the son of a Quaker staymaker, he served his father's trade, ran briefly and failed at several ventures, and became an officer of excise, a posting he lost after he had petitioned Parliament on his colleagues' pay. Frustrated and in debt, he went to London, fell in with Benjamin Franklin and reached Philadelphia at the end of 1774 with letters of introduction. He began to write for the Pennsylvania Magazine, where in March 1775 appeared his first and sharpest attack on American slavery, and in January 1776 Common Sense, arguing for independence and a republic in prose the mechanic could read. The American Crisis papers, written through the war, were read to Washington's troops; he served the American cause as a writer and in public office, and after the war was rewarded by several states. He returned to England in 1787, and his Rights of Man (1791) and the first part of The Age of Reason (1794), both after the period covered here, made him a prosecuted and then an exiled figure; he died in New York in 1809.
authors.profile: The democrat of plain style, who treated government as a common trade, monarchy as an imposture, and the reader's good sense as the only authority worth obeying.
authors.style: Short declarative sentences, homely metaphor and moral indignation; argument as address, with the cadence of a sermon and the directness of a handbill; sarcasm directed at rank and priestcraft.
authors.concerns: Natural rights and the consent of the governed; the corruption of hereditary and ministerial power; the sin and economics of slavery; deistical religion against priestly and scriptural authority; the interests of labouring men.
authors.significance: He made the case for American independence to the people who had to fight for it, and his later radicalism set the template for popular republicanism, free-thought agitation and the nineteenth-century radical press.
authors.uncertainty: His early manhood is dimly documented, and some of the works attributed to him in the 1770s have been disputed.

works.title: Dissertation on First Principles of Government

authors.name: Thomas Parnell
authors.identity: Anglo-Irish poet and Anglican clergyman, a friend of Pope and a member of the Scriblerus Club, admired for his meditative and light verse.
authors.biography: Parnell was an Irish scholar, commonly held to have been born about 1679 and educated at Trinity College Dublin, where he took holy orders in the Church of Ireland. He rose to hold benefices near Dublin and was archdeacon of Glendalough. Close to Alexander Pope and Jonathan Swift, he joined the Scriblerus Club, and Pope borrowed the theme of his own early Pastoral from Parnell's The Hermit. His short poems circulated in manuscript and periodicals during his lifetime, and a collected Poetical Works appeared posthumously in 1721. He died in Dublin in 1718.
authors.profile: A poet of modest output but high reputation, best known for a single reflective piece, The Hermit, together with light, witty songs and hymns that display ease and quiet moral feeling.
authors.style: Smooth Augustan couplets and lyric measures; a calm, meditative tone; graceful wit; and a plainness and sweetness praised by Pope as a model of true ease.
authors.concerns: Quietist contentment and retirement; moral self-examination; religious resignation; and the pleasantries and vanities of social life.
authors.significance: A transitional poet whose The Hermit anticipated the grave-mediation and churchyard current of later eighteenth-century verse, and a valued link within the Pope and Swift circle.
authors.uncertainty: His year of birth is uncertain and given as about 1679; some details of his Irish benefices and his family background rest on later biographical tradition.

works.title: Essay on the Different Stiles of Poetry
Peri Bathous, the Art of Sinking in Poetry
The Works of Mr. Martinus Scriblerus

authors.name: Thomas Percy
authors.identity: English scholar, bishop, and antiquary whose Reliques of Ancient English Poetry revived the ballad and shaped the study of old English verse.
authors.biography: Percy, born in Shropshire to a modest family, was educated at school in Shrewsbury and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he became a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries. In 1765 he published the Reliques of Ancient English Poetry, drawing on an old manuscript folio of ballads, which set off a great vogue for the popular ballad and influenced poets from Cowper and Burns to the Romantics. He edited and translated northern and antique material, including Five Pieces of Runic Poetry (1763) and a translation of Paul-Henri Mallet's Northern Antiquities, and prefaced the Reliques with a learned essay on the ancient minstrels. Advanced in the Irish church, he became Bishop of Dromore, where he died in 1789.
authors.profile: An antiquary-bishop and editor whose taste for the ballad, romance, and the early popular poetry of Britain made him a pivotal figure in the recovery and celebration of native literary tradition.
authors.style: In the Reliques, a taste for the simple lyric and the harmony of old ballads; in his own verse, easy, sometimes humorous antique and pastoral imitation; and a scholarly, glossarial editorial method.
authors.concerns: The native and popular origins of English poetry; ballad and romance as genres; national and northern literary antiquities; and the history and manners of the minstrels and their patrons.
authors.significance: The Reliques is one of the most influential anthologies in English literary history, launching the ballad revival, aiding the Romantic revaluation of popular poetry, and stimulating Burns and the later folk movement.
authors.uncertainty: His exact birthplace in Shropshire is given variously; the extent to which he silently revised and modernised the old ballads in the Reliques, rather than reproducing them, has long been debated.

authors.name: Thomas Reid
authors.identity: Minister and professor of Glasgow, founder of the school of common-sense philosophy, who answered the ideal theory of Locke, Berkeley and Hume by appealing to the first principles of human understanding.
authors.biography: Born in the manse at Strachan in the Mearns in 1710, the son of a Church of Scotland minister, he studied at King's College, Aberdeen, was licensed as a preacher in his teens and served the parish of New Machar from 1737. He left the ministry for teaching in 1752, when he was appointed regent in moral philosophy at King's College, Old Aberdeen, where the lectures sharpened his case against the ideal theory. His Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense (1764) argued that perception, memory and belief are original faculties that need no deduction, and that the way of ideas ends in Humean doubt. His Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense (1764) argued that perception, memory and belief are original faculties that require no deduction, and that the way of ideas ends in Humean doubt. Called in 1764 to the Glasgow chair of moral philosophy after Smith's resignation, he held it until failing health forced his retirement in 1781, publishing the Essays on the Intellectual Powers (1785) and the Essays on the Active Powers (1788). He died in Glasgow on 7 October 1796.
authors.profile: A pastor-philosopher who treated scepticism as a disease of theory and met it with an inventory of the mind's innate testimonies.
authors.style: Patient, encyclopaedic and repetitive exposition; classification of faculties and first principles; concrete appeals to sight, testimony and the language of common life, in a minister's measured tones.
authors.concerns: Perception, suggestion and the belief in external existence; the principles that precede reasoning; testimony, language and the rights of common sense; moral obligation, conscience and liberty of agency.
authors.significance: He gave philosophy its common-sense tradition, shaped the Scottish and American schools of mind, and set the problem of how to answer idealist scepticism that later thinkers from the Scottish realists to the twentieth century inherited.
authors.uncertainty: His published output is slight compared with his lectures, and the ordering of his intellectual development before 1764 must be reconstructed from manuscripts.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense
Essays on the Active Powers of Man
Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man

authors.name: Thomas Robert Malthus
authors.nationality: English; political economy and the prose of argument of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Clerman, mathematical political economist and the first professor of a modern political economy chair in England; the writer who fixed the population argument and its relation to famine, preventive checks and the Poor Laws.
authors.biography: Malthus was born at the Rookery, the family estate near Dorking in Surrey, on 13 or 14 February 1766, the second son of Daniel Malthus, a cultivated landowner and friend of David Hume and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and of Henrietta Graham. He was taught largely at home by tutors and by his father, then studied at Jesus College, Cambridge, where he took prizes in Latin and Greek and became a fellow in 1789. Ordained in the Church of England in 1791, he married in 1804 against the terms of his fellowship and lost it, but was in 1805 appointed professor of history and political economy at the East India Company's college at Haileybury, the first such professorship in England. His Essay on the Principle of Population, first issued anonymously in 1798 as a reply to his father's acquaintance the Marquis de Condorcet and to William Godwin's expectation of indefinite improvement, was enlarged in a second edition of 1803 into a documented historical and statistical work, with the added argument that vice and misery were the necessary consequences of population exceeding food. He became a central figure of London political economy, a friend and antagonist of David Ricardo, a frequent contributor to the debates on the Corn Laws and the Poor Laws, and from 1819 a member of the Political Economy Club and of the royal and statistical societies. His Definition of Political Economy (1827), his Measures of Value (1829) and his mathematical statements of rent were widely read and contested. He died unexpectedly at Bath on 29 December 1834 while on a visit, and was buried in the parish church at Bath, with a monument later placed in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: His writing is argumentative prose of the highest order of its kind: an anonymous pamphlet of 1798 that grew by repeated and heavily rewritten editions into a two-volume treatise of history, arithmetic and observation, followed by shorter analytic works on the nature, measure and laws of value, on rents and tithes, and on the deposits and currency. He wrote also a substantial article on Population for the Supplement to the Encyclopaedia Britannica, extended in 1836, and a work of moral philosophy, the Principles of Political Economy, whose first volume appeared in 1820. His manner is less technical than that of the economists who followed: he reasons on evidence drawn from travellers, parish registers and the history of nations, and he writes to persuade a cultivated reader as well as a specialist.
authors.style: Clear, measured and heavily qualified expository prose, built on the recurring couple of a check and a tendency, on numbered divisions and on the patient accumulation of instances; a polemical edge reserved for the openings and the conclusions of chapters. Abstract nouns and careful definitions are handled as instruments, and the argument advances by concession and exception rather than by system. Later economic writing becomes drier, more definitional and more preoccupied with measuring terms.
authors.concerns: The ratio of population to food and the geometric and arithmetic growth of the two; the moral and physical checks that keep the balance; the effects of parish relief and early marriage on the labouring poor; the reality of a general glut in contrast to Say's doctrine of markets; the theory of rent and the interests of landlords; the limits of perfectibility arguments and the uses of inequality; the education and moral discipline of the industrious classes.
authors.significance: The Essay on the Principle of Population set the terms on which famine, marriage, wages and relief were argued for a century, gave political economy its first professional professorship in England, and through Ricardo's debates defined the classical theory of rent. Its argument was taken up, and fought over, by poor-law reformers, by the reviewers of the Edinburgh and Quarterly, and by the evolutionary theorists who read in its competition for food the mechanism of natural selection; its pessimistic version of economics earned the science the name the dismal one. As a specimen of Romantic-period prose of argument he stands between the philosophical reformers of the 1790s and the professional social science of the 1830s.
authors.uncertainty: The day of his birth is given variously as 13 or 14 February 1766 in the biographies, and the parish and estate are described both as Westcott and as the Rookery near Dorking. The anonymous first edition of 1798 was long attributed to others, and its precise relationship to the much enlarged second edition of 1803 is a matter of continuing scholarly description rather than of settled fact.

works.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population

authors.name: Thomas Sackville
authors.identity: poet; dramatist; statesman
authors.biography: Born in 1536 at Buckhurst, Sussex; educated at Oxford (Inner Temple, and Cambridge). He entered Parliament in 1558 and rose through the law and the council to become Baron Buckhurst (1567), a commissioner at the trial of Mary Queen of Scots, and Earl of Dorset and Lord Treasurer (1599–1608). He died suddenly at the council table at Whitehall on 19 April 1608.
authors.profile: Co-author with Thomas Norton of Gorboduc (performed 1561–62), the first English tragedy in blank verse, and author of the great 'Induction' and the 'Complaint of Henry Duke of Buckingham' contributed to A Mirror for Magistrates (1563), which he planned and edited with others.
authors.style: Grave, stately, Senecan moral verse; the Induction's descent into the underworld is the finest English poetry between Chaucer's death and Spenser.
authors.concerns: The dangers of a divided succession; the falls of princes; counsel and the commonwealth.
authors.significance: Gorboduc founded English tragedy and political drama; the Mirror for Magistrates he fathered became the great poetic storehouse of Elizabethan tragedy.
authors.uncertainty: The exact division of the Gorboduc acts between Sackville and Norton is unknown.
sources: Letitia Elizabeth Landon: Selected Writings

authors.name: Thomas Shadwell
authors.identity: Dramatist, Whig, and poet laureate; a self-professed disciple of Jonson who wrote vigorous comedies of humours and low life (Epsom Wells, The Squire of Alsatia) and whose quarrel with Dryden made him the target of Mac Flecknoe and the 'Og' of Absalom and Achitophel.
authors.biography: Born c. 1642 at Stanthall, Norfolk, educated at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn. A committed Protestant and Whig, he wrote some eighteen plays, including the comedies The Sullen Lovers (1668), Epsom Wells (1672), and The Squire of Alsatia (1688), the tragedy Psyche (1674), and the anti-Catholic The Lancashire Witches (1681). He succeeded Dryden as poet laureate and historiographer royal after the Revolution of 1688 (Dryden, a Catholic, having been deprived). He died on 19 November 1692.
authors.profile: The Jonsonian satirist-comedian of the Restoration, whose plays championed 'humours' comedy, Protestant Whiggism, and a plain, moral, low-comic realism against what he saw as the immorality and wit of Dryden's party.
authors.style: Comedy of humours and dialect; realistic low-life and provincial settings; moral satire; verse prologues and epilogues of political bite; and, in his operas and masques, spectacle.
authors.concerns: Protestant and Whig politics; the satire of vice, foppery, and popery; the moral purpose of comedy; Jonsonian 'humours'; and the defence of plain English sense.
authors.significance: Shadwell's importance lies both in his substantial, socially observant comedies and in his role as Dryden's antagonist — his defeat in the Mac Flecknoe quarrel made him a permanent emblem of literary dullness, though modern critics have reassessed his real comic talent.
authors.uncertainty: Shadwell's birth year is approximate; the Dryden–Shadwell quarrel is well documented, though Shadwell's reputation suffered from its partisan literary afterlife.
sources: The Letters of Edgar Allan Poe (2 volumes)

authors.name: Thomas Southerne
authors.identity: Irish-born Restoration dramatist; author of the pathetic tragedy The Fatal Marriage (1694) and of the stage adaptation of Behn's Oroonoko (1695), which held the repertory for over a century and made the 'noble slave' a staple of the eighteenth-century theatre.
authors.biography: Born 1660 at Stranorlar, County Donegal, educated at Trinity College, Dublin and the Middle Temple. He came to London, was befriended by Dryden (for whom he wrote a prologue), and produced comedies (The Wives' Excuse, 1691; The Maid's Last Prayer, 1693) and tragedies. His Oroonoko (1695), adapting Behn's novella into a tragedy with a comic subplot, and The Fatal Marriage (1694), built for the actress Elizabeth Barry, were enormously successful. He made a fortune from an Irish sinecure and a government post, retired from the stage early, and lived to the great age of 86, dying on 28 May 1746.
authors.profile: The successful practitioner of pathetic tragedy and the adapter who transmitted Behn's Oroonoko to the eighteenth-century stage in a form that shaped the period's imagination of slavery and noble suffering.
authors.style: Pathetic, sentimental blank verse; tragic suffering heroines; a mixture of tragedy and comic intrigue (in Oroonoko); and a commercially astute dramaturgy.
authors.concerns: Suffering innocence and pathetic tragedy; slavery and the 'noble savage'; love, marriage, and misfortune; and the moral appeal to pity.
authors.significance: Southerne's Oroonoko was the standard stage version of the story for 150 years and the vehicle through which Behn's anti-slavery narrative reached mass audiences; his pathetic tragedies exemplify the sentimental turn of Restoration serious drama.
authors.uncertainty: Southerne's life is documented; the extent of Dryden's hand in his early work and the sources of some plays are matters of scholarship.

works.title: The Fatal Marriage; or, The Innocent Adultery

sources: Stedman's Surinam: Life in an Eighteenth-Century Slave Society. An Abridged, Modernized Edition of Narrative of a Five Years Expedition against the Revolted Negroes of Surinam

authors.name: Thomas Sprat
authors.identity: Clergyman, poet, and historian of science; his History of the Royal-Society of London (1667) was the first account of the Society and a manifesto for the plain, factual prose style that the new philosophy demanded.
authors.biography: Born 1635 (baptised) at Henstridge, Dorset, educated at Wadham College, Oxford (Fellow), where he joined Wilkins's circle. He wrote a Pindaric ode on Cromwell (1659) and served as a chaplain and preacher after the Restoration. At the request of the Royal Society he composed its History (1667), celebrating its method and advocating a 'close, naked, natural way of speaking'. He rose in the church to become Dean of Westminster (1683) and Bishop of Rochester (1684), and was involved in the politics of James II's reign and the Revolution. He died on 20 May 1713.
authors.profile: The apologist and historian of the Royal Society whose prose ideal — plain, precise, free of rhetorical 'swelling' — became the manifesto for the modern scientific and plain style.
authors.style: Clear, expository, persuasive prose; historical narrative of an institution; advocacy of the plain style; and occasional Pindaric verse.
authors.concerns: The new experimental philosophy and its institution; the reform of language toward the plain style; the reconciliation of science and religion; and public and ecclesiastical affairs.
authors.significance: Sprat's History of the Royal-Society is the foundational document of the Society's early ideals and the classic statement of the plain-style programme, widely quoted in the history of science and of English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Sprat's birth year is approximate; his ecclesiastical and political career is documented, and his History is partly propagandistic for the Society's ideals.

works.title: The History of the Royal-Society of London for Improving of Natural Knowledge

sources: Lady Caroline Lamb: A Biography

authors.name: Thomas Traherne
authors.identity: Anglican priest, mystical prose writer, and poet, discovered only in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries; author of Centuries of Thankfulness and the Roman Forgeries, whose ecstatic celebration of innocent vision and divine felicity is unlike anything else in English.
authors.biography: Born c. 1636–37 in Hereford, son of a shoemaker; educated at Brasenose College, Oxford (BA 1656–57), and ordained, holding the living of Credenhill near Hereford (1657–72) while serving as chaplain to Sir Orlando Bridgman at Teddington from 1669. He wrote prolifically in prose and verse but published little in his lifetime (only the anti-Catholic Roman Forgeries, 1673). He died of smallpox on 27 September 1674. His major works — Centuries of Thankfulness, The Kingdom of God, and the poems — circulated in manuscript and were misattributed to Vaughan until Bertram Dobell's editions of 1903–08 established his fame.
authors.profile: The mystic of felicity and wonder, who celebrated the infant soul's apprehension of the infinite in the world and argued that happiness consists in rightly valuing creation as God's gift.
authors.style: A rhapsodic, cumulative prose of wonder and thanksgiving; long flowing 'centuries' or meditative paragraphs; visionary imagery of light, infinity, and childhood; and a lyric poetry of ecstatic innocence.
authors.concerns: Felicity and the desire for God; innocence and the vision of childhood; the infinity of the soul; gratitude and thanksgiving; the goodness of creation; free will and love.
authors.significance: Once unknown, Traherne is now recognised as a major mystical writer whose Centuries and poems anticipate Romantic and modernist celebrations of childhood vision and influenced figures from Christopher Smart to the twentieth century.
authors.uncertainty: Traherne's birth year is uncertain (1636 or 1637); his manuscripts were long misattributed, and the dating and arrangement of his works remain subjects of scholarship.
sources: The Poetical Works of Fitz-Greene Halleck: Now First Collected

authors.name: Thomas Usk
authors.identity: poet; political writer; clerk
authors.biography: A London scrivener and clerk who attached himself first to the party of John of Northampton and then betrayed it to Nicholas Brembre and the royalist faction, serving as under-sheriff of Middlesex. Imprisoned after the Merciless Parliament of 1388, he wrote the Testament of Love in the Tower and was executed at Tyburn on 4 March 1388.
authors.profile: Author of the Testament of Love (c. 1384–88), an allegorical prose apologia in the Boethian and Chaucerian manner — for centuries printed as Chaucer's — in which Love consoles the imprisoned author and vindicates his political life.
authors.style: Elaborate allegorical prose with Chaucerian echoes; the fusion of love allegory with political self-defence; Boethian consolation adapted to a treason trial.
authors.concerns: The justice of his political career; fortune, free will, and the consolations of love and philosophy.
authors.significance: The Testament is the first major prose work in the Chaucerian line and a unique document of Ricardian factional politics; its false attribution to Chaucer long shaped the poet's canon.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his political career come from hostile records.
movements: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy
sources: Leviathan: The English and Latin Texts

authors.name: Thomas Warton
authors.identity: English literary historian, poet, and scholar, professor at Oxford and Poet Laureate, best known for the foundational History of English Poetry.
authors.biography: Thomas Warton the younger, son of the poet Thomas Warton the elder and brother of the critic Joseph Warton, was educated at Oxford, where he became a fellow of Oriel College and later Professor of Poetry. He published early verse, including The Pleasures of Melancholy (1747), contributed odes written jointly with his brother, and wrote an Essay on the Genius and Writings of Pope. His lifelong work, The History of English Poetry, whose first volumes appeared in 1774, 1778, and 1781, pioneered the historical study of medieval and Renaissance verse and its French and Italian sources. He became Poet Laureate in 1785. He died in 1790.
authors.profile: A poet and a literary historian of romantic and antiquarian sympathies who, reacting against strict neoclassicism, prized imagination, the medieval tale, and the historical development of national literature.
authors.style: In his verse, a melancholy, descriptive, and occasionally antiquarian manner; in his History, a learned, digressive, source-hunting scholarly prose that valued imaginative romance and native tradition.
authors.concerns: The origins and historical development of English poetry; the romance tradition and its sources; the imagination versus rules; national literary identity; and the pleasures of melancholy and retirement.
authors.significance: The History of English Poetry is a founding work of English literary history and scholarship, establishing the study of medieval and early modern literature and anticipating Romantic interest in romance and imagination.
authors.uncertainty: He must be carefully distinguished from his father and his brother Joseph, also literary figures, and his exact birthplace is given variously; the completion and dating of the later volumes of his History are uneven.

works.title: Observations on the Faerie Queene of Spenser

authors.name: Timothy Dwight
authors.nationality: American; the New England Congregational letters of Hartford and New Haven, the Yale presidency and the Federalist clerical interest of the 1790s
authors.identity: Preacher, theologian, poet and educator; the president of Yale who made the college the training ground of the New England clergy and of the Federalist interest, the most influential Congregational divine of his generation in America, and the author of the most considerable American descriptive poem of the 1790s.
authors.biography: Dwight was born at Northampton in Massachusetts, of a family long connected with Yale and with the New England ministry, and on his mother's side grandson of the Northampton preacher of the Great Awakening, whose theology and papers were the inheritance of his whole life; he was taught first at home under his mother's direction, reading the classics and the divines before he was a student in the ordinary sense. He entered Yale at thirteen and graduated at seventeen in the class of 1769, taught for two years at the grammar school at New Haven and returned to the college as a tutor, and was licensed to preach in the years of the Revolution, serving with the armies as a chaplain while he preached by contract in the villages of Connecticut and Massachusetts. He came to the public eye as a poet with the epic of the conquest of Canaan published in 1785, belonged in the Hartford and Wethersfield circle of wits whose satires and miscellany defined the Federalist letters of the 1780s, and about 1791 settled at a farm at Greenfield Hill near New Haven, where in the intervals of teaching and preaching he wrote the topographical, historical and didactic poem which bears the place's name. In 1795 he accepted the presidency of Yale, which he held until his death, governing the college through two decades of political agitation, religious revival and war, filling the classes with students from every part of the country, lecturing and preaching against the deistic and revolutionary principles of the age, and superintending an undergraduate community which he treated at once as a school of religion and as a nursery of the New England establishment. His presidency saw the revival of 1802 and the controversies with the Republicans and with the liberal Christians, and he was the most attacked and most quoted clerical Federalist of the embargo years. He wrote much besides: sermons, theological lectures, a defence of the scriptural scheme against the infidelity of the day, biographical and religious memoirs, and the survey of the northern country compiled from the journals of his tours, which was printed from his papers after his death with an enlarged issue following.
