He died at New Haven on 11 January 1817, having been president of the college for twenty-two years, and was buried in the Grove Street cemetery there, leaving his college the leading school of Congregational New England and his theological writings the standard course of instruction for a generation of ministers.
authors.profile: His verse divides between the early epic on the Israelite conquest, which drew the American continent into the machinery of scriptural history, and the descriptive-poetical essay of Greenfield Hill, which passes from landscape through the settlement, institutions, commerce, religion and morals of the American township. His prose is chiefly clerical and educational: sermons and charges, the theological lectures printed after his death, controversies on the French Revolution and on infidelity, biographical memoirs, religious tracts for the young, and the Travels in New-England and New-York, part journal, part statistical survey and part moral argument, which is the fullest early American example of the traveller's national survey. He edited and used the papers of his grandfather's house, and his editorial and documentary work belongs to the same piety of records which produced the historical societies of the next generation.
authors.style: In verse a competent and stately command of the eighteenth-century couplet and of the Thomson and Goldsmith manner of descriptive didactic poetry, with a weight of enumeration, moral reflection and historical recapitalization laid over the landscape; in prose a clear, energetic and frequently contentious pulpit style, argumentative in the theological and political writing, and detailed, table-laden and morally earnest in the Travels, where observation of farms, schools, canals and denominations is always pressed toward religious and civic instruction.
authors.concerns: The fate of religion and of sound learning in a republic, and the danger of deistic and revolutionary principles; the Congregational covenant and the education of the ministry; the moral history of New England and the meaning of its townships, colleges and churches; providential national history read through the Bible and through settlement; the duties of the educated to the commonwealth, and the government of students, churches and a people.
authors.significance: As president of Yale for twenty-two years he made the college the central institution of New England Congregationalism and of the Federalist interest, and the ministers, editors and statesmen of the next generation were formed under his government; his theological lectures and his controversies gave the standing clergy their most influential defence against the infidelity of the 1790s and against the rising liberal theology, and his Greenfield Hill was the most ambitious American poem of its decade. His Travels supplied the first systematic portrait of the northern states, and his career remains the type of the American clerical man of letters exercising public influence through an institution.

authors.name: Tobias Smollett
authors.identity: Scottish novelist, pamphleteer, and historian, a vigorous picaresque writer and editor who was among the major novelists of his generation.
authors.biography: Born in 1721 (baptized in that year) at Dalquhurn in Dunbartonshire into a Scottish family, he was apprenticed to a printer in Glasgow and began writing. He moved to London, where his first novel, The Adventures of Roderick Random (1748), established his reputation, followed by The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle (1751), The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom (1753), and The Adventures of Sir Launcelot Greaves (1766). He edited periodicals and histories and traveled, including a journey that produced The Expedition of Humphry Clinker (1771). He died at Livorno on 17 October 1771.
authors.profile: A novelist of satiric vigor and abrasive humor whose picaresque journeys expose corruption, misanthropy, and the rougher edges of society, and whose late epistolary novel is a landmark of sentimental and travel-inflected fiction.
authors.style: Coarse, energetic, satirical realism; episodic picaresque plotting; caricatured and misanthropic characters; invective and humor; and in Humphry Clinker a comic polyphony of contrasting epistolary voices.
authors.concerns: National identity and Anglo-Scottish tension; cruelty and benevolence in society; travel, observation, and the state of the nation; the politics of faction; and misanthropy versus social feeling.
authors.significance: A leading figure in the rise of the novel and of Scottish letters within British culture, whose picaresque satires shaped later fiction and whose Humphry Clinker remains a touchstone of the comic epistolary novel.
authors.uncertainty: The year of his birth rests on baptismal records, and some details of his early life, apprenticeship, and the full extent of his journalistic and editorial work remain imperfectly documented.

works.title: A Journey Through France and Italy
The Adventures of Ferdinand Count Fathom
The Adventures of Gil Blas of Santillane
The Adventures of Sir Launcelot Greaves

sources: Hope Leslie: Or, Early Times in the Massachusetts (American Women Writers series)

authors.name: Venture Smith
authors.birthplace: Baa, on the West African coast (the African name and the place as given in his own narrative; the modern identification is disputed)
authors.nationality: American (born in West Africa); the earliest Afro-American slave narrative and the life-writing of the free Black communities of New England
authors.identity: A man born in Africa, enslaved in Rhode Island and Connecticut, who purchased his own freedom and that of his family and dictated the earliest secular slave narrative printed in the United States; the author-assert, in his own first person, of an African past, of the Middle Passage and of a lifetime of labour, contract and lawsuit.
authors.biography: He was born Broteer Furro, as he said, the eldest son of a ruler in an African country on the coast known to him as Baa, and was taken in a raid on his father's town when he was a boy of about sixteen, marched to the coast and sold; the year and the place of his birth he gave only as his memory and his account could give them. He was carried across the Atlantic, passed through the markets of the West Indies and was sold at Newport in the Rhode Island colony; he took the name Venture from an English word written on papers of his purchase, and the surname Smith from his last Connecticut owner, and he passed through several New England masters, serving in households, on the water and in the labour of the seaport towns. By the labour of many years, by contracts of hire he kept to the letter, and by the help of friends among the free Black people and the white neighbours of the Connecticut coast, he bought his own freedom at New London in 1746 and afterwards the freedom of his wife Meg and of his children, paying the prices and recording them. He worked as a mariner, a farm labourer, a woodcutter and a small proprietor, saved money, bought land, and in his later years lived at Haddam in Connecticut as a free landholder and parent of a considerable family, pursuing in the courts a man who had illegally sold his wife and recovering something of the loss. In his seventies he caused the history of his life to be drawn up and published at New London in 1798, taken down from his own mouth by a local compiler, and the volume sets out the African succession and politics of his father's country, the manner of his capture, the voyage, the slave markets of the West Indies and of the northern colonies, and the exact sums of his earnings and purchases. He died in 1805 at Haddam and was buried in the graveyard of the church at East Haddam, where his headstone, raised long afterward by his descendants and by the historical society, records the dates he gave him.
authors.profile: His Narrative is a short first-person life taken down from his mouth and printed as related by himself, and it divides between the African chapters, an account of the country, the succession and the raid that ended his childhood which has no parallel in the later genre, the Middle Passage and the sale, and the long American record of labour, wages, contracts, prices paid and lawsuits. The economic detail is its distinguishing feature: the sums earned and paid, the terms of hire, the cost of his own and his family's freedom, and the final pursuit of the man who sold his wife are set down with a specificity absent from the religious narratives that followed. It is autobiography and evidence at once, and it closes with the facts of his property and his family.
authors.style: A flat, concrete and unsentimental narrative voice, in the first person and without appeal to the reader's pity, resting on date, place, name and amount; the phrase of the account rendered rather than of the complaint made. The compiler's literary hand is visible in the framing and in the moralising touches, but the matter and the manner of counting are his own, and the effect of plain statement is the more powerful for the absence of rhetoric.
authors.concerns: The fact of an African history, name and family before enslavement; the actual conduct of the trade from the coast through the voyage to the market; the meaning of freedom as the power to earn, to contract, to buy persons out of slavery and to hold land; the law as an instrument available, however imperfectly, to a free Black man; the worth of labour and the record of its price; the duty of a father and a husband in a condition that denied both.
authors.significance: His narrative is the earliest secular slave narrative printed in the United States and one of the strongest surviving first-person accounts of African origins, the Middle Passage and the slave markets of the northern colonies and the West Indies; it antedates and differs from the religious confession-model that hardened in the genre. Its records are used as primary evidence for the trade, for the labor and wages of enslaved and free Black people in New England, and for the founding of a free Black propertied community, and it stands at the origin of the Afro-American autobiography.
authors.uncertainty: His birth year and his African origin are self-reported and approximate: the narrative gives the place as Baa and the country of his father's rule in his own terms, and modern scholars have placed it variously in what are now Nigeria, Ghana and Guinea, with the date of his birth estimated at about 1729 from his account of his age at capture, while older editions and notices put it nearer 1700. His African name, his age, the dates of his sale and of his several transfers, and the details of the lawsuit for his wife come only from the dictated narrative and from such local records as survive, and the compiler's share of the composition cannot be measured. The date of his death and the inscription of the gravestone are recorded in Haddam and East Haddam sources and in the family account.

works.title: A Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Venture, a Native of Africa: But resident above sixty years in the United States of America. Related by Himself

authors.name: Walter Hilton
authors.identity: mystic; devotional writer; Augustinian canon
authors.biography: Probably educated at Cambridge and trained in canon law before becoming an Augustinian canon of Thurgarton Priory, Nottinghamshire; he died on 24 March 1396. His writings circulated widely and were printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1494.
authors.profile: Author of the Scale of Perfection (Book I c. 1380s, addressed to an anchoress; Book II c. 1390s), the most influential English treatise on contemplation; of the Epistle on the Mixed Life, addressed to a devout layman; and of other works including Of Angels' Song and the translation of the Stimulus Amoris attributed to him.
authors.style: Measured, theologically precise prose; the famous image of the spiritual life as a ladder or scale; cautious discrimination between true and false mystical experience; clarity and pastoral warmth.
authors.concerns: The reformation of the soul in the image of God; the relation of active and contemplative lives; the discernment of spirits.
authors.significance: The classic systematizer of English mysticism; the Scale of Perfection remained a standard of English devotional reading into the seventeenth century (used by Augustine Baker and his circle).
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early career conjectural; some works attributed to him are disputed.
sources: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

authors.name: Walter Map
authors.identity: satirist; courtier; churchman
authors.biography: A Herefordshire-born clerk of Welsh descent who studied at Paris and served Henry II as a royal justice and travelling ambassador; he attended the Lateran Council of 1179 and became a canon of St Paul's and archdeacon of Oxford. The archsatirist of the Angevin court, he died c. 1210.
authors.profile: Author of De Nugis Curialium (Courtiers' Trifles, c. 1181–92), a miscellany of satire, gossip, marvels, and history that preserves some of the earliest Arthurian and fairy material in Latin; the Goliardic poems once attributed to him are not his.
authors.style: Biting, allusive, deliberately disordered satire of the court and the religious orders; the anecdote raised to moral fable; a proto-Renaissance pessimism about the world he served.
authors.concerns: The vices of courts and monasteries; the vanity of worldly service; the relations of the sexes; the marvels of Wales and the Celtic past.
authors.significance: De Nugis is the supreme literary monument of the twelfth-century courtier's disenchantment and a key source for the early Arthurian and Herla/fairy traditions.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the De Nugis survives in a single manuscript and its text is unstable.
movements: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume D: The Romantic Period

authors.name: Walter Savage Landor
authors.identity: Poet and prose writer, principally a writer of Latin-English lyric and of imaginary dialogue; one of the great English prose stylists, and a Jacobean-reviving romantic classicist rather than a participant in the Lake or Cockney schools.
authors.biography: Landor was born in 1775 at Ipswich into a prosperous Warwickshire family, the eldest son of a doctor and a mother who died while he was young. He was sent to Rugby and then to University College, Oxford, where he was rusticated for firing a gun in his rooms and for the quarrels that followed, and where he wrote the verse that became Gebir. His marriage in 1797 to Julia Guadagni, daughter of a Florentine nobleman, brought wealth and a long domestic estrangement which ended in separation in Italy in 1819 and in the loss of access to his children, a wound he never stopped writing about. He lived chiefly in Italy, at Como, Bagni di Lucca, and above all at Bath and then at the Villa Fiesole and in Florence, with a long residence at Bath in the 1830s. In 1836 he quarrelled with his friend and patron Robert Forster, whose family he had attacked, and the resulting scandal and the loss of a share of his income shadowed his last decades. He published steadily but poorly from the 1820s, with Imaginary Conversations in 1824, Pericles and Aspasia in 1836, and the last volumes of verse in the 1860s, and he died at Florence in 1864, aged eighty-nine, leaving a large posthumous prose and verse collection.
authors.profile: His canon is small for its length of years and almost wholly made up of short or modular forms: the Spenserian romance of Gebir, the anonymous epic of The Battle of Hastings, the compact elegies, and above all the prose conversations, which he kept revising and regrouping for half a century. He wrote in a double register, English and Latin, and thought of style as the chief moral possession of a writer. His reputation rests less on any single large work than on the intensity and compression of the whole manner, and on a handful of short poems which stand outside the main currents of romanticism.
authors.style: Austere, epigrammatic, and archaising: periods of balanced subordination, monosyllabic emphasis at the close of a passage, and a habitual refusal of transition and explanation. His dialogue dispenses with stage direction and narration, letting character appear wholly through speech, and his lyric reduces diction to the barest nouns and verbs. He is capable of extreme tenderness in the shortest space and of sustained invective in the same syntax.
authors.concerns: Liberty of private judgement against priest, king, and party; the claims of the affections against the family and the law; style as an ethical achievement; the study of Greek, Latin, and Italian literature as a living constitution; the moral history of tyranny and exile, and the dignity of the cultivated individual in a degraded public life.
authors.significance: He stands outside the metropolitan schools of romanticism and supplies its classical and archaising counter-tradition, handing on to later writers the imaginary conversation as a form of criticism and the short elegy as a model of condensation; his life and quarrels also document the economics and the family politics of the professional man of letters in the nineteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: The dating of the poems of the 1790s, including the elegies addressed to Rose Aylmer, rests on manuscript evidence and on later recollection rather than on a settled chronology, and the first printing of several short pieces is imperfectly recorded.

works.title: Pericles and Aspasia; a Series of Dialogues, Letters, and Epitaphs
The Battle of Hastings; an Epic Poem in Twelve Books
The Gebir; a Spanish Romance, Poetical, in Four Books

authors.name: Washington Irving
authors.nationality: American; essayist, tale-writer, sketch-writer, biographer and historian of the early republic, the central figure of the Knickerbocker group and the first American author of prose to obtain a wide British and European reputation
authors.identity: A writer of prose in several related modes: the comic antiquarian history, the periodical paper and character sketch, the legend and ghost tale of the Dutch country, the familiar essay of English scene and society, and later the romantic history and biography of the Spanish and American past. He wrote no poetry and no fiction of the systematic novel kind; his characteristic form is the sketch, in which observation, memory, humorous invention and moral reflection are left unwelded.
authors.biography: He was born in New York City on 3 April 1783, the youngest but one of eleven children of a Scotch settling family, and was named, it was said, in honour of the recent declaration of independence. He was apprenticed to a law firm, was admitted to practice without ever taking much interest in the bar, and from about 1802 began to write for the New York papers with his brothers. In 1807 and 1808 he shared with his friend James Kirke Paulding the periodical Salmagundi, and in 1809 he brought out at New York the burlesque history which established the persona of Diedrich Knickerbocker. Business disaster in the family importing house sent him to England on its affairs from 1815 to 1823, and there he wrote the English and American sketches of The Sketch Book, issued in parts from 1819 to 1820 and making his name on both sides of the Atlantic. He published miscellaneous histories and sketches of the British and Spanish field through the middle 1820s, travelled in the American prairies in 1832, and in 1835 settled at Sunnyside on the Hudson, where he built up a reputation as the senior man of letters of the country. He served as United States minister at Madrid from 1842 to 1846, wrote the life of Washington in five volumes at Sunnyside, and died there on 28 November 1859, a few weeks after finishing the last volume.
authors.profile: His work falls into a humorous historical group, a group of essays and tales in the manner of the periodical sketch, and a late group of biography, history and travel; between them he compiled lives of western and Spanish personages and a great deal of occasional address and preface. The History of New York and the Salmagundi papers are the native and comic beginning; The Sketch Book, with its two companion collections of 1822 and 1824, is the characteristic body of his work and the source of the American short tale. His later prose is antiquarian and diplomatic in tone, and his Spanish histories and biographies of Columbus and of the conquerors of Granada belong to the romantic treatment of national past rather than to scholarly history.
authors.style: A smooth, old-fashioned, consciously literary English, shaded from easy irony into sentiment without the reader being warned of the turn. He is an excellent describer of quiet scenery and of ruined places, a droll narrator in the personating vein, and a writer who prefers the half-light of the legend and the sketch to the resolved plot; his humour is generated by persona, by the assumption of a naive or pompous voice, and by the pedantic accumulation of invented authority.
authors.concerns: The making of an American literary past out of Dutch, Indian and revolutionary materials; the depreciation and the admiration of the old country by a colonial writer; the value of tradition, holiday and legend to a calculating republic; the commerce of the nations and the fate of the settled and displaced peoples of America; the education of taste through English scene and architecture; the dignity of the man of letters in a country of lawyers and merchants.
authors.significance: He gave the American short prose tale its first durable models and the sketch essay its American manner, and by his success with British publishers and readers he established that American writing could be a European commodity. Diedrich Knickerbocker named a school, a city's mythology and a literature's self-image, and The Sketch Book was the most widely read American book of its generation. His late life of Washington and his prairie travel also fixed the sentimental and legendary treatment of the national story for a century.
authors.uncertainty: The story of his naming in honour of the declaration of independence is family tradition rather than documented fact; the precise extent of Paulding's and of his brother's share in the Salmagundi papers has never been settled to general satisfaction.

works.title: A History of New York from the Beginning of the World to the End of the Dutch Dynasty
The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.

authors.name: Werferth
authors.identity: translator; bishop
authors.biography: Bishop of Worcester from c. 872 to his death (c. 915); one of the scholars of King Alfred's court circle named by Asser.
authors.profile: Translator of Gregory the Great's Dialogues into Old English (c. 890s), a work commissioned by Alfred and prefaced by him; the earliest extensive Old English translation of a major patristic text.
authors.style: Faithful, competent Mercian-flavoured prose, somewhat more literal than the other Alfredian translations.
authors.concerns: The transmission of Gregory's hagiographical and pastoral teaching to a vernacular audience.
authors.significance: A key figure of the Alfredian translation program; his Dialogues preserve a major stage in the development of Old English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the attribution of the translation rests on Asser's Life of Alfred and Alfred's own Preface.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume II: 1042–1189

authors.name: William Baldwin
authors.identity: satirist; editor; corrector of printing
authors.biography: Born about 1515; a scholar of Oxford who became corrector of the king's printing under Edward VI and a prolific editor and compiler. His Treatise of Moral Philosophy appeared in 1547; his prose satire Beware the Cat, written in 1552–53, was printed in 1561. He planned and partly compiled A Mirror for Magistrates, printed in 1559 after his death. He died about 1563.
authors.profile: The author of the first English work of sustained prose fiction and the begetter of A Mirror for Magistrates. Beware the Cat — a night-long exchange of stories about cats, set in a London printing house and framed as a fantastic listening experiment — is the first English novel in embryo, and its anti-Catholic satire made it dangerous enough to be suppressed. The Mirror, which he edited and contributed to, became one of the most influential books of the Elizabethan age.
authors.style: Framed narrative in the plain style; printer's-shop realism; satirical fable with a serious theological edge.
authors.concerns: Protestant polemic against the old religion; the uses of fiction for truth-telling; the moral instruction of magistrates through the falls of great men.
authors.significance: A founding figure of English prose fiction and of the complaint tradition; his Mirror for Magistrates supplied subjects and rhetoric to Spenser, Shakespeare, and the whole Elizabethan tragic imagination.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the division of authorship within the Mirror is editorial.
themes: Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
sources: John Keats: The Complete Poems (Penguin Classics)

authors.name: William Beckford
authors.identity: English writer, collector, and politician, the fabulously wealthy author of the Gothic-Oriental tale Vathek.
authors.biography: Born on 29 September 1760 in London, the son of William Beckford, twice Lord Mayor of London and a West Indian planter and politician, he inherited great wealth and entered public life as a Member of Parliament and briefly a sheriff. As a young man he wrote the Oriental romance Vathek, originally composed in French and published in English in 1786. He built the eccentric country house at Fonthill Abbey and pursued collecting and writing. He died on 2 May 1844.
authors.profile: The author of Vathek, a tale of oriental magnificence and forbidden knowledge that fused Gothic luxury with the Arabian Nights tradition and helped define the decadent and exotic strain in Romantic-era fiction.
authors.style: Ornate, sensational, orientalizing prose; lavish descriptive excess; a framing of wonder and magic; and a deliberate artificiality and luxury of detail inherited from the Arabian Nights vogue.
authors.concerns: Curiosity, power, and transgression; the pursuit of forbidden knowledge; orientalism and exotic magnificence; pleasure and damnation; and aesthetic luxury.
authors.significance: A distinctive and influential author of Gothic-Oriental fiction, whose Vathek became a landmark of the supernatural tale and an important source for later decadent and fantasy writing.
authors.uncertainty: His birth date is well attested; some details of the composition and translation history of Vathek, and of the dating of his writings, remain subjects of scholarly note rather than of real dispute.
sources: Timothy Dwight, 1752-1817: A Biography

authors.name: William Blackstone
authors.identity: Oxford don, serjeant at law, judge and Tory MP, whose four-volume Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765-1769) made English law a readable rational system.
authors.biography: Born in Cheapside in London in 1723, the posthumous son of a City merchant, he was educated at a London grammar school and at Pembroke College, Oxford, with the help of relations, and was elected a fellow of All Souls. Called to the bench of the Middle Temple and practising on the Oxford and home circuits, he won fame by a book on gavelkind and by lecturing on English law, which led to his appointment as the first Vinerian professor in 1758. His Analysis of the Laws of England (1756) and his Discourse on the Study of the Law (1765) prepared the Commentaries, published in four parts between 1765 and 1769 and immediately made his name. He sat in the Commons, was appointed to the bench of the Common Pleas and knighted in 1770, and was transferred to the King's Bench in 1779, where his rigorous, sometimes unpopular judgments tested his own theory of law. He died in London on 14 February 1780.
authors.profile: The great systematiser and apologist of the common law, who presented its intricacies as an ordered, decent and largely admirable inheritance.
authors.style: Clear, stately, judicious prose that explains difficulty without hiding it; balanced periods and a scholar's courtesy; historical narrative used to legitimate existing doctrine.
authors.concerns: The reasonableness and continuity of the common law; the rights of persons and of things; the nature of law, sovereignty and the reach of parliamentary authority; the legal condition of servants, women, children and colonial subjects; the relation of law to religion and morality.
authors.significance: The Commentaries became the standard education of English-speaking lawyers for two centuries and, with their American reprints, one of the chief sources of early American legal and political vocabulary; Bentham's attack on them opened the age of law reform.
authors.uncertainty: The order and dating of his lectures and of the several editions of the Commentaries, which he revised to his death, are complex and disputed.

works.title: An Analysis of the Laws of England
Commentaries on the Laws of England

authors.name: William Blake
authors.birthplace: London, in the Golden Square quarter, of a dissenting shopkeeping family
authors.nationality: English; poet, engraver and visionary painter of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Poet-engraver who made his books by his own hands, the creator of a private prophetic mythology, and the most uncompromising visionary writer of the English Romantic generation.
authors.biography: Blake was born in London, the son of a hosier, and showed from early childhood a disposition to drawing and an familiarity with visions; he was not sent to school but was bound apprentice to an engraver at about fourteen, served the seven years, and then entered the schools of the Royal Academy, where the academic manner of the presidents offended him. He set up as an engraver and print-seller, married in 1782 a woman whom he taught to read and to work at his printing, and produced the illuminated books by a method of etching and relief-printing of his own invention, colouring the plates by hand and selling them in numbers far below their merit. He knew and was friendly with the painter of the Nightmare and with the publishers and dissenting writers of the revolutionary decade, visited France in 1792, and wrote and engraved the prophetic books of the years of hope and reaction. From 1800 to 1803 he worked under the patronage of a poet of the earlier school at Felpham in Sussex, where a soldier's complaint brought him before a magistrates' court and an acquittal; the last decades brought commissions for illustrations to a book of scripture and to the vision of the Italian poet, a small circle of devoted younger painters, a display of his own designs at his own price, and death in 1827 in lodging in the Strand, his wife beside him and his funeral attended by friends of both his arts.
authors.profile: His writing divides between the songs and shorter lyrics of the two illuminated collections, the prophetic books in verse and prose, and the mass of annotations, memoranda, letters and designs; his mythology of the four powers of the human mind, of the fallen reason and of the labouring imagination is the most systematic private system in English. He was also a designer and engraver whose plates carry his poems, so that text and image must be read as one, and a painter in water-colour and in tempera who executed a series of large designs and illustrations.
authors.style: Lyric verse of great simplicity in song measures, with reiterated lines and a balance of innocent and terrible images; prophetic verse of stern and rapid accentual lines, filled with proclamation, question and catalogue; prose of aphoristic vehemence, with the rhetoric of the angel and the devil and a continuous war of contraries.
authors.concerns: The contraries by which the soul progresses, and the falseness of a morality of patience and restraint; imagination as the divine body in man and the enemy of single reason; the guilt of law, priesthood and empire, and the bondage of the slave, the child and the inhibited lover; the redemption of the divided giant and the building of a city of vision in England.
authors.significance: He anticipated by a decade the ballad revolt against polished verse, and he left the only fully developed personal mythology in English. His illuminated books are the foundation of the art of the printed page in which poem and design are one object, and his prophecy of a redeemed imagination, with his phrases for the dark satanic mills and for the child and the sweep, has entered the language of literature, of religious radicalism and of national song.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of the first issue of several illuminated books and the order in which the plates were executed and sold are disputed, and the account of his visions rests almost wholly on his own statements and on those of his wife and his friends.

works.title: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
Visions of the Daughters of Albion

authors.name: William Camden
authors.identity: antiquarian; historian; herald; schoolmaster
authors.biography: Born 2 May 1551 in the Old Bailey, London. Educated at Christ's Hospital and St Paul's School, then at Magdalen and Christ Church, Oxford. He taught at Westminster School (1575–97), where his pupils included Ben Jonson, and ended his career as Clarenceux King of Arms (1597). He died on 9 November 1623 at Chislehurst, Kent.
authors.profile: Britannia (1586, in Latin; English translation by Philemon Holland, 1610), the chorographical description of Britain, and the Annales of the reign of Elizabeth I (1615–25).
authors.style: Exact, methodical, elegant Latin and an English style of grave plainness; the scholar's impartiality joined to patriotic purpose.
authors.concerns: The recovery of British antiquity; the writing of sober, documented history against legend; national identity through the past.
authors.significance: The father of English antiquarianism; his Britannia launched the great tradition of county and national history that runs through the seventeenth century and beyond.
authors.uncertainty: The accuracy of the Annales on some episodes is disputed by later historians.
sources: Memorials of the Life of Amelia Opie, Selected and Arranged from Her Letters, Diaries, and Other Manuscripts

authors.name: William Caxton
authors.identity: printer; translator; merchant
authors.biography: A Kentish mercer who spent three decades in the Low Countries, rising to governor of the English merchants at Bruges, where he learned printing at Cologne and produced the first book printed in English, his own Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (Bruges, c. 1473–74). In 1476 he set up the first English press at Westminster, printing some hundred books — Chaucer, Malory, Gower, Lydgate, the Golden Legend, and his own translations — before his death c. 1491.
authors.profile: Printer and translator: the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (c. 1473–74), The Game and Playe of the Chesse (1474), the History of Reynard the Fox (1481), the Golden Legend (1483), and numerous prologues and epilogues that constitute a body of critical prose.
authors.style: Lucid, idiomatic translation from French sources; a merchant's plain style enriched by courtly vocabulary; the prologues' genial self-presentation as servant of the 'comyn wele'.
authors.concerns: The provision of good books in English; the standardization of the language ('ouer rude termes' and the dialect of Kent); the moral and chivalric education of the nobility and gentry.
authors.significance: The introducer of printing to England: his press fixed the form of the English classics, began the standardization of written English, and made the fifteenth century's literature the sixteenth century's inheritance.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the exact site and date of his first printing remain debated.
themes: The education of princes and magistrates

works.title: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye

sources: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne

authors.name: William Cobbett
altNames: Peter Porcupine (as used in his American writing)
authors.identity: Journalist, polemicist, farmer, and political historian; the greatest writer of English plebeian radical prose, and the founder of the weekly political journal as an instrument of class argument.
authors.biography: Cobbett was born in 1763 at Goodwood near Chichester, the son of a farm bailiff, and grew up with field work, book learning, and the grammar schools within reach but not taken. He ran to sea at nineteen, married an Irish servant girl, Anne Reid, in 1791, and after a period as a clerk and a soldier, set himself up as a writer. He went to America in 1792, made his name in Philadelphia as Peter Porcupine, editor of a fiercely loyalist newspaper and of a series of pamphlets, and returned to England in 1800 disillusioned with the republic. In 1802 he founded the Political Register, which he edited almost without interruption until 1835. His imprisonment in 1810 for an attack on flogging earned him a popular martyrdom, and from the end of the war he turned his agrarianism into a systematic attack on paper credit, the funds, the taxes, and the corn laws. He fought the six Acts, defended the reformers, was repeatedly prosecuted, and in 1832 was elected to parliament for Oldham, where he spoke briefly against poor-law policy before his death at Kensington in 1835.
authors.profile: His work is at once journalistic, agricultural, historical, and autobiographical, and it was written overwhelmingly for a weekly serial audience of mechanics, small traders, and farm labourers. The Rural Rides, the currency letters, the grammar, and the polemic against the Protestant Reformation share one method: concrete observation, a documented grievance, and an appeal to the reader's own experience against 'the system'. He also wrote extensively on husbandry, on timber and planting, on style, and on education, and he was a serious editor of documents.
authors.style: Plain, Anglo-Saxon, rhythmic, and spoken: short words, direct address, repetition, and an idiom built from the workshop and the field. His prose carries invective and endearment in the same sentence, uses figures drawn from farming and from money, and treats the familiar noun as an argument in itself. He is the great English example of writing that refuses gentility without becoming colloquially vague.
authors.concerns: The political economy of paper money, taxation, and the national debt; the property confiscations of the Reformation as the origin of modern pauperism; the dignity and the wages of agricultural and artisanal labour; representation and corruption; the education of the labouring child in the standard language; and the defence of the small producer against both aristocracy and manufactured capital.
authors.significance: He created the popular weekly journal in England, shaped the language in which reform was argued before and after 1832, and made the condition of the labouring poor a subject of literary as well as political analysis; the documentary force of his prose is one of the two or three foundations of the social history of the romantic period.
authors.uncertainty: The details of his childhood schooling and of the farm where he was born are variously reported, and the extent to which the Parliamentary History and other compilations was composed by others working for him was disputed in his lifetime and remains so.

works.title: A Grammar of the English Language
A History of the Protestant "Reformation" in England and Ireland
A Parliamentary History of England, from the earliest Period to the Year 1803

authors.name: William Collins
authors.identity: English lyric poet of the Odes, associated with Gray and with the rise of imaginative, impassioned, and personified poetry.
authors.biography: Collins was born at Chichester, the son of an insurer, and studied at Winchester College and at Queen's College, Oxford. A volume of odes appeared in 1746 but sold poorly and was effectively withdrawn, and the pieces came to be prized chiefly after his death. Later poems such as Ode on the Poetical Character and his oriental and Persian imitations mark his range. Mental illness and early death cut short his career; he was tended in his last years by his lifelong friend the painter Joseph Hammell, and he died at Chichester in 1759. Gray, who admired him, did much to secure his posthumous reputation.
authors.profile: A short-lived lyric poet whose best work casts abstract qualities as personified figures in an atmosphere of imaginative reverie, enthusiasm, and melancholy; he stands between the Augustans and the pre-Romantics.
authors.style: Rich, sustained personification; lyric and ode measures of great musicality; elevated, sometimes archaic diction; and an intoxicating, enthusiastic imaginative tone distinct from Pope's point.
authors.concerns: The power of imagination and poetic enthusiasm; the personified emotions and qualities of the mind; the appeal of the exotic, the supernatural, and melancholy; and the poet's isolation.
authors.significance: One of the most important lyric poets between Pope and the Romantics; his odes were championed by Samuel Johnson and later admired for prefiguring Romantic imagination and sensibility.
authors.uncertainty: The number and publication history of his odes are complicated by the suppression of his 1746 volume and later editorial reconstruction; the nature and onset of his mental illness are imperfectly documented.

works.title: Odes on Several Descriptive and Allegorical Subjects
The Passions: An Ode for Music

authors.name: William Congreve
authors.identity: The greatest master of the comedy of manners; author of The Way of the World (1700), Love for Love (1695), and the tragedy The Mourning Bride (1697), whose flawless comic prose and brilliant repartee represent the summit of English wit comedy.
authors.biography: Born 24 January 1670 at Bardsey, Yorkshire, son of an army officer; raised in Ireland and educated at Kilkenny and Trinity College, Dublin. He came to London, studied law at the Middle Temple, and astonished the town with The Old Bachelor (1693), followed by The Double Dealer (1693), Love for Love (1695), and The Mourning Bride (1697, the most successful tragedy of the decade). His masterwork The Way of the World (1700) was coolly received, and, sensitive to criticism and enjoying a comfortable government sinecure and the friendship of the Whig Junto (and a long liaison with Henrietta Godolphin, Duchess of Marlborough), he wrote little after 1700. He died on 19 January 1729 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The consummate artist of comic prose, whose plays achieve a perfection of wit, structure, and tone — 'the prose Shakespeare' — treating the negotiation of love, marriage, and money in a society of manners with ironic elegance.
authors.style: Brilliantly epigrammatic prose; the 'proviso' scene of negotiated marriage; balanced, ironic repartee; elegant plotting; and, in The Mourning Bride, sonorous blank-verse declamation.
authors.concerns: Wit and true wit; love, marriage, and money; hypocrisy, affectation, and scandal; the social code of the town; and the relation of art and manners.
authors.significance: The Way of the World is universally regarded as the finest comedy of manners in English; Congreve defined the genre, influenced Sheridan and Wilde, and his tragic lines ('Musick has charms to soothe a savage breast') became proverbial.
authors.uncertainty: Congreve's life is well documented; his early retirement from writing is explained by his finances, health, and sensitivity to criticism, though the reasons remain partly conjectural.
sources: The Letters of Thomas Babington Macaulay: Volume 2, March 1831-December 1833

authors.name: William Cowper
authors.identity: English poet and hymn-writer of the evangelical and sentimental age, whose Task and Olney Hymns opened a new nature poetry and whose life was marked by depression and religious terror.
authors.biography: Cowper was born in Hertfordshire, the son of a clergyman, was called to the bar, and after a breakdown and an attempt at self-destruction found a measure of religious assurance in evangelical Christianity. He lived much of his life in retirement under the shelter of the Hill family, at Olney and later in Norfolk. With John Newton he contributed to the Olney Hymns (1779), writing such hymns as God Moves in a Mysterious Way. His long conversational poem The Task (1785) established his fame, followed by translations of Homer and shorter poems including The Castaway and an account of his despair. Plagued all his life by melancholy and by a recurring conviction of reprobation, he died in 1800.
authors.profile: A poet of retirement, domestic life, nature, and religious feeling, who combined the descriptive, meditative, and comic-familiar modes and wrote with startling honesty of depression and faith.
authors.style: Smooth, conversational blank verse of the familiar line; descriptive tenderness and homely humour; a passionate, troubled religious lyricism; and a gift for hymn and melancholy song.
authors.concerns: Providence, evangelical assurance, and despair; the consolation of rural and domestic life; anti-slavery and humane feeling; nature, retirement, and melancholy; and the critique of luxury and city life.
authors.significance: A leading poet of sensibility and the evangelical revival and one of the most influential nature poets before the Romantics, admired by Wordsworth and Coleridge for the honesty and feeling of his verse.
authors.uncertainty: A lifelong fear of eternal reprobation makes his own accounts of his religious states hard to date precisely; the chronology of his breakdowns and his late poem on despair is partly conjectural.

authors.name: William Cullen Bryant
authors.nationality: American; poet, political editor, critic and translator, the first American poet of the nineteenth century to command an international audience and the founder of the American nature lyric in the Wordsworthian manner
authors.identity: A poet of short and middle-length meditative and descriptive pieces and of a few longer topographical poems, together with an enormous body of editorial, critical and political prose. His verse is predominantly blank verse and the didactic or descriptive stanza; his later work included the prose retelling of the Latin tale, a national poem of the Revolution's memory and the blank verse translation of Homer which completed his career. As editor of a New York daily for near half a century he was also a principal political writer of his time.
authors.biography: He was born at Cummington, in the hill country of western Massachusetts, on 3 November 1794, the second son of Peter Bryant, a physician and occasional writer of the neighbourhood, and he learned his first Latin and Greek at his father's table. He went to Williams College in 1810 and left in the following year without a degree, then studied law, was admitted to the bar and for a short season practised in the same western counties. In 1811 he married his cousin Frances Fairchild, and about these same years he wrote the pieces which first made his name, including the brief satirical poem on national policy which he gave out under a disguise to spare his father's Federalist connections. His early meditative poem was printed in a Boston review in 1817 and was for long treated as the beginning of his reputation, and the volume of 1821 established him as a poet of the American scene. Finding no support for literature in Massachusetts, he removed to New York in 1825, took a share in the editing of periodicals, and from 1829 until his death was the leading spirit of a great daily newspaper, in which he wrote the political and literary argument of a generation of New York conservatives and reformers. He lectured on the national literature, edited a poetical and prose anthology, wrote the long poem on the American prairies at the end of his active work, and in the last years completed his blank verse Homer. He died in New York in June 1878, having been for half a century the most public of American men of letters.
authors.profile: His verse is small in bulk compared with his prose and is built around a few durable meditations, a group of short lyrics on waterfowl, flowers, death and the seasons, and two long descriptive poems of the prairie and of American history. His editorial and critical work fills an enormous file of newspaper columns and a course of lectures and addresses, and his translations, Latin fables, Homer and the prose romance retelling, occupy a large part of his later labour. The theory he held of poetry as moral and serious thought in elevated numbers gave the American nature lyric its first sustained practice, and he was the acknowledged centre of the New York literary world for thirty years.
authors.style: A grave, sustained and deliberately elevated diction in blank verse of great smoothness, with long sentences, frequent inversion, apostrophe and a moral close; in the shorter lyrics a plain descriptive accuracy which passes into meditation. He is a poet of twilight, winter, water and the death of the year, and his strength is the slow descriptive paragraph in verse rather than the quick stroke of passion or the comic vein, which he rarely attempted.
authors.concerns: Death, immortality and the consoling proof drawn from the order of nature; the soul's instruction by landscape and solitude; the transience of earthly glory and the permanence of moral truth; the dignity and the destiny of the republic and of its western wilderness; the religion of a reasonableness hostile to sect and to fanaticism; the education of a nation's taste by criticism and by the daily press.
authors.significance: He fixed the American nature meditation in the blank verse and the diction of the English eighteenth century, and through a long editorial career he gave poetry and criticism a recognised place in American public life. His shortest poems entered the schoolbook and the recitation as no American verse had done, and his Homer remained for a generation the standard English rendering. As a political editor he also shaped the antislavery and reform opinion of the North, so that his literary and his public authority were exercised in one continuous career.
authors.uncertainty: The first printing of his earliest printed poem, and the exact relation between the 1811 and later texts, are imperfectly documented; the long dispute over how much of the meditative poem was his own work and how far his father's papers have been counted in it remains only partially settled.

works.title: The Embargo; or, Sketches of the Times

authors.name: William Dunbar
authors.identity: poet; courtier; priest
authors.biography: A graduate of St Andrews (MA 1479) and a Franciscan novice in his youth, he served from c. 1500 as a clerk and poet at the court of James IV, for whom he wrote the celebratory poems of the marriage to Margaret Tudor (1503); he received a royal pension from 1500. He disappears from record after the battle of Flodden (1513), and died c. 1520.
authors.profile: Author of some eighty poems preserved chiefly in the Bannatyne and Maitland manuscripts: the Lament for the Makaris (c. 1505), The Goldyn Targe, The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo (c. 1500–07), the flying with Kennedy, the dream allegories, and the great occasional verse of the court.
authors.style: The most technically virtuosic of the makars: aureate magnificence (The Goldyn Targe) alternating with scabrous colloquial satire (the Tretis); the refrain, the flying, the alliterative line, and the French formes fixes all mastered; a voice by turns celebratory, venomous, elegiac, and devout.
authors.concerns: The vanity of life and the power of death (Timor mortis conturbat me); the hypocrisies of court and clergy; the duties and pleasures of the royal court.
authors.significance: With Henryson, the greatest poet of medieval Scotland; the Lament for the Makaris is one of the supreme elegies in the language and gave the Scottish tradition its name.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; his clerical status and career details are conjectural.
movements: The Early American Republic and Its Letters
themes: Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo

sources: The Cambridge Companion to Milton, 2nd edition

authors.name: William Ellery Channing
authors.nationality: American; the Unitarian Boston circle of Federal Street and the review writers about Harvard and the Connecticut Valley, and the liberal preaching of New England in the 1820s and 1830s
authors.identity: Preacher and moralist, the most influential religious writer and the most quoted preacher of New England in his generation, the chief expounder of American Unitarianism, and the centre of the Boston circle from which the liberal religion and the liberal literature of New England together proceeded.
authors.biography: Channing was born at Newport in Rhode Island, of a family connected with the commerce and the revolutionary leadership of the State, and was marked early for the professions by a precocity of reading joined to a diffidence of manner. He went to Harvard, graduated in 1798, and earned his living for some years as a tutor in the families of Virginia, where the leisure of the country house gave him his formative reading in the rational dissenting divinity and where, after a season of religious depression and moral struggle, he ceased to believe the doctrines of the Trinity and of the Calvinist scheme of salvation. He was licensed to preach, and in 1803 was settled over the Federal Street congregation at Boston, a church of merchants, physicians, lawyers and scholars, which he served for the rest of his life and which he kept at the centre of the intellectual and charitable affairs of the city. For years he avoided the doctrinal controversy into which his position carried him, preaching instead the moral and religious themes of duty, culture, self-denial and the likeness of man to God, until the occasion of an ordination at Baltimore in May 1819 drew from him the sermon which gave the liberal party its public confession of faith and its answer to the charge of unbelief. From that time he was the most quoted and most attacked divine in the United States; his sermons, discourses and reviews built up a body of practical theology which made the nature of God, the credibility of revelation, the dignity of the human mind and the duties of the Christian the ordinary subjects of American religious discourse. His writings on the character and the treatment of the slave, called out by the violence of the antislavery controversy of the middle and later 1830s, made him an authority on the abolition question and an outlaw in the Southern states, and he was at once a friend, a patron and at last a problem to the younger writers who went beyond him. He was an adviser of education and reform movements, a constant contributor to the American and the British journals, and a preacher whose discourses on public occasions were taken as moral events; the most famous of them gave its name and its programme to a religious party. Failing health sent him in search of strength out of Boston in his last years; he died at Old Bennington in Vermont on 2 October 1842, and was buried in the cemetery at Cambridge, leaving a congregation, a denomination and a generation of preachers formed on his manner.
authors.profile: His works are almost wholly the sermon, the discourse and the review article: the confession of faith of 1819 and the subsequent defences of the Unitarian position against the charges of the Orthodox review press; practical and theological discourses on the attributes of God, on the likeness of the human soul to God, on self-denial, on the culture of the mind, on the union of religious profession with common life, and on the duties of a Christian people; the letters and treatise on slavery; remarks on education, on the character of the age and on the religion of a republic; and a considerable body of review writing on books of theology, history and biography. He projected greater works of history and of doctrinal argument which he never executed, and the journals, letters and conversations of his later years were printed by his family and friends after his death.
authors.style: A prose of deliberate, candid and moral argument: the long qualifying sentence, the repeated appeal to reason and to the sentiments, an evident diffidence carrying itself into authority, and a preaching manner that expounds rather than terrifies; the sermon constructed as an essay, with numbered propositions, illustrations from common life and an unction of benevolence; and the review article written with the same courtesy and the same weight of moral assertion.
authors.concerns: The unitary being and the moral attributes of God, and the wrong done to them by a creed which divides or debases them; the dignity and capacity of the human soul and its likeness to God as the ground both of religion and of education; the credibility of revelation judged by reason and by the conscience; the duties of self-culture and of the Christian in society; slavery as a national sin and as a trial of character; the union of churches and of the States, and the obligations of the citizen in a republic.
authors.significance: His sermon of 1819 is the founding document of American Unitarianism as a distinct religious body, and through him Boston became the capital of a liberal Protestantism which supplied the clergy, editors and professors of New England for two generations. His writings on the mind, on culture and on the divine humanity prepared the language which the Transcendentalists inherited and reacted against; his public letters on slavery gave the moderate conscience of the North a text; and his preaching remains the standard example of the moral and reasonable sermon in American religious history.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of his Virginia tutoring and of the changes of his father's fortunes are given variously, and the exact course of his religious conversion is known chiefly from his own memoranda and from the recastings of his biographers; the chronology of his unpublished projections, and the extent of his share in the journals for which he wrote, are imperfectly reported, and opinions attributed to him on abolition in his last months rest on letters and conversations of doubtful authority.

authors.name: William Godwin
authors.nationality: English; Rationalist dissenting and radical philosophical prose of the 1790s
authors.identity: Dissenting minister turned philosopher, essayist and novelist; the systematic exponent of justice, private judgement and the indefinite perfectibility of the mind, and the era's most influential builder of a rational anarchism.
authors.biography: Godwin was born at Wisbech in Cambridgeshire on 3 March 1756, the son of a Strict Baptist minister, and was intended for the dissenting ministry. He was trained at Hoxton Academy and served as an independent pastor at Ware and then at St Alphage's, Canary Street, in London, where he began to move from Calvinism towards Socinian and philosophical opinions. Publicly avowing deist and anti-monarchical views, he resigned his pulpit around 1783 and lived thereafter by his pen, befriending Samuel Holcroft, Thomas Holcroft and the circle of the radical book-seller and reform. An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice (1793) made his name overnight; his second edition, rewritten while the printers waited, already softened the strictest conclusions. In 1797 he married Mary Wollstonecraft, whose Rights of Men and Vindication of the Rights of Woman he had long admired and whose Memoirs of the Author of a Vindication of the Rights of Woman he published in 1798 to general disgust; their daughter Mary, later Mary Shelley, was born a few months before Wollstonecraft's death in childbed. The reopening of the Baker Street lecture rooms after the Gagging Acts, his campaign against the war with France, the essays of the Political Register and the Friend of the People, and the Enquiry's revised third edition of 1798 kept him at the centre of a shrinking radical public. His later career was long and increasingly domestic and literary: the novels and romances of the 1800s, the Life of Chatham, histories of England and of Commonwealth, a Life of Marat and the Essays; and the Courtauld lectures on necromancy. He was by then regarded as a venerable rather than a dangerous figure, died in London on 7 April 1836, and was buried beside Wollstonecraft in Bunhill Fields.
authors.profile: His work is a continuous prose project rather than a body of separate genres: a philosophical treatise on justice and government, a series of novels that test the same principles in the passions, and a large occaional literature of biography, history, political pamphlet and review essay. Enquiry Concerning Political Justice states the system in three parts on political justice, its application to government and punishment, and the morals and opinions that a rational institution would produce; the Dissertation on First Principles of Government of 1795 reissued the political portions as a shorter, more practical argument. Caleb Williams (1794) is at once a gothic narrative and an illustration of how institutional power and curiosity destroy an individual. His late prose turned to the history of ideas, to literature and to elaborate accounts of opinion, superstition and civilisation, in a manner closer to learned essay than to polemic.
authors.style: A severe, unhurried argumentative prose of long balanced periods, abstract nouns and repeated key terms, in which a proposition is stated, qualified and restated until its consequences are exhausted; occasional polemic sharpened by irony and by plain contempt for argument from authority. In the novels and romances the same analytical habit appears as an insistence on motives, causes and the chain of reasoning that betrays a character, and the narrative voice is frequently intrusive and explanatory. Late work is digressive, bookish and cumulative rather than epigrammatic.
authors.concerns: Private judgement and the duty to follow the evidence of one's own reason; the opposition of justice to institution, and of general utility to promise, contract and allegiance; the critique of government, of coercion, of property held by inheritance and of marriage as an exclusive compact; the perfectibility of the mind and the gradual withering of political authority; the relation of opinion to virtue, and of literature and narrative to moral improvement; the morality of publication and the duty to tell truth.
authors.significance: Godwin supplied the first fully reasoned anarchism in English and gave radical thought of the 1790s its most systematic text; the Enquiry became a recognised authority for reformers, and its fame was such that it was read widely, answered in the press and cited in Parliament. He shaped, more than any single writer, the philosophical temper of the Romantic generation that grew up under the reputation of his principles, and his domestic history, as Wollstonecraft's husband and Mary Shelley's father, places him at the source of Frankenstein. His novels established the analytical, socially-caused English narrative; his Essays and histories kept the eighteenth-century argument about superstition, opinion and civilisation alive into the nineteenth century.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of his education at Hoxton Academy and the precise dating of his early pastorates at Ware and in Canary Street are variously given in the biographies; the full account of his marriage and of Wollstonecraft's death depends on his own Memoirs, published in 1798 and immediately contested by readers as injudicious.

works.title: Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of Caleb Williams

authors.name: William Harrison Ainsworth
authors.identity: Popular historical and romance novelist; editor of Bentley's Miscellany
authors.biography: William Harrison Ainsworth was born in Manchester, the son of a lawyer, and was educated at Manchester Grammar School. He was called to the bar but abandoned law for writing and moved to London. His early work included the novel Rookwood (1831-32), which established his reputation with its mixture of Gothic and highwayman romance. He succeeded Dickens as editor of Bentley's Miscellany and contributed to it his most famous novel, Jack Sheppard (1839), which provoked controversy over its glorification of a criminal. He went on to publish a long series of historical and Newgate romances, including Old St. Paul's, Windsor Castle, and The Lancashire Witches, which appeared well beyond the Romantic period.
authors.profile: Ainsworth is the popular novelist who bridged the late Gothic of the Romantic period and the Victorian romance of criminal history and topography. His subjects are real places and historical events populated with legendary and criminal figures; his mode is melodramatic, fast-paced, and strongly visual.
authors.style: Melodramatic prose; strong sense of place and topography; embedded illustrations (often by George Cruikshank); serial structure with cliff-hangers; the Newgate Calendar as source and model.
authors.concerns: London's criminal and historical past; the legend of the highwayman and the apprentice; the Gothic survival in popular narrative; the visual dimension of fiction and illustration; the moral boundaries of popular entertainment.
authors.significance: Rookwood fixed the modern Dick Turpin legend and inaugurated Ainsworth's long career as the most prolific popular novelist of early Victorian London; his serial novels represent a transitional form between Romantic Gothic and Victorian sensation fiction.

authors.name: William Hazlitt
authors.nationality: English; Radical criticism and the periodical essay of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Critic, essayist and polemicist, the leading English reviewer of his generation and the most forceful writer of character-sketches in prose, who also held an office in the Excise and tried for a while to earn his living as a painter.
authors.biography: Hazlitt was born at Maidstone, the son of a Unitarian minister who took the family to America during the Revolutionary war and returned to England in the middle of the 1780s. He was educated for his father's profession at the Warrington Academy, where the new philosophical theology was taught, and for a short time afterwards attended lectures in Scotland; he never took holy orders. He tried painting, working as a portrait painter and as an engraver of portraits, and he held a salaried post in the Excise, which for years made his literary work possible. From about 1813 he wrote theatrical and political criticism for the liberal journals of the day, most importantly for Leigh Hunt's Examiner, and he contributed essays and reviews to other periodicals until his death. He lectured on poetry and on the drama in London in 1818, 1819 and 1820, and his published lectures, his characters of the dramatists and his series of contemporary portraits made him the most discussed critic of the period. A long attachment, exposed in a printed confession in 1822, coincided with the breach of his marriage and with years of quarrel, debt and ill health; his books were sold to meet his obligations, and he died in Frith Street, Soho, in September 1830, in the poor circumstances his own essays had often described.
authors.profile: His work divides between criticism, philosophical writing and the essay. He edited and annotated the English poets, wrote continuously on the stage, and practised in his magazines and lectures the character-writing that he defined as the critic's proper task; his earliest and most ambitious book was a treatise on the human mind in its action, which he long considered the foundation of all his other work. His prose subjects are the theatre and the poets, the painting of Italy, the political conflict of his own decade, and the temper of the ages he read. He is at his strongest in the short analytical sketch, where a single quality of a writer or a public figure is followed out to its consequences.
authors.style: An assertive, colloquial and heavily accented prose, built on balance, contrast and blunt verdict, with a sustained rhetorical momentum in the paragraphs of the essays; a habit of opening with a general proposition and closing with a personal one; imagery drawn from painting, from the theatre and from the landscape, and an unapologetic first person that turns criticism into a form of autobiography.
authors.concerns: The association of ideas as the ground of mind and of taste; liberty of thought and the hatred of tyranny, in politics as in the theatre; the distinction between power and genius; imagination as the faculty that enlarges sympathy; the prejudice and self-interest of the established orders; the relation of the age to its writers.
authors.significance: He is the principal English critic between Johnson and the Victorians, and his method of describing the dominant faculty of a writer set the pattern for later character-writing; his Shakespearean and Jacobean criticism, his account of the poets of his own age, and his essays on the principles of the mind together form the most complete body of Romantic critical prose outside German idealism, and his political writing is a primary record of English Radicalism in the years of repression.
authors.uncertainty: The dates of his student years in Scotland and of his first contributions to the periodicals are not exactly settled, and the chronology and the details of the attachment described in the printed confession of 1822 are known chiefly from his own account, which is a literary representation rather than a record.

works.title: Lectures on the Dramatic Literature of the Age of Elizabeth
Lectures on the English Comic Writers

authors.name: William Langland
authors.birthplace: probably Cleobury Mortimer, Shropshire, or the Malvern Hills area
authors.identity: poet; satirist; allegorist
authors.biography: Almost everything known of him is inferred from Piers Plowman, whose dreamer 'Will' is a long-clothed clerk of the Malvern country, married, and living in London in poverty among the Cornhill folk; the poem's A-text (c. 1367–70), B-text (c. 1377–79), and C-text (c. 1386–88) show a career of continuous revision. He is commonly identified with the William Langland recorded at Oxford and in London in the 1390s, though the identification is uncertain.
authors.profile: Author of Piers Plowman, the greatest English allegorical poem: a sequence of dream visions in which Will searches for Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest amid the estates of fourteenth-century England.
authors.style: Unrhymed alliterative long lines of extraordinary range — satiric, homiletic, apocalyptic, tender; the allegorical dream vision fused with estates satire and biblical exegesis; the personification of abstract virtues with concrete social observation.
authors.concerns: The reform of society and church through penance and truth; the theology of grace and merit; poverty, labour, and the social order.
authors.significance: With Chaucer and Gower, the third summit of Ricardian poetry; Piers Plowman became the rallying text of reformist and radical traditions (it was read by the rebels of 1381 and printed by the Tudor reformers) and one of the most studied poems in English.
authors.uncertainty: Biography almost entirely conjectural; the attribution of the poem rests on manuscript rubrics and internal evidence.
sources: The Poems of Andrew Marvell

authors.name: William Law
authors.identity: Nonjuring clergyman and devotional writer, author of A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life (1728) and of the Christian perfection tracts that shaped Methodist and Anglo-Catholic piety.
authors.biography: Born at King's Cliffe in Northamptonshire in 1686, he was educated at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and held a fellowship there. He refused the oaths to the Hanoverian succession in 1715, lost his fellowship and spent the following decade as a schoolmaster in London. Retiring to his birthplace in 1727, he lived there, writing and governing his household, until his death in 1761. In 1726 he entered the stage controversy with an attack on theatrical entertainment as a snare of Satan; in 1728 A Serious Call applied the rules of devotion to the ordinary hours of a gentleman's or a lady's day. From the 1730s his letters on the spirit of prayer and on the spirit of faith set him against Bishop Warburton; with the help of the lawyer William Bryan he edited and translated Jacob Boehme and printed a selection of Boehme's works in 1745.
authors.profile: A practical diviner of the daily closet, whose prose makes the whole of life, and not its religious intervals, an offering.
authors.style: Plain, urgent, exact devotional prose; moral portraiture and example; a rule-of-life cadence of precept, reproof and prayer; later a mystical exuberance of type and figure.
authors.concerns: The universality of devotion; Christian perfection and the death of self-will; church, oath and civil obedience; the stage, dress and the amusements of the world; the hidden God of Boehmean mysticism.
authors.significance: The Serious Call made him the most read English devotional writer between Bunyan and the Tractarians; it formed the religious imagination of Samuel Johnson and of the Oxford movement, and his mystical writings fed Methodist and Anglo-Catholic holiness.
authors.uncertainty: His reasons for conforming outwardly after 1727 are debated, and the serial publication of his letters makes their chronology awkward.

works.title: A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life

authors.name: William Lily
authors.identity: grammarian; first High Master of St Paul's School
authors.biography: Born at Odiham about 1468; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek. Appointed by John Colet as the first High Master of St Paul's School in 1512, he wrote the Latin grammar that, revised by Colet and Erasmus, became the standard school grammar of England. He died in February 1522 (new style 1523).
authors.profile: Author of the grammar that schooled England for three centuries. The Short Introduction of Grammar ('Lily's Grammar'), with its English accidence and its Latin Brevissima Institutio, was prescribed by royal proclamation under Henry VIII and Edward VI and memorized by every grammar-school boy from Shakespeare to Johnson — who quotes it, and its misquotations, throughout the literature of the period.
authors.style: The schoolmaster's clarity: paradigms, rules in English for boys, Latin examples; a grammar written to be memorized.
authors.concerns: The reform of Latin teaching on humanist principles; the founding of a public grammar school; the union of Greek learning with Christian education.
authors.significance: The author of the most widely used textbook in English history; Lily's Grammar structured the linguistic formation of the entire literate class of early modern England.
authors.uncertainty: The exact division of the grammar's authorship among Lily, Colet, and Erasmus is editorial.
genres: Moral Philosophy and the Theory of Society
themes: Imagination as a way of knowing
sources: The William Blake Archive

authors.name: William Lloyd Garrison
authors.nationality: American; the Garrisonian reform press of Boston and the immediatist abolitionist movement
authors.identity: Journalist, editor and agitator; the founder and editor of The Liberator and the chief architect of American immediate-emancipation doctrine, of the reform newspaper as an instrument of mass moral agitation, and of the moral-suasion wing of the movement.
authors.biography: Garrison was born at Newburyport, Massachusetts, on 10 December 1805, the son of a sailing captain of difficult circumstances who emigrated to Europe and died abroad, and he grew up in partial want. He was apprenticed as a boy to a Newburyport printer, worked in Boston composing rooms, and by his early twenties was printing and editing on his own account; he took up the temperance cause, protested the treatment of seamen, and was at first friendly to the colonisation enterprise. He became agent for the American Colonization Society in 1828, but the friendship of Benjamin Lundy and his growing conviction that the society was a plan for expelling rather than freeing the enslaved turned him to immediate emancipation. On 1 January 1831 he began The Liberator in Boston with the famous resolution not to equivocate, not to retreat and to be heard, and it ran weekly for thirty-four years to 1865. The New England Anti-Slavery Society followed in 1832, the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1833, and the movement's mail, its meeting-house and its agent's lives were attacked: a mob tried to seize him in 1835 and the post office excluded abolitionist matter from Southern delivery. His principles widened into a general reform programme of nonresistance, women's rights and moral suasion, and he broke with the political abolitionists and with most of his former allies in 1840 over the participation of women and over his refusal of voting and office-holding as support for a slaveholding constitution. The disunion slogan of the 1840s and his public burning of the Fugitive Slave Law and of a pro-slavery sermon in the 1850s expressed the same logic; the Thirteenth Amendment and the end of slavery in 1865 allowed him to close the Liberator. He lived his last years in Boston, engaged in women's suffrage, education and prison and labour reform, and died in New York on 24 May 1879 at his daughter's house. He left behind the movement he founded and the model of the reform editor who makes a weekly paper into a book of argument.
authors.profile: His literary medium was the periodical: four thousand weekly numbers of The Liberator, with its leading articles, its reprinted testimony, its correspondence, its poetry and its documentary appendix, together with the open letters to public men, the remonstrances to legislatures, the 1832 tract on the colonisation society, and the speeches of his two lecture tours in Britain. He wrote also pamphlets of doctrine on the character of the federal compact as an agreement with slavery, and a large body of correspondence which is itself part of the movement's literature. His editorial practice is itself a literary achievement: he built a paper out of letters, testimony, and reprinting, and made the aggregate of documents into argument.
authors.style: A plain New England prose of high moral pressure, in which short declarative sentences and anaphora of resolution give way to long periods of indictment; directness deliberately courted, with the plain style of Quaker remonstrance fused to the jeremiad and to the revival address. The prose shifts between the editorial we, the first-person vow and the second-person arraigning of the reader, and it is unreservedly figurative, turning on the language of blood, compact, altar and judgment.
