authors.concerns: Immediate and unconditional emancipation without compensation; the Constitution and the churches as compacts with slavery; moral suasion as the means of reform against political and clerical management; the identity of the slave's cause with the freedom of speech and of the press; the rights of women as inseparable from the rights of the enslaved; nonresistance, pacifism and the refusal of oaths and office; the brotherhood of humanity and the sin of colonisation and of prejudice.
authors.significance: Garrison converted American abolition from a charitable and gradualist project into a mass movement with its own vocabulary, its own press and its own full-time agents, and The Liberator remains the model of the reform periodical that makes an agitation. His intransigent rhetoric, and his willingness to be hated, made slavery a national question of conscience rather than of policy, and his quarrels over politics, women and the Constitution shaped the party and clerical lines of the movement for thirty years. He is the central figure of the sectional literature of the 1830s and 1840s and a defining instance of the Romantic reform writer whose paper is his book.
authors.uncertainty: The day of his birth is given as 10 December 1805 in most accounts and as 12 December in some official biographical notes. The details of his apprenticeships and of the first years of his own printing and editing are recorded mainly from his own later reminiscence and from the memories of associates, and the chronology of his conversion from colonisation agency to immediatism in 1828-29 is variously assigned between the influence of Lundy, his own reading and his quarrel with society managers. His authorship of unsigned leading articles in his own paper is a matter of editorial convention rather than of itemised record.

authors.name: William Mason
authors.identity: English poet, dramatist, and garden theorist, author of blank-verse tragedy and essays on poetry and gardening, associated with pre-Romantic sensibility.
authors.biography: Mason, sometimes called the younger to distinguish him from a kinsman of the same name, was educated at Westminster School and Queen's College, Oxford, and inherited an estate at Nuthall in Nottinghamshire. His Poems (1754) won immediate attention, and he followed with elegiac and didactic verse, including essays on eclogues and on garden design. He turned to blank-verse historical tragedy with Elfrida (1763) and Caractacus (1769), and he wrote a Life of his friend Thomas Gray. A keen gardener and man of letters, he corresponded widely within the literary circles of the age. He died at Nuthall in 1797.
authors.profile: A poet, dramatist, and man of letters whose work spans the sentimental elegy, the garden essay, and declamatory blank-verse tragedy, reflecting the movement from Augustan taste toward pre-Romantic feeling.
authors.style: Correct, elevated blank verse; didactic ease in the essay poem; mournful sensibility in the elegy; and a rhetorical, declamatory grandeur in the tragedies, with a cultivated taste for the picturesque garden.
authors.concerns: Taste and the design of gardens; moral and heroic virtue in historical drama; friendship, biography, and literary memory; melancholy, retirement, and religious consolation.
authors.significance: A transitional figure of later-eighteenth-century letters whose garden writings and blank-verse tragedy reflect the spread of picturesque taste and pre-Romantic sensibility; his Life of Gray is an important literary document.
authors.uncertainty: His birthplace is given variously in biographical accounts; the precise chronology of his poems and essays, and his relation to the older William Mason of the same family, require careful distinction.

works.title: Edwin and Morcar, the Earls of Mercia and Northumberland

authors.name: William of Malmesbury
authors.identity: historian; Benedictine monk
authors.biography: A monk and librarian of Malmesbury Abbey, where he spent his whole career, becoming precentor and, late in life, refusing the abbacy; he died c. 1143. The greatest English historian since Bede, he gathered his materials from libraries across England and corresponded with the learned of his day.
authors.profile: Author of the Gesta Regum Anglorum (first version 1125, revised to c. 1135), the Gesta Pontificum Anglorum (1125), the Historia Novella (c. 1140–43), and saints' lives including those of Wulfstan, Dunstan, and Aldhelm.
authors.style: Polished, allusive Latin modelled on classical historians; critical assessment of sources; a gift for anecdote and character; patriotic pride in English history tempered by Norman loyalties.
authors.concerns: The continuity of the English kingdom from the Anglo-Saxons to his own day; the moral exemplarity of history; the recovery of the English past after the Conquest.
authors.significance: The founder of critical English historiography after Bede; his Gesta Regum is the principal narrative source for Anglo-Norman history and the model for the century's chroniclers.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his Anglo-Saxon sources were largely lost in the Reformation.
sources: The Life of Samuel Johnson, 6 volumes (Birkbeck Hill edition)

authors.name: William of Ockham
authors.identity: philosopher; logician; political theorist; Franciscan friar
authors.biography: A Franciscan who studied and taught at Oxford, where his teaching was denounced to the papal court at Avignon (1324); while awaiting judgement he became embroiled in the Franciscan poverty controversy, fled Avignon with Michael of Cesena in 1328, and spent the rest of his life under the protection of the emperor Louis of Bavaria at Munich, writing political works against the papacy until his death in 1347.
authors.profile: Author of the Summa Logicae (c. 1323), the Ordinationes on the Sentences, the Quodlibeta, and a series of political treatises on poverty and papal power.
authors.style: The 'razor' of terminist logic: relentless elimination of superfluous entities and distinctions; a new theory of signs and mental language; clear, devastating polemic in the political works.
authors.concerns: The foundations of logic and knowledge; universals and nominalism; the limits of papal power; apostolic poverty.
authors.significance: The most consequential English philosopher of the Middle Ages: his nominalism reshaped European philosophy and theology (via Buridan, the via moderna, and Luther), and his political theory laid groundwork for conciliarism and modern notions of sovereignty.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his early works rests on internal evidence.
themes: Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
sources: The Rise of the Novel: Studies in Defoe, Richardson and Fielding

authors.name: William Paley
authors.identity: Archdeacon of Carlisle and the century's master of utilitarian divinity, whose Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy (1785) made happiness and obedience the whole of duty.
authors.biography: Born at Peterborough in July 1743, the son of a clergyman who later became headmaster of the free school at Giggleswick, he was educated at that school and at Christ's College, Cambridge, where an idle first year was retrieved by hard reading, a fellowship and a tutorship that made him the most successful coach of his university. He took orders in the Church of England, held a succession of northern livings at Musgrave, Dalston and Appleby, and was made archdeacon of Carlisle in 1782. His Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy (1785) soon became a standard university text and the target of reviewers who thought it reduced virtue to expedience. His argument for the undesigned coincidence of the apostolic letters appeared in the Horae Paulinae of 1790, and his Evidences of Christianity (1794) and Natural Theology (1802), both later than the period covered here, long stood as textbooks in the schools of theology. He was installed at Bishopwearmouth in his last years and died on 25 May 1805.
authors.profile: A clear-eyed churchman who wrote the morality of obedience and the evidences of belief for a reading public that wanted argument in plain terms.
authors.style: Conversational, concrete and unornamented; cases and common-life examples carried through a single rule; the plainness of a good tutor, with a polemicist's patience in reply.
authors.concerns: Utility as the measure of duty; the obligations imposed by civil government and by the established church; the evidences of revelation and the credibility of miracle; design in nature and the relation of pleasure to virtue.
authors.significance: He gave utilitarian ethics its first systematic ecclesiastical form and supplied the teleological argument in the version Mill and Darwin had to answer; his textbooks governed English theological education for a generation.
authors.uncertainty: The order in which his preferments and lecture texts were produced is complicated by posthumous edition and by his own revisions.

works.title: A View of the Evidences of Christianity
The Principles of Moral and Political Philosophy

authors.name: William Robertson
authors.identity: Minister of the Church of Scotland, principal of Edinburgh and royal historiographer, whose History of America (1777) made philosophical history a professional discipline in Britain.
authors.biography: Born at Borthwick near Langholm in 1721, the son of a country clergyman, he was educated at Edinburgh, entered the ministry and served a southern parish before he removed to Edinburgh and became one of the city's most fashionable preachers. The History of Scotland (1759) established him as the leading historian of his generation, and the great work on the reign of Charles V (1769) displayed his command of archives and of the European sixteenth century. Appointed principal of the University of Edinburgh in 1762 and royal historiographer, he at last produced the History of America (1777), three volumes of sources, geography, conquest and character which were translated across Europe, and the History of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth (1787). His disquisition on the ancients' knowledge of India came in 1791, after the period with which this record deals. He was a leader of the moderate interest in the church, a friend of Hume, Smith, Ferguson and Home, and died in 1793.
authors.profile: The historian of states and religions who wrote narrative as instructed enquiry, combining Scottish church politics with the sources of the Spanish and Italian archives.
authors.style: Dignified, lucid, well-paced narrative; disquisitions and notes carrying the argument; a preacher's moral seriousness and an editor's restraint; balance of character, cause and consequence.
authors.concerns: The origins of American civilisation and conquest; the political and religious history of Europe in the age of Charles V; feudal law, ranks and the rise of the commons; the character of Queen Elizabeth and of the Reformation.
authors.significance: He professionalised historical writing in Britain, gave the English-speaking world its standard account of America's discovery and conquest, and set the model of philosophic narrative that Gibbon and the nineteenth century inherited.
authors.uncertainty: His early parish years are documented thinly, and his use of other men's manuscripts and collections has been re-assessed by later scholarship.

works.title: The History of the Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic
The History of the Reign of the Emperor Charles V

authors.name: William Roper
authors.identity: biographer; lawyer; More's son-in-law
authors.biography: Born about 1496; a lawyer of Lincoln's Inn who married Margaret, Thomas More's eldest daughter, in 1521, and lived in More's household at Chelsea for sixteen years. He wrote The Life of Sir Thomas More between about 1553 and 1558 from intimate memory; it circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1626. He died on 4 January 1578.
authors.profile: Author of the first great English biography of a private man. The Life of Sir Thomas More — the portrait of the Chancellor at Chelsea: his prayers, his jests, his relations with his family, and his final refusal of the oath — is the classic of Tudor life-writing and the foundation of the More legend that Shakespeare's play and the later tradition inherited.
authors.style: Plain, affectionate, anecdotal prose; the vivid recalled dialogue of the Chelsea household; a son-in-law's reverence without hagiographical inflation.
authors.concerns: The memory and example of More; conscience against the state; the sanctity of the family and the household.
authors.significance: Established the English biographical tradition and supplied the human More to every later age; a primary source of the first importance for the English Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: The Life of Sir Thomas More

sources: Shelley's Poetry and Prose (Norton Critical Edition)

authors.name: William Roscoe
authors.nationality: English; the commercial, dissenting and abolitionist culture of Liverpool, and the Whig historical scholarship of the revolutionary decade
authors.identity: Merchant, banker, lawyer, historian of Renaissance Italy, abolitionist poet and patron of arts and botany; the first considerable English historian of the Medici and one of the earliest and most consistent English poet-critics of the slave trade.
authors.biography: Roscoe was born at Liverpool on 8 March 1753, the only surviving son of a small trader in the market-garden and bowling-green line, and was educated at the dissenting and proprietary schools of the town before being bound apprentice to a Liverpool merchant house. Called upon to support a widowed mother and young sisters, he studied law, was admitted an attorney, and in the years of the town's enormous prosperity built up a mercantile and banking business of large reputation, at the same time pursuing scholarship, botany and the collection of pictures and books with a single-mindedness unusual in a tradesman. The Wrongs of Africa, a poem, published in two parts in 1787 and 1788 for the cause of the abolition committee, made him at once known beyond Liverpool and marked him permanently in his own town, where the slave-trade interest was powerful and where he was afterwards burnt in effigy. His two great historical works, the Life of Lorenzo de' Medici called the Magnificent of 1796, with its introductory view of Italian history, and the Life and Pontificate of Leo the Tenth of 1805, were built partly out of manuscripts which he obtained in Italy at his own cost, and gave the English reading public its first scholarly account of the age in which the revival of letters and the Reformation met. Elected in 1806 one of the first two members for the newly enfranchised town, he sat a single session, voting against the trade and against the party that had returned him, and withdrew from Parliament with his banking interests already embarrassed. The commercial crash of the post-war years ruined his firm about 1814-1815, and the sale of his library, his garden and his pictures, which included the sculptures and the collection of prints he had gathered with so much care, was a public event in the town. He gave his remaining years to letters, to botanical and artistic patronage and to the small poems and fables for children of which The Butterfly's Ball and the Grasshopper's Feast is the survivor, and he died at Liverpool on 27 June 1831, leaving a reputation as the scholar-tradesman of the great trading community and a family of sons, one of whom wrote his Life.
authors.profile: His work runs in three unrelated veins, all of them considerable. The abolitionist poem The Wrongs of Africa, in two parts, puts the whole progress of the trade, from the coast of Africa through the voyage to the colonies, into the heroic line of the moral plea. The Italian histories are scholarly narrative biography on the model of the eighteenth-century life, prefaced by disquisitions on the state of Italy and of the papacy and resting on printed authorities and on transcripts gathered in Italian libraries. The nursery verse, of which the insect masquerade is the most durable, belongs to the new small-book trade of the years after 1800, and he wrote also fables, translations from the Italian, botanical and historical essays, and the manuscripts on painting and on his own collection which his son printed after his death.
authors.style: A decorous and deliberate eighteenth-century prose, grave in the histories, heavily qualified in the argumentative prefatory disquisitions, and circumstantial in the narrative of courts and councils; the abolition verse is in a stately heroic line of moral appeal, addressed to the conscience of a nation, with the enumeration of instances doing the rhetorical work. The nursery pieces are light, quick and plain, in short common metres of the child's ear, and show the same gift of concrete description that marks his botanical writing.
authors.concerns: The sin and the national interest of the slave trade, and the duty of a trading community to examine its own gains; the civilisation of Renaissance Italy, the papacy, and the fate of Italian liberty; the study of the age of the Medici as a case in the relation of letters, power and church; the encouragement of the fine arts and of botany in a commercial town; the instruction and the innocent fancy of very young children; the education and patronage of a manufacturing community.
authors.significance: The Wrongs of Africa was the first of the great abolition poems and gave the movement its earliest sustained verse indictment, published by the friends of the cause in the year of the first petition to Parliament; his Italian biographies founded the scholarly English study of the Renaissance and long stood as the standard accounts of Lorenzo and of Leo the Tenth. As a banker, collector and civic patron he made Liverpool a provincial centre of art and learning, and his ruin and the sale of his collections became the cautionary case of the merchant-scholar; his nursery poem passed into the childhood of two continents.
authors.uncertainty: A few older biographical accounts place his birth in London rather than Liverpool, and the day of his death is given as the 27th or the 30th of June 1831. The extent of his responsibility for anonymous pamphlets on the trade and on the affairs of the town is not settled, and the account of his Italian manuscript researches depends largely on the prefaces to the two lives and on the family Life edited by his son, which is a defence as well as a record.

works.title: The Butterfly's Ball, and the Grasshopper's Feast
The Life and Pontificate of Leo the Tenth
The Life of Lorenzo de Medici

authors.name: William Shakespeare
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and actor; the central figure of English literature, author of some 39 plays, 154 sonnets, and two narrative poems.
authors.biography: Baptized 26 April 1564 at Stratford-upon-Avon, son of the glover and alderman John Shakespeare; educated at the Stratford grammar school. He married Anne Hathaway in 1582 (children Susanna, and the twins Hamnet and Judith), and by 1592 was established in the London theatre (Greene's 'upstart crow' attack). He wrote for the Lord Chamberlain's Men (from 1594) and its successor the King's Men (from 1603), was a sharer in the Globe (1599) and Blackfriars, and prospered as actor, playwright, and investor, buying New Place in Stratford in 1597. The narrative poems Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594) were his first printed works; the Sonnets appeared in 1609. He retired to Stratford around 1613 and died there on 23 April 1616; the First Folio of his plays was published by Heminges and Condell in 1623.
authors.profile: The supreme dramatist of the language and its greatest poet of the human interior: his histories, comedies, tragedies, and romances transformed every genre they touched, and his sonnets reinvented the Petrarchan sequence as a meditation on love, time, and art.
authors.style: Unmatched range of register — from the euphuistic wit and sonneteering of the early plays to the metaphysical density of the great tragedies and the late romances' verse of reconciliation; mastery of blank verse, prose, and song; the invention of character through soliloquy.
authors.concerns: Kingship, legitimacy, and the body politic; love, jealousy, and self-deception; time, mortality, and the immortality of art; the theatre itself as the mirror of nature; conscience and the divided self.
authors.significance: The measure of English literature: his works constitute the largest single achievement of the language's canon, translated into every tongue and performed continuously since the 1590s.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of the plays rests on printed dates, records of performance, and stylistic evidence; the authorship of several plays (Titus Andronicus, Pericles, Henry VIII, The Two Noble Kinsmen, Edward III, Sir Thomas More) is collaborative, and the biographical record between 1585 and 1592 is a blank.
sources: The Poetical Works of James Montgomery (2 volumes)

authors.name: William Shenstone
authors.identity: English poet and gardener, of the Leasowes, a pastoral writer and letter-writer whose ornamental garden became an eighteenth-century landmark of taste.
authors.biography: Shenstone was born into the Worcestershire gentry, educated at Halesowen and at Pembroke College, Cambridge, and succeeded to the family estate, the Leasowes, which he laid out as a celebrated ornamental farm. He wrote the pastoral poem The Schoolmistress (1742) and other pastorals, songs, and epistles, publishing his Poetical Works in a collected form in 1763. His letters and his critical and horticultural writings circulated among friends and were partly printed after his death, notably his account of the Leasowes and his essays on taste and gardening. He died unmarried at the Leasowes in 1763.
authors.profile: A poet of retirement, rural sympathy, and sensibility, and a practised maker of landscapes; his verse and his garden together embody the cult of the picturesque and the ornamented farm.
authors.style: Gentle, conversational pastoral and occasional verse; Spenserian and Thomsonian descriptive influence; a warm, familiar, sometimes digressive epistolary prose; and an aesthetic of artless variety.
authors.concerns: Rural life and the education of rustic minds; taste, the picturesque, and the design of landscapes; retirement, friendship, and benevolence; and the integration of art and nature.
authors.significance: A central figure in the development of the English landscape garden and picturesque taste, and a respected pastoral and epistolary writer linking Thomson's nature poetry to later sensibility.
authors.uncertainty: His exact birthplace is given variously in accounts of the Worcestershire parish; the precise dating of his garden improvements and of the circulation of his letters and essays remains partly conjectural.

authors.name: William Tyndale
authors.identity: Bible translator; reformer; martyr
authors.biography: Born in Gloucestershire about 1494; educated at Oxford (BA 1512, MA 1515) and Cambridge. Denied episcopal patronage for an English Bible, he left England in 1524 and worked in Germany and the Low Countries: his New Testament was printed at Worms in 1526 and smuggled into England; the Pentateuch followed in 1530 and a revised New Testament in 1534. Betrayed at Antwerp in 1535, he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde on 6 October 1536.
authors.profile: The father of the English Bible. His translations — made from the Greek of Erasmus and the Hebrew — gave English scripture its enduring shape: the Authorized Version of 1611 retains perhaps ninety per cent of his New Testament phrasing. As a polemicist he wrote the most effective Reformation tracts in English: The Obedience of a Christian Man (1528), The Parable of the Wicked Mammon (1528), The Practice of Prelates (1530), and An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue (1531).
authors.style: The plain style at its greatest: short sentences, monosyllabic Saxon diction, and rhythms tuned for reading aloud; learned argument made colloquial and urgent.
authors.concerns: The authority of scripture over church and prince; justification by faith; the translation of the Word into every ploughboy's language; the duty of obedience and its limits.
authors.significance: The principal architect of English biblical prose and of the language of English devotion; his translation work shaped the King James Bible and, through it, the speech of the English-speaking world.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his early Gloucestershire life rest on Foxe's Acts and Monuments.
themes: The public sphere, print, and the periodical

works.title: An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue
The Obedience of a Christian Man
The Parable of the Wicked Mammon

sources: A Treatise of Human Nature (Clarendon Edition of the Works of David Hume)

authors.name: William Wordsworth
authors.nationality: English; the Lake school of the Romantic period
authors.identity: Poet and theorist of poetry of the Lake District, the maker of the lyrical ballad and of the Romantic blank-verse meditation, and the most authoritative English voice on nature, memory and the growing mind.
authors.biography: Wordsworth was born at Cockermouth in Cumberland, the second of five children of an estate agent, and was educated at Hawkshead grammar school and at St John's College, Cambridge. He walked the mountains in his student holidays, and stayed in France in 1790 and again in 1791-95, when the early promise of the Revolution made a lasting impression on him and a daughter, Caroline, was born there. Settling with his sister Dorothy first at Racedown and then at Alfoxden in the west, he began in 1797-98 the collaboration that produced the anonymous ballad volume; in 1802 he married Mary Hutchinson, and after the Keswick years he settled at Allan Bank and then at Rydal Mount, where he lived until his death. The later decades brought public employment as Distributor of Stamps for Westmorland, an unfinished scheme of a philosophical poem, the volumes of 1807, The Excursion of 1814, the Ecclesiastical Sketches of 1822, and a national fame marked by a civil pension and by the laureateship accepted in 1843. The autobiographical poem on the growth of a poet's mind, long revised and never published by its author, appeared after his death in 1850. His politics moved from revolutionary sympathy to a conservative attachment to church, state and the rural order, a change much used against him by later critics.
authors.profile: His work divides between the lyrical ballads and short lyrics of humble life, the blank-verse meditations and sonnets, and the long philosophical and autobiographical poem planned as The Recluse, of which only The Excursion was published in his lifetime. He wrote also a prose guide to his own country and a large body of letters and memoranda, and his Preface to Lyrical Ballads is the period's most quoted theory of poetry. His subjects are the mountain landscape, the labouring poor, children, grief and endurance, and the education of the imagination, and his characteristic form is the poem that passes from an observed scene to a history of the mind that remembers it.
authors.style: A deliberate plainness of diction drawn from ordinary speech, rising in the blank verse to great weight of syntax; long suspensive periods, apostrophe, repetition and an insistent use of general nouns; in the lyrics a song-like regularity of stanza and refrain, and in the sonnets a compressed and Latinate turn. The manner changes markedly between the deliberate roughness of the experimental ballads and the serenity of the later lyrics.
authors.concerns: The mind's intercourse with nature and the shaping power of landscape; memory and the pleasure re-created in tranquillity; the imagination as a moral and perceptual faculty; childhood as the season of vision; the loss of revolutionary hope and its consolation in duty, the church and the permanences of rural life; the proper language and audience of poetry.
authors.significance: With the collaborators of the ballad volume he opened the English Romantic period and supplied its most durable account of how poems are made; his blank-verse meditation and his autobiographical poem founded the modern poetry of the self's education, and his sonnets helped revive the English sonnet. His practice and his theory together changed the subject and the diction of English verse, and his later career remains the central case in the long argument about the relation between Romantic poetry and political allegiance.
authors.uncertainty: The sequence of his French sojourns of the early 1790s and the circumstances of his daughter Caroline's parentage and upbringing are recorded imperfectly and are variously stated in the biographies.

works.title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
Lines Written a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey

authors.name: William Wycherley
authors.identity: Restoration dramatist; author of the two fiercest comedies of manners, The Country Wife (1675) and The Plain Dealer (1676), whose savage wit and moral seriousness about lust, hypocrisy, and jealousy set him apart from his more elegant contemporaries.
authors.biography: Born c. 1640–41 at Clive, Shropshire, educated at Queen's College, Oxford, the Middle Temple, and in France (where he briefly became a Catholic before reverting). He served at sea in the Second Dutch War and moved in court circles. His plays — Love in a Wood (1671), The Gentleman Dancing-Master (1672), The Country Wife (1675), and The Plain Dealer (1676) — won him fame but little money. A secret marriage to the Countess of Drogheda ruined him; he spent seven years in the Fleet for debt, was briefly reconciled to his father, and lived in obscurity and poverty until, in old age, he married a young heiress days before his death on 1 January 1716, leaving his manuscripts to the young Alexander Pope.
authors.profile: The most savage and morally earnest of the Restoration comic writers, whose comedies expose sexual appetite, jealousy, and hypocrisy with a harsh, near-Jacobean intensity beneath the manners-comedy surface.
authors.style: Biting, energetic dialogue; intrigue plotting drawn from Molière and the Spanish; sexual frankness and dark comedy; and a moral seriousness unusual in the comedy of manners.
authors.concerns: Lust, jealousy, and cuckoldry; social and sexual hypocrisy; the corruption of town and country; misanthropy and plain dealing; and the vanity of pretence.
authors.significance: The Country Wife and The Plain Dealer are among the greatest English comedies; Wycherley's moral ferocity influenced Congreve and later satirists, and his late-life friendship with Pope linked Restoration and Augustan letters.
authors.uncertainty: Wycherley's birth year is uncertain (c. 1640–41) and much of his biography, especially his marriages and debts, is recorded only in anecdotal sources.

works.title: Love in a Wood; or, St. James's Park

sources: The Journals of Thomas Babington Macaulay (5 volumes)

authors.name: Wulfstan
authors.identity: homilist; lawgiver; archbishop
authors.biography: Bishop of London 996–1002, bishop of Worcester 1002–1016, and archbishop of York 1002–1023; the principal counselor and draftsman of law under kings Æthelred II and Cnut.
authors.profile: Author of the Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (1014), the most famous Old English sermon, preached in the crisis of the Danish invasions; the Institutes of Polity (a treatise on the orders of Christian society); the Canons of Edgar; the law codes of Æthelred and Cnut; and a series of eschatological homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis) warning of the approaching end.
authors.style: A distinctive, urgent rhythm built on two-stress phrases, alliteration, intensifying repetition, and cumulative word-pairs; the most recognizable idiolect in Old English prose.
authors.concerns: National repentance; social order and the duties of each estate; the coming of Antichrist; the law of God as the foundation of earthly law.
authors.significance: With Ælfric, the last great writer of Old English prose; his homilies and law codes shaped the response of the English church and state to the conquest of 1016.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early career unknown; the canon of his writings rests on stylistic analysis.

works.title: Wulfstan's Eschatological Homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis, and related sermons)

sources: Dictionary of Old English: A to I online

authors.name: Wulfstan the Cantor
authors.identity: poet; hagiographer
authors.biography: Monk and precentor of the Old Minster, Winchester, active in the 990s; a leading figure of the literary culture of the Benedictine Reform.
authors.profile: Author of the Narratio metrica de Sancto Swithuno (c. 996), a verse life of St Swithun with an important prose preface describing the rebuilding of the Old Minster; also credited with the Life of St Æthelwold.
authors.style: Accomplished Latin hexameters in the classical revival manner of the tenth-century reform; encomiastic tone.
authors.concerns: The cult of the saints as the glory of the reformed church; the commemoration of Winchester's patrons and builders.
authors.significance: The principal Latin poet of the late Old English period; his Narratio is a major source for the architecture and liturgy of the Old Minster.
authors.uncertainty: Little biographical detail known; attributions of the Æthelwold life debated.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500

authors.name: Ælfric Bata
authors.identity: Latin colloquy writer; schoolmaster
authors.biography: A pupil of Ælfric of Eynsham who identifies himself by the nickname 'Bata' and addresses his master with affectionate humour in the colloquies. He probably taught at a monastic school in the first quarter of the eleventh century (fl. c. 1005-1025). His life is otherwise unknown.
authors.profile: Author of the Colloquia and the Colloquia difficiliora, Latin conversation manuals modelled on Ælfric's Colloquy but far more expansive and boisterous: they dramatize daily life in the monastic school with dialogue about food, drink, beatings, and petty theft.
authors.style: Colloquial, hyperbolic Latin with a taste for comic exaggeration and insult; the texts deliberately enlarge the vocabulary of daily life beyond the classroom classics.
authors.concerns: The teaching of spoken Latin; the discipline and everyday realities of the monastic school; the relationship between master and pupil.
authors.significance: His colloquies preserve a uniquely vivid picture of eleventh-century English school life and document the vitality of the vernacular-Latin classroom tradition founded by Ælfric.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from his texts; floruit approximate (c. 1005-1025); birth and death dates unknown.
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

authors.name: Ælfric of Eynsham
authors.identity: homilist; hagiographer; grammarian; translator
authors.biography: Educated at Winchester under Bishop Æthelwold, the leading figure of the Benedictine Reform; monk and mass-priest at Cerne Abbas (c. 987–1005); first abbot of Eynsham (1005–c. 1010). The greatest and most prolific writer of Old English prose.
authors.profile: Author of the two series of Catholic Homilies (c. 989–995), the Lives of Saints (c. 993–998), the Grammar and Glossary (the first Latin grammar in a European vernacular), the Colloquy, translations of Genesis and other Old Testament books (the Old English Hexateuch), De temporibus anni, pastoral letters, and numerous shorter homilies and treatises.
authors.style: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of extraordinary clarity and control — a deliberately plain style designed to be read aloud and understood; careful avoidance of apocryphal excess.
authors.concerns: Orthodox teaching for clergy and laity; the dignity and capacity of the English language; the education of the young; resistance to superstition and error.
authors.significance: The culmination of the Old English prose tradition; his works circulated more widely than any other vernacular prose of the period and influenced English religious writing for centuries.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; several works are attributed to him on stylistic grounds.
sources: Beowulf: A Verse Translation

authors.name: Æthelweard
authors.identity: chronicler; ealdorman; patron
authors.biography: Ealdorman of the western provinces and descendant of King Æthelred I; patron of Ælfric of Eynsham; died c. 998.
authors.profile: Author of the Chronicon (c. 980), a Latin version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle down to 973, written for his kinswoman Matilda, abbess of Essen, with a famous prologue praising King Alfred.
authors.style: Dense, hermeneutic Latin of the sort parodied by his contemporary William of Malmesbury's sources; learned vocabulary and Grecisms.
authors.concerns: The antiquity and dignity of the West Saxon royal line; the cultivation of Latin learning among the secular aristocracy.
authors.significance: An important witness to the text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and to lay Latin literacy in late Anglo-Saxon England.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; identification with the ealdorman Æthelweard of the charters is standard but rests on prosopography.
sources: The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

authors.name: Æthelwold of Winchester
authors.identity: monastic reformer; Latin and Old English prose writer; translator
authors.biography: Born into a noble Winchester family c. 904-909, brought up at the court of King Æthelstan, and ordained with Dunstan. He became a monk at Glastonbury under Dunstan, was made abbot of the derelict monastery of Abingdon (c. 954), and in 963 was appointed bishop of Winchester, where he expelled the secular clerics of the Old and New Minsters and installed monks. He was the most radical and effective leader of the Benedictine Reform, a teacher of Ælfric, and a patron of manuscript production and the arts. He died on 1 August 984.
authors.profile: Author of the Regularis Concordia (c. 970), the customary that unified English monastic observance under royal patronage; traditionally credited with the Old English translation of the Rule of St Benedict (c. 960s) and associated with the Old English New Minster Charter (966) and possibly the Benedictine Office. His school at Winchester created the standardized literary language ('Winchester words') used by Ælfric.
authors.style: In the Regularis Concordia, clear expository Latin organized for practical liturgical use, with vivid prescriptions for ceremony (the Visitatio Sepulchri, the 'tropes'); in the vernacular Rule, plain idiomatic Old English translating Benedict's Latin closely.
authors.concerns: Uniformity of observance; the king as protector of reformed monasticism; the education of monks in Latin and the vernacular; the liturgy as the centre of the religious life.
authors.significance: The architect of the English Benedictine Reform and of the alliance between the crown and the reformed monasteries; his Winchester school and standardized Old English shaped the literary language of the late tenth century and of Ælfric's and Wulfstan's prose.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (c. 904-909). The attribution of the Old English Benedictine Rule and Benedictine Office to him is traditional and widely but not universally accepted.
movements: English Petrarchism and the Sonnet Vogue
themes: Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: The Old English Rule of St Benedict

sources: TEAMS Middle English Texts Series

works.title: 'Tis Pity She's a Whore
works.description: John Ford's notorious tragedy of incestuous love between the siblings Giovanni and Annabella in Parma, and of Giovanni's murder of his sister and his entrance bearing her heart on his dagger.
works.plot: Governing himself by passion rather than religion, Giovanni declares his love to his sister Annabella; she yields, marries the noble Soranzo to conceal her pregnancy, is discovered, and is killed by Giovanni, who then dies fighting Soranzo's followers.
works.significance: The most powerful and most discussed Caroline tragedy; it pushed the theatre's moral limits further than any contemporary play and remains a central text in the study of early modern incest and tragic passion.
works.meter: Blank verse of sustained lyric intensity, with Ford's characteristic repetition and lament.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Phoenix in Drury Lane, probably c. 1629-33, and published in 1633 with a remarkable author's dedication defending the play's seriousness.
works.characters: Giovanni; Annabella; Soranzo; the Friar Bonaventura; Vasques; Grimaldi; Bergetto; Philotis; Richardetto; Hippolita
works.structure: Five acts of a single, tightly driven tragic action with subordinate comic plots, ending in the public catastrophe at the cardinal's feast.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Bold Stroke for a Wife
altTitles: A Bold Stroke for a Wife: A Comedy
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: The author's best-known comedy, a comic campaign in which a clever lover wins an heiress by personating the several guardians who have been charged with keeping her from him. It is a sustained satire on religious and political cant, each guardian standing for a species of enthusiasm.
works.plot: A colonel loves a young woman whose fortune is controlled by four guardians, a Quaker, a nun, a Whig knight and a Tory general, each pledged to keep her from him. He and his friends disguise themselves as a Quaker preacher, a confessor and a petitioning politician, and by playing each guardian's own cant against him they obtain her consent. The exposure of the tricks reconciles the guardians and the lovers marry.
works.significance: It is the most durable English comedy about enthusiasm as a social language, and a central text for the study of the woman dramatist in the Augustan theatre; its personation structure was a model for later comedy of disguise.
works.meter: Predominantly prose dialogue with verse epilogue, the humour carried by the stylised cant of each guardian - Quaker plainness, Romish casistry, party phraseology.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in February 1718, in the season of the Whig split and the Jacobite scare, and held a repertory place through the century; its portraits of Quaker and papist enthusiasts draw on the controversy comedy of the previous age.
works.characters: Colonel Fainwell; Miss Lovely; Obadiah Prim the Quaker; the nun Perpetua; Sir Simon Affection; the Tory general
works.structure: Five-act comedy built on a single conceit of successive personation, with an epilogue and prologue addressing the party divisions of the house; the disguise scenes are arranged as set pieces of mimicry.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play was published with the author's name, though the pirated acting editions of the century alter its lines.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Book of Airs
works.description: The songbook of 1601 by Thomas Campion (words and music) and Philip Rosseter (music): twenty-one lute songs and one masque song, including 'My sweetest Lesbia', 'Follow thy fair sun', 'When to her lute Corinna sings', and 'I care not for these ladies' — the volume that made Campion the supreme English lyricist of the lute-song golden age.
works.plot: No plot: the airs set the commonplaces of love — carpe diem, the lady's beauty, the lover's complaint, the joys of country over court — each song a perfected miniature in the courtly lyric tradition.
works.significance: The classic of the Elizabethan lute-song tradition — poetry and music fused as nowhere else in the language, and a touchstone for every later English lyricist.
works.meter: Short-line lyric stanzas of exquisite finish — trochees, iambs, and the quantitative experiments of Campion's 'observations' — composed for music and printed with tablature.
works.context: Published 1601 in the first great decade of the English ayre, alongside Dowland's and Jones's books; Campion's preface defends the new union of English verse and music against the metrical pedants.
works.characters: the singer-lover; Lesbia; Corinna; the beloved ladies
works.structure: A printed songbook of twenty-one airs plus the masque song, arranged for voice and lute (some also for viol consort), in the standard format of the English ayre books.
works.attributionNotes: Words by Campion throughout, with one masque song; music by Campion for half the airs and by Rosseter for the rest.

editions.title: The Works of Thomas Campion

works.title: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside
works.description: Middleton's comedy of London's sexual economy: the goldsmith Yellowhammer's daughter Moll, betrothed by her parents to the decadent knight Sir Walter Whorehound, loves the poor Touchwood Junior; the city's trades in food, sex, and legitimacy — the Allwits' household, the promoters, the puritans feasting at a christening — fill the play, until Sir Walter's ruin and Moll's mock-death restore the lovers.
works.plot: Sir Walter finances the Allwits and fathers their 'children' while courting Moll; Touchwood Senior's fertility and his brother's love-plot run through the middle acts; the christening feast and the arrest of the gallants expose the city's corruptions; and the final scene, with Moll's pretended death and revival, joins the lovers and topples the knight.
works.significance: The sharpest of the Jacobean city comedies — a play that makes money, sex, and religion a single system of exchange.
works.meter: Prose and verse of Middleton's quickest, cruellest wit, with the christening scene's hypocritical feasting as its summit.
works.context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men at the Swan in 1613 and printed in 1630; its satire of the Jacobean marriage market and puritan hypocrisy is the most scathing of the age.
works.characters: Moll Yellowhammer; Touchwood Junior; Touchwood Senior; Sir Walter Whorehound; Yellowhammer; Maudlin Yellowhammer; the Allwits; the Kixes; the promoters; the wench; the puritans
works.structure: A five-act cross-section of Cheapside — multiple households joined by Sir Walter's purse — in Middleton's most populous and corrosive comic design.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside (New Mermaids)

works.title: A Collection of Hymns for the Use of the People Called Methodists
works.description: John Wesley's canonical hymnal, gathered from the brothers' earlier collections into some five hundred and twenty-five hymns, his last great editorial act and the book Methodism long sang from. He meant it as a compact scripture of heart and doctrine, its order teaching the whole Methodist way of salvation in verse.
works.plot: The collection orders the Christian and Methodist life from general hymns of praise through the acts and sufferings of Christ, the operations of the Spirit, the states of the believer, the means of grace, the sacraments, and the seasons of the year, a walk through divinity in song. Its nucleus is Charles Wesley's lyric theology, with the best of Watts, Doddridge, and the older hymnists admitted beside John's own translations and paraphrases. The editor pruned, altered, and regularized the texts of forty revival years into a single honest compass of experimental religion. Its preface states the design plainly: that the people called Methodists should own the whole of their religion and hope in one small book they could sing.
works.significance: It is the parent of almost all later Methodist hymnals and one of the most influential hymn books in the language, fixing the canon of Charles Wesley's lyrics in the worship of the whole communion.
works.meter: The common, long, short, and varied eight-line hymn metres of Augustan psalmody, the texts regularized in diction and measure by the editor.
works.context: Published in 1780 as the societies entered the last decade under John Wesley's sole governance, it deliberately canonized the revival's song against the multiplicity of earlier collections and became the standard of Methodist worship.
works.structure: An ordered hymnal in heads following the course of divinity and the church year, with preface and indices by subject and first line.
works.attributionNotes: Edited throughout by John Wesley; the majority of hymns are Charles Wesley's, with others by Watts, Doddridge, and earlier hands.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Collection of Psalms and Hymns
works.description: The Wesleys' first London hymn collection, issued in 1738 for the society they met with and drawing on the psalter versions and hymns then in use among the Oxford and London methodists. It carries the earliest printed fruits of Charles Wesley's hymnwriting alongside metrical psalms and the brothers' translations.
works.plot: The collection sets David's psalms in metrical version beside hymns for the chief seasons and doctrines: Advent, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, repentance, faith, and the last things. Its prefatory address pleads the conscience of the writers in choosing and mending the old versions, and its hymns already display Charles's gift for first-person assurance and tender doctrine. The volume thus forms a bridge from the Psalm-singing of the Church of England to the full Methodist hymnody of the Bristol collections.
works.significance: It marks the moment the Wesleyan movement began to sing in print, the first public shape of the revival's lyric theology and the ancestor of the great Methodist collections.
works.meter: Common, long, and short metre psalm stanzas and hymn measures of iambic lines; the language plain and singable, after the style of the earlier methodist psalmody.
works.context: Published in London in 1738 in the months of Aldersgate and the societies' forming, after the Oxford Psalm and Hymn pocket book of 1733 and before the Bristol Hymns and Sacred Poems of 1739.
works.characters: the London society
works.structure: A dual collection, psalms in metre followed by hymns arranged by seasons and subjects, with preface and occasional doxologies.
works.attributionNotes: Prepared by John and Charles Wesley; Charles is the author of the new hymns, the psalter versions being collaborative and largely rehandled from earlier hands.

works.title: A Compendious Dictionary of the English Language
works.form: Lexicography and philological writing; school and usage dictionary
works.description: The first considerable dictionary published in the United States, a single-volume compendium intended to fix American spelling, pronunciation and usage. It gathers the common English vocabulary with the new words of the republic and adds a grammatical and orthographical preface. It is the working ancestor of the great dictionary of 1828.
works.plot: The work defines the ordinary vocabulary of the language, marking parts of speech and offering usage notes rather than literary quotation. It sets out the American preferences in spelling that its author had long argued for, and it appends tables of words pronounced and spelled alike but differently written. Its front matter states the case for a national language independent of British decision. The whole is designed for the schoolroom and the counting house rather than for the scholar.
works.significance: It established the authority of the American dictionary and made the lexicon a question of national policy. Its spellings passed generally into American use. It is the necessary predecessor of the 1828 work and a document of the linguistic nationalism of the early republic.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1806 after two decades of the author's spelling books and political pamphlets on language, and in the season of the American argument that a republic needed its own dictionary. Its spelling reforms answered the Federalist and nationalist claim that language is an instrument of national character. It drew on Johnson and on the technical vocabulary then entering American speech.
works.structure: Alphabetical dictionary with a doctrinal preface and appended tables; no narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

works.title: A Defence of Poetry
works.form: Critical treatise and occasional essay of the Romantic theory of imagination; a polemical defence written in the manner of the reply pamphlet and enriched by aphoristic prose rhythm.
works.description: The period's most influential essay of poetic theory, written in a few weeks as a reply to a friend's prose argument that poetry must inculcate moral truth. It defines poetry as the expression of the imagination, morality as the calculation of the relations of action to effect, and argues that a man who is good must love the beautiful, so that the poet who only creates is the unacknowledged legislator of the world. Its aphoristic manner and its argument for the utility of the useless have made it the centre of the Romantic theory of imagination.
works.plot: The essay opens by accepting that poetry is a branch of the art whose end is pleasure, and then distinguishes reasoning, which tabulates the relations of what is known, from imagination, which represents action as it is affected by the qualities of the mind that contemplates it. It argues that poetry is connected with the principles of our nature by the same ties as language and that the reasoning and the imaginative faculties are as the measure and the harmony of composition. It passes to a history of the civilizing power of poetry, from the ballad and the drama to the great works of the age it lives in, and defends the modern poets against the charge of indifference to moral instruction. Its close asserts that the influence of the poet is all-sufficient, that poetry is the record of the best and happiest moments of the happiest and best minds, and that the world's moral regeneration is the work of imagination.
works.significance: It is the most compact statement of the Romantic doctrine of imagination and, with its companion essay on the same occasion, the standard text of the defence of poetry's utility against a utilitarian age. Its definition of reason and imagination, and its claim for the poet as an unacknowledged legislator, have governed most later discussion of the social function of literature.
works.meter: Prose; a highly rhythmic periodic style, built on balanced clause, reiteration and the sententious closing member, much quoted as prose aphorism.
works.context: Written at Bagni di Lucca and at Pisa between February and March 1821 in reply to a prose essay, published in a review by a friend, on the demand that poetry should inculcate moral truth, and at a moment when the poet was defending his own longest and most philosophical drama against the charge of irrelevance. It was not printed in the author's lifetime; it first appeared posthumously in a collection of his prose edited by his widow, and its fame belongs to the reprints of the later century.
works.structure: A continuous occasional essay in twenty numbered sections, opening with the concession to the opponent's definition, proceeding by distinction, example and historical survey, and closing with the aphorisms on the legislator and on the happiness of the imaginative mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the essay was unfinished, the closing section fragmentary, and the printed text rests on a copy made by a friend of the author in the last year of his life.

editions.title: Shelley's Poetry and Prose (Norton Critical Edition)
editions.editor: Donald H. Reiman and Sharon B. Powers (editors)

works.title: A Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament
altTitles: The Defence of the True and Catholike Doctrine of the Sacrament of the Body and Bloud of Our Saviour Christ
works.description: Cranmer's principal theological work, published in 1550, defining the eucharist against both transubstantiation and mere memorialism; the fullest statement of the Reformed doctrine of the sacrament in English.
works.plot: The book argues from scripture and the fathers that Christ is truly but spiritually present in the eucharist, received by faith; it refutes the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (against Stephen Gardiner) and the Zwinglian reduction of the sacrament to a bare sign, distinguishing 'sacramentally' from 'corporally', and it defends the vernacular liturgy and communion in both kinds.
works.significance: The classic English statement of the Reformed eucharist and Cranmer's most sustained piece of theological prose; it fixed the middle course of Anglican sacramental doctrine for centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1550 during Cranmer's ascendancy under Edward VI, in the controversy with Bishop Stephen Gardiner (imprisoned for his opposition); the doctrine of the Defence shaped the communion rite of the 1552 Prayer Book, and Cranmer recanted it under Mary before renouncing his recantations at the stake in 1556.
works.structure: Five books of doctrinal argument with patristic citation, cast as a reply to Gardiner's defence of the corporal presence.

works.title: A Description of the Villa of Mr. Horace Walpole
altTitles: A Description of the Villa of Mr. Horace Walpole at Strawberry Hill
works.form: antiquarian description and catalogue of a collection
works.description: A room-by-room account of the author's Gothic villa at Strawberry Hill, its collections, its chapels and its libraries, written for the guidance of visitors and printed at his own instance. It is the founding document of the Gothic revival house as a literary and antiquarian artefact.
works.plot: The description leads the visitor through the exterior and the several apartments, reporting the arrangements of the Gothic chambers, the painted glass, the armour, the books and the relics with their provenances. It explains the taste and the scholarship that assembled them, and defends the villa's imitations of the old styles as faithful and instructive. The account of the collection ends with the library and the collections of prints and drawings, the whole forming a theory of antiquarian pleasure.
works.significance: It established the model of the described Gothic house and is the primary source for the taste, the antiquarian methods and the humour of the century's most famous literary residence.
works.meter: A plain descriptive prose of measurement, provenance and modest comment, with the epigraphic and heraldic phrases of the antiquarian tradition.
works.context: Printed in 1784 in the season of the vogue for Strawberry Hill and of the author's late quarrels over the authenticity of the relics he displayed; the villa itself, built and altered over some thirty years, is the work the book describes.
works.structure: A topographical and inventory description ordered by the plan of the house, with inserted catalogues and historical notes on individual pieces; there is no argument beyond the tour.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work was printed by the owner's direction, and the later editions were enlarged by other hands after his death.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Dialogue Concerning Heresies
altTitles: A Dialogue of Sir Thomas More, Knight
works.description: More's first and longest English polemical work against the Lutheran heresy, cast as a four-book dialogue between More and a young 'messenger' sent by a friend who is tempted by the reformers.
works.plot: In Book I More defends the veneration of images, pilgrimages, and miracles; Book II discusses the authority of the Church and the corruption of Tyndale's New Testament translation; Book III refutes Luther's and Tyndale's views on faith and works; Book IV defends the clergy and the burning of heretics, arguing that Luther's doctrine leads to sedition and the destruction of the sacraments.
works.significance: The major English Catholic response to the early Reformation, documenting the doctrinal battle over scripture and tradition, and one of the fullest exhibits of More's prose — combative, witty, and colloquial — outside the Latin works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written 1528–29 after More had read Tyndale's New Testament and his Obedience of a Christian Man; part of the print war between More (with Bishop John Fisher) and the English reformers conducted under Bishop Tunstall's licence to read heretical books.
works.characters: Thomas More (as speaker); The Messenger
works.structure: Four books of continuous dialogue; the anonymous messenger relays objections while More answers at length with authorities, anecdotes, and comic deflation of the reformers.

works.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation
works.description: More's last and greatest English work, written in the Tower of London while awaiting execution, a dialogue in which an elderly Hungarian uncle instructs his nephew on bearing tribulation, especially the fear of death under persecution.
works.plot: Set in Hungary on the eve of a Turkish invasion, the dialogue moves from the general consolation of tribulation, through the temptations of fear, scruple, and despair, to the specific comfort of martyrdom, culminating in the uncle's meditation on the passion of Christ as the pattern of all suffering.
works.significance: The masterpiece of English devotional prose of its age, and one of the great prison writings in the language; its controlled serenity under sentence of death has made it the most widely read of More's English works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the Tower between More's arrest (April 1534) and execution (6 July 1535), after his refusal of the Oath of Succession; the manuscript was smuggled abroad and first printed in London by Richard Tottel in 1553, under Mary I.
works.characters: Anthony (the uncle); Vincent (the nephew)
works.structure: Three books of dialogue between the aged Anthony and his nephew Vincent, with inset parables and a famous treatment of the temptation to suicide; the fictional frame thinly veils More's own imprisonment.

editions.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation (The Yale Edition of the Complete Works of St. Thomas More, vol. 12)
editions.editor: Louis L. Martz and Frank Manley

works.title: A Dictionary of the English Language
altTitles: A Dictionary of the English Language, in Which the Words are Derived from the Originals, and Illustrated in Their Different Significations by Examples from the Best Writers (first edition title)
works.form: two-volume folio dictionary with a prefixed grammar and prospectus; lexicographical and philological writing
works.description: The two folio volumes that settled the lexicography of English for half a century and remained the standard authority until the Oxford English Dictionary. Johnson gave some 42,773 words and illustrated their senses with a vast body of literary quotations, treating the language as a national literature rather than as a set of logical terms. The work was performed largely by Johnson's own labour, assisted by a small body of clerks, on the booksellers' contract signed in 1747.
works.plot: Each entry gives the orthography, the etymology where it can be traced, the parts of speech and the senses arranged from the primary to the derived, each authenticated by a quotation from an approved writer. Johnson's discussions of the difficulty of fixing a living language, of the limits of etymology and of the treatment of low or indecent words are recorded in the Grammar and the Plan prefixed to the volumes, and the illustrative citations - Shakespeare, Milton, Dryden, Pope and hundreds more - amount to an anthology of English writing.
works.significance: It established quotation-as-evidence, the historical treatment of senses and the idea that a dictionary is a record of a literature, all of which passed into later lexicons; it also created the modern image of the independent professional writer. Its definitions remain a literary document, and the work is a central text for eighteenth-century theories of language, usage and national letters.
works.meter: Prose of extreme compression in the definitions, with the illustrative quotations supplying the rhythm and the authority; the Grammar is written in the same periodic style as the Plan.
works.context: Produced in the decade after Chesterfield's indifference to projects for an English academy and in the same years as the Rambler papers; the booksellers' share system, the labour of the six copying clerks and Johnson's lodging in Gough Square provide the physical conditions of the work, and the Seven Years' War had already begun when it was published.
works.structure: A reference work: an alphabetical macrostructure, preceded by the Plan and a Grammar of the English tongue; no narrative order, but a strict microstructure of word, etymology, senses, examples.
works.attributionNotes: Johnson is the author of the whole design and of the definitions; the clerks and later bibliographers assisted the execution, and the etymologies relied on the philology then available, including Junius, Skinner and Tooke's predecessors.

editions.editor: W. Jackson Bate and James L. Clifford (general editors)

works.title: A Discourse of the Grounds and Reasons of the Christian Religion
works.description: Collins's historical-critical pamphlet, treating Christianity as a this-worldly political phenomenon whose grounds lie in Jewish messianic expectation and whose reasons for assent are those of the Jewish religion it answered. Published amid the Woolston trials, it provoked a swarm of replies and a parliamentary outrage.
works.plot: Collins argues that the Jews expected a temporal Messiah, and that the first preachers addressed purely political hopes shaped by that expectation. On this account Christianity's rise is explained by causes within history: a deluded expectation later corrected by an allegorical reading after the failure of the temporal kingdom. The spiritualizing interpretation, he suggests, is a shift that saved the sect from extinction and made prophecy serve whatever happened. He closes with a proposal: the true Messiah remains to come, and the grounds of Christian assent, being historical and political, are weaker than those of the Jewish religion they displaced.
works.significance: It is the most political of the deist attacks, turning the evidences inside out by explaining religion from the interests it served, and a decisive provocation for the historical and moral apologetics of the following decades.
works.meter: Level, deadpan argumentative prose, with startling conclusions reached through a series of apparently neutral historical enquiries.
works.context: Published in 1724, the same year as Tindal's Christianity as Old as the Creation and in the shadow of Woolston's libel trial; the House of Commons resolved to prosecute the author, making it a cause celebre of the deist decade.
works.structure: A compact single discourse moving from the political state of the Jews, through the causes of Christianity's rise, to the allegorizing solution and a concluding query about the true Messiah.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: A Discourse on the Love of Our Country
altTitles: A Discourse on the Love of Our Country, on a Review of the Revolution of 1688
works.description: Price's sermon to the Revolution Society on the centenary of the Glorious Revolution, delivered two months after the fall of the Bastille and read as a blessing upon the French Revolution. It defined true love of country as attachment to liberty and to the rights of mankind, not to soil, state, or church establishment, and it provoked Burke's Reflections directly.
works.plot: Price argues that the love of our country, rightly understood, is a moral attachment to the commonwealth of free people, not a jealous patriotism set against the rest of the world. He reviews the English Revolution of 1688 as a real assertion of the rights of mankind, and insists that the same principles authorize the French people's resistance to tyranny; the glory of Britain lies in having taught the lesson, not in reserving it. He warns that churches and courts which turn religion into an engine of state betray both, and closes with a universalist prayer for the progress of liberty, knowledge, and virtue among all nations. The discourse was answered by loyal addresses, by clerical replies, and above all by Burke.
works.significance: It is the great text of cosmopolitan British radicalism and the book that called Burke into print, defining the argument about the rights of nations and the love of country that ran through the revolutionary decade.
works.meter: Sermonic prose of grave, sustained warmth, the periods built by parallel and antithesis, its rhetoric deliberately pacific and universal.
works.context: Delivered on 4 November 1789 to the Revolution Society at the Old Jewry in the first fever of the French Revolution, printed by the author's appointment and reprinted within the year; it was the immediate occasion of Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France.
works.structure: A single commemorative sermon, the centenary meditation opening into a universal theory of liberty and its love.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: A Fragment on Government
altTitles: A Fragment on Government; or, A Comment on the Commentaries
works.description: Bentham's anonymous first book, a savage critique of Blackstone's Commentaries that made the greatest legal oracle of the age the enemy of rational law. Its preface planted the principle of utility - the greatest happiness of the greatest number - at the foundation of legislation, and its commentary exposed fiction, prescription, and mystery as the armour of misrule.
works.plot: Against Blackstone's account of original contract and passive obedience, Bentham argues that government rests on the obedience actually rendered, and that the test of institutions is their utility, not their antiquity or the lawyer's applause. He dissects the Commentaries passage by passage: the state of nature fable, the fictional contract, the praise of English law's mystery and its trifling with the people's interest under the name of ease. The celebrated passages expose Blackstone's apology for the equity of the judges, the vagueness of natural law, and the treason-law's tyranny, until the famous declaration that the standard of right and wrong is the greatest happiness of the greatest number. The fragment thus turns a commentary into a manifesto for radical reform.
works.significance: It founded utilitarian radicalism and the critique of the common-law mystique, gave the English reform movement its watchword and its method, and made its author, unknown for years, the legislator of the reforming century.
works.meter: Ferocious, vivid, quotational prose, the polemical repetition of an opponent's own phrases turned against him by emphasis and scorn.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1776, the year of the Wealth of Nations and Common Sense, after Bentham's youthful revolt in the Temple from Blackstone's lectures; its first public detection as Blackstone's critic scandalized the profession.
works.structure: A double work: a preface of principle and then a running paragraph-by-paragraph commentary on selected sections of Blackstone.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously, with only the advertisement's clues; authorship known within the circle of Bentham's friends and declared openly in later years.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A General History of the Pyrates
altTitles: A General History of the Pyrates, From Their First Rise and Settlement in the Island of Providence
works.form: collective biography and historical narrative in prose
works.description: The chief narrative source for the lives of the great pirates of the American station, compiled and dramatised as a history of the profligate colony of the Bahamas. Its first volume is a continuous series of captains' lives, and its style is a hybrid of the criminal biography, the sea narrative and the moralising tale.
works.plot: The work traces the rise of pyrating after the peace discharged the privateers, describes the settlement at New Providence under Hornigold and the seizures made by the new confederacy, and then gives the careers, customs, articles, trials and deaths of the principal captains. It dwells on Roberts's articles and discipline, on the terrors of Teach, and on the female pirates' disguise and capture. It moralises throughout on the inevitable end of the pyrating course, so that even the successful captains are reported into the gallows or the desert.
works.significance: It is the sourcebook of the modern image of piracy, the black flag, the articles and the ship's democracy, and one of the most influential of the Newgate-derived prose series; its uncertain authorship makes it a test case for the attribution of hack history.
works.meter: Plain narrative prose of the criminal life, with sea-cant, trial reportage and the abrupt sentences of the hanging report; the inserted documents preserve official and notarial styles.
works.context: Published in London between 1724 and 1728 in the wave of public interest following the vice-admiralty trials of the pirates, and drawing on the court records, the colonial news sheets and the captains' own depositions.
works.characters: Henry Every; Blackbeard; Bartholomew Roberts; Henry Jennings; Charles Vane; Anne Bonny; Mary Read
works.structure: A serial of biographical lives inside a short historical introduction, with inserted documents such as articles and trial reports; a second volume extends the series with a more evidently inventive manner.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution disputed: the first volume was entered in the name of Captain Charles Johnson, a pseudonym many scholars have identified with the novelist and pamphleteer of the same publishing circle, while others deny the identification and question the second volume; the record is held for that disputed ascription and the pseudonym alone is named in the text.

works.title: A Grammar of the English Language
works.form: Grammar and didactic prose, a schoolbook consciously written as an instrument of popular education rather than as scholarship.
works.description: The author's grammar, first written for his son at school in America and then issued as a book for the English labouring classes. It teaches parts of speech, syntax, prosody and composition through sentences drawn from ordinary speech and from the best writers, and it is candidly polemical against Latin and French derived rules. The volume also carries his famous account of the 'Saxon' idiom and his insistence that clear writing is a moral as well as a civic accomplishment.
works.plot: The rules are set out in question-and-answer form, with parsing exercises on sentences of farm, shop and workshop, and with corrections of faulty examples. The writer argues that English is a language of short Saxon words which should be preferred to long derived ones, and that the grammar of the tongue is learned by use and imitation rather than by translation from Latin. He gives instructions on spelling, on the choice of words, and on writing plain prose, and adds advice on reading the best English authors. The later part addresses composition, punctuation and versification, and argues that a labourer's child properly taught has the same access to the language as a gentleman's.
works.significance: One of the most widely read English grammar books of the nineteenth century, long a standard school text in Britain and America, and a key document of the period's belief that control of the standard language was a route to political enfranchisement.
works.meter: Prose, with illustrative verse passages on prosody.
works.context: Written after its author's American exile and his son's schooling at Bristol, and issued cheaply as part of the series of useful knowledge for mechanics and labourers that flourished in the later 1810s alongside the Lancasterian schools and the mechanics' institutes.
works.structure: Didactic treatise in progressive lessons with exercises and examples, addressed in a first-person voice to a pupil and to his parent; prefaced by an account of the book's origin in correspondence with the author's son.

William Cobbett: The Politics of Style (Cambridge Studies in Romanticism)
