works.title: Aenigmata
works.description: Aldhelm's collection of one hundred Latin riddles in hexameters, enclosed as the final part of the Epistola ad Acircium (addressed to King Aldfrith of Northumbria). The first riddle collection of medieval England and the direct model for the vernacular Exeter Book riddles.
works.plot: Each riddle speaks in the first person, obliquely describing its subject — the elements, creatures, household objects, tools of learning — with the last line of each revealing or hinting the solution (water, the wind, the raven, the pen, the alembic, and so on).
works.significance: The model and quarry of the entire insular riddle tradition, Latin and vernacular.
works.meter: Dactylic hexameters, technically virtuosic.
works.context: Written c. 686-700 as part of the Epistola ad Acircium, a treatise on Latin metre for King Aldfrith; imitated by Tatwine, Eusebius, and Boniface, and translated into Old English in the Exeter Book tradition.
works.characters: the speaking objects of the riddles
works.structure: A numbered sequence of one hundred enigmas, framed by the prefatory acrostic poem on Aldhelm's own name.
works.attributionNotes: Aldhelm's authorship is certain.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography

works.title: Aenigmata (Hwætberht's Riddles)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.C.xxiii (tenth century), with the riddles of Tatwine
works.description: Forty Latin riddles composed by Hwætberht (Eusebius), abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow (c. 716-c. 747) and associate of Bede, in the tradition of Symphosius and Aldhelm. The riddles range over the natural world, the cosmos, and the tools of learning — the sun and moon, the winds, the sea, the alphabet, and the liberal arts.
works.plot: The riddles personify their subjects, from celestial bodies and elemental forces to letters and numbers, each speaking obliquely of its nature and powers; the collection moves from the macrocosm of heaven and earth to the microcosm of human learning.
works.significance: The Northumbrian counterpart to Aldhelm's and Tatwine's riddle cycles, completing the Anglo-Latin riddle corpus that inspired the vernacular riddles of the Exeter Book.
works.meter: Latin hexameters modelled closely on Aldhelm, with his alliteration and ornamental diction; the verse is learned and allusive, written for readers trained in the monastic school.
works.context: Composed at Wearmouth-Jarrow in the age of Bede, when the twin monastery was the richest centre of learning in western Europe; the riddles show Aldhelm's influence carried into Northumbria and the riddle form serving the encyclopedic ambitions of the Northumbrian Renaissance.
works.structure: Forty self-contained hexameter riddles in an encyclopedic sequence, deliberately continuing and answering the tradition of Aldhelm's century of riddles; the arrangement suggests a curriculum of knowledge from cosmology to grammar.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Hwætberht (Eusebius), abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow, by manuscript tradition.
themes: Puritan inheritance and the secret sin
sources: The North American Review

works.title: Aenigmata (Tatwine's Riddles)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.C.xxiii (tenth century), with the riddles of Hwætberht
works.description: Forty Latin riddles with a verse preface composed by Tatwine, monk of Breedon-on-the-Hill and archbishop of Canterbury (731-734). The riddles treat theological, philosophical, and grammatical subjects — faith, hope, charity, the five senses, the letters of the alphabet, the books of the Bible — in the manner of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
works.plot: Each riddle speaks in the first person about its own nature, requiring the reader to identify abstractions (the virtues, the liberal arts, grammatical categories) and objects (the pen, the sword, the book) from oblique descriptions built on learning rather than natural history.
works.significance: With Aldhelm's and Hwætberht's collections, Tatwine's riddles define the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition that stands behind the Exeter Book Riddles; they document the teaching of abstract theology through the schoolroom genre.
works.meter: Latin hexameters of schoolmasterly correctness, plainer than Aldhelm's hermeneutic verse; the riddles average six to eight lines and often begin with a paradoxical self-description.
works.context: Composed in the learned milieu of Breedon and Canterbury in the generation after Aldhelm, the riddles show the classroom union of grammar, theology, and verse composition that characterized early Anglo-Latin culture and fed the vernacular riddle tradition.
works.structure: A preface followed by forty self-contained riddles arranged in a deliberate sequence from theological virtues through philosophical abstractions to grammatical and physical subjects; the collection is the earliest complete Latin riddle cycle composed in England.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Tatwine by manuscript tradition and internal evidence; the riddles are contemporary with his Canterbury years or earlier.
themes: Republican nationhood and the claim to a national literature
sources: The Letters of William Cullen Bryant (6 volumes)

works.title: Aglaura
works.description: Sir John Suckling's first and most famous play, a tragicomedy of courtly love and intrigue performed by the King's Men in 1638 and lavishly printed at the author's expense, reflecting the gallant, platonic-love ideals of the Caroline court.
works.plot: The King of Bithynia's court is troubled by the amorous conflicts surrounding the Princess Aglaura, involving love, jealousy, and a plot against the throne, resolved in the tragicomic mode.
works.significance: A characteristic Caroline courtly drama, notable for its production history, its expression of Caroline platonic-love ideals, and its author's social prestige.
works.meter: Blank verse and prose with a gallant, witty, courtly manner.
works.context: Performed and printed in 1638 at Suckling's own great expense, reflecting his wealth and his standing among the Caroline court wits.
works.characters: Aglaura; the King of Bithynia; Ardebert; Orbella
works.structure: A five-act tragicomedy in blank verse and prose, produced in two alternative endings (tragic and comic).
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Agrarian Justice
altTitles: Agrarian Justice Opposed to the Agrarian Law
works.form: pamphlet in political economy and social project; argumentative tract with a scheme of public provision
works.description: A short pamphlet of political economy and justice, addressed to the problem of property in land and proposing a national fund paid from landed and inheritable wealth. It distinguishes the earth in its natural state, the common inheritance of all, from the earth in a state of cultivation, whose improvements are property, and argues that the landholder owes a rent to the community for the ground he holds. Its practical proposal, an endowment paid to every citizen at majority and a pension in old age, is the most quoted part of the work.
works.plot: The pamphlet begins by rejecting both the levelers and the defenders of prescription: agrarian laws confounding property with the land are unjust, but the exclusive private ownership of the earth by inheritance is a theft of the common stock. It then dates the revolution of property: cultivation created the value of land, and with it the inequality that dispossessed the many for the benefit of the few, so that civilization, instead of diminishing, has increased the mass of misery. From this it concludes that the occupant of land owes a ground-rent to the national estate, but that the improvements belong to the holder and are not to be confiscated. The scheme follows: a national fund raised by a duty upon inheritances beyond the direct line, and administered as a payment to every person reaching adulthood and as an annuity for those advanced in years, with the poor laws to be repealed as inefficient and degrading. The argument closes by claiming that this plan relieves the poor without pauperising them, and enriches no one at the expense of the donor.
works.significance: It is the classical statement of the doctrine that landed property is a social creation carrying a debt to the community, the source of the long tradition that connects the unearned increment to public endowment, and one ancestor of both the single-tax tradition and the modern case for a social dividend. Its tone also made it a permanent weapon in the argument over property, quoted alike by radicals and by their opponents.
works.meter: Ardent, arithmetical prose of the plain school: declaratory openings, numbered cases, and a repeated rhythm of 'it is not, but it is' distinctions, pitched for the popular reader.
works.context: Written in France during the Directory, in the aftermath of the constitutional pamphlets of the same years and of the debate over agrarian law in the American states, and published in 1797 in Paris, Philadelphia, and London. Its appearance coincided with the British controversy over the poor laws, of which the tract's argument was a radical version.
works.structure: A continuous short argument in nine numbered sections: the statement of the common right, the history of cultivated property, the refutation of confiscation, the ground-rent principle, the plan of the national fund, and the objections answered.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, and its dedication to the French Directory is printed in the first issue.

works.title: Aids to Reflection
works.form: Moral and religious reflection in the aphoristic and commentarial manner, a work of practical philosophy written for the private reader and drawing on the seventeenth-century devotional writers as its quoted authorities.
works.description: The author's book of moral and religious reflection, published in 1825 and drawn from aphorisms, commentaries and letters on the conduct of the mind and the grounds of faith; the maxims and passages quoted from earlier writers, chiefly from a seventeenth-century divine, are set out with a running commentary that makes the book a work of applied philosophy rather than of devotion. Its purpose is to teach the reader to reflect, distinguishing the faculties by which he is governed and the order of knowledge proper to each, and its argument about reason and understanding became one of the most influential pieces of psychological vocabulary in the nineteenth century.
works.plot: The work proceeds by aphorism and exposition. It divides the internal man into the powers of the flesh or appetite, the understanding with its prudence, and the reason with its moral and spiritual ideas, and argues that the errors of the age arise from applying the logic of the understanding to the objects of reason, so that prudence is mistaken for wisdom and the evidence of things seen for the evidence of things not seen. Against the philosophy of mere prudence it maintains that the moral will is the seat of personality and that the ideas of reason are not generalisations from experience but conditions of thought; the Christian faith is presented as a temper of heart requiring a readiness to be taught rather than a conclusion from proof. The closing letters and appendixes pursue the same distinction in disputes on free-will, on the character of the religious teacher, and on the temper of the church and its clergy, and it was these passages that drew the book into controversy with the author's own family and with the liberal religious bodies.
works.significance: One of the most widely read and most quoted books of Victorian thought, exercised through the distinction between reason and understanding and through its claim that religion is a temper of heart rather than a system of proof; readers from the schoolmaster and the cleric to the American transcendentalists formed their vocabulary of the faculties from it. It also remains the standard document of the religious turn of the later Romantic movement and of the author's own career.
works.meter: Prose of a deliberately weighty and periodic style, full of distinction and definition, with long sentences that enact the act of reflection and a repeated vocabulary of faculties, grounds and temper; it is the author's most quoted English prose.
works.context: Published in 1825, in the years of the author's settlement as a household writer, of the controversies over the unitarian and Trinitarian questions, and of his public quarrels with the political and religious opinions of his early friends; the book's use of a seventeenth-century divine's maxims reflects the period's recovery of the older English theological writers.
works.structure: A book of aphorisms with continuous commentary, arranged in several divisions and followed by letters and appendixes on the disputed questions; there is no narrative, and the design is that of an education of the reader's faculties, each division taking up one power of the mind.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the quoted aphorisms are the author's selection from an earlier divine and are acknowledged as such in the text.

works.title: Al Aaraaf, Tamerlane, and Minor Poems
altTitles: Al Aaraaf, Tamerlane and Minor Poems
works.form: Romantic philosophical poem and lyric collection; vision-poem of the intermediate state
works.description: The author's second pamphlet of verse and his first attempt at a cosmological poem. Its central fancy is an island or star of the same name, the residence of souls too imperfect for heaven and too delicately raised for earth. The volume reprints the earlier Tamerlane confession and adds short lyrics, and it shows the romantic habit of the sublime pushed to the verge of abstraction.
works.plot: The title poem places the reader in a kingdom of the sky where the spirits of the imperfect dead await their final elevation, and describes its lakes, its night flowers and its waiting inhabitants. The poem then descends to earth and to the love and ambition that could not be satisfied there, and closes with a prophecy of the soul's eventual passage. Tamerlane supplies the second long poem, the wanderer's confession of forfeited love. The minor pieces treat the memory of the dead and the power of beauty to detain the mind.
works.significance: It contains the earliest American poem to make a cosmology the scene of moral instruction, and it documents the ambitious, unreadable side of the author's imagination. Its revision history shows the author reshaping his early verse into a canon. It is the middle term between the 1827 pamphlet and the collected volume of 1831.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter with irregular stanzaic grouping, and shorter lyric stanzas in the minor poems
works.context: Printed in 1829 for the author, after his expulsion from West Point and during his brief association with the family that had supported him. Its astronomical fancy borrows from the popular astronomy and from the German romantic example then reaching American readers. The volume sold poorly and was disowned by its author in later years.
works.characters: The spirits of the island of Al Aaraaf; the wanderer of Tamerlane; the lost beloved
works.structure: Two long poems followed by shorter lyrics; the principal poem proceeds by description of an imagined place, then by reflection, then by prophetic conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the volume names its author on the title-page.

works.title: Alastor; or, The Spirit of Solitude: And Other Poems
works.form: Romantic narrative meditation in blank verse, with the conversation poem and the sonnet sequence of the revived school; the volume is the apprentice statement of a theory of imaginative self-sufficiency.
works.description: The first volume of verse issued through the trade by its author, dominated by a long narrative of a poet who dies of the pursuit of an ideal form he once saw in a dream. The title poem states the case for and against imaginative solitude in a single fable, and the accompanying pieces, sonnets, a blank-verse meditation on the sea and the recollections of an unrequited devotion, display a manner learned from the older lake school. Its reviews were severe and the volume sold poorly, and the book marks the point at which a philosophical radical began to write as a poet of mood.
works.plot: A young poet, nurtured by the Genius of the lonely mountains and refusing the company of human love, walks the earth in pursuit of the ideal beauty once shown him in a vision, passing through the caves and valleys of the north and the plains of Asia. He finds at last, by a stream in a desert valley, the form he sought in the likeness of a dead woman who was his mother's love, and dies in the act of clasping the shadow, while his wild companion the eagle and the hind mourn over the stream. The shorter poems add the poet's own creed, the power of the intellect and of beauty, and the consolation of the mountain scenery remembered in absence. The argument is that imagination which refuses the human bond consumes itself, though the poem's own rhetoric admires the refusal.
works.significance: It gave the century one of its definitive parables of the dangerous self-sufficiency of the imaginative mind, and its title figure was at once read as the poet's own portraiture, making the volume a founding document of the Romantic myth of the solitary genius. Its diction, a deliberate reproduction of the older nature school's compound style, is the clearest record of that school's conquest of the younger generation.
works.meter: Chiefly blank verse of five-beat iambic lines with rich compound adjectives and long periodic movement; the shorter pieces are Pindaric or Spenserian stanzas and sonnets after the revived manner.
works.context: Written largely between the autumn of 1815 and the spring of 1816, in the months of the author's first marriage and his withdrawal from his family, and published in 1816 with a prefatory advertisement that complained of the coldness of the metropolis; the review of the volume by the anti-Jacobin quarterlies attacked its egoism and its atheism together. The book's failure pushed the author toward the more public and philosophical verse of the following years.
works.characters: the solitary poet of the title; the Genius of the mountains; the mother beloved of his infancy; the eagle and the hind of the desert stream; the fire-side hearers of the frame
works.structure: A frame of an evening fireside and a winter storm introduces the long narrative in continuous blank verse, with the lyric and sonnet pieces of the volume printed after it and an authorial advertisement in prose.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume's shorter pieces include work of the author's schoolfellow in the accompanying advertisement's account, but the title poem and the principal lyrics are single-handed.

works.title: Alciphron
works.description: Berkeley's dialogue against the freethinkers of his own day, figured as the ancient minute philosopher Alciphron, whose scepticism about religion, morality, and providence is answered not by metaphysics but by the visible evidence of Christianity's civilizing power. Its defence of the church as an historical and moral phenomenon was Berkeley's most publicistic work.
works.plot: The dialogue opens on the minute philosopher Alciphron rejecting religion as enthusiasm and priestcraft, until the older Euphranor promises to prove Christianity by facts any candid critic must weigh. They examine the evidence of the founder's miracles and the prophecy of the church's enduring spread, arguing that a scheme which has tamed nations, fixed morals, and produced learning and charity cannot rest on a known imposture. Alciphron's scepticism about providence is met with the analogy of a well-governed state whose end exceeds present view. The closing dialogues answer the charge that Christianity has been the spoil of priests, showing it instead the patron of civil liberty and national union.
works.significance: It became the classic apologetic of evidential Christian moral history, influential in America and reprinted for debates at Harvard and Yale, and it is the century's fullest dialogue answer to freethinking ridicule.
works.meter: Measured, courteous dialogic prose, more expansive than the Hylas dialogues, with set-piece historical argumentation.
works.context: Published in 1732 in the immediate wake of the deist flush of Tindal and Collins and of the Shaftesburian reign of ridicule, and as Berkeley returned from his failed American college project; its portraits of the minute philosopher and of Lysicles were read as sketches of the freethinking club wits of the day.
works.characters: Euphranor; Alciphron; Lysicles; Hippias; Cleontes
works.structure: Four consecutive dialogues, each answering one branch of the minute-philosopher's assault: miracles and evidence, prophecy and the church's spread, providence, and priestcraft and civilizing power.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Alcuin's Letters
works.description: The surviving correspondence of Alcuin of York — over 280 letters to kings, bishops, and friends, from Charlemagne and his court to the monks of Lindisfarne and the school of York: the richest epistolary record of the Carolingian Renaissance and of the network that carried Anglo-Saxon learning to the Continent.
works.plot: The letters range from affairs of state and church (the condemnation of adoptionism, the imperial coronation, the Danish raids) to friendship, consolation, and literary patronage; the most famous is the letter of 793 to the community of Lindisfarne after the Viking sack, interpreting the disaster as divine correction and urging repentance.
works.significance: The principal documentary source for the intellectual life of the Carolingian age and its English foundations.
works.meter: Latin prose, with verse epistles among the corpus.
works.context: Written 780-804 from York and the Frankish court; edited by E. Dümmler in MGH Epistolae IV (1895).
works.characters: Charlemagne; Arno of Salzburg; the monks of Lindisfarne; Æthelhard of Canterbury; Eanbald of York
works.structure: A chronologically arranged correspondence of over 280 items.
works.attributionNotes: Alcuin's authorship is certain.
themes: The public theatre and the players' world
movements: The Knickerbocker Group and the American Sketch
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Alexander's Feast; or, The Power of Music
works.description: Dryden's second Cecilia ode, a dramatic narrative of the Greek musician Timotheus singing at Alexander the Great's victory feast and rousing him through pity, love, and finally revenge.
works.plot: Timotheus's song moves Alexander from triumph to tears to drunken fury, so that he burns Persepolis; the poem concludes that a nobler master of harmony — St Cecilia — raised the sacred organ and the divine affections.
works.significance: The culminating English ode of the seventeenth century; Handel's 1736 setting made it internationally famous and it remained a touchstone for poetic theories of versification through the eighteenth century.
works.meter: Irregular Pindaric stanzas; Dryden claimed to have written it in a single night and considered it his best work.
works.context: Written for the Music Society's St Cecilia's Day celebration of 1697 and set by Jeremiah Clarke.
works.characters: Alexander the Great; Timotheus; Thaïs; St Cecilia
works.structure: A continuous dramatic narrative in irregular stanzas, ending with an abrupt change of key in the final chorus.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

The Poems and Fables of John Dryden

works.title: Alfred
works.description: Thomson's masque on Alfred the Great and the deliverance of the Saxon kingdom, written for the prince's country house and closed by the ode on the dominion of the sea which became the national song.
works.plot: The young Alfred, nursed in exile and instructed in the history of his house, is restored against the Danish power by the counsel and the example of the ancient British worthies; the vision of the nation's future is disclosed to him, and the masque ends with the invocation of the ocean's rule.
works.significance: It is the most successful of the century's literary masques and the source of the song that became the anthem of the naval nation, and it shows the Augustan language of liberty converted into entertainment.
works.meter: Alternating recitative lines, the regular stanzas of the song and the anthem measure of the closing ode, written for composition.
works.context: Prepared for the court of the Prince of Wales at his country seat, with music by the century's chief theatre composer, in the season when the patriot circle made the ancient British mythology of Alfred the vehicle of its opposition politics.
works.characters: Alfred; the Saxon counsellors of the exile; the Danish power; the choruses of the British worthies
works.structure: A masque in one act with the recitative, the chorus and the prophetic vision, closing in a separately numbered ode.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Thomson's, the music being another hand's; the closing ode has been separately credited to the poet.

works.title: Alfred's Domboc
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: King Alfred's law book: an introduction translating the Ten Commandments and Mosaic law into English, followed by Alfred's own code and an appendix of Ine's laws. A founding document of the idea of English law as the law of a Christian people, consciously modelled on the Old Testament.
works.plot: The prologue renders Exodus 20-23 — the commandments, the laws of injury, slavery, and property — as the ancient foundation of law; Alfred's own clauses then regulate oaths, treachery against lords, sanctuary, the church, marriage, wounds, theft, and the ordeal, closing with the principle of compensation where no earlier provision exists.
works.significance: The classic statement of Anglo-Saxon kingship as Christian legislation; the foundation text of the later English common law tradition.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued in the later years of Alfred's reign, c. 893; preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 173 (with the Chronicle).
works.characters: Alfred (legislator); Moses (prologue)
works.structure: Tripartite: Mosaic introduction, Alfred's code, and the appended code of Ine.
works.attributionNotes: Alfred's authorship of the prologue and code is certain.
movements: Civil War Radicalism: The Levellers and the Diggers
sources: The Cambridge Companion to English Renaissance Drama, 2nd edition

works.title: All for Love; or, The World Well Lost
works.description: Dryden's rewriting of Antony and Cleopatra in blank verse, observing the unities of time, place, and action and confining itself to the last day in Alexandria; it is his own favourite among his plays.
works.plot: After Actium, Antony refuses to fight Octavius again, is drawn into suspicion by Ventidius and Alexas, and Cleopatra feigns death; the lovers die together, and the world is 'well lost' for love.
works.significance: The greatest heroic tragedy of the Restoration and the standard version of the Antony story on the English stage for more than a century; it remains Dryden's most frequently performed play.
works.meter: Blank verse, written, Dryden said, 'in imitation of Shakespeare's style'; the prologue declares it the first play he ever wrote without rhyme.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in December 1677 and published in 1678 with a preface defending the choice of blank verse and the observance of the unities.
works.characters: Marc Antony; Cleopatra; Ventidius; Alexas; Octavia; Serapion; Dolabella; Myris
works.structure: Five acts within the classical unities, with a single place (the temple of Isis at Alexandria) and a single day.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: All Ovid's Elegies
works.description: Marlowe's translation of Ovid's Amores into English heroic couplets — the first complete English version of the Roman love elegies, in which the poet-lover's campaigns in the bedroom, his mistress Corinna, and the whole erotic repertoire of Augustan Rome are rendered with Marlowe's characteristic audacity; the book was condemned and burned by the bishops' ban of 1599.
works.plot: The three books of the Amores move through the lover's slavery to Corinna, the rivalries, quarrels, and reconciliations of the affair, the impotence elegy, and the final renunciation of love elegy for tragedy — each poem an erotic set piece in the Ovidian manner.
works.significance: The first full English Ovid of the Renaissance erotic tradition — the text that made Marlowe's name a byword for atheism and licence, and a model for Donne's elegies.
works.meter: Heroic couplets — Marlowe's chosen form for Ovid's elegiacs — of a frankness that scandalized the authorities.
works.context: Printed surreptitiously in the late 1590s and burned under the Bishops' Ban of 1599 along with the satires of Marston and Hall; all early editions survive only in fragments.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Corinna; the eunuch Bagoas; the bawd Dipsas; Aurora
works.structure: A sequence of some forty-eight elegies in three books, translated in order from the Amores, with Marlowe's ten elegies to a serving-wench translating Ovid with his usual freedom.
works.attributionNotes: Translation; uncontested.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Poems and Translations

works.title: All the Works of Epictetus
altTitles: All the Works of Epictetus, Which are Now Extant: Consisting of His Discourses, Collect'd by Arrian; The Enchiridion; and Chapters, Collect'd by Stobaeus
works.form: translation of a philosophical text, with preface and notes
works.description: A complete English version of the surviving works of the Stoic teacher, made from the Greek with an historical and critical preface and with annotations explaining the philosophy and its phrases. It was the work by which a woman scholar became a European byword for Greek learning.
works.plot: The translation renders the discourses reported by Arrian, the handbook and the extracts preserved by Stobaeus, giving the reader the whole of Epictetus's practical philosophy. The prefatory account explains the life, the doctrine and the value of the author, and the notes open the terms of the schools. The work presents Stoic ethics as a discipline of judgement, desire and duty, useful to Christian readers as well as to philosophers.
works.significance: It is one of the great achievements of eighteenth-century women's scholarship and long remained the standard English Epictetus, its reception being a decisive argument for female classical learning.
works.meter: A plain and capable prose translation of the Greek homily and diatribe, its sentences kept close to the spoken manner of the school; the prefatory matter is in the essay style of the day.
works.context: Published in 1758 with the encouragement and the practical support of the learned women of her acquaintance, in the season of the revival of Stoic and moral-philosophical interest and of the controversy about the study of Greek by women.
works.characters: Epictetus; his interlocutors and reporters, Arrian and Stobaeus
works.structure: A scholarly translation in several books with a prefatory dissertation and commentarial notes; the order follows the arrangement of the Greek discourses.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the translator's name, the undertaking having been assisted by a borrowed Greek text and by the counsel of friends.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: All's Well That Ends Well
works.description: Shakespeare's 'problem comedy' from Boccaccio: Helena, the physician's daughter, cures the King of France and claims as her reward the reluctant Bertram, who flees to the wars of Italy — forcing Helena to win him by the bed-trick: taking Diana's place in the dark to fulfil his impossible conditions (his ring and his child), and exposing him at the play's end.
works.plot: Helena heals the King, chooses Bertram, is rejected and abandoned; in Florence she substitutes herself for Diana in Bertram's bed and secures ring and child; the final scene unravels Bertram's lies until Helena appears with both proofs and his conversion is wrung from him.
works.significance: The most disquieting of the comedies — a study of merit against rank, and of a woman's will — that has found its audience only in the modern era.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose for the exposure of Parolles; the style is spare and riddling, matching the play's moral knot.
works.context: Dated about 1604–05, in the same phase as Measure for Measure; its tone reflects the Jacobean darkening of Shakespeare's comedy.
works.characters: Helena; Bertram; the Countess of Rousillon; the King of France; Parolles; Lafew; Diana; the Widow; the two French lords (the Dumaine brothers)
works.structure: A fairy-tale plot (the healing of the king, the impossible tasks) crossed with the bed-trick of Renaissance novella, framed by the choric commentaries of the Countess, Lafew, and Parolles.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

works.title: Alliterative Morte Arthure
works.description: The great alliterative tragedy of King Arthur: some 4,300 lines recounting Arthur's continental conquests, his war against the emperor Lucius, and his fall through Mordred's treason and his own pride, culminating in his dream of Fortune's wheel and his death. A poem of imperial ambition and Christian judgement, preserved in the Thornton manuscript, and a principal source of Malory's Morte Darthur.
works.plot: Arthur, refusing tribute to Rome, leads his army across the Channel, defeats the giant of Mont St Michel, and conquers the emperor Lucius; at the height of his power the dream of Fortune's wheel warns him of the fall to come, and the news of Mordred's rebellion and Guinevere's adultery brings him home to the final battle, where Gawain dies and Arthur, mortally wounded, is buried at Glastonbury.
works.significance: The most powerful Arthurian poem of the alliterative tradition and the classic English statement of Arthur's tragedy; its influence on Malory and on the modern Arthurian revival (Tennyson read it in Malory's shadow) is profound.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line at its most heroic, with formulaic battle diction.
works.context: Composed c. 1400 in the north of England, blending chronicle history with romance matter and the tragedy of Fortune; preserved in the Thornton manuscript (Lincoln Cathedral MS 91, c. 1440) and used by Malory in his tale of Arthur and Lucius.
works.characters: Arthur; Gawain; Mordred; Guinevere; Lucius; the giant of Mont St Michel; Fortune
works.structure: A two-movement tragedy of rise and fall, with the dream of Fortune as its pivot and the battles as its set-pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: Memoirs of Modern Philosophers (Broadview Editions)

works.title: Alms-Giving
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A nine-line homiletic poem urging the giving of alms while one still lives, since after death no gift can avail the soul. It is the briefest complete poem in the Exeter Book.
works.plot: The poet exhorts his audience to clothe the naked and feed the hungry now, in life, because the opportunity ends at death, when the soul must face judgment with only what it has given away.
works.significance: A miniature of the Old English homiletic tradition in verse, showing the poets' capacity for lapidary moral statement.
works.meter: Nine alliterative long lines; compressed formulaic phrasing typical of the Exeter gnomic-homiletic manner.
works.context: Almsgiving was a central obligation of Anglo-Saxon Christianity, legislated in the law codes and urged in the homilies of Ælfric and Wulfstan; the poem distils that teaching into a single memorable exhortation.
works.structure: A single compact exhortation built on the antithesis between the living body's power to give and the corpse's helplessness.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
sources: John Keats: The Complete Poems (Penguin Classics)

works.title: Alnwick Castle, with Other Poems
works.form: Romantic meditation and lyric collection; topographical verse with elegy and occasional poem
works.description: The first collected volume of the Knickerbocker poet of the group, containing the title meditation on the English baronial castle and the shorter pieces that had made his reputation in the newspapers. Its lyrics celebrate friendship, the ruins of the old world and the Grecian cause. The volume established the author as the poet of the New York literary group.
works.plot: The long title poem visits the castle on the English border and draws from its state rooms and its ruins a meditation on the transience of feudal power and on the surviving dignity of the mind. The shorter poems include tributes to a dead friend, patriotic pieces and the lyric of the hunter's death, with versified recollections of the American scenery. The volume as a whole argues that a young country may inherit the picturesque through sympathy. Its closing pieces turn from European ruin to native promise.
works.significance: It is the volume by which the Knickerbocker group possessed a poet, and its elegies on early death became a staple of the annuals. Its treatment of the castle ruin brought the European picturesque fully into American verse. It fixed the author's reputation, which stood high through the century and fell afterwards.
works.meter: Chiefly blank verse in the longer poem; iambic stanzas of varying length in the lyrics
works.context: Published at New York in 1827, in the decade when the Knickerbocker group was defining itself against Boston and against British review criticism. The author's friendship with a fellow poet who died young gave the elegies their public currency. Its English subject answers the American claim that only Europe possessed ruins worth poetry.
works.structure: Collected volume organized by length and occasion, with a dominant topographical meditation and a group of occasional and elegiac lyrics.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

editions.title: The Poetical Works of Fitz-Greene Halleck: Now First Collected

works.title: Amelia
works.form: novel; domestic and moral prose fiction in twelve books
works.description: The last and most serious of the comic histories, the story of a virtuous woman tried by her husband's imprudence, by debt and by the pursuit of a corrupt seducer. It abandons the road and the country house for the garrison, the fleet, the alehouse and the gaol, and is the most directly argumentative of the author's fictions.
works.plot: Colonel Booth, an officer of honour and no prudence, marries Amelia against her guardian's will and carries her through the campaigns and stations of his career. His loss of money at the dice, his friendships with the designing, and the machinations of Bellers and of a lewd colonel bring him into arrest and Newgate. Amelia's conduct under every trial - seduction, bankruptcy, prison and the death of her child - converts her husband and exposes the laws and the customs that ruin good men, and the closing papers promise a recompense.
works.significance: It is the eighteenth century's boldest attempt to make the novel an instrument of social reform and to place a good woman's suffering at the centre of its argument, and its cold reception marked the limit of the comic-history form.
works.meter: An earnest, periodic prose with the lawyer's and magistrate's precision in the passages of argument; the dialogue of the lower rooms is reported in a broad colloquial idiom.
works.context: Published in 1751 by the author then a sitting magistrate at Bow Street, in the same season as his enquiry into robbers and the debate over the gin acts and the discipline of the metropolis; its law, finance and gaol detail come from official experience.
works.characters: Colonel Booth; Amelia Booth; William Bellers; Colonel James; Mrs. Patience; the gaolers and officers of Newgate
works.structure: Third-person narration in twelve books with a strong didactic current, framed by a prefatorial address to the fair sex and by an appendix of argument; the plot is a continuous trial rather than an intrigue.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in his correspondence of the last years.

works.title: America a Prophecy
works.form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, a political prophecy that casts the American Revolution as the first act of a spiritual emancipation.
works.description: An illuminated prophecy etched and printed in 1793, written as a vision of the American war of independence seen as an act of spiritual liberation, and addressed in its preface to the inhabitants of a great republic. Its machinery centres on a youth born of a woman's terror on the night when the king's son was slain, who becomes the fire of revolt, and on the watchful angel and the dark power of the deep who would hold the old world in its chains; the poem makes the Atlantic revolution the opening of a new age for the nations of the west.
works.plot: The preface, addressed to the people of the newly founded republic, declares that the moment is come when the oppressor shall fall, and that the blood of the victims cries from the ground. In the vision that follows, the Angel of England, watchful on the rock of the hoary king, is driven from his sleep, and the spectre of the old king calls on the dark spirit of the deep to arm; meanwhile the youth Orc, born in a night of terror when his mother saw the king's son slain by the sinner who was also the avenger, grows up in the wild and is fed by the vultures of the morning, and at sixteen is drawn to the burning fires of revolution. Orc, joined by the female spirit of the west who weeps over him and is bound in chains of the sun's rays, breaks the doors of the dungeon where the hoary black Angel keeps his books, and with him the multitude of the oppressed, driven mad with the expectation of a coming day, pass across the ocean; the poem ends with the fall of the cities of the west and with the voice of the liberated land, the nations of the ocean and the children of the new age crying aloud at the opening of the morning.
works.significance: The boldest of the poet's revolutionary prophecies and the standard instance of his identification of political insurrection with imaginative liberation; its figure of the youth Orc, born in terror and bred in rebellion, became the central recurring personage of his later myth. It is a permanent document of the literature of the Atlantic revolutions and of the claim that a new nation might be the subject of a new prophecy.
works.meter: Blank verse of a rapid and reiterating kind, with long breathless periods, apostrophe and the short shouted lines of the closing chorus; the preface is in prose of an oracle-like brevity.
works.context: Etched and published in London in 1793, in the year of the war with France, of the trial of the author's fellow-citizen for his Corresponding Society, and of the height of the English debate about the American and French revolutions; the poem's dedication to the inhabitants of a great republic and its figure of the oppressor's fall belong to that moment of revolutionary hope.
works.characters: Orc, the youth who is the spirit of revolt; his mother, the terrified woman of the vision; the Angel of England, hoary and watching on the rock; the dark power of the deep; the female spirit of the west, bound in chains; the multitude of the oppressed and the inhabitants of the new republic
works.structure: A prophecy in two parts, a prose preface and a blank-verse vision, organised as the birth and the action of a spirit of revolt, with the machinery of angels, kings' spirits and chained female powers; the argument moves from the watchful angel over the rock to the breaking of the dungeon and the passage of the oppressed to the new world.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: American Writers
altTitles: American Writers: A Series of Papers
works.form: Critical review and periodical essay; the first history of American literature in serial form
works.description: A series of critical papers surveying the literature of the United States for a Scottish monthly, and the earliest attempt to write the whole of American writing as a single history. It reviews the colonial poets, the pre-war dramatists, the novelists and the critics with an energy that is as often abusive as judicious. Its polemic against cultural dependence is the most concentrated statement of American literary nationalism of the 1820s.
works.plot: The papers take up the writers of the colonies and of the early republic in turn, from the Puritan sermons and the verse of the eighteenth century to the native novelists and critics then living. Each account is used to argue that American letters have been misjudged by British condescension and underserved by American caution. The series demands a literature of national character, produced by native conditions and judged by native standards. Its closing papers turn the argument against the timidity of the American writer himself.
works.significance: It is the founding document of American literary history and of the claim that a national literature exists as a subject for criticism. Its quarrel with Edinburgh and London defines the terms of transatlantic cultural dependence for a generation. It established the review essay as an instrument of literary nationalism.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Contributed to Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine from December 1824 into 1825, at the centre of the transatlantic quarrel over American books conducted in British monthlies. Its author was then the American correspondent of the Scottish magazine and a pioneer of the professional review-writer. The series was written between his novels and helped to make the phrase American literature current.
works.structure: Serial critical survey in a succession of magazine numbers, organized by author and period rather than by theme, with a running polemical argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution established from the author's own later claims and from the magazine's records; the series was published in the periodical's customary manner.

works.title: Amis and Amiloun
works.description: A romance of sworn brotherhood and sacrifice, adapted from the widespread European legend of the two friends: Amis and Amiloun, identical in appearance, exchange places in trial by combat and marriage, and Amis slays his own children to cure his friend's leprosy — before a miraculous restoration rewards their loyalty. One of the most powerful of the Auchinleck romances.
works.plot: The sworn brothers part; Amiloun takes Amis's place in a judicial combat over a false accusation, and later, when Amiloun is struck with leprosy for the deception, Amis learns in a vision that his children's blood will cure him — and the sacrifice, made in secret, is rewarded by the children's resurrection.
works.significance: The classic English treatment of the friendship-and-sacrifice legend, and a favourite test case for the romance's religious and ethical codes.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the Auchinleck manner.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from an Anglo-Norman source (Ami et Amile), in the East Midlands; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and three later copies.
works.characters: Amis; Amiloun; Belisaunt; the steward (villain); Amiloun's wife
works.structure: A double-plot of symmetrical substitution (combat; wedding-night; sacrifice), resolved by miracle and final reunion.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Principles of Political Economy: With a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science (Cambridge Library Collection)

works.title: Amoretti and Epithalamion
works.description: Spenser's sonnet sequence of eighty-nine sonnets tracing his courtship of Elizabeth Boyle, followed by the great marriage ode Epithalamion, which celebrates their wedding on 11 June 1594 through the hours of the wedding day.
works.plot: The Amoretti move from the lover's unrequited suit and the lady's proud refusals through reconciliation to the secure mutual love of the final sonnets, which lead directly into the wedding song; the Epithalamion summons the muses, the hours, and the guests, and blesses bride and bridegroom through the day and night of the feast.
works.significance: One of the greatest sonnet sequences in the language and, in the Epithalamion, the supreme English wedding poem.
works.meter: The Spenserian sonnet form (abab bcbc cdcd ee) throughout, followed by the long-lined stanzas and refrain of the Epithalamion.
works.context: Written during Spenser's courtship of his second wife Elizabeth Boyle at Kilcolman, Ireland, and printed together in 1595, the year after the marriage.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Elizabeth Boyle (the beloved); the assembled wedding guests
works.structure: A Petrarchan sequence with a calendrical design (the sonnets allude to Lent and Easter of 1594) climaxing in the 24-stanza Epithalamion, which is built on the canonical hours and the refrain of the echoing woods.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: An Account of the Growth of Popery and Arbitrary Government in England
altTitles: An Account of the Growth of Popery
works.description: Marvell's anonymous political tract (late 1677/early 1678) warning that a design was afoot to establish both popery and arbitrary monarchy in England by dissolving Parliament and using a standing army; a foundational text of Whig resistance theory on the eve of the Exclusion Crisis.
works.plot: Marvell argues that the prorogation of Parliament and the court's policies reveal a plan to subvert English liberties, religion, and law, and that the people must resist arbitrary power.
works.significance: An important document of Restoration political radicalism and Whig ideology, attributed to Marvell and central to understanding his later politics.
works.meter: Vigorous, urgent argumentative prose of political polemic.
works.context: Published just before the Popish Plot (1678) and during the Exclusion Crisis, it expressed the emerging Whig critique of the court of Charles II and the Catholic succession.
works.structure: A political pamphlet of sustained argument and warning, published anonymously.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; attribution to Marvell is long-established and accepted.

works.title: An American Dictionary of the English Language
works.form: Lexicography and philological writing; the national standard dictionary
works.description: The two-volume dictionary that completed the author's life work and gave American English its standard of authority. It carries a much enlarged vocabulary, definitions built from actual usage, and a preface arguing that a language grows from the people who speak it. Its spellings, its encyclopaedic entries and its moral and religious illustrations define the American reference book.
works.plot: The volumes alphabetically define the whole range of ordinary, technical and scriptural words then in use in the United States, with parts of speech, etymologies and examples of application. The prefatory dissertation argues for the maturity and independence of the American language and for the authority of national usage. The appended plates and tables treat weights, measures, coins and the divisions of learning. The dictionary's entries on American institutions and words register the new republic's vocabulary as evidence.
works.significance: It is the foundation of American lexicography and the source of the orthographical system that American spelling still follows. Its preface is the most influential statement of the doctrine of a national language. It fixed the dictionary as an instrument of public instruction in the United States.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1828 after more than two decades of preparation and a tour of Europe for the study of the kindred languages, and in the year of the republic's second half-century of independence. Its claims for American linguistic independence belong to the nationalist program of the 1820s. Its scriptural and moral illustrations reflect its author's religious and political conservatism.
works.structure: Two-volume alphabetical dictionary with prefatory dissertations on the origin, development and national character of the English language, and with appendix tables.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the work is lexicographical and its authority rests on its editor's long labour rather than on collective authorship.

editions.title: An American Dictionary of the English Language (2 volumes)
A Common Heritage: Noah Webster's Blue-Back Speller

works.title: An Analysis of the Laws of England
altTitles: Analysis of the Laws of England
works.description: Blackstone's elementary chart of the law, first printed in 1756 from his Oxford lectures and designed as a skeleton of heads and subdivisions by which a student might master the whole compass of the science. It distils the architecture that the Commentaries would later fill with narrative.
works.plot: The Analysis divides the law into rights of persons and rights of things, private wrongs and public wrongs, and under each head lists the subordinate institutions in their logical order. Blackstone prefixes short historical remarks on the laws of the English before and after the conquest, and adds analytical tables that let the student see the law at a glance. The text assumes a reader of general cultivation, compressing doctrine into definitions and distinctions. Later editions, revised with the assistance of others, expanded the commentary around the skeleton.
works.significance: It became the standard mnemonic frame for legal study in England and America for decades, and a monument of the eighteenth century's faith that knowledge could be ordered in tables.
works.meter: Bare, condensed enumerative prose, maximally compressed definitions with minimal connectative tissue.
works.context: Produced from the lectures Blackstone read as Vinerian student and tutor at Oxford, published in 1756 as a teaching aid and repeatedly reprinted with enlargements, it anticipates the architecture of the Commentaries and the century's mania for analyses and tables.
works.structure: A tabular analysis: prefixed historical sketch, then four divisions resolved into numbered heads, with synoptical tables.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue
altTitles: An Answere unto Sir Thomas Mores Dialoge
works.description: Tyndale's reply to More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies, published in 1531; the central exchange of the great English print war between the two men.
works.plot: The book answers More point by point: Tyndale defends his translation of the New Testament against More's charges of corruption, argues that the church is the congregation of believers known by scripture, not the pope's institution, denies that he teaches rebellion, and attacks More's church of ceremonies with the full battery of scriptural citation, closing with a devastating personal address to 'Master More'.
works.significance: One half of the greatest controversy in early English prose: the Tyndale–More exchange fixed the rhetorical terms of the Reformation debate, and the Answer remains the fullest statement of Tyndale's ecclesiology and translation theory.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1531 as the direct reply to More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies (1529); More answered with the Confutation of Tyndale's Answer (1532–33), completing the most sustained intellectual duel of the English Reformation, conducted from exile and the chancellorship respectively.
works.structure: A point-by-point refutation following the order of More's Dialogue, in Tyndale's plain and urgent prose; the first major English controversy conducted wholly in print.

works.title: An Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs
altTitles: Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs
works.form: political pamphlet and party argument; polemic in the form of an appeal to authorities
works.description: A party pamphlet written as the author's Whig colleagues adopted the French Revolution as a principle, and addressed to the older Whig tradition of the Revolution of 1688 as he understood it. Its quarrel is less with France than with the leaders at home, and its method is quotation: it accumulates the language of the party's own classics to show that the new doctrines of popular sovereignty contradict the settled faith of the old.
works.plot: The Appeal insists that the Revolution of 1688 was made to preserve the ancient law of the kingdom, not to create a right in any generation to model its government anew, and that the declaratory parts of the settlement bound Posterity as well as the present age. Against the position that the people at any moment may alter everything that offends them, it cites the party's own writers and the great common-law authorities, and it argues that an unlimited right of innovation is in fact a denial of all settled constitution. The book then examines the character of the new Whiggism, which it takes to have substituted metaphysical speculation for historical prescription, and it pleads that a party which abandons its own recorded principles forfeits its title to the name. Its closing judgement is that the true Old Whig is the man who holds the constitution as an inheritance to be transmitted unchanged.
works.significance: It is the classic statement of prescriptive, party-based constitutionalism, and one of the earliest analyses of how a political language changes when a party adopts philosophy in place of history. Its method of appealing to an older canon of authorities became a permanent move in British conservative argument, and its account of the Revolution of 1688 was quoted for a century by both sides of the debate.
works.meter: Forensic, cumulative prose, heavy with quotation and with the mannered courtesy of parliamentary invective; its characteristic movement is the citation followed by the dry comment.
works.context: It followed the summer of 1791, when the leading figure of the parliamentary Whigs openly approved the French Revolution and when a meeting of the party's friends declared for the rights of men, driving the older, more constitutional Whigs into a separate allegiance. It arrived between the Reflections and the vindication of the rights of man, and it was read as the pamphlet that completed the rupture of the Whig interest.
works.structure: A continuous argument in long paragraphs, organized as an induction of witnesses: authorities and declared party opinions are quoted in sequence, then applied to the modern profession of faith.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested as to the authorship of the argument; the manuscript was revised and corrected by a colleague in the Whig opposition whose share the author himself acknowledged in correspondence, a fact long recorded in the standard editions.

works.title: An Argument against Abolishing Christianity
altTitles: An Argument to Prove that the Abolishing of Christianity in England May Answer as Effectual to the Intended Ends as an Act of Indemnity
works.description: Swift's ironised pamphlet, spoken by a profession-deist who argues that Christianity should be quietly abolished because it is the source of all the nation's divisions, debt and enthusiasm, and that the nominal believers have nothing to lose.
works.plot: The speaker enumerates the factions of the nominal Christians, the Whig deists, the fanatics and the heathen projectors, and urges that the name of Christ be removed from the currency, the liturgy and the oaths; the satire turns on the fact that the abolition he describes is already what the age's irreligion wants.
works.significance: It is the sharpest short example of Swift's method of arguing in the voice of the enemy, and its diagnosis of a Christianity reduced to a party name made it a permanent scandal in the debate on toleration and irreligion.
works.meter: The dry prose of the parliamentary argument, with the accumulating catalogue and the flat declarative close.
works.context: Written at the height of the deist and blasphemy controversies that followed the Toleration, and long held to have been intended for The Examiner; it was first printed in 1711 in the miscellaneous volumes that gathered Swift's tracts.
works.characters: the profession-deist speaker; the nominal Christians; the heathen and deist projectors
works.structure: A single continuous ironical argument, in the order of a speech or pamphlet, with enumerated categories of opponents and a closing peroration of apparent advice.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Swift's, though it was published anonymously and its first printing was not authorised under his name.

works.title: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
works.description: Hume's reconstruction of the first part of the Treatise as a polished Enquiry, recast when it appeared as Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding and retitled in 1750. It is the classic statement of the problem of induction, the analysis of causation, and the sceptical discussions of miracles and of the arguments for providence.
works.plot: Hume divides all objects of the mind into impressions and ideas, fixes the copy principle, and finds in custom the answer to how experience reaches beyond what is immediately present: our reasonings concerning matters of fact are founded not on demonstration but on habit. Causation is then analysed as constant conjunction with a felt determination of the mind, and necessary connection is projected onto nature. The sections on liberty and necessity reconcile the will with determinism by redefining freedom as a power of acting according to the will's determination, and the celebrated section on miracles argues that no testimony can amount to proof of a miracle unless its falshood would be more miraculous than the fact, while the discussion of design demurs that an order in nature argues only to an artisan's artifice, not to a benevolent Providence. The book ends by committing the school metaphysics to the flames.
works.significance: It is the most influential text in the empiricist tradition, source of the induction and causation problems in their standard modern form, and the founding document of the philosophical discussion of miracle testimony and natural theology.
works.meter: Supple, lucid, often epigrammatic prose of deliberate literary polish, with famous rhetorical closers on the metaphysicians and on miracle testimony.
works.context: Published at London in 1748 in the wake of Butler's Analogy and the Woolston controversy over miracles and evidence, after Hume's failed candidacy for the Edinburgh chair; it recast his earlier metaphysics for the general reader.
works.structure: Twelve successive enquiries, each isolating and enlarging one chapter of the Treatise's argument, the later sections turning to liberty, miracles, and natural religion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice
works.form: philosophical treatise of politics and morals; systematic enquiry in essays
works.description: The most ambitious attempt of the revolutionary decade to found a system of politics, morals, and the human mind upon the single principle of private judgement. Written in three volumes by a dissenting minister who had abandoned his pulpit, it argues that government is an evil, that institutions corrupt the understanding, and that a rational society could dispense with punishment, property, and marriage. It fixed the creed of the radical philosophical circle and drew upon its author a lifetime of controversy.
works.plot: The enquiry opens from the perfectibility of man: a rational creature, governed by opinion, is capable of indefinite improvement, and the mischief of the world proceeds from institutions that fix and pervert his judgement. Government it treats as a necessary evil at best, a force that substitutes the decision of one for the decision of the many and that rests on the very error it is meant to correct; it should therefore be reduced to the smallest possible extent, and its functions of punishment and of legislation dissolved into the verdict of unprejudiced understanding. On property the first edition argues that each has a claim upon the surplus of another's stock when his own wants are greater, that accumulation is the child of law and of opinion, and that a rational distribution would follow the general good. Marriage and the obligations of promise are examined as contracts which an independent judgement cannot be bound to keep; and the same argument is applied to oaths, to colonies, to wealth, to the theatre, to literature, and to population, each of which is shown to be a corruption of a simple moral truth. The closing books defend truth-telling as a duty absolute enough to outweigh the claim of a murderer, and treat political reform as a question of opinion, to be advanced by discussion and not by violence.
works.significance: It is the founding text of philosophical anarchism and one of the two or three works that shaped the radical romantic imagination of the 1790s, converting the doctrine of private judgement into a complete social criticism. Its influence on the poets of the following generation, on the communitarian and freethought movements, and on the later debate over justice, property, and punishment, is one of the main lines of intellectual history of the period.
works.meter: Austere, impersonal, relentlessly syllogistic prose: short paragraphs of premise and conclusion, the abstract noun as the subject of almost every sentence, and an absence of ornament that became itself a style.
works.context: Published in the same months as the counter-revolutionary constitutional writings were provoking the vindication of the rights of man, and composed by a minister of the new philosophy of necessity who had already written a treatise on the same system of morals. It circulated as the creed-book of the radical societies and of the philosophical circle, and it provoked the most famous of all its replies, an essay on population written to disprove the perfectibility it assumed.
works.structure: Three volumes of essays in strict sequence: the principles of political morality and of the mind, the actual institutions of civil society criticized one by one, and the practical conduct of reform; each chapter a self-contained argument with a numbered heading.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the text is not, however, a single stable work, since the author recast and retracted much in the second edition, and the editions differ enough that any claim about his doctrine of property and of promise must specify its year.

works.title: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals
altTitles: Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals
works.description: Hume's recasting of Treatise Book III, the mature sentimentalist ethics, and in his own judgment incomparably the best of his writings. It argues that moral distinctions arise from a sentiment of approbation attentive to utility and agreeableness, and re-reads the catalogue of the virtues as a catalogue of their value to life.
works.plot: Hume first shows that our moral sentiments respond to characters as a whole and not to single acts, and that utility, public or private, is a principal source of the esteem we pay to benevolence, justice, fidelity, and honour. He confutes the rationalist and egoist systems by exhibiting the calm general sentiment, the moral taste, which makes virtue lovely and vice odious independently of self-interest, and explains the artificial virtues of justice and allegiance by the evident usefulness of their general systems. A celebrated appendix attacks the monkish virtues of self-denial and humility as enervating and useless to society, and the closing section asks whether morality be founded on reason or sentiment, answering in favour of sentiment. The whole is written as a cheerful vindication of virtue as the charm and benefit of life.
works.significance: It is the classic document of sentimentalist ethics and one of the sources of utilitarian moral theory, decisive for Adam Smith, the classical utilitarians, and the later virtue tradition.
works.meter: Hume's most generous and polished prose, ironic and rhetorically enriched, with sententious closes and an extended set-piece against the monkish virtues.
works.context: Published in 1751 against the Glasgow debates with the rationalist moral school and the critical neglect of the Treatise; its appendix on the monkish virtues made its anti-austerian temper unmistakable to every reader.
works.structure: Nine sections progressing from the origin of moral distinction through utility, benevolence, and justice to the reason-versus-sentiment dispute, with three appended sections.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Enquiry into the Causes of the Late Increase of Robbers
altTitles: An Enquiry into the Causes of the Late Increase of Robbers, and Other Disorders of the Present Times
An Enquiry into the Late Increase of Robbers
works.form: public enquiry and policy pamphlet in prose
works.description: A magistrate's enquiry into the disorder of the metropolis, occasioned by the observations made in a late riot trial and arguing that the increase of robbers follows from the diffusion of gin, the decay of the moral restraint of the poor and the failure of the laws. It is the most influential of the criminal-enquiry pamphlets of the mid-century.
works.plot: The writer examines the causes of the late growth of street robbery and riot, laying the first weight on the spirit trade and the gin houses, then on the dissolution of family and apprenticeship discipline, the idleness of Journeymen, and the corruption of the constables and the watch. He compares the severity and the execution of the existing laws, and argues that the theater and the price of admission spread the same loose principles. His remedies are regulation of the spirits, better police, and the restraint of the common plays.
works.significance: It is a primary document of the century's urban policing and social investigation, and it supplies the professional basis of the novelist's later fictions of the metropolis; its analysis of pleasure, drink and disorder shaped reform argument for a generation.
works.meter: Clear magistrate's prose of instance and enumeration, with the periodic sentence of the argumentative close and frequent appeal to reported fact.
works.context: Written from the Bow Street office in the spring of 1751 during the debates on the Gin Act and after the Covent Garden riot over the price of seats at Drury Lane, an event the pamphlet treats directly.
works.structure: A single continuous argument in numbered sections, each cause being stated, illustrated from the office books and answered against objection; the pamphlet closes with proposals rather than a conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name as a sitting magistrate and reprinted in his collected tracts.

works.title: An Enquiry into the Present State of Polite Learning in Europe
altTitles: Enquiry into the Present State of Polite Learning
works.form: Critical and social dissertation in prose, in numbered sections, in the manner of the comparative enquiry; issued by subscription with printed proposals.
works.description: Oliver Goldsmith's first important prose work, and one of the most quoted books of the age about the condition of letters: an enquiry into the state of polite learning in the nations of Europe, written by a man about to try his fortune in London. It is at once a comparative survey of national cultures, a history of the progress of the arts, and a bitter account of the decay of patronage and of the degraded condition of the modern writer.
works.plot: The enquiry proceeds from the general to the national and from the historical to the immediately contemporary. Goldsmith argues that the polite arts have in general advanced, that ignorance and superstition have been expelled by the spread of learning, and that the modern nations of Europe, France, Italy, Spain, Germany, Poland and the northern kingdoms, each display their own mixture of cultivation and remaining barbarism. Turning to England, he complains that while every other branch of knowledge has improved, literature alone has declined, and he assigns the decline to identifiable causes: the withdrawal of noble and royal patronage, the pride and avarice of the great who would direct as well as reward, the multiplication of critics and reviewers, the corruption of the theatre, and the deplorable economics of the book trade, which leaves the man of letters dependent upon his humour and his creditors. The book's most durable passages are those in which the writer's poverty, his patience and his independence are analysed as a social condition rather than as private misfortune.
works.significance: It supplied the classic eighteenth-century statement of the decay of patronage and of the miseries of the professional author, and its survey of European politeness is an early specimen of comparative cultural history written for a general reader. Its complaints are the background to everything Goldsmith later wrote, and its diagnosis was soon taken up by Johnson and by the moralists of the literary marketplace.
works.context: It was published in the year before Goldsmith's periodical papers began, as the book trade was expanding, the subscription and the magazine were replacing the patron, and the argument about politeness, commerce and national taste carried on by Shaftesbury, the reviewers and the Scottish societies was becoming an argument about the material fate of authors. Its tone reflects the impoverishment of a recently arrived Irish graduate in Grub Street.
works.characters: The enquiring author-voice; the critics and reviewers; the cold and self-interested patron; the needy writer of the new age
works.structure: A sustained argumentative enquiry in twenty sections, proceeding historically and comparatively, with each nation and each branch of the polite arts taken in turn and with the English case reserved for the closing and most personal complaints.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work was published with Goldsmith's name and its authorship was never in doubt. The precise dates of composition are not fixed and are left null.

works.title: An Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot
works.description: Pope's apologia pro vita sua in couplets, addressed to his friend the physician John Arbuthnot: an account of the poet's peacable retirement, his parents, his enemies' persecution and the proper use of satire.
works.plot: The epistle answers the pestering of the importunate poetaster, defends the poet's education and his independence, then reviews the masks of his attackers and ends by committing his cause to the candid reader and to his friend's judgment.
works.significance: It is the century's most complete statement of the professional writer's defence of himself, and its personae, Atticus and Sappho above all, became the standard masks for the criticism of literary celebrity.
works.meter: Heroic couplet of extraordinary conversational energy, with the interrupted address, the quoted opponent and the closing lapidary pair.
works.context: Written in the season of the Horace imitations and of the quarrels over the Dunciad's enemies, when Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's verse attacks and the reviews of the poet's Homer had made personal satire a public business.
works.characters: Dr Arbuthnot; the poet; Atticus; Sappho; Bavius; Mola; the importunate poetaster
works.structure: A single verse epistle of argument and gallery, opening with the visitation scene, passing through the catalogue of offended persons, and closing on the valedictory portrait of the retired poet.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the identification of Atticus with Addison and of Sappho with Lady Mary Wortley Montagu is long established, though a few minor masks remain debated.
