works.title: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding
works.description: Locke's founding work of modern empiricism, an enquiry into the origin, certainty, and extent of human knowledge, which rejects innate ideas and argues that all thought derives from sensation and reflection.
works.plot: Book I refutes innate ideas; book II sets out the theory of simple and complex ideas derived from sensation and reflection; book III treats the philosophy of language and the abuse of words; book IV defines knowledge and probability and examines the grounds of belief.
works.significance: The founding text of British empiricism and of the Enlightenment theory of mind; it shaped Berkeley, Hume, and Kant, and its influence on eighteenth-century literature, psychology, and educational theory was pervasive.
works.meter: A clear, deliberate, sometimes conversational prose; Locke's plain style was consciously opposed to scholastic Latinism.
works.context: Begun in 1671 in discussion with friends including James Tyrrell, completed during Locke's exile in Holland, and published in December 1689 (dated 1690) after the Revolution.
works.structure: Four books in a systematic argument of 71 chapters.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Locke; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: An Essay Concerning the Art of Political Lying
works.form: Satirical essay and character in the mock-didactic manner
works.description: A short satirical essay in the person of a professor of political lying who reduces mendacity in public affairs to a methodical art with rules, divisions and praise of its practitioners. Dr John Arbuthnot writes in dead-pan mock panegyric, treating falsehood as the great instrument of party, credit and war finance, and the reader supplies the indictment. It is the most perfectly sustained single joke of Scribleran prose and a lasting analysis of how political language works.
works.plot: The narrator first compliments his age on the perfection to which the art of lying has been brought, then divides political lying into species, including the proof-lie, the lie of the first and second figure, the offence-defensive lie, and the equivoque, each illustrated by public practice. He next argues that the art is essential to party management, to the support of public funds and to the conduct of a war that must be concealed from the people who pay for it. He claims the greatest masters of the art for his own party's opponents while complimenting all sides, and ends with the modest proposal that a college or society should be founded for the better cultivation of the science.
works.significance: It gave the Augustan vocabulary a durable name for organised public untruth and remains the standard early analysis of political spin. Its method, a taxonomy built wholly out of irony, became a model for later satirists from Cobbett to the twentieth-century mock manual, and it is the clearest non-Popean expression of the Scribleran war against dullness and imposture.
works.meter: Prose only, in a level, ironical, precept-giving Augustan plain style
works.context: Published in the last months of the Harley ministry's attack on the Whig moneyed interest, amid the Examiner and Scriblerus campaign against party falsehood, stock-jobbing and the news-peddling of the addresses. It presupposes the 1711-12 debates over the public funds and the conduct of the war.
works.structure: Continuous mock-institutional essay, organised as panegyric, taxonomy of the species, application to current practice, and closing project.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Arbuthnot in the Scriblerus collections and accepted by modern scholarship; it was sometimes placed among Swift's pieces in early collected editions, which accounts for the older doubt.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: An Essay Concerning the Use of Reason
altTitles: A Discourse of the Use of Reason in Learning and Religion
works.description: Anthony Collins's early rationalist treatise arguing that reason is the adequate judge of all revelation and that nothing can be believed on authority that is contrary to or beyond clear perception. It generalizes the scriptural rule of trial by reason into a standard by which every pretended revelation must stand or fall.
works.plot: The Essay first settles what a proposition must be before it can be assented to, insisting that ideas must be clear and their agreement or disagreement perceived. Applying this to revelation, Collins argues that we can know a revelation to be divine only by the same rational evidence by which we know anything, so that what seems contrary to knowledge must be rejected, whatever its pretences. Mystery pleaded as super-rational assent is shown to collapse into either plain nonsense or a concealed contradiction. He then answers the argument from the shortness of reason's sight and from the necessity of a divine commission, and concludes that faith is rational assent, not a surrender of judgment.
works.significance: It is the boldest pre-deist statement of the ratio principle, the text that made freethinking a named intellectual cause and set the agenda to which Butler and the evidentialists answered.
works.meter: Dry, closely reasoned lockean prose with numbered definitions and repeated test questions driving the advance.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1707, it provoked Samuel Clarke's Defence of the Natural Instability of Humane Reason (1707) and Collins's own Reply (1708), and supplied the terms on which the Christian evidence controversy continued into the 1720s.
works.structure: A systematic essay in numbered chapters: theory of proportion and assent, application to revelation, confutation of mystery and of the standard replies, and a closing vindication of rational faith.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; authorship established by Clarke's reply naming Collins and by contemporary attribution.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: An Essay of Dramatic Poesy
works.description: Dryden's foundational work of English dramatic criticism, a dialogue among four friends on a barge during the Second Dutch War in which the merits of the ancients and moderns, and of the French and English stages, are debated.
works.plot: Crites defends the ancients; Eugenius defends the moderns; Lisideius argues for French regularity; Neander (Dryden's spokesman) defends the English drama's variety and life, arguing that rhyme may be natural to serious plays.
works.significance: The first major work of English literary criticism and the text that established Dryden as the father of English criticism; its comparative method and generous assessment of Shakespeare were decisive for the later canon.
works.meter: Elegant argumentative prose, one of the earliest examples of a distinctively modern English critical prose style.
works.context: Composed during 1666-8 and dedicated to Charles Howard, Earl of Dorset; it responds to the neoclassical controversy ignited by Corneille and the Académie française.
works.characters: Crites; Eugenius; Lisideius; Neander
works.structure: A four-part dialogue with an opening narrative frame.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; the speaker Neander is Dryden's anagrammatic self-portrait.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: An Essay on Criticism
works.description: Pope's verse treatise on the rules of taste: it argues that criticism is a polite and necessary art learned from nature and from the ancients, catalogs the vices of partial, arrogant and pedantic judging, and ends by demanding that the critic's manners answer the critic's learning.
works.plot: The first movement derives the laws of judging from the practice of nature and of the classical writers; the second catalogs the causes of false taste, pride, partiality and the worship of parts; the third passes from the ancients to the moderns, to the French rules, and to the moral duty of candid, instructive criticism.
works.significance: It became the century's handbook of critical common sense, supplied the durable phrases by which English criticism discussed wit, nature and the rules, and fixed the couplet as the vehicle of serious argument.
works.meter: Closed heroic couplets of exceptional regularity, with the balanced antithetical line, run-on enjambed passages for difficulty, and deliberate sound-imitation of the sense being described.
works.context: Published in the year between Windsor-Forest and the Rape of the Lock, when Rymer's and Dennis's dramatic controversy, Temple's ancient-modern essay and Addison's periodical criticism had made the rules of art a popular subject; the essay consolidates the Shaftesburian and neoclassical language of taste.
works.characters: the poet-critic; the false critic; the ancients as a court of appeal
works.structure: A continuous argument in numbered parts, each built as a succession of linked sententiae and examples rather than as narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Poems of Alexander Pope, Twickenham Edition (11 volumes)

works.title: An Essay on Man
altTitles: An Essay on Man in Four Epistles
Of the Nature and State of Man with Respect to the Universe
works.description: Pope's philosophical theodicy in four epistles, arguing that man's proper study is himself and his station in a graded creation, that what appears as evil in the part is good in the whole, and that self-love and social love are the same principle rightly directed.
works.plot: Epistle I measures human knowledge against the immensity of the system and condemns presumption; II examines man's state as the middle creature of the chain of being; III argues that providence orders the passions to good ends; IV closes with the identity of interest and virtue and the sufficiency of happiness to the present life.
works.significance: It was the most read English philosophical poem of the century, translating the Leibnizian and Shaftesburian theodicy into a schoolbook style, and drawing a century of attack from Kantian and romantic critics who thought its optimism a sophistry.
works.meter: Heroic couplet at its most gnomic and compressed, with the balanced pair, the interrogative sententia and the abrupt closing maxim.
works.context: Written largely within the circle of St John, Viscount Bolingbroke, whose philosophy of nature it popularised, and published in the year of the deist and moral-philosophy controversies which drew the replies of Butler and of the clergy; its claim that whatever is, is right became a byword for optimism and its target for the satire of the following generation.
works.characters: the poet-arguer; the friend addressed; the deist and the sceptic as imagined opponents
works.structure: Four numbered epistles in verse, each an continuous argument of proposition, instance and correction rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though its dependence on Bolingbroke's prose philosophy has made its originality a long-standing question.

works.title: An Essay on the History of Civil Society
altTitles: Essay on the History of Civil Society
works.description: Ferguson's philosophical history of society, the founding text of the Scottish stage theory of social development, tracing mankind from the hunter and shepherd through tillage, commerce, and polished policy. It warns that the very arts and refinements which advance civil society may enervate the citizens and endanger liberty, and it argued for a science of man attentive to unintended consequences.
works.plot: Ferguson begins from human nature as active, ingenuous, and perfectible, a species whose history is the slow education of the race. He then traces the stages of society, the hunter's tent, the shepherd's camp, the tiller's village, and the commerce that peoples cities with arts, ranks, and laws, showing each institution to be the result of human action but not of a design to found it. Polished society brings the division of labour, the machinery of state, credit, and standing armies, and with them the danger that a people of traders will surrender public freedom to private ease. The essay closes on the contingency of history, the possibility of corruption even in republics, and a Stoic counsel that the species, like the individual, must earn its character through exertion.
works.significance: It created the science of society's vocabulary of stages, unintended consequences, and civic humanism in a commercial age, standing between the civic republicanism of the ancients and the sociology of the nineteenth century.
works.meter: Nervous, energetic, sententious prose full of rhetorical questions and republican apostrophes, alternating cool analysis with moral alarm.
works.context: Composed after Ferguson succeeded Adam Smith in the Edinburgh chair of moral philosophy, the fruit of the lecture theatre and the Select Society circle, and published in 1767; it was translated into German and French within a decade.
works.structure: A continuous essay moving from the philosophy of human nature through the successive stages of society to the moral and political diagnosis of polished commercial life.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Essay on the Learning and Genius of Shakespeare
works.form: critical essay and dissertation on a poet
works.description: A critical essay defending Shakespeare's learning and his genius against the neoclassical objections of the previous age, and arguing that his excellences are those of an observing moralist rather than of a regular artist. It was the most influential piece of Shakespearean criticism by an eighteenth-century woman and went through several issues in its first year.
works.plot: The essay reviews the charge of ignorance and of barbarous taste, and answers it by showing the reach of Shakespeare's knowledge of nature and of mankind. It defends his violation of the rules by the higher rule of probability and of instruction, and sets his moral seriousness against the formal regularity of the French and classical models. The conclusion places him among the great teachers of life, whose faults are those of an age and whose beauties are of all ages.
works.significance: It gave the apologetic tradition of Shakespeare its most composed statement by a woman critic and helped to fix the moral, rather than formal, justification of his supremacy in later taste.
works.meter: A firm and well-tempered critical prose of the mid-century essay, with the balanced refutation and the quoted line of proof; the sentences are periodic and the argument explicit.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1769, in the season of the revived Shakespeare editions and of the debate about his regularity kindled by the previous generation's critics, and within the society of the Bluestockings, whose conversations had prepared the argument.
works.structure: A continuous argumentative essay in sections, the objections stated and answered, with the illustrations drawn from the plays and with the comparative examples of the ancients and of Milton.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is established rather than asserted on the title-page: the essay was published anonymously in 1769 and has been assigned to the writer on the grounds of her own papers, her circle's testimony and the later acknowledgement; authorship is therefore recorded as single with this explanation.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: An Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, with Illustrations on the Moral Sense
altTitles: Essay on the Passions and Affections, with Illustrations on the Moral Sense
works.description: Hutcheson's anatomy of the affections, mapping calm and violent passions, theocentric and sympathetic affections, and the pleasures they bring, and appending the Illustrations on the Moral Sense against Clarke, Wollaston, and Mandeville. It is the sentimentalist psychology that underwrote his ethics.
works.plot: The Essay classifies the affections into calm and violent, self-, other-, and God-directed, and shows that our happiness depends on the temper of the heart rather than its outward objects. Benevolence yields the sweetest, most steady enjoyments; malice, envy, and excessive self-love torment themselves, while the approbation of the moral sense attends every generous affection. The Illustrations then attack the rationalist moralists for mistaking cool self-interest for virtue and for making utility the measure of moral good, showing by examples that we approve disinterested benevolence immediately and independently of interest. The instruction of the passions by habit and the place of the moral sense in education conclude the argument.
works.significance: Its psychology of the passions became the standard sentimentalist textbook, training Hume, Adam Smith, and the preachers in the moral cultivation of the affections and the priority of benevolence.
works.meter: Warm, exemplum-rich prose of the preacher-philosopher, long in sympathetic description and sharp in polemic rejoinder.
works.context: Published in 1728 after the Inquiry and amid Hutcheson's Glasgow disputes with the rationalist school; the Illustrations take up the cause of Shaftesbury's sentimentalism against the moral philosophy of the English rationalists and of Mandeville.
works.structure: Two paired parts: a systematic essay on the affections and a group of Illustrations conducted as critical essays against named opponents.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population
altTitles: Essay on the Principle of Population
works.form: treatise of political economy and social theory; statistical essay with polemic
works.description: The tract that refused the perfectibility of the species a place in the rational political future, published anonymously and written to answer the philosophy of indefinite improvement then current among the radical writers of the day. Its principle is arithmetical and pitiless: population, if unchecked, doubles in a generation, while food cannot be made to increase beyond a far slower rate, and the surplus must therefore be taken off by vice, by misery, or by restraint. It is the founding document of population science and of the political economy of the poor.
works.plot: The essay lays down two postulates in the constitution of man, the passion between the sexes and the need of food, and a third proportion, that population in a country without checks goes on doubling every five-and-twenty years while the produce of even improved agriculture advances only in an arithmetical series. From these it deduces that the race of man cannot be improved away from suffering, since every improvement of subsistence is consumed by the increased numbers it supports, and that equality and a community of goods would in a few years reproduce all the inequality they abolished. It then surveys the checks actual and possible: vice and misery, war, famine, disease, and late and unfruitful marriage as the only check consistent with virtue and with the happiness of the poor. The argument is applied to the parish provisions of England, which it holds to accelerate population without creating food and so to aggravate the evil they profess to cure, and to the laws of settlement, to interest, and to the practice of charitable accumulation of grain. In the second edition, recast on an enlarged scale, the historical and statistical evidence of the checks is worked out through the ages and nations of the world, with the American states as the proof of what a cheap land and prudent marriage can do, and with the moral check of delayed marriage advanced as the practical remedy.
works.significance: It is the origin of demography as a science and one of the two or three books that made the argument from necessity indispensable to social thought; it defeated the philosophy of perfectability on its own ground, supplied the naturalists of the next century with the premise of the struggle for existence, and set the terms in which poverty, marriage, relief, and empire were debated for a hundred years. Its tone, at once humane and unsparing, made it the most attacked book of the generation and the standard example of the 'dismal' science.
works.meter: Cool, numerate, candid prose of the investigating mind: postulate, ratio, and consequence, with a candour of pessimism that became a rhetorical pose in itself.
works.context: It grew out of a family discussion on the schemes of human perfectability and was published in the year after the war, the scarcity, and the agitation that followed the revolutionary decade, when the English controversy over the poor laws was opening. Its author, a fellow of a Cambridge college and the holder of the first English chair of political economy, wrote into the second edition the agricultural and statistical evidence of the following years, and the work went through successive editions to the middle of the century.
works.structure: In the first issue a short sequence of numbered chapters stating the principle, its illustration, and its consequences for the systems of improvement; in the recast edition a much enlarged two-volume argument of statistical history, of the checks in the ancient and modern world, and of the applications to the law and the politics of the poor.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously, and the authorship was openly acknowledged by its author within a few years and in the later editions; the two very different forms of the first and second editions raise no question of attribution but do require the text to be cited by edition.

works.title: An Essay on Truth
works.description: James Beattie's verbose, pugnacious vindication of common sense against scepticism, published by subscription at Aberdeen and London in 1770 and aimed squarely at Hume's philosophy. It argued that the principles of common sense are the testimony of the Creator and that sceptical reasoning, followed honestly, refutes itself.
works.plot: Beattie first defends the general rules of logic and the original perceptions of the mind against the sceptical geometry of probabilities, insisting that a man must believe his faculties before he can dispute them. He then attacks the theory of ideas directly: the reductions of mind to a bundle of perceptions, the definition of cause as mere sequence, and the sceptical account of personal identity, each he answers by appeal to the plain judgments of mankind and to the moral interests of society. He closes with a defence of the common-sense philosophy, an appeal to testimony and miracle, and a warm apology for the Christian scheme against Hume's Natural History. The book's energy lay less in argument than in the moral outrage it professed at the sceptics' treatment of truth, virtue, and the Deity.
works.significance: Long dismissed by professional philosophers, it was the most widely read popular answer to Hume of its generation, fixed common-sense rhetoric in Scottish letters, and is now studied as the rhetorical and religious face of the Aberdeen Enlightenment.
works.meter: Diffuse, declamatory, often comic prose of the high moral pulse, swollen periods alternating with blunt invective and exclamatory common sense.
works.context: Written at Aberdeen by the Marischal College professor who had published juvenile poems there and was soon made principal of the college, the Essay appeared in 1770 in the current of Reid's common-sense campaign; several editions followed at once, and Boswell reported Johnson's scorn for its logic with his praise of its honesty.
works.structure: Two books? use: a single long essay in successive chapters: logic and the general rules, the original perceptions, the confutation of the theory of ideas, and the closing moral-theological defence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Essay to Defend the Women's Cause
altTitles: An Essay to Defend the Womens Cause
Essay to Defend the Women's Cause
works.form: polemical and argumentative essay in prose
works.description: A prose defence of women's rational capacity and of their title to education, written in answer to the libels of the stage and of the pamphlets and arguing the equality of souls and of understanding. It circulated in manuscript before its printing and stands among the earliest English essays in the systematic defence of the sex.
works.plot: The essay examines the usage by which women are reproached as fools and as unfit for learning, and denies the charge by the evidence of the understanding and of virtue. It argues that the defects charged on women are the effects of their education and of their law, not of their nature, and that the same capacity appears where the same advantages have been given. It closes with the claim that the defence of the sex is a cause of reason and of religion.
works.significance: It is a founding text of the English argument for women's rational equality, standing between the defence tradition of the previous century and the educational proposals of the following one.
works.meter: A direct and closely reasoned prose of the plain style, with the quick retort and the summed antithesis; the argumentative paragraphs close on a balanced sentence.
works.context: Written in the aftermath of the stage reform quarrel and of the pamphlet war on the women question, and circulated among the learned women of the western circles before being printed at the beginning of the eighteenth century.
works.structure: A continuous argumentative essay, the objection stated, the particulars answered one by one, and the general conclusion drawn on the capacity and the deserts of women.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the essay circulated in manuscript under the author's name and was printed at the beginning of the eighteenth century, the date of the first printing being given here as conventionally assigned.

works.title: An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision
works.description: Berkeley's first philosophical essay, arguing that distance and magnitude are not perceived by sight itself but learned by experience through association with touch and the straining of the eyes. It rewrote the geometry-based optics of the Cartesians and became a foundation stone of empiricist psychology of perception.
works.plot: Berkeley shows that the immediate objects of sight are colours and figures with no necessary connexion to distance, and that distance is perceived only because certain visible ideas suggest ideas belonging originally to touch. He denies that the eye judges distance by lines, angles, or refractions known to the mind, and reinterprets Molyneux's problem of the cube and the globe: a person born blind, on receiving sight, would not identify by vision alone what he knew by touch. Apparent magnitude and the perception of situation follow from the same associative mechanism, and visual experience is shown to work like a language of signs. The essay closes by making vision a universal grammar divinely instituted, not a school of geometry.
works.significance: It founded the science of perception on association rather than geometry, influenced Hume, Reid, and the empiricist tradition of psychology, and fed the eighteenth-century idea of nature as a language of signs.
works.meter: Sparse, exact, demonstrative prose of short numbered paragraphs, the style of an experimental natural philosopher turned psychologist.
works.context: Published in 1709 out of Berkeley's Dublin debates on the geometry of vision and framed by the new optics after Newton's Opticks of 1704; William Molyneux's question about distance perception gave it its shape.
works.structure: A continuous argument in numbered sections, each proposition built on the previous analysis of the immediate objects of sight.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language
altTitles: An Essay towards a Real Character
works.description: Wilkins's ambitious scheme for a universal philosophical language in which the characters would correspond directly to the things and ideas they signify, with a full classification of knowledge as its foundation.
works.plot: Wilkins proposes a 'real character' — a written symbol system independent of any natural language — and a taxonomic arrangement of all ideas into genera and species, so that the language would itself be a philosophy.
works.significance: The most elaborate of the seventeenth-century universal-language projects and a landmark in the history of taxonomy, semiotics, and information science; it influenced Leibniz and later classification systems.
works.meter: Systematic technical prose with extensive tables.
works.context: Published in 1668 for the Royal Society, of which Wilkins was a founding fellow and first secretary; it belongs to the seventeenth-century quest for a universal language.
works.structure: Four parts: the design of the character, the philosophical tables, the grammar, and a vocabulary.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Wilkins; authorship undisputed.

works.title: An Exhortation to Christian Living
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (eleventh century)
works.description: A homiletic poem of ninety-two lines urging its audience to keep God's commandments, resist the devil, and live in readiness for death and judgment. The poem is direct, urgent, and practical in its moral teaching.
works.plot: The poet exhorts the faithful to love God, keep his commands, avoid sin and the devil's snares, and remember the brevity of life and the certainty of judgment; wealth and pleasure are fleeting, but the soul's fate is eternal.
works.significance: A representative of the reform movement's verse catechesis, showing the homiletic mode of late Old English poetry at its most direct.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic formulas of late Old English preaching; the verse is plain and expository rather than ornamental.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English group of CCCC 201 (with Judgement Day II, A Summons to Prayer, and the Menologium), texts associated with the Benedictine Reform's devotional and catechetical programme.
works.structure: A sequence of direct exhortations in the second person, each grounded in the antithesis between this world's brevity and the soul's eternity, closing with the promise of heavenly reward.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus: The 1818 Text

works.title: An Experiment in Education, Made at the Male Asylum of Madras
altTitles: An Experiment in Education, Made at the Male Asylum of Madras; Suggesting a System by which a School or Family may teach itself, under the Superintendence of the Master
works.form: educational report and treatise; the institutional experiment with the evidence and the plan of extension
works.description: The founding document of the monitorial system of education, a brief report by the medical officer of the asylum of the Company's settlement at Madras of the experiment by which the fatherless children kept there were taught by one another, and by which a school might, in his phrase, teach itself under the superintendence of the master.
works.plot: The report states the condition of the male asylum at Madras, the insufficiency of its funds, the idleness and ignorance of the boys, and the failure of the common method of teaching them by the master alone; and it then describes the device by which the difficulty was overcome: the most advanced of the scholars were made the instructors of the rest under him, the school being divided into classes, the boys examined and promoted, the meritorious marked and rewarded by badges and by the honour of the station, the monitors responsible for the proficiency of their several classes, and the master retaining only the general superintendence and the religious instruction. He sets out the progress made, the smallness of the expense at which the boys were thus taught, and the certificates of the officers and of the directors who had seen the school; and he argues that the same machinery, applied in England to the children of the labouring poor, would give a national education at a price within the reach of a parish or a subscription. The whole method rests, in his statement, upon the emulation of the boys and upon the economy of the pupil-teacher.
works.significance: The originating text of the monitorial or mutual system of instruction, and one of the few short pamphlets of its age whose machinery was copied into the schoolrooms of three continents; the arrangement of pupil-monitors, classes, badges, and registers which it described became the working form of the elementary schools of the established religious society and of its rival, and so of the mass schooling of the nineteenth century, which makes it a central document of the history of education and of the education of the poor.
works.meter: The blunt, particular, unadorned prose of the practical man stating a case, with the enumeration of the classes, the marks, and the rewards, the figures of the expense, and the appeal to the testimony of persons of authority who had visited the school; the style is that of the official memorandum rather than of the essay, and its force lies in its air of evidence.
works.context: Written out of the eleven years' residence of the author's experiment at Madras, where he had taken the asylum in hand in the years after the American war, and published in London in 1797, in the season of the charity and Sunday school, of the societies for the education of the poor, and of the first anxiety about the instruction of the manufacturing and labouring classes. The notice it obtained among the directors, among the friends of the missions, and at length in the highest families, prepared the way for the great monitorial controversy of the following twenty years, in which the same method was promulgated in England by another schoolmaster with the public credit of the metropolis.
works.structure: A short report of an experiment, in the manner of the statement of facts: the case of the asylum, the method pursued, the proof of the progress made, the account of the expense, the appended letters and certificates, and the closing proposal of the system's extension.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to a single hand is uncontested; but the dating of the several tracts and the priority of the invention were the subject of a long and bitter dispute with the other promulgator of the same method, in which the parties pleaded the Madras experiment of the 1780s and the Southwark school of the 1790s against each other, and the controversy must be consulted wherever the claim to the invention is in question.

works.title: An Historical and Moral View of the Origin and Progress of the French Revolution
altTitles: An Historical and Moral View of the Origin and Progress of the French Revolution; and the Effect It Has Produced in Europe
works.form: Philosophical and national history; political treatise and moral essay on a contemporary event.
works.description: A philosophical history of the Revolution written partly on the scene itself, which treats the French event as the symptom of a long civilisation and asks what its moral effects have been on Europe. It defends the original causes of the Revolution while condemning the violence that followed, and explains both by the corrupt institutions of the old regime and by the temper of a people unprepared for free inquiry. It is the period's clearest attempt to hold revolutionary hope and revolutionary disappointment in a single argument.
works.plot: The work first states the general causes: the accumulated superstition, the inequality of ranks, the vices of an exhausted monarchy and the progress of letters that had prepared the crisis. It then traces the opening acts of the Revolution, the conduct of the assemblies, the errors of the court and the character of the parties, with sustained attention to the motives of individuals. The later chapters examine the effects produced in Europe, the spirit of party, the tendency of the violence to discredit the cause, and the prospects of a slower moral improvement that may yet fulfil the expectations the Revolution defeated. The conclusion is cautious: the principles are vindicated, the event is mourned.
works.significance: A key document of the transatlantic Revolution Controversy and one of the earliest attempts to write the history of a living revolution as moral philosophy. It supplies the period's most articulate statement of disappointed yet unretracted revolutionary hope. Its reading of enthusiasm, prejudice and national character links it to the philosophical history of the Scottish schools.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a cool analytical style enlivened by rapid characterisation and by rhetorical generalisation.
works.context: Composed during the author's residence in Paris and on the return journey in 1792-93, through the trial of the king, the wars and the Terror, and published after the executions had made optimism difficult to defend. It belongs to the literature of the revolutionary exile and of the British debate over sympathy with France. Its argument answers both the conservative prediction of ruin and the radical expectation of regeneration.
works.structure: Systematic historical essay in preface and numbered sections, moving from general causes to narrative sequence to moral reflection; no continuous chronicle but an argumentative arrangement of events.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute.

works.title: An Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland
works.description: Marvell's famous and much-debated ode on Oliver Cromwell's return from the Irish campaign in 1650, balancing admiration for Cromwell's irresistible, almost elemental force with a poignant lament for the executed Charles I — a masterpiece of political ambiguity.
works.plot: The ode urges the poet to leave the Muses and sing of Cromwell's active power, describes his campaign and the regicide (with the memorable image of Charles at the scaffold 'as the Royal Actor born'), and looks to Cromwell's future conquests.
works.significance: One of the greatest political poems in English, admired for its balance, its compression, and its capacity to hold conflicting judgments about power and legitimacy.
works.meter: A regular Horatian quatrain (alternating four- and three-stress lines) of restrained, balanced power.
works.context: Written in 1650, in the crisis after Cromwell's Irish campaign and before Dunbar; circulated in manuscript and published only in the 1681 Miscellaneous Poems, its political sympathies have been argued ever since.
works.characters: Oliver Cromwell; Charles I; the poet
works.structure: A Horatian ode in quatrains moving from the call to celebrate to the account of Cromwell's rise, the king's death, and the prospect of further conquest.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: An Inquiry Concerning Virtue or Merit
altTitles: An Inquiry Concerning Virtue, or Merit
An Essay upon the Conduct and Passions of the Mind
works.description: Shaftesbury's foundational treatise of moral sense theory, first circulated privately in 1699 as An Essay upon the Conduct and Passions of the Mind and given substantially its final form in the Characteristics. It argues that moral distinction arises from a natural sentiment responding to the balance of the affections, not from law, contract, or self-interest.
works.plot: The Inquiry analyses the mind into natural, social, and selfish affections and shows that a reflective sense approves the system in which the social affections hold due proportion to the rest. Virtue is thus the right balance of a secondary, reflective nature, and the sense of it is as immediate as the sense of beauty. Shaftesbury refutes at length the egoism of Hobbes and the voluntarism of Pufendorf, arguing that obligation cannot be grounded in self-love or in will alone. He extends the account to a 'theology of the moral sense', showing the same harmony in the universal system, and closes with a defence of the claim that virtue is the interest of the species and of each person within it.
works.significance: It founded the British sentimentalism of Hutcheson, Hume, and Adam Smith and set the terms for a century of debate whether moral distinction is sentiment or reason.
works.meter: Tight, reflective prose built on numbered distinctions and recurring triads (affections, senses, systems), with a tendency toward balanced periodic closers.
works.context: Written in the shadow of Locke's Essay and of the Locke-Filiimerde-Stillingfleet controversies, and shaped by Shaftesbury's own Journals; its 1699 essay version circulated among the Whig wits before its authorized appearance in the Characteristics of 1711.
works.structure: A sustained analytical treatise in two parts, moving from the division of the affections through the definition of virtue to the confutation of opponents and the enlarged cosmological conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae
altTitles: An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, Known by the Name of the Cow Pox
works.form: medical and scientific writing; case-based experimental inquiry and practical proposal
works.description: The short pamphlet which founded vaccination, published at its author's own expense and containing the evidence for a proposition drawn from the observation of the dairy counties: that the cow pox, a disease of the udder of the cow transferred to the hand of the milker, confers upon the human being an immunity from the small pox which nothing else does. It is a model of the patient accumulative method, twenty-three cases stated, compared, and argued.
works.plot: The inquiry begins with the history of the opinion in the western counties, that a person who has taken the cow pox from the hand of a milking woman cannot afterward be infected by the small pox, and with the examination of the several circumstances of the disease in the cow and in the human subject. It then reports the cases in order: the progress of the inoculated cow pox from the pustule to the areola and the scab, its mild constitutional effect, and its unlikeness to every other pustular disease; and after the series of cases it records the decisive experiment, the insertion of the matter of the small pox into subjects who had previously taken the cow pox, with the finding that no disease followed. The causes of the irregular and failing cases are then examined, the identity of the matter and of the disease in the several instances is discussed, and the differences between the cow pox and the greedy itches of the horse are distinguished. The argument closes with the practical inference that an inoculation so safe may be made universal, and with the proposal of the procedure to the profession and to the public.
works.significance: It is one of the few short books which changed the practice of medicine and the destiny of populations, the founding text of immunology and of the public vaccination which in the following century abolished the worst of the endemic scourges of the world; and as a document of method it is a classic of the argument from accumulated cases, often cited for the combination of country observation, experiment, and caution with which a national prejudice was turned into a universal practice.
works.meter: Modest, deliberate, evidential prose of the country practitioner: the case stated in order of date with the particulars of the subject and of the pustules, the careful qualification, and the unhurried generalisation from the accumulated instances.
works.context: Published in the year when the inoculation of the small pox, long practised and long disputed, was at once fashionable and distrusted, when the cattle trade of a grazing county carried a disease of the udder into the hands of the dairy people, and when an English physician of Gloucestershire, trained in the metropolitan schools and a correspondent of the great experimenters of the day, was able to test a country tradition by the method of the hospital. Its reception ranged from instant adoption to the warmest professional ridicule.
works.structure: A single pamphlet of some seventy pages in three movements: the historical and medical statement of the disease, the series of twenty-three reported cases with the experimental proofs, and the general remarks on the causes, the irregularities, and the practice.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the priority of the observation and the several shares of the country practitioners and of the metropolitan institutions in the trials are matters of a well-documented contemporary controversy which concerns the honour of the discovery rather than the authorship of the pamphlet.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Effects of Putting a Stop to the African Slave Trade, and of Granting Liberty to the Slaves in the British Sugar Colonies
altTitles: An Inquiry into the Effects of Putting a Stop to the African Slave Trade
works.form: Polemical inquiry in political economy and colonial evidence
works.description: The book that turned Anglican clerical opinion against the slave trade, written by the Reverend James Ramsay after nineteen years as a surgeon and then a planter's chaplain in Saint Christopher and a rectorate in Kent. Ramsay argues from long residence in the sugar islands that stopping the African trade and gradually freeing the colonial slaves would strengthen rather than ruin the colonies. The Inquiry supplied the abolitionists with first-hand evidence in economic form and made Ramsay the witness whom Wilberforce and the Clapham circle consulted throughout the campaign.
works.plot: Ramsay estimates the numbers of the trade and of the colonial population, then shows that the annual loss of imported Africans must be replaced by costlier purchase and by the constant renewal of a workforce that is worked to death. He next argues that a resident planter and a proportion of free or indentured labour would improve cultivation, that the islands need not be depopulated by emancipation, and that the West Indian interest in the trade is the interest of a few merchants rather than of the colonies. He closes with a gradual scheme: the stop of the importation, the registration and protection of the enslaved, incentives to planters to breed and to treat their people as families, and a progression toward freedom, warning that injustice long tolerated invites judgment upon the nation.
works.significance: It was the first substantial abolitionist argument built on colonial experience and economic calculation rather than on scripture and sympathy alone, and it converted the question from one of conscience into one of policy. It established the evidential method that Clarkson and Equiano would use and gave the parliamentary campaign its most trusted clerical witness.
works.meter: Prose only, in a plain clerical and statistical style, argumentative rather than ornamental
works.context: Written in the years of the Bristol and Liverpool petitions against the trade, the Somersett precedent and the emerging evangelical humane politics, it answers the planters' claim that abolition would be national ruin and shares the political-arithmetic method of the period's economic writing.
works.structure: Single argumentative inquiry in numbered sections combining statistical estimate, case-based description of colonial management, refutation of planter objections and a positive proposal for gradual emancipation.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by James Ramsay is established; the earlier pamphlet letters on the trade are sometimes separately numbered but the Inquiry is his own consolidated argument.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense
works.description: Reid's founding statement of the philosophy of common sense, begun as a challenge to the way of ideas and first delivered as Glasgow lectures in the early 1760s. It argues that the faculties of perception, memory, and conception are original powers given by nature and trusted by every human being, and that scepticism is the inevitable harvest of treating the mind's natural testimony as a hypothesis.
works.plot: Reid reviews the history of speculative philosophy and the essence of language as prefaces to a grammar of the human mind. He distinguishes sensation from perception and shows that perception of external objects is a natural and original judgment, not an inference from ideas or a calculus of signs. The chapters on the five senses demonstrate, against Locke, Berkeley, and Hume, that the mind is endowed with faculties whose deliverances carry their own authority; the same argument is run through memory, conception, and belief. The concluding chapters expose the ideal theory as scepticism's engine and defend the common judgments of mankind as first principles, the judge and party together in the cause of reason.
works.significance: It founded the school of common-sense philosophy, reshaped the epistemology of perception, and is the central document of the Aberdeen and Glasgow resistance to sceptical empiricism, revived in modern philosophy of mind and epistemology.
works.meter: Vigorous, plain, hortatory prose of a preacher-philosopher, direct address, rhetorical questions, and blunt refusals of technical jargon.
works.context: Published in 1764 with a dedication to the Glasgow physician who had pressed the lectures into print, after Reid's appointment to the Glasgow chair and amid the faculty's running controversy with Hume; it was answered, and answered again, through the following decade.
works.structure: Seven chapters of progressive anatomy of the faculties, each opening from common observation and closing against the theoretical philosophy, with prefatory chapters on language and the history of speculation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
works.description: Adam Smith's founding book of political economy, an inquiry into how the wealth of nations grows through the division of labour, free mutual exchange, and the accumulation of stock, and why monopoly, mercantilist regulation, and colonial exclusive trade obstruct that growth. Published in two volumes in London in 1776, it reframed the science of society's material life.
works.plot: Book I derives the division of labour from the propensity to truck and barter, limits it by the extent of the market, and resolves the price of commodities into wages, profit, and rent, with the famous observation that the butcher, brewer, and baker serve us from self-love rather than benevolence. Book II classifies stock, capital, and money, and distinguishes productive from unproductive labour as the real determinant of national accumulation. Book III narrates the history of European development from the fall of Rome: the rise of towns, the slow victory of urban manufactures over rural dependence, and the commerce that introduced order and personal liberty. Book IV dismantles the mercantile system, the restraints on import, and the project of colonial monopoly, with the East India company among its indicted villains, and Book V grounds the necessary public works, institutions of education, and revenue of a civilized state. The whole makes commercial interdependence, not state power, the engine of national opulence.
works.significance: It is the foundational text of classical political economy and of liberal thought about markets and empire, the book against and from which all later economics, from Ricardo and Marx to the present, has defined itself.
works.meter: Long analytic prose of lecture-derived clarity, built on homely exemplars of pin-makers and corn-farmers, its argumentative climaxes in sustained ironic indictments of the interested systems of commerce and law.
works.context: Written after Smith's tutorial tour abroad and years of Edinburgh and Glasgow teaching, amid the American crisis and the East India company's scandals, it was published in the year of the Declaration of Independence and read immediately across Europe and in Parliament.
works.structure: Five books moving from first principles of value and distribution through the real history of Europe to the polemic against the mercantile system and the policy of natural liberty.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue
altTitles: An Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue, in Two Treatises
works.description: Hutcheson's two-treatise defence of the moral sense and the sense of beauty against Hobbes and Mandeville, arguing that the determinations of taste and virtue are immediate, disinterested senses of the human frame. It gave the Scottish Enlightenment its founding vocabulary of benevolence and moral sense.
works.plot: The first treatise shows that beauty and deformity are perceived at once by an internal sense, not by calculation of advantage, and that the harmony of parts, novelty, and the intellectual beauties of science and art obey the same sense. The second treatise argues that virtue is loved for benevolence, the quality of intending happiness to others, against the egoism that resolves all affection into self-love; the moral sense approves disinterested affection immediately. Calculations of utility, Hutcheson insists, follow rather than found our approvals, and the pleasure of virtue is proportioned to the extent of its benevolence. A concluding mathematical language of morals attempts to express praise as benevolence multiplied by the number possessed.
works.significance: It fixed the moral-sense scheme, taught the century to speak of benevolence as the essence of virtue, and directly shaped Hume, the American founders' idea of the pursuit of happiness, and the whole sentimentalist tradition.
works.meter: Clear, modest, scholastic-plain prose of a teacher's lecture-room, with numbered distinctions and the famous arithmetic notation of moral worth.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1725 as Hutcheson had begun his Glasgow lectureship amid the row over his appointment; the third edition of 1729 was greatly enlarged. The Inquiry answered Mandeville's Fable of the Bees and the rationalist ethics of Clarke and Wollaston within the debate Shaftesbury had opened.
works.structure: Two linked treatises on beauty and virtue, each an analytic demonstration with objections answered, plus a closing section proposing a calculus of morals.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
altTitles: Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
The Principles of Morals and Legislation
works.description: Bentham's systematic statement of the utilitarian science of legislation, printed in 1789 after a decade of elaboration and issued with a preface surveying the field of legal reform. It grounds morals and law in the sovereign masters of pain and pleasure, furnishes the hedonist calculus, and classifies offences for a rational code.
works.plot: Bentham begins that nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure, whose dominion the legislator must reconstruct as the greatest happiness of the community, and he analyses actions, motives, and acts by the seven dimensions of their tendency. He examines the limits of the principle of utility, its rejectors, and the four sanctions of pleasure and pain, natural, political, moral, and religious, then classifies offences against the state, the subject, and the individual, defining the proper measure of punishment by its prospect of utility. Private ethics and legislation are one science, and the fictitious entities of the law - obligation, right, corporation - are reducible to the reality of pains and pleasures. The book ends as an architect's plan for a complete legal code.
works.significance: It is the foundation document of classical utilitarianism and of analytical jurisprudence, the book that formed James Mill, Bowring, and the codification movements, and remains the standard statement of the felicific calculus.
works.meter: Architectonic, enumerating, taxonomic prose, numbered divisions and definitions, its rhetoric of exactitude lashed by irony against lawyers' mysteries.
works.context: Long maturing after the Fragment, the manuscript circulated among reformers and was published in 1789 on the eve of the French Revolution, in the year its principles were carried into the American and French debates on codes and punishment.
works.structure: Twenty-one chapters of graduated theory: foundation, calculus, limits, sanctions, then the taxonomy of offences and punishments, with prefatory and appended analyses.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Ancrene Wisse
works.form: rule and devotional treatise in prose
works.description: A rule of life for three anchoresses, written in the West Midlands 'AB language' c. 1225–40: eight parts treating the devotional routine, the custody of the senses, temptation, confession, penance, love, and the inner life. It is the greatest prose work of early Middle English, celebrated for its psychological acuity, its homely and exact imagery, and its humane severity.
works.plot: Addressing the anchoresses as a loving director, the author regulates their prayers and reading, anatomizes the temptations of the solitary life (with the famous allegory of the royal wooing of the soul), teaches the art of confession, and unfolds the degrees of love culminating in union with Christ.
works.significance: The masterpiece of early Middle English prose and the supreme English contribution to the literature of the solitary life; its influence reaches the Cloud-author and beyond.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of great art; concrete domestic metaphor (the anchorhold as house, the heart as its lady).
works.context: Written in Herefordshire or the Welsh Marches for three sisters enclosed near a church, in the milieu that produced the Katherine Group; revised and translated into French and Latin, and copied into the sixteenth century.
works.characters: the three anchoresses (addressees); Christ as lover-king (allegorical)
works.structure: Eight books moving from outer rule (devotions, senses) to inner rule (heart, conscience) and love; interlaced with exemplary tales and allegories.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; authorship_status reflects scholarly consensus (the author is sometimes speculatively identified with a Dominican or Augustinian director).

works.title: Andreas
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 1,722 lines on the apocryphal Acts of Andrew and Matthias: the apostle Andrew, sailing incognito with Christ himself as his helmsman, voyages to the cannibal city of Mermedonia to rescue his fellow apostle Matthew. The poem recasts the apostle as a heroic seafarer in the manner of Beowulf, with some of the corpus's most vivid voyage imagery.
works.plot: Christ, disguised as a ship's captain, ferries the reluctant Andrew over the stormy sea, hearing his preaching on the way; in Mermedonia, Andrew is seized, tortured, and imprisoned, but a flood released from a stone pillar drowns his tormentors and revives them, converting the city; Andrew establishes a church and departs, leaving the poem's didactic epilogue.
works.significance: The fullest Old English saint's life in verse and a celebrated example of the heroic adaptation of hagiography.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in the classical heroic manner.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 29v-52v); based on a Latin version of the apocryphal Acts, itself known in Old English prose from the Blickling manuscript.
works.characters: Andrew; Christ (the helmsman); Matthew; the Mermedonians
works.structure: A sea-voyage frame enclosing the martyrdom-and-conversion narrative, with speeches, miracles, and a flood scene modelled on Exodus; the poem borrows formulaic lines directly from Beowulf.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the Beowulf borrowings are stylistic, not evidence of authorship.
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer
movements: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Gothic Fiction

works.title: Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis
altTitles: The Satire of the Three Estates
works.description: Lindsay's great morality drama of the Scottish Reformation: King Humanitie, seduced by Sensualitie and the vices, is recalled to virtue by Divine Correction, and summons a parliament of the three estates — Spirituality, Temporalitie, Merchant — where John the Common-Weill indicts the church's abuses and the vices are tried and hanged. Played at Linlithgow in 1540 and enlarged at Cupar in 1552.
works.plot: Rex Humanitas falls under the rule of Wantonness, Placebo, and Solace; Divine Correction reforms him; the estates meet in parliament, hear John the Common-Weill's complaint, and pass the acts of reform, the play closing with the sermon of Folly.
works.significance: The greatest Scottish play and the dramatic summa of the northern Reformation; its parliament scene made drama an instrument of national reform and remained a living text into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Scots couplets of great stage energy; songs, interludes, and the sermon of Folly closing the action.
works.context: First played before James V at Linlithgow in 1540; the enlarged Cupar performance (1552) addressed the eve of the Scottish Reformation, and the play remained in performance for a century.
works.characters: Rex Humanitas; Divine Correction; Sensualitie; Flatterie; Falset; Dissait; John the Common-Weill; Spirituality; Temporalitie; Merchant
works.structure: A two-part morality expanded to a national parliament: the king's moral fall and recovery (Part I) and the public trial and reformation of the estates (Part II).
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Annals of the American Revolution
altTitles: Annals of the American Revolution; or, A Record of the Causes and Events which Produced, and Terminated in the Establishment and Independence of the American Republic
works.form: History and chronicle with documentary editing; the national annalistic record
works.description: A year-by-year record of the war of independence, compiled from documents, state papers and the published histories, and issued with a documentary apparatus. It treats the Revolution as a providential national history and arranges its matter chronologically for reference. It belongs to the wave of centennial-era preservation of founding records.
works.plot: The annals follow the progress of the war from its political origins through the campaigns, the councils, the correspondence and the treaties, entering each year's principal events in order. They interweave the operations in the northern and southern states and at sea, and record the civil measures of the states and of Congress. Documents and letters are printed at length or abstracted, with notes identifying their sources. The work ends with the peace and with the establishment of the government it treats as the fruit of the contest.
works.significance: It is an early American attempt to fix the chronology of the Revolution from sources rather than from memory, and it stands beside the editorial work of the same generation. Its providential reading of national history was characteristic of the clerical nationalism of New England. It supplies a reference frame for the historical fiction of the 1820s.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published at Hartford in 1824, in the decade of the fiftieth-anniversary celebrations, the tours of Lafayette and the first great editorial enterprises for the founding records. Its compiler was a Congregational minister and geographer who read the Revolution as a religious as well as a political event. The book anticipates the documentary series edited by the historical societies of the following decade.
works.structure: Chronological annals with entries arranged by year and campaign, supported by printed documents and editorial notes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the volume also contains edited documentary papers relating to the war.

works.title: Annals of the Parish; or, The Chronicle of Dalmailing
works.description: the author's first and most celebrated novel, the affectionate memoir of the Rev. John Halcyon Balwhidell, minister of a west-of-Scotland parish, chronicling nearly fifty years of rural transformation. A foundational text of the Scottish regional novel, it records agricultural improvement, Methodism, and the French wars from inside the old kirk.
works.plot: The minister Balwhidell narrates the history of his parish from his settlement in 1758 through to 1805. He records the coming of agricultural improvement, the disputes between the old and new husbandry, the inroads of Methodism and secession churches, the enthusiasm and disillusion of the French wars, and the quiet passing of the patriarchal laird system. The narrative's gentle irony arises from the gap between Balwhidell's complacent self-satisfaction and the reader's perception of the world passing him by.
works.significance: Annals of the Parish invented the Scottish parish chronicle and is a direct ancestor of Kailyard fiction and of Hardy's Wessex; its dialect realism and ironic memoir form make it one of the major experiments in voice in Romantic fiction.
works.context: Written by the author, an Ayrshire-born friend of Byron and admirer of Ferguson and Burns, and published in 1821 as the Waverley vogue opened the market for regional Scottish fiction. Its subject — the death of the old parish under improvement — reflects the author's own experience of rapid social change in southwest Scotland.
works.characters: The Rev. John Halcyon Balwhidell; Bailie Blair; Mr. McCorkindale; Andy Glovers; Miss Broun; Robert Lang; Gavin Mossgiel
works.structure: First-person memoir covering 1758-1805; episodic and digressive, organised by ecclesiastical and agricultural events rather than plot; the unreliable but lovable narrator generates the novel's irony.

works.title: Annus Mirabilis
altTitles: Annus Mirabilis: The Year of Wonders 1666
works.description: Dryden's long historical poem on the two disasters of 1666 — the Second Anglo-Dutch War and the Great Fire of London — written from Charlton in Wiltshire, offering the nation an optimistic, providential reading of catastrophe.
works.plot: The poem narrates the naval victories over the Dutch, then the Fire, and concludes with a prophecy of London's rebirth as a greater commercial empire under Charles II.
works.significance: The major English public poem of the 1660s; it demonstrates Dryden's ability to turn current events into national myth and anticipates the scientific imagery of his later verse.
works.meter: Quatrains (alternately rhymed iambic pentameter, ABAB), deliberately chosen over couplets to imitate the stateliness of history writing.
works.context: Composed while Dryden was absent from plague-stricken London; dedicated to the City of London in the year of the Great Fire, and closely engaged with the Royal Society's new empiricism.
works.structure: A two-part public narrative (war, fire) framed by dedication and prophetic conclusion, with episodic set-pieces for individual battles.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Antonius
authors: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
works.description: Mary Sidney Herbert's translation of Robert Garnier's Senecan tragedy Marc-Antoine (1578), the first English version of a French classical tragedy: a closet drama in which Mark Antony, after Actium, debates his ruin with his friends and Cleopatra, and falls on his sword.
works.plot: Antony, defeated and despairing, rejects the counsel of his followers, is reproached and forgiven by Cleopatra, and kills himself; the play closes with the chorus's meditation on Fortune and with Cleopatra's grief and resolve.
works.significance: The bridge by which French neoclassical tragedy entered English, and the first English tragedy of Cleopatra.
works.meter: Blank verse with rhyming choruses, matching Garnier's French alexandrines with English iambic pentameter.
works.context: Published in 1592, amid the English vogue for Senecan tragedy and the Pembroke circle's literary patronage; it anticipated the Antony plays of Shakespeare and Daniel.
works.characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Charmian; Philostratus; Lucilius; the Chorus of Egyptians
works.structure: Five acts of Senecan structure with choruses, designed for reading rather than performance.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by Mary Sidney Herbert from Robert Garnier's Marc-Antoine (1578); uncontested.

works.title: Antony and Cleopatra
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of empire and desire: the ageing Antony, caught between Rome and Egypt, duty and Cleopatra, loses the world at Actium and, hearing the false report of her death, falls on his sword; Cleopatra, refusing Octavius's triumph, dies by the asp, and the play ends with the lovers' deaths transfigured into myth.
works.plot: Antony's dalliance in Alexandria draws him back to Rome and the marriage to Octavia; the breach with Caesar sends him back to Cleopatra; the sea-fight at Actium is lost when she flies and he follows; his rage, her feigned death, his botched suicide, and her staged one complete the tragedy — 'I am fire and air' — with Caesar left to bury them side by side.
works.significance: The greatest English poem of erotic grandeur — the tragedy in which the lovers outgrow tragedy itself.
works.meter: A hyperbolic, sensuous verse of superlatives — Enobarbus's barge speech its summit — with the prose of Egypt's court as the foil to Roman plainness.
works.context: Written about 1606–07 from North's Plutarch, whose phrasing Shakespeare follows at the barge and the death scenes; the play's imperial themes shadow the Jacobean debate over empire and union.
works.characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Octavius Caesar; Enobarbus; Octavia; Charmian; Iras; Lepidus; Pompey; Alexas; Eros; Dolabella; the Clown
works.structure: A tragedy of scenes, not acts — forty-two rapid movements between Rome and Alexandria — in which the lovers' deaths are deliberately drawn out across the final acts as ceremony and apotheosis.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Apollonius of Tyre
works.form: prose romance in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English prose translation of the Historia Apollonii regis Tyri — the story of the shipwrecked prince Apollonius, his lost wife and daughter, and their final reunion: the first prose romance in English and the ancestor of Shakespeare's Pericles and of the Apollonius tradition that runs through Gower and the Middle Ages.
works.plot: Apollonius of Tyre, having solved the riddle of the incestuous king Antiochus, flees by sea; shipwrecked at Pentapolis, he wins the king's daughter in marriage; at sea their daughter is born and the queen, apparently dead, is cast overboard in a sealed coffin; the daughter, raised at Mytilene, is sold to a brothel-keeper but preserves her honour by her wisdom; the story ends in the great recognition scene, when the family is reunited at Ephesus and Mytilene.
works.significance: The first English prose romance; the bridge between the classical romance tradition and the Middle English romances and Shakespeare's Pericles.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated c. 1000-1050 from the Latin Historia Apollonii (a late antique romance); the unique manuscript is Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201, which also contains Wulfstan's homilies.
works.characters: Apollonius; Antiochus; Arcestrates of Pentapolis; the queen; the daughter (Thasia); Athenagoras of Mytilene
works.structure: A continuous romance narrative of adventure, loss, and recognition, in the incest-riddle frame of the Latin source.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translator.

works.title: Apology for the Life of Colley Cibber
works.form: Autobiographical memoir and theatrical history in prose.
works.description: An autobiographical memoir published in 1740 after the writer's retirement from the stage, at once a defence of a career and the richest contemporary account of the London patent theatre in its first brilliant half-century. Written in a garrulous, self-admiring prose that rarely distinguishes vanity from evidence, it reviews the author's own plays and acting, the quarrels and collapses of the companies he helped to manage, and the attacks of his enemies, the most formidable of which had long since enthroned him as the emperor of dullness.
works.plot: The narrative runs from a boyhood in the theatre world and a first sight of a play to management at Drury Lane, feuds with rival companies and with the poets who succeeded, and final retirement; it is interrupted by set defences of the author's treatment of the Shakespearean text, of his own dramatic writings, and of the actors and actresses he employed. Passages of portraiture of players, managers and their noble patrons are worked up from memory and were repeatedly borrowed by later historians of the stage. The memoir prints or paraphrases the prologues, epilogues and occasional verses by which its author had advertised himself, and quotes the insults levelled at him at length so as to return them with good humour.
works.significance: It is the principal source-book for the company history, repertory and acting style of the London stage between the 1680s and the 1730s, and the standard illustration of how a manager turned autobiography into reply. Historians use its testimony with caution because self-love governs its dates and its judgments, and its apology for adapting the national dramatist to modern taste is the fullest contemporary defence of that practice.
works.context: The memoir was put together in the years of the author's retirement, when the theatre he described had been reconstituted by new managers and licences, and when the satire that had made his name a byword for dullness was still in circulation. It belongs to the flourishing of theatrical memoir and anecdote that also produced the biographical prefaces of the play collections of the 1730s and 1740s, and it is a specimen of the Augustan practice of answering lampoon with autobiography.
works.characters: the author himself as boy, actor, manager and old man; the players and actresses of the two patent houses; the booksellers and rivals with whom he quarrelled; the noble patrons and box-keepers of the theatre
works.structure: Continuous first-person prose narrative running in one line from youth to old age, with documentary matter - verses, letters, the published records of quarrels - embedded in it and with digressive chapters on the drama and on editorial dealings with the national dramatist.

works.title: Appius and Virginia
works.form: tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: Dennis's blank-verse Roman tragedy, drawn from the decemviral history of Livy, in which the lust of the mighty magistrate for a plebeian maid and the father's pious murder of her become a study of corrupt power, chastity and republican fury. Severe in its moral register and unstinted in its invective against the decemvirs, it is the dramatic illustration of the theories of enthusiasm and of the terrors of virtue set out in the treatises of 1701 and 1704. Its failure at the playhouse and the quarrel over its re-use by other authors made it also the most famous case in the century of the professional writer's grievance.
works.plot: Appius, one of the decemvirs, designs to get Virginia, the betrothed of Icilius, by a judicial fiction of sale, and uses his authority to defeat her advocates in the forum; Virginius, her father, rather than yield her to the tyrant's power, kills her in the street with a sentence that at once frees and destroys her; the outraged commons secede, the decemviral yoke is attacked, and Appius, stripped of office and abandoned by his patrons, dies in captivity. The play thus moves from the corruption of law into tyranny, to private catastrophe, and then to the restoration of public liberty.
works.significance: Its severity and its political indignation made it a permanent exemplum of the neglected Augustan tragedian, and the anecdote attached to it entered the common lore of authorial property in dramatic texts; it also survives as the practical test case of a critical theory that demanded terror, enthusiasm and moral gravity in the same play.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, declamatory and heavily sententious, with long impassioned periods and a deliberate accumulation of terror-words proper to Dennis's account of poetical enthusiasm.
works.context: First acted in London in 1709, in a season when the theatre was contested ground for Whig and Tory interpretations of Roman liberty; it held the stage for only a very short run, and the later revival of its scenes in another company's play provoked Dennis's well-known public protest against the appropriation of his work.
works.characters: Appius Claudius; Virginia; Virginius; Icilius; the seceding commons of Rome
works.structure: Regular five-act tragedy in the neoclassical manner, with a public forum action, a central recognition and killing, and an offstage political resolution; the catastrophe is reported rather than represented, and the political action closes the design.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Dennis's ownership of the text is documented by his own publication and by the anecdote of the reclaimed scenes.
