works.title: Colloquia (Ælfric Bata)
works.manuscriptDate: Oxford, St John's College MS 154 (eleventh century), alongside Ælfric's Colloquy
works.description: A pair of Latin conversation manuals by Ælfric Bata, a pupil of Ælfric of Eynsham: the Colloquia and the harder Colloquia difficiliora. Modelled on Ælfric's Colloquy, they dramatize the daily life of the monastic school with boisterous, hyperbolic dialogues about food, drink, beatings, theft, and the relations of master and pupil.
works.plot: The dialogues stage conversations among schoolboys and between pupils and master: bargaining for food, complaining of hunger, confessing petty theft, enduring (and threatening) beatings, and practising the vocabulary of daily life in the monastery — shoes, clothes, bedding, the refectory, the infirmary, and the latrine.
works.significance: The most vivid surviving picture of eleventh-century English school life, and evidence of the living tradition of spoken Latin that the Benedictine Reform established in English monasteries.
works.context: Composed in the generation after Ælfric's Colloquy (c. 998), the dialogues show the continuity of the reform's vernacular-Latin classroom tradition into the eleventh century, and their earthy realism is a deliberate antidote to the classicizing curriculum.
works.characters: Ælfric Bata (speaker), his pupils, stock schoolboys and masters
works.structure: A loose sequence of dramatic dialogues without sustained plot, each built to drill vocabulary through exchange; the speakers are stock schoolboys and masters, and the humour is deliberately exaggerated.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ælfric Bata, who names himself in the texts and addresses Ælfric of Eynsham as his master; the attribution is conventional and generally accepted, though the texts are transmitted anonymously in their manuscript.
themes: The marriage market and the limited estate
sources: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson

works.title: Colloquy
works.form: grammar and didactic prose (dialogue) in Latin with Old English gloss
works.description: A school dialogue between a master and his pupils who impersonate the trades — ploughman, shepherd, oxherd, hunter, fisherman, merchant, shoemaker, smith, cook — composed by Ælfric for the teaching of Latin conversation, with an Old English interlinear gloss added later by a teacher (Ælfric Bata). The liveliest classroom text of the Anglo-Saxon period.
works.plot: The master questions each boy about his craft: the ploughman feeds the oxen, the hunter takes deer and boar for the king, the fisherman risks the sea for his catch, the merchant crosses the sea to sell and buy; each defends the dignity of his work, and the dialogue ends with the master's advice on industry and good counsel.
works.significance: The most vivid picture of Anglo-Saxon daily life and trades in the period's literature.
works.meter: Latin prose with interlinear Old English gloss.
works.context: Composed c. 998-1005 at Cerne Abbas or Eynsham; the unique manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Tiberius A.iii (mid-eleventh century).
works.characters: the Master; the pupils (ploughman, shepherd, hunter, fisherman, fowler, merchant, shoemaker, salter, baker, cook, and others)
works.structure: A question-and-answer dialogue of some 75 exchanges, each trade a set piece.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ælfric on stylistic grounds; the Old English gloss is by another hand (Ælfric Bata).
themes: The English vernacular and national letters
movements: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling
sources: The Diary of Samuel Pepys

works.title: Colonel Jack
altTitles: The Life and Unexpected Fortunes of Jack the Thoughtful
The Fortunes and Misfortunes of Jack the Thoughtful
works.description: The life of a boy taken from a Newgate-connected childhood into a career of theft, transportation, soldiering and finally plantation ownership. It is the third and most openly autobiographical of the 1722 criminal narratives, with a narrator whose self-examination is obsessive and whose social climbing is a study in the making of a gentleman.
works.plot: Jack, the son of a widowed mother left in want, is apprenticed to a dancing master, runs away to London, and is drawn into a gang of child thieves drilled by an old pickpocket. He is tried and transported, escapes in America, and after a series of raids and duels becomes a planter; he raises horse in the wars in Flanders, takes the title in the army, and returns to England to marry. Throughout, the narrative pauses to audit his own motives and to count his shifts from honour to criminality and back.
works.significance: It is the most candid analysis in early fiction of class mobility and of the moral vocabulary of repentance as a social credential, and its child-thief episodes are a primary source for the history of London street life.
works.meter: Colloquial, garrulous first-person prose heavy with cant terms of the flash languages and with the accounting idiom of estates; the repentance sections adopt the periodic syntax of the serious address.
works.context: Published in the same current of Newgate biography as the criminal lives of 1722, and drawing on the post-1718 transportation trade and on the war in the Low Countries, which supplies the military career of the title.
works.characters: Colonel Jack; his mother and sister; the dancing master; the old pickpocket and the child gang; the Virginia and Carolina landlords; his several wives
works.structure: First-person autobiography in two parts closing in a conversion narrative, moving from picaresque episode to moral accounting; the narrator repeatedly interrupts himself to examine his own designs.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested in modern scholarship; the first part's title-page attributes the work to the author of Moll Flanders.

works.title: Commentaries on the Laws of England
altTitles: Commentaries on the Laws of England, in Four Volumes
works.description: Blackstone's four-volume systematization of the common law, grown from his Oxford Vinerian lectures of 1753 onward: rights of persons, rights of things, private wrongs, and public wrongs. It made English law a teachable rational science and became the most influential legal book of the English-speaking world.
works.plot: Volume I narrates the rise of the laws, the kingdom's constitutional structure, and the rights of persons, from royal prerogative and parliamentary independence to domestic relations. Volume II reduces property, tenure, inheritance, and title to an intelligible historical grammar. Volume III treats civil wrongs and remedies, wrongs to things, and the law of actions. Volume IV defines crimes, their justifications and extenuations, and the machinery of public justice from arrest to pardon. Throughout, Blackstone presents the common law as a repository of collective wisdom, mild in its proportion of punishments and jealous of liberty, though later reformers found its apologetic tone and its fictions indefensible.
works.significance: It fixed the vocabulary in which English and Americans spoke of law, liberty, and property; Bentham's attack on it founded philosophical radicalism, while its account of the balanced constitution entered the Federal Convention's debates.
works.meter: Elevated,periodic expository prose deliberately written for gentlemen as well as lawyers, with set-piece characterizations of the constitution and frequent literary allusion.
works.context: Published by Clarendon Press at Oxford and W. Strahan in London between 1765 and 1769 after the lectures of the 1750s, it appeared in the age of Mansfield, of American rights rhetoric, and of Bentham's first Fragment; American lawyers before 1800 read it as a declaration of inherited liberty.
works.structure: A four-part systematic exposition ordered by the analytical divisions of the law, each volume a continuous argument from history to institution to remedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Common Sense
altTitles: Common Sense; Addressed to the Inhabitants of America
works.description: Paine's pamphlet of January 1776, written in a plain man's vernacular to carry the American colonists from grievance to independence. It sold by the hundred thousand, renamed the war's cause, and became the model of the revolutionary pamphlet as an instrument of mass politics.
works.plot: Paine opens by separating society from government, society a blessing produced by our wants and government a necessary evil produced by our wickedness, and then strikes at the royal constitution as an absurdity of hereditary succession in which a brutish herd of kings succeeds over a nation of cattle. He argues from common sense, scripture, and the natural order that a remote island ruling a continent is an inversion, that the true interest of America is independence, trade, and foreign alliance, and that the hour of separation has arrived while the colonies are armed and united. The closing parts on the present ability of America and on a continental frame of government turn the pamphlet into a practical argument for declaring war in the name of a new era.
works.significance: It is the most influential pamphlet in American history and a world-historical specimen of the plain style in politics, establishing the rhetoric of rights, republican modernity, and a new era that Paine's later writing extended.
works.meter: The new demotic: short declarative sentences, biblical cadences, single-word emphatic closes, the pulpit and the tavern fused into a political style.
works.context: Written in Philadelphia in late 1775 with Franklin's countenance and published anonymously in January 1776, sold in every colony and read aloud in the camps, it made independence thinkable within weeks and was cited by Washington and delegates as the turn of the crisis.
works.structure: A short pamphlet in numbered sections: of the origin of government, of monarchy and hereditary succession, of the present American dispute, of present ability, and of thoughts on a form of government, with preface, appendix, and a postscript added in later issues.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously, by 'AN OLD Englishman'; Paine's authorship was acknowledged in the colonies within months and he became its known author in Europe after the Rights of Man.

works.title: Complaints
altTitles: Complaints: Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie
works.description: A volume of shorter poems on the vanity of worldly things, gathering The Ruines of Time, The Teares of the Muses, Virgils Gnat, Prosopopoia (or Mother Hubberds Tale), The Ruines of Rome (from du Bellay), Muiopotmos (or The Fate of the Butterflie), and Visions of the Worlds Vanitie.
works.plot: The poems vary from the beast-fable of Mother Hubberds Tale — the Fox and the Ape swindling their way to courtly power — to the mock-heroic tragedy of the butterfly Clarion in Muiopotmos, and the elegiac ruins meditations translated and adapted from du Bellay.
works.significance: The chief English monument of the Renaissance 'ruins of time' tradition and the home of the most influential Elizabethan beast satire.
works.meter: Varied: rhyme royal, ottava rima, and the Spenserian experiments of the translations from du Bellay.
works.context: Printed in 1591 while Spenser was in Ireland; Mother Hubberds Tale was long read as a satire on Burghley's court, and the volume was among the works attacked by the authorities in the 1599 satires ban.
works.characters: The Fox; the Ape (Mother Hubberds Tale); Clarion the butterfly; Aragnoll the spider (Muiopotmos)
works.structure: A miscellany of independent poems unified by the complaint-and-vanity theme, in varied forms from fable to vision.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Composed upon Westminster Bridge
works.form: Romantic sonnet and descriptive topographical lyric; the poem applies the vocabulary of the picturesque and of the sublime to an urban scene rather than to mountain scenery.
works.description: A single descriptive sonnet written on the morning passage over the Thames, when the city lay asleep and its houses, ships and temples appeared in the beauty of the morning. It is remarkable in the poet's work as a wholly urban sublime, and in the history of the English sonnet as one of the few lyrics of the period that praise a great city without moralising about it.
works.plot: The opening declares that no touch of solemn beauty is greater than this, and that the city wears the splendour of the earliest morning as though it were a garment, the houses seeming asleep while the bright and glistening Thames flows at his own sweet will and cares nothing for the hearts that stir below. The steeples, the theatres and the temples glitter in the dawn pure and bright, the fields are open and the air is smokeless, and the speaker insists that the dulllest eye must feel the stillness and the mighty spectacle. The closing lines name the reason of the calm: the great heart of the city lies at rest, its thousand homes are yet asleep, and the awake multitude that will fill the shops with strength has not yet risen. The argument is a paradox inherited from Augustan descriptive verse and here reversed: the loveliest hour of the busiest city is that in which it does nothing.
works.significance: One of the most quoted short poems in the language and the standard instance of the Romantic urban sublime, much discussed for its stillness, its impersonality and its defiance of the wilderness as the only seat of greatness. It helped revive the English sonnet after its long eclipse in the mid-eighteenth century.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter in a Petrarchan-style sonnet with an irregular rhyme scheme that runs in the opening through interlocking and repeated sounds, making the form closer to Milton's English sonnets than to the fashionable Miltonic imitation of the day.
works.context: Dated by its title to the morning of 3 September 1802, on the journey that took the poet and his sister from London towards Calais; it belongs to the cluster of early sonnets on public and topical subjects, and it was first printed several years later in the 1807 collected edition.
works.characters: The sleeping city of London; the Thames, rolling at his own sweet will; the passing observer on the bridge
works.structure: A compressed occasional lyric in sonnet form: statement of theme, sequential description of river, buildings and sky, an appeal to the reader's sensibility, and a closing restatement of the stillness observed.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: Comus (A Masque Presented at Ludlow Castle)
works.description: A masque written for the installation of the Earl of Bridgewater as Lord President of Wales and performed at Ludlow Castle on Michaelmas night 1634: the Lady, separated from her brothers, is tempted by the sorcerer Comus to sensual pleasure but preserves her chastity through steadfast virtue, and is freed by the Attendant Spirit and Sabrina.
works.plot: Comus ensnares the Lady with an enchanter's cup, immobilising her body while her mind remains free; her brothers and the Attendant Spirit rout Comus, and the water-nymph Sabrina releases the Lady, who is presented to her parents.
works.significance: Milton's longest early poem and a transformation of the masque into serious moral poetry; its celebration of chastity and virtue anticipates the ethical concerns of Paradise Lost.
works.meter: Blank verse interspersed with lyric songs; a grave, elevated style unusual for the court masque.
works.context: Composed in 1634 with music by Henry Lawes, who played the Attendant Spirit; it adapts the court masque to a serious moral and Puritan-inflected theme of chastity.
works.characters: the Lady; Comus; the two Brothers; the Attendant Spirit (Thyrsis); Sabrina
works.structure: A masque in blank verse and song, with a moral-allegorical debate between the Lady and Comus, a masque-typical resolution by a deity, and a concluding song and epilogue.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published anonymously in 1637, then in the 1645 Poems under Milton's name.

works.title: Confessio Amantis
works.description: John Gower's English masterpiece: a collection of some 140 exemplary tales, mostly from Ovid, framed by the confession of the aging lover Amans to Genius, priest of Venus, who anatomizes the seven deadly sins as they corrupt love. Over 33,000 lines of octosyllabic couplets, with a Latin apparatus, it is the most substantial English poem of the century after the Canterbury Tales.
works.plot: Amans, sick with unrequited love, prays to Venus and Cupid, who assign him Genius as confessor; book by book, Genius examines him on the sins of love, illustrating each with exemplary narratives — Florent and the loathly lady, Constance, Apollonius of Tyre, the tale of the Three Questions, and the story of Nebuchadnezzar's dream that closes the poem with a mirror for kings — until Venus cures him, shows him his aged face, and dismisses him 'John Gower' from love's service.
works.significance: The classic English poem of the seven sins and the great 'mirror' collection of the Ricardian age; its tales (Apollonius, Florent) entered Shakespeare and the English narrative tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of great smoothness — the 'middle style' Gower made his own.
works.context: Composed c. 1386–90 at the request of Richard II (first recension) and revised for Henry of Lancaster (c. 1392–93), in the period of the Peasants' Revolt and the king's fall; preserved in some fifty manuscripts and printed by Caxton (1483).
works.characters: Amans (John Gower); Genius; Venus; Cupid; the exemplary figures of the tales
works.structure: An eight-book confessional frame (prologue, seven sins, epilogue) enclosing the exemplary tales, with the lover's cure as the poem's comic-pathetic resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Gower's authorship secure; the poem's Latin verses name him throughout.

works.title: Confessions of an English Opium-Eater
altTitles: Confessions of an English Opium-Eater: Taken from an Old Manuscript
works.form: Inward confession and autobiographical prose narrative, combining the memoir, the dream vision and the analytical self-examination in a single confessional form.
works.description: An autobiographical narrative first published in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine in the autumn of 1821 and in book form in London in 1822, giving the account of a young man's years of opium consumption and of the dreams, the terrors and the miseries that it produced. Its matter is the writer's own student life, his flight from his family home, his wandering in Oxford and in the streets of London, his first acquaintance with laudanum as a remedy for bodily pain, and the cascades of dream imagery and of fear that followed, ending with a resolution to moderate but not to abandon the habit. It created the literature of the intoxicating confessional and remains the standard document of opium in English letters.
works.plot: The narrative moves in two parts. The first gives the prehistory of the dreamer's terrors: the death of his mother in his earliest childhood, the tyranny of a schoolmaster at a grammar school in the west, the quarrel with a stern home authority which drove the boy from his family to the lodging of a fellow-student at Oxford, and the weeks of solitary wandering in Oxford and in the streets of London with little money and no protection, in which a friendless outcast girl received such shelter as he could give, and in which opium was first taken as a remedy against bodily suffering. The second part reports the effects of the confirmed habit: the long sleep of some days' duration, the architecture and the populations of the dreams, the mystic stairs and the rooms and the faces without number, the Malay and the persecuting powers, and the recurring sense of space and of eternity in which the hours of sleep became ages. It closes with the account of the bettered and moderated use of the remedy, the plain statement that the writer had no intention of abandoning opium, and the acknowledgement of the consolations and the powers of the faculty which the habit had also given him.
works.significance: The founding text of the literature of intoxication and of the analytic confession in English, and the work that gave the language its vocabulary for the dream and for the pleasure and the terror of the altered mind. Its influence on later confessional writing and on the literature of drugs has been permanent, and it is a standard text for the history of autobiography and of the Romantic study of the mind.
works.meter: Prose of a highly finished and Latinate periodic style, with long accumulating sentences in the passages of terror and short declarative sentences in the moral reflections, and a constant use of parenthesis and of the apostrophe to the reader.
works.context: Written after the author's settlement in the northern lake country, in the character of a private record of the years of the opium habit, and published in a Scottish monthly magazine in 1821 and in book form in 1822, at a time when the use of opium and laudanum was widely practised and unregulated and when the review journals were the chief vehicle of autobiographical revelation.
works.characters: The English opium-eater as narrator; his mother, lost in his earliest childhood; the schoolmaster of the grammar school; the stern authority of the broken home; the fellow-student of the Oxford lodging; the friendless girl of the London streets; the Malay and the persecuting forms of the dreams
works.structure: A first-person confessional in two parts, the prehistory and the dreams, with a closing section on the uses of the remedy; the sequence is chronological in the outer life and associational in the accounts of the dreams, and the book's unity is that of a self examined by its own memory.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the narrative was published anonymously at first, and the author's later edition of his own works revised and enlarged the text, so that the magazine version of 1821 and the revised book form differ.

works.title: Conjectures on Original Composition
altTitles: Conjectures on Original Composition in a Letter to a Friend
works.form: critical essay in the form of a letter
works.description: Young's critical essay on original genius, arguing that the great writer is made by nature and by his own industry rather than by the rules and the imitation of the ancients, and that an original composition is the only true growth of a literary nation.
works.plot: The letter distinguishes the original from the imitation writer, compares the modern scholar to the child of a later age who is dwarfed by his parents, pleads the cause of native genius and of the invention that copies nature rather than books, and closes on the religious dignity of the creative mind.
works.significance: It is the charter of the cult of genius in English criticism, translated into German almost at once and used by the romantic theorists and by the continent's argument about originality.
works.meter: Aphoristic prose of the maxims and the numbered head, with the sustained metaphor of growth, nature and the child.
works.context: Published in the same years as the first fragments of the Gaelic forgeries and of the debate on barbarism and genius, when the rules of taste were being displaced by the theory of original composition; Young's essay gave that theory its most quotable English statement.
works.structure: A continuous epistolary argument in numbered reflections, with the aphoristic proposition and the analogy carrying the sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Contemplations
altTitles: Several Poems Compiled with Great Variety of Wit and Learning (Contemplations)
works.description: Bradstreet's greatest and most personal poem, written in her later years and published posthumously in 1678: a meditation on nature, time, and mortality that moves from the beauty of the New England landscape to the vanity of the world and the hope of eternity.
works.plot: Contemplating the trees, rivers, sun, and seasons, the poet reflects on human mortality and the fall, envies the seeming permanence of nature, and turns to the promise of resurrection and heavenly bliss.
works.significance: Widely regarded as Bradstreet's finest poem and one of the first great American meditative lyrics, it influenced later nature and devotional poetry.
works.meter: A seven-line stanza (ababbcc) with a reflective, musical cadence and vivid natural imagery.
works.context: Composed in the 1660s–70s and published in Several Poems (1678) after Bradstreet's death; it reflects her mature Puritan faith and love of the New England landscape.
works.characters: the poet; nature
works.structure: A meditative lyric sequence of 33 seven-line stanzas moving from nature to spiritual reflection.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published posthumously.

works.title: Conversation
works.form: didactic-satiric familiar essay in verse, in the Thomsonian blank-verse manner
works.description: Cowper's first blank-verse essay poem, a gentle satire on the fashionable round of society written in the manner of Thomson's Castle of Indolence. Its speaker surveys the card-tables, the assemblies and the small talk of the great, and finds the whole machinery of politeness a study in emptiness and affectation. The poem is the opening movement of Cowper's long argument with the world that continues in Retirement and the Task.
works.plot: Addressed to a friend who proposes a day of company, the poem describes in order the scenes of fashionable intercourse - the thronged assembly of the great room, the card table, the opera and the playhouse, the talebearer and the prude - and shows each producing its own bored and envious characters. The satire closes not in despair but in a plea for conversation that is civil, instructive and cheerful, and for the society of a few chosen friends over the noise of many.
works.significance: It establishes the characteristic Cowperian voice - domestic, moral, mildly ironic, strongly opposed to the metropolitan world of display - and supplies the prosodic model for the Task. Its treatment of politeness makes it a useful document for the eighteenth-century debate on the codes of conduct.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of Thomson's school, with a colloquial ease, occasional couplet-like closures and much enjambement.
works.context: Written late in Cowper's Olney and early St Albans period and printed with the Poems of 1782, in a decade when the manners of the ton were a staple of periodical and novelistic satire; its Thomsonian manner reflects the revived esteem for the author of The Castle of Indolence.
works.characters: The advising speaker; the man of the world; the prude and the scandal-monger of the great room
works.structure: A familiar epistle in continuous blank verse, organised as a sequence of social scenes united by the addressing speaker's comments rather than by incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition rests on the biographical reckoning of Cowper's letters and on his own account of the poems of this period.

works.title: Conversations, Introducing Poetry to the Young
works.form: Juvenile, School and Educational Book; Conduct, Education, and Domestic Prose
works.description: Charlotte Smith's last educational work, issued in two volumes by Joseph Johnson in 1804, in which an elder sister and brother teach their younger relations to read and value poetry by conversation on walks and at home. The volume was also a repository of Smith's own shorter verse: several of the poems introduced and quoted there reappeared after her death in Beachy Head, and the book therefore preserves the last stage of her poetic as well as her pedagogical practice.
works.plot: The dialogues put poems and passages of poetry into the mouths and hands of children and of their instructress, using commentary, correction, and recollection to teach taste, sympathy, and moral judgement; the conversations argue that poetry is a form of knowledge proper to youth, and they model an education founded on pleasure and inquiry rather than on rote.
works.significance: Conversations is important as Smith's statement of a poetics for the young and as the source of her late shorter lyrics; it documents the transmission of Romantic verse into the educational market, and it preserves the last poems she lived to see prepared for the press.
works.meter: Prose dialogue interspersed with quoted lyric and descriptive verse in the traditional metres of the poems selected, some of them Smith's own.
works.context: Published in the last years of Smith's life, when her income depended on commissioned and educational work and when her juvenile trilogy had established her authority in children's publishing; it belongs to the same Joseph Johnson circle that had printed her poetry and fiction for two decades, and its poems were reserved for the posthumous volume that appeared in 1807.
works.characters: the young pupils of the conversations; their elder sisters and brothers who conduct the teaching; the poets quoted and explained
works.structure: Conversational and dialogic prose framed as family instruction, with quoted verse and explanatory comment, continuing the method of Rural Walks and Rambles Farther but turning specifically to the teaching of poetry.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

works.title: Cooper's Hill
works.description: Sir John Denham's topographical and reflective poem on the view from Cooper's Hill overlooking the Thames, Windsor, and Runnymede (1642), which yoked landscape description to history, politics, and moral meditation and established the English prospect poem.
works.plot: From the hill Denham surveys the Thames (praised for its useful, moderate, 'deep but clear' current as an emblem of ideal verse and government), Windsor, and the field of Runnymede, reflecting on Charles I, the Stag-hunt as allegory of the Civil Wars, and the balanced constitution.
works.significance: Cooper's Hill founded the English topographical and estate-meditation tradition (Marvell, Pope's 'Windsor-Forest', Thomson's Seasons) and its couplets shaped Augustan versification.
works.meter: The balanced closed heroic couplet, praised by Pope as 'strong sense ... most correctly writ'.
works.context: Written in 1642 at the outbreak of the Civil Wars and revised in later editions (1650, 1655, 1668); the stag-hunt episode was read as an allegory of the war and of Strafford's fate.
works.characters: the poet; Charles I (alluded to)
works.structure: A prospect poem in heroic couplets moving through the view from the hill with historical and moral digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Coriolanus
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of the aristocratic warrior against the people: Caius Martius, conqueror of Corioli and now 'Coriolanus', refuses to court the plebeians for the consulship, is banished by the tribunes, and joins his Volscian enemy Aufidius to march on Rome — until his mother Volumnia's plea in the Volscian camp breaks him, and his capitulation costs him his life at Aufidius's hands.
works.plot: The grain riots open the play; Coriolanus wins his name at Corioli; the tribunes Brutus and Sicinius manoeuvre him into rage and banishment; he defects to Aufidius and leads the Volscian army to Rome's gates; Volumnia, Virgilia, and the boy plead with him; he yields — 'O mother, mother!' — and Aufidius's faction cuts him down in Corioli.
works.significance: The most rigorously political of the tragedies — a study of pride, populism, and the state that speaks with undiminished force to every later oligarchy.
works.meter: A hard, sinewy verse of contempt and defiance, with the fable of the belly as the play's emblem of the body politic.
works.context: Written about 1607–08 amid the Midland grain riots and the Commons' assertiveness under James I; its class politics have made it the most divisive of the Roman plays in performance.
works.characters: Caius Martius Coriolanus; Volumnia; Virgilia; Menenius Agrippa; Tullus Aufidius; Cominius; Titus Lartius; Brutus; Sicinius Velutus; young Martius; Valeria
works.structure: A political tragedy built on the confrontation of the one and the many, with the plebeians' crowd-scenes as chorus and Volumnia's embassy as the play's reversal.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Count Basil: A Tragedy
works.description: The first play of a planned series in which it was attempted to delineate the stronger passions of the mind, and the number nominated by its own introductory discourse as the tragedy of love. It stands first in a volume published anonymously, prefaced by a long critical discourse on the analysis of passion on the stage, and it was long read as the manifesto of a new dramatic theory rather than as a theatre piece. Its hero is a general whose love is tried by the competing enthusiasm of glory.
works.plot: Count Basil, a general in the Emperor's service, loves Victoria and is beloved in return, while the honour of his house and the demands of the Italian wars in the time of the contest between the emperor and the French king press him to action. The play moves through the Mantuan court and camp, with rival suitors, a countess whose own feelings complicate the negotiation, and old-family opposition, to the battle after which the hero is cut off and killed by an unknown hand among the wreck of the field he has won. The catastrophe is the destruction of the lovemaking by the very martial virtue the passion of glory enforced, and the closing scenes are given to mourning rather than to settlement.
works.significance: Count Basil, with the companion pieces in its volume, is the most systematic attempt by any writer of the period to found a drama of psychological analysis on the older tragedy of humours, and the volume's discourse is a document of first importance for Romantic dramatic theory. Its modern recovery has made it central to the study of women's closet drama and of the theory of passion.
works.meter: Sustained blank verse of the closed eighteenth-century school, with a strong rhetorical line, set speeches of analysis and apostrophe, and little of the loose lyricism of the Romantic drama; the dialogue is built to expose the progress of one feeling.
works.context: Published anonymously in the last years of the eighteenth century in a volume printed in London for two Strand booksellers, at a moment when the licensed stage was closed to serious tragedy of this kind and when the analysis of a single passion was offered as a substitute for theatrical effect. The volume's critical preface explains the design of the whole series, of which this is the first number, and the anonymity led early reviewers to suppose the writer a man.
works.characters: Count Basil; Victoria; Count Rosinberg; the Duke of Mantua; the Countess of Albini; Geoffry; Mirando
works.structure: A regular five-act tragedy in blank verse with an argument prefixed, single-action construction, and a progression from domestic negotiation through the field of battle to death and lamentation; no sub-plot is allowed to divide the governing passion.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in the first volume; the author's identity was established within a few years and the series was reissued under her name.

works.title: Creation, a Philosophical Poem
altTitles: Creation: A Philosophical Poem, Written in the Measure of Milton's Paradise Lost
works.description: Blackmore's physico-theological poem, which reads the frame of nature, the senses, the faculties of the mind and the order of the creation as evidence of one intelligent and benevolent Maker, and defends reason against enthusiasm and atheism.
works.plot: The poem contemplates the chaos and the formation of the world, the parts of animals, the mechanisms of the senses and the passions, and the immateriality of the soul, drawing from each the argument for a Deity and for a moral order established in nature.
works.significance: It is the largest English attempt to put the physico-theological argument in Miltonic verse, and its quarrel with Pope over the originality of the Essay on Man makes it a document of the century's dispute about optimism.
works.meter: Unrhymed five-beat lines in the Miltonic measure Blackmore claims on his title page, of a deliberate and often lumbering fullness.
works.context: Written in the season of the Boyle lectures and of the vogue for the argument from the frame of nature, after Ray, Derham and the new mechanical philosophy had made the observation of the creatures a branch of natural religion.
works.characters: the poet-teacher; the Deity addressed; the mind of man as the spectacle
works.structure: A continuous argument in numbered books, each a course of natural and philosophical reflection rising to a theological conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Crotchet Castle
works.description: the author's last major novel, a savage comic satire on the mania for educational and social reform in the Reform Bill era, in which the Rev. MacGurry gathers a party of literary projectors at Crotchet Castle. It is the author's broadest assault on the pretensions of systematic thinking.
works.plot: The Rev. Dr. MacGurry, a London publisher and collector of manuscripts, invites his literary friends — a political arithmetician, a school-reformer, a civil architect, and others — to Crotchet Castle in Wales. Each proposes a scheme for the regeneration of society; the castle and grounds become a comic laboratory of incompatible reforms. The party's attempts at arranged marriages and philosophical education collapse in chaos; the novel ends with the party dispersing and MacGurry returning to London, his manuscripts unimproved.
works.significance: Crotchet Castle is the fullest expression of the author's satire of the 'projector' tradition reaching back to Ben Jonson and the Augustans; its assault on systematic reform anticipates Victorian critiques of Utilitarianism and is a central document of the intellectual reaction against progress in late Romantic England.
works.context: Published in 1831, on the eve of the Great Reform Act, during the surge of Utilitarian and evangelical social-reform projects; the author satirises the reform mania with an intensity shaped by the political crisis. It is his most explicitly political novel.
works.characters: The Rev. Dr. MacGurry; Miss MacGurry; Mr. Pip; Mr. Short; Miss Lory Rickburst; Mr. Thrigmorton; Countess Pearl
works.structure: Single country-house setting; episodic sequence of project-arrivals and practical failures; intellectual comedy carried by dialogue rather than conventional plot.

works.title: Croxton Play of the Sacrament
works.description: An East Anglian miracle play of c. 1461 on the host: the Jewish merchant Jonathas and his fellows buy the consecrated wafer from the Christian merchant Aristorius, subject it to their tests — and when they stab it, it bleeds, and the image of Christ appears, converting them all. Its staging directions (the cauldron, the severed hand, the miraculous oven) make it the most spectacular of the English miracle plays.
works.plot: Aristorius, tempted by gold, sells the host to Jonathas, who with his companions proves it in their own body of tests: boiling, oven, and dagger; the host bleeds, sticks to Jonathas's hand, and the image of Christ as a child reproves them; their conversion follows, the church is reconciled, and the play ends with the doctor's epilogue and the procession.
works.significance: The fullest English miracle play and the most spectacular document of the late medieval eucharistic cult; its staging is central to the history of English theatre.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, with stage directions prescribing spectacular effects.
works.context: Composed c. 1461 at Croxton, Norfolk (the banns name the village), when the cult of the host and the Corpus Christi confraternities flourished; its treatment of Jews reflects the period's anti-Judaism, and its conversion plot the theology of eucharistic miracle; preserved in Trinity College, Dublin, MS F.4.20.
works.characters: Jonathas; Aristorius the merchant; the priest Isoder; the Jews Jason, Jasdon, Masphat, Malchus; the Bishop; the Image of Christ
works.structure: A two-part miracle (the bargain and the testing; the miracle and conversion), framed by the banns and the closing sermon.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Cursor Mundi
works.description: A vast northern verse history of the world, some 24,000 lines, 'running' (cursor) through sacred history from Creation to Doomsday: Old Testament narrative, the life of Christ, the Virgin, the apostles, and the finding of the cross. The most comprehensive biblical paraphrase in Middle English, designed to rival secular romance in the affections of its audience.
works.plot: The poem retells the Old and New Testament story in chronological sequence — Creation, the patriarchs, Christ's life and Passion, the early church — with moralizations and legends (including the harrowing of hell) woven into the biblical narrative.
works.significance: The largest Middle English biblical poem and the principal popular scriptural compendium before the Wycliffite Bible; a major witness to lay biblical culture.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets (with some septenary sections) in the northern dialect.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 in the north of England (Durham or Yorkshire), in the tradition of the Historia Scholastica and vernacular biblical paraphrase; preserved in nine manuscripts, with a southern version made c. 1400.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the patriarchs, apostles, and saints
works.structure: A seven-part chronicle following the ages of the world, with prologue and epilogue framing the narrative as a book for 'lewed' men.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: Perdita: The Life of Mary Robinson

works.title: Cygnea Cantio
works.description: Leland's Latin poem in praise of the Thames, in which a swan sings as it glides down the river from Oxford to London, celebrating the towns, palaces, and worthies along its banks; published with a long commentary by the author in 1545.
works.plot: The swan's song follows the Thames from its source past Oxford, Windsor, and Hampton Court to Westminster and London, praising each place and the Tudor dynasty; the commentary supplies the antiquarian and topographical learning that the verse compresses.
works.significance: The earliest sustained literary celebration of the Thames and the model for the river-poems of Spenser (the Thames–Medway marriage) and Denham's Cooper's Hill; a key monument of Tudor antiquarian humanism.
works.meter: Latin hexameters
works.context: Published 1545 during Leland's final productive years, as part of his programme of celebrating the antiquities of Britain in Latin verse (the unpublished Genethliacon and the unfinished De uiris illustribus).
works.characters: The Swan (speaker)
works.structure: A single long Latin poem with Leland's own prose commentary, a form modelled on the Renaissance edition of a classical text.

works.title: Cymbeline
works.description: Shakespeare's romance of ancient Britain: Imogen, married secretly to the low-born Posthumus, is slandered by the villain Iachimo's wager; banished and betrayed, she flees in disguise as the boy Fidele to Wales, where her lost brothers live in the cave of Belarius; the Roman war, the dream of Jupiter, and the final scene's cascade of recognitions restore the family and the kingdom.
works.plot: Iachimo hides in Imogen's trunk to 'prove' her infidelity; Posthumus orders her death; Pisanio spares her and she flees; the potion's mock-death, the cave, and Cloten's pursuit lead to the war with Rome; Posthumus fights for Britain in disguise; and the last scene unravels every knot — brothers, husband, father, and the tribute of peace.
works.significance: The most experimental of the romances — a laboratory of plot whose final scene outdoes all its rivals in the theatre of recognition.
works.meter: A late style of extreme compression and ellipsis, with the dirge 'Fear no more the heat o' the sun' and the vision of Jupiter as its lyric heights.
works.context: Written about 1609–10 from Holinshed's British matter and Boccaccio; its peace with Rome mirrors James I's pacific foreign policy.
works.characters: Imogen (Fidele); Posthumus Leonatus; Cymbeline; the Queen; Cloten; Iachimo; Pisanio; Belarius; Guiderius; Arviragus; Caius Lucius; Jupiter (in the apparition)
works.structure: A romance of three worlds — court, Wales, Rome — braided into the single great recognition scene of Act 5, with the wager-plot from Boccaccio at its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Cædmon's Hymn
works.manuscriptDate: margins of eighth-century manuscripts of Bede
works.description: A nine-line praise poem to God the Creator, composed, according to Bede's Historia ecclesiastica (IV.24), by the illiterate cowherd Cædmon after a dream in which he was commanded to sing of the beginning of created things. It is the earliest datable poem in Old English.
works.plot: The poem praises the heavenly Father, the measurer of fate, who established the beginning of every wonder: first he created heaven as a roof for the children of men, then the middle-earth, the guardian of mankind made the earth for men. (This is the traditional five-line paraphrase; the text runs to nine lines with epithets varying by version.)
works.significance: The earliest surviving English poem and the foundation of the English religious poetic tradition.
works.meter: Nine lines of alliterative accentual metre, with formulaic epithets ('heofonrices weard', 'moncynnes weard').
works.context: Composed c. 657–680 at Whitby under Abbess Hild; Bede gives a Latin paraphrase and says the vernacular text was preserved; it survives in Old English in the margins and endleaves of some twenty-one manuscripts of the Historia, the earliest (the 'Moore Bede') datable to 737.
works.characters: God the Creator
works.structure: A single doxological period: address, epithets of God, and the two works of creation (heaven, earth).
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally attributed to Cædmon on Bede's authority; the extant Old English texts are translations back from oral memory of the original, which Bede knew only in paraphrase.

sources: A Book of Middle English, 4th edition

works.title: Dame Sirith
altTitles: The Interlude of the Clerk and the Girl
works.description: The earliest English fabliau: a comic tale of 450 lines in which the clerk Wilekin, failing to seduce Margery, buys the services of the old bawd Dame Sirith, whose trick with a weeping dog convinces Margery to yield. The poem may have been designed for performance by one or two speakers.
works.plot: The lovesick clerk Wilekin woos Margery without success; Dame Sirith, hired for a fee, persuades Margery that her weeping bitch is a transformed woman punished for refusing a clerk — and Margery consents rather than share that fate.
works.significance: The first English fabliau and a landmark in the history of English comedy and secular drama; the bawd-and-trickster plot anticipates Chaucer's fabliaux.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets with dialogue assignable to speakers (semi-dramatic form).
works.context: Composed c. 1275 in the East Midlands; preserved in Bodleian Library, Digby MS 86 (c. 1300).
works.characters: Wilekin the clerk; Margery; Dame Sirith
works.structure: A short fabliau of courtship, trickery, and capitulation, largely in dialogue, with explicit staging cues.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: Hobomok: A Tale of Early Times (Broadview Edition)

works.title: Damon and Pythias
works.description: A blank-verse tragedy of friendship and tyranny, first acted at Covent Garden in May 1821 with a success that carried it through many reproductions and provincial revivals. Its subject is the classical legend of the two Pythagoreans and the tyrant of Syracuse, treated as an illustration of fidelity proved by the pledge of a life. The play is the Irish tragic revival of the Regency stage in the hands of a Kilkenny painter turned dramatist, and its power rests on the declaration of trust rather than on political argument.
works.plot: Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, condemns to death the Pythagorean philosopher whom he has accused of plotting against his government. The condemned man asks leave to go home and order his affairs and to settle the obligations of his family, and his friend offers himself as hostage on the condition that the prisoner's life forfeits his own if he fails to return. The tyrant grants the delay out of curiosity to see friendship tested, and watches the days pass with the hostage in his power. The friend returns at the hour of danger, and the demonstrated fidelity turns the tyrant's sentence and, in the play's resolution, his character. The action closes on the triumph of the bond over the despotic will.
works.significance: Damon and Pythias was the most performed Irish tragedy of the 1820s and remained a stock piece of provincial and declamatory recitation for half a century, giving the legend of friendship a modern theatrical form. It is also the central document of the author's reputation and the point at which the question of joint Irish dramatist authorship has been argued.
works.meter: Correct and sustained blank verse in the declamatory school of the early nineteenth century, with set speeches of friendship and of tyranny and little lyrical experiment; the line is regular and the caesura frequent, fitted for declamation by the tragedy actors of the patent houses.
works.context: Written after the author's removal from Kilkenny to London, where his drawings and his Irish tales made him known, and produced in the season when Covent Garden was reviving classical and moral tragedy for a mixed house. The play's subject had an English schoolroom currency through the eighteenth-century versions of the legend, and its treatment belongs to the Regency taste for proofs of virtue made in the presence of a tyrant.
works.characters: Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse; Damon, the hostage for his friend's life; Pythias, the condemned philosopher; the courtiers and officers of the tyrant
works.structure: A regular five-act tragedy in blank verse with a single moral experiment as its skeleton; the delay, the counting of the days, and the return form the mechanical centre, and the scenes of the court supply the pressure that tests it.
works.attributionNotes: The play is constantly said to have been a joint work with an older Irish dramatist; the author's biographer denies the shared claim, and the first edition and the contemporary accounts carry the Kilkenny writer's name alone. The matter remains unresolved, and the record here follows the printed attribution.

works.title: Daniel
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 764 lines on the book of Daniel, from the Junius manuscript: the three youths in Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace, the king's dream of the tree and his madness, and the fall of Babylon to the Medes and Persians under the writing on the wall — with the liturgical Canticles of the three youths (the 'Azarias' material) expanded into songs of praise.
works.plot: The poem follows Daniel and his companions at the Babylonian court; Nebuchadnezzar's idol and the furnace; the king's dream of the great tree, interpreted by Daniel as his own pride and coming fall; his seven years of bestial madness and restoration; Belshazzar's feast, the writing on the wall, and the city's fall to Cyrus. The youths' prayers and songs in the furnace (the Canticum trium puerorum) are rendered as extended lyric passages.
works.significance: A sustained meditation on pride and the fall of kings, central to the Junius manuscript's providential scheme.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the canticle passages show a more ornate, lyrical style.
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11); related to the Exeter Book poem Azarias, which preserves a version of the first canticle.
works.characters: Daniel; Nebuchadnezzar; Belshazzar; Azarias, Ananias, and Misael (the three youths); Cyrus
works.structure: Episodic biblical narrative punctuated by lyric set-pieces (the canticles), with an admonitory frame on pride and the fall of kings.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: The New Science and experimental philosophy
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Alexander Pope

works.title: Davideis
altTitles: Davideis: A Sacred Poem of the Troubles of David
works.description: Abraham Cowley's unfinished biblical epic in four books (in Poems, 1656), retelling the persecution of David by Saul in heroic couplets, with a preface defending the modern epic and arguing for a Christian verse built on rhyme rather than Milton's blank verse.
works.plot: The poem narrates David's flight and troubles under Saul's jealous pursuit, drawing on the books of Samuel, with digressions and a prefatory argument on epic theory and the state of English poetry.
works.significance: An influential, if unfinished, attempt at a modern Christian epic, important for its couplet form and its theory of epic, and as a foil to Milton's practice.
works.meter: Closed heroic couplets, which Cowley advocated against rhymeless verse in his preface.
works.context: Published in 1656 during the Interregnum; its preface engages the debate about epic form and the future of English poetry that Milton would answer with Paradise Lost's blank verse.
works.characters: David; Saul; Jonathan
works.structure: A heroic epic in rhymed couplets (four books of a planned twelve), with a critical preface on epic conventions.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: De Cive
altTitles: Philosophical Rudiments Concerning Government and Society
works.description: Hobbes's first published statement of his political theory, the third part of his philosophical system, which argues from the state of nature to the necessity of an absolute sovereign and was published in Latin in Paris in 1642.
works.plot: In three parts — Libertas (the state of nature), Imperium (the establishment of government), and Religio (the kingdom of God) — Hobbes derives the sovereign's absolute authority from the natural right of self-preservation.
works.significance: The prototype of Leviathan and the first full modern statement of social contract theory; its influence on seventeenth-century political thought was immediate and enormous.
works.meter: Latin philosophical prose; translated into English as Philosophical Rudiments in 1651.
works.context: Published at Paris in April 1642, on the eve of the English civil wars, which Hobbes said determined his subject; expanded edition 1647.
works.structure: Eighteen chapters in three sections.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Hobbes; authorship undisputed.

works.title: De Civili Dominio
works.description: John Wyclif's most explosive treatise (1375–76), expounding his doctrine of dominion: lordship is founded on grace, so that the sinful clergy — the pope included — forfeit their right to temporal possessions, and kings may and must strip the church of its wealth. The book that made Wyclif the theorist of disendowment and the target of papal condemnation.
works.plot: Wyclif argues that all dominion derives from God and is held only by the righteous; the reprobate hold possessions unjustly; the clergy's endowment was conditional on their holiness and may be revoked by lay lords; and the English king, as God's vicar in his realm, is bound to reform and disendow the delinquent church.
works.significance: The theoretical charter of Lollardy's attack on ecclesiastical wealth and the most consequential political theology written in medieval England.
works.meter: Latin prose in the Oxford scholastic manner, relentlessly syllogistic.
works.context: Composed at Oxford and Lutterworth in 1375–76, when the papal-imperial politics of the Great Schism's prelude and the English crown's anti-papal statutes (Provisors, Praemunire) gave Wyclif's theories immediate political force; nineteen propositions from it were condemned by Gregory XI in 1377.
works.characters: none (theological treatise)
works.structure: Three books of scholastic argument, from the metaphysics of dominion through its application to the church to the duties of the king.
works.attributionNotes: Wyclif's authorship secure.
sources: Timothy Dwight, 1752-1817: A Biography

works.title: De Emendata Structura Latini Sermonis
altTitles: On the Correct Structure of Latin Prose
works.description: Thomas Linacre's treatise on Latin syntax, published in London by Richard Pynson in 1524; the first systematic Latin grammar composed by an Englishman and a landmark of the humanist reform of grammar.
works.plot: The work analyses Latin construction in six books, replacing the medieval speculative grammars with a descriptive account of syntax based on the usage of Cicero and the best classical authors, illustrated with abundant quotations.
works.significance: A founding document of English classical scholarship; its descriptive method influenced the whole European tradition of Latin grammar, and it secured Linacre's European reputation among humanists.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Linacre, physician to Henry VIII and the foremost English Greek scholar of his generation, composed the work over 1512–24 after his return from Italy; it was printed by Pynson and used in the schools alongside the authorized grammar.
works.structure: Six books of systematic grammatical exposition with a preface to Prince Arthur's tutor and a dedication to the grammar-school masters.

works.title: De excidio et conquestu Britanniae
altTitles: On the Ruin and Conquest of Britain
works.description: Gildas's jeremiad against the sins of the British kings and clergy, opening with the only near-contemporary narrative of the Saxon settlement of Britain, including the battle of Mount Badon. The principal source for post-Roman Britain and the foundation of the providential reading of British history that Bede adopted.
works.plot: Part I narrates the Roman occupation, the coming of the proud Saxons as mercenaries, their revolt, and the British resistance culminating in Ambrosius Aurelianus and the victory at Mount Badon. Parts II and III denounce the five tyrant kings (Constantine, Aurelius Caninus, Vortipor, Cuneglas, and Maglocunus) and the corrupt British clergy in the manner of the Old Testament prophets.
works.significance: The indispensable (if tendentious) source for the adventus Saxonum and for the moral theology of national disaster.
works.meter: Rhetorical Latin prose saturated with biblical allusion.
works.context: Composed in Britain, traditionally c. 540s, a generation after Mount Badon; the earliest surviving extended insular text after the Roman period.
works.characters: Ambrosius Aurelianus; the five tyrant kings; the Saxon mercenaries
works.structure: A tripartite sermon-polemic: historical prologue, royal denunciations, clerical denunciations — history entirely subordinated to moral exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Gildas's authorship is traditional and generally accepted; the dating rests on inference.
sources: English Literature in the Sixteenth Century, Excluding Drama

works.title: De Monfort
works.form: Drama; domestic and analytic tragedy of a single passion; closet-originated stage tragedy
works.description: A domestic tragedy in blank verse founded, in the author's own account, on the passion of hatred. De Monfort, raised by a benefactress and in love with her daughter, discovers that the man he has befriended is the son of his father's destroyer, and his settled hatred overmastering every other feeling drives him to kill him in a duel and confesses his hatred publicly. The play's power comes from the analysis of a single passion held up against softer domestic affection, and from its heroine's horrified discovery that the man she loves is an avenger. It was the most performed Romantic tragedy by a woman and a repertory piece for leading actors into the 1820s.
works.plot: De Monfort, adopted in childhood after his father's ruin and death, is beloved by Jane, the daughter of his benefactress, and is bound as well by a warm friendship with the amiable count, whose wife Rezenza had been De Monfort's own earlier attachment. When he learns that this friend is the son of the man whose prosecution destroyed his father, he resolves on revenge yet cannot extinguish his affection, and the strain of the two passions is dissected in long soliloquies. At a public entertainment Rezenza is accidentally shot by De Monfort's hand while he aims at the count, and she dies in a scene of terrified innocence. De Monfort then denounces the count before the company, abandons his love, and gives himself up to justice and despair.
works.significance: The most influential verse tragedy written by a woman in the Romantic period and a central text for study of the analysis-of-the-passions drama, of the debate between closet and acting texts, and of the nineteenth-century repertory's revival history. Its treatment of hatred as a self-consuming passion has been read as a case study in Romantic psychological determinism.
works.meter: Blank verse throughout, with a few rhymed passages for heightened effect; the idiom is conversational and argumentative rather than declamatory
works.context: Published in 1798 as the second volume of a series designed to delineate the stronger passions, and first played at Drury Lane in the spring of 1800 in a season when regulation domestic tragedy was competing with Gothic melodrama and with Shakespeare revivals. Its psychological method belongs to the late-eighteenth-century analysis of the passions carried on from the moral-philosophical tradition, and its female-authored domestic tragedy responded to the period's debate about women's access to the stage. A celebrated revival with a famous performer in the title role in the early 1820s re-established it in the repertory.
works.characters: De Monfort; Jane, the daughter of his benefactress and his beloved; the Count Montaigue, his friend and his father's son; Rezenza, his friend's wife and his early attachment; his old attendant and household dependants
works.structure: Regular five-act tragedy with a single ruling passion as its organising principle; dialogue and soliloquy carry the psychological analysis, and the catastrophe depends on a public scene of accidental death and open denunciation.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name in the series title page; no dispute. The play's prefatory argument naming the governing passion is the author's own critical statement.

Joanna Baillie: A Selection of Poems and Plays

works.title: De Nugis Curialium
works.description: Walter Map's miscellany of court gossip, satire, Welsh legend, ghost story, and moral anecdote, assembled piecemeal during his service at the court of Henry II; 'a jest book and a jest at the same time', as one editor put it, and the only certain work by one of the wittiest Latin writers of the age.
works.summary: Five distinctiones gather tales of the court of Henry II, satirical portraits of monks and courtiers, the legend of Sadius and Galo, the story of the Welsh king Herla and the fairy bride, and the earliest surviving connected account of the birth of Lancelot; Map's dissuasio to his friend Ruffinus against marriage closes the work.
works.significance: A unique window onto the oral culture and court life of Henry II's England, an early witness to Arthurian material, and a masterpiece of twelfth-century Latin satire and narrative.
sources: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice (Oxford World's Classics)

works.title: De temporum ratione
works.form: didactic and scientific prose (computus) in Latin
works.description: Bede's treatise on time and its reckoning, the standard medieval textbook of computus: the calculation of Easter, the solar and lunar cycles, the ages of the world, and — decisively — the practice of dating years from the Incarnation of Christ (annus Domini), which the work made universal in western Europe.
works.plot: The treatise proceeds from the smallest units of time (moments, hours, days) through the calendar, the lunar cycles, and the Easter tables to the great divisions of world history — the six ages of the world and the seventh age of rest — closing with a chronicle of the world's six ages down to 725.
works.significance: The most influential computistical work of the Middle Ages; the origin of the BC/AD dating convention in general use.
works.meter: Latin prose.
works.context: Composed at Jarrow in 725 for the monks' instruction; a revision and expansion of Bede's earlier De temporibus (703).
works.characters: none
works.structure: A systematic didactic treatise in 71 chapters, concluding with the world chronicle (chapter 66) as the practical demonstration of its chronology.
works.attributionNotes: Bede's authorship is certain.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume II: 1042–1189

works.title: De virginitate (prose and verse)
works.form: didactic treatise in Latin prose and hexameter verse
works.description: Aldhelm's double treatise in praise of virginity, composed in both prose and verse: a celebration of chastity sustained by a vast catalogue of exemplars — biblical heroes, virgin martyrs, and ascetics — in the ornate 'hermeneutic' Latin that made Aldhelm the model of insular style.
works.plot: The prose treatise (addressed to the nuns of Barking, headed by Hildelith) argues the superiority of virginity over marriage and the other states of life, adducing the patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, and virgins as witnesses; the accompanying Carmen de virginitate recasts the argument in hexameters with a culminating allegorical battle of the vices and virtues.
works.significance: The founding text of the Anglo-Latin literary tradition and of its characteristic learned style.
works.meter: Ornate hermeneutic Latin prose; the Carmen is in dactylic hexameters.
works.context: Composed for the double monastery of Barking, probably c. 675-705; the prose was praised by Bede and widely imitated.
works.characters: Hildelith and the nuns of Barking (addressees); the exemplars: Elijah, Daniel, the Maccabees, Agnes, Cecilia, and others
works.structure: A thematic treatise built from scriptural and hagiographical exempla, concluded by the allegorical psychomachia of the verse version.
works.attributionNotes: Aldhelm's authorship is certain.
themes: Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: English Petrarchism and the Sonnet Vogue
sources: TEAMS Middle English Texts Series

works.title: Death and Doctor Hornbook
works.form: debate poem and personal satire in the popular 'Death and the Doctor' dialogue tradition
works.description: Burns's rollicking dialogue-poem of Death and the parish schoolmaster-doctor, a personal pamphlet against Peter Buchan, the Tarbolton excisier and poet who had insulted him in print. Death comes to drag the quack Hornbook to his trial, and the schoolmaster protests his useful ignorance of theology till the summons is served. The poem converts a local quarrel into a full-scale comic debate of the Death and the Doctor type, and a satire on pedantic presumption.
works.plot: Death, in the homeliest terms, rouses the doctor from his bed to answer for his misdeeds, and the schoolmaster protests that he was never taught to fear such visitors and that his learning has been of the bookish and useless kind. The two dispute the merits of learning, of practice and of preparation for the hour of death, with the doctor's excuses running out as Death presses the account. The dialogue ends with the parson's discomfiture and with an author's appeal to common sense against the pretensions of the professional neighbour.
works.significance: It is the best example of Burns's power to turn private pique into durable poetry, and one of the liveliest surviving instances of the Death-and-doctor debate in British verse. Its portrait of the schoolmaster-poaster has become a standard document for the history of the parish school and of rural self-education.
works.meter: Stanzaic Scots in the rambling six-line measures of the old Scottish comic narrative, with colloquial idiom, internal rhyme and a running dialogue of matched speeches.
works.context: Written in 1784 as a reply to Buchan's The Farmer's Ingle, which had caricatured Burns and his friends, and thus belongs to the local literary quarrels of Tarbolton and Mauchline; at the same time it works in a folk tradition of Death-dialogues and in the eighteenth-century contempt for the quack and the small pedant.
works.characters: Death; Doctor Hornbook (a portrait of Peter Buchan); the poet-speaker of the argument
works.structure: A two-voice debate poem in continuous dialogue, opening with Death's arrival, sustaining the exchange of summons and excuse, and closing with a direct address of the poet to his adversary.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the quarrel with Buchan and the poem's occasion are documented by Burns's correspondence and by the rival pamphlets, and the identification of Hornbook with Buchan is accepted in the standard editions.

works.title: Death's Jest-Book; or, The Fool's Tragedy
works.description: The author's last and greatest drama, begun in 1825, carried through to completion about 1829, and revised against the manuscript until his death; it was printed posthumously in 1850 with a memoir by the friend who inherited the papers. A tragedy of a court fool who murders his duke, it turns the jest-book of death into a metaphysical drama of immortality, revenge, and the visible world's contempt for the soul. Its lyrics, including the dirge of a dead child and the song of the swallow, are among the finest short verse of the period.
works.plot: The play is founded on the chronicle story of a Silesian duke of Münsterberg stabbed by his court fool, and it builds from that nucleus a drama in which the fool undertakes the duty of revenge for a wronged household. The Duke and his courtiers pass through scenes of hunting, drinking, and instruction in which the fool's licensed speech conceals a settled purpose, and the murdered man's family, with a child whose dirge is sung, furnish the tragedy's pathos. Death appears as the only serious character, and the jest with which the fool's hand completes the killing is at once a trick and a sacrament. The play closes in the dissolution of nearly every figure who moves in it, and its imagery of the body, the grave, and the surviving spirit is continuous to the end.
works.significance: Death's Jest-Book is the supreme English closet tragedy of the later Romantic period and the source of the author's modern reputation, much quoted by later symbolists and decadents and by twentieth-century detective and gothic writers. Its treatment of mortality, laughter, and revenge has made it a central text for the study of Romantic pessimism and of the Gothic dramatist.
works.meter: Blank verse of great density and compression, full of compound epithet, broken syntax, and riddling address, varied by songs, a dirge, and nursery rhyme; the prosody is deliberately difficult and shifts between declamation and lyric intensity.
works.context: Begun at Oxford and completed during the author's years of travel and medical study on the continent, where he pursued the hope of physical evidence for a surviving human spirit; the play's debt to the German romance of the fool and to the Jacobean revenge drama is constant. It was never offered to the stage, and it passed from manuscript to print through the editorship of a literary friend after the author's death in 1849.
works.characters: Isbrand, the court fool and avenger; the Duke of Münsterberg, whom he kills; the wronged household whose cause he undertakes; the child whose dirge is sung in the second act
works.structure: A five-act tragedy with a prologue, constructed in short scenes of confrontation, song, and dumb-show rather than in a steady plot; multiple revisions left the text uneven, and the printed version reflects the editor's reading of a lifetime of manuscript change.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship, but the text printed in 1850 is an editor's reading of manuscripts revised over more than twenty years, and the several states of the drama make the printed play an editorial reconstruction rather than a final authorising impression.

works.title: Defensio Pro Populo Anglicano
works.description: Milton's Latin defence of the English Commonwealth and the regicide, answering the Defensio Regia of Claudius Salmasius; written for a European audience in his capacity as Latin Secretary, it vindicates popular sovereignty and the English people against royalist propaganda abroad.
works.plot: Milton refutes Salmasius's defence of monarchy and attack on the regicide point by point, arguing that kings are accountable to the people, that tyrants may be judged, and that the English republic is lawful and honourable.
works.significance: The most important Latin political work of the English Revolution, defending republicanism to the continent and establishing Milton's international reputation as a political thinker.
works.meter: Eloquent, erudite Latin prose with powerful oratorical and satirical force.
works.context: Commissioned by the Council of State in 1650 and published in 1651; Milton's exertion on it (while already losing his sight) is said to have hastened his total blindness, and it earned him European fame.
works.structure: A learned Latin polemic of sustained argument, structured as a rebuttal of Salmasius's treatise.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name.

works.title: Dejection: An Ode
works.form: Romantic ode and meditation in the conversation manner, combining the eighteenth-century irregular ode with the letter of apology and the poem of psychological analysis.
works.description: An occasional ode of the spring of 1802, written over some days in a season of despair over a love that could not be answered and over the poet's own loss of imaginative power, and addressed to a woman named in an earlier version of the text. It is the most explicit verse statement of the Romantic theory of perception, since its argument is that the passion we bring to a scene is the source of its worth, and that a mind which cannot feel gives nothing to what it sees. The storm that gathers outside the window, watched without emotion, is the emblem of the speaker's condition.
works.plot: The opening invokes the evening wind, the last leaves that fall from the tree, and the storm gathering over the sea, and the speaker reports how he looks upon the face of the world with no sense of joy and no fear of loss, able neither to weep nor to sleep for want of feeling. Turning to the addressee, he says that grief without the imaginative power is a dumb and shapeless misery, and recalls that there was a time when the beauty of the world was attended by a holy light and by a joy too keen not to be painful. The central assertion is then laid down plainly: what we seem to receive from outward things is given and borrowed from ourselves, and the passion and the intelligence of the mind are the wedding garments of the world it beholds; a creature without imagination has no power to create or to enjoy. The closing stanzas return to the storm and to the prayer that the listener, whose life is bound to a household and to a child, may keep the fancy and the feeling that make the world fair, while the speaker accepts his own duller fate and asks only to be left to his silence and his penance.
works.significance: The classic Romantic poem on the failure of the imaginative faculty and one of the plainest statements of the mind-dependent view of perception; its claim that the mind supplies what it seems to receive from the world became a central tenet of Romantic theory. It remains a touchstone for readings of the relation between biography, intoxication and the Romantic ode.
works.meter: Irregular ode stanzas of unequal line-length with a complex rhyme scheme and persistent exclamatory and interrogatory periods; the alternation of long storm lines and shorter reflective lines marks the alternation of feeling and argument.
works.context: Written in April 1802, in a season of estrangement from his family, of increasing dependence on laudanum, and of hopeless attachment to a member of his wife's family; it belongs to the years in which his public lectures and his periodical were in difficulty, and its theory of the imagination was restated in prose in his critical work of 1817.
works.characters: The speaker beneath the storm in his room; the addressee, a woman loved and unattainable, whose household is named in the poem; the wind, the clouds and the sinking moon of the opening
works.structure: An irregular ode in eight sections, moving from the description of the storm, through the confession of impotence, to the philosophical assertion about the mind's agency, and back to the address to the listener; the design is that of a passionate self-analysis rather than of a close argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the identity of the addressee is a matter of biographical inference and does not affect the question of authorship.

works.title: Delia
works.description: Samuel Daniel's sonnet sequence of fifty sonnets to Delia, with the appended complaint 'The Complaint of Rosamond' (1592): a polished, plaintive sequence in which the lover vows constancy against time and the lady's coldness, and finds his best weapon in the immortalizing power of verse.
works.plot: The lover serves Delia through her disdain, argues with time and death, warns her that her beauty will fade unless his verse preserves it, and closes with the complaint of Rosamond — Henry II's mistress telling her ghost-story of seduction and murder by poison.
works.significance: The purest Elizabethan expression of the sonnet convention; Shakespeare borrowed from its phrasing, and its complaint of Rosamond founded the female-voiced 'mirror' complaints of the 1590s.
works.meter: The English sonnet form, handled with Daniel's characteristic smoothness and grave music.
works.context: Printed in 1592, in the first flush of the sonnet vogue after Astrophel and Stella; Delia's name glances at Sidney's Stella and at the 'Delia' of Tibullus.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Delia; Rosamond (in the Complaint); Henry II (in the Complaint)
works.structure: A sequence of fifty sonnets framed as a lover's diary, followed by the narrative complaint of Rosamond in rhyme royal.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.
