works.title: Fingal
works.form: Ancient epic in the restored or reconstructed manner, in books, with argument or analysis prefixed to each book and with introductory and explanatory dissertation; accompanied by a group of shorter songs and laments.
works.description: Macpherson's first long Ossianic poem, offered as an ancient epic in six books on the deeds of Fingal, the Caledonian hero, together with several shorter translated poems. It greatly enlarges the manner of the 'Fragments' into a narrative machine of invasions, single combats, ghosts and bardic recitation. Its publication, with a prefacial dissertation, provoked both enthusiasm in Europe and attack at home.
works.plot: The epic frame is a war in which the forces of the north and of Ireland contend, and Fingal, aged, venerable and supreme in judgement as well as in arms, leads his Caledonians to the relief of the distressed. The action is interrupted and deepened by the recursive method of the poems: bards sing the past, heroes recount their own sorrows, and the ghosts of the departed appear to hasten or to lament a death. Love, friendship and the observance of hospitality are the governing virtues, and the great motive power is grief, expressed in lamentation over the slain and over fallen greatness. The shorter poems appended are mostly laments and narratives of private calamity, and they supply the tenderness the epic's battles refuse.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the Ossianic vogue in its full epic form, and one of the most widely translated and imitated poems of the later eighteenth century in Europe; its machinery of grief, mist, ghosts and heroic moderation supplied preromantic poetry with a whole repertoire. Its claim to have supplied Britain with an ancient epic of its own remains the centre of the authentication controversy.
works.meter: Unrhymed cadenced verse of great uniformity and weight, with inversion, accumulation of epithets, and long rolling periods; the measure is deliberately unlike heroick couplet or blank verse of the Augustan school, and was admired as a recovery of ancient harmonious barbaric numbers.
works.context: Published in 1762, in the war years, when Scottish and English readers were being offered national epics on every side, and when the dissertation on ancient poetry prefixed to the work was itself a contribution to the criticism of taste and sublimity. The volume's success established Macpherson's position and his claim to have recovered a Homeric-age literature from the Gaelic.
works.characters: Fingal; his sons and warriors; the heroes and heroines of the appended poems; the spirits of the dead and the reciting bards
works.structure: An epic in six books with a strongly episodic and recursive organisation: the present action is repeatedly suspended by songs, recitations and visions of the past, so that the temporal structure is that of an ancient tradition recollected by bards rather than of a continuous plot.
works.attributionNotes: Recorded as disputed because Macpherson published the work as a translation of an ancient epic and contemporaries, and many since, have held that the ancient original is largely or wholly his own composition, made from such Gaelic tradition as he genuinely gathered. The ascription to 'Ossian' and to the ancient bards is not verifiable; Macpherson's own responsibility for the printed text is undisputed.

works.title: Five Varieties of Blank Verse
altTitles: Five Varieties of Blank Verse, which are found to have been practised by some of our best English Poets
works.form: Critical treatise in versification, printed as a separate tract and reissued among the apparatus of the collected editions of old English poetry; its method is definitional and illustrative, with quoted specimens.
works.description: A short metrical treatise by Percy, issued as a companion to the historical criticism of the 'Reliques', which distinguishes five varieties of unrhymed English verse and traces them from the age of Gower to that of Milton. It is one of the earliest attempts in English to describe the history of blank verse as a system of measurable forms rather than as a single practice, and it belongs to the editorial apparatus of the antiquarian revival of native poetry.
works.plot: The treatise argues that English unrhymed verse is not one measure but several, and it sets out the varieties with specimens of each, arranged in chronological order so that the reader may see the progress of the metre towards the established iambic pentameter of the later poets. The point is both technical and national: the Old English and early writers had a metrical art of their own, and the modern habit of reading them as irregular or barbarous arises from ignorance of the distinction. Percy's evidence is scanned quotation, and his method is that of the antiquary-critic who lets specimens carry the argument. The essay thus supports the larger case of the 'Reliques', that native antiquity deserves critical as well as historical attention.
works.significance: It is a foundation-stone of the history of English metrics, the first systematic attempt to classify the varieties of unrhymed native verse, and it prepared the way for the later scholarship of the early English measures and for the antiquarian defence of blank verse as a national form.
works.meter: Prose argument on verse: the subject-matter is the analysis of English accentual and syllabic measures, including the long unrhymed line, the twelve-syllable line of the Romance school, and the several varieties of the decasyllable, with scanning of each.
works.context: It appears with the first vogue of the 'Reliques' and in the middle of the 1760s debate about old English verse, blank verse and the rules, in which the antiquaries were revising the neoclassical account of the metrical history of the language. It is a scholarly by-product of the ballad collection's enterprise.
works.structure: A continuous argument in a single short tract: proposition, definition and naming of each variety, illustrative specimens in sequence, and concluding remarks on the ascent of the measure to Milton.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Percy is regular and undisputed. Its precise first-print circumstances and its relation to the several editions of the 'Reliques' are complicated, and the composition dates are not fixed; the year recorded is that of its publication as a separate metrical tract of the same moment as the collection.

works.title: Floris and Blancheflour
works.description: An idyllic romance of young love, adapted from the Old French Floire et Blancheflor: the Saracen prince Floris and the Christian captive Blancheflour, brought up together, are parted by his parents, and Floris pursues her to the emir's tower in Babylon, where love and loyalty overcome jealousy and force. The gentlest of the early English romances.
works.plot: Floris's parents sell Blancheflour to merchants to end the match; she is taken to the emir of Babylon's harem tower; Floris follows, bribes his way in, is discovered in the maidens' tower, and is saved from death when the lovers' mutual devotion moves the emir to mercy and their marriage.
works.significance: The classic English romance of young love and constancy, and a key witness to the transmission of the sentimental romance from France to England.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, gently lyrical in tone.
works.context: Composed c. 1250 in the south-east from the French Floire et Blancheflor (c. 1150), one of the most widely translated romances of the Middle Ages; preserved in four English manuscripts from c. 1300 onward.
works.characters: Floris; Blancheflour; the emir of Babylon; Clarice; Darys the porter
works.structure: A quest-romance in two movements (parting; pursuit and rescue), with the tower and the garden as symbolic settings.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: Rural Rides (Penguin English Library)

works.title: Foliage; or, Poems Original and Translated
works.form: Miscellaneous lyric volume of original songs, sonnets, and meditations with translations, chiefly from the Italian
works.description: A collection of short poems, translations, and familiar verses by Leigh Hunt, published in 1818 and giving its name to the volume that gathered much of his best-known lyric work. Foliage mixes original songs, sonnets, and meditations with translations from the Italian and with verse rendered from other languages, and it opens with the poem 'Foliage' itself, a protest against the pride of authorship and a plea for the humble, unassertive gift of poetry. The volume is the chief treasury of Hunt's lyric manner: graceful, sympathetic, and tuned to the pleasure and pity of ordinary feeling.
works.plot: The volume presents no continuous argument but a range of pieces: the opening 'Foliage' reflects on the poet's dependence and the modest offering of verse; songs and sonnets treat love, friendship, absence, and death; meditations draw feeling from natural scenes and from the sight of suffering; and the translations render Italian and other poetry into English. Together they assemble Hunt's creed of a poetry of simple, humane, sensuous truth.
works.significance: Foliage is the principal collection of Hunt's lyric verse and the source of many of his most reprinted poems; its opening address on the unpretentious gift of poetry became a statement of Hunt's poetics and of the sympathetic, familiar current of Romantic lyric associated with his name and with Keats's early allegiance to him.
works.meter: Original and translated pieces in varied lyric stanzas, sonnets, and smooth iambic measures; Hunt's prosody is easy, musical, and end-stopped, favouring sweetness and regularity over experiment, and the translations strive to keep the lilt of their originals.
works.context: Published in 1818 by Taylor and Hessey, the volume appeared at the height of Hunt's influence over the younger Romantics and of the Hunt circle's activity in publishing and criticism; it collects work from the years of the Examiner and of Hunt's imprisonment and reflects the Italian vogue the circle was promoting.
works.characters: the meditative lyric speaker; friends and the absent beloved; the figures of the translated and Italian pieces
works.structure: A miscellaneous collection ordered loosely by kind and length, the programmatic 'Foliage' standing first, followed by lyric, sonnet, meditation, and translation; the reader moves piece to piece with no framing narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; Hunt's authorship of the original poems and his editorship of the translations are undisputed. The volume is Hunt's, not, as has sometimes been confused, Shelley's.

works.title: Fowre Hymnes
works.description: Four philosophical hymns on love and beauty — 'An Hymne in Honour of Love', 'An Hymne in Honour of Beautie', 'An Hymne of Heavenly Love', and 'An Hymne of Heavenly Beautie' — in which the Platonism of earthly desire is answered and completed by the Christian ascent to divine love.
works.plot: The first two hymns celebrate Cupid's power and the beauties of the beloved as earthly ladder; the second pair, written (the dedication says) to 'reform' the first, ascend through the creation to the love of Christ and the beauty of the divine wisdom enthroned in heaven.
works.significance: The classic English statement of the Neoplatonic ladder of love, and a key text for the devotional Platonism of the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Rhyme royal, with an elevated, liturgical diction.
works.context: Published in 1596 with a dedicatory epistle to the Countess of Cumberland and the Countess of Warwick explaining that the first two hymns were written in youth, the second two in maturity.
works.characters: the poet as lover and worshipper
works.structure: Two matched pairs of hymns, the earthly pair answered point by point by the heavenly pair in a deliberate palinode.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Fragmenta Aurea
altTitles: Fragmenta Aurea: A Collection of All the Incomparable Pieces
works.description: The posthumous collection of Suckling's poems and plays (1646), including his best-loved lyrics — 'Why so pale and wan, fond lover?', 'A Ballad upon a Wedding', and 'The Session of the Poets' — which capture the rakish wit and careless grace of the Cavalier generation.
works.plot: The lyrics treat love, gallantry, friendship, and wit with an easy, sceptical charm, deflating romantic pretension while celebrating the pleasures of court life.
works.significance: Fragmenta Aurea is the classic record of Cavalier wit and song; 'Why so pale' and 'A Ballad upon a Wedding' remain among the most lively lyrics of the century.
works.meter: Light, witty, conversational songs with a deliberately 'careless' aristocratic ease.
works.context: Published in 1646, four years after Suckling's death in exile, by his friends, with an engraved frontispiece; it preserved the voice of the doomed Cavalier court.
works.characters: the poet; mistresses; fellow wits
works.structure: A collection of songs, poems, letters, and four plays, gathered by friends after Suckling's death.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published posthumously.

works.title: Fragments of Ancient Poetry, Collected from the Bards
works.form: Anthology of translated fragments in prose-verse arrangement, with prefatory and paratextual matter asserting their antiquity and their source language; the unit is the short lyric or the broken narrative.
works.description: James Macpherson's first Ossianic publication: a thin collection of short pieces offered as translations from the Gaelic or Erse of 'ancient bards', with the names of the heroic cycle attached to them. It appeared anonymously, with a list of subscribers prefixed, and its success sent its author into the Highlands to collect more. It is the opening document of one of the great literary controversies of the century.
works.plot: There is no sustained argument, only a series of brief lyrical and narrative fragments: invocations of heroes, laments for the dead, addresses to the night, to mountains and to departed glory. The pieces are unified by a tone of mournful sublimity and by a supposed antiquity, since the speaker throughout is a bard of an unrecorded heroic age reporting what older bards sang. The effect the collection aims at is the impression of a native epic tradition surviving in ruins, and its politics of the fragment is deliberate: what is missing is made to appear lost rather than never written. The book's dedication and advertisements frame the fragments as a national restoration of ancient Scottish poetry, and they promised further and larger recoveries.
works.significance: It started the Ossian phenomenon and with it the European fashion for the primitive sublime, the forged or reconstructed national epic, and the cult of the bard. Its manner is traceable through the following decade's poetry, and its controversy set the terms in which authentication, national literary property and editorial honesty were debated.
works.meter: A stern, inverted, cadenced English prose-verse of long periods and heavy latinate diction, modelled on no existing English measure; the irregular 'ancient' rhythm was one of the features that readers seized on as evidence of sublimity and sceptics seized on as evidence of imposition.
works.context: It was published in Edinburgh in 1760, in the moment after the 'Forty-five' when Scottish Highland antiquity was being simultaneously romanticised and policed, and within the wider European argument about primitive genius, Homer and the origins of national poetry that had been sharpened by Hurd, Blair and the Warton circle. Hugh Blair's encouragement and the subscription model made the first collection possible.
works.characters: The supposed ancient bards; the heroes and heroines of the Gaelic cycle invoked in the fragments
works.structure: A collection of independent short pieces, sequenced for variety of tone rather than chronology, prefaced by subscriber list and advertisements and annotated with the names of the heroes and the occasions of the songs.
works.attributionNotes: Macpherson is the author in the sense that he produced and published the texts; whether he translated genuine Gaelic and Irish sources or largely composed his 'ancients' himself has been disputed from 1760 to the present, and the 'ancient bard' authorship the title asserts is certainly not verifiable. The present record assigns the book to Macpherson and marks the ancient attribution as disputed.

works.title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
works.form: Gothic novel and romance of terror with a philosophical tale of creation inside an Arctic narrative.
works.description: The tale of a modern Prometheus: a Genevan student who learns to kindle animation in dead matter, and the reasoning creature his labour brings into being. It is written as a series of confessions nested inside the letters of an Arctic navigator, and its argument concerns the duties of a maker to his work, the miseries of an unprotected intelligence, and the revenge of knowledge pursued without sympathy. Its 1831 revision, prefixed by a new account of its composition, is the text most often read.
works.plot: Robert Walton, wintering in the northern ocean, takes aboard a half-dead traveller who tells his history: Victor Frankenstein, bred in prosperity, masters natural philosophy, assembles a being from materials and, horrified at his own success, abandons it. The creature, instructed by observation and by a lost volume of philosophy, demands companions; refused, it murders Victor's brother, allows an innocent servant to be executed for the deed, destroys the mate intended for it, and kills Victor's bride on his wedding night. Victor pursues his maker's enemy to the north, is there lost in the ice, and dies on board the navigator's ship, having warned him from the same ambition. The creature appears at the bedside and vows to consume itself in the frozen ocean.
works.significance: The most durable myth of modern culture, supplying the vocabulary in which the responsibilities of the scientist, the grievances of the made and the terrors of solitary ambition are discussed. It transformed the gothic tale of terror into a philosophical narrative with two contested narrators, and founded a line of fiction and stage spectacle that continues. Its composition history makes it a central document of the period's scientific and poetic circles.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; elevated eighteenth-century rhetorical narration, with the creature's set speeches in a more Latinate and self-taught idiom.
works.context: Conceived in the summer of 1816, the year without a summer, among a party of exiles and experimenters on the lake of Geneva, out of a wager to produce tales of the supernatural, and written out after the return to England. Its science reflects the current interest in galvanism and in the chemistry of life, and its frame draws on the published narratives of polar voyages. The 1831 revision was made in response to a demand for a standard collected text and quietly altered the account of its own origin.
works.characters: Victor Frankenstein; the creature he makes; Robert Walton, the Arctic captain; Elizabeth Lavenza; Henry Clerval; Alphonse Frankenstein; Caroline Beaufort; William; Justine Moritz
works.structure: Triple-frame narration: the letters of the Arctic captain enclose the traveller's first-person confession, which in turn encloses the creature's own long defence; the three accounts contradict and confirm each other without a final arbitrating voice.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1818 with a preface unattributed; authorship established by the 1831 edition, which carries the writer's name and a new introduction, and by family and publisher records.

works.title: Freedom's Journal
works.form: Reform newspaper and group-editorial periodical: the race-paper of the early Black public sphere, combining the programmatic editorial, the biographical sketch, occasional verse and the abolitionist reprint.
works.description: A weekly New York newspaper founded in 1827, the first African American-owned and operated newspaper published in the United States. It was established by a group of free Black citizens and clergymen to plead the cause of their people in their own print, and it was edited first jointly and then solely by one of its founders after the other left to found a successor title. Its columns carried editorial matter, correspondence, obituaries of race worthies, marriage and death notices, and reprints from British and American abolition writing.
works.plot: As a serial it has no single argument but a declared programme: to disseminate useful knowledge among the coloured population, to rebut the prejudice of the white press, and to assert the capacity and citizenship of free Black Americans. Its editorials attacked the colonisation schemes then urging emigration to Africa, argued for manual-labour and common schools, and reported on African American institutions, temperance and industry. It also printed poems and biographical sketches that constructed a public history of Black achievement, and it reprinted testimony against slavery and the colour line.
works.significance: It marks the beginning of the African American press, and its existence is the decisive fact for the literary history of Black print before immediatism: it made the community's own editors the narrators of its condition. Its pages are the principal evidence for an antebellum Black reading public, and its editorial arguments prefigure the language of the 1830s and 1840s.
works.meter: Prose; its occasional verse is in standard hymn and ballad stanzas. Editorials are argumentative and restrained rather than declamatory.
works.context: Founded in New York City in 1827, when a substantial free Black community had built churches, mutual aid societies, schools and a reading public, and when the debates over the American Colonization Society and over New York's suffrage restrictions made Black print a political necessity. It appeared two years before the great pamphlet agitation of the later 1820s and four years before the immediatist press of the 1830s.
works.structure: Serial weekly: four columns of editorial, correspondence, notices and reprints, with the inaugural number stating the paper's design for its own community.
works.attributionNotes: Jointly founded and initially co-edited; the paper's first number carries the announcement of the group of free Black citizens who established it, and editorship passed to one of the founders after the other resigned in 1827-1829.

works.title: Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay
works.description: Greene's romantic comedy of Oxford magic and Suffolk love: Friar Bacon, England's great magician, works his brazen head and his glass of distant seeing while the Prince of Wales, the earls, and the keeper's daughter Margaret of Fressingfield play out their love-plot — the play moving between the scholars' cell and the country fair to its double ending of broken magic and honest marriage.
works.plot: Prince Edward and Lacy both love Margaret; Lacy woos her in the prince's name and wins her for himself; the prince's rage, the rivals' duel, and the disguises of the middle acts complicate the match; Bacon's glass shows the fathers' deaths and is shattered; the brazen head speaks 'Time is, Time was, Time is past' and falls; and the play ends with the marriages and the friar's renunciation of magic.
works.significance: The masterpiece of the University Wits' romantic comedy — the play in which magic, love, and England's own legends met on the popular stage.
works.meter: Blank verse for the court and scholars, prose for the rustics — the mixed style that became the Elizabethan comic norm.
works.context: Performed about 1589 and printed in 1594; its Oxford setting and national hero-magician answered the vogue for conjuring plays after Faustus.
works.characters: Friar Bacon; Friar Bungay; Prince Edward; Lacy, Earl of Lincoln; Margaret of Fressingfield; the Keeper; Miles; the two scholars (the sons of Lambert and Serlsby); the Devil (in the conjuring); the brazen head
works.structure: A two-world comedy — the university cell and the Fressingfield household — braided by the magic glass, in Greene's most accomplished construction.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Friendship in Death
altTitles: Friendship in Death: In Twenty-Six Letters, Between Two Persons of Distinction, Of the Other World
works.description: A series of letters between two departed friends who write to each other from their tombs in Westminster Abbey, reviewing the lives they have left and the affections they have not lost. It is one of the most original of the pious fictions of the early century, and a landmark both of the women's friendship tradition and of the literature of the other world.
works.plot: Two women long deceased carry on a correspondence from their respective sepulchres, each reporting the state of the other's family and the changes of the world below. They review their own past conduct, the trials of marriage, the uses of study and the comfort of religion, and they intercede and sympathise with one another across the boundary of death. The letters pass to the deaths of those still living and to the reunions of the friends, the whole closing on the hope of a friendship perfected in another state.
works.significance: It stands between the conduct fiction and the novel of female friendship, and its device of the correspondence of the dead anticipates both the Gothic letter and the sentimental fiction of bereavement; it was long read and reprinted through the century.
works.meter: A warm and elevated epistolary prose of the female devotional style, with the apostrophes to the dead and to the Abbey as its characteristic movement; some of the pieces are versified.
works.context: Published in 1728 by a poet already known as the author of pious verse and of the poems of the earlier years, in the season of the vogue for the letters of the dead and for the conversation of the other world, an amusement that had been licensed by the essays of the previous generation.
works.characters: the two departed friends who write from their tombs; the surviving families and friends reported to them; the several characters of the inset histories
works.structure: A serial epistolary fiction of short letters, the sequence of correspondents and of posthumous reports supplying the order; the inset histories of the living make it a collection of tales within a correspondence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in the posthumous collections of her works.

works.title: Frost at Midnight
works.form: Conversation poem and lyric meditation in meditative blank verse, the form in which the period replaced the Augustan imitation and the estate poem with a private scene of thought.
works.description: The most perfect of the conversation poems: a short blank-verse meditation written in a west-country cottage at night, where the speaker sits with his infant sleeping near him and the only visible motion is the film of frost that settles on the languid flame of his fire. Out of that stillness he argues that the mind creates its own moods from what it hears, recalls the school days when such silence and the few small sounds of an evening were all the variety he had, and ends with the hope that his child, reared among hills and lakes, shall learn his language from the eternal forms of nature.
works.plot: The poem begins with the strange patience of the frost, which hangs on the fire-wood and performs its ministry in silence, and from that observation the speaker turns to the question of how the mind supplies its own sound, illustrating it by the listeners who borrow from themselves the melancholy or the comfort of an hour. He then recalls his own rearing in a great city, where nothing of the living seasons was visible and the eye found no familiar shapes of hill or field to which it could go in sympathy; all that variety was made for him by the changing sounds of evening, the flutter of a film on the fire, the note of a cricket or the hoot of an owl. In the closing movement he addresses the babe sleeping by its mother's side, and pledges that the child shall walk among the hills and the lakes, and shall see and hear the seasons as they change, and that nature, in every living thing, shall be a teacher to him; the poem ends with the confession of his own childhood's want and with the prayer that the eternal Beauty, which is present in all the forms of the world, shall be the child's guide and guardian.
works.significance: The standard example of the Romantic conversation poem and one of the most quoted blank-verse meditations on childhood, education and the perception of nature. Its account of the mind's creation of its own mood, and its blessing on the child who is to learn from the living landscape, became common property of later nature writing and of Romantic pedagogy.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of exceptional quietness, with a high proportion of soft monosyllables, delayed predicates and suspended syntax, and long vowel music; the tempo of the line imitates the pace of a mind listening to its own silence.
works.context: Written in the cold spring of 1798 in the cottage in which the collaboration of the ballad volume was beginning, and addressed to the first years of the poet's married life and to his infant son; its educational hope for the child answers the contemporary debate about schooling and about the formative influence of place, and it draws on the associationist psychology the poet had lately been reading.
works.characters: The speaker alone in his cottage at night; his infant son, asleep in the cradle; the absent mother of the child; the school-hours and the town of the speaker's childhood
works.structure: A single meditative movement in one voice, built as a sequence of retirements and returns: the outer stillness of the frost, the inward memory of the city and the school, the image of the sleeping infant, and the closing hope for the child's future education; the transitions are made by association rather than by argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: Fulgens and Lucrece
works.description: Henry Medwall's interlude of the wooing of Lucrece, performed at the household of Cardinal Morton; the earliest surviving secular English play, printed by John Rastell c. 1512–16.
works.plot: The Roman senator Fulgens promises his daughter Lucrece to the suitor of greater nobility, Publius Cornelius or Gaius Flaminius; the debate on true nobility (virtue versus birth) is interwoven with a subplot in which two serving-men, A and B, woo Lucrece's maid and re-enact the contest in comic parallel. The play breaks off in the unique surviving copy before the conclusion.
works.significance: The first surviving secular English play and a landmark in the transition from medieval moral drama to Renaissance comedy; its debate on true nobility and its pairing of serious and comic plots anticipate the structure of Elizabethan drama.
works.meter: Rhyme royal and couplets, with prose dialogue in the comic scenes
works.context: Written for performance at a feast given by Cardinal John Morton (probably Christmas 1497), in whose household Medwall was chaplain; the play adapts Buonaccorso da Montemagno's De vera nobilitate (translated by John Tiptoft c. 1460), and Rastell's printing (c. 1512–16) preserved it for the sixteenth-century stage tradition.
works.characters: Fulgens; Lucrece; Publius Cornelius; Gaius Flaminius; A (servant); B (servant); Joan (Lucrece's maid)
works.structure: Two-part interlude alternating the serious debate of the senators with the comic subplot of the servants, with direct addresses to the banqueting audience.

works.title: Gallathea
works.description: Lyly's pastoral comedy of disguise and desire: to appease Neptune's demand for the fairest virgin of the land, the fathers of Gallathea and Phillida disguise both girls as boys; the two 'youths' fall in love with each other, and the play ends with Venus's promise that 'one of them' shall be transformed into a man — a resolution whose gender the text leaves teasingly open.
works.plot: Neptune's sacrifice is evaded by the two disguises; the shepherds' loves and the fair's episodes (Rafe, Robin, and the alchemist) fill the middle; the 'boys'' mutual love complicates everything; and the final scene, with Diana and Venus contending, produces the metamorphosis promise and the virgin's reprieve.
works.significance: The most daring of Lyly's gender comedies — the play in which the Elizabethan stage's play with sexual identity becomes the plot itself.
works.meter: Prose with verse for the divine scenes — the gods speak verse, the mortals prose, in Lyly's careful decorum.
works.context: Probably performed at court on 1 January 1588, the Armada year; printed 1592; its same-sex desire, licensed by the boy actors' convention, has made it a touchstone of queer reading of the Renaissance stage.
works.characters: Gallathea; Phillida; Neptune; Venus; Diana; Cupid; the fathers (Tityrus and Melibeus); Hebe; the fair folk (Rafe, Robin, the Alchemist, the Mariner)
works.structure: A five-act pastoral built on the cross-dressing device, with the fair scenes and Neptune's wrath as frame and counterpoint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Gammer Gurton's Needle
altTitles: A Ryght Pithy, Pleasaunt and Merie Comedie: Intytuled Gammer Gurtons Nedle
works.description: The classic English village farce of the lost needle, composed c. 1552–53, probably at Christ's College, Cambridge, and printed in 1575; the second of the two earliest English comedies (with Ralph Roister Doister).
works.plot: Gammer Gurton's precious needle is lost while mending the breeches of her servant Hodge; the whole household turns out to search, suspicion falls on the neighbour Dame Chat, and the village curate Doctor Rat is beaten in a confusion of break-ins and brawls; the needle is at last discovered — in the seat of Hodge's breeches — with a resounding yell, and the company shares the ale in reconciliation.
works.significance: One of the two founding comedies of the English stage: its picture of village life, its rich dialect comedy, and its plot of the lost needle set the pattern for English farce from Shakespeare's Merry Wives to the twentieth century.
works.meter: Rhyming couplets ('rhyming fourteeners'), with the famous drinking song 'Back and side go bare'
works.context: Composed c. 1552–53, with the title-page attribution of the 1575 edition to 'Mr. S. Master of Art' generally identified as William Stevenson of Christ's College, Cambridge, where the play was probably acted; it belongs to the university revival of classical comedy in the 1550s.
works.characters: Gammer Gurton; Hodge; Diccon the Bedlam; Dame Chat; Doctor Rat; Master Bayly; Tib; Cock
works.structure: Five acts in a single village setting, modelled on Roman comedy but filled with native farce: the plot turns on the lost object, the false accusation, and the comic discovery.
works.attributionNotes: The 1575 title page ascribes the play to 'Mr. S. Master of Art', identified by modern scholarship (most fully by Charles W. Whitworth) as William Stevenson of Christ's College, Cambridge; the attribution is probable rather than certain.

works.title: Gaston de Blondeville; or, The Court of Henry the Third, Keeping Festival in Ardenne. A Romance; St. Alban's Abbey, a Metrical Tale; with Some Poetical Pieces
altTitles: St. Alban's Abbey, a Metrical Tale
works.form: Posthumous fragmentary historical romance, metrical tale and shorter verse, with a prose memoir compiled from journals
works.description: The posthumous collection that closed Ann Radcliffe's printed career, issued in four volumes by Henry Colburn in 1826, three years after her death, and prefixed with the Memoir of the Author with Extracts from her Journals, the first life of her, edited from her papers by her husband. It contains Gaston de Blondeville, her historical romance of the court of Henry III of England keeping festival in Ardenne, left as a large fragment, and St. Alban's Abbey, a metrical tale in the antique mould, with other poetical pieces. The volume is the chief witness of her later temper: the romances of the 1790s abandoned, the picturesque journals and the ballad and metrical tale preferred, and the whole career surveyed by the Memoir that made her literary testament public.
works.plot: Gaston de Blondeville, in its unfinished sweep, brings together the Saxon and Norman factions, the outlaws of the forest and the court festival of Henry III in Ardenne, tracing Gaston's fortunes, the love of Matilda of Dinant, the tyranny of the house of Mountfort and the forest legend of the fatal assembly; St. Alban's Abbey, in verse, tells the tale of Edwy, of the abbey and of the lost heiress of the house of Walderie, the metrical descendant of her own prose romances; the Memoir prefixed records the life, the retirement from publication, the journals of tour, and the death of the authoress.
works.significance: Gaston de Blondeville with its Memoir is the foundation document of Radcliffe's biography and reception, the source of nearly all knowledge of her life and character, and the record of her post-1797 imaginative writing; the metrical tale and the fragment are the evidence of the Gothic novelist's turn to romance in the antique and to verse at the close of her career, and the volume's account of her journals anchors the study of her travel writing.
works.meter: The metrical tale is in the antique romantic stanza and measure of the ballad and the old romance, deliberate in its archaism; the fragment of Gaston is in prose of historical elevation; the Memoir is plain domestic prose.
works.context: Published in 1826 to a literary scene remade by Scott's historical novel, of which Radcliffe's Ardenne romance is an unconscious antecedent; the Memoir and journals were the husband's disposal of her papers after her death in February 1823, answering a public that had known nothing from her in prose fiction since The Italian in 1797.
works.characters: Gaston de Blondeville; Matilda of Dinant; the Saxon Outlaw of the Woods; the house of Mountfort and the court of Henry III; in St. Alban's Abbey, Edwy and the outcast of Walderie; Ann Radcliffe herself as the subject of the Memoir
works.structure: A posthumous miscellany: the romance fragment, the metrical tale and shorter poems gathered after the author's death and presented with a prose Memoir compiled from her journals and papers by her husband; the parts are independent, unified by the life that frames them.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name, the posthumous authorship of the romances and metrical tale by Ann Radcliffe established by the Memoir of her husband; the Memoir itself is compiled by William Radcliffe from her journals and papers and is not by her hand.

works.title: Genesis A
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 2,935 lines paraphrasing Genesis 1-22, from the creation and the fall of the angels to the sacrifice of Isaac. The longest of the Junius manuscript poems, it is the foundational Old Testament epic of the period, composed in the plain style of the 'Cædmonian' school.
works.plot: The poem recounts the fall of the rebel angels, the six days of creation, the fall of Adam and Eve and their expulsion, Cain and Abel, the generations to Noah, the Flood and the covenant, the tower of Babel, and the story of Abraham to the near-sacrifice of Isaac, concluding with the promise of the seed.
works.significance: The earliest sustained biblical epic in English; a primary witness to the vernacular reception of scripture.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in a relatively plain, narrative style.
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11); its opening lines were long known as 'Cædmon's Genesis' from the early editor Junius's attribution.
works.characters: God; Adam; Eve; Satan; Cain; Abel; Noah; Abraham; Sarah; Isaac; Lot
works.structure: Continuous biblical paraphrase in epic form, with an interpolated passage (Genesis B, lines 235-851) translated from Old Saxon treating the fall in greater detail.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attribution to Cædmon is traditional and no longer accepted.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Eighteenth-Century Poetry

works.title: Genesis B
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 617 lines, interpolated into Genesis A (lines 235-851), translated from an Old Saxon original and containing the most celebrated scenes of the fall in Old English: Satan's proud rebellion ('better for me to be a king in hell'), the temptation of Adam by the disguised tempter, and the grief of Eve.
works.plot: The poem opens with Satan's boast against God and his binding in hell; an envoy demon journeys to Eden and, taking the form of a serpent, tempts first Adam (unsuccessfully) and then Eve, deceiving her with the promise of a vision of heaven; Eve eats and persuades Adam; the poem closes on their shame and the beginning of repentance, with the original ending lost in the transition back to Genesis A.
works.significance: Contains the finest dramatic treatment of the fall in early English poetry; its Satan anticipates Milton's in power and pathos, a connection first argued by Sievers in 1875.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with occasional hypermetric lines betraying the Old Saxon original.
works.context: Translated into Old English from an Old Saxon poem (possibly connected with the ninth-century Heliand milieu) and interpolated into Genesis A in the Junius manuscript; the Old Saxon original survives only in a few Vatican fragments.
works.characters: Satan; the Tempter (demon); Adam; Eve
works.structure: A dramatic expansion of the fall narrative built on lengthy speeches — Satan's monologue, the tempter's persuasions, Eve's lament — unique in the corpus for its psychological interest.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the interpolation was first detected by Eduard Sievers (1875).
themes: Restoration politics: party, succession, and Exclusion
sources: The Cambridge Companion to the Eighteenth-Century Novel

works.title: Gentleness and Nobility
works.description: A debate interlude on the nature of true nobility, printed by John Rastell c. 1529 and attributed to Rastell (or, by some, to John Heywood); an early dramatic statement of the humanist case that virtue, not birth, makes the gentleman.
works.plot: A Knight, a Merchant, and a Ploughman dispute whether gentleness resides in ancestry or in virtue; the Ploughman, arguing that nobility of birth without worth is empty, is supported against the Knight's hereditary claims, and the debate — refereed by the Philosopher — concludes with the definition of true gentleness as virtuous living, with a sharp satire of idle gentlemen who live off others' labour.
works.significance: The first English play devoted wholly to the question of true nobility, and a rare dramatic voice for the commonwealth critique of hereditary privilege; it anticipates the social debates of Elizabethan drama.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Printed c. 1529, in the year of the Reformation Parliament; the play's defence of labour and its satire of idle gentry voice the social criticism of the humanist commonwealth tradition (More's Utopia, Starkey's Dialogue), and its attribution to Rastell connects it to the More circle.
works.characters: The Knight; The Merchant; The Ploughman; The Philosopher
works.structure: A formal disputation in two parts, with the Philosopher as moderator and the three estates as speakers; the debate is enlivened by comic abuse between the Knight and the Ploughman.
works.attributionNotes: Printed without author's name; the play is traditionally attributed to John Rastell (whose press produced it), with John Heywood also proposed; modern scholarship accepts Rastell as the likeliest author without certainty.

works.title: Gertrude of Wyoming
altTitles: Gertrude of Wyoming; A Pennsylvanian Tale, and Other Poems
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse: an sentimental frontier narrative in the revived Spenserian stanza, drawing on the ballad revival and on the poetry of domestic pathos.
works.description: A narrative poem in Spenserian stanzas set on the frontiers of Pennsylvania during the American Revolutionary war, and the most successful romance in verse of its decade. It tells of Gertrude, bride of a colonial settler, whose household is destroyed in an attack on the Wyoming valley, and who dies in her husband's arms. The volume also contains shorter tales and lyrics which helped fix the poet's popular reputation.
works.plot: The poem opens on a settler household in the Wyoming valley and on the marriage of its heroine, and it dwells on the friendly compact between the colonists and the neighbouring Native Americans before that compact is broken by war. The settlement is surprised and destroyed, parents perish, and the heroine dies in the arms of those she loves, while an infant survivor is carried to safety. A wandering bard, who has himself lost family in the same catastrophe, recovers the child and transmits the story, so that the tale reaches the reader as a remembered and recited romance. The massacre of 1778 in the Wyoming valley supplies the historical kernel, and the poem's emotional argument turns on conjugal and filial fidelity tested by frontier violence. Spenserian stanzas lend the tale an archaising dignity that contemporary reviewers thought at once its ornament and its limitation.
works.significance: It supplied the nineteenth century with its most widely read verse account of the American frontier and helped legitimate sentimental domestic tragedy in heroic-measure romance. Its fame travelled to the United States, where the Wyoming story was already national myth, and it was attacked and praised chiefly for the archaism of its stanza. Later historians of the ballad revival treat it as the moment when popular Romantic narrative verse turned from Scottish border matter to transatlantic colonial subject.
works.meter: Spenserian stanzas (nine lines, ababbcbcc), iambic pentameter with the closing alexandrine.
works.context: Written when British readers were avid for American frontier material and when the Wyoming massacre of 1778 had already become a transatlantic cause celebre. Its publication coincides with the vogue for historical romance in verse that the leading Scottish poet-novelist of the generation soon dominated, and its treatment of Native Americans recycles the enlightened vocabulary of the noble savage current after the Scottish Enlightenment's theories of society. The poem was repeatedly reprinted, pirated in America, and used by its author as the anchor of his collected edition.
works.structure: A framed romantic narrative in six cantos: an idyllic settlement, a betrayed compact, a catastrophe, and a survival carried into a reciting frame by a bard who has himself been bereaved by the same violence.

works.title: Gesta Regum Anglorum
altTitles: Deeds of the Kings of the English
works.description: William of Malmesbury's history of the English kings from the arrival of the Anglo-Saxons (449) to the twenty-eighth year of Henry I (1127–28), the most learned English history of the twelfth century, deliberately modelled on Bede and written with a polished Latinity that set a new standard for English historiography.
works.summary: Five books carry the narrative from the adventus Saxonum through the kings of Wessex and the Norman Conquest to Henry I; the work combines narrative history with biography, anecdote, and documentary research, drawing on a library of sources now partly lost and on William's own travels and enquiries.
works.significance: The outstanding English historical work between Bede and the later twelfth century; a model of critical method and style, cited and pillaged by later chroniclers, and a primary witness to Anglo-Saxon history after the Conquest.

works.title: Gloria I and II
altTitles: The Greater and Lesser Doxology Poems
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: Two short Old English versifications of the liturgical Gloria: Gloria I (57 lines) paraphrases the Greater Doxology sung at Mass, praising the Trinity and Christ the Lamb of God; Gloria II (20 lines) is a brief rendering of the doxology of praise to Father, Son, and Spirit.
works.plot: Gloria I moves from the angels' song of praise through the attributes of the persons of the Trinity to Christ the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, ending with a prayer for mercy. Gloria II offers a compact doxology in verse.
works.significance: Evidence of the Old English church's project of rendering the central texts of the liturgy into the vernacular poetic idiom.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the balanced parallelism appropriate to liturgical praise; the shorter poem is notably compact.
works.context: The Benedictine Reform's devotion to the liturgy gave new prominence to the sung ordinary of the Mass; vernacular paraphrases like these made its texts accessible to those whose Latin was limited.
works.structure: Both poems are direct liturgical paraphrases; Gloria I is organized by the successive clauses of the Gloria in excelsis, closing with the Agnus Dei petitions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two poems are separate compositions.
themes: Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
sources: Byron's Letters and Journals (12 volumes with index and supplement)

works.title: Godfrey of Bulloigne
works.description: Edward Fairfax's translation of Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata (1581), under the title Godfrey of Bulloigne, or the Recovery of Jerusalem (1600): the crusaders' siege and taking of Jerusalem — Godfrey's command, Rinaldo's enchantment in Armida's garden, Tancred and Clorinda's tragedy — in English ottava rima of grave and musical fidelity, the translation Dryden ranked with the originals.
works.plot: The Christian army besieges Jerusalem; the pagan enchantments of Armida and Ismeno delay the victory; Rinaldo is rescued from the garden of Armida; the duel of Tancred and Clorinda, the battles, and the final assault take the city; and the poem ends with Godfrey's worship at the Sepulchre.
works.significance: The great English Tasso — the version through which the Italian romantic epic entered English poetry, and a landmark of translation as an art.
works.meter: Ottava rima (abababcc) of sustained dignity and sweetness — the metre Fairfax naturalized for English heroic verse.
works.context: Published 1600, in the decade of the English epic translations (Harington's Ariosto, Sylvester's Du Bartas); Fairfax's Tasso was read by the Spenserians and praised by Dryden as the model of translation.
works.characters: Godfrey of Bouillon; Rinaldo; Armida; Tancred; Clorinda; Erminia; Peter the Hermit; Ismeno; Solyman; Argantes
works.structure: Twenty cantos of ottava rima following Tasso's order, with Fairfax's 'Allegory of the Poem' appended as the moral key.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by Fairfax; uncontested.

editions.title: Godfrey of Bulloigne: A Critical Edition of Edward Fairfax's Translation of Tasso's Gerusalemme Liberata
editions.editor: Kathleen M. Lea and T. M. Gang (eds.)

works.title: Godly Queen Hester
altTitles: A New Interlude Drawn out of the Holy Scripture of Godly Queen Hester
works.description: An anonymous interlude on the biblical story of Esther, printed in 1561 but composed c. 1525–29; a political allegory in which the virtuous queen and her wise counsellor save the realm from the wicked minister.
works.plot: King Ahasuerus, misled by the proud Aman, signs a decree against the Jews; Queen Hester, advised by the wise Mardocheus, intercedes with the king at the risk of her life, exposes Aman's malice, and obtains his overthrow and the deliverance of her people — with the collop-eating scene of Aman's gluttony played as comic Vice-business.
works.significance: The first surviving English dramatization of the Esther story and a striking example of the interlude as political counsel; it shows biblical drama absorbing the new humanist debate on counsel and tyranny.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed c. 1525–29, almost certainly for a noble household: the story of Esther had long served as an allegory of good counsel and royal deliverance, and the play has been read (by Greg Walker and others) as a veiled commentary on the fall of Wolsey, in which the virtuous queen intercedes against an overmighty minister.
works.characters: King Ahasuerus; Queen Hester; Mardocheus; Aman; Ardion (Aman's servant); Hardydardy; Pride; Adulation; Ambition
works.structure: A continuous interlude alternating the counsel scenes of Hester and Mardocheus with the comic scenes of Aman and his servants, ending in judgement and the elevation of Mardocheus.

works.title: Goostly Psalmes and Spirituall Songes
works.description: Miles Coverdale's collection of metrical psalms, hymns, and carols translated from the German (chiefly Luther), printed c. 1535; the first English hymn book, intended for congregational singing.
works.plot: Forty-one pieces — metrical versions of the psalms, Luther's hymns (including 'Ein feste Burg' as 'Our God is a defence and tower'), the Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and canticles — each with its tune indicated, prefaced by an epistle on the right use of psalmody in church and home.
works.significance: The first English hymn book and the beginning of English congregational song; its psalms anticipate the metrical psalters of Sternhold and Hopkins, and its translation of 'Ein feste Burg' entered the English hymnic tradition.
works.meter: Metrical stanzas in ballad and hymn metres, set to German tunes
works.context: Printed c. 1535 during Coverdale's continental exile, drawing on the Wittenberg hymn books; Henry VIII's 1546 proclamation against 'ballads, rhymes, and lewd songs' included it among the books to be burned, and only one complete copy survives (Queen's College, Oxford).
works.structure: A hymn book arranged by liturgical use, with a preface on singing and notes of the tunes to which the pieces are set.

works.title: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners
works.description: Bunyan's spiritual autobiography, written in Bedford Gaol during his twelve-year imprisonment for preaching without a licence, which records his agonising struggle with doubt, temptation, and the assurance of salvation.
works.plot: Bunyan traces his life from a childhood of swearing and bell-ringing through his conversion under John Gifford, his long torments of doubt and despair, his reading of Luther's Commentary on Galatians, and his final assurance of grace; the narrative is organised around biblical typology rather than chronology.
works.significance: The greatest spiritual autobiography in English and a foundational text of the Protestant confessional tradition; it supplied the raw material of inner experience that Bunyan transformed into the allegory of The Pilgrim's Progress.
works.meter: Vigorous, colloquial prose saturated with biblical language, especially the Psalms, Paul, and Hebrews.
works.context: Written in 1666 during Bunyan's first long imprisonment (1660-72) and published in the same year with a preface addressed to his Bedford congregation; a seventh edition appeared before his death.
works.characters: John Bunyan (the narrator); John Gifford; his first wife; his second wife Elizabeth; the Bedford congregation
works.structure: A first-person retrospective narrative in numbered paragraphs, with scriptural glosses on the margins, following the pattern of the Pauline conversion.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bunyan; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Graham Hamilton
altTitles: Graham Hamilton; a Tale of the Old School
works.description: A two-volume historical novel of Scottish covenanting and border material, written after the author's notorious first romance and issued anonymously with the publisher's explanation that the manuscript had been placed in his hands two years earlier with an earnest injunction neither to name the writer nor to publish it at that time. It is the novel in which the author tried the plan of writing a book that would offend nobody. The tale takes the form of a family history set in the old Scottish school of persecution and covenant.
works.plot: Graham Hamilton grows up under the instruction of a stern covenanting household, is bound to an unequal love, and is drawn into the troubles of the Scottish southwest, where the old covenanters' feud with the civil and ecclesiastical authority supplies the machinery of the plot. The narrative moves between the house, the moor, and the field of arms, and the hero's education in honour and enthusiasm is tested by the disasters of his family's cause. A tale of the older religion and of the lovers divided by it, the novel ends with the destruction of the generation it has followed. The romance is deliberately gentler than the author's first book in its handling of society and of persons.
works.significance: The novel marks the attempt of a woman author of scandalous celebrity to convert the Waverley model into a decorous covenanting romance, and it records the pressure of anonymity on the women's fiction market of the 1820s. Its publication history, with the manuscript held back two years at the writer's request, is a document of authorial anxiety in the period.
works.context: Written in the early 1820s when the Scottish historical novel had become the dominant form of fiction and when its author, having published a violent personal roman a clef in 1816 and a verse satire in 1819, was advised by an exile poet friend to write a book that would offend nobody. It appeared from a Conduit Street publisher in two small volumes in 1822, anonymously, the delay and the anonymity being stated in the publisher's own note.
works.characters: Graham Hamilton; the covenanting elder of his household; the woman he loves and cannot marry; the soldiers and preachers of the southwest rising
works.structure: A conventional multi-volume historical novel of education and persecution, with a continuous third-person narrative interrupted by letters and by explanatory notes on the covenanting period.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1822; the publisher's note records the request for concealment, and the authorship rests on contemporary knowledge of the writer and on the collected editions.

works.title: Grammar and Glossary
works.form: grammar and didactic prose in Old English
works.description: Ælfric's Latin grammar written in English — the first grammar of Latin composed in any European vernacular — with its companion glossary of Latin words arranged by subject. A landmark in the history of education and of the vernacular as an instrument of learning.
works.plot: The Grammar adapts the Excerptiones de Prisciano to teach the parts of speech, declensions, and conjugations entirely through the medium of English, explaining Latin forms with English equivalents; the Glossary lists vocabulary by topics (the body, kinship, the church, tools, birds, beasts) in Latin with English glosses.
works.significance: The first vernacular Latin grammar in Europe; a milestone in the history of English education.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Composed c. 998, when Ælfric was at Cerne Abbas or Eynsham; at least fifteen manuscripts survive, evidence of its use in schools into the twelfth century.
works.characters: the schoolboys of Eynsham (addressees)
works.structure: A systematic school grammar in sections on the eight parts of speech, followed by the thematic glossary.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship is certain.
themes: Tyranny and the abuse of power
movements: The Graveyard School and Preromantic Meditation
sources: The English Poems of George Herbert

works.title: Greenfield Hill
altTitles: Greenfield Hill: A Poem, in Seven Parts
works.form: Topographical and descriptive poetry with didactic and historical argument; the estate and township poem transferred to America
works.description: A topographical, historical and didactic poem on a hill settlement in New Haven county, and the most ambitious verse of the early American republic before the 1820s. Its seven parts pass from the scene of the grove to the history of the country, its institutions, its commerce, its religion and its morals. It gives the American township as a subject for the Thomsonian and Goldsmithian descriptive manner.
works.plot: The poem opens on the grove and the vale of Greenfield Hill and its seasons, and then retells the settlement of the country from the first planting of the colony. It passes to the survey of the neighbouring towns, to the character of the people, to the pleasures of study and to the claims of religion and of public duty. Admonitions against intemperance, gambling and irreligion are woven through the descriptive passages. The close commends the hill, its church and its schools to the reader as a model of a republican community.
works.significance: It is the largest American poem of the 1790s and the standard example of the transplanted British topographical manner. Its social survey makes it a primary document for the cultural history of Connecticut. Its reputation stood high through the nineteenth century as the work of the president of Yale.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, with occasional longer stanzas
works.context: Published in 1794 at New York, in the president's second decade, and written from the author's settled life at Greenfield Hill in Connecticut. Its models were Thomson, Goldsmith and the British descriptive school, and its subject was the newly confident Congregational township. Its political passages reflect the 1790s quarrel over French revolutionary principles and over the fate of religion in a republic.
works.structure: Descriptive and didactic poem in seven parts, moving from local scene to colonial history to moral and religious instruction, with long topographical and catalogue passages.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

works.title: Greenland, and Other Poems
works.form: Descriptive and elegiac poem in the Thomsonian and mission-inspired mode, gathered with shorter lyrics in a miscellaneous volume
works.description: A volume of poems by James Montgomery of Sheffield, published in 1819, whose title piece is a melancholy meditation on the vanished Norwegian colony of Greenland. The volume mixes the descriptive and missionary imagination with lyric and moral pieces, reflecting Montgomery's double life as a radical editor and a hymn-writer. Greenland itself, the chief poem, imagines the lost settlements of the Norse in the frozen north and the extinguished Christian community that once flourished there, turning topography into an elegy for a perished people.
works.plot: The title poem traces the rise and disappearance of the old Norse settlements in Greenland: the faith and labour of the colonists, their isolation and gradual extinction, and the modern traveller who finds only ruins, ice, and the Inhabitant where a Christian people had been. The companion poems of the volume move among moral, descriptive, and sentimental subjects, several touched by Montgomery's interest in missions, distant lands, and the transience of human establishments.
works.significance: The volume is the principal example of Montgomery's Romantic descriptive verse and of his poetry of vanished peoples and missionary sympathy; Greenland gave the lost Norse colony its best-known English poetic treatment of the period and helped fix the vanished-settlement theme in Romantic literature of the North.
works.meter: Greenland is written in smooth iambic pentameter couplets suited to swelling description and moral reflection; the accompanying lyrics use regular song and hymn stanzas with simple rhyme, the whole marked by Montgomery's clear, tuneful, and unforced prosody.
works.context: Published in 1819, when the Arctic, the vanished Norse settlements, and the great missionary societies were vivid topics for a reading public fascinated by lost civilisations and distant heathendom. Montgomery, editor of the Sheffield Register and a committed Evangelical, wrote within a current that joined Romantic topographical melancholy to a missionary and humanitarian interest in perished and un evangelised peoples.
works.characters: the lost Norse colonists of Greenland; the extinguished Christian settlement; the modern traveller or speaker who surveys the ruins; the Inuit inhabitant met in the emptied land
works.structure: A miscellaneous volume dominated by the single long descriptive-elegiac poem Greenland, with shorter lyric and moral pieces grouped after it; there is no continuous plot across the volume, and Greenland itself proceeds as a historical meditation from settlement to ruin rather than as a story with characters in action.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; Montgomery's authorship of the volume and of Greenland is undisputed.

works.title: Gulliver's Travels
altTitles: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World
works.description: Swift's four-part voyage satire, narrated by the surgeon and captain Lemuel Gulliver, which reduces the scale of mankind to Lilliput, enlarges it in Brobdingnag, sends him to the flying island and the projectors of the Academy, and ends among the Houyhnhnms and the Yahoos.
works.plot: Gulliver is cast away and reaches a nation of six-inch men whose politics, war and parties are a miniature of Europe; then a land of giants where his own species is judged; then the projects of the mechanicks and the shades of the dead; and finally a country of rational horses whose human brutes, the Yahoos, force him to see his own kind as vermin, till his return and his disgust.
works.significance: It is the century's largest satiric fiction, converting the travellers' tale into an anatomy of human pride, and it founded the tradition of the constructed utopian and satirical voyage that runs to the nineteenth century.
works.meter: The deliberately unadorned prose of the navigator's log, with the exact measurement, the enumeration of customs and the flat statement of the most outrageous conclusion.
works.context: Written in the years between the fall of the Harley ministry and Swift's retirement to Dublin, and published anonymously in 1726 at a moment when the travel narrative and the new fiction of Defoe were making the invented first person respectable; the contemporary key identified nearly every personage of the first part.
works.characters: Lemuel Gulliver; the court and army of Lilliput; the farmer and the queen of Brobdingnag; the sages of the flying island; the Houyhnhnms; the Yahoos
works.structure: Four independent voyages in the first person, in the plain manner of the travel relation, each with its own ascent from curiosity to judgment; the sequence tightens from the political satire of the first two to the philosophical conclusion of the fourth.
works.attributionNotes: Published as the work of Lemuel Gulliver, initially a surgeon and lately a captain, with the printer's pretence of an unauthorised copy; Swift's authorship was understood at once and is uncontested.

works.title: Guthlac A
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 818 lines on the Mercian hermit Guthlac of Crowland: his arrival in the fenland retreat, his battles with the demons who tempt and torment him, and his vindication by the apostle Bartholomew. Based on Felix's Latin Vita, the poem turns the saint's spiritual warfare into heroic combat in the native manner.
works.plot: The young Mercian warrior Guthlac, renouncing war, takes up the solitary life in the fens of Crowland; demons assault his cell, carry him to the gates of hell, and accuse him of pride; the apostle Bartholomew commands his release and the devils obey; Guthlac returns victorious, and the poem closes with his death and the angels' reception of his soul.
works.significance: The classic vernacular treatment of the hermit-warrior and of the fenland as spiritual battlefield.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with the diction of heroic combat applied to spiritual warfare.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 32b-44b); source: Felix of Crowland's Vita Sancti Guthlaci (c. 730-740).
works.characters: Guthlac; the demons; Bartholomew; the angels
works.structure: A hagiographical epic in the heroic mode: renunciation, the demonic wars (a psychomachia in narrative form), heavenly vindication, and death; speeches dominate the central combat scenes.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
sources: The Works of Mary Wollstonecraft, 7 volumes

works.title: Guthlac B
works.description: A poem of 561 lines on the death of St Guthlac of Crowland, from the Exeter Book: the saint's illness, his last conversation with his servant Beccel, and the ascent of his soul, which flies like a bird to heaven. Distinct from Guthlac A in style and emphasis, it is one of the most tender poems in the corpus.
works.plot: Stricken with his final illness, Guthlac instructs his disciple Beccel, foretelling his own death on the seventh day; his soul departs like a bird to the heavenly home, and a light shines over the fen; Beccel, instructed to tell his sister Pega, buries him and the poem closes with a prayer. The poet's meditation on death — 'death is no man's friend' — frames the narrative.
works.significance: The finest Old English poem on the death of a saint; its bird-image for the soul's flight is among the period's most memorable figures.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; gentler and more meditative than Guthlac A.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 44b-52b); source: Felix's Vita Sancti Guthlaci.
works.characters: Guthlac; Beccel; Pega; the angels
works.structure: A single, intimate deathbed narrative: prophecy, farewell dialogue, and the ascent of the soul, framed by prologue and prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; distinct authorship from Guthlac A is generally accepted.
genres: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
themes: Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
sources: Reflections on the Revolution in France

works.title: Guy Mannering; or, The Astrologer
works.form: Historical novel and romance of Border society with a strong comic and dialect component; the mystery of identity gives it an early detection plot.
works.description: The second tale of the new school of Scottish fiction, a romance of Borders gentry, smuggling and legal fraud in which the fortunes of a family are read in advance by an astrological prediction. A colonel from India, quartered at a Border inn, becomes the witness and friend of the heir who had been carried off in childhood, and the tale's curiosity is sustained by the concealment of that identity. Its portraits of a sour landlady, a starved pedant and a terrier-fancier became some of the most reproduced types of Scottish popular fiction.
works.plot: Colonel Mannering, seeking a lodging in the south of Scotland, is warned by an astrologer's figure of the child then missing from the neighbouring house; the infant heir Bertram had been abstracted in his mother's chamber years before, and his kinsman Glossin, the heir presumptive, had profited by the loss. Bertram returns unknown to himself, takes a farm under another name, and is entangled with the smuggler Hatteraick and with the treachery of Glossin's factor. Meg Dods, the innkeeper who loves him spitefully, Dominie Sampson, the scholar whom a marriage would starve, and Dandie Dinmont, whose puppies end the quarrels of the county, carry the novel's comedy. Detection, a trial at the circuit court and a recovery of name and estate bring the prediction to its fulfilment.
works.significance: Established the second, comic-native mode of the historical novel and supplied the period's stock of Scottish character types. Its treatment of stolen inheritance and legal title made it a source for later sensation and detection plotting. Its dialect comedy was widely imitated and remains a document of Scots speech at the Union.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; heavy use of Scots speech for the servant and border characters, with songs and ballad tags interpolated.
works.context: Written in the same season as the author's antiquarian work on Border legends, and dependent on the record of smuggling along the Solway coast and of the civil law of entail and hypothec then being modernised. The East India interest represented by the colonel reflects the returns of Anglo-Indian wealth into Scottish land. Its publication, within months of the former tale, created the commercial pattern of the anonymous national series.
works.characters: Colonel Guy Mannering; Henry Bertram, the lost heir; Glossin, the heir presumptive; Hatteraick the smuggler; Dominie Sampson; Meg Dods; Dandie Dinmont; Julia Mannering; the astrologer
works.structure: Third-person narrative with Colonel Mannering as the chief intelligence-gathering witness; a large cast observed through dialect talk; a concluding assembly of evidence in court supplies the discovery of the lost heir.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as by the Author of Waverley; attribution undisputed.
