works.title: Guy of Warwick
altTitles: The Romance of Guy of Warwick
works.form: romance in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas
works.description: The longest and one of the most widely read of the English romances, in couplets and tail-rhyme stanzas: the career of Guy, earl of Warwick, who wins the lady Felice by feats of arms, then renounces the world to fight as God's champion and die as a hermit. Its hero was England's favourite romance champion for three centuries.
works.plot: Guy, a steward's son, wins Felice through tournaments and foreign wars; struck by remorse, he leaves her to do penance as a pilgrim, returning in disguise to defend England against the giant Colbrond at Winchester; recognized only at his death, he is buried by Felice, who follows him in holiness.
works.significance: The romance of Guy fixed the image of the penitent knight in English culture and remained a bestseller until the Civil War; it is central to the study of romance readership.
works.meter: Couplets in the Auchinleck version; tail-rhyme stanzas in later copies.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from Anglo-Norman sources, drawing on Warwick legend and the cult of Guy; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript and many later copies and prints, into the seventeenth century.
works.characters: Guy; Felice; Colbrond the giant; Reinbrun (their son); Herhaud
works.structure: A two-part structure — chivalric career, then penitential career — with the Colbrond episode and the deathbed recognition as climaxes.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes
works.description: Samuel Purchas's four-volume continuation of Hakluyt's collections: the voyage narratives and geographical documents left unpublished at Hakluyt's death — the travels of the East and West Indies, the relations of China and Japan, the Arctic voyages, and the Virginia enterprises — gathered and framed in Purchas's 'pilgrimage' of the world's records, the great Jacobean storehouse of travel literature.
works.plot: No single plot: the Pilgrimes arranges its hundreds of narratives by region and voyage — Purchas's own summaries and moral reflections interlacing the documents — from the voyages of the ancients to the discoveries of his own day.
works.significance: The great Jacobean continuation of Hakluyt — the book that carried the age of discovery's records into the age of colonization.
works.meter: Prose of many hands within Purchas's devout editorial frame.
works.context: Published 1625, the year of Purchas's death and of the Virginia Company's dissolution; the collection preserved many accounts that survive nowhere else and fed the English imagination of empire for two centuries.
works.characters: the voyagers and travellers (Hudson, Baffin, Cavendish, and hundreds of others)
works.structure: Four folio volumes of documentary compilation, with Purchas's prefaces, indices, and the running apparatus of his editorial 'pilgrimage'.
works.attributionNotes: Compiled and edited by Purchas from Hakluyt's papers and other sources; uncontested.

editions.title: Hakluytus Posthumus or Purchas His Pilgrimes, 20 vols.

works.title: Hali Meiðhad
works.description: An alliterative prose epistle in praise of virginity, addressed to young women contemplating the religious life, in the AB language of the Katherine Group. It contrasts the blessedness of the virgin bride of Christ with the miseries of married life, in a rhetorical tradition going back to patristic treatises on virginity.
works.plot: The author extols virginity as the highest estate, describes the joys of the heavenly bridegroom, and — in famously vivid passages — details the pains and humiliations of marriage and childbearing to urge his readers to choose the better part.
works.significance: The classic Middle English statement of the virginity ideal, and a prime exhibit of the period's energetic anti-matrimonial rhetoric (the counterpart of the Wife of Bath's prologue).
works.meter: Rhythmical, heavily alliterative prose of the AB language group.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, in the circle of Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii.
works.characters: the virgin reader (addressee); Christ as bridegroom
works.structure: A single sustained exhortation moving from praise of virginity through satiric anatomy of marriage to the rewards of the heavenly marriage.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: Maria W. Stewart, America's First Black Woman Political Writer: Essays and Speeches

works.title: Hamlet
altTitles: The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of revenge and consciousness: the ghost of Hamlet's father charges him to avenge his murder by Claudius, who now wears the crown and the queen; Hamlet's feigned madness, the play-within-the-play ('The Mousetrap'), the deaths of Polonius and Ophelia, and the final duel — poisoned rapier and cup — in which the stage is cleared of the whole royal house.
works.plot: Hamlet tests the ghost's word by staging a murder-play before the king; Claudius's guilt is exposed; Hamlet spares the praying king, kills Polonius, is sent to England with a death warrant he reverses; Ophelia drowns; Laertes returns for revenge; and the poisoned duel at Elsinore kills Gertrude, Laertes, Claudius, and Hamlet himself, with Fortinbras inheriting Denmark.
works.significance: The most famous play ever written — the tragedy of modern consciousness itself, and the summit of the English language's claim on world literature.
works.meter: The widest range in Shakespeare — soliloquy, prose, song, the Player's speech, the graveyard quibbles — with 'To be or not to be' at its centre.
works.context: Written about 1600–01 in the wake of the lost ur-Hamlet and of the death of Shakespeare's son Hamnet; the three texts (Q1 1603, Q2 1604–05, F 1623) present the classic problem of Shakespearean textual scholarship.
works.characters: Hamlet; Claudius; Gertrude; the Ghost; Polonius; Ophelia; Laertes; Horatio; Rosencrantz; Guildenstern; Fortinbras; Osric; the First Gravedigger
works.structure: A five-act revenge tragedy infinitely deferred and interiorized — soliloquies, plays, and feigned madness displacing action — until the catastrophe of Act 5.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the relationship of the three early texts remains the central problem of its bibliography.

editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

works.title: Handlyng Synne
works.description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's English verse adaptation (begun 1303) of the Anglo-Norman Manuel des péchés of William of Wadington: a manual of penance in some 12,000 lines expounding the commandments, the deadly sins, the sacraments, and the art of confession, illustrated with scores of exemplary tales. It is the classic Middle English penitential handbook.
works.plot: The poem moves systematically through the commandments and sins, each doctrine illustrated by cautionary exempla — the dancing carolers cursed by a priest, the usurer, the witch of Ely — and concludes with instruction on confession, contrition, and satisfaction.
works.significance: The principal English treatment of penance between the thirteenth-century homilies and Chaucer's Parson's Tale (which draws on related material), and a treasury of the exemplum tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of plain, efficient didactic verse in the Lincolnshire dialect.
works.context: Begun in 1303 by the Gilbertine canon Robert Mannyng at Sempringham Priory, Lincolnshire, translating Wadington's manual for an English lay audience; preserved in the Vernon and Bodleian Digby manuscripts among others.
works.characters: the exemplary sinners and saints of the tales
works.structure: A didactic sequence organized by commandment, sin, and sacrament, with narrative exempla inset throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed by the author's own preface to 'Robert of Brunne'.
sources: The Writings and Speeches of Edmund Burke

works.title: Harrington
works.form: Prose fiction; novel of education and moral reformation; the autobiographical child-narrator novel
works.description: A novel of the education of a spoiled only child, and the writer's most serious study of the formation and the unlearning of prejudice. The boy is made irrational by indulgence and by a tyrannical schoolmaster, and the book then shows how the habits of a generous nature are recovered through shame, friendship and the example of suffering. Its central and most discussed passage is an embedded tale of an injured Jewish family, which converts the boy's unreasoned contempt into a lesson on the persecution he has himself helped to inflict. It was the last of the writer's major novels and is the most explicitly moral in purpose.
works.plot: An only child of a weak father and an indulgent mother is tortured at school by a brute master whom his family will not believe against, and his character is warped by sympathy denied and by flattery accepted. He is rescued and educated by a plain-spoken friend of his father, whose method of honour and reason restores his judgement. The middle of the book is taken up with the history of a money-lender of the wronged faith and of his daughter, whose injuries at the hands of the boy's own family expose the cruelty of a prejudice inherited and never examined. The young man's life is then governed by reparation, by a friendship tested in illness, and by the choice of a wife whose worth he is at last able to recognise.
works.significance: A founding text of the English novel of childhood and of the literary argument against religious prejudice, and the writer's last important fiction. Its embedded tale is a standard document for study of writing about Jews in the Romantic period, and its first-person education design anticipates the nineteenth-century novel of development.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a plain, reflective first-person style, changing from the speech of an injured child to the measured idiom of an examining adult
works.context: Published in 1817, it belongs to the post-war debate on the civil condition of Jews in Britain, to the controversy over classical schooling and the punishment of children, and to the writer's long engagement with the education of judgement begun in the family's educational books. Its plea for the recognition of a persecuted minority is a direct answer to the treatment of Jewish characters in contemporary romance, and its school chapters draw on the reports of English academies of the period.
works.structure: First-person autobiographical fiction in three volumes, looking back on a boyhood and young manhood; the embedded tale of the injured family interrupts the forward movement and reframes the whole education as an argument about prejudice.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.

works.title: Havelok the Dane
altTitles: The Lay of Havelok the Dane
works.description: A Lincolnshire romance of some 3,000 lines on the dispossessed prince Havelok, brought up as a kitchen-boy at Grimsby, whose royal birthmark, strength, and marriage to the princess Goldeboru lead to the recovery of the thrones of Denmark and England. Its sympathetic depiction of labouring life and its Lincolnshire topography make it unique among the romances.
works.plot: The orphaned Havelok is saved from the usurper Godard by the fisherman Grim, who flees with him to England; in disguise he serves as a kitchen hand at Lincoln, where the usurper Godrich marries the princess Goldeboru to him in mockery; Havelok's revealed royalty, his defeat of the usurpers, and his double coronation conclude the poem.
works.significance: One of the finest English romances: its realism about work and poverty, and its fusion of folk-tale, dynastic, and hagiographical elements, make it a classic of the genre.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with marked northern (East Midland/Lincolnshire) dialect features.
works.context: Composed c. 1280–90 in Lincolnshire, drawing on local legend (Grimsby's foundation) and Anglo-Norman sources (Lai d'Haveloc, Gaimar); preserved uniquely in Bodleian Library, Laud Misc. 108.
works.characters: Havelok; Goldeboru; Grim the fisherman; Godard; Godrich; Ubbe
works.structure: A double exile-and-restoration plot (Havelok and Goldeboru in parallel), with an interpolated miracle episode and a long climactic battle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Headlong Hall
works.description: the author's first novel, a short comic dialogue novel in which seven guests of opposite intellectual temperaments are locked in a country house and talk past each other until a marriage plot resolves the chaos. It is the earliest of the author's novel-length satires of Romantic-era thought.
works.plot: Sir Arkandale Silkworm, a wealthy patron, gathers at Headlong Hall seven guests representing incompatible intellectual positions — a phrenologist, a metaphysician, an historian, a political economist, a beautist, a linguist, and others — each with a theory of human perfectibility. Their interminable argument is punctuated by practical jokes and forced to resolve by Sir Arkandale's arrangement of advantageous marriages among them. The novel's comedy is entirely conversational; the plot is a device for the clash of ideas.
works.significance: Headlong Hall established the 'novel of ideas' form in which the novelist became the century's master; its dialogue comedy influenced Huxley and the later campus novel. It is a key document of the reception of Romantic intellectual culture by its wittiest sceptical observer.
works.context: Published in 1816, the annus mirabilis of English Romanticism, in the immediate wake of Scott's Waverley novels; the author satirises the specialist intellectual vocabularies — phrenology, political economy, historicism — fashionable in Regency drawing rooms.
works.characters: Mr. Glossop; Mr. Floggington; Mr. Pammacassus; Miss Bellomyst; Sir Arkandale Silkworm; Mr. Skellet; Mr. Mavis; Mr. Fustifier
works.structure: Single setting, almost wholly dialogue-driven; the 'conversation piece' structure replaces conventional plot; intellectual types clash and are comically reconciled.

works.title: Hellas
works.form: Closet drama and lyrical drama in the classical masked form, with the chorus of the older Attic tragedy; a political ode cast as a scene.
works.description: A short lyrical drama written in a few weeks to celebrate the Greek rising against the Ottoman power, and built on the poet's own statement in its preface that its scenery and machinery are drawn from the hills and gulf of the modern Morea. A phantom of the ancient glory of Hellas appears to a worshipper by the sea at Lepanto and shows the regeneration of the race, while the chorus of captive women doubts and the despairing old men answer with the prophecy of a new age. It is the most purely political of the author's dramas and the shortest of his serious verse plays.
works.plot: A devotee of the ancient muse keeps the vigil of the year at Sunium and by the Gulf of Lepanto, mourning that Greece has no voice left, and the phantom of her buried glory rises upon the waters to promise a coming day of deliverance. The chorus of captive women and the despairing chiefs of the race dispute the promise, and the vision passes to the triumph of a regenerated people, the tyrant's power broken and the altars of the free rebuilt. The close retracts the certainty, the poet's own voice acknowledges the doubt of the human heart, and the drama ends with the invocation of the immortal spirit of the scene. The argument is that a nation's ancient memory is the warrant of its political resurrection.
works.significance: It became the lyrical testament of philhellenism and one of the most recited and quoted political lyrics of the following century, its stanzas used in the cause of Greek and of Italian freedom. Its preface is also a document of the author's late theory of poetry and of his disillusionment with the immediate effect of verse, and its treatment of national memory as a political force shaped the later poetry of liberation movements.
works.meter: A variety of lyric measures, free iambic and trochaic lines for the dialogue and short responsive strophes for the chorus, with the anapestic movement of the prophetic passages.
works.context: Composed at Pisa between October and December 1821, in the months of the outbreak of the Greek revolution, the rise of the eastern question in European politics and the execution of the patriarch, and published in London in 1822 with a prose preface on the poet's design and his own account of the poem's failure to sell. The dedication to the friends who had fought and died in the cause made it a public act of subscription to a foreign war of liberation.
works.characters: the devotee of the ancient glory; the phantom of Hellas; the chorus of captive women; the despairing chief of the race; the tyrant of the East as the power denounced
works.structure: A dramatic scene of some four hundred lines with choral entry and exit, opened by the devotee's soliloquy, the vision and its questioning in the middle and the retracting close; the movement is entirely lyric and prophetic.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published in the author's lifetime and its text is stable, with minor revisions in the posthumous collections.

editions.title: Shelley's Poetry and Prose (Norton Critical Edition)

works.title: Helpstone
altTitles: Helpstone. A Local Scenery on the Banks of the Welland
works.form: Topographical and Descriptive Poetry; Nature Lyric and Meditation
works.description: A sequence of eleven fourteen-line sonnets addressed to the author's native village on the Welland in the Northamptonshire fens, and the opening poem of his first published volume. The sequence moves from affectionate greeting of an unlettered place to mourning over the loss of common grazing, of sheep-walks and of the neighbours who knew them. It is the founding statement of a labouring-class poetry in which local topography becomes the evidence of dispossession.
works.plot: The first sonnets hail Helpstone as a village unknown to fame, where humble genius tries to rise above the vulgar, and recall the sports, birds, and seasons of childhood. The middle numbers name specific losses: the trees felled, the bushes cleared, the banks and waters changed by new husbandry. One sonnet curses Wealth as the cause that levels every tree and takes away labour and bread, and complains that the impounding and cutting of the Welland destroyed the sheep-herds' feeding grounds. Later numbers turn to the aged and dead who are gone, to the poet's own dependence and infirmity, and finally to the spot itself as a comfort in life's decline.
works.significance: The sequence made the author the most famous of labouring-class poets and gave the enclosure controversy its most quoted verse complaint, in which the loss of common grazing is stated as a loss of memory, pleasure, and personal identity. It established the local-poem convention later poets of rural labour imitated, and it remains the touchstone for discussions of a plebeian Romanticism distinct from the Lake school.
works.meter: Eleven sonnets of fourteen lines in iambic pentameter rhymed in running couplets (aa bb cc dd ee ff gg), the sequence closing each number on a pointed rather than a turned couplet; the diction is plain, with frequent enjambment. Verified from the first-edition text, where the sequence occupies pages 1 to 11.
works.context: Written when the author was a day-labourer in husbandry whose father had fallen to parish relief, in a village whose commons and sheep-walks were being destroyed by enclosure, drainage, and the cut of a river navigation. The poems were gathered for publication after a Stamford bookseller and a London publisher took up a manuscript of a labouring poet, and the volume appeared with an introduction stressing that the poems were the genuine productions of a young peasant.
works.characters: the poet-speaker of Helpstone; the shepherd and sheep-heard of the Welland banks; the father on parish relief; the dead and absent village neighbours; Wealth, personified as the agent of destruction
works.structure: A linked sonnet sequence without plot, each fourteen-line number a self-contained meditation that repeats the heading HELPSTONE in the volume; the progression is associative, from salutation through complaint and recollection to resignation.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name on the title page of the first volume; no dispute attaches to the sequence.

works.title: Henrietta
works.form: novel; domestic and moral prose fiction
works.description: A novel of a portionless young woman, a poor relation in a great house, whose virtue is tried by presumption, by a fraudulent seduction and by the world's readiness to believe the worst of a woman alone. It is darker and more analytical than the author's earlier fiction and much concerned with the opinion of the world as a tribunal.
works.plot: Henrietta, dependent on relations of consequence, is pursued by a man of fortune who offers protection rather than marriage, and later by one whose design is outright seduction. She defends herself with spirit, is compromised in appearance, and must bear the verdict of society while the men who injured her are spared. Her constancy and the exposure of her persecutors prepare a marriage on equal terms, the narrative arguing that a woman's reputation is a social construction.
works.significance: It is one of the most acute mid-century analyses of the sexual double standard in fiction and a key text in the development of the novel of the unprotected woman.
works.meter: An argentine prose of reflection and reported conversation, with the narrator's essays on female dependency interrupting the narrative.
works.context: Published in 1758, in the decade of the mid-century novel's turn to the analysis of reputation and dependency, and after the author's critical work on the drama had fixed her place in letters.
works.characters: Henrietta; her protectress and the great family; the two pursuers, one coarse and one designing; the suitor who finally offers equality
works.structure: Third-person narration in two volumes with a strong current of moral essay; the plot turns on the difference between Henrietta's conduct and the world's report of it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name.

works.title: Henry IV, Part 1
altTitles: The First Part of Henry the Fourth
works.description: The first play of the Henriad proper: Prince Hal's education between the tavern of Falstaff and the field of Shrewsbury, where he kills the rebel Hotspur and redeems his reputation — the comedy of Eastcheap and the tragedy of the Percys joined in the greatest of the English history plays.
works.plot: Hotspur and the Percys rebel against the king they helped make; Hal plays truant with Falstaff until the crisis calls him to arms; at Shrewsbury he saves his father, kills Hotspur, and leaves Falstaff to counterfeit death and claim the honour — a claim the prince allows, 'for my part, if a lie may do thee grace, I'll gild it with the happiest terms I have'.
works.significance: Contains Shakespeare's greatest comic creation in Falstaff, and his profoundest study of a prince's education in power.
works.meter: The fullest range of Shakespeare's early style: Hotspur's verse, Falstaff's prose, Hal's movement between them, and Glendower's Welsh lyricism.
works.context: Written about 1596–97 from Holinshed and the anonymous Famous Victories of Henry V; Oldcastle's name was changed to Falstaff after protest from the Cobham family.
works.characters: Prince Hal (Henry, Prince of Wales); Sir John Falstaff; King Henry IV; Hotspur (Henry Percy); the Earl of Worcester; the Earl of Northumberland; Owen Glendower; the Earl of Douglas; Poins; Bardolph; Mistress Quickly; Lady Percy
works.structure: A double plot of court/camp and tavern braided by Hal's movement between the two worlds, with the Gadshill robbery as hinge and the battle as convergence.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Henry IV, Part 2
altTitles: The Second Part of Henry the Fourth
works.description: The darker sequel: rebellion flickers out at Gaultree Forest, the king sickens under the weight of his usurped crown, Falstaff conscripts the rag-tag army of Gloucestershire and runs up his tavern score, and the play ends with the new king's public rejection of his old companion — 'I know thee not, old man' — and Falstaff's ruin.
works.plot: Northumberland's rebellion collapses; Prince John tricks the rebels into disbanding; the dying king and Hal are reconciled; Henry V's coronation is followed by the rejection of Falstaff and the justice's promise of the new reign.
works.significance: The most sombre of the histories — a study of the costs of power whose rejection scene is among the most painful in the canon.
works.meter: Prose dominates the Falstaff scenes and verse the court; the play's elegiac music belongs to its age and sickness.
works.context: Written about 1597–98; its Epilogue promises the further adventures of Falstaff, fulfilled instead in The Merry Wives of Windsor.
works.characters: Prince Hal; Sir John Falstaff; King Henry IV; the Lord Chief Justice; Prince John of Lancaster; the Earl of Northumberland; the Archbishop of York; Justice Shallow; Justice Silence; Pistol; Doll Tearsheet; Mistress Quickly; Bardolph; Poins; Lady Percy
works.structure: A chronicle of endings — of rebellion, of reign, of friendship — built on scenes of age, disease, and memory, with the Gloucestershire justices and the tavern as the comic underworld.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Henry V
altTitles: The Life of Henry the Fifth
works.description: The climax of the second tetralogy: the Chorus's apology for the 'wooden O' frames the epic of Agincourt — Henry's claim to France, the traitors at Southampton, Harfleur's breach, the night before battle, and the victory of the 'band of brothers' — followed by the comic peace of the wooing of Katherine.
works.plot: Henry, urged by the church and provoked by the Dauphin's tennis balls, invades France; the campaign moves through Harfleur to Agincourt, where the outnumbered English win; the play closes with the treaty of Troyes and the king's rough wooing of the French princess.
works.significance: The national epic of the English stage — and, in its ambivalences, the most debated of the histories in every age of war.
works.meter: The great set speeches — 'Once more unto the breach', the Crispin's Day oration — in verse, against the prose of the soldiers and the dialect comedy of the captains.
works.context: Written 1599, the year of the Globe and of Essex's Irish expedition (to which the Chorus looks forward); the play made Agincourt the founding myth of English arms.
works.characters: King Henry V; the Chorus; the Duke of Exeter; Fluellen; Pistol; Bardolph; Nym; Mistress Quickly; the Dauphin; the Constable of France; Katherine; Princess of France; Alice; Montjoy; Williams; the King of France
works.structure: A choric five-act epic, each act introduced by the Chorus, alternating the high rhetoric of war with the low comedy of the tavern remnants (Bardolph, Pistol, Fluellen) and ending in the romance of the wooing scene.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Henry VI, Part 1
altTitles: The First Part of Henry the Sixth
works.description: The first play of Shakespeare's earliest tetralogy, probably written in collaboration: the loss of France, the rise and burning of Joan la Pucelle (Joan of Arc), the quarrels of Gloucester and Winchester, and the white rose and the red plucked in the Temple Garden that plant the Wars of the Roses.
works.plot: Henry V's funeral opens the play; the French recover their towns through Joan's victories; Talbot, the English Achilles, dies at Bordeaux; the factions of York and Lancaster form in England; and the play ends with Suffolk's capture of Margaret of Anjou as Henry's bride — and his own instrument.
works.significance: The foundation of the English history-play cycle, and the apprenticeship of its greatest master.
works.meter: Early blank verse, often stiff and end-stopped, with the play's documentary sweep compensating for its poetic unevenness.
works.context: The Talbot scenes were celebrated by Nashe in 1592; the play is the first in the sequence that runs through Richard III.
works.characters: King Henry VI; Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester; the Bishop of Winchester; Richard, Duke of York; the Earl of Warwick; Talbot; Joan la Pucelle; Charles the Dauphin; the Duke of Suffolk; Margaret of Anjou; Edmund Mortimer
works.structure: An episodic chronicle alternating English and French scenes, unified by Talbot's tragedy and the growth of the court factions.
works.attributionNotes: Generally regarded as collaborative (the shares of Nashe and others are debated); assigned to Shakespeare by the Folio.

works.title: Henry VI, Part 2
altTitles: The First Part of the Contention
The Contention of the Two Famous Houses of York and Lancaster
works.description: The second play of the tetralogy: the fall of Duke Humphrey of Gloucester, the rebellion of Jack Cade, and the rise of Richard, Duke of York, through the disintegration of Henry VI's England toward the first battle of St Albans.
works.plot: The court faction destroys Gloucester; York exploits the Cade rebellion to test his claim; the play's great set pieces — Gloucester's murder, the miracle at St Albans, Cade's insurrection — carry England from anarchy to open war, with Margaret and Suffolk's fall along the way.
works.significance: The first English play to put the whole commonwealth — commons, court, and crown — on stage together.
works.meter: Blank verse growing more assured, with the prose of the Cade scenes as the first great crowd-comedy in English drama.
works.context: The Cade rebellion scenes dramatize the 1450 rising through Elizabethan anxieties about the commons; printed in 1594 as The First Part of the Contention.
works.characters: King Henry VI; Queen Margaret; Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester; Eleanor Cobham; the Duke of Suffolk; the Duke of York; Jack Cade; the Earl of Warwick; the Cardinal (Beaufort); Lord Say; Dick the butcher
works.structure: A chronicle of successive falls (Gloucester, Suffolk, Cade) leading to York's armed claim, in the de casibus pattern of the Mirror for Magistrates.
works.attributionNotes: Possibly collaborative with Marlowe or Nashe in debated shares; the Folio canon is followed here.

works.title: Henry VI, Part 3
altTitles: The True Tragedy of Richard Duke of York
works.description: The third play of the tetralogy: the Wars of the Roses in full blood — York's death on the molehill at Wakefield, Margaret's taunting of him with the paper crown, the slaughter of young Rutland, and the rise of Richard of Gloucester through the battles of Towton, Barnet, and Tewkesbury to his soliloquized ambitions at the play's end.
works.plot: York breaks his oath and claims the crown; the wars swing between Lancaster and York; Edward IV wins the throne and marries Elizabeth Woodville; Warwick changes sides and dies at Barnet; and Richard murders Henry VI in the Tower, then turns to the audience to announce his design on the crown.
works.significance: The bridge from the Henry VI plays to Richard III — and the first sketch of Shakespeare's greatest villain.
works.meter: Blank verse of mounting power, culminating in Richard's first great soliloquy.
works.context: Written about 1590–91, the play's cycles of revenge answered the Senecan fashion while its national matter spoke to the post-Armada moment.
works.characters: King Henry VI; Queen Margaret; Richard, Duke of York; Edward IV; George, Duke of Clarence; Richard, Duke of Gloucester; the Earl of Warwick; Lady Grey (Elizabeth Woodville); the Duke of Exeter; Rutland; Clifford
works.structure: A rapid battle-chronicle built on reversals of fortune, with Richard's emergence as the play's climactic revelation.
works.attributionNotes: Possibly collaborative in debated shares; the Folio canon is followed here.

works.title: Henry VIII
altTitles: The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eighth
works.description: The last of the history plays, written with John Fletcher: the pageant-like fall of Buckingham, the trial and divorce of Katherine of Aragon, the rise of Anne Bullen and of Cranmer, and the christening of the infant Elizabeth — ending in Cranmer's prophecy of the golden age to come under the 'maiden phoenix'.
works.plot: Buckingham falls to Wolsey's faction; the king's conscience turns against his marriage; Katherine defends herself at the legatine trial; Wolsey's fall follows; Anne is crowned and Elizabeth christened, with Cranmer's prophetic blessing on the new reign.
works.significance: The Stuart court's official version of the Reformation, and the last flowering of the history play Shakespeare had invented.
works.meter: Verse of late-Shakespearean looseness with Fletcherian run-on lines; the trial scene of Katherine is its moral and poetic summit.
works.context: First performed 29 June 1613 at the Globe, when the firing of the chambers set the theatre alight and burned it down — the play's alternate title, All Is True, is the one recorded at that performance.
works.characters: King Henry VIII; Cardinal Wolsey; Queen Katherine of Aragon; Anne Bullen; the Duke of Buckingham; Thomas Cranmer; the Duke of Norfolk; the Duke of Suffolk; Gardiner; Cromwell; the Old Lady
works.structure: A series of state show-scenes — trials, coronations, christenings — in the masque-like mode of late Jacobean spectacle, structured as successive falls and risings.
works.attributionNotes: Collaboration with John Fletcher established by stylistic and metrical evidence; the Folio assigns the play to Shakespeare alone.

works.title: Hero and Leander
works.description: Marlowe's unfinished Ovidian epyllion, left at the lovers' first night and completed by George Chapman in 1598: the priestess Hero of Sestos and the youth Leander of Abydos meet at Venus's festival and fall in love; Leander swims the Hellespont nightly, and the poem breaks off with the consummation — 'Love is not full of pity, as men say' — before Hero's death in the familiar myth.
works.plot: Leander, 'amorous Leander, beautiful and young', woos Hero at the feast of Adonis; her vows to Venus yield to his eloquence; the first swim, the first embrace, and the lovers' debate with the dawn occupy the completed portion, with Neptune's dalliance with the swimming Leander as its most celebrated episode.
works.significance: The masterpiece of the Elizabethan epyllion and the direct ancestor of the Restoration erotic couplet — the poem Shakespeare's Venus and Adonis answered and vied with.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of extraordinary wit and sensuousness — the poem that defined the English erotic couplet for the next two centuries.
works.context: Written in 1593, the year of Marlowe's death; printed first by Edward Blount in 1598 and again the same year with Chapman's continuation ('Hero and Leander: Begun by Christopher Marloe; and finished by George Chapman').
works.characters: Hero; Leander; Neptune; Venus; Cupid; the Nurse (Chapman's continuation)
works.structure: Two completed sestiads (Marlowe's) followed by Chapman's four, the whole framed as a narrative of seduction and delay in the epyllion manner.
works.attributionNotes: Marlowe's two sestiads are uncontested; the continuation is Chapman's.

works.title: Hesperides
altTitles: Hesperides; or, The Works Both Humane and Divine of Robert Herrick
works.description: Robert Herrick's vast collection of some 1,400 poems (1648), divided into the pagan 'Hesperides' and the Christian 'Noble Numbers', which celebrates the seasonal rites, courtships, and superstitions of rural Devon and the pleasures of the present, shadowed by mutability and Anglican faith — including 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time' ('Gather ye rosebuds while ye may').
works.plot: The poems range over love, wine, flowers, country customs, kings and loyalty, and devotion, urging carpe diem while acknowledging death, and pairing classical festivity with Christian piety.
works.significance: Hesperides is the most varied and charming of Cavalier collections, a treasury of English rural folklore and lyric, and 'Gather ye rosebuds' the most famous carpe diem poem in English.
works.meter: Short, musical, epigrammatic lyrics in a great variety of meters with a light, mellifluous touch.
works.context: Written largely during Herrick's years as vicar of Dean Prior (1629–47) and published in 1647/48 after his ejection by Parliament as a royalist; it preserves the ceremonial culture of the English countryside.
works.characters: the poet; Julia and other mistresses; the rural folk
works.structure: A large collection of short lyrics, epigrams, and songs in two parts, loosely grouped by theme.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Hickscorner
works.description: An anonymous early morality interlude of the conversion of three rogues — Freewill, Imagination, and the Vice Hickscorner — printed by Wynkyn de Worde c. 1513–15.
works.plot: Freewill and Imagination, fallen into idleness and vice, meet the hardened rogue Hickscorner, who boasts of his crimes and rails at virtue; Pity and Contemplation reprove them, and the three rogues are brought to repentance, confess their sins, and set out on pilgrimage, with the play ending in a vision of the joys of heaven.
works.significance: One of the earliest printed English moralities and the first to centre on the conversion of rogues; its Vice, Hickscorner, is a landmark in the development of the stage devil's comic heir, and its tavern realism anticipates the rogue literature of the Elizabethans.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Printed c. 1513–15 by Wynkyn de Worde, in the generation after Everyman; the play's tavern scenes and rogue-cant document the underworld of early Tudor London, and its popularity carried it through editions to the 1560s.
works.characters: Freewill; Imagination; Hickscorner; Pity; Contemplation; Perseverance
works.structure: A continuous morality play in two movements — the rogues' boasting fellowship and their conversion — with the Vice Hickscorner as the play's comic engine.

works.title: Historia Anglorum
works.description: Henry of Huntingdon's history of England from the earliest times to the accession of Henry II in 1154, notable for its vivid battle narratives, its interest in the English past as national history, and the substantial body of original verse — including the political poems addressed to Henry I — embedded in the prose.
works.summary: Ten books (the latest recension) move from Roman and Anglo-Saxon Britain through the Norman kings to the anarchy of Stephen's reign; the work incorporates earlier sources (Bede, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) while supplying independent contemporary witness for the twelfth century, including the famous account of the Battle of Lincoln.
works.significance: A principal narrative source for the reign of Stephen, and a central text of twelfth-century English national historiography; its verse makes it a bridge between Anglo-Latin and vernacular literary traditions.

editions.title: Historia Anglorum: The History of the English People

sources: Robert Bloomfield: Selected Poems (revised and enlarged edition)

works.title: Historia Brittonum
works.form: history and chronicle (composite) in Latin prose
works.description: A composite history of the Britons compiled in Wales in 829/30 and traditionally attributed to Nennius: genealogies, origin legends (the Trojan descent of the Britons), the lives of St Patrick and St Germanus, and the earliest datable Arthur material — the list of Arthur's twelve battles culminating at Mount Badon.
works.plot: The work assembles disparate materials on the age of the world, the Trojan origins of the Britons, the Roman occupation, Vortigern and the coming of the Saxons, the boy-prophet Ambrosius, the wars of Arthur ('dux bellorum'), the genealogies of the Saxon and Welsh kings, and the 'wonders of Britain' — an anthology of British historical memory rather than a continuous history.
works.significance: The earliest extended Arthurian text in insular literature; the principal quarry of later Welsh and English Arthurian history (Geoffrey of Monmouth).
works.meter: Latin prose of varying registers.
works.context: Compiled in Gwynedd c. 829/30 during the Mercian ascendancy in Wales; preserved in some forty manuscripts in Welsh, English, and continental recensions.
works.characters: Vortigern; Ambrosius; Arthur; Patrick; Germanus; Hengist and Horsa
works.structure: Compilatory: a sequence of heterogeneous sections of varying provenance, several marked as the work of 'Nennius the disciple of Elvodugus'.
works.attributionNotes: The prologue attributes the compilation to Nennius, but not all manuscripts carry it; the work is demonstrably composite.
sources: The Oxford Handbook of Tudor Literature, 1485–1603

works.title: Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum
altTitles: Ecclesiastical History of the English People
works.form: history and chronicle (ecclesiastical history) in Latin prose
works.description: Bede's masterpiece, completed in 731: the history of the English church and people from Caesar's invasions to 731, in five books. It is the primary narrative source for early Anglo-Saxon history, the origin of the AD dating system's general use, and the conduit through which Cædmon's Hymn and much else survives.
works.plot: The five books trace the conversion of the English kingdoms — the mission of Augustine to Kent (597), the Northumbrian mission of Paulinus and Aidan, the Synod of Whitby (664) — interspersed with saints' lives (Cuthbert, Æthelthryth), miracles, letters, and the famous account of the poet Cædmon; the work closes with a summary of Britain's ecclesiastical state and Bede's autobiographical colophon.
works.significance: 'The father of English history'; the indispensable source for the first three centuries of English Christianity and for the early vernacular poetic record.
works.meter: Latin prose of classical clarity; contains the earliest recorded English verse (Cædmon's Hymn) in paraphrase.
works.context: Composed at the twin monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow from earlier annals, lives, and documents; dedicated to King Ceolwulf of Northumbria.
works.characters: Augustine of Canterbury; Æthelberht; Edwin; Oswald; Aidan; Hild; Cuthbert; Cædmon; Theodore; Wilfrid
works.structure: Annalistic-chronological within each book, organized by kingdom and diocese; documentary (letters, synods) and hagiographical materials are woven into the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Bede's authorship is certain (his own colophon).

works.title: Historia Regum Britanniae
altTitles: The History of the Kings of Britain
works.description: Pseudohistorical chronicle tracing the kings of Britain from the legendary Brutus of Troy to the Saxon conquest, the principal source of the Arthurian legend in England. Geoffrey claims to translate 'a certain very ancient book in the British tongue' given him by Walter, archdeacon of Oxford; its authority was attacked by William of Newburgh and Gerald of Wales but it decisively shaped medieval British historiography.
works.summary: Geoffrey of Monmouth narrates the foundation of Britain by Brutus, a descendant of Aeneas, and proceeds through the reigns of the legendary kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests extend over much of Europe — to the Saxon domination and the prophecies of Merlin (the Prophetiae Merlini, later incorporated as Book VII). The work made Arthur a pan-European figure and provided the framework for Wace, Layamon, and the later chronicle tradition.
works.significance: The single most influential piece of British historical writing of the Middle Ages: over 200 manuscripts survive, and it furnished the matter of Britain for romance, chronicle, and national myth from Wace's Roman de Brut to Malory and beyond.

editions.title: The History of the Kings of Britain

works.title: Historic Doubts on the Life and Reign of King Richard the Third
altTitles: Historic Doubts on the Life and Reign of King Richard the Third
Doubts on the History of Richard III
works.description: A controversial historical argument that the standard history of Richard III is a fabrication of the victorious house, the evidence being examined point by point against the chroniclers. It is an early and influential piece of critical historical method, and its defence of the king's reputation provoked a long pamphlet war.
works.plot: The work reviews the charges against Richard - the murder of the princes, the death of his wife, the tyranny and the usurpation - and finds in each case either no contemporary evidence or evidence contradicting the received story. It argues that the chronicles were composed under the new dynasty and that the most damning particulars were invented after the event. The conclusion leaves the king's guilt undemonstrated and his character to be reformed by the reader.
works.significance: It founded the modern defence tradition of Richard's reign and is a landmark in the application of evidential scepticism to English history, anticipating the source criticism of the following century.
works.meter: A cool, ironical and closely reasoned prose of the case and the query, with the rhetorical understatement used as a weapon against authority.
works.context: Published in 1768 in the season of the antiquarian revival and of the new criticism of the chronicles, and answered by several hostile pieces before the century's end; its composition coincided with the author's own historical and edition work.
works.characters: King Richard the Third; the princes in the Tower; the chroniclers and their patrons; the historians of the Tudor age
works.structure: A dissertation in numbered particulars, each charge stated, its authorities compared and its improbability urged; the argument is juridical and accumulative rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published anonymously at first and acknowledged by the author, the dispute with the answerers being documented in his letters.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Holy Sonnets
works.description: Donne's nineteen divine sonnets — 'Batter my heart, three-personed God', 'Death be not proud', 'At the round earth's imagined corners', 'Since she whom I loved hath paid her last debt' — in which the erotic and argumentative energies of the love poems are turned on God, sin, death, and the soul's terror of damnation.
works.plot: The sonnets dramatize the soul's wrestling with God: pleas for violent grace, meditations on death and judgment, griefs of bereavement, and the final sonnets' fear and love of a God who must be wooed with the poet's whole art.
works.significance: The supreme English devotional sonnets — the bridge from the Elizabethan love sonnet to the sacred poetry of Herbert, Crashaw, and Hopkins.
works.meter: The Italian and English sonnet forms strained to the breaking point — spondaic openings, abrupt turns, and the metaphysical conceit turned to devotion.
works.context: Composed chiefly between 1609 and 1619, the years of Donne's ordination (1615) and of his wife's death (1617); the poems circulated in manuscript and were printed posthumously in 1633.
works.characters: the speaker; God (as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit); Death; the soul; the angels
works.structure: A cycle of nineteen sonnets (in the standard canon; twelve in the earliest manuscript group, with the later 'Westmoreland' sequence adding the rest), not a plotted sequence but a linked series of meditations.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the canon of nineteen and the ordering are the work of later editors, from the manuscript groups.

works.title: Homiletic Fragment I and II
works.manuscriptDate: Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII), late tenth century
works.description: Two homiletic poems in the Vercelli Book. Homiletic Fragment I (47 lines) is a meditation on deceitful friendship, comparing the false friend to the bee whose honey is sweet but whose sting is deadly. Homiletic Fragment II (20 lines) laments man's hardness of heart amid the world's sorrows.
works.plot: Fragment I warns against the friend who speaks fair but plots evil, elaborating the image of the bee through biblical and proverbial wisdom. Fragment II meditates on grief and the human failure to heed the truth, in a fragmentary surviving text.
works.significance: Witnesses to the close relationship between Old English homiletic prose and verse, and to the moral psychology of the late Anglo-Saxon church.
works.meter: Alliterative long line in the homiletic manner of the Vercelli Book's prose sermons; both texts are imperfectly preserved.
works.context: The Vercelli Book pairs these poems with its collection of doomsday homilies and with The Dream of the Rood, Elene, and Andreas; the fragments belong to the same culture of vernacular preaching and moral verse.
works.structure: Fragment I develops a single governing simile (the treacherous friend as bee) with proverbial expansions; Fragment II is a broken meditation on sorrow and heedlessness.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two fragments are distinct poems.
sources: Confessions of an English Opium-Eater and Other Writings (Oxford World's Classics)

works.title: Hope Leslie
works.form: Historical novel and romance of the colonial period, with domestic and frontier plotting
works.description: The most ambitious early American historical novel by a woman, set in the Massachusetts Bay colony of the 1630s and 1640s. It makes the Pequot war, the treatment of Indians and the position of women in a theocratic commonwealth its joint subjects. Its famous argument is that the children of a Puritan generation may dissent from its creed and still be loyal.
works.plot: Two sisters, one spirited and one gentle, are left in the care of a severe Puritan governor after their father is ruined by a quarrel with him. The younger elopes with a young Indian of the Pequot nation and passes out of the colony's world, while the elder is bound to an accomplished English youth whose loyalty to the settlement is tried by her obstinacy. The narrative passes to the Pequot war, to the burning of the fort at Mystic, and to the death of the sister whom the colony has lost. It closes by asking whether justice between cultures is possible in a country founded on conquest.
works.significance: It is the central fiction of the Puritan inheritance by a woman writer and one of the earliest American novels to make Indian dispossession its explicit moral subject. Its sister-plot supplies the structural model for later domestic historical fiction. It has been recovered as a canonical text of early American women's writing.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1827, in the year of the removal debate, and written from the author's family recollections of New England colonial history. Its use of the Indian war answers the contemporary argument over the rights of the Cherokee and the conduct of the state. Its treatment of the cavalier and the roundhead inherits the Scottish historical romance.
works.characters: Hope Leslie; Faith Leslie; Everell Whittingham; Governor Winthrop
works.structure: Third-person historical romance alternating between domestic plot and public history, with a frame of chronicle and legend and a closing appendix of historical documents.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

works.title: Horae Paulinae
altTitles: Horae Paulinae; or, New Confirmed Evidences of the Divine Authority of the Holy Scriptures
works.form: critical dissertation and biblical commentary in the evidential manner
works.description: A critical-apologetical experiment, comparing the letters of the apostle Paul with the narrative of the Acts and with one another, and finding in their accidental agreements a proof of authenticity no forger could have produced. It is a work of scholarship used as evidence, and its method of undesigned coincidence became one of the most copied arguments in the defence of the scriptures.
works.plot: The treatise first states its rule: if two writers, writing independently and for different purposes, touch upon the same place, person, or incident in ways neither intended nor adverted to, and yet without contradiction, their concurrence is evidence that both were dealing with real transactions. It then applies the rule, setting the letters of the Thessalonians and of the Corinthians beside the narrative of the missionary journeys, and showing that the history and the epistles supply each other's omissions, that the characters, fortunes, and fellow-labourers agree without apparent study, and that the notices of the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem fall into place only when the two records are read together. A second line of comparison is drawn between the epistles themselves, whose differences of tone, of phrase, and of circumstance are shown to be marks of genuine correspondence rather than of a designed uniformity. The conclusion is that these writings are neither forged nor colluded, and that the same method may be extended to the rest of the canon.
works.significance: It created a permanent instrument of scriptural apologetic, the argument from undesigned coincidence, which passed into commentaries, into the popular evidential manuals, and into the literary criticism of the next century, where the same test was used to date and to authenticate documents. As criticism it anticipates the modern treatment of a correspondence as historical evidence, and as rhetoric it is the neatest example of the period's habit of arguing religion from the rules of proof.
works.meter: Quiet, patient, expository prose of the close reader: parallel text, minute comparison, and the restrained exultation of a reasoner who believes he has found a new class of proof.
works.context: Published in the year of the counter-revolutionary pamphlets and of the quarrel over infidelity, out of the same school of evidential divinity that produced a popular view of the Christian proof, and built upon a method its author had already worked out in private study before the sceptical crisis made such arguments a public need.
works.structure: Parts, each pairing one epistle or group of epistles with the corresponding portion of the narrative, and closing with general remarks on the extent and force of the concurrence; the argument proceeds by accumulated particulars rather than by deduction.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, who afterwards re-cast and enlarged portions of it in the collected editions of his theological works.

works.title: Hours of Idleness
altTitles: Hours of Idleness; Original and Translated
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Juvenile verse miscellany: pre-Romantic sensibility lyric and verse epistle in the manner of the 1790s school of sensibility, with Augustan translation and imitation as its display of education.
works.description: The first book of verse by a noble minor, gathered from school exercises, imitations and occasional poems written between the Harrow years and the coming of age. It mixes lyric meditations, verse epistles to friends and relations, elegies on the dead, descriptive pieces on Newstead Abbey and translations from the classics and from French. The prevailing manner is that of the sentimental school of the 1790s: a sensitive young poet, estranged from his schoolfellows, consoling himself with memory, friendship and the pleasure of verse. Its hostile review in 1808, and the satirical reply it provoked, turned a private printed book into the opening quarrel of the poet's public career.
works.plot: The volume has no sustained argument but is arranged as a miscellany, opening with odes and lyric meditations and passing through epistles, elegies on friends and dead kinsfolk, and descriptive verse on the abbey and the Harrow playing-field. Its recurring subjects are the loss of schoolfellows, the isolation of a boy among boys, the deaths of maternal relatives in Scotland, and a claim to feeling refined by misfortune. Several pieces address the poet's half-sister directly, and a group of epistles is written to Harrow friends, among them a schoolmate who became a lifelong companion. The close turns on the poet's own prospects and on the consolation of verse, in a diction borrowed from the Scottish school of Beattie and from Campbell. The imitation of prior poets, ancient and modern, is not concealed but presented as the honest exercise of an undeclared hand.
works.significance: It is the documentary starting point of a career that became the most famous in European poetry within five years, and the evidence that the later manner was an argument with the school of sensibility rather than an inheritance from it. Its reviews fixed the posture of the insulted young nobleman that the satire of 1809 exploited and that the pilgrimage poem later dramatized. It also preserves the private mythology of family, home and loss on which the public pose of the tale poems was built.
works.meter: Chiefly iambic pentameter couplets and quatrains, with irregular ode stanzas, an imitation of the walk-verse of the country poem, and a few lyric measures in the manner of song; the handling is competent and heavily modelled rather than inventive.
works.context: Printed at a provincial press in 1807 at the author's cost for private circulation, the book was refused by the publisher whom its dedicatee had served, and its augmented London issue of 1808 drew the severe Edinburgh Review notice of April of that year, which treated a noble minor's private verses as public folly. The attack, and the satirical answer it produced, exemplify the new power of the review journals to make or wound a career, and the sensitivity of class, patronage and the booksellers' market in the years of the anti-Jacobin settlement.
works.characters: the poet-speaker; the half-sister addressed in several poems; the Harrow schoolfellows of the epistles; the dead kinswomen of the elegies; the ghost of the abbey in its descriptive piece
works.structure: A miscellany in three loose groups, odes and lyric meditations, then epistles and elegies, then translations and imitations; the ordering is by mood and manner rather than theme, and the 1808 issue added prose argument in the form of a prefatory advertisement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume appeared over the author's peerage title and initials, and pieces from it were reused and revised in the collected editions.

works.title: Hudibras
works.description: Samuel Butler's mock-heroic satire in three parts on Presbyterian and Independent hypocrisy, following the knight-errant Hudibras and his squire Ralpho through a series of absurd adventures in the wake of the Restoration.
works.plot: Hudibras, a Puritan knight of absurd learning and courage, sets out with his squire Ralpho to suppress bear-baiting, is beaten by the widow's champion Trulla, is rescued by the astrologer Sidrophel, and courts the wealthy widow; each part satirises a different aspect of sectary enthusiasm.
works.significance: The most popular poem of the Restoration — Charles II carried a copy in his pocket — and the principal English model of low mock-heroic, influencing Swift, Pope's Dunciad, and the whole tradition of comic verse satire.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with grotesque double and triple rhymes, deliberately anti-heroic; the 'Hudibrastic' verse.
works.context: Part I published 1663, Part II 1664, Part III 1678; written from Butler's experience as secretary to the Presbyterian Sir Samuel Luke during the civil wars.
works.characters: Sir Hudibras; Ralpho; Trulla; Magnano; Cerdon; Sidrophel; Whachum; the Widow; Talgol; Orsin
works.structure: Three parts in eight cantos each, a picaresque sequence of digressive episodes with extensive marginal notes and a prose epistle.
works.attributionNotes: Part I published anonymously but immediately ascribed to Butler; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Human Life
works.form: Didactic and meditative poem in the eighteenth-century descriptive tradition, descended from the 'Pleasures' poems of the earlier century and from the school of pastoral and domestic moral verse.
works.description: A reflective poem on the ordinary cycle of domestic and civic life, treating the common-place as the proper subject of serious verse. Its speaker moves through the daily round of labour, rest, friendship, illness and death, arguing that a quiet, moral and sociable existence yields more genuine poetry than romance or heroics. It was published as a single long poem in three books and was re-issued with additional pieces in 1821 and in the collected edition of 1827.
works.plot: The poem's argument is that human life, in its homeliest and most recurring features, is at once the surest subject and the severest test of verse. It passes from the morning and labouring round of a community to the consolations of friendship, religion and domestic affection, and then to sickness and mortality, refusing to resolve these into a grand narrative. Episodic pictures of the poor, of the town at work and of the sickroom carry the moral reasoning. The closing books widen the scope to history and to the poet's own station, ending in a meditation on the small services a verse of observation can render. Its plainness of subject, earned by elaboration of revision, was the poem's provocation to a age of the exotic and the heroic.
works.significance: It established the model of the deliberately undramatic Romantic meditative poem, and its insistence on the ordinary as poetic material was praised by later poets who wanted a via media between Lake-school simplicity and Byronic rhetoric. Victorian school anthologies fixed a phrase from its closing lines as a definition of the practical value of poetry. Its reputation now rests less on argument than on the example it gives of revision as a poetic method.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, with sententious closures and frequent apostrophe.
works.context: Written across the war years and published just after peace, when the vocabulary of 'human life' was being contested by radical, evangelical and Wordsworthian writers alike. Its celebration of ordinary labour and polite sociability belongs to the Regency book trade's well-fed middle-class readership, and its anti-romantic plainness was a deliberate contrast with the Oriental romances then selling widely. The poet's Unitarian family background and his position in London finance and patronage inform its quiet moral didacticism.
works.structure: A continuous reflective argument in numbered books, held together by a single meditating voice and by episodic tableau rather than by plot.

works.title: Hungarian Traductions
altTitles: Hungarian Traductions, from the Best Latin and Other Historians
works.language: English (translated from Latin and other languages)
works.form: Translation and editorial compilation in prose, of historical and antiquarian material, with notes and prefatory argument; a work of national history in the translated-compiler manner of the period.
works.description: Percy's earliest book-length publication as a translator and compiler: a volume of renderings from the Latin and other historians of Hungary, offering the English reader an account of the Hungarians and of the long frontier warfare of eastern Europe with the Ottoman powers. It is a work of the same antiquarian-historical imagination that produced the 'Reliques', applied to the origins and fortunes of a nation rather than to its poetry.
works.plot: The volume has no plot but an assembling argument: that the history of Hungary, its people, their migrations, their institutions and their struggles, can be recovered for English readers from the foreign historians and made intelligible as a single narrative of national fortune. Its substance is the rise and the trials of a nation placed on the border of empires, with the incursions of eastern peoples, the contests with the Turks, and the revolutions of its own dynasties treated as a lesson in the mutability of states. Percy's editorial interest shows itself in the choice and arrangement of the pieces and in the notes, which pursue the origin, manners and antiquities of the nations described. The implicit argument is that national character, like national poetry, is a proper object of study and of sympathetic curiosity.
works.significance: It is the lesser-known but revealing foundation of Percy's career, showing that the editor of the 'Reliques' began as a translator of national history, and that his project throughout was the recovery of the particular character of nations. It is a useful document of the eighteenth-century habit of making other countries' histories available through compiled translation.
works.context: It was published a year before the 'Reliques', when Percy was establishing himself as a compiler-antiquary supported by noble patronage, and when the history and present condition of the eastern European frontier was of live interest to a British reading public following Habsburg and Ottoman affairs. It belongs to the same antiquarian temper as his ballad collection, an interest in the origins and character of nations.
works.characters: The Hungarian nation as collective subject; the kings and commanders of the translated histories; the Ottoman and neighbouring powers
works.structure: A compiled and translated historical miscellany: independent rendered pieces and extracts arranged to give a continuous account of the nation and its wars, with editorial notes and prefatory matter.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Percy as translator and compiler is uncontested; the underlying historians are of course several and are named in the volume. The dates of the original pieces and of Percy's work upon them are not fixed here, so the composition fields are left null.

works.title: Hyde Park
works.description: Shirley's comedy of fashionable London society, set on the day of the horse races in Hyde Park, in which the wooing contests of the gentry, the tricks of a returned 'dead' husband, and the rivalry of suitors are resolved in a multiple marriage.
works.plot: Three gentlemen compete for the hands of three ladies while a fourth, presumed dead, returns; the Park scene provides the public arena in which the rivalries are settled.
works.significance: A key document of Caroline court society and one of the earliest plays to make fashionable London topography its subject.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose in the comic low scenes.
works.context: First performed at the Cockpit in 1632 and dedicated to Queen Henrietta Maria; Hyde Park had been opened to the public by Charles I in 1637.
works.characters: Bonavent; Trier; Rider; Carol; Mistress Bonavent; Mistress Bonny; Juliet; Anne; the Hostess
works.structure: Five acts, moving from the London lodgings to the Park and back.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Hydriotaphia; or, Urn-Burial
works.description: Browne's treatise on the burial of the dead, occasioned by the discovery of Roman urns in Norfolk, which moves from antiquarian description to the great meditation on mortality and oblivion that is its famous second half.
works.plot: Chapters I-III survey the burial customs of the ancient world; chapter IV reflects on the vanity of funerary monuments; chapter V, the peroration, meditates on the certainty of oblivion and the Christian hope of resurrection.
works.significance: The supreme English meditation on death and oblivion; it has influenced writers from Johnson and De Quincey to W. G. Sebald, and its phrases ('that vulgar arithmetic of antiquity', 'to be ignorant of evil') are part of the language.
works.meter: The most magnificent prose of the seventeenth century; the closing paragraphs of chapter V are among the most quoted passages in English.
works.context: Published in 1658, in the same year as The Garden of Cyrus and the death of Cromwell; it was written during the Commonwealth when Browne was living quietly at Norwich.
works.structure: Five chapters of increasing rhetorical intensity, ending in the celebrated chapter V.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Browne; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Hymn to Adversity
altTitles: Hymn to Adversity: Written on the Approach of Winter
works.description: Gray's short hymn addressed to Adversity as the grim daughter of Power and Wisdom, which thanks the harsh teacher for the discipline of sorrow and for the humanising effect of misfortune.
works.plot: The hymn invokes Adversity, attends her from the throne of the supreme, and shows how her stern schooling teaches compassion, self-knowledge and the value of the fleeting good, closing with the prayer that her discipline may not be in vain.
works.significance: It is the most perfect English short hymn of the school of feeling, converting the stoic and Christian argument of affliction into a regular lyric.
works.meter: Regular short stanzas of the hymn measure in the manner of the Horatian ode, with the clear close and the balanced personification.
works.context: Written in the same year as the Eton ode, in the circle of the poet's college retirement and of the Horatian revival, and long read as a companion to the century's discipline of sorrow.
works.characters: Adversity addressed as a power; the parent powers of Wisdom and of the chastening will
works.structure: A regular stanced hymn of invocation, argument and prayer, following the order of the Horatian and the church hymn.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Hymns and Sacred Poems
altTitles: A Collection of Hymns and Sacred Poems (1739)
works.description: The first hymn book of the Wesleyan revival, published at Bristol in 1739 by the two brothers and containing Charles Wesley's earliest great hymns. Its preface marked the break with the Church of England and gave Methodism its programme of 'Scripture, Reason, and Experience' in worship.
works.plot: The volume gathers hymns for the seasons, sacraments, and occasions of Christian experience: the nativity and passion, the resurrection and ascension, justification, assurance, prayer, and the close of the year. Its poems move from the 'little flock' of the societies through calls to repentance to the triumphant hark of the wedding hymn and the self-dedicating 'Leave all thy self behind'. The preface defends extempore singing in the field assemblies, answers the charges of enthusiasm, and sets out the Wesleyan reading of salvation by faith. The collection establishes the pattern of the Methodist hymn book: experience sung in the first person plural.
works.significance: It founded Methodist hymnody and introduced Charles Wesley's lyric voice, the most prolific and enduring hymn writer in English, into worship that spread through the Atlantic world.
works.meter: Chiefly common and long metre hymn stanzas of four and six lines in iambic measures, with the brothers' varied tunes indicated; the diction is deliberately plain and homiletic.
works.context: Published at Bristol in 1739 in the first open-air season of the revival, after the Aldersgate year and the brothers' American voyage, as the field preaching needed its own songbook against the established psalmody.
works.characters: the singing society; the Wesley family
works.structure: An ordered hymn collection with prefatory defence, the hymns arranged by Christian seasons and doctrinal heads rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Joint collection of John and Charles Wesley; individual hymns are generally assignable, with Charles as author of the great majority.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Hymns and Spiritual Songs
altTitles: Hymns and Spiritual Songs, in Three Books
works.description: Isaac Watts's first hymn collection, three books of Scriptural, moral, and devotional songs, the foundation of English hymnody as a literate genre. Its preface argued the duty and privilege of singing 'new songs under the gospel dispensation' and freed nonconformist worship from the exclusive metrical psalter.
works.plot: Book I sings selected Scriptures into verse, psalm and canticle paraphrase with didactic edges; Book II offers moral and divine subjects, the temper of the soul, death, judgment, and grace; Book III gathers divine songs of a more spiritual and affectionate cast, the longest and most quoted. Watts moves the hymn from catechism to meditation, making the first person plural of the church the voice of the awakened individual. Its best texts, from the drowsy falling sleep of the slumbering Jesus to the cross, the throne, and the coming of the Lord, became staples of every later collection. The whole carries the Puritan sermon into tuneful, rationally ordered praise.
works.significance: Watts is 'the father of English hymnody' and this book the charter document, the collection from which the English-speaking churches have most drawn their songs of worship through three centuries.
works.meter: Chiefly common, short, and long metre iambic stanzas of Augustan psalmody, plain diction, strong syntax, and the memorable simple phrase.
works.context: Published in London in 1707 with the author's early independent-ministry years at Bury and London behind it, in the reforming decade when dissent began to sing hymns of modern composition beside Sternhold and Hopkins.
works.structure: Three books arranged by source and subject, the later books progressively more experimental, with preface defending gospel hymnody.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Hymns for the Feasts of the Church
works.form: Hymn-cycle for the liturgical year, in the tradition of the paraphrase and of the church-meter hymn, with the poet's characteristic Hebraic and typological diction; the pieces are short, strophic and singable.
works.description: Smart's devotional hymns for the seasons and principal feasts of the Christian year, belonging to the liturgical side of his work and to the same religious imagination as the 'Song to David' and 'Jubilate Agno'. They were written for the uses of the church calendar rather than for the poetical market, and they survive outside any lifetime collection of his verse.
works.plot: The hymns take the anniversaries and offices of the church year as their occasions, and each is built upon the scriptural and typological material proper to its feast. Their argument is not doctrinal but doxological: the year is presented as a sequence of mercies and manifestations, and the worshipper is taught to rejoice in each in its order. As in the longer poems, the concrete and the created world is pressed into service as the imagery of praise, and the personal voice of the poet is subdued to the demands of a congregation's utterance.
works.significance: They complete the picture of Smart as a poet of the prayer book and the psalms rather than of the magazine, and they are the least Augustan of his verse in their intention to be sung by a congregation. Their survival outside print in his lifetime is part of the history of his neglect.
works.meter: Hymn measures of the common and long metre types, with the plain, accented and heavily parallelist phrasing Smart used for devotional verse; the stanzas are regular, in contrast with the experimental measures of his odes.
works.context: They belong to the religious culture of Smart's later years, in which hymn-writing for the church year was a work of party and of devotion, between the Latitudinarian and the evangelical and High-Church traditions. The same decade saw the great flowering of English hymnody by Watts, Doddridge and the Wesleys, against which Smart's church-year hymns assert an older and more liturgical model.
works.characters: The worshipping church addressed and instructing itself; the persons and events of scripture invoked at each feast
works.structure: A cycle of independent liturgical hymns arranged by the feasts and seasons of the church year, with no continuous narrative and with the calendar supplying the order.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Smart is not contested; what cannot be settled here is their chronology and their first publication, since the cycle was not issued as a book in his lifetime and the separate hymns have complicated reprinting histories. The year fields are therefore left null rather than estimated.

works.title: Hymns for the Nativity
works.description: Charles Wesley's season collection for Advent and Christmas, published at Bristol in 1745 and the turning-point in which his nativity hymns took their permanent forms, including the text of Hark! the Herald Angels Sing after the 1739 Harks! how the joyful voices sound. It is the most nearly complete single-occasion volume of eighteenth-century English hymnody.
works.plot: The hymns run the Christian year's opening: the anticipation of the messiah, the forerunner, the annunciation, the birth in David's town, the shepherds, the wise men, the circumcision, and the presentation, closing with the childhood at Nazareth. Charles turns each scene into doctrine sung as experience, the little child and the mighty God joined in paradoxes of incarnation, and the season's joy poured out in invitation and praise. The volume's revision of the earlier wedding-hymn text set the pattern of Charles's practice of rewriting his own hymns toward their best forms. Its short songs for families and social worship make the Christmas narrative a domestic liturgy.
works.significance: It gave the English-speaking churches their Christmas hymnody, the source of the most sung nativity text in the language, and remains the central exhibit of Charles Wesley's lyrical theology.
works.meter: Varied hymn measures, chiefly common metre and the eight-line 8s with refrain patterns, in tight iambic lines with Charles's characteristic internal rhyme and exclamatory openings.
works.context: Published at Bristol in 1745, in the season of Charles Wesley's marriage and mature Bristol hymnwriting and the brothers' separate but parallel collections, when the revival's songbook was becoming a literature.
works.structure: A cycle of hymns following the gospel events of the nativity in seasonal order, with invitation, praise, and close-of-season pieces attached.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.
