works.title: Hymns in Prose for Children
works.form: prose hymn and devotional writing for children, in the dissenting hymn tradition renewed in prose
works.description: Barbauld's devotional prose for the young, published in 1781 and designed to teach a child to address the Deity through the visible world. Each hymn takes some part of creation - the morning, the seasons, the insect and the elements, the breath of life - and turns its observation into praise, so that natural knowledge becomes the school of piety. The book is the most original religious writing of its author's middle period and one of the enduring children's texts of the century.
works.plot: The hymns proceed by address and by observation of nature, leading the child from the creature and the scene to the attributes of the Creator, and from the gifts of the earth to the duties of gratitude, gentleness and truth. They insist that the Divine presence is to be found in every part of the world, and that praise is the proper employment of a mind that has learned to look. Their moral teaching is of benevolence extended to animals and to other men, and their religious temper is a reasoned and affectionate deism rather than a doctrine of terror.
works.significance: It created the model of nature as a book of praise for the child reader and influenced both religious instruction and the nature-writing tradition of the nineteenth century. Its combination of sensibility, natural history and devotion makes it a central document of the culture of feeling applied to education.
works.meter: Rhythmed prose of short clauses and balanced address, pitched for recitation, with the cadences of prayer and of the hymn preserved without verse.
works.context: Published in 1781 alongside the elementary books that had made Barbauld's name in education, in a period when the hymn and the prose devotional were being addressed to children as never before, and within a Unitarian and dissenting culture that preferred rational piety to the language of dread.
works.characters: The child addressed; the speaking instructor; the creatures and elements of the meditations
works.structure: A series of short prose hymns, each a single meditation on an aspect of creation followed by ascription and petition, arranged for reading aloud with a child.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was published under the author's name as the writer of her elementary books, and the date of composition is not separately fixed, so the composition start is left null.

works.title: Hyperion: A Fragment
works.form: Heroic epic of the Miltonic school, projected as a theogony and left a fragment; the Titanomachy matter of the classical epic in English blank verse.
works.description: The author's attempt at a Miltonic epic on the fall of the elder gods, abandoned in the autumn of 1819 and published as a fragment of two books in the volume of that year's poems. The deposed Saturn mourns in the caverns of the old sea, the Titaness urges him to rise, and the ocean-god argues that the elder powers have yielded by a law of gradation to a younger and fairer rule. The second book brings the messenger of the new reign and the assembly of the Titans, and the poem breaks off before the battle and the fall.
works.plot: Saturn, dethroned and hidden in the deep caverns by the mouth of the ocean, laments his lost empire, and the earth-goddess who has kept his company reproaches him for his unmanly grief. The elders debate their condition, and Oceanus answers that no throne is kept for ever, that the elder gods have fallen by gradation from the Titans to the Olympian rule, and that the new order is more beautiful; the voice is answered by the Titan of the east, who refuses the argument. The second book opens on the mourning of the fallen race and brings the rainbow-messenger from the seat of the new god, whose look of settled splendence overthrows the counsel of resistance; the gods deliberate whether to rise, and the fragment ends.
works.significance: It is the period's most impressive attempt at a non-religious epic and the standard case in the argument about whether the epic could be written after Milton, a question the fragment's own incompleteness answers. Its account of the gradation by which orders of the mind succeed one another became a permanent text for the philosophy of cultural progress, and its diction marks the point where the poet's rich sensuous style begins to be disciplined.
works.meter: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, loaded with compound epithets, Latinate inversion and a sustained end-stopped dignity designed to imitate the older epic's stateliness; it is the author's only considerable effort in pure epic measure.
works.context: Begun in the summer of 1818, in the months of the poet's northern tour and of his brother's fatal illness, and worked at through the winter, the poem's argument of the inevitable succession of powers was written in the season of the Italian and Spanish revolutions and their suppression; abandoned late in 1819, its books were published in 1820 in the volume of the later poems with an explicit mark of incompleteness. The poet's own letters on the causes of its abandonment, which turn on the failure of its diction and the impossibility of its Miltonic mask, are among the most searched documents of Romantic composition.
works.characters: Saturn, the deposed elder god; the earth-goddess his mate and reprover; Oceanus, the arguer of gradation; the eastern Titan of the last line; the rainbow-messenger of the new reign
works.structure: Two books of continuous epic narrative in blank verse, the first a council and argument in the caverns, the second the arrival of the messenger and the debate; a sketch for a third book and a projected theogony survive in the drafts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the two published books and the surviving drafts, with the alternative dream-version of the same argument, are all in the poet's hand and are printed together in the standard edition.

works.title: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
works.form: Nature lyric and lyrical ballad of the collected manner; a short meditative lyric that makes the process of remembering its explicit subject.
works.description: A lyric of four stanzas comparing the poet to a lone cloud floating over a valley, who comes upon a host of golden daffodils beside the lake and beneath the trees. Written two years after the walk that suggested it, and revised after its first publication, it is the period's most familiar poem and a working model of its own poetic theory: an accidental sight, remembered at leisure, becomes a source of repeated pleasure. Its first printed form bore the title The Daffodils.
works.plot: The speaker, wandering solitary as a cloud, sees suddenly a long belt of daffodils stretching along the bay, tossing their heads in a sprightly dance, countlessly many as the stars that line the Milky Way. He at first gives the sight no value, gazing without thinking of the wealth the show had brought him; the second part of the poem transfers the scene to the mind, where, on a couch in a vacant or pensive mood, the flowers flash upon the inward eye which is the bliss of solitude, and the heart fills with pleasure and dances with the daffodils. The argument is thus a demonstration that the richest gifts of nature are received afterwards, in recollection, and that the imagination stores sensible forms as a permanent possession.
works.significance: The most anthologised and most parodied lyric of the English Romantic period, and the shortest complete illustration of the theory of emotion recollected in tranquillity. Its image of the inward eye became a common property of Victorian and later discussion of imaginative memory.
works.meter: Four stanzas of six iambic lines, the first four of four beats and the last two of a shorter beat, with a strongly marked rhyme pattern; the regularity and the repeated gestures of the stanza give the poem the quality of an air.
works.context: Suggested by an afternoon walk by Ullswater in April 1802, recorded in the same words by the poet's companion in her journal of the tour, and composed in 1804 for the collection of short lyrics published in 1807. The revised text, with its second stanza added and its phrasing heightened, belongs to the edition of 1815.
works.characters: The solitary speaker, figured as a cloud; the host of daffodils; the lake, the trees and the breezy bay
works.structure: Two-part movement within a single lyric: the outward scene of 1802 told as an event in the past tense, then the inward scene of later hours, with the turn signalled by the contrast between the thoughtless gaze and the pleasure recollected.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the suggested wording and the incident were shared with the companion named in the journal, but the poem is uniformly assigned to the writer.

works.title: Idea
works.description: Michael Drayton's sonnet sequence, first published as Ideas Mirrour (1594) and revised across five editions into its final 63-sonnet form as Idea (1619): a sequence of farewells — to the lady, to the sonnet form itself, and to love — crowned by the great sonnet 'Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part'.
works.plot: The lover's suit to the lady moves through adoration and complaint to the sequence's famous gesture of renunciation — a farewell to love that is also a virtuoso leave-taking of the sonnet convention.
works.significance: Home of the most famous valedictory sonnet in the language and a case study in the Elizabethan sequence as revisable form.
works.meter: The English sonnet, in Drayton's plain-spoken, muscular style.
works.context: Drayton revised the sequence continuously from 1594 to 1619, mirroring the rise and self-conscious decline of the sonnet vogue he had helped create.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Idea (the beloved)
works.structure: A sequence revised over twenty-five years, ending in the 1619 form with its valedictory design.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Imaginary Conversations
altTitles: Imaginary Conversations of Literary Men and Statesmen
works.form: Literary dialogue and dramatic prose conversation: a Neoclassical revival of the humanist dialogue, distinguished by the absence of stage direction and by epigrammatic compression.
works.description: The author's masterpiece of prose and the first series of conversations in which two historical personages talk together about art, power, religion, and death. The dialogue form is stripped of narration: almost nothing but speech, with the characters' tempers doing the work of plot. The series ranges from Greek and Roman pairs to Italian, Spanish, and modern authors, and it established its author's reputation as the finest English prose stylist of his generation.
works.plot: Each conversation places two figures in a single situation and lets their disagreement disclose character: Plato with Aristarchus on the worth of poetry, Dante with Beatrice on the price of knowledge, Pope with the Earl of Oxford, or Thrasylachus with Amycus on tyranny. There is no developing action across the volume, but within each piece pressure rises as one speaker is driven to say what he has never said before. The political conversations test whether a good man can serve a bad cause, and the literary ones argue for style as a moral rather than a decorative achievement. Recurring presences are the dignity of the private mind against public power, and the consolation of letters at the end of life.
works.significance: The most important English prose style since the seventeenth-century worthies, and the origin of the modern imaginary dialogue; it shaped how later writers from Stevenson to Eliot thought about the ethics of style and the use of historical speech as argument.
works.meter: Prose, in a deliberately punctilious and Latinate idiom of balanced periods and short retorts.
works.context: Issued while its author was settled in Italy and after the Bath and Pisa years, when his quarrels with publishers and with his family had made him a professional man of letters; the series appeared while the review journals were the chief organ of literary authority, and it was received first coolly and then reverently.
works.characters: Plato; Aristarchus; Dante; Beatrice; Alexander; Thrasylachus; Pope; the Earl of Oxford; Joanna of Naples
works.structure: A series of self-contained prose dialogues without framing narrative, each with its own speakers, setting, and turn; the volume's unity is tonal and moral rather than sequential.

works.title: Immediate, Not Gradual Abolition; or, An Inquiry into the Shortest, Safest and Most Effectual Means of Getting Rid of West Indian Slavery
works.form: Abolitionist polemic pamphlet in the form of an inquiry or analysis: reasoned, scriptural, addressed to a British public, and built on the countersuggestion that the opposing party's own premises prove the immediate case.
works.description: A short London pamphlet that broke with the gradualist strategy of the older British abolition movement by arguing that immediate emancipation was at once morally obligatory and practically the shortest, safest and cheapest policy. It circulated first as a printed circular and then as a pamphlet, and it supplied the slogan and the logic for the new organisation founded in 1831. Its tone is that of the Quaker plain-style remonstrance, addressed to the conscience of the slave-holder and to the West India interest.
works.plot: The argument runs on three levels. On principle, the writer holds that the slave-holder has no right to the labour of other human beings, so that postponing emancipation is continuing a crime; justice cannot be gradual. On interest, she claims that free labour would be more productive than coerced labour and that the planter's ruin is the product of his own system, not of emancipation. On safety, she answers the standard fear that liberation brings massacre by contending that patience and religion have preserved the enslaved so far, and that injustice itself, not emancipation, is the provocation. The pamphlet closes by urging the abolitionists to drop compensation to slave-holders and to appeal directly to public opinion, and it recommends a plain remedy for the transitional difficulty: apprenticeship of the emancipated under contract, with wages.
works.significance: It is the pivot text of British immediatism, the pamphlet that shifted the movement's demand from gradual apprenticeship to unconditional emancipation, and it directly shaped the programme of the society founded in 1831 and the debate over compensation before the abolition legislation of 1833. It is also an early example of a woman's political pamphlet setting the terms of a national agitation.
works.meter: Plain prose, lucid and unhedged; emphasis by antithesis and by direct question rather than ornament.
works.context: Written in the long debate that followed the British abolition of the trade in 1807, when the West India planters were urging amelioration and Parliament was moving cautiously toward measures to improve the condition of the enslaved. Its appearance coincides with the emergence of women as organisers of anti-slavery agitation, including the female anti-slavery societies and the sugar-boycott campaigns of the later 1820s.
works.structure: Continuous argument in a single movement: statement of the question, argument from principle, argument from interest, argument from safety, practical plan, closing appeal.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to its author is certain; it was signed by her in later editions and was well known to contemporaries as her work.

works.title: Improvements in Education, as it Respects the Industrious Classes of the Community
works.form: educational report and treatise; the school statement with the plan for the education of the labouring classes
works.description: The published account of the school at Southwark by its Quaker founder, the book which brought the monitorial method before the public of the metropolis and made the mutual system a party, a subscription, and in time a national institution; a report of an experiment like the Madras statement, but written for the town and its subscribers rather than for the Company's settlement.
works.plot: The work describes the school of the author's opening in Southwark, in which a great number of children of the labouring classes were taught by one another under his single superintendence at an expense of a few shillings for each child in the year, and it sets out the machinery by which this was done: the classes, the monitors, the patrol of the yard, the slate, the sand, the wall for the first lessons, the marks of merit and of demerit, the register of the progress, the rewards of the badge and the public inspection, the arrangement of the hour of study, and the moral and religious teaching delivered to all without the doctrine of any party. It argues that the poor may thus be taught numerously, cheerfully, and at a price which makes the education of the industrious classes a subject for the subscription of the public, and it urges the political uses of the method, the obedience, the cleanliness, the habit, and the knowledge which it gives being the securities of the order of the country. The several parts are supported by the account of the expenses, the examination of the visitors, and the evidence of the masters of other schools.
works.significance: With the Madras statement of 1797 it is the foundation text of the monitorial system, and through the British and Foreign School Society, the free schools, and the model normal schools of the nineteenth century its machinery became the working form of popular education in Britain, America, and the colonies; its claim to teach the children of the poor cheaply, in numbers, and without sectarian doctrine is one of the governing ideas of English social reform, and the book itself is a primary document of the history of the elementary school.
works.meter: Plain, businesslike, persuasive prose of the schoolmaster addressing his subscribers, with the minute enumeration of the arrangements, the repetition of the figures of cost and numbers, and the frank appeal to the feelings of the reader for the children of the poor; less technical and more hortatory than the Indian statement of the same method.
works.context: Published in 1803, after five years of the school at Southwark which he had opened for the children of the labouring poor under the inspection of a friendly society of subscribers, in the season of the anxiety about the discipline of the manufacturing population, of the Sunday-school movement, and of the project of a national education; the book won the subscriptions and the visits of the great, including at length the countenance of the court, and it set forward the rival claim of priority to the Indian system which the same method had already obtained, the two parties dividing the public and the religious aid of the following generation.
works.structure: A report in the manner of the second edition of the educational statement: the account of the school, the description of the method in its order of proceeding, the evidence of the proficiency made, the estimate of the expense, the replies to the objections, and the appeal to the public, with the papers of the inspecting society and the certificates appended.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to a single hand is uncontested; the title is variously abridged in the many editions, and the enlarged later issues, given out in parts and with the memoir of the author prefixed, contain matter not in the first; the long priority controversy with the promulgator of the Indian system obliges the careful citation of the edition.

works.title: Incendium Amoris
works.description: Richard Rolle's principal Latin treatise (c. 1340–43), an autobiographical and doctrinal account of the contemplative life as he himself had experienced it: the warmth of divine love (calor), its sweetness (dulcor), and its song (canor), with instruction on prayer, meditation, and the discernment of spirits. The founding text of the English mystical tradition.
works.plot: Rolle recounts his own conversion and his experience of the three degrees of love — fire, sweetness, and heavenly song — defends the contemplative life against its critics, and teaches the reader to progress from reading through prayer to the 'fire of love' that unites the soul to God.
works.significance: The first major work of the English mystical tradition and the fountainhead of its characteristic language of warmth, sweetness, and song.
works.meter: Latin prose, rhetorical and warm, with the psalm commentary woven in.
works.context: Composed c. 1340–43 in the north of England, early in Rolle's hermit career, and later translated into Middle English (the Fire of Love); among the most widely read Latin spiritual works of the English fourteenth century.
works.characters: Rolle (as witness and teacher)
works.structure: A prologue and forty-two chapters mixing autobiography, doctrine, and scriptural commentary, with the author's own experience as the organizing proof.
works.attributionNotes: Rolle's authorship secure.
sources: Memoirs of the Life and Writings of Thomas Chalmers, D.D., LL.D. (4 volumes)

works.title: Institutes of Polity
altTitles: Institutes of Polity, Civil and Ecclesiastical
works.form: didactic treatise (political theology) in Old English prose
works.description: Wulfstan's treatise on the orders of Christian society: the duties of the king, the bishops, the clergy, the nobles, and the people in a rightly ordered realm — 'eight columns that support the kingdom'. The clearest statement of Anglo-Saxon political theology and the seedbed of Wulfstan's law codes.
works.plot: The treatise defines each estate's office: the king shall protect the church and rule justly; bishops shall teach and judge; the clergy shall keep chastity and learning; ealdormen shall give righteous judgments; the people shall labour and obey — all bound by the law of God, whose breach brings ruin on the land.
works.significance: The fullest Anglo-Saxon statement of the theory of the Christian commonwealth.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical two-stress prose.
works.context: Composed c. 1008-1020 in the crisis of Æthelred's reign and revised under Cnut; preserved in later eleventh-century manuscripts, chiefly Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.characters: the Christian king; the bishops; the estates of the realm
works.structure: A systematic treatise in chapters on the estates of the realm, from the heavenly king down through the earthly orders.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is established on stylistic grounds.
sources: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden

works.title: Intercepted Letters; or, the Two-Penny Post-Bag
works.form: Verse epistle and periodical-style social satire in the Horatian-Butlerian familiar line, with a pseudonymous paratext of the kind used for Regency lampoon.
works.description: A sequence of satirical verse epistles published under a pseudonymous Irish correspondent's name, affecting to have been stopped in the post. The letters report the manners, fashions and quarrels of Regency London society, its theatres, its politicians and its literary parties, in a light familiar rhyme. The prefatory apparatus treats the supposed author as a young provincial introduced to the metropolitan world.
works.plot: The volume advances no plot but a progression of observations: a country relation arrives in London and reports, letter by letter, the spectacle of a society organised around card tables, the opera, the playhouse, the publisher's table and the political club. Persons of rank and letters are characterised through gossip and through the writer's professed simplicity, so that the satire works by apparent naivety. The closing letters widen from social portraiture to comment on war-time politics and on the vanity of public fame. The machinery of interception is itself part of the argument, since it justifies both the freedom of the attack and the pose of accidental disclosure.
works.significance: It established the satiric persona on which the author's later and more successful lampoons were built, and it is an unusually full poetic record of Regency high society and its literary economy. Contemporary readers treated its portraits as identifiable, which makes it useful evidence for the social history of the period. It marks the survival of Augustan verse epistle technique inside Romantic print culture.
works.meter: Heroic and octosyllabic couplets, iambic, with familiar conversational pauses and occasional lyric interpolations.
works.context: Written at the height of Regency society journalism, when the quarterly reviews, the fashionable publishers and the theatres formed a single contested public, and when Catholic emancipation and Irish representation were live issues. Its pseudonymous disguise answers the risk of libel and reflects the period's enthusiasm for detected and private correspondence. The author was already a known contributor to newspapers and to the music trade, and his Irish position sharpens the outsider's eye.
works.characters: The pseudonymous young Irish correspondent; his country family; the London society of politicians, actors, critics and fashionable hostesses he reports upon
works.structure: An epistolary sequence in verse, loosely progressive from arrival to disenchantment, unified by a single pseudonymous writing voice and by the fiction of intercepted correspondence.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the pseudonym of a young Irish correspondent, with prefatory matter affectedly assigned to a different hand; authorship has never been in doubt.

works.title: Interlude of Youth
works.description: An anonymous morality interlude of the fall and repentance of Youth, composed c. 1513–14 and printed c. 1530–35; a compact dramatization of the prodigal's return.
works.plot: Youth, flattered by Riot, Pride, and Lechery, abandons Charity and Humility for the tavern and the stews; Charity and Humility lament and warn him, and Youth, brought low, repents and returns to virtue, ending with a prayer for the king and the audience's amendment.
works.significance: A compact and influential example of the early Tudor morality, dramatizing the prodigal theme that would run through the century to the Elizabethan stage; it survives as a witness to the interlude's household origins.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Composed c. 1513–14, probably for a noble household (the prayer for the king suggests courtly performance), and printed c. 1530–35; it belongs to the same early Tudor wave as Hickscorner and Magnificence, in which the morality play becomes a vehicle for aristocratic moral counsel.
works.characters: Youth; Charity; Humility; Riot; Pride; Lechery
works.structure: A short two-part morality play of temptation and return, with the Vices' songs and taunts alternating with Charity's warnings.

works.title: Intimations of Immortality
altTitles: Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood
works.form: Romantic ode in the reflective and meditative manner, drawing on the English Pindaric and on Platonic and Christian ideas of the soul, and on the period's taste for the philosophical meditation in verse.
works.description: The poet's greatest ode and the central Romantic poem about the loss and recovery of imaginative vision, begun in the spring months of the early 1800s, completed in stages, and printed in 1807. Its speaker finds that the glory and the dream of childhood sight have fled, and seeks a reason for the decay that shall also console him; the answer is a Platonising myth that the soul comes to us from God and hither trails clouds of glory, so that the child is finest in the vision which the adult increasingly loses.
works.plot: The opening stanzas complain that a glory has passed away from the earth, and that the same flowers and the same sight of the heavens bring to the grown man none of the rapture they gave the child, for whom a cloud or a tale could fill the eye with tears. The central stanzas set out the myth of pre-existence: our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting, the soul that is our life's star has had its setting elsewhere and comes from afar, trailing clouds of glory from God who is our home, so that the infant, newest come from that country of light, sees most, and the growing boy sees least, until the shades of the prison-house begin to show upon him and the man is bound to the light of common day. The later stanzas recover the loss: the visionary gleam is gone, but the poet may still draw power from what remains behind, may read in the meanest flower that blows thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears, and may thank the human heart, with its tenderness, its joys and its fears, for the pity and the endurance that make the sober year of mature life richer than the rapturous first hours of childhood.
works.significance: The most ambitious Romantic statement of the relation between childhood, memory and loss, and the poem from which the language of the child as father of the man and of the glory that has passed away entered general use. It set the terms for later Victorian and modern discussions of imaginative decay, and it is the touchstone for readings of the poet's philosophy of the mind.
works.meter: Stanzas of irregular length and varied line, running from four to six beats, with an elaborate recurring rhyme pattern and refrains; the later ode stanzas lengthen and slow, so that metre is used to mark the difference between the child's quick vision and the adult's meditative periods.
works.context: Begun in 1802, in the months of the poet's engagement and of the sonnets on liberty and on public subjects, continued in 1803-04, and completed in 1806; the poem's philosophy of pre-existence and its account of the child drew on the Platonism current among the poets and critics of the day and on the associationist psychology then standard in education.
works.characters: The adult speaker; the child, infant, boy and youth whose successive stages are traced; Nature, personified as the nurse and guide of the child's days
works.structure: An irregular Romantic ode in stanzas of unequal length, moving from a general complaint about the loss of vision, through the pictures of the infant, the boy and the youth, to the philosophical myth and then to the turn of consolation; the design follows the movement of feeling rather than a logical argument, and the later stanzas lengthen and slow as reflection displaces description.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: Irish Melodies
altTitles: Irish Melodies, with Accompaniments and Songs
works.form: Lyric and song cycle for voice with piano arrangement: a national-air setting sequence in the ballad and song tradition, with editorial prefaces arguing for the recovery of Irish music.
works.description: A series of lyric settings written to recovered Irish airs, issued in numbered parts over more than two decades and later gathered into complete volumes. The verse supplies new English words to traditional melodies, and the accompanying prefaces and advertisements argue the case for an Irish national music rescued from neglect. Its songs move between tenderness, Jacobite and patriotic grief, and witty accommodation with the English market that bought them.
works.plot: There is no continuous argument: each lyric takes a single air and builds a short dramatic situation around it, often a rejected lover, an exile, a minstrel, or a mourner for a lost national cause. Recurrent patterns of loss and memory give the series a political colouring, since the fallen glories of Ireland are figured as abandoned harps, broken thrones and forgotten friends. Several songs turn on the figure of the bard whose instrument is the nation's last surviving voice, and others quietly rework the language of union and emancipation current after 1800. The accompanying prose notes defend the antiquity of the music and the author's fidelity to Irish tradition, while the lyrics themselves often avoid direct polemic in favour of sentimental indirection.
works.significance: It was the most widely circulated body of Irish verse of the nineteenth century and fixed the Victorian and later image of Irish national song, exercised influence on popular music, and made the recovered air a model for other national lyrical revivals. It also generated lasting critical debate about the compromise between cultural nationalism and the metropolitan literary market. Its best-known lyrics remained standard recital pieces long after the surrounding politics had faded.
works.meter: Stanzaic lyric measures strictly adapted to the pre-existing airs, chiefly ballad and song metres with regular rhyme schemes and repeating refrains.
works.context: It appeared after the failure of the 1798 rising and after the Act of Union, when Irish national identity was being renegotiated in cultural rather than political terms, and when the collection and setting of national airs was a fashionable European enterprise. Its publication was shaped by Dublin and London music publishers and by the demand of the drawing-room market, and its author was simultaneously an emancipation advocate and a London celebrity. The series continued to grow through the 1820s and into the 1830s, so that its politics shift with the agitation for Catholic emancipation.
works.structure: A serial anthology of short lyrics organised by numbered publication rather than by any narrative plan, with paratextual notes on the airs; unity is musical and national rather than sequential.

works.title: Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil
altTitles: Isabella, or the Pot of Basil
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the Italian novella in English ottava rima, with the gothic and the ballad's treatment of devoted female grief.
works.description: A short romance in ottava rima taken from a novellieri's tale of the fourteenth century, in which a merchant's sister, married by a trick to a young man of her own choosing, is robbed of her lover by her brothers, who murder him while he sleeps in the woods. The lady finds the body, carries the skull and bones away in a pot of basil, and waters it with her tears until the basil withers and her brothers take it from her. It is the most concentrated of the author's narrative poems and a study of jealous wealth against devoted grief.
works.plot: Isabella, the daughter of a wealthy family of Messina, loves a young clerk of her brothers' house, and by an artifice obtains her marriage to him; the brothers, ashamed of the match and anxious for their fortune, take their brother on a journey and kill him in a forest. The girl, told in a dream where her lover lies, goes to the spot, digs up the body, and carries the skull and bones away in a pot of basil, which she tends and waters, never leaving it, so that the plant grows strangely and the neighbours marvel. Her brothers at last steal the pot from her, and she pines and dies praying that her tomb may hold what they have taken; the pot was never afterwards found. The argument is that a mercantile family's honour can murder love, and that the devotion of grief is a thing which money cannot seize.
works.significance: It gave the English ottava rima one of its most finished narrative poems and made the pot of basil a permanent image of a grief that tends its own loss; the tale was repeatedly reprinted in the annuals and retold on the stage of the later century. Its handling of a woman's devotion against familial avarice became a touchstone for the discussion of the author's narrative sympathy.
works.meter: Ottava rima, seven-line iambic pentameter stanzas rhyming abababcc, used here with great fluency and a frequent closing couplet of sentiment; the song of the pot is set apart in shorter lyric measure.
works.context: Composed at the house of a friend's family in the north of London in the February of 1819, in the weeks after the death of the poet's younger brother and during the same season which produced the Belle Dame ballad and the beginning of the titan poem, and published in the 1820 volume. Its choice of an old Italian tale and its scorn for a mercantile brothers' world belong to the same argument about the poetry of sensation as the longer romance of the moon.
works.characters: Isabella, the merchant's daughter; her lover, the clerk of the house; her three brothers of the merchant's honour; the old nurse of the household; the people and priests of Messina
works.structure: A continuous narrative in some sixty ottava-rima stanzas, the exposition of the family and the love, the murder reported, the dream and the discovery of the grave, and the long middle of the basil's tending, closing on the lady's death and the lost pot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is dated by the letters of its composition and exists in a fair copy in another hand made for the printer.

works.title: Italy
works.form: Topographical and descriptive poem in the line of eighteenth-century Italian travel verse, inflected by the Romantic meditation on art, Catholicism and exile.
works.description: A topographical and historical meditation on Italy, written by a poet who had travelled there twice but who refused the conventions of the travel poem. The Italian scene is treated as a series of moral, artistic and personal reminders: ruins, pictures, monasteries and mountain villages prompt reflections on exile, faith, art and lost affection. Short songs, ballads and romances are intercalated in the reflective texture, so that the volume alternates between argument and lyric.
works.plot: The poem proceeds from place to place, letting each site draw out a meditation rather than narrating a journey with a fixed itinerary. It returns repeatedly to a personal history of disappointment and to the fate of the exiles and outlaws among whom the poet numbers himself, and it treats Roman Catholic ceremony and Italian banditti romance as objects of sympathetic curiosity rather than of antiquarian display. Painters, poets and historical sufferers appear as companions in the landscape, and several passages take the form of embedded tales or songs. The result is a poem whose real subject is the mind of the traveller meeting a country already overloaded with association. Its closing movements draw the reflection back from Italy to the poet's own loss and to the consolation of verse.
works.significance: For much of the nineteenth century it was the standard English poem about Italy, quoted by tourists and taught in schools, and its intercalation of songs inside a reflective structure was widely imitated in the annuals. It preserves a version of Romantic travel writing that is suspicious of the sublime and attentive to painting, ritual and social observation. Modern accounts of second-generation Romanticism treat it as the chief alternative to Byronic and Wordsworthian models of the topographical poem.
works.meter: Chiefly rhymed five-beat couplet lines in the descriptive tradition, broken by songs and ballad-measure lyrics of irregular stanzaic length.
works.context: Written after the Napoleonic wars reopened Italy to English tourists, at the height of the fashionable Italian sojourn and of the English debate over Catholic emancipation which the poem's treatment of monastic and ritual life inevitably touched. Its first part was published anonymously and the second under the author's name, a publishing history typical of a poet who cultivated reticence. Later editions supplied with engraved plates after the drawings of a famous landscape painter turned the poem into one of the century's most successful gift books.
works.structure: A loosely sequential meditation on places, interrupted by intercalated lyrics, romances and songs; no continuous plot, and a strong lyrical undertone running beneath the descriptive argument.
works.attributionNotes: The first part was issued anonymously in 1822; the second part appeared under the author's name, and the whole was revised and enlarged across several editions.

works.title: Itinerarium Cambriae
works.description: Gerald of Wales's account of the preaching tour of Wales undertaken in 1188 with Archbishop Baldwin of Canterbury to recruit for the Third Crusade, combining topographical description, ethnography of the Welsh, anecdote, and vigorous self-promotion; the companion work to the Descriptio Cambriae (1194).
works.summary: Gerald narrates the itinerary of Baldwin's mission through south and north Wales, recording the sermons, the reception of the party, local marvels and legends, the character and customs of the Welsh, and his own prominent role in the enterprise; the two books culminate in the preaching of the cross.
works.significance: One of the finest works of twelfth-century travel and ethnographic writing, a primary source for medieval Wales, and a major witness to the Latin literary culture of the Welsh marches.
sources: The Poetical Works of Barry Cornwall

works.title: Ivanhoe
works.form: Historical romance and adventure novel of chivalry, with comedy of the lower Saxon characters and a tragedy of the outsider.
works.description: The romance of twelfth-century England that moved the historical novel away from Scotland and supplied the nineteenth century with its image of medieval chivalry, tournament and Jewry. Its disowned Saxon heir, returned in secret, and its two opposed heroines - the disinherited Rebecca and the Saxon Rowena - carry an argument about tolerance, race and national fusion. The author's dedicated account of the change of subject in the introductory 'Dedicatory Epistle' is itself a famous piece of theory.
works.plot: Wilfred of Ivanhoe, disinherited for following King Richard abroad, appears incognito at the Saxon house of Cedric of Rotherwood, who plans to marry his ward Rowena to a rival claimant of the blood royal. The tourney at Ashby of the Tor, the insults of Prince John's party, and the abduction of the guests at Torquilstone leave the field to outlaws and to the medicine and charity of Rebecca, the Jewess, whom the Templar Brian de Bois-Guilbert pursues to the accusation of trial by combat. Richard returns in disguise, the baronial plot against John is broken, Bois-Guilbert falls dead in the lists, Rebecca is driven out of England by her own people, and Ivanhoe marries Rowena while the disinherited Saxon patrimony is restored.
works.significance: Fixed the popular image of medieval England and made the tournament, the castle and the outlaw band the standard equipment of romance; it also made the suffering Jewess one of the century's most discussed fictional creations. Its explicit theory of how a modern writer may fabricate a past has been continuously cited. Its influence on the medieval revival, in fiction, stage design and costume, is extensive.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; minstrel songs, brindisi and a Jewish hymn are interpolated; the dialogue is keyed to rank, from Norman French-inflected speech to Saxon plainness.
works.context: Written in the years of the post-Waterloo reaction, when medievalism, national theatre and the question of the civil status of minorities were in the air, and when the author's antiquarian studies had produced a command of the cast, armour and law of the middle ages. The treatment of the Templars and of the Jews draws on a long tradition of English prejudice and on the records of persecution. The book's instant commercial success changed the terms on which historical fiction was commissioned.
works.characters: Wilfred of Ivanhoe; Cedric of Rotherwood; Rowena; Rebecca; Brian de Bois-Guilbert; Front-de-Boeuf; Isaac of York; King Richard I; Prince John; Athelstan; Wamba; Gurth; the Prior Aymer; Ulrica
works.structure: Third-person romance in nineteen sections with a 'Dedicatory Epistle' and a 'Letter Prefixed to the Second Edition' on the composition of medieval fiction; the plot is episodic and set-piece driven, with the tournament, the feast and the trial as its pivots.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the Author of Waverley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Jack of Newbury
altTitles: The Pleasant History of John Winchcomb
works.description: Deloney's fiction of the clothier's golden age: John Winchcomb of Newbury rises from apprentice to the greatest clothier in England, his hundred looms employing hundreds, his wealth commanding kings, and his virtue (he feeds the poor, arms his men for Flodden, refuses a knighthood) making him the hero of England's craftsmen — the first English novel of the working world.
works.plot: Jack's rise, his marriage to his late master's widow, the great household of the looms, the visit of Queen Katherine, the expedition to Flodden, and the pranks of the courtiers against the honest clothier fill the episodic narrative, which closes on his death and the praise of his charity.
works.significance: The first great novel of English working life — the book that gave the artisan class its own literature, and the ancestor of the industrial novel.
works.meter: Plain, vigorous prose with interpolated songs and ballads, in the speech of shop and street.
works.context: Published 1597, in the decade of the cloth trade's crisis and the apprentices' unrest; its celebration of the clothier's charity answered the dearth and the poor laws with fiction.
works.characters: Jack (John Winchcomb); his wife (the widow); Queen Katherine; King Henry VIII; the courtiers; the clothiers of England
works.structure: An episodic biography in the jest-book and chronicle manner, built of set pieces — the banquet, the expedition, the courtiers' gulling — in the popular prose Deloney perfected.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Jacob and Esau
altTitles: A New Mery and Wittie Comedie or Enterlude, Newely Imprinted, Treating upon the Historie of Jacob and Esau
works.description: An anonymous Protestant biblical interlude on the story of Jacob and Esau from Genesis, printed in 1568; one of the liveliest mid-century dramatizations of the doctrine of election.
works.plot: The play follows Genesis 25–27: the differing natures of the twins Jacob and Esau, the sale of the birthright for a pottage, Isaac's blessing of Jacob obtained through Rebecca's counsel, and Esau's rage and reconciliation; the serious matter of election is framed by the comic servants of the household (Ragan, Mido, and the boy Abra) whose tricks and misadventures mirror the plot.
works.significance: The most accomplished of the mid-century biblical interludes and an important document of Protestant dramatic theory; its comic subplot anticipates the structure of Elizabethan biblical and history plays.
works.meter: Couplets and 'rhyming fourteeners'
works.context: Composed c. 1550–58 in the Edwardian and Marian years, when the doctrine of predestination was at the centre of English religious debate; the play's prologue makes the case for the godly theatre, and it was printed in 1568 for the Elizabethan market.
works.characters: Isaac; Rebecca; Jacob; Esau; Ragan; Mido; Abra; Deborah; Hanan
works.structure: Five acts with act and scene divisions, alternating the biblical action with a fully developed comic subplot, and a prologue arguing that election is the play's theme.

works.title: James IV
altTitles: The Scottish History of James the Fourth
works.description: Greene's Scottish romance-play: King James IV of Scotland, married to Dorothea, falls in love with the English lady Ida and plots his queen's murder; Dorothea escapes in disguise, is saved by the English knight Sir Eustace and nursed back to health, and the play ends with the king's repentance, the recognition scene, and the reunion — a history play turned romance, framed by the chorus of Oberon and the fairies.
works.plot: James, corrupted by the flatterer Ateukin, orders Dorothea's death; the honest lords refuse and the queen flees in disguise; wounded, she is healed by Lady Anderson; the wars with England and the king's remorse lead to the final scene, where the disguised queen reveals herself and all is forgiven in the play's comedy of errors and recognitions.
works.significance: The bridge between the chronicle play and Shakespearean romance — the play in which Greene's pastoral art and the history vogue met.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose for the comic scenes, and the fairies' songs in the induction.
works.context: Printed in 1598 and performed about 1590; its Scottish matter predates James VI's accession to the English throne, and its 'history' is romance from the first.
works.characters: King James IV of Scotland; Queen Dorothea; Ida; Sir Eustace; Ateukin; Lady Anderson; Sir Cuthbert Anderson; the Bishop of St Andrews; Oberon; the fairies
works.structure: A five-act romance on a chronicle frame, with the fairy induction and interludes of Oberon, and the Anderson sub-plot as the comic engine of the recognition.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Jane Shore
works.description: Rowe's tragedy of the mistress of Edward the Fourth, reduced from her court favour to penance and poverty: the most persistent example of the fallen woman's tragedy on the eighteenth-century stage.
works.plot: Jane Shore, cast off with the king's death and pursued by the malice of Gloucester, abandons her riches, does public penance in the streets of London and dies in the humility of her own repentance, while the politics of the court and the fate of Hastings carry the action.
works.significance: It fixed the penitent courtesan as a permanent figure of English moral drama and, with The Fair Penitent, established the female calamity plot that Richardson and the sentimental drama later inherited.
works.meter: Blank verse of a deliberate plainness, with the prose of the lower stations and the sententious couplet at the scene's close.
works.context: Acted at Drury Lane in the last months of the reign and the season of the succession, when the mirror of princes and the fate of the king's mistress were transparently political subjects.
works.characters: Jane Shore; King Edward the Fourth; Hastings; Gloucester; Alicia
works.structure: Five acts of court history and private fall, with the public penance and the closing deathbed scene as the two calculated crises.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Jerusalem
altTitles: Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion
works.form: Visionary and illuminated prophecy in verse, the sum of the poet's myth, and a national prophecy in the form of a scripture of the imagination.
works.description: The last and largest of the illuminated books, begun in the year of the poet's settlement at Felpham and completed in plates over many years of work, which gathers the whole of his earlier myth into a single vision of the awakening of a giant and the rebuilding of a city in England. It is written in two kinds of verse, a measured line for the narrative of Albion and a long blazing line for the prophecies, and it opens with a prose preface that states the poet's duty to build a system of his own rather than to be governed by another's.
works.plot: The prose preface declares the poet's cause as vision and the defence of imagination against the men of single reason, and ends by invoking a new Jerusalem to be built in England's green and pleasant land among those dark satanic mills. The poem then tells how Albion, the ancient giant of all mankind, lies fallen and divided into the four Zoas or states of the soul, and how, in the night of his sleep, his emanation and the powers of loss and of error hold him in chains; the books trace the labours of the prophetic and creative power who works in the furnaces of the world to bring him back to unity. The argument passes through the histories of the daughters of Albion, of the priests of the law of one, and of the cities built in the name of measurement, and closes with the awakening of Albion, the reconciliation of the divided powers, and the vision of the Emanation gathered to the Man, the last plates declaring that the hour is come and that all the nations shall see the mercy of the Divine Humanity.
works.significance: The most ambitious illuminated book and the final shape of the poet's prophetic system, and, through the lyric placed in its preface, the source of a poem that became one of the most sung of all English verses. Its claim that a city of imagination is to be built in the midst of a labouring nation is a permanent text both of Romantic theory and of later writing about England.
works.meter: Two metres are used throughout: a measured and stately accentual line for the narrative and songs, and a long, reiterated and vehement line for the prophetic books, the verses being printed as part of the illuminated plates; the opening lyric and the closing hymn-like lines are among the most set to music in English.
works.context: Begun at Felpham in Sussex in 1804, in the years of the poet's quarrel with his patron and of his return to London, and worked at in plates until the last decade of his life, when copies were issued by himself and by his wife; its imagery of the fallen giant and of the dark mills answers the industrial and national condition of England during and after the long war with France.
works.characters: Albion, the ancient giant of all mankind; Los, the prophetic and creative power who labour in the furnaces; Enitharmon, his emanation; the four states or Zoas into which Albion is divided; Rahab and the powers of loss; the priests of the law of one and the builders of the cities of measurement
works.structure: A great illuminated book of over a hundred plates, divided into its own internal books and chapters, mixing narrative prophecy, song and dramatic dialogue, with the two metres and the two orders of argument alternating; the design is a single movement from the sleep of Albion to his awakening.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of completion and of the several issues of the plates, and the order in which the parts were executed, are matters of scholarship rather than of authorship.

works.title: Joan of Arc
altTitles: Joan of Arc, an Epic Poem
works.form: National epic in the heroic manner, on the model of the Christian epics of the older poems and of the war epic then being revived; its politics and its machinery mark it as a poem of the revolutionary decade.
works.description: An epic poem in twelve books on the Maid of Orleans, written in the first fervour of the author's republican enthusiasm and published in 1796 when he was barely over twenty, by subscription and through a Bristol printer, with a prefatory address that announced the plan of a national epic on a subject of Christian chivalry. It is a war epic and a poem of prophetic voices: the French shepherdess who hears the saints and leads an army, is rejected at the court and at the siege, and is finally taken and burnt, is the subject of a poem that gives its supernatural machinery a serious moral function.
works.plot: The poem opens in the civil war of France and England and in the divinely warned dream of the maid, who is sent to relieve Orleans and to lead the Dauphin to his coronation. Books of council and of battle follow, in which the English commanders take counsel with dark powers and the maid's visions and prayers counter the machinery of her enemies; the field-worship of the French is raised above the war-craft of the invaders in a series of sieges, single combats and nights of watch, and the poem closes with the Maid taken at the last, condemned and committed to the fire, the epic ending in martyrdom rather than in triumph. The argument is at once patriotic and moral, making the virtue of an untaught peasant girl the measure of the kingdoms about her and the promise of deliverance the ground of her authority.
works.significance: The earliest ambitious English epic of the Romantic generation and the document of a radical young poet's attempt to found a national poem on the subject of a martyred maiden; its reputation rests mainly on its history and on the contrast between its politics and its author's later years, and its subject was a standing point of reference in the controversy over the epic in English.
works.meter: Blank verse, iambic pentameter, sustained through the twelve books with an unrhymed flow and occasional apostrophical excursions, in a style imitating the epics of the previous century rather than the polished diction of recent narrative verse.
works.context: Composed during the author's undergraduate years at Oxford, in the first years of the French Revolution and of the English debating societies, and in the company of the communitarian scheme on the American frontier which occupied the same circle; its republican sympathy with France against England put it squarely in the radical poetry of the 1790s, from which the writer's later career was a long retreat.
works.characters: Joan, the Maid of Orleans; the Dauphin, afterwards Charles the Seventh; the shepherds and the parents of the maid; the English commanders and their counsellors of the dark power; the saints who visit and encourage the heroine
works.structure: An epic in twelve books with a continuous war narrative, framed by invocations, councils of gods and powers, prophetic dream and prophetic speech, and by long episodes of battle and siege; the machinery is distributed between the celestial guardians of the heroine and the dark advisers of her enemies.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: Johan Johan
altTitles: A Mery Play between Johan Johan the Husbande, Tyb his Wyfe, and Syr Jhan the Preest
works.description: John Heywood's one-act farce of a cuckolded husband sent on errands by his wife and her lover the priest; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
works.plot: Johan Johan, suspecting his wife Tyb of entertaining Sir John the priest, is dispatched by her on a series of errands — to mend a pail, to fetch wax — while she dines with the priest; returning to find them feasting on a pie he was sent away from, Johan at last drives the priest out with blows, and the play ends with the husband's triumphant threat to beat Tyb too.
works.significance: The first English farce on the theme of the cuckolded husband and the anticlerical triangle that would recur through the century; its rapid domestic action makes it the most theatrically economical of Heywood's plays.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Printed in 1533 by Rastell, the year that saw the first parliamentary attacks on clerical marriage jurisdiction and mortuary fees; the play's satire of the lecherous parish priest draws on the fabliau tradition of Chaucer's Miller's Tale and the popular anticlerical jest.
works.characters: Johan Johan; Tyb (his wife); Sir John (the priest)
works.structure: A single-scene farce of errands and discovery, ending in a cudgel-fight; the play is a dramatization of the anti-clerical fabliau of the priest, the wife, and the credulous husband.

works.title: John Bull
works.form: Political allegory and character tract in epistolary form
works.description: A political allegory in three letters, published anonymously in 1712 in support of the Harley ministry's peace policy and instantly the most effective piece of war-time argument of its decade. Dr John Arbuthnot turns the Grand Alliance into a family law suit in which John Bull, the plain honest Englishman, has been brought to ruin by trustees, lawyers and a foreign partner. Its homely, low-comic manner made the figure of John Bull the standing personification of the English nation.
works.plot: John Bull, a freeholder of old family, puts his estate in the hands of trustees who hire a foreign partner, Lewis Baboon, and a crew of lawyers and projectors who out-spend the rents, mortgage the land and make John fight to keep what he no longer owns. When John falls into the power of the court of Chancery and the law's bottomless pit, his old servants and neighbours conspire to recover the estate, and the allegory urges the removal of the trustees, the ending of the war and the settlement of the account. Arbuthnot's point is that a people may be enslaved by debt, law and management while believing themselves free.
works.significance: It created the national personification that British cartoon and political language used for two centuries, and it is the purest surviving example of Scriblerian political satire in the Augustan public sphere. Its diagnosis of a nation captured by creditors, lawyers and standing armies became a durable idiom for constitutional argument.
works.meter: Prose only, in a colloquial, proverb-laden, bunyanesque-narrative register
works.context: Written during the negotiation of the Preliminaries of the Peace of Utrecht by a physician-close to the Tory ministry and to the Scriblerus circle, it belongs to the ministerial journalism of the Examiner and the Memorials of 1711-12, and to the Scriblerian strategy of using low humour and popular form against the Whig moneyed interest.
works.characters: John Bull; Lewis Baboon
works.structure: Three letters forming a continuous comic allegory, later expanded into a four-part version, with the argument carried by incident and legal farce rather than by direct declamation.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; Arbuthnot's authorship was established by his friends' testimony and by the Scriblerus correspondence, and is not now disputed. The later parts and reprints include additions of uncertain extent.

works.title: Joseph Andrews
altTitles: The History of the Adventures of Joseph Andrews, and of His Friend Mr. Abraham Adams
works.form: comic novel in prose, described as a comic epic poem
works.description: A comic history of the road, the first English novel to announce itself as a comic epic poem in prose, following a footman and a poor scholar on their journeys out of and back into their master's house. Its prefatorial essay on the ridiculous supplied the age with its most used comic theory.
works.plot: Joseph, a footman who keeps his chastity against his mistress's importunity, is turned out of the house and sets out to find his beloved Fanny. With his friend Mr. Adams, an absent but good-hearted parson, he travels by stage-coach, foot and waggon through a sequence of inns, beggars, gypsies, justices and physicians. Affection, hypocrisy and the affectation of virtue are exposed on the way, and the discovery that Joseph is Adams's future son-in-law by birth removes the last obstacle to the marriage.
works.significance: It created the self-conscious comic novel in English and set the terms of the century's debate about humour, affectation and the ridiculous, from its own prefatory essay to its later critics.
works.meter: A narrative prose of high comedy with the periodic digression of the critical chapters; the style takes up and exaggerates the diction of the romance and dramatic writers it holds up to burlesque.
works.context: Written and published between the two Pamela-answer volumes of 1741-2, in the season of the war of the theatre and the new copyright debates; its theory of the ridiculous answers both the sentimental and the licentious vogue.
works.characters: Joseph Andrews; Mr. Abraham Adams; Fanny Goodwill; Lady Booby; Mrs. Slipslop; the various innkeepers, justices and physicians of the road
works.structure: Third-person picaresque narration in book form with an intrusive narrator, digressory critical chapters and a discovery plot; the road supplies the sequence, the digressions the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the first volume appeared in the author's name, and the prefatory essays are signed by the design of the work.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides
altTitles: Journal of a Tour to the Hebrides, with Samuel Johnson
works.form: travel journal and autobiographical narrative, in the daily-notebook manner of Boswell's habit of recording
works.description: Boswell's account of the 1773 journey with Johnson to the western islands of Scotland, kept as a day-by-day journal and withheld from print for twelve years. It records the conversation, the arguments on Jacobite memory, religion, slavery and the worth of an island life, and the scenery of Skye and Mull, together with Boswell's own admiration and impatience. It is the companion to Johnson's own account of the same tour and one of the founding texts of the literature of Scottish travel.
works.plot: The journal follows the party from Edinburgh through St Andrews and Aberdeen to Inveraray, across to Skye and Mull and back by the west coast, noting what they saw and what Johnson said. The great subjects are the memory of the '45 and of the clan chiefs, the condition of the islanders, the debate over the Union and over the poverty of the islands, and Johnson's moral observations on the people he met, many of them at odds with Boswell's warmer sympathy. Boswell's own part - his devotion to Johnson, his flirtations, his pride in Scotland - is recorded as frankly as his companion's.
works.significance: It is one of the most reliable documents of Johnson's spoken mind and one of the classic travel narratives of Scotland, and its representation of Highland and island life belongs to the literature of the nations in the age of Ossian and of the romantic tour. It also shows how the journal of a single tour became a mode of autobiographical realism.
works.meter: Prose; plain, rapid and colloquial, with long passages of reported conversation and short topographical and antiquarian comment.
works.context: Written in the season of the Highlands' touring vogue opened by Pennant and others, when the aftermath of the '45, the cleared estates and the debate over the Union made the western islands an argument about national character; publication in 1785 followed Johnson's own Journey of 1775 and the long delay caused by the political and personal delicacy of the material.
works.characters: James Boswell; Samuel Johnson; the chiefs and families of the islands; the old Jacobites of the West
works.structure: A chronological day-by-day journal of a single tour, with continuous dialogue reported in the first person and no retrospectively imposed plot; the text prepared for 1785 retains the diary form.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the journal was kept by Boswell in 1773 and revised for the press, and the date of the tour and the date of first publication are both firmly documented.

works.title: Judith
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A fragmentary poem of 349 lines (the opening is lost) retelling the apocryphal Book of Judith: the Hebrew heroine beheads the Assyrian general Holofernes in his tent and rouses her people to victory. The poem recasts the biblical heroine as a figure of the heroic tradition — a maiden of God wielding the sword against the enemies of her people.
works.plot: Judith, beautiful and wise, is brought to the drunken Holofernes's tent; praying for aid, she seizes his sword and strikes off his head in two blows, then carries the head back to Bethulia in a food-bag. At dawn she shows the head to her people and delivers a speech of triumph; the Hebrews attack the leaderless Assyrians, who flee; Judith receives the spoils of Holofernes as her reward, and the poem ends with praise of God.
works.significance: The finest Old English poem on a female biblical hero; a masterly fusion of heroic style and devotional purpose.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with vigorous battle diction.
works.context: Preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv) immediately after Beowulf; the biblical book of Judith was known to the Anglo-Saxons through the Vulgate and Ælfric's later prose homily on the same subject.
works.characters: Judith; Holofernes; the Bethulians
works.structure: Dramatic narrative in the heroic manner: the tent scene, the return, the battle, and the distribution of spoils; the heroine's speeches drive the action.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Liberty of conscience and religious toleration
sources: The Poems of Robert Burns, 3 volumes

works.title: Juliana
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: Cynewulf's signed poem of 731 lines on the passion of St Juliana of Nicomedia: the virgin martyr who withstands her pagan suitor, defeats a demon sent to tempt her, and endures torture and death. The poem contains the most extended debate between saint and demon in Old English.
works.plot: Juliana refuses to marry the prefect Eleusius unless he converts; denounced by her father, she is beaten, hung by the hair, and thrown in prison, where a demon disguised as an angel urges her to yield; she seizes him and forces him to confess his works, then is subjected to fire and a boiling cauldron, and finally beheaded — her soul received into heaven, her persecutors drowned at sea. The epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature.
works.significance: The classic Old English virgin-martyr poem and the fullest statement of the saint-demon debate.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 65b-76v); based on a Latin passio of Juliana.
works.characters: Juliana; Eleusius; Africanus (her father); the demon; the angel
works.structure: A debate-driven passio: successive confrontations (suitor, father, demon, judge) leading to martyrdom, framed by the demon's confession of the history of evil and the poet's runic prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes.
sources: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, 2 volumes

works.title: Julius Caesar
works.description: Shakespeare's Roman tragedy of the republic's death: Brutus, honour's fool, joins the conspiracy against Caesar for Rome's sake; Caesar falls at the Capitol; Antony's funeral oration turns the crowd; and the play moves through the proscriptions and the quarrel of the conspirators to Philippi, where Brutus and Cassius die on their own swords.
works.plot: Cassius seduces Brutus into the conspiracy; Caesar, warned by the soothsayer and Calpurnia's dream, goes to the Senate and is murdered; Antony's 'Friends, Romans, countrymen' speech swings the mob to vengeance; the triumvirate proscribes its enemies; and the battles of Philippi complete the tragedy of Brutus, the noblest Roman of them all.
works.significance: The schoolroom tragedy of the English-speaking world — the standard by which political drama, and political oratory, have been measured ever since.
works.meter: A restrained, 'Roman' verse — no rhyme — with the prose of the plebeians and the two great orations as the peaks of its rhetoric.
works.context: Written 1599, the year of Essex's fall, from North's Plutarch; its anatomy of mob, coup, and civil war spoke to a court obsessed with succession and rebellion.
works.characters: Julius Caesar; Brutus; Cassius; Mark Antony; Portia; Calpurnia; Casca; Octavius Caesar; Cicero; Decius Brutus; the Soothsayer; Cinna the poet
works.structure: A two-part structure of conspiracy and war hinged on the assassination, with the funeral orations as the pivot of the play's rhetoric and the ghost of Caesar as its revenant.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Kenilworth
works.form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of court and domestic tragedy
works.description: A historical romance of the Elizabethan court, built on the tradition that the favourite of a queen secretly married an English heiress and that her death removed the obstacle to his ambition. The novel gives that gossip a fully imagined domestic and political history: a young woman of noble expectations, married in secret and then deserted, is destroyed by the machinery of her husband's design while the court celebrates the queen's progress to a Warwickshire castle. The public magnificence of the entertainment and the private concealment of a imprisoned wife are cut against each other throughout. It is the most purely tragic of the later romances of this series.
works.plot: An English heiress of an old family, persuaded into a secret marriage by an ambitious courtier, finds herself concealed in a distant house and abandoned as her husband's chances at court improve. The queen's progress to the Midlands brings festivals, pageants and reconciliations, while the deserted wife, tended by a faithful dependant, wastes in confinement and is terrorised by an hired agent of her husband's design. Her death, arranged in secret, removes the impediment to the favourite's suit for the queen's own hand, and the closing disclosures expose the instrument of the murder while leaving the courtier's ambition unpunished. The narrative also follows a boy's flight, a pursuivant's hunt, and the old servants of the wronged house.
works.significance: The standard example in English fiction of the Elizabethan court romance, and the most quoted treatment of the rumoured murder of a secret wife; its progress and pageant chapters are a much-studied instance of the historical novel's use of ceremonial spectacle. Its reconstruction of a domestic tragedy inside a court history made it a source for later plays, ballads and pictorial treatments of the legend.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a courtly and ceremonial diction for the progress scenes, contrasted with homely Scots and west-country speech in the domestic chapters
works.context: Published in 1821 and founded on the Elizabethan gossip and chronology surrounding a famous favourite, the queen's progress, and the mystery of a gentlewoman's death, material then being reworked by historians and antiquaries. The romance belongs to the second great phase of the series which had remained anonymous, issued when its author's public fame was established but his name still withheld, and written in the depressed years immediately after the war with France.
works.characters: The favourite of the queen and secret husband; Amy Robsart, his concealed wife; Queen Elizabeth; the agent of his secret business; a faithful retainer of the wronged house; a runaway boy and the pursuivant set to take him
works.structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes; a public court plot and a private domestic plot are conducted in parallel and meet in the last volume, with pageant, festivity and lower-class by-plot used to release and to comment on the central tragedy.
works.attributionNotes: Published as the work of the author of the Waverley romances, whose name was still withheld; the attribution is undisputed.

works.title: King Arthur; or, The British Worthy
works.description: The Dryden-Purcell dramatic opera in five acts, celebrating Arthur's wars against the Saxons and his love for the blind Emmeline; it was originally conceived as a political allegory for the Exclusion Crisis and revived in the 1690s.
works.plot: Arthur pursues the Saxon Oswald, who has stolen Emmeline; through enchantment, battles, and the restoration of Emmeline's sight, Arthur defeats the Saxons and unites Britain.
works.significance: The greatest of the English semi-operas and the finest collaboration between a poet and a composer in the period; Purcell's score (including 'Fairest Isle' and the Frost Scene) is a landmark of English music.
works.meter: Mixed blank verse, rhyme, and song.
works.context: Drafted in the 1680s as a Whig allegory of the Exclusion Crisis and rewritten for performance by the United Company at the Queen's Theatre, Dorset Garden, in June 1691 with music by Henry Purcell.
works.characters: King Arthur; Emmeline; Oswald; Merlin; Osmond; Philidel; Grimbald; Conon; Aurelius
works.structure: Five acts with extensive music, masque episodes, and spectacular machinery; the spoken roles are limited to the principal characters.
works.attributionNotes: The text is by Dryden, the music by Purcell; the 1691 quarto names Dryden.

works.title: King Hart
works.description: Douglas's allegory of the life of man: King Hart rules his castle of the body with the five senses as his servants until Dame Pleasance and her court — Youthheid, Fresche Delyte, Wantonness — enter and corrupt him; age, sickness, and death storm the castle, and the soul departs. The great Scots allegory of the body politic and the body natural.
works.plot: King Hart, counselled by Ressoun, admits Dame Pleasance and her court; the castle falls into riot; Conscience, Ressoun, and Wisdome are driven out; Age besieges and takes the castle, and Hart dies, leaving his soul to God's judgement.
works.significance: The finest Scots allegory of the body's rule and a bridge between the moralities and the Renaissance anatomy of the self; admired by the later Scots poets.
works.meter: Stanzaic verse in the Chaucerian tradition; vigorous personification allegory.
works.context: Written in Douglas's maturity, perhaps after the death of James IV at Flodden (1513); the castle's fall shadows the fall of the king's court.
works.characters: King Hart; Dame Pleasance; Youthheid; Fresche Delyte; Ressoun; Conscience; Age; Decrepitness
works.structure: A sustained allegory of the besieged castle in the morality tradition, moving from the entrance of pleasure through riot to death and judgement.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Douglas on manuscript authority; the attribution is generally accepted.

works.title: King Horn
works.description: The earliest surviving Middle English romance, some 1,500 short couplet lines telling the exile, adventures, and restoration of Horn, son of the murdered king of Suddene, who wins the love of Rymenhild, defeats the Saracen invaders, and regains his kingdom. Its spare, ballad-like narrative makes it the classic of the 'ancestral romance' of exile and return.
works.plot: Horn, cast adrift by the invaders who killed his father, grows up at the court of King Aylmar, where Rymenhild loves him; exiled through the envy of Fikenhild, he proves himself in Ireland, rescues Rymenhild from a forced marriage in disguise as a beggar, and returns to avenge his father and reclaim Suddene.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the English romance tradition and the earliest witness to the exile-and-return plot that governs the genre.
works.meter: Short rhyming couplets, often of three stresses, with formulaic diction.
works.context: Composed c. 1225 in the south of England from an Anglo-Norman source (the Romance of Horn of Thomas); preserved in Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27 (c. 1300) and two later manuscripts.
works.characters: Horn; Rymenhild; Fikenhild; King Aylmar; Athulf; the Saracen invaders
works.structure: A tripartite exile-and-return plot with disguise, recognition, and wedding scenes; narrated in terse couplets with abrupt transitions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
