works.title: King Johan
works.description: John Bale's historical morality play of King John, composed c. 1538 and surviving in a single manuscript revised in the 1550s; regarded as the first English history play.
works.plot: King John, the champion of England's ancient liberties against the papal usurpation, is beset by the allegorical forces of Rome — Sedition, Dissimulation, Usurped Power, Private Wealth — and the clergy, who stir rebellion and bring about his poisoning by Dissimulation disguised as a monk; Widow England and her allies Verity and Imperial Majesty restore the true succession, and the play ends with John vindicated as a proto-Protestant martyr and the papal power expelled.
works.significance: The first English history play: its fusion of the morality tradition with national history and its anti-papal reading of King John set the pattern for the Elizabethan history play, directly anticipating Shakespeare's King John.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed c. 1538 during Bale's Protestant exile/activity under Cromwell's patronage, at the moment when Henry VIII's break with Rome made King John a usable hero; Bale revised the play for Elizabeth (the manuscript addresses her), aligning it with the Elizabethan settlement's anti-papal politics.
works.characters: King John; Widow England; Sedition; Dissimulation; Usurped Power; Private Wealth; Verity; Imperial Majesty; Nobility; Clergy; Civil Order; Stephen Langton; Pope Innocent III
works.structure: A two-part play mixing historical persons (John, Stephen Langton, the Pope) with morality personifications, revised by Bale to address Elizabeth I; the structure alternates the king's historical action with the Vices' comic plotting.

works.title: King John
altTitles: The Life and Death of King John
works.description: Shakespeare's stand-alone history play of the Angevin crisis: King John's disputed title, the Bastard Faulconbridge's satirical commentary, the struggle with the papal legate Pandulph, and the play's terrible centre — the blinding of the boy Arthur and the grief of his mother Constance — ending in John's poisoning at Swinstead and the Bastard's closing appeal to England's unity.
works.plot: John defies Rome, battles France, captures Arthur, and orders his death; Hubert cannot blind the boy, but Arthur dies in his leap from the walls; the French invasion, the defection of the nobles, and John's poisoning follow, until the Bastard's loyalty and the Dauphin's withdrawal restore the kingdom.
works.significance: Shakespeare's boldest experiment in the history genre — a play without heroes, held together by the Bastard's irony and England's idea of itself.
works.meter: Blank verse of strong rhetorical sweep, with Constance's grief and the Bastard's 'commodity' soliloquy as the peaks.
works.context: Probably written 1595–96 in the anxious interval over the succession; its resistance to papal and foreign power spoke to Reformation England.
works.characters: King John; the Bastard (Philip Faulconbridge); Queen Elinor; Constance; Prince Arthur; Hubert; Cardinal Pandulph; King Philip of France; Lewis the Dauphin; Salisbury; Pembroke
works.structure: An episodic chronicle held together by the Bastard's choric commentary and by the Arthur tragedy at its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: King Lear
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of divided kingdom and broken nature: Lear abdicates, dividing Britain between the daughters who flatter him and disinheriting the one who loves him; cast out by Goneril and Regan, he goes mad on the heath in the storm with his Fool and the disguised Edgar, while the parallel plot of Gloucester and his sons runs to the blinding at Cornwall's hands — and the end brings Cordelia's death and Lear's over her body.
works.plot: Lear's love-test sets the tragedy in motion; Goneril and Regan strip him of his hundred knights; he rages into the storm, meets 'poor Tom' (Edgar), and is saved by Cordelia's French army; Gloucester, betrayed by Edmund and blinded, is led by Edgar to Dover; the battle is lost, Cordelia is hanged, and Lear dies of grief, leaving Edgar and Albany to close the play with its bleakest lines.
works.significance: By common consent the greatest tragedy in the language — the play that tests the limits of what tragedy can say about nature, justice, and the gods.
works.meter: A verse pushed to the edge of its resources — the storm scenes, Lear's curses, Edgar's mad speech, and the spare final lines — with prose for madness and the Fool's riddles.
works.context: Performed at court, 26 December 1606; the play draws on the old Leir play, Holinshed, and Sidney's Arcadia, and its two early texts (Quarto 1608 and Folio 1623) differ substantially.
works.characters: King Lear; Goneril; Regan; Cordelia; the Fool; the Earl of Gloucester; Edgar (Poor Tom); Edmund; the Duke of Albany; the Duke of Cornwall; Kent (Caius); Oswald; the King of France
works.structure: A double plot of Lear and Gloucester mirroring each other, built on the medieval morality pattern inverted — the trial of the daughters, the hovel, the cliff — and ending in the catastrophe that refuses consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the Quarto/Folio textual divergence is the play's standing editorial problem.

works.title: Kubla Khan
altTitles: Kubla Khan: A Vision in a Dream. A Fragment.
works.form: Visionary lyric and metrical romance in verse; a dream-poem in the line of the medieval vision, written as a study in the power of sound to carry what the argument cannot complete.
works.description: A short visionary fragment published in 1816 with a prose account of its origin in a sleep induced by an anodyne on a west-country tour, when the poem is said to have risen entire in the dreamer's mind and to have been lost, except for a few hundred lines, through interruption by a person on business from the village. The poem sets the pleasure-dome of the Mongol emperor against the image of a poet able to recreate such a place in song, and ends in terror at the power of the inspired man.
works.plot: The first movement decrees the stately pleasure-dome of Kubla Khan, with its gardens bright and its walls and towers, and the rivers that run with swift ecstatic friction through forests and measureless caverns to a sunless sea. The second movement turns to the deep romantic chasm that slanted down the green hill athwart a cedarn cover, wild with the woman wailing for her demon-lover, and to the fountain that rises in suspense, flinging up half-intermitted blocks and throwing logs and kottles into the labouring cavern, until the dome and the cavern-wonders are mingled in one hearing of the thunder of the waters. The closing movement abandons the description for the poet himself: could he revive within him the hollow and inspiring song of the Abyssinian maid, he would rebuild that dome and those caves of wonder, and his hearers, seeing the gleam and hearing the music, would fear and cry aloud at the sight; for the poet has fed on the paradise of the vision and drunk the milk of its divine woman. The argument is thus an image of the imaginative act, of the palace built in the air by the poet and of the terror that attends such power.
works.significance: The most celebrated fragment in English and a central text for all later writing on dream, intoxication and imaginative creation; its pleasure-dome and its caverns of measureless depth entered the language of literary and general discourse. It is also the most quoted example of the Romantic poem that makes the interruption of vision and the failure of memory its subject.
works.meter: Irregular accentual verse of exceptional richness, with lines running from two to six beats in a scheme of recurring rhyme, internal echo and repeated words, and a marked difference of pace between the flowing opening, the agitation of the chasm and the terror of the closing lines.
works.context: Composed, on the author's own later account, in the years of the western collaboration and of the opium experiments that followed; the date has been debated on the evidence of the manuscript and of contemporaries who heard the poem read before the turn of the century, and it was printed at last in 1816 at the instance of a brother-poet then abroad.
works.characters: Kubla Khan, the emperor who decrees the dome; the poet-speaker who would recreate the vision in song; the woman wailing for her demon-lover; the Abyssinian maid with her stringed instrument
works.structure: A fragment in three movements of unequal length and without a completed argument: the scene of the dome, the chasm and its supernatural music, and the poet's visionary ambition, the transitions being made by sound and by image rather than by exposition.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date and circumstances of composition are debated, reliance falling on the author's own 1816 preface and on the evidence of readers who heard the poem before 1800.

works.title: L'Allegro and Il Penseroso
works.description: A pair of companion poems contrasting two temperaments and ways of life: L'Allegro celebrates the active, social, cheerful mirth of the day and the countryside, while Il Penseroso praises the contemplative, melancholic, studious and religious delights of night and solitude.
works.plot: L'Allegro banishes melancholy and summons Mirth, tracing a day of rustic and urban pleasures culminating in music and masque; Il Penseroso banishes vain deluding joys and invokes 'pensive Nun', tracing a life of study, woodland meditation, church music, and a hoped-for prophetic vision.
works.significance: Among the most admired of Milton's shorter poems, they established his command of the English lyric and became models for eighteenth-century descriptive and meditative verse.
works.meter: Mixed tetrameter and pentameter couplets with varied lyric effects; the two poems mirror each other in structure.
works.context: Written during Milton's years of private study at Horton (c. 1632), published in the 1645 Poems; they reflect the Renaissance contrast of the active and contemplative lives.
works.characters: the poet; Mirth (Euphrosyne); Melancholy; the pensive Nun (Contemplation)
works.structure: Two matched lyrics in alternating tetrameter and pentameter couplets, structured as a balanced debate between the active and contemplative lives.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Lacnunga
works.form: medical manual and charm collection (Old English prose and verse)
works.description: A less orderly but more eclectic collection of remedies, charms, and prayers than Bald's Leechbook, compiled in the early eleventh century. It is best known for preserving the pagan-tinged metrical charms — above all the Nine Herbs Charm — alongside Christian prayers and learned Latin-derived recipes.
works.plot: The collection gathers remedies for wounds, fevers, eye and ear complaints, and childbirth, mixing herbal preparations with spoken charms and ritual instructions; its metrical charms invoke Woden and the herbs' powers while concluding with Christian formulas, in a characteristic fusion of traditions.
works.significance: The richest source of Old English charms, including the great Nine Herbs Charm, and a unique window onto the interface of learned medicine, popular healing, and pagan survival in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: The embedded charms are in alliterative verse (the Nine Herbs Charm, the Journey Charm); the surrounding recipes are plain instructional prose.
works.context: The manuscript belongs to the late Old English period's flourishing of vernacular medicine, when remedies circulated in monastic and lay households; the charms preserve elements of Germanic pre-Christian ritual under a Christian surface, a central document of the 'Christian-pagan synthesis'.
works.structure: A compilation in no strict order, grouping remedies by source rather than ailment; the metrical charms stand out from the surrounding prose as the collection's literary high points.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous compilation; the name 'Lacnunga' ('Remedies') is editorial, from the first remedy's heading.
themes: Early death and the mourning of poets

sources: Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine

works.title: Lady Susan
works.form: Epistolary novel of conduct and dissembling, inheriting the eighteenth-century letter-novel and turning it against the sentimental use of the form.
works.description: A short novel entirely in letters, dominated by a beautiful, penniless and unscrupulous widow who secures a home with her estranged in-laws, attaches their brother-in-law to herself, and markets her daughter to the richest suitor she can trap. It is the most ruthless and least reconciliatory of the early epistolary fictions of the period, and the only completed novel of its school to give the whole stage to a heroine-villain. The fair-copy manuscript in the author's hand survives.
works.plot: Lady Susan Vernon, having compromised herself in London by an intimacy with the married Mr. Manwaring, retreats to the country house of her late husband's brother, Mr. Vernon, where she flatters and plunders the credulous Sir James Martin and captivates his young kinsman Reginald De Courcy. Her daughter, the gentle Catherine, whom she means to foist upon Sir James for a dowry, is taken into the family's protection and forms friendships that defeat her mother's plan. When Manwaring's jealous husband exposes the correspondence, Lady Susan abandons Reginald, extorts a settlement for herself, and at the end marries the elderly Mr. Vernon, whose estate she will command.
works.significance: An important document of the transition from epistolary to narrated fiction, and one of the very few early nineteenth-century novels wholly controlled by a manipulative female protagonist. Its unfinished, unrepentant ending makes it a constant subject of editorial and feminist discussion. The survival of the fair-copy manuscript gives it exceptional value for the study of the period's composing habits.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; the style differentiates characters by their letters, from Lady Susan's studied blandishment to the blunt remonstrance of the country gentry.
works.context: Written in the years of the author's earliest maturity, when the letter-novel was being displaced by narrated realism and when the dependence of widows and unmarried women on male property was the dominant plot problem of women's fiction. Its cynicism about the marriage market belongs to the 1790s reaction against the doctrine of sensibility. The work remained in family hands for three quarters of a century and reached print only as an appendix to a biographical memoir.
works.characters: Lady Susan Vernon; Frederica Vernon; Reginald De Courcy; Mr. Vernon; Mrs. Johnson; Sir James Martin; Mr. Manwaring; Mrs. Manwaring; Alice Woodford
works.structure: Complete epistolary form: letters, notes and memoranda exchanged among Lady Susan, her confidante Mrs. Johnson, Catherine, De Courcy and the Manwarings, with the reader largely at the mercy of a manipulative correspondent; a brief documentary conclusion rounds the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship established by the manuscript and family tradition; no serious dispute.

works.title: Lalla Rookh
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse: a framed oriental romance sequence in the line of the Arabian tales and of eighteenth-century oriental fiction.
works.description: An oriental romance in verse in which a princess of Cashmere, travelling to her betrothed, is diverted by four tales told by an attendant poet. The frame gives the four separate romances - of the Paradise and the Peri, of the veiled prophet of Khorassan, of the fire-worshippers, and of the city of the Sultan - their common situation and their lyrical ease. It was the most financially successful poem of its decade and the volume that confirmed the poet's European fame.
works.plot: The frame follows the princess's journey towards her bridegroom's court, with the poet who rides beside her supplying tales that modulate from celestial love to religious imposture, to forbidden love under conquest, and to the magnificence and cruelty of an eastern city. Each embedded romance has its own plot: a peri's quest for acceptance into Paradise through a martyr's love; a prophet's veil and the exposure of his imposture by a detected lover; the amours of a captive prince and a fire-worshipper maid under Muslim conquest; a Sultan's clemency and a slave's self-sacrifice. The frame's own history turns on the discovery that the teller of the tales is the woman the princess is destined to love, so that romance and narrative machinery close together. The volume is unified by its treatment of love, faith and religious jealousy as the motives of eastern history. Its lyrical effusiveness and its scenery were held by later readers to exemplify both the attraction and the superficiality of Oriental romance.
works.significance: It was the best-selling English poem of its years, secured the author's international reputation, and supplied the Victorian stage and the school anthology with their stock image of the poetic East. Its framing of tale within tale was one of the most widely imitated structures of Romantic narrative verse. Later criticism treats it as the term against which a more exacting Orientalism, and a more severe lyric practice, defined themselves.
works.meter: Highly varied lyrical stanzas, including anapestic and mixed measures with frequent refrains, adapted to each embedded tale.
works.context: Published when eastern scenery, translated Arabian tales and the Oriental narratives of the period's most famous living poet had made the form a staple of the fashionable market, and when British interests in India and Persia were being extended. The poem's religious subjects engage a period fascinated and uneasy about zeal, imposture and fanaticism. Its huge advance from the publisher was itself a celebrated incident in the literary marketplace, and the volume was quickly translated across Europe.
works.characters: Lalla Rookh, princess of Cashmere; the poet who accompanies her as her guide and tale-teller; the Peri; the veiled Prophet of Khorassan; the fire-worshippers of Ispahan; the Sultan of the city
works.structure: A framed tale: a journey narrative containing four independent metrical romances, with the frame returning at the end to reveal the relation between teller and hearer.

works.title: Lament for the Makaris
works.description: William Dunbar's elegy on the poets ('makaris') of Scotland and the world (c. 1505, 100 lines): a procession of the dead — Chaucer, Lydgate, Gower, Henryson, and the court poets of the Stewart kings — each stanza closed by the refrain 'Timor mortis conturbat me' (the fear of death troubles me). The greatest short elegy of the Scottish tradition, and the poem that gave the makars their name.
works.plot: The poet, reflecting that all things must die, calls the roll of the dead poets: first the great English trio of Chaucer, Gower, and Lydgate, then the Scottish makers — Barbour, Hary, Holland, and above all 'the noble rhetor' Henryson — and finally the court poets of his own youth, closing with the fear of death and the petition that God provide for the poet before he joins them.
works.significance: One of the great elegies in the language: its roll-call fixed the canon of the makars and its refrain became the proverbial voice of late medieval mortality.
works.meter: Four-line stanzas with the Latin refrain, austere and musical.
works.context: Composed c. 1505 at the court of James IV, when Dunbar's generation was passing and the print era beginning; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508); it names the Scottish tradition 'makaris' for all later criticism.
works.characters: Dunbar (speaker); the dead poets (Chaucer, Gower, Lydgate, Barbour, Hary, Henryson, and others)
works.structure: Twenty-five stanzas of single-movement elegy, the refrain tolling each catalogue entry, in the ubi sunt tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Dunbar's authorship secure.

works.title: Lamia
altTitles: Lamia. Isabella. The Eve of St. Agnes. Ode to a Nightingale. Ode on a Grecian Urn. To Autumn, and Other Poems
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the fable of the enchantment and the exposure, in the couplet manner of the older romance translation, with the philosophical argument carried by the second part.
works.description: A two-part narrative poem of a serpent-woman who, having been given a human form by the magic of her lover's devotion, is destroyed at a banquet by the cold eye of a philosopher who will not let an illusion stand. It is the author's most polished couplet poem and the subtlest of his statements of the quarrel between the imaginative and the analytic life. Its first part tells the love of Lamia and a young knight of Corinth, its second the banquet and the exposure, and the moral is left unresolved.
works.plot: A serpent of golden grain, who is in truth a woman and who has been seen by a youth of Corinth in the shape of a serpent, is granted her human form by the power of the love she wakes in him, and she builds a palace of cloud and shadow for their dwelling. The pair pass into Corinth as bride and lord of a house, and the lover's friends and the whole city are drawn to the splendour of the feast, while the philosopher Apollonius, asked to the banquet by the lovers, fixes his eye upon the bride and discovers the phantom nature of the palace. At his word the illusions fall away, the bride is seen as the serpent of the field, and the lover dies of the loss; the philosopher goes on his way rebuked. The argument is that the loveliness which the imagination creates may be the only truth by which a human life can be sustained, and that the analytic knowledge which exposes it is not innocent.
works.significance: It is the most complete of the period's couplet romances and the source of the enduring formula for the sacrifice of the world's loveliness to a philosophy of cold analysis. Its two-part design, the enchantment and its exposure, became a model for later poems of the destructive intellect, and its couplets are the standard instance of the poet's mastery of a measure he was accused of not possessing.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of iambic pentameter, handled with extraordinary fluency and a sustained use of the closed line, with short interpolated lyric passages and the famous lines of the exordium in a looser movement.
works.context: Written in the late summer and autumn of 1819 at Wentworth Place, Hampstead, where the poet lodged with a friend, in the season which produced the great lyrics and the two titan poems, and published in the volume of July 1820 which was his last in his lifetime. Its attack on the analytic coldness of the philosopher was read at once as a squib on the metaphysics of the day, and its treatment of an illusion which knowledge destroys gave it a permanent place in the argument about the value of the imagination.
works.characters: Lamia, the serpent-woman of the field; the young knight of Corinth her lover; Apollonius the philosopher; the guests and friends of the banquet; the mother of Lamia named in the exordium
works.structure: Two parts, the first of some hundred and forty couplets on the metamorphosis and the building of the palace, the second of the banquet and the exposure, with the second part carrying the poem's reflection on the philosopher's office.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was kept for the volume of July 1820 rather than given to the periodical press, and the manuscript and the printer's copy are the basis of the modern text.

works.title: Lancelot of the Laik
works.description: A Scottish romance of some 3,500 lines adapting the French prose Lancelot: Arthur's war with Galiot, Lancelot's secret love for Guinevere, and the dream-vision in which the lover's conscience anatomizes his state. The only Scottish Arthurian romance, composed in the age of the makars for a court that read both Chaucer and the French cycles.
works.plot: Arthur, weakened by tyranny and war with the rebel Galiot, is saved by Lancelot, who fights incognito and compels Galiot's submission; the second half turns inward, as a dream allegory of love's joys and pains lays bare Lancelot's adulterous devotion to the queen.
works.significance: The sole Scottish Arthurian romance and a significant witness to the reception of French Arthurian prose in the Stewart court.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in Older Scots, with aureate ornament.
works.context: Composed c. 1460–79 in Scotland, adapting the French prose Lancelot and the amatory allegory tradition; preserved uniquely in Cambridge University Library MS Kk.1.5 (c. 1500).
works.characters: Lancelot; Arthur; Guinevere; Galiot
works.structure: A two-part structure — chivalric war, then amatory dream vision — that joins the French romance of arms to the Chaucerian allegory of love.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Laterculus Malalianus
altTitles: The Laterculus Malalianus of Theodore of Tarsus
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 139 (twelfth century)
works.description: A Latin exegetical and chronographical treatise on the life of Christ, attributed to Theodore of Tarsus, archbishop of Canterbury, and written at Canterbury in the 670s. Based on the Greek chronography of John Malalas, it expounds the gospel account of Christ's life in the light of eastern exegesis and computes the ages of the world; it is the principal surviving witness to the school of Theodore.
works.plot: The treatise moves through the life of Christ from the Incarnation to the Passion, glossing each episode with eastern exegetical traditions (on the Virgin, the baptism, the temptations, the crucifixion) and interweaving chronographical calculations of the world's ages drawn from Malalas's chronicle, concluding with eschatological reflection on the last things.
works.significance: The earliest theological work composed in England, and the founding document of the Canterbury school that made England a centre of Greek-influenced Latin learning; a unique witness to the eastern roots of Anglo-Saxon exegesis.
works.context: Written when Theodore and Hadrian were building the school of Canterbury, the treatise shows the direct importation of Greek and Syriac learning into England; the same exegetical traditions appear in the Canterbury biblical commentaries preserved in Milan, and Theodore's pupils carried them into the Northumbrian Renaissance of Bede.
works.structure: A continuous exegetical treatise organized by the gospel narrative, with digressions into chronology and typology; the style is dense and allusive, marked by the Greek learning of its source.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Theodore of Tarsus on the basis of its Greek sources, its Canterbury origin, and its consistent transmission with Theodore's school texts; the attribution is widely accepted but rests on inference rather than explicit ascription.
sources: Nightmare Abbey (The Cambridge Edition of the Novels of Thomas Love Peacock, volume 7)

works.title: Layamon's Brut
works.description: Layamon's verse chronicle of Britain, some 16,000 lines adapting Wace's Roman de Brut with additions from Welsh and English tradition, from the Trojan Brutus to the Saxon conquest, including the fullest early English account of King Arthur. It is the first major treatment of the Arthurian legend in English.
works.plot: Following the Trojan Brutus's settlement of Britain, the poem recounts the line of British kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests, Round Table, and death it narrates at length — down to the Saxon victory and Arthur's prophesied return.
works.significance: The first Arthurian epic in English and the bridge from the alliterative tradition to Middle English romance; its Arthur material influenced the entire subsequent Arthurian tradition in England.
works.meter: A hybrid line blending the native alliterative half-line with loose rhyme and French-derived couplets; formulaic and archaic diction.
works.context: Composed by the priest Layamon of Areley Kings, Worcestershire, c. 1190–1215, in the generation after the loss of Normandy, when English was re-emerging as a literary language; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ix (earlier, longer) and Cotton MS Otho C.xiii (later, shortened, fire-damaged).
works.characters: Brutus; King Lear; Arthur; Guinevere; Merlin; Vortigern; Hengest; Cadwalader
works.structure: A continuous regnal chronicle organized by successive kings, with Arthur as its structural and emotional centre.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship secured by the prologue's self-naming of Layamon, priest of Ernleye (Areley Kings).

works.title: Le Morte Darthur
altTitles: The Whole Book of King Arthur and of His Noble Knights of the Round Table
works.description: Sir Thomas Malory's great prose compilation of the Arthurian legend, completed in prison in 1469–70 and printed by Caxton in 1485: from the sword in the stone and the winning of Guinevere, through the adventures of Lancelot, Tristram, and the Grail quest, to the breaking of the Round Table, the last battle, and Arthur's passing to Avalon. The definitive English Arthurian book.
works.plot: Malory weaves the French prose cycles and English alliterative poems into a single tragic narrative: Arthur's accession and marriage, the founding of the Round Table, the quests and loves of its knights, the Grail quest that divides the fellowship, the adultery of Lancelot and Guinevere, and the final war against Mordred in which Arthur falls — his body borne to Avalon, his epitaph 'Rex quondam Rexque futurus'.
works.significance: The summit of English Arthurian literature and the conduit of the Arthurian story to Spenser, Tennyson, and the modern novel; its vision of chivalry — at once idealized and doomed — is the period's most enduring legacy.
works.meter: Prose: paratactic, ritual, and rhythmic, with the famous Malorian cadence of balanced clauses and repeated key words.
works.context: Completed by the 'knight prisoner' Thomas Malory in the ninth year of Edward IV (1469–70), during the Wars of the Roses; Caxton's 1485 print fixed the text for three centuries until the discovery of the Winchester manuscript (1934) revealed the pre-print version.
works.characters: Arthur; Lancelot; Guinevere; Gawain; Tristram; Isolde; Galahad; Merlin; Morgan le Fay; Mordred
works.structure: Eight books (Caxton's twenty-one divisions) of interlaced adventure compressed into linear narrative, with the Grail and the Lancelot-Guinevere tragedy as the arcs that break the fellowship.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel (d. 1471) on the evidence of the colophons; the identification is widely though not universally accepted.

works.title: Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres
works.form: critical treatise and professorial textbook, with anthologised extracts and commentaries
works.description: The published substance of Blair's professorial course at Edinburgh, the first institutional chair of rhetoric and belles lettres in Britain, and the most influential textbook of taste and composition of its generation. It joins a theory of taste, a history of the styles of writing and an analysis of the genres - epic, tragedy, ode, satire, the periodical essay - with precepts on pronunciation and elocution. For half a century it was the standard manual of literary judgment in Britain and America.
works.plot: The lectures begin with the principles of taste and with the sublime and the beautiful, proceed through the historical stages of literature and the study of the ancient and modern writers, and then examine the species of composition in prose and verse, the passions, the figures, the kinds of style and the rules of delivery. Blair argues that taste is founded on common sense and on the sympathy of mankind, that genius must be disciplined by rule and by the ancients, and that the criticism of a work must consult the sentiments and the manners of its own age.
works.significance: It codified the century's criticism of taste, sublimity and genre into a teachable system and became the grammar of literary judgment for the nineteenth century, for readers and for institutions on both sides of the Atlantic. Its treatment of primitive and national poetry, of the sublime and of elocution also makes it an index to the movements of taste that produced the graveyard and the ballad revivals.
works.meter: Prose; clear, temperate and exemplary, written to be a model of the styles it prescribes, with the illustrative extracts supplying the metrical variety.
works.context: Delivered after Blair's appointment to the new Edinburgh chair and published in 1783, in the full tide of the Scottish Enlightenment's analysis of taste, sympathy and the progress of the arts, and in the same years as the vogue of the fine arts and of the history of literature. Its use in universities and academies made it a vehicle of the period's educational programme.
works.structure: A course of lectures in three broad parts - the principles of taste and the history of literature, the species of composition with illustrative extracts and remarks, and elocution and delivery - each number a self-contained lesson with examples.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the lectures are those of Blair's course at Edinburgh, and the printed edition was prepared by him from the matter used in teaching, with several later editions revised.

works.title: Lectures on the Dramatic Literature of the Age of Elizabeth
altTitles: Lectures, Chiefly on the Dramatic Literature of the Age of Elizabeth
works.form: Lectures on the history of the drama, combining the portrait of the playwright, the account of the stage and its conditions, and the argument about the rules.
works.description: The third course of printed lectures, delivered and published in 1820, on the drama of the Elizabethan and Jacobean age, and the author's most concentrated book on the theatre. It argues that the drama of that age lived by the sense of character and of passion, by novelty of situation and by the sympathy of a mixed audience, and it opposes to the criticism that measures plays by rule a defence of the irregular abundance of the stage of the playhouses.
works.plot: The first lecture states the general character of the age, its mixture of the tragic and the comic, its freedom from the rules, and the conditions of the public theatre that produced it. The lectures that follow give a succession of portraits of the dramatists of the period before and after the great poet of the age: the university wits and their learning, the writers of city comedy and of the humours, the writers of civic and of domestic tragedy, the romancist of the stage and his sensitive and moralised plays, the satirist of the court and his strength and his meanness, and the poet of the later plays whose dialogue and whose scenes of suffering are placed with honour beside the greater masters. Against these the author sets the French and the classical model, and the argument concludes that the true test of the drama is not its observance of the rules but its power over the imagination and its passion of character.
works.significance: The book that shaped the modern estimate of the secondary dramatists of the age of the national theatre, and a foundation of the historical study of the Elizabethan stage; its portraits long stood as the standard introduction to the writers it discusses. Its defence of the irregular drama against rule is the most complete statement of the Romantic case for the older English stage.
works.meter: Lecture prose of a vigorous and summary kind, with short sentences of judgment balanced against long periods of description, and frequent quotation from the plays discussed.
works.context: Delivered and published in London in 1820, in the years of the revivals of the old drama on the nineteenth-century stage and of the new attention to the unrevised plays and the accounts of the players; the course followed the lectures on the poets and on the comic writers, and was issued from the institution that had engaged the lecturer.
works.structure: Five delivered lectures, one of general account of the age and four of succession of dramatists, with a closing comparison between the national drama and the regulated stage of the Continent; the plan is critical and historical rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: Lectures on the English Comic Writers
works.form: Lectures on the history of prose humour and satire, in the Romantic critical manner, combining the theory of laughter with the portrait and the historical survey.
works.description: A course of lectures on the English writers of humour and satire, delivered in 1819 and printed in the same year, which together with the lectures of the previous year made its author the historian of English prose as well as of English poetry. Its argument is that humour is a moral and social faculty, that it requires a sense of the absurd arising from self-love and from the contradictions of manners, and that the great comic writers are serious men who have turned their observation of themselves and of the world upon its mistakes.
works.plot: The opening lecture distinguishes humour from wit and from satire, and makes the laugh of the comic writer a product of contrast and of the unexpected, with a constant reference to the sense of power that laughter gives. The following lectures take the writers in a loose succession: the essayists and character-writers of the Elizabethan age and their humours, the comic drama of the Restoration and its picture of manners, the writers of the spectator papers with their politeness and their moral machinery, the novelist and romancer of the same school, the greater humorist of the century who satirised learning and dulness, the philosopher of humour and his theory of the laughable, and the novelists and essayists of the author's own day. The argument runs through the whole that the best humour has its seat in a tenderness and a self-forgetfulness which the mere satirist wants, and that the age of good humour is an age of ease and of good nature rather than of struggle.
works.significance: The first English history of comic prose as a serious subject and a standard authority for the reading of the essayists, the character-writers and the novelists of humour; its definitions of humour, wit and satire long held place in handbooks of the subject. It also fixed the canon of English prose for later schoolmen and is a central document of the Romantic essay's account of itself.
works.meter: Lecture prose of an easy and discursive kind, with the period built for the ear and a frequent use of the illustrative quotation and of the short verdict; the style is less weighty than that of the lectures on the poets and more conversational.
works.context: Delivered and published in London in 1819, in the season of the lecture institutions and of the new market for printed criticism, following the lectures on the poets of the previous year and preceding those on the drama of the Elizabethan age; the book takes in the controversy about the theory of the laughable then current from the older essays.
works.structure: Four delivered lectures, printed as spoken, with a general lecture of principle and three of historical succession, the several writers grouped rather than systematised, and with digressions on the theory of laughter and on the state of contemporary letters.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: Lectures on the English Poets
works.form: Lectures on the history and theory of poetry, in the Romantic critical manner, combining the portrait essay, the historical survey and the argument about the faculties.
works.description: A course of five lectures on the English poets, delivered in the early months of 1818 before a subscribers' institution in London and printed in the same year. The lectures trace the poetry of the nation from the Elizabethans to the living writers, on the principle that poetry is the language of the imagination and of passion, and they are at once a history, a theory and a quarrel with the criticism of the day.
works.plot: The first lecture states the general argument: poetry is not a matter of taste or of rule but of the passions and the imagination, and it arises from a sense of the power of the mind over its objects. The following lectures pass over the period in a sequence of portraits: the Elizabethan drama and its great contemporaries, with their abundance and their want of system; the poet of the paradise lost, whose sublimity is that of a mind conversant with the terrible and the great; the age of the couplet and of the school of polish, with the strength and the limits of its satire and its didactic verse; and the romantic and the modern poets, among them the living writers of the Lake school, the poet of the Oriental tales, and the younger revolutionary singers. The lectures estimate each by the degree of imagination found in them, praise the passion of the old drama, and argue that the age of criticism and of the couplet has lost something of the poetry of the imagination.
works.significance: A shaping book of the Romantic history of poetry, influential in fixing the canon and in the vocabulary by which English verse was judged for the next century, and the classic statement of the doctrine that poetry is the speech of imagination and passion. Its portraits of the Elizabethans and of the poet of the lost Paradise, and its account of the living poets of its own day, are still standard quotations in the history of criticism.
works.meter: Spoken prose, with the period built for the ear, the frequent antithesis, the abrupt sentence of judgment, and the long accumulation of illustration that distinguishes a lecture from an essay.
works.context: Delivered at a London institution for the diffusion of knowledge in the spring of 1818, in the season of public lecture courses and of the new profession of the man of letters, and printed the same year by a publisher of the lecture series; the course followed the author's first book of dramatic criticism and preceded the lectures of the following year on the comic writers.
works.structure: Five delivered lectures, printed much as they were spoken, with an opening lecture of principle and four of historical succession; the design is critical rather than narrative, and the portraits are linked by the recurring distinction between imagination and mechanical ingenuity.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: Legends of Holy Women
works.description: Osbern Bokenham's collection of thirteen verse lives of female saints, written 1443–47 at the request of a circle of East Anglian patrons, several of them women: Margaret, Anne, Christine, the Eleven Thousand Virgins, Faith, Agnes, Dorothy, Mary Magdalene, Katherine, Cecilia, Agatha, Lucy, and Elizabeth of Hungary. The major fifteenth-century English legendary of women's sanctity.
works.plot: Each life narrates the saint's birth, conversion, and martyrdom (or holy death), with the debates, torments, and miracles of the genre; the framing prologues record the patrons who commissioned each legend, making the work a document of literary patronage as much as of hagiography.
works.significance: The principal fifteenth-century English collection of female saints' lives and a uniquely documented instance of women's literary patronage in the period.
works.meter: Couplets and rhyme royal in the Lydgatean style, aureate but warm.
works.context: Composed 1443–47 by the Augustinian friar Osbern Bokenham of Stoke by Clare, Suffolk, for Lady Katherine Denston, Isabel Hunt, and other East Anglian gentry women; preserved in BL Arundel MS 327 (the author's own manuscript).
works.characters: St Margaret; St Anne; St Katherine; St Mary Magdalene; St Cecilia; and the other saints; Bokenham (narrator)
works.structure: A sequence of independent verse legends, each with its own prologue naming the patron, in the Chaucerian-Lydgatean manner.
works.attributionNotes: Bokenham's authorship secure; he names himself and his patrons throughout.
sources: Mason Locke Weems, His Works and Ways (3 volumes)

works.title: Lessons for Children
works.form: children's educational prose and verse, in the graduated reading-lesson tradition
works.description: Barbauld's elementary books for the very young, begun in 1778 and issued in graduated classes, the first widely successful example in English of a reading course calculated for the mind of a child. The lessons move from single words and short dialogues about the household, the animals and the weather to longer narrative and moral pieces as the child's capacity grows. Their method of steady progression, of the familiar object and of the question-and-answer dialogue made them the model of children's teaching books for a century.
works.plot: The earliest classes consist of short exchanges about things within a child's reach, naming, seeing and doing, and pass by easy steps to little stories and to the plainest duties of kindness, truthfulness and attention. Later classes introduce narrative, fable and reflection, still pitched to the child's experience and governed by the principle that instruction should follow the interests of the learner. The whole proceeds on the conviction that the mind of a child is to be led, not driven, and that pleasure is the proper engine of learning.
works.significance: It is the founding text of English literature written for the nursery and the direct ancestor of the progressive reading series, and it changed expectations of what a child could be given to read. Its doctrine of instruction through pleasure and familiar objects became orthodoxy in elementary education and in children's writing.
works.meter: Plain short sentences and dialogue in the earliest classes, with simple rhymed and rhythmic pieces introduced as the series proceeds.
works.context: Written in the train of Locke's thinking on education and of the new interest in the education of infancy, and in the practical context of Barbauld's own teaching circle and of the nonconformist academies; the books belong to the 1770s revolution in the literature made for children, which treated the child as a reader with rights of its own.
works.characters: The child addressed; the instructing voice of the book; the household and animal figures of the dialogues
works.structure: A graded series of short lessons in several classes or parts, each rising in difficulty, arranged for sequential use rather than as a continuous story.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the classes appeared successively from 1778 and the dates of the several parts differ, so the composition start is left null with the series described in the note.

works.title: Letter to the Earl of Chesterfield
altTitles: Letter to the Right Honourable Philip Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield, 7 February 1755
works.form: familiar letter in the state paper manner; epistolary prose of the Augustan school
works.description: The brief reply that closed Johnson's nine years of expectation of patronage, sent days before the publication of the Dictionary after Chesterfield had revived his acquaintance at its approach. Its courteous refusal - that favour is unwelcome when it comes 'delayed till I am indifferent, and cannot enjoy it; till I am obstinate, and cannot repay it' - is the most celebrated letter in English literary history and the classic statement of the independent professional writer. It was copied, circulated and printed soon after and became part of the lore of letters.
works.plot: Johnson recounts how he first approached Chesterfield nine years earlier, was repulsed, and nonetheless worked on without help; he observes that the Earl has now thought it convenient to remember him, and declines the favour on the ground that it comes too late to be welcome. He insists that he has needed no patron and will owe no obligations he cannot repay, and closes with a wish for the Earl's happiness that is decorously but unmistakably cold. The argument is not a personal quarrel but a claim about the dignity and self-sufficiency of learned labour.
works.significance: The letter fixed the image of authorship against patronage for the next century and supplied the standard anecdote of Johnson's independence. It is a touchstone for the history of the literary marketplace, and its rhetoric has been read as the perfect example of the period's controlled, judicial prose.
works.meter: Prose, balanced and judicial in cadence, moving from ironic gratitude to the famous refusal that favour arrives 'delayed till I am indifferent, and cannot enjoy it; till I am obstinate, and cannot repay it', and ending with a decorately cold wish for the Earl's happiness.
works.context: Written in the week before the Dictionary was issued, when the subscription and copyright economy of bookselling had already made the old aristocratic patronage relation embarrassing to both parties; Chesterfield's own letters to his son had publicly recommended a very different model of literary dependence.
works.characters: Samuel Johnson; Philip Stanhope, Earl of Chesterfield
works.structure: A single brief formal letter of a few short paragraphs, ordered chronologically through the history of the acquaintance and rhetorically from courtesy to refusal to the closing wish.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the letter is documented by Johnson's holograph copies and by early print, though no holograph of the final version survives.

works.title: Letters and Journals of Lord Byron
altTitles: Letters and Journals of Lord Byron, with Notices of His Life and Writings
works.form: Edited correspondence and journal with literary biography and prefatory commentary; an edition of papers accompanied by a critical life.
works.description: The edition of a dead poet's correspondence and journals, with a biographical and critical memoir, assembled from manuscripts in the publisher's hands and from letters recovered from correspondents. Its prefatory life became the foundational Byron biography for the rest of the century. The editor's task was at once scholarly and defensive, since the reputation of the subject and the sensibilities of surviving parties were all in dispute.
works.plot: The collection presents Byron's life through his own letters and journal entries, arranged with continuous biographical commentary that supplies the connections, dates and persons the manuscripts alone left obscure. The Notices trace the poet's schooldays and Irish inheritance, the fame of the first cantos, the separation, exile in Italy and the last Greek campaign, and they interpret the letters as evidence of a nature generous but fatally ungoverned. Editorial judgements on the poetry, on Byron's politics and on his religious opinions are woven through the narrative, sometimes apologetically. The work also records, in its silences and in its protests of necessity, the business of suppression: material was withheld on the instruction of parties who feared the consequences of publication, and the missing final journal volume became a permanent scandal. The result is a document of Romantic biography's arrival as a commercial and ethical form.
works.significance: For most nineteenth-century readers it was the authoritative Byron, and its portraiture set the terms of biographical discussion for decades. It is a primary source for the correspondence and journals on which all later editing depends. Its handling of withheld papers made it a touchstone case in the ethics of editing and in the history of literary reputation.
works.meter: Prose correspondence and journal, with verse quotation and reminiscence throughout the commentary.
works.context: It appeared a decade after its subject's death, when the poet's papers, his unpaid debts and his posthumous reputation were all still contested, and when the publisher who owned the manuscripts had destroyed part of the record. Memoirs of living and recently dead celebrities were a major branch of the book trade, and the quarterlies conducted the argument over editorial discretion. The edition also falls within the agitated politics of the late 1820s, when the memory of Byron had become a resource for reform and for continental liberal causes.
works.structure: A chronological correspondence and journal interleaved with a continuous biographical commentary; the life is told in the editor's connective narrative and the letters are the primary exhibit.
works.attributionNotes: The edition and the prefatory Notices are the editor's own work, though the letters and journals quoted are another writer's; a supplement volume followed the first issue.

works.title: Letters for Literary Ladies
works.form: Conduct, education and domestic prose in epistolary form; a polemic and open letter addressed to a reading public.
works.description: An early polemical work in the form of letters addressed to women readers, arguing that the cultivation of the understanding is the duty and the happiness of their sex, and that the fashionable restrictions on female study rest on authority rather than on reason. It replies directly to the influential prescription of the period that women should be amused rather than instructed. The book is also a piece of family literary history, since one of its letters is addressed to a young woman of the household for whom the writer's educational books had been made.
works.plot: The letters urge that women may read history, philosophy and the sciences without loss of tenderness or of domestic virtue; they argue that the pleasures of the imagination are a support in adversity and that an uncultivated mind makes an unequal marriage. They concede the danger of pedantry and of public display, and insist that the improvement of the female understanding will improve the education of children and the morals of the family. The argument is conducted through example, quotation and courteous concession rather than through declaration.
works.significance: An important document of the transition from conduct literature to the argument for women's intellectual cultivation at the end of the eighteenth century. It supplies evidence of how a woman writer entered the print public sphere by way of the familiar letter. Its arguments were to be reworked, without polemic, in the fictional illustrations of the tales.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a light, ironical, conversational period style with frequent quotation.
works.context: Written in the aftermath of the 1790s debate about female education, on which the revolutionary controversy had made the instruction of women a political question as well as a domestic one. It belongs to the household educational enterprise of its author, whose writing was first done for the instruction of younger members of her family. Its publication preceded by five years the national tale that made her name, and it shows her first use of the printed public.
works.structure: Epistolary argument in two volumes, addressed to named private correspondents; no plot, and the sequence is one of theme rather than event.
works.attributionNotes: The first edition did not print the author's name; her authorship was established immediately within the family and publishing circle and is undisputed.

works.title: Letters from Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple
works.description: The seventy-seven surviving letters written by Dorothy Osborne to William Temple during their long courtship in 1652-4, in which she discusses her family's opposition to the match, the books she is reading, and the state of the country under the Commonwealth.
works.plot: The letters trace the progress of the courtship against Osborne's brother's opposition and her own reluctance; they range freely over literature, gossip, politics, and the difficulty of a woman's position.
works.significance: The finest English letters of the seventeenth century and a crucial document of women's writing; their spontaneous style was admired by Virginia Woolf and they are the standard by which later familiar letters are judged.
works.meter: An easy, natural, unselfconscious prose that is the earliest great example of familiar English letter-writing.
works.context: Written 1652-4, during the Commonwealth, when Osborne was confined at Chicksands and Temple was travelling; they married in 1654.
works.characters: Dorothy Osborne; Sir William Temple; Sir Peter Osborne; Osborne's brother Henry
works.structure: A sequence of letters over about two years, with gaps.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Osborne; the manuscripts were printed in 1847 from the family papers (first partly published in 1713).

works.title: Letters from England
altTitles: Letters from England: by Don Manuel Alvarez Espriella
works.form: Periodical essay in epistolary form, a deliberate continuation of the Spectator paper and of the travel letter, with embedded disquisition and satire.
works.description: The author's most influential prose work: a long series of letters on England written in English but affected to be the observations of a fictitious Spanish refugee correspondent. The persona lets the writer praise and blame his own country as though seeing it for the first time, in a manner consciously modelled on Addison's Spectator papers. The range is enormous - lakes and manufactories, Dissent and the slave trade, duelling, the theatre, the poor laws.
works.plot: The personating correspondent, a South American of Spanish descent resident in England, writes to friends in Philadelphia and Lisbon about the country he has settled in. He tours the Lake District, the Scottish border, the industrial towns and London, and uses each place to draw out an argument about national character, religion, commerce or liberty. His foreign eye permits both extravagant praise of English institutions and satiric attack on Methodism, political corruption and the treatment of the poor. Alongside the travel letters are essays on the slave trade, on the Roman Catholic Question, and on literature and the drama, and a running quarrel with the Review journals.
works.significance: It made its author famous to a broad reading public as the poet of the Lakes, supplied the earliest substantial romantic prose celebration of the Lake District, and gave later guide-book writers and travellers the model of the foreign persona criticising England.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: The letters first appeared in the Anti-Jacobin Review from 1804 and were collected in the three volumes of 1806-08, when its author had broken with his early radicalism and was building a Tory public identity; the Spanish mask answers the decade's war with Spain and its hunger for picturesque domestic travel.
works.characters: the personating Spanish-refugee correspondent; his Philadelphia and Lisbon addressees
works.structure: Epistolary periodical sequence: numbered letters of unequal length gathered into volumes, loosely organised by journey and by subject rather than by argument.
works.attributionNotes: Published under a pseudonymous by-line personating a Spanish refugee correspondent, a persona properly recorded with the author rather than in this work record; the authorship was an open secret and the by-line was dropped in later collected printings.

works.title: Letters on a Regicide Peace
altTitles: First Letter on a Regicide Peace
Letters on a Regicide Peace, and on the Prospects of a Regicide Success
works.form: political pamphlet in the form of open letters; war polemic and state-paper argument
works.description: Four open letters, the first two appearing in the autumn of 1795 and the remaining two in 1797, arguing against any negotiation with the French Directory. Their title is the argument: a state founded on the judicial murder of its king is a criminal association rather than a government, and to treat with it is to license regicide among the nations.
works.plot: The first letter urges that the French power is not a France but a sect, organised for the destruction of all established government, so that peace with it would be a surrender disguised as moderation. The second argues at length that the apparent resources of the enemy are real and growing, and that the financial and military strength of the Republic has been systematically underrated by its British admirers. The third and fourth letters turn on the consequences of a pacification, prophesying the loss of the colonial and naval contest and the infection of the British constitution by a doctrine of untrimmed rights; the fourth, the most rhetorical, calls the Directory a military aggression in the shape of a civil government. Throughout, the letters press for the war as a war of principle rather than of balance, and for the internal restraint of the corresponding societies at home.
works.significance: They carry the argument of the Reflections from constitutional theory into the diplomacy of ideological war, and they gave British political writing its most influential vocabulary for describing revolutionary power as a sect rather than a state. Their reading of the trade, finance and manpower of the enemy also marks an early attempt to argue grand strategy from social statistics.
works.meter: Amplified, declamatory prose of the late parliamentary style: long periods charged with metaphor, classical allusion, and invective, with an invectory rhythm the reviewers of the day imitated and mocked.
works.context: Written during the debate on the negotiations at the close of 1795 and the talk of a congress in 1796-97, when the corresponding societies, the famine and the suspension of habeas corpus made the French question a domestic one. The letters were circulated as separate publications bought widely, and they fixed the language of the war party for a generation.
works.structure: Four letters of very unequal length forming a single sustained argument; the first two carry the case against negotiation, the third supplies the historical and philosophical defence of European society, the fourth is the closing peroration on the terms of a possible peace.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the four letters are securely documented among the undisputed writings of their author, and their separate publication is well attested.

works.title: Letters on the Improvement of the Mind
altTitles: Letters on the Improvement of the Mind, Particularly with Regard to the Conduct of the Life
Letters on the Improvement of the Mind
works.form: conduct and educational letters; familiar essay in epistolary form
works.description: A series of letters of instruction to a young woman, on the government of the temper, the use of learning, the choice of company, religion and the conduct of the common day. It became one of the most widely read of the century's female conduct books and passed through many editions.
works.plot: The correspondent is guided through the duties of the mind, the culture of the understanding, the discipline of the passions and the ordering of time and fortune. Learning is recommended for judgement rather than for show, and the dangers of sensibility, of company and of expense are weighed with practical counsel. The later letters turn to religion, to the conduct of the understanding in divine matters and to the duties of the active life.
works.significance: It is a central text of the practical education of women in the later eighteenth century and a document of the Bluestocking argument that improvement of the mind and conduct of the life are one subject.
works.meter: A clear, warm and unrhetorical epistolary prose of the middle style, with the balanced sentence of moral advice and the occasional quotation of the poets.
works.context: Published in 1773 from the circle of the Bluestocking correspondents, whose letters on female education and taste had prepared the public for such a work, and in the season of the new attention to the academies and to women's rational improvement.
works.structure: A serial of familiar letters on connected heads, the sequence moving from the culture of the mind to the conduct of the life and to religion; each letter closes with a practical direction.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name after the circulation of the letters among friends.

works.title: Letters to Serena
altTitles: Letters to Serena, Occasioned in a Stay in France
works.description: Toland's Spinozist-tinged philosophical letters, written during and after a stay in France, which develop a necessitarian, materialist account of mind, matter, and the eternity of the species. The letters to his correspondent Serena are prefixed by a discourse on the eastern philosophy arguing that European learning derived from the East.
works.plot: The prefatory discourse maintains that philosophy migrated east-to-west and that the Greeks learned from barbarian sages, demoting the miracle of Greek originality. The letters then argue that motion is essential to matter, so that an immaterial, unmoved mover is unintelligible; thought likewise arises in organized matter, and the mind is not a separable substance. From this Toland draws the eternity of the universe and of the species of creatures, against creation out of nothing and against the doctrine of a naturally mortal soul, reading Genesis as a natural history of this world only. Personal immortality is dissolved into the perpetuity of nature, and religion is reinterpreted as the homage of a mind that contemplates the whole.
works.significance: It introduced a Spinozist necessitarianism into English philosophical letters and became a standard citation in the pantheist scares of the century; its eastern-philosophy thesis early globalized the history of ideas.
works.meter: Supple epistolary prose, argumentative but conversational, with long distinctions worked out through examples and retorts.
works.context: Written after Toland's 1707-08 continental visit, where he studied the reception of Spinoza on the continent, and published amid the post-Clarke debates on the soul and on the sufficiency of reason.
works.characters: Serena (the addressee); the writer
works.structure: A sequence of familiar letters on connected philosophical topics, framed by a prefatory historical discourse.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Letters written during a short residence in Spain and Portugal
altTitles: Letters written during a short residence in Spain and Portugal, in 1795 and 1796
works.form: Travel letters / topographical epistle: a pedestrian tour narrative in the manner of Young and Arber, enlarged with antiquarian essay and political economy.
works.description: The author's Iberian travel letters, worked up from notes taken during his walking tour of northern Spain with John Favero in 1795-96. The volume combines picturesque description of coast, mountain and monastery with antiquarian discussion, political observation and an open sympathy with the Spanish and Portuguese poor. It is the founding text of his career as a traveller-author and the source of the Iberian colour he later used in verse.
works.plot: The letters narrate a pedestrian tour from Lisbon through the valleys of Asturias and Old Castile and back, pausing at mines, cathedrals, baths and fishing villages. The writer estimates populations, agriculture and monastic wealth, and argues that Iberian poverty is the product of misgovernment rather than of climate or national character. Antiquarian detours on early Spanish poetry, Moorish remains and local institutions are woven into the route. The closing letters weigh the prospects of reform in the peninsula and the consequences of the war with Revolutionary France.
works.significance: It fixed the Iberian setting later exploited in the romances of the same author, and it is a primary document of 1790s pedestrian tourism and of the romantic picturesque applied to the peninsula.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Written by a twenty-two-year-old former Jacobin just after the French Revolutionary War began on the peninsula, the book refracts its author's desertion of radical politics through a sympathetic but Protestant, anti-monastic view of Catholic Spain.
works.structure: Epistolary sequence in dated letters following a geographical itinerary; description, disquisition and correspondence with friends alternate without a sustained argumentative thread.

works.title: Letters Written in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark
altTitles: Letters Written during a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark
works.form: Travel letters and familiar essay in epistolary form; topographical and political observation fused with a diary of feeling.
works.description: A book of travel letters written on a northern tour in the summer and autumn of 1795 and revised for the press the following year; it is at once a scenic account of Sweden and Norway, a survey of their commerce, manners and government, and a journal of private grief. The letters are addressed to the partner whose commercial interests the journey was meant to recover, and are signed with a single initial. Its mixture of picturesque observation, political economy and lament makes it the most subtle of the period's travel narratives.
works.plot: The letters follow a ship and a coach from London through Elsinore, Gothenburg and the Swedish coast, up the Norwegian rivers and to the cascade of Rjukanfoss and Telemark, and then through Denmark and back. Along the road the writer records the faces of the poor, the condition of women, the management of forests and mines, the laws of Sweden, the manners of the Norwegian peasants and the scenery of rock and waterfall, and repeatedly tests the theories of the sublime and of taste against what she has seen. Interwoven with this is the account of a failed negotiation, of a deserted woman's tenderness and of thoughts of death that the northern landscape seems to invite and then to dispel. The closing letters turn from the individual complaint to a project of moral and political improvement for the nations of the north.
works.significance: The most admired prose narrative of its author's later work and a central text of Romantic travel writing; it influenced the northern travelogue and the lyric meditation on landscape for a century. Its analysis of the sublime from a woman's travelling consciousness is a much-studied contribution to the period's aesthetic debate. It is also a primary document of the history of feeling, commerce and gender in the 1790s.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; an elastic, exclamatory style that moves from precise observation to apostrophe, with quoted verse and song fragments.
works.context: Written in the aftermath of the revolutionary decade, when travel in the north had become an object of commercial and diplomatic interest and when the picturesque was the dominant vocabulary of landscape description. Its economic observations belong to the debate about national prosperity opened by the new political economy. The tour was undertaken to retrieve a partner's failing speculation in Scandinavian trade, and the book's private address reflects that entanglement.
works.structure: Twenty-five familiar letters in chronological order of travel, shifting between report, essay and confession; the second-person addressee gives the sequence its emotional continuity, while the description and the disquisition carry its argument.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute.

works.title: Leviathan; or, The Matter, Forme, and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill
works.description: Hobbes's masterwork of political philosophy, in which the commonwealth is conceived as an artificial man whose soul is sovereignty, founded on a covenant by which individuals transfer their right of self-government to an absolute sovereign.
works.plot: Part I ('Of Man') sets out Hobbes's materialist psychology and his state of nature, in which life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'; part II ('Of Common-Wealth') derives the sovereign's absolute authority from the social contract; part III ('Of a Christian Common-Wealth') subordinates the church to the state; part IV ('Of the Kingdom of Darkness') attacks scholastic and papal claims.
works.significance: The foundational text of modern political philosophy and of social contract theory; it transformed the vocabulary of politics, founded the modern theory of sovereignty, and provoked responses from Locke, Rousseau, and every subsequent theorist of the state.
works.meter: A powerful, lucid English prose deliberately free of rhetorical ornament; Hobbes's style became a model of the plain philosophical sentence.
works.context: Composed in Paris during Hobbes's exile and published in London in 1651, two years after the execution of Charles I; it was condemned by royalists and by Presbyterians alike and was later attacked in Parliament as an encouragement to atheism.
works.structure: Four parts in 47 numbered chapters, with the famous engraved frontispiece of the giant sovereign composed of his subjects.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Hobbes; authorship undisputed.
