works.title: Sense and Sensibility
works.form: Novel of manners and domestic moral comedy, inheriting the 1790s vogue for the fiction of sensibility while inverting it through irony and conditional endings.
works.description: A social novel of two orphaned sisters, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, who illustrate contrasting regimes of feeling and judgement after being displaced from their father's estate. The work grew out of an epistolary juvenile experiment of the late 1790s and was reworked into a third-person narrative of discretion, disappointment and eventual settlement. Its argument is not that sensibility is false but that unexamined feeling needs the discipline of principle.
works.plot: Sir John Dashwood, influenced by his wife Fanny, keeps the promised provision from his stepmother and half-sisters, who remove to a cottage on the estate of a distant relation. Marianne attaches herself passionately to the charming, impecunious John Willoughby, who is recalled to London and marries a rich heiress instead; Elinor quietly endures the secret engagement of her own beloved Edward Ferrars to the artful Lucy Steele. Marianne's exposed grief carries her to illness and near death, while Edward is disinherited for honouring his early pledge and is only freed when Lucy transfers herself to his brother. The novel closes with double marriages, Marianne's cooler second choice of the steady Colonel Brandon, and a modest restoration of family order.
works.significance: The first work of the school of social realism that displaced the romance of sensibility, and the founding text of the novel of manners in the Regency mode. Its treatment of female feeling as both social currency and private suffering set the terms for later women's fiction. Its revision from epistolary draft to narrated tale is a documented case of 1790s experimental form being absorbed into nineteenth-century realism.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; balanced periodic sentences, epigrammatic dialogue, and a famous antithetical title-phrase in iambic rhythm.
works.context: Written through the 1790s controversy over sensibility and the education of women, and revised during the Napoleonic Wars when the commercial and clerical careers open to gentle families were precarious. The novel's entailed estates, half-pay officers and drawing-room politics register the specific economic vulnerability of the landless gentry. It was offered to a London publisher at a moment when the three-volume novel had become a financial as well as a literary form.
works.characters: Elinor Dashwood; Marianne Dashwood; Edward Ferrars; Colonel Brandon; John Willoughby; Mrs. Jennings; Lucy Steele; Fanny Dashwood; Sir John Dashwood; Mrs. Dashwood; Robert Ferrars
works.structure: Third-person narration with sustained free indirect discourse anchored now in Elinor and now in Marianne; linear, episodic plot of removals between Devonshire, Sussex, London and Cleveland; letters and reported conversation carry offstage information.
works.attributionNotes: Published as 'By A Lady'; identification of the author rests on publisher's records and family documentation and is not in dispute.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Jane Austen

works.title: Sensibility
altTitles: Sensibility. A Poem. In Two Parts
works.description: A moral essay in couplets on the culture of feeling, distinguishing a true from a false sensibility and arguing that tenderness without principle is a form of self-love. It was the first considerable poem of its author and established her reputation in the fashionable literary world.
works.plot: The poet examines the temper of the age, in which the refinement of feeling has been mistaken for virtue, and shows the man of sensibility pursuing his own pleasure under the colour of sympathy. Examples of the false and the real are contrasted - the suffering of the poor, the distress of friendship, the duties that a feeling heart evades. The second part passes to the consolation of religion and to the assertion that sensibility must be governed by duty and by the hope of another world.
works.significance: It is one of the clearest early statements of the case against the ethics of feeling, and it announced a career that was to span the century's passage from fashionable sensibility to evangelical duty.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of the Augustan school, with the closed and balanced antithesis of the sententious line and the occasional pathetical pause.
works.context: Published in 1773, in the height of the cult of sensibility and of the first attacks upon it, and written by a young woman of the Bath and London literary circles who was shortly to become a dramatist and a conduct writer.
works.structure: A discursive poem in two parts, opening with a complaint of the manners of the age, passing through instances and characters, and closing in an elevation of principle.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in her collected verse.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sensus Communis: An Essay on Wit and Humour
altTitles: Sensus Communis, an Essay on Wit and Humour
authors: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
works.description: Shaftesbury's essay on wit, written as a friendly critique of Anthony Collins's Essay Concerning the Use of Reason and issued the same year as the Letter Concerning Enthusiasm. It proposes ridicule as the proper test of wit and of whatever claims assent, and distinguishes true raillery, which supports sociability and liberty of thought, from the spleen and ignorance of the mere witling.
works.plot: The essay opens on the character of a book and the conditions of free examination, then passes to an anatomy of wit and humour, classifying wits by their governing humour. Shaftesbury insists that ridicule, like reason, must be exercised freely and without fear, since a doctrine or religion that cannot endure to be ill-used deserves to be. He distinguishes genuine raillery, addressed to opinions and manners, from personal abuse, and traces modern wit to a mixture of the fine and the humorous. The argument closes with a defence of good manners in raillery and an appeal to common sense as the public standard of the ridiculous.
works.significance: It gave the century its most influential account of ridicule as a criterion of truth and civility, directly conditioning Addison's papers, Pope's doctrine of wit, and later theories of humour and the comic.
works.meter: Conversational, pointed prose in the manner of a letter to a friend, rich in distinctions, short definitions, and barbed asides; passages of rhythmic tripartite enumeration give it the feel of spoken raillery.
works.context: Printed in 1709 amid the freethinking debates opened by Collins and Toland, and written in dialogue with the author of A Discourse of the Liberty of the Press, whose press Shaftesbury praises while disagreeing with his conclusion. It forms part of what became the Characteristics.
works.structure: A single discursive essay in loose epistolary form, moving from the conditions of free enquiry through a classification of wits to the doctrine of ridicule as test.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Serious Reflections During the Life and Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
altTitles: Serious Reflections During the Life and Afflicting Circumstances of Robinson Crusoe
works.form: meditative and didactic prose essays in a fictional persona
works.description: The third Crusoe volume, a collection of meditations, dialogues and practical essays put into the mouth of the retired islander. It abandons narrative for moral reflection on providence, solitude, the fear of man, temperance and the duties of a master, and is organised as a set of numbered serious thoughts.
works.plot: The narrator, now settled and prospering, meditates on the religious meanings of his preservation, debates with imagined interlocutors the questions of conscience and enthusiasm, reflects on the condition of servants, wives and children, and argues that a Christian's true business is the government of his own passions. The volume adds visionary and allegorical papers on the invisible world, including a dialogue with the soul and a description of the world of spirits.
works.significance: It supplies the strongest internal evidence of the moral and religious frame that contemporaries read in the first volume, and its mixed reception marked the boundary between fiction and edification in the early-eighteenth-century book trade.
works.meter: Serious plain prose of the conduct-book manner, with balancing clauses, scriptural tags and the interrogative turn of meditation; the allegorical papers admit a more ornate visionary rhetoric.
works.context: Published in the same year as the second volume and in the wake of controversies over enthusiasm and natural religion, it draws on the Puritan tradition of the serious meditation and on the 1710s vogue for soliloquy on the passions.
works.characters: Robinson Crusoe; the imagined interlocutor; Friday as a figure of natural religion; the narrator's own soul
works.structure: A serial of short reflective papers rather than a continuous plot, with inset dialogues and a few narrative fragments; the Crusoe persona functions as a mask for a moralist.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested, though the volume has conventionally been treated as the weakest of the three; the title-page carries the same fictional persona as its warrant.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos
altTitles: The Sermon of the Wolf to the English
works.description: Wulfstan's most famous sermon, preached in the crisis year 1014 as the Danish conquest of England was completed: an impassioned jeremiad interpreting the Viking devastation as God's punishment for the nation's sins, culminating in the vision of the enslaved nation — 'an Englishman is not worth more to a Dane than a dog'. The masterpiece of Old English pulpit rhetoric.
works.plot: The sermon catalogues the nation's sins — betrayal of lords, perjury, oppression of the poor, the violation of churches — and reads the tribulations of Æthelred's reign (the treachery of Eadric Streona, the burning, plundering, and enslavement of the people) as the biblical pattern of divine wrath; it calls the nation to repentance before the last things overtake it, in a crescendo of Wulfstan's two-stress rhythms.
works.significance: The greatest Old English sermon and the classic statement of the period's theology of national sin.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical prose: two-stress phrases, alliteration, anaphora, and word-pairs ('byman and bærnan' — burn and ravage).
works.context: Preached in 1014, after the expulsion of Æthelred and before Cnut's final conquest (1016); preserved in five manuscripts, including British Library, Cotton MS Nero A.i.
works.characters: Wulfstan (preacher, as 'Lupus'); the English nation
works.structure: A single continuous exhortation built on the antithesis of sin and punishment, with the historical crisis framed as the fulfilment of prophecy.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is certain ('Lupus' is his Latin signature).

editions.title: The Homilies of Wulfstan

sources: The Pilgrim's Progress

works.title: Sermon of the Plough
works.description: Hugh Latimer's most famous sermon, preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548 and printed the same year; the classic Protestant sermon of social criticism, built on the text of the sower.
works.plot: Taking the gospel of the sower, Latimer expounds the 'plough' of preaching, the 'seed' of God's word, and the spiritual husbandry required of clergy and laity alike; he attacks the idleness of prelates ('unpreaching prelates'), the rack-renting of landlords, and the neglect of the poor, calling the realm to the work of the spiritual plough — a sustained sermon of estates satire turned to gospel ends.
works.significance: The most celebrated English sermon of the Reformation: its homely agricultural allegory and its fearless attack on clerical and landlord abuses made it the model of the Protestant pulpit's social criticism from the sixteenth century to the nineteenth.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548, in the first months of Edward VI's reign, as part of the reform campaign against images and non-residence; printed by John Day in 1548 and reprinted through the century, the sermon made Latimer the voice of the Edwardian Reformation's social conscience.
works.structure: A single sermon structured by the parable's allegory — the plough, the seed, the soil — with digressions into the abuses of church and commonwealth.

editions.title: Sermons by Hugh Latimer

works.title: Sermons (Hugh Blair)
works.form: published pulpit oratory and practical divinity, in the polite sermon tradition of the eighteenth century
works.description: The collected sermons of Blair, minister of St Giles's in Edinburgh and the most widely read Scottish preacher of his generation, issued from the later 1770s and reprinted across the English-speaking world. They exhibit the temperament of moderated Augustan pulpit oratory: practical, moral, polished, addressed to the feelings and to the conduct of ordinary life rather than to doctrinal controversy. Their success made Blair the standard model of the polite sermon and a central presence in the rhetoric of the Scottish Enlightenment.
works.plot: The discourses take up the duties of the Christian life - the government of the passions, the duties of social and family conduct, the improvement of the mind, the conduct of affliction and the hope of a future state - and expound their texts with an orderly argument from observation of human feeling to practical application. Blair's handling of the parables and of the gospel history is narrative and affective, and his perorations press the auditor toward self-examination without invoking terrors.
works.significance: The Sermons were among the most reprinted religious books of the age, admired for their style by Blair's Scottish auditors and by the French and German translators who used them. They supply the practical counterpart to the Lectures on Rhetoric and remain the standard illustration of polite pulpit oratory in the culture of feeling.
works.meter: Prose; the balanced period, the graduated triple, the measured cadence and the clear syllabic emphasis for which Blair's theory of elocution was written into his own practice.
works.context: Preached and collected in the decades of Blair's incumbency at St Giles's and of his Edinburgh professorship of rhetoric and belles lettres, when the moderated Calvinism of the Scottish church and the culture of feeling met in the pulpit, and when the sermon was a literary genre with a substantial print market.
works.structure: A serial volume of separately preached discourses, each a single argument with an opening explication of the text, a progression of reflections and a closing application; the several series were gathered in successive volumes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the several series of Blair's Sermons appeared across the later eighteenth century and the volumes are documented by his own publication of them, so the date entered here is that of the first collected series, with the later volumes described in the note.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
altTitles: Fifteen Sermons Preached at the Rolls Chapel
Sermons, Founded on Several Occasions, Preached at the Rolls Chapel, in Chancery Lane
works.description: Butler's early sermon sequence on human nature, conscience, and the authority of reflection, preached at the Rolls in the 1720s and published as a philosophical defence of the natural constitution of moral agents. Its central claim, that conscience is by nature authoritative in man, answers Mandeville, Hobbes, and Shaftesbury at once.
works.plot: Butler argues first that human nature is a system, not a heap of instincts, in which self-love and benevolence are naturally implanted and commonly coincide. Against psychological egoism he shows that particular passions have their own objects, and that pursuing them, not self, is the true path to happiness. Reflection or conscience surveys our actions and approves or disapproves with a natural authority that is one of degree as well as strength; to follow it is the case of the whole creature. The later sermons treat self-deception, the pursuit of pleasure, and the respect owing to conscience, grounding religion in the same constitution that grounds morality.
works.significance: The Preface and sermons anticipated the theories of benevolence, conscience, and authority debated by Hume, Reid, and the intuitionists, and remain the most-cited eighteenth-century text in moral philosophy besides the Treatise.
works.meter: The plain, exact, cumulative prose of the pulpit turned to analytic purpose: distinction after distinction, quietly weighted, with an unwonted precision of definition.
works.context: Preached between 1719 and 1725 before a Rolls audience drawn from the chancery bar, amid the Mandeville and Shaftesbury debates on self-love; the sermons were published in 1726 with a Preface that became a locus classicus of moral philosophy.
works.structure: A collected series of fifteen sermons with an analytical Preface, each sermon isolating one branch of the argument from human nature.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sermons upon Several Occasions (Tillotson)
altTitles: The Works of the Most Reverend Dr John Tillotson
works.description: The collected sermons of John Tillotson, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1691, published posthumously by his chaplain Ralph Barker; they are the model of latitudinarian preaching and were among the most widely read religious works of the eighteenth century.
works.plot: The sermons expound a rational, moral, and tolerant Christianity: the reasonableness of revelation, the duties of charity and justice, the evil of strife and persecution, and the practical character of true religion.
works.significance: Tillotson's sermons defined latitudinarian prose style and were a principal influence on Addison, Swift's models of plain preaching, and the moral temper of eighteenth-century Anglicanism.
works.meter: Clear, balanced, plain prose that became the standard of English pulpit eloquence.
works.context: Tillotson preached at St Lawrence Jewry and at court through the Restoration and after the Revolution; he was made Archbishop of Canterbury in 1691 and died in 1694; the folio of his Works appeared in 1696.
works.structure: A collection of occasional sermons arranged by subject and occasion.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Tillotson; the posthumous collection was edited by Ralph Barker.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Seventy-Six
works.form: Historical novel of the Revolutionary period in the comic and popular manner
works.description: A novel of the year of the Declaration of Independence, and one of the earliest American attempts to write the Revolution as popular comedy rather than as civic legend. Its scene is a New England town and its personages a company of ordinary men swept into the war. The book treats patriotism as a matter of temperament and of incident.
works.plot: In a community on the eve of the war, neighbours are divided by interest, habit and fear as the crisis arrives, and the call to arms draws each of them into the contest by a different motive. The narrative follows the enlistments, the quarrels and the comic misadventures of a company raised from the town. Private interest and public duty are played against one another until the war settles the argument. The book ends with the Revolution established and the community transformed by the demands made on it.
works.significance: It is among the first American fictions to make the Revolution available as popular comedy, and it anticipates the later native treatment of the founding as everyday history. Its crowded speech and provincial idiom are an early experiment in American vernacular. It documents the range of the historical novel in the 1820s.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published at New York in 1823, in the efflorescence of centennial and semi-centennial interest in the founding events. Its plebeian treatment of patriotism belongs to the author's quarrel with the dignified historical novel. The book was written when its author was editing a newspaper and preparing his move to English publishing.
works.structure: Third-person popular novel of a community in crisis, episodic and crowded with speech-types, with the historical year imposed as frame and title.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

editions.title: Observations on American Art: Selections from the Writings of John Neal (1793-1876)

works.title: Shakespear Illustrated
altTitles: Shakespear Illustrated: Containing the Genuine Plot of His Best Plays, Proving That They Are Translations from the Italian, Spanish and French
Shakespear Illustrated, with Essays Proving His Plays Translations
works.form: critical treatise with comparative abstracts of sources
works.description: A critical collection proving from the antecedent tales that the plots of Shakespeare's best plays are borrowed from Italian, Spanish and French originals, each play being faced with an abstract of the source. Its prefatory discourse on the properties of drama is an early statement of neoclassical plot doctrine in English criticism.
works.plot: The work examines a sequence of the plays - among them Othello, Measure for Measure, All's Well That Ends Well, Romeo and Juliet and The Taming of the Shrew - and sets against each the story Shakespeare found. It shows the plot as given, the alterations as made, and argues that the poet's judgement rather than his invention is to be praised or blamed. The prefatory discourse draws the conclusion that fidelity to probability and to the unities is the measure of dramatic merit.
works.significance: It is an important document of source study before scholarship and of the eighteenth-century argument about Shakespeare's obligations to the romance tradition, anticipating later source criticism.
works.meter: Plain argumentative prose of the mid-century critical essay, with the quoted abstracts in a deliberately bald narrative style.
works.context: Published in 1753 in two volumes, in the season of the great editions of Shakespeare and of the quarrel over his regularity, and written by a novelist-critic with access to the Italian and Spanish sources through translation.
works.structure: A series of comparative essays, each pairing an abstract of the source with remarks on the play, framed by a general discourse on the drama; the argument is cumulative and evidential.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, though early bibliographers occasionally misassigned it.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Shakespeare's Sonnets
works.description: The 154 sonnets printed in 1609, with the long poem 'A Lover's Complaint' appended: a sequence to a beautiful young man urging him to marry and immortalizing him in verse, shadowed by a rival poet and by the 'dark lady' of the later sonnets — the greatest sonnet collection in the language, and the most argued-over book of poems in English literary history.
works.plot: The first seventeen sonnets press the youth to marry; the middle poems anatomize love, jealousy, absence, and the rival poet; the dark lady sequence (127–152) turns on lust and self-betrayal; and the final poems rework Cupid and the cures of love, closing with 'A Lover's Complaint' spoken by a forsaken maid.
works.significance: The summit of the English sonnet tradition; its identities, erotic shapes, and textual mysteries have made it a permanent site of scholarship and dispute.
works.meter: The Shakespearean sonnet (abab cdcd efef gg) brought to its definitive form, with 'A Lover's Complaint' in rhyme royal.
works.context: Composed across the 1590s and early 1600s, partly circulating in manuscript; printed by Thomas Thorpe in 1609 with the dedication 'To the onlie begetter of these insuing sonnets, Mr. W.H.' — the most famous crux in English bibliography.
works.characters: the poet; the young man (Fair Youth); the dark lady; the rival poet; the maid (in the Complaint)
works.structure: A sequence of 154 sonnets with a detectable narrative arc — courtship, crisis, self-reproach — followed by the appended complaint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Shakespeare's; the identities of the Fair Youth, the dark lady, and 'Mr. W.H.' remain unknown.

works.title: Shamela
works.form: short epistolary burlesque and prose satire
works.description: A short burlesque of the servant-girl novel, published anonymously in the same season as its original, which turns the heroine's letters into the devices of an artful seductress pursuing her aim. It is the earliest and sharpest of the answers to the conduct fiction, arguing from inside the form that its morality was interested.
works.plot: Shamela Andrews, a country servant with an eye on her mistress's estate, writes letters home rehearsing her own arts of attack and defence. She is courted, resisted and finally complied with on her own schedule, her scruples being the scruples of design, and she secures a proposal from the squire while keeping the old woman and the parson in play. The piece ends with her married and in possession, the pretence of virtue having served the whole design.
works.significance: It invented the technique of the ideologically inverted parody and remains the standard instance of the eighteenth-century argument that the novel of moral reward was a fiction of interest; it also led directly to the author's own theory of comic prose.
works.meter: A debased copy of the servant style, with the idiom and misspellings of the original mocked and the candid sentences of the design breaking through the piety.
works.context: Published in April 1741, three months after the conduct novel it answers, in a season crowded with its imitations and abridgements; the pamphlet war over the education of women and the price of virtue formed its immediate context.
works.characters: Shamela Andrews; Squire Booby; Parson Williams; Mrs. Slipslop; the old lady of the family
works.structure: An epistolary burlesque in a single short volume, the letters' dates and self-exposures replacing the original's suspense; the prefatorial apparatus directs the reading as party attack.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution long anonymous and established by internal evidence, the contemporary advertisement and later acknowledgment; recorded here as single.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: She Stoops to Conquer; or, The Mistakes of a Night
works.form: Laughing comedy in five acts, dialogue prose, for the London theatre, printed with prologue and epilogue and with the customary dramatis personae; built on the comic conceits of mistaken place and assumed condition.
works.description: Goldsmith's masterpiece for the stage and one of the two or three comedies that survived continuously in the English repertory from the eighteenth century: a laughing comedy in which a mistake about the identity of a house sets the whole plot going and in which a young woman deliberately 'stoops' in order to win the man she loves. It was written in explicit opposition to the sentimental comedy of distress and was dedicated to Samuel Johnson.
works.plot: Young Marlow, ardent and forward with women of easy reputation but dumb and bashful before a modest woman, is brought by his father's arrangement to the house of the neighbouring Mr Hardcastle, whom he is to marry. The idler Tony Lumpkin, who has no wish to be married himself and delights in mischief, directs the travellers to Hardcastle's house as though it were an inn; Hardcastle, learning of the mistake and determined to cure his son's bashfulness by it, plays the landlord. Marlow therefore behaves with insolent freedom towards the real daughter of the house, whom he takes for a barmaid, and Kate, perceiving what has happened, consents to the deception and 'stoops' to the character in order to be loved for herself. The subplots of Tony's own refused match and of the elopements are gathered into the same night's confusion, and the discovery of the mistake at the end restores order, consent and the couple.
works.significance: It is the most durable English comedy between Congreve and Sheridan, and the practical vindication of Goldsmith's theory that comedy should correct by laughter rather than by distress. Its Tony Lumpkin and its Kate Hardcastle became standards of the repertory, and its plot of the assumed condition remains the best-known illustration of the eighteenth-century effort to reconcile sentiment with mirth.
works.context: It was produced in the season in which the managers were rebuilding the comedy of the London stage and in which Goldsmith's quarrel with the theatre of sentimental distress had been running for years; its success is part of the theatrical regeneration associated with the great players and managers of the 1770s. Its satire upon provincial idleness and upon the fashionable manners of London belongs to the same decade's comedy of national character.
works.characters: Young Marlow; Kate Hardcastle; Mr Hardcastle; Mrs Hardcastle; Tony Lumpkin; Mr Hastings; Constance Neville
works.structure: A five-act comedy of errors and disguised identities with a single night's duration, driven by one sustained mistake and by characters' knowledge of it, and resolved by the discovery scene; the amatory main plot is supported by the comic country plot of the idler and his intended.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the play is Goldsmith's, its production history is documented, and the printed edition carries his name and his dedication. Its relation to the earlier project of 'The Mistakes of a Night' is a matter of editorial chronology rather than of authorship.

works.title: She Would if She Could
works.description: Etherege's second comedy, a brilliant but famously unsuccessful intrigue play in which two rakes, Courtall and Sir Joslin Jolly, pursue two masked beauties through a series of crossed appointments.
works.plot: Courtall and Sir Joslin arrange assignations with Ariana and Gatty; the women appear in disguise, the men are deceived, and a series of farcical failures leads to the marriages the title promises.
works.significance: Now recognised as one of the finest and most formally daring Restoration comedies, its plotless brilliance anticipating Congreve.
works.meter: Sparkling prose throughout.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields on 6 February 1668 and failed with the audience, though Pepys admired it; it was long undervalued before the twentieth-century revival.
works.characters: Courtall; Sir Joslin Jolly; Ariana; Gatty; Lady Cockwood; Rakehell; Mr Trim; Betty
works.structure: Five acts of almost pure intrigue with a single day's action and minimal plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Etherege; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Silex Scintillans
altTitles: Silex Scintillans; or, Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations
works.description: Henry Vaughan's great collection of mystical religious verse (1650, expanded 1655), whose poems seek God through nature, childhood memory, and visionary longing — 'The Retreat', 'The World', 'Peace', and the 'Rules and Lessons' — earning him the title 'the Silurist' and a place among the metaphysical poets.
works.plot: The poems move between longing for a lost innocence and eternity glimpsed behind the world ('Eternity' in 'The World'), meditations on scripture and the sacraments, elegies, and practical rules for holy living.
works.significance: Once obscure, Silex Scintillans was recovered by the Romantics and Coleridge (whose 'intimation of immortality' echoes 'The Retreat') and is now recognised as major mystical poetry of the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Luminous, musical verse with emblematic structure and a visionary intensity drawn from Herbert but wilder and more personal.
works.context: Written in the aftermath of the Civil Wars and Vaughan's royalist seclusion in Breconshire, and deeply influenced by Herbert's Temple; the 1655 edition added secular and satirical pieces.
works.characters: the poet; God; the soul; natural and biblical figures
works.structure: A two-part collection (1650, then 1655 with 'Flamma sine Fumo') of devotional lyrics, translations, and epigrams loosely ordered around themes of nature, eternity, and faith.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under the initials 'H.V.' and the title 'the Silurist'.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sir Degaré
works.description: A Breton lay of the foundling knight: Degaré, son of a fairy knight who ravished his mother, is exposed at birth, raised by a hermit, and wins his spurs through combat with a dragon; his search for his father ends in recognition, reunion, and the marriage of his widowed mother to her long-lost lover. Preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
works.plot: Degaré, given his father's broken sword at birth, defeats the dragon, unhorses the knights of Arthur's court, and proves himself; seeking his father, he jousts with the fairy knight himself, and the two recognize each other; the poem ends with the father's return and the family's reunion.
works.significance: A representative minor lai valuable for the incest-anxieties and recognition patterns of the genre, and a staple of romance anthologies.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, plain and rapid.
works.context: Composed c. 1325, probably in the south-east; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and later copies including the Percy Folio.
works.characters: Degaré; the fairy knight (his father); his mother; the hermit
works.structure: A foundling-quest in the lai manner, with the father-son combat as its climactic recognition scene.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.

works.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
works.description: The supreme masterpiece of the Alliterative Revival and one of the greatest poems of the English Middle Ages: 2,530 lines in alliterative stanzas with the 'bob and wheel' close, recounting Gawain's beheading-game with the Green Knight and his testing in the castle of Sir Bertilak. A romance of courtesy, chastity, and shame, in which the pentangle and the green girdle measure the hero against an ideal he cannot perfectly keep.
works.plot: At Arthur's Christmas court, the Green Knight offers his axe-blow for a return stroke a year hence; Gawain beheads him, and the knight rides off alive. The following winter Gawain journeys to the Green Chapel, is entertained for three days at Hautdesert — where his host's wife tests his chastity with escalating temptations while the host hunts deer, boar, and fox in parallel scenes — and, having accepted the protective green girdle and concealed it, receives at the Chapel a nick on the neck: the girdle's shame is revealed as the whole adventure was Bertilak's design, set on him by Morgan le Fay.
works.significance: The most admired English romance ever written: its fusion of alliterative craft, courtly ideals, and moral seriousness — and its unmatched winter landscapes and temptation scenes — have made it a touchstone of English literature (translated by Tolkien, Armitage, and many others).
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line in stanzas of varying length, each closed by the five-line rhymed 'bob and wheel'.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by an unknown north-west Midlands poet (the 'Gawain-poet'), probably in the household circle of the Cheshire/Staffordshire gentry; preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Nero A.x, with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness.
works.characters: Gawain; the Green Knight (Sir Bertilak); Lady Bertilak; Arthur; Guinevere; Morgan le Fay; the guide
works.structure: A two-part structure (the beheading game at Camelot; the journey, temptations, and exchange of winnings at Hautdesert), interlaced by the three parallel hunts and the three bedroom temptations, and closed by Gawain's return and Arthur's court's adoption of the girdle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributed with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness to the single 'Gawain-poet' on grounds of style, dialect, and shared manuscript.

works.title: Sir Launfal
works.description: Thomas Chestre's late fourteenth-century Breton lay of the fairy mistress: the knight Launfal, impoverished and slighted at Arthur's court, receives boundless wealth and the love of the fairy lady Tryamour on condition of secrecy, and is saved from death by her at his trial. The most accomplished English version of Marie de France's Lanval.
works.plot: Launfal, neglected by Arthur, rides out in despair and meets Tryamour, whose gifts restore his magnificence; his boast of her beauty at court — provoked by the queen's advances — brings trial for treason, but Tryamour appears at the judgement, vindicates him, and carries him to the fairy isle of Olyroun.
works.significance: The finest English fairy-mistress lay and the standard version of the Lanval story in English; a key text for the romance's treatment of women and power.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas of the popular romance kind.
works.context: Composed c. 1390 by Thomas Chestre (who names himself in the poem), reworking the earlier Sir Landevale and Marie de France; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
works.characters: Launfal; Tryamour; Arthur; Guinevere (unnamed queen); the mayor of Caerleon
works.structure: The classic lai structure: courtly exclusion, otherworld encounter, transgression, trial, and translation to the otherworld.
works.attributionNotes: The author names himself 'Thomas Chestre' in the poem's opening lines.

editions.title: The Middle English Breton Lays

works.title: Sir Orfeo
works.description: The masterpiece of the English Breton lay: the classical myth of Orpheus and Eurydice retold as a Celtic fairy romance, in which King Orfeo, harper of Winchester, loses his queen Heurodis to the fairy king and wins her back through the power of his music. Some 600 lines of haunting narrative, preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
works.plot: Heurodis is taken by the fairy king from under the ympe-tree; Orfeo abandons his throne to live as a harper in the wilderness, sees his queen among the fairy riders, follows them into their castle, and recovers her by his harping; the poem ends with the steward's loyalty tested and the kingdom restored.
works.significance: Universally regarded as the finest of the Middle English Breton lays and one of the great short narratives of the period; the classical myth's medieval transformation is a touchstone of romance criticism.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with lyrical set-pieces; economical and evocative.
works.context: Composed c. 1300, perhaps in the London area, reworking the Orpheus myth through Celtic fairy-lore and the Breton lai tradition; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and two fifteenth-century copies.
works.characters: Orfeo; Heurodis; the fairy king; the steward
works.structure: A lai of loss, wilderness exile, and recovery, framed by the steward episode; the Otherworld journey is its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: William Cobbett: The Politics of Style (Cambridge Studies in Romanticism)

works.title: Sir Thomas More; or, Colloquies on the Progress and Prospects of Society
works.form: Humanist dialogue and moral-philosophical prose, a Christian-humanist colloquy of the kind written by More himself, turned to the question of social progress.
works.description: The author's late prose colloquy, long gestating and issued in two volumes, in which the writer converses with the ghost or the spirit of Sir Thomas More about the condition and the future of society. It is the most systematic of his prose works, ranging over education, the press, the working classes, pauperism, Rome, and the colonies in a humanist dialogue form. The book is a storehouse of the period's anxieties about progress, and was later quarried by Marx for its evidence on the manufacturing system.
works.plot: More, learned and sceptical, is made to survey the modern world from the vantage of a man who knew another civilisation before the Reformation and the age of commerce. He questions the writer about the diffusion of knowledge through cheap print, about the education of the poorer classes, and about whether the increase of reading has improved the readers. Other colloquies treat the condition of labour, the growth of the towns, the state of Ireland, Roman Catholic claims, the colonies and slavery, and the prospects of Christianity in an age of machinery and of political change. The argument throughout is conservative in method but genuinely alarmed: material progress is admitted, and then weighed against the moral and religious cost, with More pressing toward a defence of counsel, conscience, and settled order.
works.significance: The most complete statement of its author's social thought and one of the most quoted conservative analyses of the manufacturing age, important both as a document of romantic-era Toryism and as a source of evidence on early industrial conditions later used by writers of the opposite opinion.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Published in the years of post-war depression, of the quarrel over Catholic emancipation, and of the first factory and education legislation; the first volume appeared in 1829, on the eve of the Reform crisis, and the second followed soon after, when the debate about the 'condition of England' was opening.
works.characters: Sir Thomas More; the enquiring writer
works.structure: Series of colloquies in dialogue form between the author and the shade of More, without dramatic setting or plot; each colloquy takes up one subject and is free to digress into report, history, and prophecy.

works.title: Siris
altTitles: Siris: A Chain of Philosophical Inquiries and Speculations concerning the Virtue of Tar-water
Siris: or, the Chain of Philosophy
works.description: Berkeley's strange and late 'chain of philosophical inquiry', occasioned by the vogue of tar-water as a medicine, which rises from remedies and agriculture through electricity, the animal fibre, and the Platonic one to a hymn to light and the divine mind. It is his most explicitly Platonizing and most idiosyncratic published work.
works.plot: Berkeley praises tar-water as a specific for many distempers and derives from its humble origin a chain of enquiry into virtue in physical things, fire, air, and electricity as the universal active medium. He speculates that a far subtler electric or aetherial spirit pervades and quickens nature, the seat of vital motion and of the animal spirits, and that light is the most universal being whose finite emanation binds the world. From physics the chain ascends to Platonic ontology: the one, the good, and intellectual light, closing with an apostrophe to the source of light and truth. The book thus makes medicine the stairway to natural theology.
works.significance: It stands as the century's most curious fusion of empiricist science and Platonist mysticism, and it renewed the ancient doctrine of the one and of vital spirit in a modern scientific vocabulary.
works.meter: A rising, sometimes rapturous prose of questions and responsive speculations, with a long hymnic peroration in rhythmic periods.
works.context: Published in 1744 after Berkeley's return from America and the failure of his Bermuda college scheme, in the season of electrical excitement following Franklin and of popular medical specifics; it was reviewed, mocked, and translated on the continent.
works.structure: A serial chain of short linked enquiries, each section drawing the previous upward, in the manner of a Platonizing rhapsody.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Sketches of the History of Mankind
altTitles: Sketches of the History of Man
works.description: Kames's anthropological history of the human species, the richest single compilation of the Scottish Enlightenment's conjectural and ethnographic history. It sketches the progress of mind, language, memory, perception, and the social and moral faculties from savagery to polish, drawing on travellers, antiquaries, and the philosophy of the stages.
works.plot: The Sketches open on the origin and progress of the mental faculties, tracing perception, remembrance, and the growth of general language from the signs of savage passion. They then follow the successive social stages from hunter and shepherd to tiller and citizen, the history of the sexes in marriage and domestic authority across nations, the progress of religion from superstition and idolatry to Christianity, and the development of the moral sense through custom, law, and the arts. Kames weaves ethnography, ancient history, and philosophical conjecture into a single narrative of the species' slow perfection, treating the savage as the living evidence of the primitive mind. The last sketches examine the influence of civil society on the faculties and close on the perfectibility of mankind.
works.significance: It is the sum of eighteenth-century Scottish conjectural history in a single work, a storehouse of Enlightenment anthropology whose method and materials shaped the later human sciences and the century's idea of progress.
works.meter: A brisk, anecdotal, aphoristic prose, travellers' facts and philosophical inference stitched in quick paragraphs.
works.context: Published in 1774 at the high tide of the conjectural history of mankind, when the circumnavigation reports and the ethnography of the north were transforming the subject, and within the circle of Millar, Adam Smith, and Robertson; it was read and translated across Europe.
works.structure: A series of sketches grouped by theme, each a short essay of conjectural history and ethnography, cross-referenced into one history of the species across the four volumes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Solomon and Saturn I and II
altTitles: The Dialogue of Solomon and Saturn
works.description: Two wisdom dialogues in which Solomon, the biblical master of wisdom, contends with Saturn, the legendary Chaldean sage, over questions of fate, prayer, and the powers of the Pater Noster — its letters imagined as armed warriors assailing the devil. The poems are the most extravagant of the Old English wisdom tradition.
works.plot: In Solomon and Saturn II, the sages debate the powers of the Pater Noster: each letter becomes a warrior with a specific weapon against the fiend ('P has a golden rod and fights the devil...'); the poem surveys the poem's battles against evil in a fantasia of personified letters. Solomon and Saturn I concerns the praise of the Pater Noster and the books it governs, with a runic passage on the letter R.
works.significance: The wildest flights of the Old English wisdom tradition; central to the study of Anglo-Saxon learned imagination.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; dense, sometimes eccentric diction.
works.context: Preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MSS 41 and 422; the dialogues draw on apocryphal Solomonic and computistical lore.
works.characters: Solomon; Saturn; the personified letters of the Pater Noster
works.structure: Question-and-answer dialogue in the wisdom-contest tradition, elaborated with the allegorical letter-warfare of the Pater Noster passages.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Prelude: 1799, 1805, 1850 (Norton Critical Edition)

works.title: Solomon on the Vanity of the World
works.description: A reflective poem on the Preacher's theme, in which the riches, pleasures and honours of the world are weighed against the wisdom that knows their end. It is the most ambitious of its author's serious pieces and the one by which his contemporaries judged him a philosopher as well as a wit.
works.plot: The poet follows the Solomon of Ecclesiastes through the trial of magnificence, building, planting and possessing, and finds the account of all his labour to be vanity. The poem passes over the conditions of the wise man and the fool, the fortune of the wicked and the rewards of the just, and resolves the enquiry into the fear of God and the government of the present heart. The close turns from the world measured to the world renounced.
works.significance: It shows the other face of the most popular light poet between the two greatest of the age, and its manner of argumentative couplet meditation was a school for the younger writers who at once imitated and dismissed him.
works.meter: Stanzaic meditative verse of the ode manner, with a regular rhyme scheme and balanced antithetical lines carrying the moral argument in the Dryden school.
works.context: Written in the later years of a career divided between diplomacy and poetry, when the poet had been disappointed of employment and had turned to the serious essay in verse; it belongs to the company of the century's vanity-of-the-world poems.
works.structure: A sustained meditative poem in the manner of the ode and the essay in verse, the argument advancing by the review of the several species of worldly good and their judgment.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem exists in more than one state and length, and the several issues are dated variously in the catalogues of the trade, so the year given is that of the earliest collected printing and no year of composition is asserted.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Some Reflections upon Marriage, Occasion'd by the Duke and Duchess of Mazarine's Case
works.description: Astell's second major feminist work, written in response to the scandalous separation of the Duke and Duchess of Mazarin, arguing that the legal subjection of wives is a form of arbitrary power inconsistent with the principles of the Glorious Revolution.
works.plot: Astell asks how it can be that all men are born free, yet every woman is born a slave; she argues that marriage as constituted gives husbands arbitrary power over wives, that women must cultivate their reason, and that a rational education would make better wives and mothers.
works.significance: One of the most powerful early feminist critiques of marriage and of the sexual double standard; its argument that arbitrary power over women is inconsistent with the principles of 1688 has made it a canonical text of political theory.
works.meter: Ironical, pointed prose with a sustained rhetorical question.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1700, with second and third editions in 1703 and 1706; the Mazarin case was a cause célèbre in Restoration and post-Revolution London.
works.characters: the Duchess of Mazarin; Hortense Mancini (alluded to)
works.structure: A continuous argument in three parts with a preface to the third edition of 1706.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; attribution to Astell is established.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Some Thoughts Concerning Education
works.description: Locke's influential treatise on the education of a young gentleman, which grew out of letters to his friend Edward Clarke and argued for physical hardiness, moral habituation, and a practical curriculum over rote learning.
works.plot: Locke advises on the health of the body, the formation of the mind through habit and example, the teaching of reading, writing, languages, history, geography, arithmetic, and a trade, and the importance of curiosity over coercion.
works.significance: The most influential English work on education of the eighteenth century; it shaped Rousseau's Emile, and its emphasis on habit and on the child's own interest transformed educational theory.
works.meter: Practical, conversational prose.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1693, expanded in the 1695 and 1705 editions; it derived from Locke's letters to Edward Clarke of Chipley concerning Clarke's son.
works.structure: A series of numbered sections following the natural order of education.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; authorship was publicly acknowledged only in the 1705 edition.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Song to David
works.form: Sacred ode or hymn of praise in the English Pindaric tradition as revised in the eighteenth century, with stanzaic response to the order of the subject and with a strongly Hebraic rhetoric of accumulation and parallelism.
works.description: Christopher Smart's great ode, a poem of praise addressed to the psalmist-king and through him to God, and the most extraordinary achievement of English Augustan verse between the odes of Dryden and those of the Romantic period. It passes from the invitation to sing to the works and the names of David, to music, to the beasts and elements attending him, and finally to the typological and prophetic range of the Israelite kingdom. Its stanzas are irregular by design, each shaped to its subject, and its diction, rhyme and vowel-pattern are among the most carefully experimental of the century.
works.plot: The poem is an invitation, a catalogue and a praise. It begins by calling the muse of Israel to her task and then proceeds through the parts of David's story and his attributes, treating the psalmist as the inventor and patron of sacred music and as the type of Christ. The middle movements are a natural history and a physics of praise: harp and organ, the vocal powers of beasts, birds and the elements, and the famous enquiry into the properties of vowels and consonants, in which Smart's theory of the inherent music of language is made the ground of the poem's own practice. The conclusion gathers the typology together, making David's kingdom and the builder of the temple figures of a spiritual and prophetic order. Praise, not narrative, is the argument, and the poem's form is an argument that variety of measure is itself a mode of devotion.
works.significance: It is the supreme religious ode of the mid-eighteenth century and the strongest claim made in the period for poetry as an act of praise rather than of instruction or of taste; its recovery in the twentieth century altered the estimation of Smart and of Augustan verse generally. Samuel Johnson's recorded admiration of parts of it is the beginning of its reputation among the poets of the club.
works.meter: A planned variety of measures: long and short lines, recurring burden-like refrains, dense internal and vowel rhyme, and experiments in the sound of the alphabet itself; the poem is the age's most self-conscious treatment of the relation of phonetic material to devotion.
works.context: It was published in the year of Smart's release from the retirement in which he had been confined, and stands with 'Jubilate Agno' and the other poems of the confinement years at the centre of his work. Its Hebraism belongs to an age of psalm translation, of the debate about 'enthusiasm' and true religious poetry, and of the High-Church and Jacobite sympathies of its author.
works.characters: David, the psalmist and king, addressed and celebrated; the personified muse and music; the created things, animal, vegetable and elemental, that attend the praise
works.structure: A continuous ode in unequal stanzas, moving by association and amplification from invocation through the subjects of David's praise to typological and prophetic conclusion; the stanzaic irregularity is planned, not accidental.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is Smart's and its authorship was never disputed. The year of first printing is recorded, but the venue of the first impression and the stages of composition within the confinement years are matters of editorial detail which are not asserted here.

works.title: Songs and Poems of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
altTitles: The Works of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
works.description: The small but influential body of verse by the Earl of Dorset — courtier, wit, and patron — including the famous sea-song 'To all you ladies now at land', written, according to tradition, the night before the battle of Solebay.
works.plot: The poems are light, graceful lyrics of love and parting, several written on public occasions and to particular women of the court; the sea-song consoles the ladies ashore while the men fight at sea.
works.significance: 'To all you ladies now at land' became one of the best-known songs of the period; Dorset's work is a touchstone for the ideal of effortless courtly wit.
works.meter: Short song stanzas in an easy, colloquial register.
works.context: Dorset's verse circulated in manuscript at the court of Charles II; he was a leading patron of Dryden and Prior and a central figure in Restoration literary society.
works.structure: A short miscellany of songs and occasional verse.
works.attributionNotes: The canon is small and some attributions are uncertain; the sea-song is traditionally ascribed to Dorset.

works.title: Songs and Sonnets
works.description: The collective title given in the 1633 posthumous Poems to Donne's lyrics of love — 'The Good-Morrow', 'The Sun Rising', 'The Canonization', 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning', 'The Ecstasy', 'The Flea', and some fifty more — in which the conventions of Petrarchan love are re-forged by argument, paradox, and the new 'metaphysical' wit.
works.plot: No single plot: the poems dramatize the phases of love — waking, parting, quarrelling, dying, transcending — each lyric a miniature drama of persuasion in which a lover argues a mistress, a rival, the sun, or himself into a truth about love.
works.significance: The founding book of metaphysical poetry — the lyric revolution that Jonson's classicism answered and that the twentieth century would re-canonize.
works.meter: Dramatic, speech-like rhythms within stanza forms of Donne's own devising — the 'strong lines' of the metaphysical manner, with conceits drawn from astronomy, alchemy, law, and cartography.
works.context: Written from the 1590s (the 'Jack Donne' of Lincoln's Inn and the Essex and Ralegh voyages) into his middle years, circulating in manuscript among the wits and Inns of Court; printed only after his death in the 1633 Poems.
works.characters: the poet-lover; the beloved (unnamed); the Sun; Death; God (in the religious lyrics)
works.structure: A group of some fifty-five lyrics gathered posthumously under a title Donne never gave them, arranged in the 1633 edition as a loose anthology of the love poems.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the group's composition dates span at least two decades, and individual datings are widely disputed.

works.title: Songs of Experience
works.form: Illuminated lyric collection and songs of the experienced state, in the line of the song and the emblem, designed as a direct reply to the earlier collection and printed with its plates as one book.
works.description: The second and darker of the two illuminated collections, etched and printed by the author in 1794 and issued with the earlier songs under a single title announcing the two contrary states of the human soul. Its lyrics answer, correct and destroy the trust of the first collection: the maker of the lamb is now questioned as the maker also of the tiger, the garden of innocence is planted with a chapel, and the poems of the city expose the institutions, the priests and the kings that keep the soul in bondage.
works.plot: The collection opens with an earth answerable to the eternal, and with the tiger, whose frightful symmetry forces the question of what hand or eye could frame such dread and what exchange of fear was made when it was given life, an answer that reverses the child's trust in the lamb. Songs of the lost childhood follow: the sick rose destroyed by the invisible worm, the sunflower pined out in the marsh, the grey-bearded physician who knows the tree by its leaf and nothing else, and the youth who is told that the garden of love, where his infant joys were planted, is now a chapel, its gates shut against the child and its altar dressed with the thorns and briars of the priest's curse. The later plates turn on London and on the moral state of the kingdom, in which every black'ning church, the palace rebuilt from the blood of the soldier, the marriage hearse and the cries of the chimney-boy are read as a state of bondage, and the poems of the harlot, of the flies of summer and of the little lost one close upon pity for the sinner and the child, so that the contrary state is presented at once as knowledge and as the loss of the power to feel. The last poem figures the bard of a new age who shall restore the departed powers.
works.significance: One of the two collections that define the Romantic reading of innocence and experience as contrary and answering states of the soul, and the source of the most discussed single lyric in English on the problem of the maker of evil. Its plates are the standard evidence of the poet's illuminated method, and its London poems are a permanent part of the literature of the city and of the critique of institutional religion.
works.meter: Song stanzas of two- and three-beat lines with a tightened and more reiterated pattern, the tiger's trochaic four-beat lines and its insistent questions being the most quoted example; the rhythm is deliberately hammer-like where the argument demands it, and the later plates allow longer and more prophetic periods.
works.context: Etched and printed in London in 1794, in the years of the author's most active experiment with illuminated relief-printing and in the decade of the repression of English radical opinion, the wars with France and the trade in wealth of the metropolis, all of which give the city poems their targets; the combined issue of the two collections under one title states the theory of contrary states from which the poems proceed.
works.characters: The tiger and the questioning singer; the rose and the invisible worm; the sun-flower and the lily of the valley; the grey-bearded sage; the child who sees the chapel in the garden of love; the harlot of the city of London; the soldier, the chimney-sweeper and the labouring poor of the London plates; the little lost one; the bard of the new age
works.structure: A plate-for-plate collection answering the earlier songs poem by poem, with a progression from the tiger and the lost garden through the city poems to the harlot and the closing promise of the bard; several pieces exist in two versions in the earlier copy, and the design of the sequence is the collection's argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the existence of earlier drafts of several poems, and the differences between the copies in the order of the plates, are matters of bibliography and of the text's several states.

works.title: Songs of Innocence
altTitles: Songs of Innocence. Written for the Children of the Age to Come
works.form: Illuminated lyric collection and songs of the innocent state, in the line of the nursery song and the devotional hymn, engraved and designed by the poet as a single art object.
works.description: A short collection of lyrics etched, printed and hand-coloured by the author himself in 1789, and issued as plates with the poems and the designs engraved on the same copper, so that text and image were made as one object. Its voices are those of children, of the piper who is taught by them, of the lamb, the nurse, the chimney-sweeper and the schoolboy, and its subject is a state of the human soul in which protection, joy and trust are still unbroken. It was later combined with a second collection to show the two contrary states of the human soul.
works.plot: The poems present a world of open country and of the city's poor in which innocence is both a fact and a condition exposed to danger. A piper hears a child asking for a song about a lamb, writes it, and rejoices; another song answers the child's question about who made the lamb by tracing the maker's meek and gentle likeness in himself. The lamb, the little black boy, the chimney-sweepers of London, the nurse whose play is over, the schoolboy who watches the winter morning and the evening's returning flock, and the shepherd and the boy who has lost his ball, give a sequence of small states of the soul; two of the poems name the cruelty of the institutions that employ children and one of them sets the child's complaint against the prayer and the doctrine taught him, so that the collection's innocence is figured as a trust that others are ready to betray. The closing poems turn to the grown-ups who have lost that trust, and the little bird, the clod and the pebble give the short lyric argument about the answerable heart.
works.significance: The founding work of the illuminated books and one of the two collections that make up the standard Romantic statement of innocence and experience as contrary states; its songs entered the anthologies of children's verse and its plates are the central example of the poet's method of making text and design one. Its account of protected and betrayed childhood remains a starting point of modern criticism of the lyric of innocence.
works.meter: Short song stanzas of two- and three-beat lines with simple recurring rhyme, many of them written as airs to be sung, with repetitions and question-and-answer patterns proper to children's verse; the irregularities are part of the song manner rather than errors of the ear.
works.context: Etched and printed in London in 1789, when the author had developed his method of illuminated relief-printing and was working as an engraver and designer of plates in the City; its concern with children, with the sweeper chimneys of the metropolis and with the teachings of the church belongs to the philanthropic and dissenting writing of that decade.
works.characters: The child who asks the piper to write a song; the lamb and its questioning child; the little black boy; the chimney-sweepers Tom Dacre and his fellow workers; the nurse and the schoolboy; the shepherd, the blossoms and the lost boy; the piper who becomes the writer of the songs
works.structure: A plate-for-plate collection of short lyrics, without a continuous story but designed as a sequence, the order of the illuminated copies varying slightly and the images supplying a running commentary on the texts; the poems answer one another by their repeated figures of the child, the maker and the guardian.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the several hand-coloured copies differ in the order of the plates and in the colouring, and the number of copies printed from the copper plates is a matter of bibliography rather than of disputed authorship.

works.title: Songs of the Affections, with Other Poems
works.form: Collected volume of short lyrics and elegies; the governing genre is the affectionate meditative lyric, with the hymn-like stanza and the topical elegy beside it.
works.description: A late collection in which its author's shorter lyric manner is gathered under a title that names its whole repertoire: affection tried by separation, loss and time. It shows the mourning and devotional lyric of her final decade.
works.plot: The poems move through states of attachment - friendship recalled, love unanswered, the dead imagined still present - without forming a sequence with a plot. Several pieces build upon a single emblem, a farewell, a lake image or a link, and develop it as a meditation. A group addresses the consolations of faith, asking whether affection dissolved by death is restored. The remaining poems are descriptive or occasional, on places, on the dead, and on the lot of the poet. The volume's argument is cumulative rather than progressive: feeling is proved durable by the repetition of cases.
works.significance: These songs supplied the idiom that middle-class Victorian mourning and devotional culture later took for granted, and their lines were set to music and reprinted without attribution for decades. The volume is the clearest evidence that the most widely circulated verse of the later Romantic period was affective, occasional and domestic rather than prophetic or rebellious. Its very popularity made it the target of later dismissal.
works.meter: Regular iambic stanzas, largely common and short measure with refrains, built for vocal repetition; occasional anapaestic and mixed measures mark the pieces written to be recited or sung.
works.context: It followed the volume of records and confirmed its author's position as the century's most borrowed poet of affection, at the moment when the literary annual was becoming the chief market for such verse. Her income and fame in these years depended on the annuals and on transatlantic reprints, and the collection gathers what those markets demanded. Its publication year falls between the Catholic Emancipation Act and the Reform crisis, a period of turbulent public verse from which the volume is entirely absent.
works.structure: An unordered company of short lyrics grouped under the affectionate design of the title; the arrangement is by tone and length, and the reading experience is one of recurring situations rather than of sequence.

works.title: Sophonisba
works.description: Thomson's regular tragedy of the Carthaginian princess who chooses death rather than the Roman triumph, written deliberately in the observance of the unities and in the manner of the antique and French classical drama.
works.plot: Sophonisba, taken between the rival African princes and the advancing Rome, is given by the conqueror to the suitor she must not love; she disappoints both by choosing the poison, and the play closes on the spectacle of her constant death.
works.significance: It is the century's most complete English attempt at the classical regular tragedy, and its death scene became a byword for the calculated pathos of the closet and the stage.
works.meter: Blank verse of studied smoothness, with the formal expiring dialogue of the last scene.
works.context: Acted at Drury Lane in the season of Thomson's struggle with the theatres and of the debate over classical regularity, when the Racine model and the unities were being reasserted against the opera and the burletta.
works.characters: Sophonisba; Syphax; Masinissa; Scipio; the attendants of the captive princess
works.structure: Five acts of strict regularity, with the set dying scene as the prepared catastrophe and the political argument of the rival parties supplying the tension.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Sophonisba; or, Hannibal's Overthrow
works.description: Lee's early heroic tragedy on the Carthaginian princess Sophonisba, who drinks poison rather than fall into Roman hands, and whose lines 'O happiness! O pleasure!' became proverbial for heroic bombast.
works.plot: Sophonisba, betrothed to Massinissa, is captured by the Romans; to save her from their triumph she takes poison given by Massinissa, and Hannibal's cause collapses.
works.significance: An important early heroic tragedy and the source of some of the most frequently quoted lines of Restoration bombast; it establishes Lee's reputation before The Rival Queens.
works.meter: Blank verse of high rhetorical strain.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1675 and published in 1676; it was one of the earliest plays in which the young actor Thomas Betterton shone in a heroic role.
works.characters: Sophonisba; Massinissa; Hannibal; Syphax; Scipio; Melbo; Narbal
works.structure: Five acts in the heroic manner with a single tragic action.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lee; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Soul and Body I and II
altTitles: The Soul's Address to the Body
works.form: religious debate poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A pair of related poems (Vercelli Book I, 166 lines; Exeter Book II, 121 lines) in which the soul, revisiting its decaying body once a week, reproaches it for the sins of the flesh and foretells the torments of judgment. The earliest English body-and-soul debate, ancestor of a long medieval tradition.
works.plot: The damned soul, forced to revisit its corpse, addresses the silent body: 'Where are the riches you gathered? The hall you feasted in?' — enumerating the body's pleasures and their price in hell, the worms and the fire; the Exeter version closes with a brief address to the blessed soul by contrast. The debate's later fortunes run through the Middle English 'Desputisoun bitwen the Bodi and the Soule' to the danse macabre.
works.significance: Inaugurates the body-and-soul debate tradition that runs through Middle English literature.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 101v-103v) and the Exeter Book (fols. 98a-100a); the genre derives from Latin and homiletic sources.
works.characters: the Soul; the Body; (in II) the blessed soul
works.structure: A monologue of reproach and warning, spoken by the soul to the body at the grave; the two versions differ in length and ending.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, 7 volumes (Bury edition)

works.title: Specimens of the British Poets
altTitles: Specimens of the British Poets, with Biographical and Critical Notices, and an Essay on English Poetry
works.form: Anthology and editorial collection with literary biography and prefatory commentary; a work of Romantic-period literary history in the handbook manner.
works.description: A seven-volume anthology of British verse with prefatory biographical and critical notices and a general essay on English poetry, assembled by a living poet rather than by a scholar. It arranges its selections chronologically from the early Tudor and Scottish writers to the poet's own contemporaries, and its notices became a standard source of information and judgement. The series of lives later circulated separately and shaped the nineteenth century's sense of a native poetic tradition.
works.plot: The work's argument is that English poetry can be understood as a continuous national tradition, recoverable through carefully selected passages and through short critical lives attached to each poet. It gives precedence to moral and imaginative seriousness, defends the older writers against neoclassical disparagement, and reserves some of its most discriminating comment for the living Romantic generation. Its selections act as a canon: what is quoted defines what a nineteenth-century reader was likely to know. The prefatory essay generalises this practice into an account of the phases of English poetry and of the conditions of patronage, print and national taste that produced them.
works.significance: For two generations its notices and selections were the ordinary medium through which readers met the earlier English poets, and its judgements on the Romantics entered the standard accounts of the period. It shows how a practising poet's editorial authority could be used to construct a national canon, and it preserves much early scholarship on forgotten writers. Later histories of canon formation cite it as a decisive instance of Romantic anthologising practice.
works.meter: Prose notices and essay framing verse extracts of every prevailing metre from the old ballad stanza to the blank verse and couplets of the eighteenth century.
works.context: It belongs to the post-war boom in national literary history and in the collected-standard-poets trade, when publishers turned poetry into a respectable branch of national education. Its compiler was by then a successful narrative poet and a London literary manager, and his judgements were conditioned by the review culture and by friendships and quarrels within the Romantic generation. The essay on English poetry addresses directly the question, urgent in the 1810s, whether a modern British school existed worthy of the name.
works.structure: A chronological anthology with prefatorial lives and critical notes, opened by a general essay on English poetry; not a narrative but an argument about literary history conducted through selection.
