works.title: The Emigrants, A Poem, in Two Books
works.form: Nature Lyric and Meditation; Meditative Blank Verse; Topographical and Descriptive Poetry
works.description: Charlotte Smith's most ambitious poem and the first long blank-verse meditation by a woman poet on the French Revolution as an English coastal spectacle: French refugees, driven out by war and proscription, are watched on the Sussex cliffs and the Downs, and their dispossession becomes the occasion for a national poem about exile, charity, and the failure of revolutionary hope. Written in two books dated November 1792 and April 1793 and offered in the lineage of Cowper's The Task, it converts topographical description into political and moral argument.
works.plot: Book I, set on the Sussex cliffs in November 1792, follows the coming of the émigrés, the suffering of the dispossessed French families, and the poet's own recollection of exile, and turns the landscape of the beach and the channel into a commentary on the Revolution and on the war now beginning between Britain and France. Book II, dated April 1793 and set on the Downs, widens the meditation to the causes and consequences of war, to the fate of the poor at home as well as of the refugees abroad, and to the disappointed expectation of liberty, closing in a mood of resigned charity rather than of prophecy.
works.significance: The Emigrants is a central work of women's political poetry in the 1790s and an important early instance of Romantic coastal topography used to think about revolution, refugee hospitality, and war; it shows the conversation-poem and blank-verse meditation traditions being reshaped by a female professional writer, and it is now read as a necessary precedent for the Lyrical Ballads politics of poverty and landscape.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of self-contained lines and passages, with the suspended syntax, apostrophe, and descriptive enumeration characteristic of blank verse after Cowper and Thomson; the poem's rhetorical cadences carry its political argument.
works.context: Published in the spring of 1793, the month Britain declared war on revolutionary France, when the arrival of émigrés made the Revolution a visible social problem on the south coast, and when Smith, who had spent part of her childhood in France, wrote from her own experience of dispossession and dependence. Its address to Cowper locates it in a tradition of national poetry that was being rapidly politicised by the Revolution controversy.
works.characters: the poet-walker of the Sussex shore; the French émigré families; the labouring and fishing poor of the English coast; the distant actors of the Revolution and of the declared war
works.structure: A poem in two books, each anchored in a dated season and a named stretch of coast and downland; the movement is that of Cowperian conversation poetry, where walking and looking generate reflection, and where the émigrés and the local poor supply the human cases on which the argument turns.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

works.title: The English Garden
works.form: Didactic poem in the Thomson school, in books, with descriptive and reflective passages embedded in the preceptive argument; related separately to his essay on topiary, here treated under the name of 'green sculpture'.
works.description: Mason's didactic poem on the theory and practice of the 'improved' English pleasure ground, and one of the two or three most influential verses ever written on garden design. It defends the modern irregular style against the geometry of the formal garden, and it treats the lay of ground, the concealment of boundaries, the planting of belts and clumps, water, and the disposition of buildings as matters at once of taste and of moral feeling.
works.plot: The poem proceeds by precept and illustration rather than by action. It surveys what the English garden had become since the reaction against the formal line, argues that its improvements should follow the 'genius' of the place rather than an imported pattern, and cautions the possessor against excess: against too much art betraying itself, against costly ornament, and against the petty tyrannies of the landscape contractor. The picturesque vocabulary of the age is translated into practical instruction, with the Chinese garden and the paintings of Claude and Salvator offered as models of composition. Throughout, the retired ground is made a figure of a well-ordered mind, so that the instruction in planting is also an argument about retirement, virtue and national taste.
works.significance: It fixed in verse the vocabulary of the improved garden and handed it on to the debate of the 1790s between the picturesque and the 'beautiful' garden, in which Price and Knight were still answering positions already stated here. As a document of the eighteenth-century marriage of ethics and landscape, it is the most substantial estate poem of the third quarter of the century.
works.meter: Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) of close, weighted and frequently epigrammatic texture, with a strongly marked caesura and a preference for the balanced period; the manner is deliberately that of Thomson's 'The Seasons' adapted to instruction.
works.context: It appears at the moment when the English landscape garden had become a national institution and a subject of open argument, between the practical doctrines of 'Capability' Brown and the more picturesque, varied taste urged by Uvedale Price's generation. Mason wrote as an amateur of gardens with a rector's income, and his poem addresses the country gentleman at a time when estate improvement and the language of taste were becoming a single conversation.
works.structure: A preceptive didactic poem organised into books, each handling its own department of the subject, with descriptive digression and historical survey running inside the framework of instruction.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Mason's name is on the first edition and he later reprinted the poem in his collected works. The years of composition are not precisely determinable and are left null.

works.title: The Eolian Harp
works.form: Conversation poem and lyric meditation in reflective blank verse, drawing on the eighteenth-century meditation upon a natural object and on the contemporary vogue for the Aeolian harp as a figure of the passive mind.
works.description: The first and shortest of the conversation poems, written at Clevedon in the summer of 1795 in the months of the poet's courtship and first marriage, and printed among his earliest collected poems. An Aeolian harp, strung by the wind in a window-frame of the cottage, supplies the occasion: the speaker listens to its random music, lets his thoughts pass into a speculation on the one life and one intelligence that runs through all things, and is then drawn back, in the closing lines, by the voice of the woman beside him to duty and to a sober faith.
works.plot: The poem opens with the description of the harp and of the breeze that plays over its strings, and with the reflection that such an instrument yields infinite variety to the attentive ear and seems to possess a faculty of its own. From this the speaker passes to the central speculation: if all animated nature were but a collection of sensitive instruments played upon by one intellectual and vital being, the whole of created life might be a member of one ever-living mind, and the sense of the beautiful and the sense of the holy would be one and the same feeling. The last part withdraws that fancy as an error of unassisted thought, and turns to the speaker's companion, whose gentle voice and hopes reprove the bewilderment of his soul; she is hailed as the guardian of a wiser and humbler virtue, and the poem ends with the prayer that her heart's affections, and the duties and the faith that belong to a life lived in domestic love, shall be the poet's portion.
works.significance: The founding text of the Romantic conversation poem and one of the earliest English lyrics to make the theory of the associative and passive mind the subject of a meditation. Its speculation and its self-rebuke have made it a standing case in discussions of pantheism, orthodoxy and the development of the poet's early thought.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of continuous and softened movement, with long vowel music and suspended syntax in the speculative passage and shorter, plainer periods in the closing address; the poem is written as a single unbroken paragraph of meditative verse.
works.context: Composed at Clevedon on the eve of the poet's marriage, at a time when associationist psychology and a nature-philosophy deriving from the German schools, with its idea of one life running through all things, were actively read in England; the Aeolian harp had become a fashionable emblem of sensibility and of the mind acted upon.
works.characters: The speaker at his window; his companion and newly married wife, whose voice interrupts the speculation; the Aeolian harp and the evening breeze
works.structure: A single meditative movement in three parts, with the turn marked by an address to the listening woman: the outward scene of the harp and the sea, the speculative flight into the philosophy of one life, and the return to domestic duty and Christian modesty. The form gives the poem its characteristic air of a thought overheard and then corrected.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was revised and its speculative passage abridged under the author's own hand in later collected editions, and the earlier and fuller text is printed in modern editions.

works.title: The Epistle to Curio
works.description: Akenside's political verse epistle, the fiercest party attack of the mid-century, denouncing the statesman who passed from the opposition to the administration and warning the nation against the corruption of its liberty.
works.plot: The poet addresses Curio as the traitor to the public cause, traces his progress from the patriotic platform to the rewards of the court, and sets the example of the true patriot against the train of ministers, place-holders and corrupt senators.
works.significance: It is the ablest of the century's verse political attacks and the work by which Akenside's public career as a moral and political poet began, and the person intended was understood at once by the party readers of the year.
works.meter: Heroic couplet of the Juvenalian and Swiftian hardness, with the long arraigning period and the closing sententia.
works.context: Written in the year of the fall of the long administration and published at the moment when the conversion of the old country leaders into the new ministry seemed to the patriot writers the ruin of the country cause; the pamphlet presented itself as an old manuscript now first printed.
works.characters: Curio the converted minister; the poet as the patriot monitor; the court and the corrupted senate
works.structure: A single long epistle of invective, moving from the character of the minister to the history of his treason and to the general argument about the fate of British liberty.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously and long uncertain in its authorship, with other names proposed by its enemies; Akenside's claim is established by his circle and by the manuscript evidence, though he is said to have wished the piece suppressed in later life.

works.title: The Essays
altTitles: Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
works.description: Francis Bacon's essays, published in three successively enlarged editions (ten essays in 1597, thirty-eight in 1612, fifty-eight in 1625): counsels civil and moral on studies, truth, death, revenge, marriage, gardens, masques, and the conduct of public life, in the aphoristic prose that made the form an English genre.
works.plot: No plot: each essay is a compact meditation on its subject — the 1625 title calls them 'counsels, civil and moral' — moving from observation through maxim to practical advice, with the famous 'Of Studies' ('Reading maketh a full man') and 'Of Truth' as its touchstones.
works.significance: The book that naturalized the essay in English — the prose counterpart of Bacon's philosophical revolution, and a schoolbook of English style for three centuries.
works.meter: Prose of aphoristic compression — antithesis, balance, and the telling image — deliberately plain and packed.
works.context: The 1597 edition was among the first English essay collections, after Florio's Montaigne was still to come; the 1625 edition, published the year before Bacon's death, is the canonical text and the foundation of the English essay tradition.
works.structure: A collection of fifty-eight numbered essays in the final edition, each a self-contained meditation in the Senecan and Montaignian modes.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Essays of Montaigne
works.description: John Florio's translation of Montaigne's Essays (1603), made from the 1595 French edition: the first complete English Montaigne, in which the Frenchman's scepticism, self-portraiture, and humane wisdom enter English prose in Florio's expansive, inventive idiom — the book Shakespeare read and quarried for The Tempest.
works.plot: No plot: the Essays proceed by subject — custom, cannibals, coaches, friendship, experience — Montaigne's 'I' the matter of the book, and Florio's version enlarging the French into the rich Elizabethan English of the translator's own invention.
works.significance: One of the great translations in the language — the book that gave English thought its sceptical conscience and Shakespeare his New World speech.
works.meter: Prose of Florio's characteristic copiousness — Montaigne's sentences doubled and ornamented into the idiom that Shakespeare knew.
works.context: Published 1603, dedicated to the Countess of Bedford and others; Shakespeare's Gonzalo in The Tempest paraphrases 'Of Cannibals' from this translation, the most famous borrowing in English drama.
works.characters: Michel de Montaigne (as speaker); his friend La Boétie (in 'Of Friendship'); the cannibals; the ancients quoted throughout
works.structure: Three books of essays in the 1595 arrangement, with Florio's dedicatory epistles, his preface 'To the Reader', and his appendix of the author's life.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by John Florio from the 1595 French text; uncontested.

works.title: The Eve of St. Agnes
altTitles: The Eve of St. Agnes: A Legendary Poem for the Year 1819
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the legendary and superstition tale of the school of the older romance, with the ritual scene and the gothic household.
works.description: The author's richest legendary poem, a romance of the eve of a virgin saint whose ritual, in the old belief, let a maiden see the shape of the husband she was to marry. It tells how a youth, banned from the house of his lady's hostile kin, is hidden by an old beadswoman in her room, enters the lady's chamber at the hour of the rite, and is persuaded by the superstition's own power to flee with him. The poem's colour, its treatment of the consecrated sleep and its music of the stanza have made it the most quoted of the narratives.
works.plot: On a night of bitter cold, with the owl and the hare abroad, a youthful lover waits at the door of the hall where a baron's company is feasting, and is admitted by an old woman servant to the shelter of her chamber; his lady's family are foes to his. Madeline, who has kept the vigil and believes that she shall see her promised lord at the rite's hour, is left alone in her rose-casemented room, and Porphyro steals in while she sleeps in the middle of the ceremony's dream. He wakes her with the sound of the charmed company, and after the scene of the feast of the senses the two escape into the storm, leaving the old beadswoman dead at the foot of the altar and the house in confusion. The argument is that the consecrated dream becomes the warrant of an outlawed love, and that the ritual's power is realised in the flesh.
works.significance: It is the period's supreme example of colour and sense carried by the Spenserian measure, and its stanzas on the casement, the feast and the storm became a stock of the later poetry of romantic intensity. Its treatment of a ritual dream fulfilled in an elopement also made it the central text of the discussion of the poet's relation to superstition and to the consecrated life.
works.meter: The Spenserian stanza of nine iambic pentameter lines with the closing alexandrine, ababbcbcc, handled with an unprecedented richness of vowel and colour, the rhyme sustained and the last line used for a slow close.
works.context: Begun at the house of a friend's family in the north of London in the winter of 1819, in the season when the poet was writing the odes and the dream-version of the titan poem, and finished at the seaside in the spring of 1820, appearing in the volume of that July. Its subject, a Catholic superstition of maidens treated with complete sympathy, belonged to the same interest in consecuted ritual which the period's romance and its controversial religion shared, and its archaic diction was a deliberate answer to the reviews which had pronounced the earlier romance the work of a school.
works.characters: Porphyro, the lover outlawed by the lady's kin; Madeline of the rose window and the vigil; the old beadswoman Angela; the baron and the riotous company of the hall
works.structure: A continuous legendary romance of forty Spenserian stanzas, the external scene of the hall, the secret chamber, the vigil and ritual in the middle, the escape and the moral close in the last stanzas.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem's early draft survives, and its title and the accompanying legend were explained in a prose note of the poet's own written for the volume.

works.title: The Examinations of Anne Askew
altTitles: The First Examination of Anne Askew
The Latter Examination of Anne Askew
works.description: Anne Askew's first-person accounts of her two examinations for heresy before the ecclesiastical authorities, printed in 1546 and 1547 with prefaces by John Bale; the most important English text written by a woman in the first half of the sixteenth century.
works.plot: Askew narrates her arrest and first examination before the bishop's chancellor (March 1545) and the second, harsher examination before Bishop Bonner, Bishop Gardiner, Wriothesley, and the privy council (1545–46), recording her scriptural answers on the eucharist, her refusal to name her fellow evangelicals, and her racking in the Tower — 'I answered that I would not deny my master and my God'; the account ends with her condemnation, the burning following on 16 July 1546.
works.significance: The first sustained autobiographical narrative by an English woman in print and the founding text of the English martyr tradition; Askew's scriptural self-defence under torture made her a model of the speaking female subject for later centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in prison in 1545–46, smuggled out, and printed by Bale at Wesel in 1546 (first examination) and 1547 (latter examination) as Protestant propaganda against the Henrician church; John Foxe incorporated the Examinations into the Book of Martyrs, making Askew the most famous of the Henrician women martyrs.
works.characters: Anne Askew (narrator); Bishop Edmund Bonner; Bishop Stephen Gardiner; Thomas Wriothesley; Christopher Dare; John Bale (editor)
works.structure: A first-person testimonial narrative in two parts, with Bale's framing prefaces and his 'elucidations' printed alongside; the latter examination includes the exchange with the council and the account of the rack.
works.attributionNotes: The text is Askew's own account, edited (and heavily framed) by John Bale; the record attributes authorship to Askew, with Bale's role as editor noted.

works.title: The Examiner Papers
works.description: The thrice-weekly ministerial paper which Swift took over and turned into the ablest organ of Harley's peace administration: a sequence of party essays examining the Whig conduct of the war, the church in danger and the state of the nation.
works.plot: The examiner reviews the party in office, the dissenters, the moneyed interest and the allies, and examines the arguments of the opposing papers, closing with the defence of the negotiation for the peace.
works.significance: It marks the moment at which periodical prose became the chief weapon of English party politics, and it is Swift's school of the ironical examination that Gulliver and the Drapier later extend.
works.meter: Swift's bare and forceful prose style, the short closing sentence and the rhetorical question, in deliberate contrast to the periodic manner of the essay papers.
works.context: The paper ran through the winter of the peace negotiation and the trial of the Sacheverell cause, and was conducted by Swift from about the autumn of 1710; Addison's Spectator was in part a reply to its method, and the contest of the two papers defined the political middle.
works.characters: the Examiner as the speaking editor; the ministry in office; the dissenting clergy; the confederate allies
works.structure: Serial numbered papers, each a self-contained argument, with the occasional re-print of an opposing text for examination.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative: the paper before Swift's direction and several numbers around him belong to other hands, and the division between Swift's papers and those of the associated writers remains a matter of bibliographical argument.

works.title: The Example of Virtue
works.description: Hawes's first major poem, an allegory of the soul's life: Youth, guided by Discretion, journeys through the world and learns virtue's lessons from Lady Sapience, marries Cleanness, and passes through Age to the vision of Eternity. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1504.
works.plot: Youth, counselled by Discretion, crosses the sea of the world, defeats the dragon of vice, and is led by Sapience and Fortune's lessons to the marriage with Cleanness; Age overtakes him, and the soul enters Eternity.
works.significance: A minor but characteristic example of the late medieval moral allegory, showing the tradition Spenser was to transform.
works.meter: Rhyme royal in the Lydgatian manner, with aureate vocabulary.
works.context: Written early in the reign of Henry VII, when the court still sustained the allegorical tradition of the fifteenth century.
works.characters: Youth; Discretion; Lady Sapience; Cleanness; Fortune; Age; Eternity
works.structure: A moral allegory in the pilgrimage form, moving from instruction through trial to the vision of eternity.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Excursion
altTitles: The Excursion. Forming a Part of the Recluse
works.form: Philosophical poem and conversational poem in blank verse, on the model of the didactic and contemplative poem; its one-day journey structure descends from the topographical tradition, while the set speeches belong to the Romantic debate about belief, consolation and social hope.
works.description: The only completed and published portion of a great philosophical poem that was planned but never written, issued in 1814 as a single volume of blank verse in nine books and described on its title page as forming part of the larger work. It records a day's walk in the northern mountains with an aged pedlar, and the conversations the walk produces among the narrator, the Wanderer, a despondent Solitary and a country Pastor. Its subject is the condition of human hope, melancholy and belief, argued through competing voices rather than by a system.
works.plot: The narrator, wandering among the hills, falls in with the Wanderer, an old pedlar of patient and cheerful mind, and with him ascends towards a hill community; at its edge they meet a Solitary, once a man of affairs and letters, whose hope for mankind has been wrecked by private losses and by the public history of the age, and who urges that the mass of the people are made miserable by institutions, by unequal wealth and by the course of the world. The Wanderer and the Pastor answer with the consolations of duty, of domestic affection, of labour, of the church and of the mind's intercourse with nature, and the middle books recount the lives of the humble dead of the village churchyard, each a small lesson in endurance. In the books set on and about the mountain height the Solitary is pressed but not converted, and the argument is carried forward rather than closed; the poem ends with the Pastor's meditations in the churchyard and with an invocation of evening and a defence of human hope against despondency, resting on the permanence of the moral law and on the strength lodged in the poor.
works.significance: The most substantial and most attacked long poem of the later Romantic period: reviewers received it as a proof of the failure of the system it served, and its fate discouraged the large philosophical poem in English for a generation. It nevertheless preserved the argument of the age about consolation, nature and social hope in a single continuous work, and its churchyard book has been central to recent accounts of Romantic mourning and of rural elegy.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter throughout, in a stately and deliberately elevated manner, with long paragraphic speeches, elaborate punctuation, and occasional lyric and hymn-like interpolations of shorter metre, notably in the Pastor's narrative of the humble dead.
works.context: Grown out of the plan of a philosophical poem announced in correspondence at the start of the century, composed in fits between 1802 and 1813, and published in 1814 as a detached part of a work whose rest never existed; its debates register the disappointment of the revolutionary hope of the 1790s, the condition of rural and manufacturing distress, and the poet's own movement towards a conservative national and ecclesiastical position.
works.characters: The Wanderer, an aged pedlar of the hills; the Solitary, a disillusioned former man of business and letters; the Pastor, a country clergyman; the Narrator, the poet's own speaking voice; the humble dead of the churchyard, several of whose lives the Pastor commemorates
works.structure: A poem of nine books in dramatic-narrative form: an external journey through a single day in an identifiable mountain district, framed so that each stage releases a long set speech, with three principal speakers whose contentions answer one another; the narrator's reflective passages and the churchyard narratives bind the debates together.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: The Exeter Book Riddles
works.description: A collection of some ninety-five riddles in the Exeter Book, ranging from the majestic (the swan, the iceberg, the storm, the bookworm) to the bawdy double entendres (the onion, the key, the churn), all spoken in the first person by their subjects — the largest surviving body of riddles in any early medieval vernacular.
works.plot: Each riddle presents an oblique first-person self-description — 'I am a wonderful creature...' — inviting the reader to name the hidden subject; subjects include weapons, tools, animals, natural forces, writing, and domestic objects, with several deliberately suggestive 'obscene' solutions masking innocent ones.
works.significance: The cornerstone of the English riddle tradition; a unique window onto the everyday and the marvellous in Anglo-Saxon imagination.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the riddles vary from four lines to over a hundred.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 101a-115a and elsewhere); the genre descends from the Latin enigmata of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
works.characters: the speaking objects (swan, iceberg, bookworm, onion, key, etc.)
works.structure: A sequence of independent enigmas, likely arranged by the compiler in thematic groups; the collection ends with a famous series of double-entendre riddles.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the collection may include compositions by several poets over centuries.
themes: The sublime, terror, and the ruin

works.title: The Expedition of Humphry Clinker
altTitles: The Expedition of Humphry Clinker. In a Series of Letters
works.form: epistolary novel of travel and opinion
works.description: The account of a family tour through England and Scotland, given in letters by five correspondents whose temperaments make the same scenes appear as five different books. It is at once the century's most successful comic novel of opinion, a handbook of the bath, road and fishery, and a study in the politics, medicine and morals of the late Georgians.
works.plot: An old bachelor of fortune, his maiden aunt, his ward and their two servants set out for the waters at Bath and travel by Bristol, Wales, Liverpool and the Scottish Highlands home to London. Each correspondent reports the places and the people - the pump-room, the manufacturers, the Highland hospitality, the electors and the mobs - according to his or her interest, and the servants' own histories turn out to matter. Humphry Clinker is discovered to be an heiress's lost lover, the aunt is married against her principle of scorn, and the invalid is cured by the journey.
works.significance: It is the richest of the eighteenth-century comic novels and the standard literary source for the geography of Georgian taste, reform and travel; its plural correspondence method was much imitated and remains a touchstone of narrative theory.
works.meter: Five sharply distinguished prose idioms - the politer satiric period, the fussy feminine epistle, the young man's essay, the servant's blundering record - the comedy arising from their collision over a single fact.
works.context: Written in the last years of the author's life at Nice and in London, and published in 1771, in the season of the heated politics of the Middlesex election and its riots, of the craze for the waters and for the Scottish tour, and of the debate on emigration and the fishery.
works.characters: Matthew Bramble Esq.; his sister Tabitha; their ward and nephew; Humphry Clinker the footman-gardener; Mrs. Winifred Jenkins; the assistant of the Scottish journey
works.structure: A correspondence in five hands, arranged so that the same events are reported at a distance by different letters; the plot is carried by the delayed recognition of the servants' histories.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in the letters of its composition.

works.title: The Fable of the Bees
altTitles: The Fable of the Bees: or, Private Vices, Publick Benefits
The Grumbling Hive, or Knaves Turned Honest
works.form: allegorical poem with prose philosophical essays
works.description: Mandeville's paradox poem and prose commentary, developing the thesis that private vices - luxury, pride, avarice, sensuality - are publicly beneficial because they set trade, ingenuity, and civility in motion. The first edition paired the 1705 poem 'The Grumbling Hive' with an enquiring essay; the enlarged edition of 1723-29 added a second fable, part of a play, and an extended discussion of the moral origins of virtue.
works.plot: A hive of prosperous bees, 'full of knaves', thrives on fraud, luxury, and emulation until a divine reformer makes them honest; virtue then starves trade, and the hive falls to a despicable abject state, the moral being that neither saints nor knaves can make a 'hiv' well governed. The prose essays that follow argue, paradox by paradox, that the most corrupt societies may be the most flourishing, that honour and shame are artificial engines of social cooperation, and that self-denial for its own sake is a sophism. Mandeville's later Defence and Enquiry extend the argument against 'virtue without renunciation' and against the church's account of moral self-love, distinguishing the 'fine gloss' of virtue from its real, self-interested sources.
works.significance: It is the century's most provocative contribution to the luxury debate, a decisive influence on Hume, Adam Smith, and the ideas of unintended social order, and a landmark of paradoxical prose satire.
works.meter: The fable is written in tight, dry heroic couplets of iambic pentameter in the manner of Auguean didactic satire; the commentary is plain, colloquial argumentative prose.
works.context: Developed from the 1705 poem printed for a Whig club, published as the Fable in 1714 and greatly enlarged in 1723-29, when it provoked formal presentments by the Grand Jury of Middlesex and a flood of replies; it belongs to the debates over luxury, commerce, and national decline opened by the 1720s economic writings.
works.characters: the bees of the hive; the God of the hive; Mandeville as essayist and respondent
works.structure: A short allegorical poem in heroic couplets followed by increasingly long prose essays, a defence, and enquiries; the second edition added a further fable, a dramatic poem 'The Grumbling Hive' turned into a play, and an examination of the reviewer.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Faerie Queene
works.description: Spenser's unfinished national epic and allegorical romance: twelve projected books of the adventures of knights who embody the private virtues, of which six were completed — Holiness (Redcrosse), Temperance (Guyon), Chastity (Britomart), Friendship (Cambell and Triamond), Justice (Artegall), and Courtesy (Calidore) — together with the fragmentary Mutabilitie Cantos (printed 1609), all moving through the fairyland that shadows Elizabeth's England and court.
works.plot: In each book a knight-errant undertakes a quest under the commission of the Faerie Queene (Gloriana): Redcrosse defeats the dragon and wins Una; Guyon destroys the Bower of Bliss; Britomart seeks Artegall through her founding vision of Britain; Artegall dispenses justice against Grantorto; Calidore wins Pastorella; the whole is shadowed by the giants, enchanters, and false knights of moral and political evil.
works.significance: The supreme poem of the English Renaissance and the fountain of English romantic narrative; Milton, Keats, and Tennyson all took their bearings from it.
works.meter: The Spenserian stanza: nine lines, eight of iambic pentameter and a final alexandrine, rhyming ababbcbcc.
works.context: Composed across the Armada decade; dedicated to Elizabeth I, with Books I–III printed in 1590 and IV–VI in 1596 during Spenser's service in Ireland; its allegories address the Reformation, the conquest of Ireland, and the cult of the Queen.
works.characters: Gloriana (the Faerie Queene); Prince Arthur; Redcrosse; Una; Guyon; Britomart; Artegall; Talus; Calidore; Archimago; Duessa; Acrasia
works.structure: Six completed books of twelve cantos each in interlaced romance structure, unified by the figure of Arthur, Prince of Britain, and by the allegorical design announced in the Letter to Ralegh.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Fair Jilt; or, The Amours of Prince Tarquin and Sister Henrietta
works.description: Behn's short prose fiction based on the real scandal of Sister Henrietta of the Convent of the Holy Sepulchre at Antwerp, who was tried for attempting to murder her sister; Behn, who sat on the jury, presents her as a beautiful and irresistible temptress.
works.plot: The beautiful Henrietta, forced into a convent, is pursued by the friar Tarquin; her intrigues with a nobleman and her attempt to murder her sister lead to her trial, and she is finally reconciled to the church.
works.significance: An important example of the Restoration scandal narrative and of Behn's exploitation of the boundary between reportage and fiction.
works.meter: Restoration prose of the scandal-chronicle type.
works.context: Published in 1688; Behn claimed to have witnessed the events while in the Spanish Netherlands in the 1680s.
works.characters: Sister Henrietta; Prince Tarquin; the Prince of Antwerp; the Prioress
works.structure: A short prose narrative with a documentary frame, presented as a true history.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Behn; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Fair Penitent
works.description: Rowe's tragedy of Calista, a woman of quality betrayed into a private guilt which is discovered and judged: the most acted and most read English tragedy of the first half of the century, and the founding play of the pathetic drama of female frailty.
works.plot: Calista, long yielded to the gay deceiver Altamonte and still engaged elsewhere, is exposed by the discovery of her correspondence; her father Sciolto pronounces and executes the family judgment, and the play closes in the deaths of the offenders and of the injured.
works.significance: It made the betrayed and penitent woman the central pathetic figure of the English stage and supplied the plot and the vocabulary that the sentimental drama and the novel of seduction later prosified.
works.meter: Blank verse of sustained pathetic declamation, with the broken address and the long-completed sentence of the penitential speeches.
works.context: Written for the players of the patent theatre in the years when the reformation of the stage was being argued in print, and long identified with the acting of the century's chief tragic actresses.
works.characters: Calista; Sciolto; Altamonte; Lavinia
works.structure: Five acts of discovery and judgment, with the private correspondence as the mechanism of exposure and the father's sentence as the catastrophe.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland
altTitles: Fairy Legends and Traditions of the South of Ireland
works.form: Fairy Tale and Romantic Legend; Ballad and Popular Song
works.description: The first series of the most influential collection of Irish fairy tradition in English, issued without any author's name on the title page in 1825 and illustrated by a native artist. It arranges the legends under the heads of the fairy people themselves, the Sheero or sidhe, the Cluricaune, the Banshee, the Phooka, the Thierna na Oge, and the Merrow, and gives each as a short tale. The book made Irish folklore a subject for the general reader and was praised by the leading Scottish novelist of the day.
works.plot: The series presents the fairy people in their several functions: the Sheero or good people of the hills, of whom the legends of Knockgrafton, Knockfierna, and Bottle Hill tell the punishment of the disrespectful and the reward of the patient; the Cluricaune, the hidden purse-keeping spirit of the old houses and the cellar; the Banshee, the woman of the house who cries at the death of her family; the Phooka, the spirit horse of the night, with the tale of the dreamer carried to the air. The Thierna na Oge, the land of the young, supplies the legends of the enchanted lake and of the sleeping host of the hill. The Merrow, the sea people, close the series. Each legend is retold as a short narrative with a moral of courtesy toward the invisible neighbours, and the whole is bound by notes on the beliefs and on the places.
works.significance: The Fairy Legends fixed the canonical vocabulary of Irish fairy belief for English readers and supplied the repertory on which the later Celtic revival drew; its classification of the fairies by type was one of the first such arrangements in a popular book. Its anonymous appearance and the rewriting of lost matter make it a significant instance of collaborative national collection.
works.meter: Chiefly prose, with the ballads and song fragments of the sections given in their popular stanzas and burdens; the quoted Irish and English staves are set out as verse within the prose narrative.
works.context: Published in the opening decade of the folklore movement, when the picture tour, the national tale, and the antiquarian society were all collecting peasant belief, and when the author's own notebooks of the southern tours had been lost. Because the manuscript was gone, friends with a knowledge of the country helped to rewrite the legends from memory and from what survived, and the volume went out anonymously; the second series followed in 1827 with the author's name attached.
works.characters: the Sheero or fairy people of the hills; the Cluricaune of the cellar; the Banshee who cries at deaths; the Phooka or spirit horse; the sleepers of the hill of youth; the Merrow or sea folk
works.structure: A framed collection organised by class of spirit rather than by county or tale-type, each section holding several independent short legends and closing with notes; the tales are retold in literary prose rather than transcribed as spoken.
works.attributionNotes: The first series was published with no author's name on the title page because the notebooks had been lost and the legends were rewritten with the help of friends; the authorship is established by the second series of 1827, which carries his name, and by contemporary correspondence.

works.title: The Fairy Thorn
works.form: Ballad and Popular Song; Fairy Tale and Romantic Legend
works.description: A ballad of the Irish fairy-faith printed in a Dublin magazine in 1836, taking its subject from a thorn tree at a west-Irish town which country opinion held to be the door of the fairy court. The poem narrates an assembly held in the neighbourhood of the thorn, the carrying-off of a young woman by a mystery-dancer, and her death, and it treats the belief with a seriousness that later collectors of folklore found exemplary. It is one of the earliest poems of the author's reputation and one of the most quoted of Irish verse of the decade.
works.plot: A company of gentle young people and their friends hold an assembly near the haunted thorn, and a stranger of noble and strange appearance joins the dancing. One of the household, a young woman of the family, is won into the dance and away, and though she returns she is marked by the other world; she pines and dies, and the poem attributes her death to the fairy captivity. The country people read the events by the old rules, and the thorn is left standing as its credit is confirmed rather than broken. The ballad closes on the warning and on the continuing honour paid to the tree.
works.significance: The Fairy Thorn became the standard English verse account of the fairy thorn tradition and was drawn on by the later Celtic twilight writers who documented the surviving belief; it is cited as an early model of the Irish ballad that treats peasant supernaturalism as fact rather than as ornament. Its reputation helped establish the poet as the first figure of the Irish academic school.
works.meter: A steady ballad measure in rhymed quatrains with narrative compression and a grave refrain-like emphasis, far removed from the bouncing energy of the earlier forge-ballad; the poetry is soft and reticent at the crisis.
works.context: Printed in the Dublin magazine that had begun to publish a self-consciously Irish verse in English in the later 1830s, and founded on a well-known local tradition of a fairy thorn in the west of Ireland, of which the country people forbade the cutting. The poem belongs to the same revival of fairy belief as the contemporary collections of southern Irish legend, with which its author's generation was intimate.
works.characters: the young woman danced away and lost; the strange noble dancer of the fairy court; the assembly company of the gentry; the country people who interpret the event
works.structure: A single continuous ballad with a framed assembly, a central sequence of abduction and return, and a closing reflection on the surviving belief; the movement is narrative rather than lyrical, with the fairy lore supplied by the speech of the country witnesses.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the poem first appeared in a magazine over the writer's name and was collected in his verse volume of the 1860s.

works.title: The Fall of Hyperion: A Dream
altTitles: Hyperion. The Dream of the Poet
works.form: Dream vision and Romantic monody of the poet's function, recasting the Miltonic titan fragment as a vision of the priestly office of the imagination.
works.description: The dream-version of the titan poem, in which the poet himself becomes the speaker and the fall of the elder gods is witnessed as the vision of an aspirant to the office of poetry. Written in the late summer and autumn of 1819 and left unfinished, it recasts the earlier epic as a monody of the poet's function, in which the mortal pain of the world is the qualification for the immortal work. It was never printed in the author's lifetime and first appeared from the manuscript in the middle of the following century.
works.plot: The dreamer, awake in an old thought and heavy as the leaves of autumn, finds himself in a temple of the dead gods where the stones breathe and the columnar spaces seem alive, and climbs the steps to the shrine where Saturn and the Titan race lie as in the earlier poem. There he meets the guide Moneta, the shadow of the faintest worn lady of the tribe, who shows him the priest's office and forbids him to touch the altar, declaring that no one may enter the lists of the immortal but those who suffer for the human race, the high souls who are the physicians of its pain. As the dreamer tries to speak the tale of the fallen gods the scene passes to the last vision of the poem, and the fragment ends with the question of the dreamer's own waking office. The argument is that the poetry of the immortal is bought only by the mortal pain of the world's misery.
works.significance: It is the period's most searching account of the poet's vocation as a suffering office, and its claim that only those who live for others may enter the lists of the immortal became one of the most quoted propositions of later poetics. Its recovery in the middle of the nineteenth century and its relation to the earlier draft have made it the standard instance of the Romantic poem existing in two authorially distinct versions.
works.meter: Blank verse of five-beat iambic lines, with a far more colloquial and self-questioning movement than that of the earlier epic draft and a heavier use of the enjambed line and of the parenthetical address.
works.context: Written in the late summer and autumn of 1819 at Wentworth Place, Hampstead, where the poet lodged with a friend, in the season of the great odes and after the abandonment of the first titan draft, and never completed nor printed in the author's lifetime. Its definition of the poet as the physician of the world's pain belongs to the same months as the letters on negative capability and on the vale of the world's making, and it became the central text of the argument about the two versions of the titan poem.
works.characters: the dreamer-poet; Moneta, the guide and priestess of the shrine, the shadow of the old seer of the tribe; Saturn and the fallen Titan race of the earlier poem
works.structure: A single continuous dream vision with a dream frame, opening on the speaker's fevered condition, passing to the temple and the address of Moneta, and breaking off in the middle of the poet's attempt to tell the titan tale.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem survives in a manuscript and in transcripts made by the author's friends, and its relation to the earlier draft was long disputed by editors before the manuscripts were fully printed.

works.title: The Family Expositor
altTitles: The Family Expositor: or, A Paraphrase and Commentary on the New Testament
works.description: Doddridge's great posthumous work, a paraphrase and commentary on the New Testament in weekly family portions, published from his manuscripts from 1756 into the 1760s. It was designed to make each section of scripture a complete act of family worship: text, sense, improvement, and devotion together.
works.plot: Each week's portion gives the biblical text with a running paraphrase that supplies the idioms and links, a commentary of doctrine and criticism, and then the practical improvement for the heart and life. Doddridge draws on the best earlier annotators, joining scholarship of a learned temper to pulpit directness. The improvements turn each passage into meditation on providence, the Saviour's love, and the duties of the common hour. The work runs its course through the Gospels and Acts into the epistles, the later volumes completed from his papers by friends.
works.significance: It set the model of the devotional commentary for family worship and, through its completion and constant reprinting into the nineteenth century, formed generations of Protestant reading of the New Testament.
works.meter: A smooth, meditative prose of paraphrase and application, the rhythms of prayer woven into exposition.
works.context: Long prepared at Northampton for the academy and for the family devotions of his people, and published after his death from 1756, it became the most popular Protestant family New Testament of the later eighteenth century.
works.structure: A continuous paraphrase-commentary in weekly family lessons through the books of the New Testament, each lesson a unit of text, paraphrase, comment, and improvement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Family Legend: A Tragedy
works.description: A Highland blood-feud tragedy founded on the traditional hostility of two western Scottish houses in the sixteenth century, published and acted in Edinburgh in 1810 with a prologue written for the occasion by a neighbouring novelist. It is the author's most openly national play, and the only one of her series to be produced professionally in Scotland. The tragedy turns on a marriage that crosses the feud and on the honour that forbids the avenger to spare his own kin.
works.plot: Maclean, chief of his line, has married Helen, daughter of the Earl of Argyll, whose house and his are bound by an old and murderous feud. When Argyll invades Mull and takes the household of his daughter prisoner, the claims of kinship and of clan honour pull in opposite directions, and the middle course offered by John of Lorne and by the captive Helen fails. The progress of the play is a sequence of demands for vengeance met by refusals grounded on the marriage tie, and the catastrophe falls on the house of Maclean itself. The Scottish border tradition of feuding is thus made the tragic subject rather than merely the setting.
works.significance: The Family Legend is the principal instance of a woman dramatist of the period writing national Scottish tragedy for the stage rather than for the closet, and it shows the series of passions method adapted to blood-feud and kinship. Its Edinburgh production, with a prologue by the leading Scottish author of the day, marks the meeting of the ballad revival and the analytical drama.
works.meter: Blank verse in the sustained rhetorical manner of the author's earlier tragedies, with a heightened and occasionally archaising diction suited to the Highland subject and with marches, gathering-calls, and border song interposed.
works.context: Written and published in the decade of the Scottish musical and ballad revival, when the Highland feud was a fashionable tragic subject and when the novelist of the border ballads supplied the prologue for the Edinburgh performance of 1810. The play's politics of clanship and of royal administration of the Isles belongs to the long afterlife of the sixteenth-century campaigns in the west of Scotland.
works.characters: Maclean; Helen, his wife and Argyll's daughter; the Earl of Argyll; John of Lorne; Sir Hubert de Grey; Benlora; Lochtavish; Glenfadden; Rosa
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of a single feud, with a choric and martial movement between the camps and the island, and with the captive scenes framing the argument; the action is continuous and closes in destruction rather than reconciliation.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship and undisputed; the prologue to the Edinburgh performance is a separate occasional poem by another hand.

works.title: The Fancy: A Selection from the Poetical Remains of the Late Peter Corcoran, Esq., of Gray's Inn, Student at Law
works.form: Volume of romantic fantasy verse, songs, and lyric meditations under a playful fictional frame
works.description: A volume of verse by John Hamilton Reynolds, published in 1820 under the playful fiction that it was selected from the poetical remains of an imaginary Gray's Inn lawyer named Peter Corcoran. The Fancy gathers lighter, fantastical, and Keatsian pieces, including the title poem and Reynolds's characteristic medley of song, ballad, and descriptive fancy, and it appeared in the same year and from the same publisher as Keats's own first volume. The book is the principal record of Reynolds's charm as a poet of romantic fantasy and playful sensibility, and it belonged to the circle of Hunt and the younger Romantics.
works.plot: The volume has no continuous plot; it presents a series of short imaginative pieces governed by fancy rather than argument. Its poems conjure castles, old romances, moonlight, music, and melancholy scenes, treating love, loss, and the lure of the imaginary with a wistful playfulness; the frame of the fictional 'Peter Corcoran' lets Reynolds offer verse of fantasy and feeling under a humorous mask.
works.significance: The Fancy is Reynolds's chief claim on the attention of literary history and the volume by which he is remembered chiefly as Keats's friend and fellow-author of 1820; its play of romantic fantasy exemplifies the lighter, sensuous current of the Hunt circle's verse and helps chart the milieu out of which Keats's own first book emerged.
works.meter: Chiefly light lyric stanzas, songs, and ballad measures in smooth musical iambics, with some sonnets; the versification is graceful, tuneful, and deliberately fanciful, close in manner to Keats's early verse and to Hunt's sweetness.
works.context: Published London, 1820, by Taylor and Hessey in the same circle and season as Keats's Poems and Reynolds's friendship with Keats and the Hunt group; the fictional 'Peter Corcoran' device reflects the playful, clubbable literary culture of the period's young Romantic poets around Hunt, Reynolds, and Keats.
works.characters: the fanciful lyric speaker; the invented Peter Corcoran as framing persona; the lovers, mourners, and romantic figures of the separate pieces
works.structure: A miscellaneous collection of short lyrics, songs, and fanciful meditations presented as the remains of an invented predecessor; the ordering is thematic and playful rather than narrative, and the framing conceit supplies unity in place of plot.
works.attributionNotes: Published under Reynolds's name behind the fictional pretence of the remains of 'Peter Corcoran'; Reynolds's authorship is established and undisputed.

works.title: The Farmer's Boy
altTitles: The Farmer's Boy; a Rural Poem
works.form: Topographical and Descriptive Poetry; Pastoral Poetry
works.description: A rural poem in four parts, Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter, written by an East Anglian journeyman shoemaker and published by the literary patron to whom the manuscript was sent. It presents the working year of a Suffolk farm household in decorous heroic couplets, published with a patron's preface and explanatory notes. For a generation it was the most widely read labouring-class poem in English, going through many editions and pirated printings.
works.plot: Spring opens with the household and field in renewal, the young cattle, the hedging and sowing, and the labourer's early journey to work before light. Summer follows the mowing, the rick-making, and the long harvest day, with the sickle, the binding, and the waggon. Autumn gives the gleaning, the stacking, the barn, and the market, and closes with the rural sports and the labourer's supper. Winter brings the frost, the fold, the fire-side, the faggot, and the poor's cottage, ending in moral reflection on contentment and on the condition of the man who labours all year for little.
works.significance: The Farmer's Boy created the market for labouring-class rural poetry and set the template of the poet discovered and edited by a patron, a template the next generation of peasant poets followed. Its prestige also provoked the lasting disparagement of labouring verse as topographical report rather than poetry, a judgement that shaped the author's relegation.
works.meter: Closed iambic pentameter heroic couplets in the manner of the eighteenth-century estate and seasons poem, with an added glancing alliteration and a plain Suffolk vocabulary; the verse is deliberately unambitious in figure and metre.
works.context: Composed in a garret after hours of journeyman work and published at the end of the dear years of the 1790s, when bread prices, enclosure, and rural depopulation made the labourer's condition a public subject. A literary magistrate and bibliophile obtained the manuscript, subscribed for copies, and secured a sumptuous first edition with wood-cut illustrations by a celebrated provincial engraver, an arrangement that made the book a publishing event.
works.characters: the journeyman poet-speaker; the farmer's boy; the hind and the shepherd; the gleaners and the housewife; the labourer's family at the winter fire-side
works.structure: A four-part seasonal sequence in continuous descriptive narration without plot, each part a self-contained month-cycle of tasks; the first edition frames the poem with an editor's preface and explanatory notes.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship, undisputed; the editor's preface and notes are by the poem's patron, who is not a claimant of the verse.

works.title: The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
altTitles: The Further Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
The Second Part of the Life of Robinson Crusoe
works.form: novel; prose voyage narrative with an inherited fictional persona
works.description: The second of the three Robinson Crusoe volumes, issued in August 1719 after a spurious continuation had appeared in London. It returns the narrator to the island, then carries him through the East Indies, the Cape and across the deserts of Central Asia in a series of voyages that replace settlement with motion.
works.plot: Crusoe revisits his island, now peopled by the mutineers he left there and by newly arrived Englishmen and Spaniards, and settles disputes over worship and government before sailing on. He is attacked off Madagascar, trades and travels through the Malay coast, China and Persia, and after a near-fatal crossing of the Great Tartary desert reaches Moscow and travels overland to England, where he finds himself unexpectedly wealthy. The volume closes with a third voyage contemplated rather than narrated.
works.significance: It fixed the model of the sequel and the return-novel, and its colony-building episode has been much discussed as a fable of plantation government, toleration and colonial ownership.
works.meter: Plainer and more hurried prose than the first volume, dominated by dates, distances and commoditues of trade; the meditative periodic sentence gives way to the listed itinerary.
works.context: Composed within months of the first volume's success, it draws on East India Company and privateering narratives and expressly supersedes the pirating Continuation of the World of Robinson Crusoe published in London in mid-1719.
works.characters: Robinson Crusoe; the island governor; Friday's brother; the Portuguese pilot; the Tartar and Muscovite guides
works.structure: First-person retrospect in an episodic voyage sequence, the island episode framing a picaresque chain of traverses and encounters; less concentrated than the first volume and more dependent on reported incident.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was advertised as the true second part to displace the anonymously pirated continuation.

works.title: The Fatal Marriage; or, The Innocent Adultery
works.description: Thomas Southerne's most successful tragedy, an adaptation of two of Behn's novellas, in which Isabella, believing her husband Alonzo dead, remarries and is destroyed when the first husband returns.
works.plot: Isabella, in poverty, believes Alonzo dead and marries Biron; Alonzo returns; Isabella, unable to bear the guilt, kills Biron's brother and then herself.
works.significance: The most popular she-tragedy of the 1690s and an important adaptation of Behn's prose fiction for the stage.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1694 and published the same year; Elizabeth Barry's Isabella was one of the great performances of the age, and the play held the stage into the nineteenth century.
works.characters: Isabella; Alonzo; Biron; Baldwin; Carlos; Anne
works.structure: Five acts in blank verse with a subordinate comic plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Southerne; he acknowledges the debt to Behn in the dedication.

works.title: The Fatal Sisters
altTitles: The Fatal Sisters: A Translation from the Norse
works.description: Gray's imitated translation of an old Norse poem of the women of the battle, in which the fatal sisters sing the names of the doomed and the course of the fight while they ply the wound and the hair.
works.plot: The daughters of the whirlwind and the battle chant their terrible weaving of the fates of the warriors, name the king whose hour is come and the land that is to be won, and ride away to the north and to the night after the song.
works.significance: It introduced the imagery and the machinery of the northern mythology into English verse, and it is the most exact of the century's poetic reconstructions of primitive poetry.
works.meter: The short paired lines of the reconstructed northern measure, with the heavy alliteration and the repeated burden.
works.context: Written in the same year as The Bard out of Gray's study of the Danish and Norse poetry in the antiquarian editions, at the moment when the northern and the primitive were being made the models of a new sublimity.
works.characters: the fatal sisters of the battle; the king whose doom is chanted; the warriors of the two hosts
works.structure: A short series of antiphonal stanzas of the imitated Norse measure, with the refrain and the enumeration of the slain.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Gray's, though the piece is an imitation rather than a literal translation and the identification of his Norse original is a matter of the antiquarian scholarship of the following century.

works.title: The Fate of Adelaide
works.form: Collected volume: a long verse romance with shorter lyrics, elegies and descriptive pieces; the governing genres are the metrical tale and the meditative lyric in a woman's voice.
works.description: The first volume of verse from the pen that would become the most cultivated poetess of the annuals, built around a long romance in stanzas and a company of shorter pieces. It introduces the characteristic situations of the whole career: the abandoned woman, the artist's vocation, and mourning figured as a landscape.
works.plot: The title romance tells of a young woman's attachment, desertion and ruin, and frames the story with reflective commentary on the fate such attachments leave behind. Around it the volume gathers lyrics of disappointment, elegies on the dead, and descriptive pieces that make scenery the language of feeling. Several poems already treat the figure of the gifted woman whose art is at once her fame and her exposure. The argument is not a single thesis but a repertoire of postures - constancy, wounded pride, and self-dramatising grief. The book ends with shorter occasional verse rather than with the romance's closure.
works.significance: The book is the starting point of a persona - the gifted, wounded, professional woman poet - that its author's later volumes and her imitators developed into an idiom of the annuals. It documents the economics by which a woman could live by verse in the 1820s, since its reception was managed through review work and periodical payment. Modern editions have restored it to the history of Romantic authorship as a case study in female self-fashioning.
works.meter: The romance runs in regular stanzic iambic verse with a rapid movement of talk and ejaculation; the lyrics use common measure, refrains and triple-metre openings, and the couplet appears in the argumentative passages.
works.context: The volume appeared while its author was still writing for the magazines and the Literary Gazette, and unusually for a woman poet of the moment it was issued under her own name rather than over initials. It was reviewed at once in the very periodical press she was herself supplying. Its register is wholly private at a moment when the book trade was saturated with public, political and scandalous verse.
works.characters: Adelaide, the heroine whose fate the title romance records
works.structure: A long narrative romance in stanzas occupies the centre of the volume, preceded and followed by shorter lyrics, elegies and descriptive pieces; the collection is ordered by length, not by design, and the romance interrupts its own story for moral and personal comment.
works.attributionNotes: The first issue carries the author's own name on the title page; the magazine verse of the same years, much of it identical in subject, was signed with initials.

works.title: The Fates of the Apostles
works.form: religious catalogue poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 122 lines cataloguing the deaths and missionary fields of the twelve apostles, signed by Cynewulf in a runic acrostic that spells his name. The catalogue frame encloses a meditation on the poet's own need for grace, the best-known of the four Cynewulfian signatures.
works.plot: The poet, speaking as a weary traveller, enumerates the apostles in order — where each preached and how each died (Peter crucified, Paul beheaded, Andrew in Achaia, John at Ephesus, and so on) — then turns to himself: begging the prayers of the reader, weaving the runes of his name into a meditation on the gifts of God and the terror of judgment.
works.significance: The earliest signature of an English poet in his own verse; a key document for the Cynewulf canon.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the runic acrostic spells CYNEWULF.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 52v-54r) and in the same collection as Andreas and the homilies.
works.characters: the twelve apostles; the poet (Cynewulf)
works.structure: A thula-like catalogue of the apostles followed by the runic signature passage, which modulates from report to prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes; accepted as authentic.
themes: Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world
sources: The Rise of the Novel: Studies in Defoe, Richardson and Fielding

works.title: The Father and Daughter
works.description: the author's first novel, a domestic sentimental tragedy of a father's unconditional love for his seduced daughter, based on the real case of a fallen woman and her broken family. It was an immediate bestseller, admired for its moral seriousness and its refusal to condemn its heroine. Mary Wollstonecraft's principles were cited in defence of the novel when critics attacked its leniency.
works.plot: Clara Franklin, the only daughter of a widowed country gentleman, is seduced by the rake Sir Edward Mordant and elopes with him. When the deception is exposed, she is abandoned; her father, rather than cast her off, takes her back and cares for her in her shame. The novel traces their years of quiet exile, Clara's suffering, and her gradual death, ending with the father's inconsolable grief. The narrative is structured around the unconditional bond between parent and erring child rather than around the seduction itself.
works.significance: The Father and Daughter is the most influential of the Romantic-era seduction novels and a landmark in the compassionate representation of the 'fallen woman'; it connects the sentimental tradition to later Victorian treatments of female vulnerability.
works.context: Published in 1801, during the aftermath of Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Woman and in the height of the sentimental 'fallen woman' novel; The author, already a celebrity by her novel The Tricks of Fiction, deliberately treats the fallen woman with compassion rather than moral condemnation.
works.characters: Clara Franklin; Mr. Franklin; Sir Edward Mordant; Mrs. Clotilde; Arthur Mordaunt
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative; the domestic tragedy is centred on the father-daughter bond; the seduction is treated as an event that precipitates but does not dominate the story of endurance and love.

works.title: The Feast of the Poets; with Notes, and Other Pieces in Verse
works.form: Mock-heroic and critical verse satire in the Augustan tradition, revived in Regency England with a lighter, more sociable manner
works.description: A mock-heroic verse satire by Leigh Hunt, first published in the Reflector in 1811 and issued as a separate poem with notes and other pieces in verse in 1814. The poem imagines a banquet to which the living British and classical poets are summoned, and, in the manner of the Dunciad and of Scottish Burns's 'Epistle to the Old Poets', treats the guest-list of contemporary verse as a comic feast of presences and conspicuous absences. Its courteous wit, its critical as well as playful manner, and its copious annotation made it a widely-quoted document of Regency literary taste.
works.plot: An invitation goes out to a feast of the poets at which the muses and their votaries gather; the poem names, praises, gently derides, or pointedly omits the poets of the day from Wordsworth and Coleridge to Rogers, Moore, and Byron. Classical poets are also invited, and the moderns are contrasted with the ancients in a running comic comparison. The notes expand the poem into a critical gloss on contemporary reputations, and the accompanying pieces in verse extend Hunt's manner into lighter lyrics.
works.significance: The Feast of the Poets is a central document of Regency literary sociology and of the mock-heroic satire's survival into the Romantic period; its catalogue of presences and omissions shaped later nineteenth-century judgments about the literary field, and its blend of courtesy and critical edge typifies Hunt's contribution to Romantic periodical culture.
works.meter: Written chiefly in smooth heroic couplets, following the Pope-Byron line of Augustan satire in a lighter, conversational tempo; the diction is witty and allusive, and the poem's argumentative edge is carried in the couplet as often as in the notes.
works.context: The poem first appeared in the Reflector, the quarterly Hunt edited for his brother John in 1810-11, and was expanded into a separate edition in 1814 as Hunt moved from journalism into open literary controversy. Its satiric guest-list engaged the quarrels over contemporary taste that would soon harden into Blackwood's and Quarterly attacks on Hunt and his circle, and Byron himself noted the poem in conversation.
works.characters: the poet-host who presides at the feast; the invited contemporary poets of Regency England; the classical poets who appear for comparison
works.structure: A single mock-heroic poem in rhymed couplets preceded by a brief epistle-like opening and followed by a set of explanatory notes and shorter verses; the design is episodic, moving through the guest-list of poets, and the prose notes carry much of the critical content.
works.attributionNotes: Published by 'The Editor of the Examiner'; authorship by James Henry Leigh Hunt is established and undisputed.

works.title: The Female Husband
works.form: fictional biography and scandalous tale in prose
works.description: A fictionalised life of the woman who passed as a man and married several women, published on the occasion of her trial at the Bristol court in 1746. It is a short scandalous biography in the Newgate manner, mixing report, invention and moral comment on the boundaries of sex and marriage.
works.plot: A young person of masculine appearance and no fortune takes to the road in male dress, learns the practice of a physic, and courtships and marries women in several counties. The marriages are consummated or refused, the wives complain of deformity and distance, and the pursuit of an affectionate partner leads at last to detection, trial and punishment. The narrative reports the exposure with a mixture of sensational detail and professed moral horror.
works.significance: It is a central text for the history of cross-dressing, gender impersonation and the legal fiction of sexual identity in eighteenth-century print culture, and evidence of the novelist's movement from amatory to documentary material.
works.meter: Plain narrative prose with the abrupt, evidential sentences of the trial report and the raised register of the moral reflection.
works.context: Published in 1746 out of the reports of a real prosecution for bigamy and deceit at the Bristol sessions, and in the same decade as the author's own conduct-oriented fiction; the case touched the law of marriage and the definition of sex.
works.characters: the female husband; the successive brides; the constables and prosecutors; the Bristol court
works.structure: A continuous pseudo-biographical life in two short parts, following the trial report and the confessional narrative conventions of criminal biography; detection serves as the structural hinge.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution generally accepted on stylistic and publishing grounds and recorded as single; the text was published without the writer's name, and its subject is a real person whose own account differs.

works.title: The Female Quixote; or, The Adventures of Arabella
works.form: comic novel; moralities of reading in prose
works.description: The comedy of a young heiress who, having read nothing but romances, governs her conduct by their laws and reads every man as a knight and every civility as a homage. It is the most sustained English treatment of the madwoman of the reading plot and one of the century's central statements about fiction's power over its readers.
works.plot: Arabella, beautiful and rich, insists upon the ceremonious courtship prescribed by the romances and refuses the plain addresses of the man she ought to marry. Her lover and her friend try various devices to cure her, including a counter-romantic treatment which makes her believe herself admired in the old style. The exposure of a designing admirer at last breaks the illusion, and the closing reconciliation is effected by a physician who prescribes history and religion against romance.
works.significance: It gave the century its most influential figure of the female reader corrupted by fiction and supplied the model for later treatments of romantic delusion, from its own imitators to the nineteenth-century novel of reading.
works.meter: A clear ironic prose that quotes and parodies the diction of the heroic romance in the heroine's speeches, the comedy lying in the mismatch of registers.
works.context: Published in 1752, in the season of the quarrel over the danger of novel-reading and of the author's own friendship with the leading writers of the day, including the lexicographer who advertised the book; its target includes the surviving vogue of translated romance.
works.characters: Arabella; her lover and friend; the designing admirer who works on her delusion; the physician and the moralist of the conclusion
works.structure: Third-person narration in two volumes, the plot a single sustained irony maintained by the heroine's misreadings; the episodes are arranged as trials of her interpretive system and resolved by an anti-romance cure.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and long, wrongly, credited to another hand by early bibliographers before being firmly reassigned.

works.title: The Female Reader
altTitles: The Female Reader: Pieces, Prose and Verse, Selected from the Most Classick Writers and Calculated as a Practical Guide to the Review of a Female Education
The Female Reader. A Practical Guide to the Review of a Female Education
works.form: anthology and critical guide to reading
works.description: An anthology of prose and verse selected for the use of young women and furnished with rules of reading and with the editor's remarks on taste, elocution and the choice of books. It was planned as the practical completion of a female education and issued in several volumes.
works.plot: The collection passes in order through the species of composition - description, argument, narration, the drama, the epic, lyric and the letters of history - each being illustrated by extracted specimens and preceded by directions for reading it well. Remarks on the choice of books, on the cultivation of the ear and on the danger of incorrect reading supply the connective argument. Its design is to make a woman's taste an instrument of judgement rather than of amusement.
works.significance: It is an important document of the pedagogy of taste for women at the end of the century and evidence of the author's methods as a critic and teacher before her political writing.
works.meter: A didactic prose of rule and remark for the connecting matter, the verse extracts being given as specimens of the several measures and the prose as models of style.
works.context: Published in 1789 in the same season as the author's work on the education of women and within the dissenting and Bluestocking projects for female improvement, the anthology genre then being a principal means of literary instruction.
works.structure: A systematic anthology in classes with the editor's dissertations and notes interposed; the order of the species governs the sequence, the extracts supplying the examples.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution established by the publisher's records and by the correspondence of the period, the work having been issued without the name of the editor; part of the compiling labour has been associated with a sister's hand, and the record is held as partial.
