works.title: The Finnsburh Fragment
works.manuscriptDate: lost; preserved in an early eighteenth-century transcript
works.description: A fragment of about 48 lines of an older heroic lay describing the night attack on the hall of Finn, king of the Frisians, in which the Danish prince Hnæf and his men defend the doors for five days. The story — later told allusively in Beowulf's 'Finnsburg episode' — is one of the great Germanic tales of feud and loyalty.
works.plot: A watchman sees the gleam of weapons as Finn's men attack the hall by night; Hnæf's Danes hold the doors, and the fight lasts five days without a man falling, until the fragment breaks off. The fuller story, reconstructed from Beowulf and other sources, involves the peace-pledge of Hildeburh, the death of Hnæf and Finn's son, and Finn's eventual slaying by the Danes.
works.significance: The sole surviving example, alongside Beowulf, of the heroic hall-fight; indispensable for reconstructing the legend and the older lay tradition.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of an archaic, compressed kind.
works.context: The story belongs to the fifth-century Germanic migrations; the text survives only in the transcript made by George Hickes for his Thesaurus (1705) of a manuscript leaf (Lambeth Palace MS 487) now lost.
works.characters: Hnæf; Finn; Hildeburh; Hengest; Sigeferth; Garulf; Guðlaf; Ordlaf
works.structure: A single vivid scene of hall-fighting, extended by speeches (the door-defenders Garulf and Guðere, the veteran Sigeferth); the poem's brevity and compression suggest the style of the older lays behind Beowulf.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The First Settlers of New-England; or, Conquest of the Pequods, Narragansets, and Pokanokets, as Related by a Father to His Children
altTitles: The First Settlers of New England
works.form: Juvenile and educational history in the tales-of-the-settlement mode: a framed narrative of war and planting designed to form national feeling in the young reader.
works.description: A historical narrative for young readers recounting the settlement of New England and the wars with the Pequods, Narragansets and Pokanokets, put into the mouth of a father telling the story to his children. It was written as part of a programme of national education, and it is notable for the way its sympathetic treatment of the conquered combines with an unrepentant account of the settlers' cause. Its frank description of atrocity on both sides makes it one of the more unusual juvenile histories of the period.
works.plot: The narrative begins with the earliest plantings and the first contact between settlers and the Native nations of the region, and moves through the Pequot war, the destruction of the fort at the Mystic, the flight and death of the Narraganset king, and King Philip's war. Each campaign is recounted as an episode of courage and cruelty, with the writer's sympathy frequently diverted from the English to their opponents, whose loss of land and people is lamented plainly. The father's frame supplies the moral instruction: the children are to love the settler's fortitude but to pity the conquered, and the tale closes on the hope that justice might yet be done to the remnant.
works.significance: It is a significant early American book for children and an unusually conflicted piece of national origin-writing, in which the elegy for the conquered sits inside a celebration of the conquest. Its treatment of the Native past anticipates the romantic Indian tale of the following decade and documents the moral ambiguity of Jacksonian-era education.
works.meter: Clear expository prose addressed to children, with occasional apostrophe and lament; no verse.
works.context: Written in the late 1820s for a national audience of children at a moment when American historical writing was being rebuilt as usable origin-myth and when Indian policy was moving toward removal. Its author was by then editing a juvenile periodical in Boston and writing the reform-adjacent fiction and pedagogy that led her, in the following years, to the great abolitionist argument of the 1830s.
works.characters: The narrating father and his listening children; the Pequot and Narraganset chiefs; the confederated king of Pokanoket; the settlers and captains of the United Colonies
works.structure: Framed juvenile history: a father's continuous narrative addressed to his children, divided into episodes of war and settlement in strict chronological sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is established and uncontested; the book was published under the author's own name in her second year of professional writing.

works.title: The Fleece
works.form: Didactic and topographical poem in the Thomson school, in books, with the technical instruction of a husbandry poem combined with the survey of a trade; issued after subscription proposals and dedications.
works.description: John Dyer's principal poem: a didactic and topographical work on the English wool trade, from the feeding of the sheep and the shearing to the staple, the marketing and the international commerce that carried the fleece to the world's ends. It was published by subscription and carries the name of the clergyman who wrote it. The ambition is at once technical and moral: to make the whole circuit of a national industry the subject of elevated unrhymed verse.
works.plot: The poem moves outward in stages from the pasture to the ocean. Its first care is practical: the breeds, the feeding, the shearing and the management of the flock, with the shepherd and the shepherdess introduced as figures of a vanishing rural order. From the fleece in the fold it passes to the wool in the warehouse and the market, and then to the merchant, the ship and the ports of the Mediterranean and the north, arguing that this single commodity has bound England into the world's trade. A moral anxiety runs under the praise: the growth of wealth threatens to corrupt the labour and the independence that produced it, and the prospect of national fullness is shadowed by the fear of decline. The argument is therefore a sustained piece of political economy in verse, closer to a discourse of the wool trade than to any earlier English poem.
works.significance: It is the most ambitious of the eighteenth-century attempts to put a national industry into elevated verse, and the crucial link between Thomson's meditative topography and Goldsmith's 'The Deserted Village' in the poetry of rural labour, commerce and depopulation. Samuel Johnson's account of its crabbed sublimity made it the standard example of a poet who mistook harshness for strength, and it remains a primary document of the age's thinking about commerce and its discontents.
works.meter: Blank verse (unrhymed iambic pentameter) of notoriously harsh and laborious texture, with long compounds, stretched and hypermetric lines, and an evident attempt to bend English measure to the weight of Latin and Italian syntax.
works.context: It was written in the decades when the wool and cloth trade was the acknowledged foundation of English national power, and when the staple, the export markets and the growing manufactures were matters of public debate. Dyer, a Welsh-born curate with a small living and large schemes for rural industry, published by subscription after earlier ventures failed, and the poem carries those projects' hopes and disappointments.
works.characters: The shepherd and shepherdess of the English hills; the wool merchant; the mariner; the labouring poor of the staple towns
works.structure: A didactic poem in books, each gathering its own department of the subject, with descriptive digression, apostrophe to the labouring poor, and an ascending sweep from local husbandry to global commerce.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published in the author's own name in the collected editions and its composition is documented in Dyer's correspondence with his friends. Precise years of composition for the individual books are not fixed here and are left null.

works.title: The Forc'd Marriage; or, A Night's Intrigue
works.description: Aphra Behn's first play, a tragicomedy of forced marriage and intrigue in which Alcander is compelled to marry Erminia while loving another, and the complications are resolved in a set of marriages.
works.plot: The King forces Erminia to marry Alcander, who loves Aminta; disguises and mistaken identities lead to a night of intrigue, and the plot ends with the rightful pairings.
works.significance: The first play by a woman to be performed on the English public stage, marking the beginning of professional female authorship in English drama.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in December 1670 and published in 1671; it ran for six nights, a modest but respectable success for a first play, and by a woman.
works.characters: Alcander; Erminia; Aminta; Cleontius; Lisander; the King; Galliard
works.structure: Five acts of heroic tragicomedy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Behn; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Forest
works.description: Jonson's collection of fifteen poems printed in the 1616 Folio, including the country-house poem 'To Penshurst', the odes 'To Celia' and 'To Heaven', the song 'That Women Are but Men's Shadows', and the epistle 'To Sir Robert Wroth' — the volume that made the estate, the court, and the virtuous life the matter of English lyric.
works.plot: No plot: the poems move from the celebration of Penshurst's hospitality and Sidneyan estate-life, through the songs and odes of love and devotion, to the epistles and epitaphs that map Jonson's moral world of patrons and friends.
works.significance: Home of the English country-house poem and of Jonson's most enduring lyrics — the classical counterweight to the metaphysical fashion.
works.meter: Couplets, odes, and songs of classical restraint, including the famous lyric 'Drink to me only with thine eyes' (a cento from Philostratus).
works.context: Collected for the 1616 Folio; 'To Penshurst' (c. 1612) founded the country-house poem that Lanyer, Carew, and Marvell would continue.
works.characters: the poet; the Sidney family (at Penshurst); Celia; Sir Robert Wroth; the Countess of Bedford
works.structure: A miscellany of fifteen poems organized by theme — place, love, virtue, mortality — with 'To Penshurst' as its opening masterpiece.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Forest of Vaud
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's later Gothic novel, set in the Swiss forest of Vaud and the Jura mountains, in which an isolated heroine encounters persecution and the supernatural. It belongs to the author's final phase of Gothic writing, after the great vogue of the 1790s had passed.
works.plot: In the Alpine canton of Vaud, a young woman is confined in a forest hermitage by a guardian whose intentions are sinister; pursuit, supernatural threat, and the wild landscape combine in the Gothic ordeal. The novel's Swiss setting draws on the Rousseauian and Gothic Alpine traditions, and its heroine's endurance under confinement is the novel's central dramatic pattern.
works.significance: The Forest of Vaud extends the author's lifelong Gothic interrogation of female vulnerability and confinement; it illustrates the Gothic mode's endurance into the late Romantic period beyond Scott and the historical novel.
works.context: Published in the mid-1820s, at the twilight of the Gothic novel vogue and at the end of the author's career; the Alpine setting reflects the enduring Romantic fascination with Switzerland and its literature of terror.
works.characters: The heroine of the forest; her persecutor guardian; her protector
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative; the Gothic captivity and pursuit plot is set against the Swiss forest landscape; a resolution restores the heroine's rightful position.

works.title: The Forest Sanctuary
works.form: Verse romance and religious narrative poem in six cantos; the metrical tale of providential preservation is the governing genre, with descriptive and meditative lyric passages embedded.
works.description: The longest serious narrative poem in the author's canon, worked out in six cantos around a providential plot of shipwreck, rescue and rearing. It converts an adventure story into a meditation on gratitude, vocation and the claims of a religious house upon a soul preserved by it.
works.plot: An infant's life is saved in a storm at sea, and the child is brought up within a monastic retreat sheltered in a forest, which gives the poem its title and its central image of sanctuary. The middle cantos pass from the discipline and kindness of that training into the world, where the grown hero meets ambition, society and a love that threatens the allegiance formed in the forest. The argument resolves not by dramatic catastrophe but by a returning sense of obligation to Providence and to the retreat that saved the child. Descriptive and reflective passages interrupt and enlarge the story, so that the fable carries a sustained argument about grace and gratitude. The close confirms the sanctuary as a moral as well as a physical place.
works.significance: The poem is the index of a reputation that was drifting toward the sentimental and the occasional; reviewers who had treated the earlier volumes as sweet now had to address a Spenserian romance with a theological argument. Its celebration of the religious house as sanctuary sits oddly with the anti-monastic current of an age formed by Gothic fiction, and that friction is its most interesting feature. Its later eclipse measures how fast the long moral poem passed out of fashion before the 1830s.
works.meter: Written in Spenserian stanzas, a choice that aligns the poem with the romance measures then being revived by the older generation of narrative poets; the stanza's closing alexandrine is used for reflective weight, and the caesura is managed for devotional pause.
works.context: It appeared after a decade in which its author had published lyrics, translations and shorter narratives, and marks her attempt to be read as a poet of sustained moral narrative rather than of occasional feeling. Its providential plot answers the age's taste for Catholic romance while insisting on a plainly Protestant devotional temper. A revised second edition in 1829 shows that the longer poem carried her name into a different critical category.
works.structure: Six continuous cantos, each opening from a different vantage and returning periodically to the sanctuary; the plot of preservation is interwoven with lyric invocation and moral reflection rather than driven by incident.

works.title: The Forget-Me-Not
altTitles: The Forget Me Not: A Christmas and New Year's Present
works.form: Literary annual and keepsake verse: the miniature lyric and the sentimental prose sketch arranged for gift presentation with engraved plates.
works.description: The first of the English literary annuals proper, a small ornamented gift book issued for the Christmas season of 1823 and continued for some years afterwards. It established the pattern the trade would make famous: a finely bound volume, a plate or plates of the fine arts, and a miscellany of short poems and prose sketches of sentiment, presented as a token of affection to be given rather than bought for reading. It belongs to the moment when the steel engraving and the seasonal gift created a new market for Romantic verse.
works.plot: The volume has no continuous argument; its design is a sequence of lyrical pieces on memory, parting and affection, and of brief prose tales of sentiment and historical colour, each framed to the plate it accompanies. Its titles and its emblematic device announce its subject: remembrance, the transience of feeling and the keeping of tokens between the absent.
works.significance: It is the prototype of the English literary annual, the object that began the gift-book economy through which much Romantic and early-Victorian verse reached its readers, and a necessary starting point for any account of the annual as a form. Its miniature aesthetic, addressed to memory and affection, defines the tone later critics associate with the annuals.
works.meter: Predominantly short lyric in song and sonnet measures, with simple rhyme schemes and a soft meditative register; prose in familiar sentimental style.
works.context: Issued at the opening of the annuals' decade, when improved steel engraving, the book trade's expansion and a new etiquette of gift-giving created demand for seasonally dated volumes. It precedes by five years the foundation of the great commercial annual and shows the form's origins in topographical and decorative publishing rather than in literary editing.
works.structure: Annual anthology miscellany: emblem plate, then an unbroken succession of short poems and prose sketches, without editorial argument.
works.attributionNotes: The volume was issued without a named editor. Its editorship has been popularly assigned to a celebrated poetess of the following decade, but the attribution rests on tradition rather than on documentary evidence and is now generally doubted; the volume is therefore recorded as anonymous.

works.title: The Forging of the Anchor
altTitles: The Forging of the Anchor: A Legend of the Bay of Carrick
works.form: Ballad and Popular Song; Lyrical Ballad and Popular Stanza
works.description: A vigorous industrial ballad published in a leading Edinburgh periodical in February 1832, the poem that made its author's reputation as an English verse-writer in Ireland before he was twenty-two. The scene is a forge on the Bay of Carrick, where a huge anchor for a ship of war is welded by a squad of smiths, and the labour of the anvil is joined to a story of love, rivalry, and death. Its bounding measure and its technical vocabulary of work made it at once celebrated and much quoted.
works.plot: The poem opens on the forge-fire and the band of smiths at Carrick, mustered to weld an anchor for the service of the navy, and it follows the labour through its stages of heating, welding, and dipping with an insistent chorus of action. A love-plot runs beneath the industrial frame: the smith's winning of the maiden whose favour is at stake, the rivalry of a proud companion, and the catastrophe which brings the work of the anchor into contact with drowning and with death. The poem's closing movements unite the forged metal and the human fate, the anchor holding where the affections failed. The diction is deliberately muscular and technical, the labour terms and the bay place-names carrying the poem's local pride.
works.significance: The Forging of the Anchor is the founding poem of the Irish academic verse tradition in English and the instance most often cited of a Romantic-period ballad that makes industrial labour itself its subject and its music. It remains a standard anthology piece and a touchstone for the argument that the ballad revival passed into a national poetry of work.
works.meter: A strongly accented, fast-running ballad measure with burdens and refrains, close to the bagatelle and the street stave, and much praised for the way its line mounts the physical work of the hammer; the stanza is regular and the rhyme pressing.
works.context: Published in the period when the Ulster and Dublin magazines were attempting a national poetry in English. A reviewer of the leading Scottish magazine school first noticed the poem and made the author's name. The anchor forged for a ship of war belongs to the working smithing and ship-supply economy of the Irish Sea coast in the 1820s, and the poem's technical pride is of an Ulster artisan world.
works.characters: the foreman smith of the forge; the maiden whose love is contested; the rival smith; the crew and the drowned of the bay legend
works.structure: A single continuous ballad in numbered sections, built on recurrent refrain and on the staged progress of the forging, with the love and rivalry plot interwoven rather than sequentially opposed to it.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship and undisputed; the poem appeared in a periodical, where its author was initially unknown to many readers, and was afterwards collected in his verse volume of the 1860s.

works.title: The Form of Living
works.description: Richard Rolle's English epistle of spiritual guidance, written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, the anchoress of Ainderby, and the most influential of his English works: a rule of the devout life in twelve chapters, from the love of God and the practice of prayer through the discernment of true contemplation to the joy of the heavenly song. It became the classic handbook of English anchoresses after Ancrene Wisse.
works.plot: Addressed to Margaret 'in the form of living', the epistle teaches the love of God above all things, the exercise of prayer and meditation on the Passion, the temptations and consolations of the solitary life, and the discernment of the true 'song' of contemplation from delusion.
works.significance: The bridge between Ancrene Wisse and the fifteenth-century devotional manuals, and the classic of the Rolle tradition in English.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative prose of the Rolle school.
works.context: Written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, recluse of Ainderby, in the last year of Rolle's life; the most widely copied of his English writings, it circulated into the fifteenth century and was printed by Wynkyn de Worde.
works.characters: Rolle (writer); Margaret Kirkby (addressee)
works.structure: Twelve short chapters of practical and mystical instruction, in the epistle form of the Rolle canon.
works.attributionNotes: Rolle's authorship secure.
sources: Selected Prose of John Hamilton Reynolds

works.title: The Forme of Cury
works.description: The earliest English cookery collection: some 200 recipes compiled c. 1390 by the master cooks of King Richard II, from potages and roasted meats to the subtleties and spiced dishes of the royal table, including the first English recipe for pasta ('macrows') and dishes with olive oil. It is the foundation document of English culinary literature.
works.plot: The collection proceeds from the 'furmenty' and potages through flesh and fish days to the elaborate final courses, with the spices of the East (saffron, cloves, mace) and the French culinary vocabulary of the court marking the recipes' royal provenance.
works.significance: The first English cookbook and the classic document of medieval English courtly cuisine; its recipes are still cooked by food historians today.
works.meter: Prose: terse, practical recipe English with French technical terms.
works.context: Compiled c. 1390 by the chief master cooks of Richard II, and preserved in the manuscript BL Additional MS 5016 (with the closely related manuscripts of the Curye on Inglysch group); first printed by Samuel Pegge (1780).
works.characters: none (recipe collection)
works.structure: A recipe collection in the medieval cookbook tradition, organized by course and occasion, with the royal headnote claiming its authority.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous (compiled by the king's cooks).
sources: The Rights of All (New York, 1829): Digitised Run, Chronicling America

works.title: The Fortunes of Men
works.description: A poem of 98 lines cataloguing the fates that befall men — one dies young, one by the sword, one from a fall, one on the gallows; the hawk dies, the wolf mourns, the singer is praised — closing with the assurance that God apportions all gifts. A companion to The Gifts of Men.
works.plot: The poem surveys the deaths and destinies of men (and, in an admired passage, of a hawk), then turns to the arts — one man learns song, one harp, one the law — and concludes that the Measurer shapes each man's lot, bestowing craft, wealth, and wisdom as he will.
works.significance: A finely crafted example of the catalogue poem and of the period's providential view of human diversity.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 87a-88b), following Widsith.
works.characters: none
works.structure: A double catalogue (fates, then gifts) closed by a doxological gnome on divine providence.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
sources: Encyclopedia of the Enlightenment

works.title: The Fortunes of Nigel
altTitles: The Fortunes of Nigel; or, Nigel Olifaunt of that Ilk
works.form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of the Jacobean metropolis
works.description: A historical romance of the reign of the first British king, in which a poor young laird of a Scottish house goes up to London to prosecute a claim at court and is thrown among the money-lenders, goldsmiths and players of the Jacobean capital. Its subject is the fortune of a dependent and a kingdom: a Scotch estate, a pawned jewel, a court favourite's malice, and the cause of an injured house which the king must finally judge. The romance is the most concentrated study of the new British politics after 1603 that the series contains, and it treats the transaction of land for money as the real event of the age. Its London topography and its portraits of a famous king and a famous goldsmith have been much quoted.
works.plot: A young Scottish laird, sent to London to secure the repayment of a debt owed to his house by the crown, finds his estate threatened by a court favourite, is arrested for debt, and is befriended by a goldsmith of the Exchange whose credit and whose household he endangers. A diamond pledged and lost, a suit of wrong, a duel, and the protection of the king himself carry the cause from the counting-house to the council, and the Scottish claimant is finally preferred while the favourite is discountenanced. The lower world of London law-writers, actors and money-lenders carries on the same argument in the by-plot.
works.significance: The most important of the series' romances of the British union and one of the earliest historical novels to make credit, pawn and legal suit the motive force of its plot. It is a standard document for the study of the representation of London, of Scottish migration to the English capital, and of the fiction of money in the 1820s.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; Scottish speech for the hero and his countrymen, and a city idiom of trade, law and the playhouse for the London chapters
works.context: Published in 1822, it uses the removal of a Scottish court to London after 1603 as a study of the union in practice, of the crown's dependence on merchants' credit, and of the favourites and suits which then determined fortunes. Its treatment of a king famously wrote, argued, and favoured supplies a political anatomy of the early British state, and the tale's money-lending and pawnbroking world reflects contemporary debate about credit, debt and the opening of professions to those formerly restricted.
works.characters: A young laird of a Scottish house; King James; the goldsmith to the Exchange and his household; a favourite of the court who wrongs the Scottish family; a law-writer, actors and money-lenders of London
works.structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, with a single hero's cause as its spine and a fully realised urban by-plot; the king's conversations and the goldsmith's house supply the two poles of the design.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute over authorship.

works.title: The Fortunes of Perkin Warbeck: A Romance
works.form: Historical novel and romance; a tragedy of imposture, legitimacy and dynastic extinction.
works.description: A historical romance on the impostor who personated one of the vanished princes of the house of York, and on the fall of that house after Bosworth. The tale treats the pretender as a gentleman bred to a name he never fairly held, and reads the Tudor settlement as the extinction of an aristocratic and romantic order. Its materials are the chronicles, the ballads and the drama that had long handled the same story; its interest is moral rather than evidential.
works.plot: Perkin Warbeck, an unhappy child of a Kentish household, is marked out by a patron of the Yorkist cause, instructed in the part he is to act, and acknowledged as one of the princes believed murdered in the Tower. He is welcomed by the duchess of Burgundy, married to a Scottish gentlewoman while the Scottish king plays the cause for his own advantage, and led through insurrection in Cornwall, through the siege of a northern town and through the mercy of a court he had hoped to inherit. Henry the Seventh's policy narrows about him; he is taken, pardoned, again entrusted and again convicted, and dies at Tyburn, while the romance's closing chapters follow the extinction of the house whose name he wore.
works.significance: An important late instance of the historical romance by a writer whose earlier fiction had reshaped the gothic tale, and a study of identity, adoption and legitimacy conducted through dynastic material. It supplies evidence of how the school of national romance was adapted to a tragic and feminine moral interest. It is now chiefly studied for its treatment of imposture and of the claims of the disinherited.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a formal romantic narrative with quoted ballad and chronicle phrase.
works.context: Written in the later 1820s, when the historical romance of the previous generation had become the dominant model for fiction on national subjects and when the pretender's story had been revived by drama and by ballad editing. The novel's Yorkist sympathy continues a tradition of dynastic romance rather than the new Whig history. It was published in the year of the French revolution that closed the post-war settlement.
works.characters: Perkin Warbeck; Margaret, duchess of Burgundy; Katherine Gordon; James IV of Scotland; Henry VII; the patron who frames his identity
works.structure: Third-person historical romance in three volumes, with ballad and chronicle material absorbed into the narrative and with an epigraphic apparatus; a rise-and-fall structure keyed to the pretender's claims.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the author of an earlier tale; authorship undisputed. Not to be confused with the seventeenth-century chronicle play on the same subject already held in this corpus.

works.title: The Four Elements
altTitles: A New Interlude and a Mery, of the Nature of the Four Elements
works.description: John Rastell's pedagogical interlude on the four elements and the new geography, printed by the author c. 1520; the first English play designed to teach natural science.
works.plot: Humanity, instructed by Nature and Studious Desire, is taught the four elements, the roundness of the earth, and the new-found lands of America; he is then tempted by Sensual Appetite into the tavern, where he wastes his learning in drinking, and the fragment (the play survives incomplete) breaks off with Experience promising his restoration.
works.significance: The first English play to teach science and geography, and a pioneering attempt to harness the stage to the new learning; it documents the arrival of the Age of Discovery in English popular culture.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Printed c. 1520 by Rastell, More's brother-in-law, who had himself attempted a voyage to the New World in 1517; the play's geography lesson celebrates the discovery of America, and its music survives in the unique fragment (British Library).
works.characters: Nature; Humanity; Studious Desire; Sensual Appetite; Experience; Ignorance; The Taverner
works.structure: A morality framework used for instruction: a series of lectures on cosmology and geography alternating with scenes of temptation and fall, with songs (including one with music) and a dance.

works.title: The Four PP
altTitles: The Play Called the Four PP
works.description: John Heywood's best-known farce, a lying contest among a Palmer, a Pardoner, a Pothecary, and a Pedlar; the earliest surviving edition is that of William Middleton, c. 1544.
works.plot: A Palmer, Pardoner, and Pothecary each boast of his trade and its profits, and the Pedlar proposes a contest: whoever tells the greatest lie wins the wager. The Pothecary's tale of a marvellous cure and the Pardoner's account of a soul released from hell's pains — capped by the Palmer's claim that he has met a woman patient and uncomplaining — end the contest, the Palmer winning the palm and the company concluding in good fellowship.
works.significance: The most famous of the Tudor interludes and the classic English stage farce before Shakespeare; its tale of the woman patient in all things circulated into later jest-books and remains the play by which Heywood is chiefly remembered.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Composed c. 1520–30 in Heywood's period as a court entertainer and virginal player to Henry VIII; the lying contest reworks the fabliau tradition (the tale of the patient wife appears in Boccaccio) and the satire of pardons and relics reflects pre-Reformation criticism of popular piety.
works.characters: The Palmer; The Pardoner; The Pothecary; The Pedlar
works.structure: A single-scene farce built of successive set-piece tales, with the Pedlar as proposer and judge of the wager.

editions.title: The Plays of John Heywood

works.title: The Fox and the Wolf
works.description: The earliest English beast fable, a comic tale of some 300 lines in which the fox, trapped in a bucket down a well, persuades the gullible wolf that he is in paradise, and escapes by the wolf's folly. It inaugurates the English Reynardian tradition that runs to Caxton's Reynard the Fox.
works.plot: The thirsty fox climbs into one well-bucket and is stranded; when the wolf asks what he does there, the fox claims the well is paradise, induces the wolf to descend in the other bucket, and is drawn up as the wolf goes down.
works.significance: The beginning of the English Reynard tradition and the earliest English fabliau-fable; an essential witness to the continental debts of early Middle English narrative.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with lively dialogue.
works.context: Composed c. 1250–75, adapted from the French Roman de Renart; preserved in the late thirteenth-century Digby MS 86 (Bodleian Library).
works.characters: the Fox; the Wolf
works.structure: A single comic episode built on the trickster's persuasive lie and the dupe's comeuppance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: Poems

works.title: The Freeholder
altTitles: The Freeholder: a Collection of Papers
works.description: Addison's late political essay paper, written in support of the Hanoverian settlement during the Jacobite rising of 1715 and addressed to the freeholder electorate; it argues the case for limited property-based liberty against both arbitrary power and popular licence.
works.plot: A freeholder addresses his constituents and a succession of imaginary opponents, tracing the constitution from the feudal conquest, defending the settled succession, and warning that a standing army, Jacobite intrigue and the demagogic temper threaten the same liberty from opposite sides.
works.significance: It became a standard textbook of the moderate Whig constitutional argument, reprinted in America through the 1760s and 1770s as an elementary school of British liberty.
works.meter: Clear argumentative prose of the Spectator manner, with heavy use of balanced pairs, historical example and closing sententiae.
works.context: Published during and immediately after the '15 rising, in the season of Whig pamphlet warfare that also produced Swift's and Steele's party papers and Addison's breach with Steele over The Drummer's circle.
works.characters: the freeholder-writer; the party opponent; the Jacobite conspirator
works.structure: A short serial of letter-like papers addressed to a named friend or to the freeholders, each taking up one branch of the argument, with an inserted historical dissertation.
works.attributionNotes: Addison's authorship is uncontested, though the paper was issued without his name; his official connection with the administration has encouraged readers to treat it as ministerial writing.

editions.title: The Spectator, 4 volumes

works.title: The Friend
works.form: Periodical essay and moral-critical miscellany in the line of the Spectator papers, transformed by the Romantic habit of self-analysis and by the projector's account of his own enterprise.
works.description: A weekly literary and moral sheet conducted by the author at his own risk between 1809 and 1810, and reissued in an enlarged edition in 1812, in which the essayist addressed a small circle of subscribers on character, ambition, marriage, the duties of the young, the politics of the day and the principles of literature. It grew out of a scheme of public lectures on government and public feeling that had failed, and it carries that origin in its habit of arguing with an imaginary audience of men of business and of men of letters. The numbers mix moral meditation, literary criticism, autobiography and editorial matter, and the enterprise lost its projector money.
works.plot: The essays proceed by proposition and appeal rather than by narrative: the writer states the condition of a private mind in a public age and then examines the resources available to it - habit, principle, the example of the ancients, the discipline of a chosen occupation. Some numbers deal with the conduct of life, warning against ambition without talent and against the love of reputation, and prescribing the economy of a character to be maintained in a world of parties; others comment on the literature and the criticism of the day, on the education of the mind and on the duties of the clergy, and on public affairs, including the conduct of the war and the state of the press. The whole is framed as a manual for a young man of character, and the series ends with the projector's plain account of the failure of the scheme, which became part of the biographical record of the author's life.
works.significance: The chief monument of the author's own attempt to found a moral-literary journal, and a document of the Romantic essayist's quarrel with the market: its numbers on ambition, on the discipline of the mind and on the conduct of a public career are part of the period's preoccupation with character, and its material was later worked up in the literary autobiography of 1817.
works.meter: Prose of a dense and hortatory kind, marked by long sentences, abstract nouns and a repeated appeal to principle, with passages of narrative simplicity in the autobiographical numbers.
works.context: Founded in London in 1809 after the failure of the author's lecture course on the state of public feeling and after the collapse of his domestic and marital prospects, at a time when the weekly literary sheet was being established as a vehicle for criticism and when the author's quarrel with his collaborator's public position was beginning; its financial failure left him dependent on lecture and periodical work for years.
works.characters: The essayist-editor addressing his subscribers; the imagined young man of character for whom the series is a manual; the friends and correspondents whose letters are inserted
works.structure: A serial periodical of weekly numbers, gathered into a volume at the close of the first series and enlarged in the second edition of 1812; the numbers are free-standing, with a continuity of voice and of purpose rather than of argument, and with occasional letters and contributions from correspondents.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; a few inserted letters and contributions by correspondents are distinguished from the projector's own matter in modern editions.

works.title: The Fudge Family in Paris
altTitles: The Fudge Family in Paris; and Other Poems
works.form: Comic verse epistle and travel satire, in the tradition of the tourists' letter and of Regency light political verse.
works.description: A verse epistolary comedy in which a middling English family reports its first season in Paris after the peace, published under the same pseudonymous Irish correspondent used for the earlier letter-poems. It reprints and frames letters from the British tourist in Paris, adding an account of the spoliated collections and of the politics of the Restoration city. Its humour depends on the gap between the family's patriotic confidence and what it actually sees.
works.plot: The letters record the family's progress through hotels, shows, sales, prefects' offices and society, each member misinterpreting French manners in a way that exposes English prejudice and greed. The father's commercial curiosity, the daughters' romantic sensibility and the young attachements of the family produce a running comedy of misreading. The volume's most sustained argument concerns the loot of European art held in Paris, and the poet anticipates the demand for its restitution. Later letters extend the satire to the diplomatic congresses and to the trading politics of post-war Britain, so that the tourist narrative becomes a general account of national character and of European reconstruction.
works.significance: It was one of the best-selling comic poems of the period and created the template for the Victorian tourists' satire in verse, remaining in print for generations in expanded editions. Its passages on the spoliation of art entered the debate that led to the restitution of the royal collections. It remains the standard illustration of how high Romantic verse and commercial light verse coexisted in the same publishing house.
works.meter: Predominantly octosyllabic and decasyllabic couplets, iambic, with inserted songs and ballad stanzas.
works.context: Published in the first season of peace travel to the continent, when Paris was crowded with English visitors and when the fate of the spoils of the public collections was a public controversy. Its politics address the restored monarchy, the Allied settlement and the commercial mood of Regency Britain. The pseudonymous Irish voice allowed the poet to satirise both English and French national vanities while his own Irish question remained implicit.
works.characters: The Fudge family; the pseudonymous Irish correspondent who reports the letters; French hosts, cicerones and officials; English tourists and speculators in Paris
works.structure: An epistolary comic sequence, loosely chronological over a single season, with additional letters supplied in later editions; the family letters are interspersed with lyric and with the correspondent's editorial comment.
works.attributionNotes: Issued under the same pseudonymous young Irish correspondent used for the earlier intercepted letter-poems; subsequent editions were enlarged by the same hand.

works.title: The Gamester
works.form: domestic and sentimental tragedy in five acts
works.description: A domestic tragedy of a gentleman undone by the gaming table, whose weakness is exploited by those about him until he destroys his family and himself. It was one of the most effective and most imitated of the century's moral tragedies and remained a stock piece of the repertory.
works.plot: Beverley, an honest man with a passion for play, is drawn on by a cheating companion and by the artifices of a serving man who wins his own ends by the ruin. His wife's remonstrances and the losses at the table drive him to despair, and he is led by a false report of her infidelity to a fatal act. The discovery of the cheat and of the innocent wife comes too late, and Beverley dies penitent on a bed of straw in the playhouse's most quoted scene of domestic ruin.
works.significance: It is the most successful of the eighteenth-century plays on the ruinous passions of the middle class and a central text of the sentimental theatre, its ending being a byword for the pathos of the domestic catastrophe.
works.meter: A grave and affective blank verse of the middle style, with the homely sentences of the domestic scenes and the long dying periods of the last act.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in February 1753, in the season of the new statutes against gaming and of the vogue for moral domestic tragedy; the writer was a periodical essayist and editor of the same years.
works.characters: Beverley the gamester; his wife; the designing servant; the cheating friend at the table; the family and the creditors of the ruin
works.structure: Five-act regular domestic tragedy, the action contracted about the game and the house, with the villainy of the inferiors supplying the machinery of the fall; the catastrophe is a death-bed discovery.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name with a dedication that argues the moral design.

works.title: The Garden
works.description: Marvell's meditation on the pleasures of a garden and the withdrawal from worldly ambition and sensual love into contemplative solitude, culminating in the famous image of the mind as a sea that 'Annihilates all that's made / To a green thought in a green shade'.
works.plot: The poem rejects the vain pursuits of ambition and the grosser pleasures of love for the superior delight of the garden, then rises to a Platonic vision of the soul's meditation and the paradise of the solitary, innocent mind.
works.significance: A central poem of retirement and contemplation in English, admired for its wit, its green imagery, and its metaphysical meditation on the mind.
works.meter: Iambic tetrameter quatrains with a serene, meditative wit and paradox.
works.context: Composed probably in the 1650s, published in Miscellaneous Poems (1681); it reflects the Neoplatonic and Epicurean ideal of retirement valued by Marvell and his contemporaries.
works.characters: the poet; the soul
works.structure: A nine-stanza lyric meditation moving from satire of worldly pursuits to celebration of the garden to visionary contemplation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; there is a Latin companion poem 'Hortus' by Marvell.

works.title: The Garden of Cyrus
altTitles: The Garden of Cyrus: Discourse on the Quincunx
works.description: The companion piece to Hydriotaphia, a learned and increasingly mystical discourse on the quincunx — the five-point arrangement — as it appears in the gardens of Cyrus, in nature, and in art, and as an emblem of cosmic order.
works.plot: Browne traces the quincunx from the Hanging Gardens of Cyrus through Roman military formations, botanical patterns, and the arrangement of the stars, arguing that the figure reveals a divine geometrical order in creation.
works.significance: A unique experiment in emblematic natural philosophy and one of the strangest and most beautiful works of English prose; it has been a touchstone for critics interested in the seventeenth-century imagination.
works.meter: Dense, incantatory prose; the concluding 'night-piece' is famous for its drowsy cadences.
works.context: Published in 1658 together with Hydriotaphia and dedicated to Nicholas Bacon.
works.structure: Five chapters of accumulating pattern and digression, ending in a nocturnal vision.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Browne; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Garden of Florence; and Other Poems
altTitles: The Garden of Florence and Other Poems
works.form: Romantic narrative verse in the Italian manner of Hunt's circle, joined to a collection of lyrics and sonnets. The form of the title poem is that of the metrical tale, colloquial, unhurried and devoted to situation and feeling rather than to incident, and it deliberately avoids the machinery and declamation of the Byronic narrative; the shorter poems continue the same interest in tenderness, music and homely detail.
works.description: Reynolds's most serious collection of verse, and the book in which his Italian narrative manner, learned from Hunt and from Boccaccio, was given its fullest scope. Its title poem, which bibliographers and earlier commentators describe as a pair of tales in verse named collectively The Garden of Florence, develops the kind of Boccaccian story that Keats was treating at the same moment in Isabella, and it stands at the head of a volume that also carries shorter poems and sonnets. Contemporary accounts of Reynolds's work single out his command of the tender and musical lyric, and the volume as a whole is the best evidence that the Cockney interest in Italian story was a shared enterprise of the group rather than Keats's possession alone.
works.plot: Scholarly accounts of Reynolds's Italian verse identify the title poem as his version of the seventh tale of the fourth day of Boccaccio's Decameron, and the earlier memorials of Reynolds describe the chief poems of the collection as taken from Boccaccio. The tale as Reynolds retells it concerns an attachment that family and money forbid, the attempt to confine the woman who is loved, and her passage at last to Florence; the interest of the poem, in the manner the Cockney school had learnt from Boccaccio, is laid on feeling, tenderness and situation rather than on incident or moral judgement. The shorter poems that follow are occasional and lyrical, among them a piece on Devon which one modern account reports as Reynolds's most successful poem, and a sonnet which he had sent to Keats before printing it here.
works.significance: The Garden of Florence is the chief witness to Reynolds's attempt to make the Boccaccian tale a serious form within the Cockney school, and it is the standard evidence for the rivalry and partnership between his verse and Keats's. Its title poem and its shorter pieces show how widely the fashion for Italian story had spread by 1821, and its reception, and the survival of single lyrics from it in later anthologies, is part of the history of how that fashion was remembered and then discounted.
works.meter: The narrative is in regular rhymed English verse of the Hunt school, with an easy decasyllabic movement and a diction chosen for plainness and for closeness to speech; the shorter poems use simple lyric stanzas and the sonnet, and Reynolds is often praised for the purity of his musical effects. There is no attempt at the spikenard of the Lake school or at Byron's variety, and the effect of sameness and softness that reviewers noticed is a property of the metre as much as of the subject.
works.context: Published in 1821 by John Warren in London, the volume belongs to the last months of the London group around Hunt and to the years in which Keats's Isabella and Reynolds's own Italian tales were written in conscious emulation of one another; Reynolds alludes to Keats in its preface, and the friendship of the school days had by then become a matter of published record. The book also appears at the point when Hunt himself had left England for Italy, so that the Cockney school it represents was already dissolving.
works.characters: The lovers of the Florentine tale; the speakers of the shorter poems and sonnets
works.structure: A volume, not a single design: the long Florentine narrative occupies the first part of the book and a section of shorter poems follows it, with the title piece itself, according to the older biographical accounts, made up of two poems carried under one collective name. Within the narrative the structure is that of the plain tale in order, without frame or digression, while the minor pieces are discontinuous lyrics, sonnets and sketches whose organising principle is the sensibility of the writer rather than sequence.
works.attributionNotes: There is no doubt of Reynolds's authorship; the volume appeared in his own name and is catalogued among his works, and the only complication is that the title piece is described in the older biographical accounts as two poems published collectively under one name. No part of the book has been claimed for another writer, though the shared habits of Hunt's circle make it difficult to isolate what Reynolds owed to Keats and what Keats's contemporaries thought of as a common manner.

works.title: The Garland of Laurel
works.form: dream vision in rhyme royal and Skeltonics
works.description: Skelton's self-crowning dream vision: the poet, wandering in a forest, is brought before Queen Fame and the assembled court of the Countess of Surrey at Sheriff Hutton, where Pallas and the ladies of the court intercede for him and Fame grants him the laurel — the poem including a catalogue of his own works that is the first English poet's bibliography.
works.plot: The dreamer debates with Occupation and Fame whether he deserves the laurel; the ladies of the court, led by the Countess of Surrey, petition on his behalf; Fame crowns him, and the poet wakes to compose the envoy of praise.
works.significance: The first English poem to canonize its own author, with a bibliography of his works; a unique document of the poet's self-understanding at the Tudor court.
works.meter: Mixed rhyme royal and Skeltonic passages; the courtly and the demotic styles deliberately alternated.
works.context: Written at Sheriff Hutton in Yorkshire, in the household of the Countess of Surrey, in 1523, when Skelton's laureate claims needed the court's support against Wolsey.
works.characters: the poet; Queen Fame; Pallas; the Countess of Surrey; Occupation
works.structure: Dream vision with debate and pageant; the catalogue of the poet's works embedded in the intercession of the court ladies.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Gebir; a Spanish Romance, Poetical, in Four Books
works.form: Romance in verse: an English Spenserian romance that revives allegorical machinery, enchanted guardians and genealogical prophecy from The Faerie Queene while treating the matter as symbolic rather than narrative.
works.description: The author's first published poem, a four-book romance in Spenserian stanzas drawn from a supposed Moorish-Spanish source about an infant heir of Spain. The story mixes dynastic exile, enchanted river-gods, and a quest for water that turns out to be a quest for the poet's own blood. It is at once a late-romantic allegory and a deliberate archaism, and it established the dense, allusive manner kept for the rest of its author's career.
works.plot: Gebir, infant son of the murdered King Alphonso of Spain, is saved from his uncle's slaughter by being laid in a brazen cradle upon the waters and nursed in secret among goatherds. Grown unknown to himself, he loves his sister Gwendolin without knowing her kinship, and marches to war against the giant Dan and the Sorayzan host. A drought afflicts his army, and Gebir descends through caves of the earth to seek water from the river-gods of the Guadalete and the Genal. There he must pass the guard of the serpent Tondalu and is shown, in visionary genealogies of Spain, his own destiny. He learns that the promised stream can flow only from his own wounded heart; he slays Tondalu, is himself destroyed in the effort of the victory, and his life-giving water rises to relieve the host.
works.significance: A landmark of the romancing reaction of the 1790s, and one of the earliest English poems to treat dynastic exile and thirst as a private mythology; Swinburne and later Pre-Raphaelite readers made it the keystone of its author's reputation as a poet rather than as a prose stylist.
works.meter: Spenserian stanzas (nine lines, ababbcbcc), iambic pentameter with the closing alexandrine; archaic diction and inverted syntax throughout.
works.context: Written in the first flush of the 1790s romancing reaction and published as its author left Oxford; its withdrawn first issue made it a bibliographical rarity for a generation, and its Jacobean archaism answers the decade's taste for romance and for Spenserian revival.
works.characters: Gebir; Gwendolin; Alphonso; Dan; Tondalu; the river-spirits Guadalete and Genal
works.structure: Continuous four-book narrative romance in Spenserian stanzas, with prophetic visions and set-piece descents interrupting the linear plot; the middle books form a katabasis framed by the two outer war narratives.
works.attributionNotes: Published without the author's name; Its author acknowledged it in later life, and the 1798 date rests on bibliographical evidence rather than a dated title page.

works.title: The Genius of Oblivion and Other Original Poems
works.form: Lyric and meditative collection; personification poem, elegy and occasional verse in the sentimental manner
works.description: A volume of occasional and meditative verse by a widowed mother of five children, published with the help of her late husband's lodge and the author's first book. Its longest poem personifies oblivion as the power that veils the past and finally releases the mourner. The book marks the beginning of the most influential editorial career in American letters.
works.plot: The title poem addresses oblivion as the gentle power that draws a veil over the sorrows and the errors of the past, and asks whether remembrance is a blessing or a burden. Shorter pieces treat death, bereavement, the seasons, the duties of the survivor and the prospects of the republic. Several poems take public occasions and national subjects, and others are elegies on private losses. The volume's movement is from grief toward resignation and then toward useful labour.
works.significance: It is the first monument of a woman of letters who would dictate the taste of American households for half a century. Its treatment of oblivion and remembrance shows the psychology of sentimental verse turned to the service of bereavement. It documents the patronage economy by which women's books were first financed.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter stanzas and heroic couplets, with hymn-like shorter metres
works.context: Published in 1823 after the death of the author's husband left her without means, and supported by subscription and lodge patronage. Its appearance belongs to the first great decade of women's periodical and gift-book writing in America. Its national poems answer the post-1815 demand for a republican verse.
works.structure: Collected volume with one dominant personification poem and a company of shorter occasional pieces; no imposed sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; the authorship was established by her own later account and by the subscription records of the first edition.

works.title: The Genius of Universal Emancipation
altTitles: The Genius of Universal Emancipation and Colonization Journal
works.form: Reform periodical in the abolitionist mould: the essay-editorial combined with printed testimony, statistical extract and reprint, in a small weekly or monthly sheet.
works.description: An abolitionist monthly, and later weekly, journal begun in 1821 and continued for nearly two decades, the first periodical in the United States devoted entirely to emancipation. Its editor was a Quaker journeying agent who made the paper a clearing-house for facts about slavery: testimony, legislative reports, prices of slaves, extracts from British abolition writing and verse on the subject. Its editorial line combined immediate emancipation with a colonisation scheme, which gave it a double character and made it the school of the movement's later leaders.
works.plot: The journal's persistent argument is that American slavery must end at once and that the slaveholder's claim of property in human beings is void. Its numbers accumulate evidence rather than build a single thesis: accounts of the internal slave trade, sketches of enslaved people's condition, memorials of cruelty, arguments for the moral and economic superiority of free labour, and reports of manumission abroad. Editorially it urged the formation of state societies, the education of the free Black population and a gradual, compensated, colonisation-based plan for emancipation; it later opposed the Texas annexation war as a slaveholding project.
works.significance: It is the founding organ of the American abolitionist press before immediatism, and the best record of how the movement learned to use periodical form as evidence-gathering. Its files preserve a large body of otherwise lost verse and pamphlet matter, and its editor's practice of travelling to collect testimony set the pattern for the movement's literature.
works.meter: Plain earnest prose, with frequent quoted evidence; the journal also printed much occasional abolitionist verse in conventional stanzas.
works.context: Begun in the decade of Missouri statehood controversy, when the American Colonization Society had just been founded and when the British abolition movement supplied American reformers with models of organised publicity. The paper gave the young editor of a later and more famous abolition weekly his first apprenticeship, and its survival into the 1830s documents the transition from gradualist to immediatist argument.
works.structure: Serial monthly and later weekly: editorial essay, documentary extracts, testimony, correspondence and verse, with annual indexes; individual numbers are compilations rather than designs.
works.attributionNotes: Editorial responsibility rests with its founder, an editor who wrote most of its leading matter; the journal's extracts and reprints are of course by other hands.

works.title: The Gentle Craft
works.description: Deloney's fiction of the shoemakers' craft: the legendary origins of the 'gentle craft' in the saints and heroes who took up shoemaking — St Hugh, St Crispin and Crispianus, Sir Simon Eyre the shoemaker Lord Mayor, and the apprentice who married a king's daughter — the book that gave Dekker his Shoemaker's Holiday and the trade its mythology.
works.plot: The frame of the shoemakers' feast encloses the tales: Hugh's love for the king's daughter Winifred and his martyrdom; Crispin and Crispianus serving the king in disguise; Simon Eyre's rise to the mayoralty; and the apprentice Tom Drum's wooing of a great lady — each tale proving the craft's gentility and the shoemaker's wit.
works.significance: The classic of the craft romance — the book that made the shoemaker's bench a seat of English legend.
works.meter: Prose of Deloney's popular register, with songs and the frame's festive setting.
works.context: Published about 1597–98; its Eyre story supplied the plot of Dekker's The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599), and its craft-patriotism answered the decade's civic pride.
works.characters: St Hugh; Winifred; St Crispin; Crispianus; Simon Eyre; Tom Drum; the master shoemakers and their guests
works.structure: A frame-tale collection in the manner of the Decameron, with each story a romance or jest of the craft's legends.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Gentleman Dancing-Master
works.description: Wycherley's second comedy, a satire on affectation of French and Spanish manners, in which a would-be Spanish grandee is fooled by his daughter's suitor disguised as a dancing master.
works.plot: Monsieur de Parelle, an affecter of foreign fashions, is outwitted by St Jago, who courts his daughter Hippolita by posing as her dancing master; the plot exposes the emptiness of the gentleman's pretensions.
works.significance: An important link between Wycherley's first comedy and his two masterpieces, notable for its satire on cultural affectation.
works.meter: Prose dominant.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1672 and published in 1673.
works.characters: Monsieur de Parelle; Hippolita; St Jago; Madame Caution; Don Diego; Mrs Flareit
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy with a strong comic central figure.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Wycherley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Giaour
altTitles: The Giaour: A Fragment of a Turkish Tale
authors: George Gordon Byron, Sixth Baron Byron
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; the oriental or gothic tale poem, with the interpolated popular song and the supernatural credulity of the ballad tradition.
works.description: The first and shortest of the oriental tale poems, subtitled 'a Fragment of a Turkish Tale' and set in Greece under Turkish rule. A Christian lover has seduced and abandoned the daughter of a Turkish lord, who drowns her in the sea; the lover lives in a monastery under a curse and in terror of the dead woman's coming judgment, and is finally killed by her father in a mountain encounter. The poem establishes the outlaw, the haunted guilty self and the eastern landscape as a theatre of conscience. Its manner is not narrative continuity but a sequence of vivid fragments, songs and interpolated voices.
works.plot: The story is given in pieces and by shifting narrators: an opening description of the evening sea, the drowned girl's funeral and the mourning songs, the father's quest for revenge, and then the long encounter at the hermit's cell in which the outlaw tells his own history of seduction, desertion and the beloved's death. The Turkish lord slays him, and he dies unreconciled under the monk's curse, while the villagers declare that the vampire of the drowned girl haunts the shore. The argument is less a tale than a study of guilt without repentance, of a will that refuses the church's remedy, and of revenge as the only honour left to an eastern lord. The interpolated songs, on the happiness of the fisherman's life and on the roses and nightingales of the east, offer a lyric counterworld to the tragedy.
works.significance: It set the pattern of the verse tale, guilty hero, eastern scene and fragmented narration, that the sequel tales and the whole school of popular romance in verse imitated. It also gave the century its first great study of a conscience that refuses forgiveness, and its vampire and superstition passages fed the gothic imagination of the following decades.
works.meter: Chiefly heroic couplets in iambic pentameter, broken by interpolated songs and lyric stanzas of popular measure, with anapestic variation in the passages of supernatural terror.
works.context: Written and published within two months of the poet's separation from his wife and the public scandal that followed his departure from England, the tale converted the materials of the recent tour into a drama of unpardonable sin. The Greek cause, the Albanian court of a local pasha and the current taste for eastern scenery supplied both its subject and its market, and its success fixed the couplet-tale as the form of popular poetry for a decade. Its treatment of seduction and its hostile portraits of monastic remedy drew moral criticism from the quarterly press.
works.characters: the Giaour; the Turkish lord, father of the drowned girl; the drowned girl; the hermit of the cell; the fisherman and the Greek villagers
works.structure: A deliberately fragmentary sequence of set pieces, told now by a fisherman, now by a monk, now by the Giaour himself, with ballad songs and a concluding apostrophe on the superstitious credulity of the Greek villagers.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was revised and enlarged across several issues in the author's lifetime, and the suppressed lines concerning the heroine's fate are recorded in the variorum.

works.title: The Gifts of Men
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A catalogue poem of 113 lines celebrating the diversity of human talents as gifts of God: one man is strong, another wise, another skilled in song, hunting, navigation, smithing, or counsel. The poem's theme is that every gift comes from the Lord and none should be despised.
works.plot: The poet enumerates the many endowments distributed among mankind — physical strength, beauty, eloquence, song, learning, craftsmanship, skill in the hunt, the sea, the harp, and the council — and concludes that God, the giver of all gifts, has so ordered the world that no one possesses everything and each talent has its place.
works.significance: A major statement of the Old English wisdom tradition's social vision, and a companion piece to The Fortunes of Men; both poems treat the same theme of distributed human destiny.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the catalogue form is carried by parallel clauses of the 'sum... sum...' (one... another...) type characteristic of Old English gnomic verse.
works.context: The poem belongs to the Exeter Book wisdom tradition alongside Maxims I and II and The Fortunes of Men, with which it is often compared; it reflects the Anglo-Saxon conviction that society is knit together by complementary gifts under divine providence.
works.structure: A sustained catalogue organized by successive human activities and skills, framed by an opening assertion of God's generosity and a closing meditation on the ordered distribution of gifts.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake

works.title: The Golden Legend
works.description: William Caxton's translation of Jacobus de Voragine's Legenda Aurea, printed at Westminster in 1483: the great medieval collection of saints' lives and feasts of the church year, in nearly 450 leaves and the first English printing of the work. It became the standard English legendary for a century, reprinted repeatedly into the 1520s.
works.plot: Following the church year, the collection narrates the lives and martyrdoms of the saints — from St Andrew through the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins — with the great feasts (Advent, Christmas, Passiontide) expounded and the legends moralized for the reader's instruction.
works.significance: The great bestseller of Caxton's press and the principal English channel of the Legenda Aurea; its saints' lives nourished English devotional reading into the sixteenth century.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's mature plain style at its most ample.
works.context: Translated by Caxton from French and Latin sources and printed at Westminster in 1483, in the orthodox devotional market of pre-Reformation England; nine editions appeared by 1527, before the Reformation ended the cult of the saints it served.
works.characters: the saints of the calendar
works.structure: A calendrical legendary in the Voragine tradition, with Caxton's additions (including lives of English saints) and his prologue explaining the work's purpose.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's translation is documented in his own prologue.
