works.title: The History of the Fairchild Family
works.form: juvenile and domestic tale; the religious family history for home instruction
works.description: The most famous and the most feared of the English books for children of the nineteenth century, a history of three children and of the religious discipline of their home, published in parts beginning in 1818 and long read in every family of the middle rank. It puts before the child the whole course of a pious day, the duty, the fault, the punishment, and the forgiveness, and it carries its lesson to the verge of the terrible.
works.plot: The history sets the Fairchild children in their house in the woods, with their father and mother as the governors of a little commonwealth of which the rule is the Bible and the catechism, and it follows their lessons, their work, their play, and their sins. Its central method is the severe object-lesson: the children are taken to the remains of the body of an executed criminal, that they may see what the wages of guilt come to; they are punished with a public severity which the modern reader finds hard, and they are taught to read, to give to the poor, to visit the cottages, and to consider their own hearts. The narrative passes through the illness and the death of one of the children, the trial of the survivors, the gipsy and the beggar episodes, and the steady government of the parents, whose religion is at once tenderness and terror. Later parts carry the family forward to the growth and the trials of the survivors, and the whole book is a manual of the discipline of the soul applied to the very young.
works.significance: It is the type and ancestor of the English religious family book for children, and one of the few children's books that has become a subject of cultural history in itself: its mixture of piety, fear, and the terrible object-lesson has been read ever since as the image of a whole method of governing the young, and its influence on the children's literature of both countries, and upon the nineteenth-century conscience about education, is very great.
works.meter: Plain, urgent, unembellished narrative prose of the devotional teacher, with the direct speech of children, the solemn parental address, and the inserted hymn and scripture; its effect rests on the plainness of the moral said.
works.context: Published from 1818 by the book-seller of the religious and the fashionable trade, in the season of the evangelical family and of the tract for the young, when the religious instruction of children at home was a serious concern of the middling ranks and when the theory of the child's depravity was taught as frankly as the theory of his innocence. Its author, an officer's wife returned from India, had already written the little Indian tale, and the Fairchild books were followed by the third part and by imitations without number.
works.characters: Mr and Mrs Fairchild; Lucy, Emily, and Henry Fairchild; the poor, the gipsy people, and the dependents of the neighbourhood; the survivors of the family in the later parts
works.structure: A continuous family history in numbered chapters, published in parts and in volumes, each part a sequence of the occasions of the home, the lesson, the fault, and the consequence, with the hymns and the readings bound into the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to a single pen is uncontested; the book is nevertheless a long series rather than a fixed text, since the later parts were given out at a great interval after the first, and the many abridgements, the edited and the expurgated issues of the later century alter the text materially, so that the work is cited by part and by edition.

works.title: The History of the Peninsular War
altTitles: History of the Peninsular War, which invaded Portugal in 1807
works.form: Military and political history in the narrative manner of the period, combining official-document editing with eyewitness inquiry.
works.description: The author's monumental narrative of the war in Spain and Portugal, written from official despatches, Portuguese and Spanish sources, and the testimony of officers he interviewed at first hand. It is at once a campaign history, a defence of the Spanish and Portuguese peoples, and a partisan account of British conduct of the war. As laureate and as an old Iberian traveller, its author made the subject his own.
works.plot: The work begins with Junot's march into Portugal in 1807 and the convention of Cintra, and follows the war through Moore's retreat, Wellington's campaigns, the Sieges of Badajoz and Ciudad Rodrigo, Salamanca, Vitoria and the Pyrenees. It gives equal space to the guerrilla and to the popular rising of 1808, insisting that the peninsula's own resistance, not British generalship alone, wore the French down. It also weighs the politics of the Cortes of Cadiz, the regency, and the restored Ferdinand VII, whose treatment of his liberators the historian records with bitterness. The final volumes carry the narrative to the close of the war and the French expedition of 1823, with copious notes on sources and on disputed dates.
works.significance: The authoritative English account of the Peninsular War for a generation and a key text of romantic-era nationalism and liberal sympathy for Spain; it also documents how a poet of the 1790s turned the historical method he had learned in Brazil against the diplomacy of the Restoration.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Written in the long peace after Waterloo, when the Peninsular War was being absorbed into national memory and into Wellington's monument, and when the Holy Alliance's intervention in Spain in 1823 made the recent past an immediate political issue.
works.structure: Multi-volume chronological campaign history with substantial notes, appendices of despatches and returns, and recurring interpretive chapters on Spanish and Portuguese politics.

works.title: The History of the Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic
altTitles: The Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic
works.description: Ferguson's narrative history of Rome from its agricultural and citizen origins through conquest, civil discord, and the loss of the republic, written by the philosopher of civil society as its practical case study. It showed how the virtues that built Rome, martial spirit and public ambition, dissolved the very constitution they had founded.
works.plot: The history opens on the earliest ages, Rome's peasant militia, patrician families, and kingless commonwealth, and follows the struggle of the orders as the engine of Roman liberty. It narrates the progress of conquest, the agrarian laws, the rise of the commons and their leaders, the civil wars of Marius, Sylla, Pompey, and Caesar, and the final extinction of the republic under Augustus. Ferguson treats the dissolution not as a mere conspiracy of great men but as the structural outcome of empire without civic capacity, the corruption of the people, and the army's transfer of loyalty from the state to its generals, closing with reflections on the fate of free states.
works.significance: It became the standard Scottish reading of Rome's fall as a lesson in the political sociology of liberty, much admired in its day and read by the founders of the American republic as a mirror of corrupt commonwealths.
works.meter: A declamatory, periodic prose in the manner of the classical historians, its judgment-sentences modelled on the moralities of republican rise and decline.
works.context: Published in Edinburgh and London in 1769, a work of Edinburgh lecture culture and of the age's Roman republicanism, written in the same years as the Wilkes and parliamentary debates that made the fate of free states a live British subject.
works.characters: Romulus; the Gracchi; Marius; Sylla; Pompey; Caesar; Cicero; Augustus
works.structure: Four books of continuous narrative from the regal and early republican ages to the establishment of the monarchy under Augustus, with inserted institutional and moral reflections.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The History of the Reformation of the Church of England
works.description: Gilbert Burnet's monumental church history in three volumes (1679, 1681, 1714), which gave the Church of England an authoritative narrative of its separation from Rome and became the standard Protestant account of the Reformation.
works.plot: Burnet narrates the reigns of Henry VIII, Edward VI, and Elizabeth I, using original documents, to show the Reformation as a lawful and providential return to primitive Christianity.
works.significance: The standard English history of the Reformation for two centuries and a principal source for the Anglican identity of the Church of England.
works.meter: Clear, vigorous, plain historical prose.
works.context: Volume I published in 1679 and rewarded with a doctorate of divinity by Oxford; volume II in 1681 and volume III, posthumously, in 1714.
works.characters: Henry VIII; Thomas Cranmer; Edward VI; Elizabeth I; Thomas Cromwell; Thomas More
works.structure: Three volumes of narrative history with collections of documents appended.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Burnet; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The History of the Reign of the Emperor Charles V
altTitles: History of the Reign of Charles V
works.description: Robertson's imperial history of Charles V and the European states system, built on the Habsburg archival and printed materials he was among the first English historians to exploit. It made the age of the Reformation and the Habsburg-Valois wars intelligible as the birth of the modern balance of power, and became the most admired British history of the decade in several languages.
works.plot: Robertson narrates the accession and inheritance of Charles, the rivalries with Francis I of France, the Turkish pressure on the empire, and the German religious division from Luther to the Peace of Augsburg, showing how the dream of universal monarchy collapsed against the particular liberties of princes and nations. He treats the Reformation as high politics: the leagues, the diets, the councils, the Schmalkaldic War, and the emperor's eventual weariness and abdication. The narrative constantly weighs the springs of state, the expedients of finance, and the maxims of a balancing Europe, in set-pieces on the constitutions of the continent. The history ends on the divided inheritance and the modern states system it left behind.
works.significance: It defined the age of Charles V for generations of English readers, established the balance-of-power narrative of modern European history, and stood among the most admired works of the Scottish Enlightenment.
works.meter: The mature philosophical style: capacious periods, weighty antithesis, and the judgment of cabinets, a prose of authority with a moralist's poise.
works.context: Published in 1769 after Robertson's appointment as Historiographer Royal and years of archival research; it was translated into French, Italian, and German and read as a textbook of statecraft in the Atlantic world.
works.characters: Charles V; Francis I; Henry VIII; Luther; the princes of the Schmalkaldic League; Suleiman the Magnificent
works.structure: A continuous political and military narrative in several volumes, with separate disquisitions on the state of Europe appended in the later editions.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave-Trade, by the British Parliament
altTitles: History of the Abolition of the Slave Trade
The History of the Rise, Progress, and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the Slave-Trade
works.form: Abolitionist history and documentary testimony: a large-scale argumentative narrative built from evidence, correspondence and reported examination, in the tradition of the state-of-the-question pamphlet enlarged to history.
works.description: A monumental two-volume documentary history of the British abolition movement, written by its chief investigator and published immediately after the abolition of the trade. It combines personal narrative, evidence gathered from ships' papers and slave testimony, and the argumentative history of a quarter-century of agitation. Its purpose is at once evidential and exemplary: to prove what the trade was, and to show how a moral crusade succeeded through organisation, enquiry and patient publication.
works.plot: The work opens on the geography, commerce and human character of Africa and then documents the mechanism of the trade with an accumulating mass of testimony about the Middle Passage and the West India colonies. It traces the formation of the abolitionist committees, the parallel histories of the movement in the United States and France, the failure of the first parliamentary bills, and the long process by which public opinion, county petitions and seamen's evidence were assembled. The narrative closes with the passing of the abolition act, which the author reads as the accomplishment of a moral revolution carried out by the British people. Throughout, the author's own research interviews and voyages of enquiry function as the movement's first documented fieldwork.
works.significance: It is the foundational documentary history of British abolition and one of the largest works of argumentative prose in Romantic-period reform writing, a model for the movement's later reliance on accumulated testimony. Its evidence remains a standard source for the history of the slave trade and its critique of commercial innocence speaks to Romantic writing about empire, sympathy and the moral economics of consumption.
works.meter: Prose of plain, earnest periodicity, with long quoted evidence passages; no verse.
works.context: Written after twenty years of enquiry, petitions and pamphlet war and published in the year the abolition act took effect, at a moment when the movement needed both a record and a defence against planter counter-argument. It preserves evidence collected earlier and answers sceptics who claimed the trade was humane or economically necessary.
works.structure: Chronological and evidential history in two volumes, with books within volumes: state-of-Africa and state-of-the-trade material first, then the agitational history, then the parliamentary accomplishment; documentation and testimony are woven into the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution is certain and the work is signed; its factual claims have been tested by later historians, with some corrections to dates and roles, but the work itself is not disputed.

works.title: The History of the Royal-Society of London for Improving of Natural Knowledge
works.description: Thomas Sprat's official history of the Royal Society, commissioned by the Society itself, which defends the new experimental philosophy against its critics and sets out the ideal of a plain, unadorned prose suited to the reporting of fact.
works.plot: Part I surveys the history of learning and the corruption of philosophy; part II describes the Society's constitution, methods, and achievements; part III answers the objections of the schools, the wits, and the clergy.
works.significance: The principal source for the early history of the Royal Society and the classic statement of the ideal of plain prose that dominated English non-fiction for a century; it has been a touchstone in the history of scientific writing.
works.meter: Elegant but plain prose; the famous passage on the Society's resolution to reject 'swelling of style' and to use 'a close, naked, natural way of speaking' became the manifesto of the plain style.
works.context: Published in 1667, five years after the Society's charter; Sprat was a chaplain and Fellow who had access to the Society's records and to Evelyn and Wren.
works.characters: Francis Bacon; Charles II; the Fellows of the Royal Society
works.structure: Three parts in a continuous history and defence.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Sprat; the work was commissioned and corrected by the Society.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The History of the World
works.description: Ralegh's great history, written during his imprisonment in the Tower: the story of the world from the Creation to the end of the Macedonian empire, told as the record of God's providence over kingdoms — with the famous preface's meditation on death ('O eloquent, just, and mighty Death!') and the running argument that the wise man serves God, not fortune.
works.plot: The five books move from the Creation and the patriarchs through Egypt, Assyria, and Persia to Greece and Alexander; the rise and fall of each empire demonstrates the providence that raises and casts down; and the closing books and the preface frame the whole as counsel to princes and consolation to the prisoner.
works.significance: The great English history of the Renaissance — the prisoner's summa of providence and power that Milton and Cromwell's generation read as scripture of state.
works.meter: Prose of grave sententiousness — the prison's composure in every period.
works.context: Written 1603–14 in the Tower, dedicated to Prince Henry, and published in 1614; James I is said to have disliked it as 'too saucy in censuring princes', and the book was suppressed after Ralegh's fall.
works.characters: Adam; Noah; Moses; the kings of Egypt, Assyria, and Persia; Alexander the Great; the historical actors of the five books
works.structure: A universal chronicle in the classical and biblical tradition, organized by empire, with the author's moral reflections interlacing the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Sir Walter Ralegh: The History of the World

works.title: The History of the Worthies of England
works.description: Fuller's great county-by-county biographical and antiquarian survey of the notable men and women of England, with descriptions of each county's natural resources, wonders, and families; it was published posthumously in 1662.
works.plot: Each county is treated in a uniform sequence: its natural commodities, manufactures, wonders, battles, families, and memorable persons, with biographical notices of its 'worthies'.
works.significance: A foundational work of English local history and biography, and the source for countless later antiquarians; it remains in use as a biographical reference.
works.meter: Fuller's characteristically digressive, witty, and compressed prose.
works.context: Written during the Commonwealth and published in 1662, after Fuller's death in 1661; it is the first systematic topographical and biographical dictionary of England.
works.structure: An alphabetical arrangement by county with a general introduction.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Fuller; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling
works.form: comic novel in prose, in the manner of a comic epic in eighteen books
works.description: The author's masterpiece and the most completely designed English novel of the century, the history of a foundling's education in good-nature and in error, from the country house of his benefactor through the road and the great city to the discovery of his birth. Each of its eighteen books opens with a chapter of critical preface.
works.plot: Tom, an unknown child taken in by the wealthy Allworthy, grows up generous, hot-blooded and imprudent, and is opposed by the artful Blifil and instructed by the tutor Thwackum and Square. His love for Sophia is cross'd by her family's design on her for another; he is expelled, she runs away, and both travel to London by separate adventures. There Tom's errors culminate in an imprisonment and a near-execution, and the discovery that he is Allworthy's own sister's son clears his title to the estate and to Sophia.
works.significance: It is the touchstone of the theory of the novel as a formally ordered art, its design and its analysis of good-nature and prudence setting the terms of discussion from the eighteenth century to modern criticism.
works.meter: A commanding narrative prose of balanced period and pointed irony, capable of the colloquial energy of the road and the oratory of the prefatory essays; dialogue is sharply differentiated by class and profession.
works.context: Composed after the author's marriage and during his essays on administration and society, and published in 1749 in the season of the riotous rejoicing over the peace and of the street disturbances which the novel's London scenes use.
works.characters: Tom Jones; Squire Allworthy; Blifil; Sophia Western; Mrs. Western; Thwackum; Square; Lady Bellaston; Jenny Jones and her husband
works.structure: Eighteen books in three great movements - country, road, London - with a doubled chronology and an elaborate chain of discoveries; the prefatory chapters form a parallel argument on the writing of comic history.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and documented in his correspondence and in the contemporary reviews.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Holy Fair
works.form: comic-descriptive tale-poem with allegorical debate, in the Scottish rambling tradition of Ramsay's Christ's Kirk
works.description: Burns's great comic survey of a Church of Scotland communion preaching in the open air, in which the religious solemnity of the Holy Fair is matched against the thronging, drinking, courting and quarrelling of the field. The poem frames the scene as the vision of a ploughman homeward on a moonlit night, and lets three personae of the fair - religion, interest and fancy - contend for the meaning of what he has seen. It is the most complete poetic record of Scottish communion-season culture and one of the most sustained satires of enthusiasm in the century.
works.plot: The poet, riding homeward at moonlight, recalls the scene of the preaching: the crowd spread over the braes, the preacher working the auditors with the terrors of the law and the glories of the gospel, the professional religionists scanning each other for signs of grace, and the young people making their own business of the day. The allegorical voices of Religion, Interest and Fancy then dispute the event, Religion pleading for the seriousness of the doctrine, Interest for its worldly uses, and Fancy for the human spectacle of appetite and mirth. The poem closes with the ploughman's sober re-entry into common life, leaving the value of the fair undecided.
works.significance: It supplies the classic literary account of the Scottish communion season and remains a primary source for the social history of Scottish popular religion. Its mixture of dialect realism, allegory and comic detachment made it a landmark of the preromantic interest in vernacular popular spectacle, and its portraits of the preacher and of the audit of grace have become standard.
works.meter: Stanzaic Scots in long running measures of four- and three-beat lines with a brisk rhyme and much colloquial idiom, adapted to the tune known as Cherry and Cream; the allegorical sections keep the same narrative pace.
works.context: Rooted in the communion preachings of the Ayrshire and Scottish west, seasonal events that drew thousands to the fields and were notorious for their profane diversions, and in the contemporary debate about enthusiasm, Methodist and evangelical preaching and the suspicion of religious enthusiasm. Burns's own experience of the revival at Kirkoswald and his acquaintance with the lay preaching of the period give the poem its technical accuracy.
works.characters: The ploughman-speaker; the preacher of the sermon; the sitters of the audit; Religion, Interest and Fancy as speaking abstractions; the courting country folk
works.structure: A framed narrative: a moonlit opening scene with the ploughman, the long descriptive middle on the preaching and the crowd, an allegorical tripartite dispute, and a brief closing retirement of the spectator.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Burns revised the poem across editions and his authorship of the earlier and later states of the text is documented in his correspondence and memoranda. The precise date of first composition is not fixed, and the range entered here follows the usual scholarly reckoning.

works.title: The Holy State and the Profane State
works.description: Thomas Fuller's most popular work, a book of 'characters' describing the ideal states of the church, the family, the court, and the commonwealth, followed by the contrary vices of the profane state.
works.plot: The first part describes the good parson, the good husband, the good magistrate, the good soldier, and the like; the second part describes their profane opposites; the third part gives the history of the Church from the creation.
works.significance: The most influential English collection of characters after Earle and the principal model of the pithy, aphoristic prose style that Johnson imitated.
works.meter: Fuller's characteristic pithy, epigrammatic, punning prose.
works.context: Published in 1642, on the eve of the civil wars, and dedicated to the Lady Montagu; it was reprinted throughout the century.
works.characters: the good parson; the good husband; the good magistrate; the good soldier; the good merchant; their profane opposites
works.structure: A series of short character-pieces followed by a historical narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Fuller; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Holy War Made by Shaddai upon Diabolus, for the Regaining of the Metropolis of the World
works.description: Bunyan's second great allegory, a military and spiritual epic of the town of Mansoul, built by Shaddai, captured by Diabolus, and recovered by his son Emmanuel; it is a complex allegory of the soul's fall and redemption.
works.plot: Shaddai builds Mansoul and gives it law; Diabolus besieges and takes it; Emmanuel, Shaddai's son, wages war to recover it, captures and pardons the town, and appoints officers; Diabolus returns by stealth and the town must be continually defended.
works.significance: Bunyan's most ambitious and most learned allegory, and a major work of Puritan theology in narrative form; it has been judged more complex but less popular than The Pilgrim's Progress.
works.meter: Plain prose with an elaborate allegorical nomenclature and occasional verses.
works.context: Published in 1682 with a copperplate frontispiece, four years after Part I of The Pilgrim's Progress, and dedicated to the reader in an allegorical address.
works.characters: Shaddai; Emmanuel; Diabolus; the Lord Secretary; Captain Credence; Mr Conscience; Mr Recorder; the captains Boanerges; the towns of Mansoul
works.structure: A prose epic in four parts with an allegorical cast of named officers, captains, and townspeople.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bunyan; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Honest Whore, Part 1
works.description: Dekker and Middleton's comedy of conversion: the courtesan Bellafront, courted by all Milan, is converted to virtue by the grief of her rejected suitor Hippolito; the madhouse of Bethlehem, where her father Anselmo feigns madness to save her, supplies the play's great scene; and the play ends with her marriage to the patient Matheo — the first part of the diptych continued in Part 2 (c. 1605).
works.plot: Bellafront plies her trade until Hippolito's lament and her father's disguise break her heart; her conversion, the testing of her suitors, and the schemes of the pander and the courtiers follow; the scene in Bedlam, with the madmen's pageant of the city's vices, is the play's moral centre; and the final act restores Bellafront to marriage and her father to peace.
works.significance: The great Elizabethan-Jacobean comedy of conversion — the play that made the 'honest whore' a type of the English stage's moral theatre.
works.meter: Prose and verse in the two authors' distinct registers, with the madmen's speeches as the play's most quoted passages.
works.context: Performed by Prince Henry's Men in 1604 and printed the same year; the Bedlam scene answered the vogue for madhouse shows, and the play's reform of the whore answered the city's moralists.
works.characters: Bellafront; Hippolito; Matheo; Anselmo (disguised as the madman); Candido the linen-draper; the Duke of Milan; Infelice; Fluello; Castruccio; Pioratto; the madmen of Bedlam
works.structure: A five-act comedy of conversion built on the two great set pieces — the madhouse and the conversion — with the Duke's disguised progress through the city as frame.
works.attributionNotes: By Dekker and Middleton jointly, as printed; the division of scenes is debated.

editions.title: The Dramatic Works of Thomas Dekker, 4 vols.

works.title: The House of Fame
works.description: Chaucer's comic dream vision of fame and rumour (2,158 lines in octosyllabic couplets, unfinished): the dreamer is carried by a talkative eagle through the heavens to the House of Fame, where the goddess dispenses reputation with sublime arbitrariness, and on to the whirling House of Rumour where every report, true and false, takes wing. A poem about poetry, authority, and the instability of language itself.
works.plot: The dreamer, pondering the causes of dreams and the nature of fame, finds himself in a temple of Venus adorned with the story of the Aeneid; an eagle (comically garrulous, in the Dantean manner) snatches him up and lectures him on sound, air, and the physics of speech; before the House of Fame he sees the petitioners — great and small — receive arbitrary reward or oblivion; and in the twig-built, whirling House of Rumour every tiding breeds and flies; the poem breaks off as 'a man of gret auctorite' appears.
works.significance: The most brilliant medieval English poem about poetry, fame, and the circulation of language; its self-reflexive comedy anticipates the metacritical concerns of modern literature.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with colloquial verve; the eagle's lecture burlesques the didactic mode.
works.context: Composed c. 1378–80, during Chaucer's Italian-inspired middle period, drawing on Dante, Virgil, Ovid, and Boethius; the invocation promises tidings 'of love or such thinges glade' — a tease never fulfilled.
works.characters: the Dreamer (Geffrey); the Eagle; Fame; Aeolus; the suitors of Fame; the 'man of great authority'
works.structure: Three movements (the temple of Venus; the eagle's flight and lecture; the houses of Fame and Rumour), with the Aeneid and the physics of sound as its digressive armature.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure.

works.title: The Husband's Message
works.description: An elegiac poem of 54 lines in which a wooden rune-stave, carved with a message, speaks on behalf of an exiled lord to the woman he loves, recalling their former vows and summoning her to join him across the sea.
works.plot: The stave tells how its lord was forced into exile by a feud, how he longs for his lady, and how he now sends word that he has wealth and a hall prepared for her; the poem closes with a runic passage (often solved as 'sige', 'rad', and other rune-names) promising their reunion and the renewal of their vows.
works.significance: An early and sophisticated use of the speaking-object device and of runic writing as poetic material.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book, following the riddles; often paired with The Wife's Lament as complementary perspectives on exile and separated love.
works.characters: the rune-stave (speaker); the lord; the lady
works.structure: A speaking object (prosopopoeia) delivers the lord's message; the closing runic riddle has prompted attempts to read the poem as part of a composite sequence with the riddles that follow it in the manuscript.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
movements: The AB Language Group (West Midlands Devotional Prose)
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume I: c. 500–1042

works.title: The Idler
altTitles: The Idler, by the Author of The Rambler (series title)
works.form: periodical essay and character-writing in the Spectator tradition
works.description: Johnson's second periodical paper, a weekly series of short essays contributed to a London newspaper between 1758 and 1760 and afterwards collected. Its persona - a man who has resolved to do nothing and to write only what comes to him - lets Johnson examine idleness, attention, marriage, reading, hopes and fears with a lighter, more playful touch than the Rambler, while still turning each subject to moral account. The 104 papers include some of his best brief criticism and his wryest analysis of self-deceit.
works.plot: Each paper takes a single topic - the danger of sloth, the pleasure of novel-reading, the conduct of life in easy circumstances, the use of criticism, the fears of the ignorant, the duty of parents and children - and pursues it by definition, example and epigram rather than by sustained argument. The framing personae of the Idler and of his club of loungers supply a comic distance from the matter, and several numbers advertise Johnson's own habits and quarrels. The series repeatedly insists that idleness is itself a labour of the mind and that the unexamined life of ease is the most dangerous of all.
works.significance: The Idler consolidated the essay serial as a vehicle for criticism as well as morals, and the numbers on Shakespeare, on the pleasure of reading and on the vanity of expectations are among the most quoted of Johnson's shorter prose. In a lighter register it carries out the same analysis of dependence and self-knowledge that makes the Rambler serious.
works.meter: Prose; shorter and less Ciceronian periods than the Rambler, with a pointed conversational sententiousness that Johnson himself thought more readable.
works.context: Written in the same years as the Dictionary and the Rambler, for a new newspaper venture that needed established hands; Johnson's authorship was recommended by the reputation of the Rambler and his papers were read as a continuation of the Addison-Steele serial, from which they differ by their scepticism about politeness.
works.characters: The Idler; the members of his club; the correspondents of the occasional papers
works.structure: A serial periodical of 104 weekly papers, first issued from 1758 within a newspaper and later gathered in volumes; the numbers are free-standing, with only a slight continuity of personae.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the Yale edition records the very few papers doubtfully assigned to other hands.

works.title: The Iliad of Homer
altTitles: The Iliad of Homer Translated from the Greek
works.description: Pope's complete translation of the Iliad, issued in parts by subscription and then in volumes: the most commercially successful and most criticised English Homer, which recast Greek epic as Augustan heroic couplet and as a national monument.
works.plot: The translation follows Homer's argument from the plague and the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon through the great battles, the embassy, the death of Patroclus and the vengeance on Hector, to the ransoming of the body, with the accompanying scholarly notes and the essay on the genius and writings of Homer.
works.significance: For a century it was the English Homer, the book by which the epics were known to readers of verse; at once the monument of Augustan neoclassicism and the translation that later critics, from Blake to the Victorian Hellenists, chose to destroy.
works.meter: Heroic couplet sustained over the longest English poem of the century, with the epic simile compressed into the closed pair and the line-end made the unit of judgment.
works.context: Subscribed for at the height of the war's aftermath and of the classical vogue, it was attacked for its fidelity by Bentley and by the scholars, defended by the fashionable, and made the centre of the quarrel over the study of the ancients; its subscription model also made Pope the century's first profiting English poet.
works.characters: Achilles; Hector; Agamemnon; Patroclus; Priam; Homer as the translated author
works.structure: A book-by-book verse translation of the twenty-four books of the Iliad, published in installments and collected in volumes, each with argument, notes and classical apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Pope's own hand, working with a library of Latin, French and English commentators and with the help of friends on the notes; the verse translation itself is not divided among several writers.

editions.title: The Poems of Alexander Pope, Twickenham Edition (11 volumes)

works.title: The Imitations of Horace
works.description: Pope's free translations of Horace's satires and familiar epistles, in which the Roman poet's circle becomes the poet's own: a sequence of personated self-defence, retirement and judgment on the age.
works.plot: Taking one Horatian poem after another, the speaker reports his own life among his friends and patrons, answers his enemies, refuses the offers of the great, and turns the ancient dialogue into an account of the modern writer's independence.
works.significance: It redefined imitation as a modern mode of citation and self-portraiture, and it is the century's fullest demonstration that the ancients could be occupied rather than copied.
works.meter: Heroic couplet made colloquial and broken by the dialogue line, the interruption and the narrative aside, in deliberate contrast to the close cadence of the Essay on Criticism.
works.context: Written across the later 1730s, after the failure of the last Scriblerian projects and in the years when the Licensing Act and the defeat of the administration changed the relation of the writer to party and patronage; Horace supplied the model of a private friendship publicly defended.
works.characters: Horace as the personated speaker; Pope; the friend; the patron; the importunate poetaster; the bookseller
works.structure: A serial of separately printed imitations, each a self-contained dialogue or epistle, accumulating by recurrence of persons into an autobiography.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the mask of Horace is a deliberate prosopopoeia and the identification of the speakers with Pope's own circle has encouraged, without proving, division of hands in the earliest pieces.

editions.title: The Poems of Alexander Pope, Twickenham Edition (11 volumes)

works.title: The Improvisatrice
works.form: Collected volume dominated by a long narrative lyric romance; the governing genres are the metrical tale and the dramatic lyric of the artist-poet, with the descriptive Italian piece beside them.
works.description: The second volume and the one that fixed its author's fame, named for its long central poem on the woman of genius who sings and loves. It consolidates the persona of the professional poetess and adds the exotic romance and the historical scene to her repertoire.
works.plot: The title poem imagines an Italian singer-poetess whose art and her sex's destinies are set against each other: she is admired, used and finally silenced, while the gift that made her survives in song. The poem moves through performance, patronage, love and renunciation, and closes the biography as a monument. Other pieces record disappointed affection, the death of friends, and the consolation or insufficiency of memory. A group of descriptive lyrics turns Italy and its arts into the scenery of feeling. The volume's argument is that the improvisatrice's gift is both her only inheritance and the cause of her exposure.
works.significance: The Improvisatrice supplied the nineteenth century with its most influential image of the woman poet as popular artist and victim, a figure that later novelists and poets of the annuals reworked without cease. It is the point at which the poetess tradition becomes self-conscious, taking its own situation as its subject. Criticism of women's professional writing now treats the poem as a founding text.
works.meter: The title poem uses a stanzic iambic measure with a rapid declamatory movement and frequent triple-time openings; the lyrics keep refrained common measure and compressed direct address, all tuned for recitation.
works.context: Published by Hurst and Robinson in 1824, the volume appeared in the season when the annual and the keepsake were remaking the market for short verse, and its success made its author the model of the gifted female contributor the annuals required. Contemporary reviews were divided, praising the facility and questioning the propriety of a woman's self-exposure in print. Its fame rested heavily on transatlantic reprinting, which was by then outrunning British copyright.
works.characters: the improvisatrice, the Italian singer-poetess of the title poem, whose career of performance, patronage and renunciation the poem records
works.structure: The long title poem is a continuous biographical romance in verse, told in successive phases of the singer's career; the rest of the volume is an unordered company of lyrics and elegies repeating its situations in shorter measure.
works.attributionNotes: Much of the magazine verse gathered here had appeared over initials, and the volume itself was put out under that signature rather than the full name used for the first collection.

works.title: The Indian Princess; or, La Belle Sauvage
works.form: Musical entertainment and afterpiece: sentimental drama with songs, scene-designs and rescue spectacle, belonging to the popular London stage convention rather than to closet drama.
works.description: A two-act musical entertainment on the Pocahontas story, played in London's theatre of the Regency years and the first American-authored drama to treat a Native American heroine of the Jamestown legend as its central figure. It converts John Smith's narrative and the older stage versions of the tale into a sentimental rescue plot with songs, spectacle and a happy ending. Its interest is double: as a piece of transatlantic popular theatre, and as an early instance of the Pocahontas myth serving a romantic account of settlement and reconciliation.
works.plot: The action follows the capture of the English captain by the Virginian people, the intercession of the chief's daughter, and the reprieve at the place of execution. The heroine, raised in the forest and called La Belle Sauvage by the English, is torn between duty to her father and affection for the captive, and she resolves the conflict by a staged death and restoration that leaves the father humiliated and the lovers free. A romantic subplot between an English soldier and a Native woman doubles the theme of crossing cultural boundaries, and the piece ends in clemency and union rather than in conquest.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the American-literature stage treatment of Pocahontas and a standard example of how Romantic melodrama turned colonial history into a moral spectacle of nature-culture reconciliation. Its design is now read against the history of Indian removal and of the noble-savage tradition, and it marks the beginning of a continuous American dramatic career.
works.meter: Spoken dialogue in prose with lyric songs of conventional stanzaic measure set to the composer's music.
works.context: Written by an American for the London stage at the height of the Regency's taste for spectacle, frontier melodrama and the Indian on the theatre, and produced at a patent theatre in 1808. The Jamestown story was then a live transatlantic property, and the play draws on the same romantic material that made the Pocahontas legend a stock subject of the period.
works.characters: La Belle Sauvage; the Indian chief; the English captain; the English soldier in love with a Native woman; the treacherous attendant who engineers the false death
works.structure: Two-act afterpiece with a linear rescue plot, set pieces of spectacle, and interpolated songs that comment on the action at its emotional turning points.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by the American dramatist is established and was stated on the title page of the printed edition; the music was by the house composer of the theatre.

works.title: The Indian Queen
works.description: The first full English heroic play in rhymed couplets, set in the conquest of Mexico, written by Dryden in collaboration with his brother-in-law Sir Robert Howard.
works.plot: The Aztec prince Acacis and the Indian hero Zempoalla are caught between love and ambition in the war against the Spaniards; Zempoalla's usurpation, the sacrifice of the captives, and the intervention of the gods lead to a final resolution.
works.significance: The founding work of the English heroic drama, and the occasion of the Dryden-Howard controversy over rhyme that led to An Essay of Dramatic Poesy.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets in iambic pentameter.
works.context: Performed by the King's Company at the Theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields in January 1664 with music by Henry Purcell's teacher John Banister; the collaboration quarrel is recorded in the prefaces.
works.characters: Zempoalla; Acacis; Zempalla's son Amexia; Montezuma; Traxalla; Garrucca; the High Priest of the Sun
works.structure: Five acts with masque-like spectacle, songs, and machinery.
works.attributionNotes: The 1664 quarto names Dryden and Howard jointly; modern attribution assigns the bulk to Dryden.

works.title: The Indicator
works.form: A weekly periodical in the tradition of the Spectator papers and of Hunt's own Examiner, and one of the chief vehicles of the Romantic familiar essay. Its constituent forms are the short critical essay, the literary character sketch, the retold tale, the note on a passage of verse and the occasional poem. The paper is a miscellany rather than a review: it carries no political intelligence and no reports of Parliament, and it subordinates book-notice to the essayist's reflection, which is why it is usually classed with Elia and Table Talk rather than with the Edinburgh Review.
works.description: A weekly literary journal founded, edited and very largely written by Leigh Hunt, issued in London by Joseph Appleyard from 1819 and continued through 1820 and into 1821; its essays were also collected in a two-volume issue dated 1820 to 1821. It was Hunt's attempt to carry the manner of the Examiner into a sheet devoted to poems, tales and short critical essays, and it became one of the founding documents of the familiar Romantic periodical style. Its pages mix definitions of poetry, notices of contemporary verse, reworkings of older stories and sketches of literary character, all in a voice that treats reading as a form of friendship. The Indicator, with The Companion of 1828, is the practical demonstration of the prose Hunt theorised.
works.plot: As a periodical the paper has no argument, but its recurring proposition is that good writing is a kind of conversation and that verse and prose alike should be judged by their humanity and their ease. Numbers carry short essays on poetry and on the poets Hunt admired, reprints and redressings of Italian and English tales, notices of current books and papers of general literary instruction, together with original verse. Its practical polemic is against the hierarchical and personal manner of the great reviews: it proposes instead a criticism of sympathy, addressed to an ordinary reader who buys a penny sheet rather than a quarterly.
works.significance: The Indicator established the model of the personal literary weekly that later Romantic and Victorian periodical writing followed, and it is the place where Hunt's idea of a criticism of humanity, rather of judgement, was worked out in practice. Through it the familiar essay became a Romantic institution, setting the manner that his contemporaries and successors copied in the cheap serial press, and shaping how the generation that included his own later collectors understood the relation of verse and criticism. It also documents the economics of authorship: a poet of real distinction earning his living by a weekly sheet. As criticism it remains a key source for Hunt's judgements, for his accounts of Shakespear, Dante and his own contemporaries, and for the quarrels of the Cockney school controversy.
works.meter: Prose throughout, in Hunt's characteristic familiar manner: short sentences, colloquial vocabulary, first-person speculation and an easy alternation of seriousness and play. Verse appears within the prose in the quoted passages and in the contributed poems, and Hunt's own occasional pieces in the paper are regular in metre, mostly simple lyric or epistle. The prose rhythm is deliberately conversational, closer to spoken ease than to the periodic style of eighteenth-century prose, and it was this quality that later essayists identified as Hunt's contribution.
works.context: The Indicator belongs to the explosion of small cheap periodicals after 1815, when technological and Circulating-library growth made the weekly sheet a livelihood for professional letters, and to the aftermath of the suppression campaigns that had imprisoned Hunt for the Examiner. Its appearance coincides with the height of the Cockney School controversy, and it gave Hunt a steady income from the press and a platform independent of the great reviews that had insulted him. Its contributors and its circle overlapped with Blackwood's and the London literary world of Hazlitt, Shelley and the younger poets, and its career, like his, ended at the point when Hunt left England for Italy in 1821.
works.structure: Discontinuous and miscellany-based: a weekly sequence of short numbers, each containing several self-contained pieces, with no plot and no sustained argument across issues. The organising principle is the persona of the editor, who moves between quotation, exegesis, criticism and remonstrance within a single number. Bound runs therefore read as volumes of essays rather than as a serial narrative, and the paper's unity is one of voice, of subject-matter and of the weekly rhythm of appearance.
works.attributionNotes: The journal was published under Hunt's editorship and reference sources state that he wrote much or most of its content, though the weekly numbers carry no consistent individual attributions and the usual practices of periodical composition of this kind mean that the assistance of his literary friends and family cannot be excluded. Its separate authorial identity is secure, but the share of its copy that is Hunt's own is a matter of scholarly inference rather than of documentation, and its collected reissues carry his name as author. Nothing in the evidence supports the transfer of any specific number to another hand.

works.title: The Inheritance
works.description: the author's second novel, a wider social comedy following the young heir, who unexpectedly inherits a great fortune and is transplanted from humble Scottish origins into English and Scottish high society. The novel examines how sudden wealth corrupts and tests character across two generations of fortune-hunters.
works.plot: Eliot, a young man of modest means, learns that an unexpected inheritance has made him one of the wealthiest commoners in Britain. His sister Julia's prospects transform correspondingly, and the pair are drawn into the worlds of Edinburgh and London society, where they encounter the mercenary calculations of the aristocracy, the manipulative Mrs. St. Clare, and the proud Lady Victoria. the author's education in wealth and Julia's trials in the marriage market trace the novel's central argument that inheritance tests moral nature more severely than poverty.
works.significance: The Inheritance is the author's broadest social canvas and her most sustained analysis of class mobility; it is a key text for the representation of wealth and gentility in Scottish Romantic fiction between Scott and later Victorian social novels.
works.context: Published in 1824, the author's most ambitious novel consolidates the Waverley-era market for Scottish social fiction and responds to the speculative excesses of post-war gentility; it draws on her knowledge of Edinburgh legal and clerical society.
works.characters: Eliot; Julia Eliot; Mrs. St. Clare; Lady Victoria; Fanny Elliot; Colonel Macquarie
works.structure: Linear three-volume narrative; the ascent plot from obscurity to wealth is the organising device; contrast between Scottish and English society structures the satire.

works.title: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African. Written by Himself
works.form: Autobiographical slave narrative with embedded travel journal and polemic
works.description: The first great slave narrative in English, published in two volumes in 1789 and subscribed by hundreds of readers, including members of the royal family. Equiano tells of his childhood in Africa, his kidnapping and sale, the Middle Passage, twenty years of slavery and service in the Royal Navy and the merchant trade, his purchase of his own freedom, and his conversion and public anti-slavery activism. The narrative combines autobiography, travel writing, commercial detail and protest, and it became the most widely used text of the abolitionist campaign.
works.plot: From an idealised account of Igbo society in what is now Nigeria the narrative moves to the horror of the middle passage, where the close-packing, mortality and torture of the ship are registered with precise numbers. Enslaved in the West Indies and then in England, Equiano serves the Royal Navy officer Michael Henry Pascal, is christened Gustavus Vassa by the Shipley family at Guernsey, works as a domestic servant and ship's crewman, and under the Philadelphia merchant Robert King learns bookkeeping and accumulates enough to buy his freedom in 1766. Later volumes recount his travels in the Arctic, Central America and Jamaica, his evangelical conversion and his circle of Methodist and Calvinistic friends, and a closing appeal to the imagination of British readers, in which the suffering of enslaved people is figured in the language of familial and Christian sympathy.
works.significance: It established the conventions of the English-speaking slave narrative, the testimony of an authenticated self that refutes the theory of African incapacity. Its argument from felt sympathy, commercial evidence and Christian providence made it a decisive instrument of public persuasion and it is now a central text of eighteenth-century studies, of Atlantic history and of life-writing.
works.meter: Prose only, in a plain, earnest, periodically structured narrative style with biblical and sentimental cadences
works.context: Published in the year of the first abolitionist petition to Parliament and of the French Declaration of the Rights of Man, it belongs to the evangelical and Quaker anti-slavery movement, to the boom in spiritual autobiography, and to the eighteenth-century literature of travel, commerce and natural history.
works.characters: Michael Henry Pascal; Robert King; Granville Sharp; the Shipley family
works.structure: Two-volume spiritual and commercial autobiography in chronological order, with a frame of providential design and a final section of documents, testimonials and abolitionist argument.
works.attributionNotes: Equiano's own authorship is accepted, though the degree of editorial help from abolitionist friends such as the bookseller and clergyman supporters is debated. Vincent Carretta has argued from contemporary records that Equiano may have been born in the British colonies rather than in Africa, which would make the opening African childhood a persuasive fiction; the narrative's factual status remains contested even where its authorship is not.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Introduction of Knowledge
altTitles: The Fyrst Boke of the Introduction of Knowledge
works.description: Andrew Boorde's popular geography and travel book of 1547, the first English printed book to describe the nations of Europe in verse and prose for the general reader.
works.plot: The book presents each nation of Europe (and beyond) through a woodcut portrait of a native in national dress, a verse dialogue spoken by the figure, and a prose description of the country's customs, currency, and distances — a compendium of travel knowledge for merchants and pilgrims.
works.significance: The first printed English survey of European nations and an early document of English ethnographic description; its woodcut national portraits founded a visual tradition that lasted into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Prose with verse interludes
works.context: Compiled from Boorde's European travels of the 1530s and printed in 1547 by William Copland; Boorde, physician and Carthusian, had been licensed to travel by Thomas Cromwell, and the book reflects the expansion of English geographical curiosity in the mid-Tudor period.
works.structure: Thirty-nine chapters, one per nation, each combining woodcut, verse self-description, and prose itinerary.

works.title: The Italian Opera
works.description: Addison's satiric essay on the Italian opera then occupying the London stage, a comic indictment of declamatory singing, castrato heroes, improbable machinery and the abdication of sense before sound.
works.plot: The spectator reports the absurdities of an evening at the Italian opera, where artificial voices command armies and melt away in affected rapture, stage machinery manufactures thunder, and the audience most admires whatever most forbids belief.
works.significance: It set the terms of the English critique of operatic convention for the century, and was reused by Gay and by the ballad-opera writers of 1728 as the obvious target of their burlesque.
works.meter: Lucid ironic prose, with exaggerated enumeration and the mock-solemn aside; the paper's couplet tag is quoted from the poets of the theatre.
works.context: Written while Handel and Handel's rivals were establishing Italian heroica opera at the Queen's Theatre, and while the English opera, the ballad entertainment and the spoken drama were competing for the same audience; the paper belongs to the long quarrel between English spoken theatre and foreign sung drama.
works.characters: Mr. Spectator; the opera singers; the applauding audience
works.structure: A single character paper: expository frame, catalogued instances of abuse, and a closing general reflection on credulity and taste.
works.attributionNotes: Standardly assigned to Addison, but the earliest Spectator numbers divide between Addison and Steele and the ascription rests on style and on the later collected arrangement rather than on external documentation.

works.title: The Italian, or, The Confessional of the Black Penitents. A Romance. In Three Volumes
altTitles: The Confessional of the Black Penitents
works.form: Gothic novel and romance of terror, with the confessional, the robbers' cavern and the Inquisition for its machinery; the last of the mature prose romances Radcliffe published in her lifetime
works.description: The last prose romance of Ann Radcliffe, advertised in the London press in December 1796 and published in three volumes with the imprint of 1797, of which she sold the copyright to Thomas Cadell. Vincentio di Vivaldi, seeing Ellena di Rosalba at church in Naples, loves her at first sight against the pride of his family; Ellena, reared in seclusion on the coast of Sorrento, is carried off on the road by the robbers who own Schedoni for their chief, is driven through the caverns of the banditti and the fortress of the suitorous Duke of Braccivalo, is accused of a murder committed in her chamber by Schedoni's assassin Spalatro, and is pressed by ecclesiastical arts into vows, while the confessional of the black penitents and the Inquisition darken the way. The disclosures at the close unite the houses of Schedoni and Ellena, establish her nobility so that Vivaldi may honourably wed her, and unbind the terrible history of the Schedoni family from which the title-piece takes its name.
works.plot: Ellena, beloved of Vivaldi, is kidnapped on the road to Naples by robbers under Schedoni, protected from harm by his own troubled conscience, and pursued by the suit of the powerful Duke of Braccivalo, whom her pride and her lover's danger oblige her to resist; a murder in her lodging, done by the assassin Spalatro, throws suspicion on herself, and she is driven toward the convent and its arts of the confessional to escape forced marriage. Schedoni's history, of anhouse disowned, a sister lost, and the black-robed penitents of his family's Easter rite, is unfolded till he finds in Ellena a kinswoman, her parentage is cleared, the crimes are brought home to their authors, and her marriage with Vivaldi is made lawful in honour.
works.significance: The Italian is by many judges Radcliffe's most accomplished romance, concentrating her method into a single tragic fable of conscience and persecution; it stood as the school-example of the explained supernatural and of Gothic's anti-clerical machinery through the nineteenth century, was a measure for Scott's and Peacock's accounts of terror, and remains the canonical companion volume to Udolpho in the Gothic syllabus.
works.meter: Prose romance without interspersed verse; the rhythm of the book is that of its tragic scene-setting, the bay of Sorrento, the caverns and the fortress, and its style is nearer to tragedy than to the lyricism of Udolpho.
works.context: Published at the close of the first vogue of the Gothic, when the campaign against the Inquisition and monastic craft was a staple of radical as well as Tory polemic, and when the Directory's wars had made Italy a subject of anxious English attention; its December 1796 press notice and the Cadell copyright mark the height of Radcliffe's fame before her withdrawal from publication.
works.characters: Ellena di Rosalba; Vincentio di Vivaldi; Schedoni, captain of the robbers; Spalatro, his assassin; the Duke of Braccivalo; Vivaldi's mother; Ellena's father; the sister and confessor of the Schedoni house; the Inquisition of Naples
works.structure: A continuous three-volume romance, close-knit and rapid beside its predecessors, moving through abduction, pursuit, accusation and trial toward a single expository revelation that ties the robbers' chief to the heroine's house and resolves the machinery of the confessional and the Inquisition.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the author of The Mysteries of Udolpho on the title page; the newspapers of December 1796 name Ann Radcliffe, and her authorship is undisputed.

works.title: The Itinerary
works.description: John Leland's topographical survey of England and Wales, the record of his itineraries undertaken with a royal commission from Henry VIII to search the libraries of the monasteries, compiled c. 1535–43 and first printed by Thomas Hearne in 1710–12.
works.plot: The Itinerary is a county-by-county record of Leland's travels: towns, rivers, bridges, castles, churches, and the antiquities of each place, noted in terse first-person entries that document the landscape of England on the eve of the dissolution of the monasteries.
works.significance: The founding text of English antiquarianism and topography; it inaugurated the tradition of the county survey that runs through Camden, Aubrey, and the eighteenth-century antiquaries, and its value as an eyewitness record of pre-dissolution England is irreplaceable.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Leland held a commission from Henry VIII (1533) to search the monastic and collegiate libraries; his itineraries of c. 1535–43 covered most of England and Wales, and his notes preserve records of books, inscriptions, and buildings later destroyed in the dissolution and after.
works.structure: Topographical notes arranged by county, preserved in autograph notebooks; the printed text of 1710–12 follows Hearne's edition of the surviving manuscripts.

works.title: The Jew of Malta
works.description: Marlowe's black comedy of Machiavellian revenge: the merchant Barabas, his wealth seized to pay Malta's tribute to the Turks, revenges himself on the Christian state by intrigue and poison, betrays the island to the Turks, and is finally caught in his own engine — the cauldron prepared for his enemies — in a play whose prologue is spoken by 'Machevill' himself.
works.plot: Barabas is stripped of his estate; through his daughter Abigail he recovers his hidden gold and buys the deaths of the governor's son and suitor; Abigail's conversion and death, his purchase of the slave Ithamore, and the double poisonings follow; made governor by the Turks, he plots the city's destruction, but the falling floor delivers him to the cauldron and the Christians' triumph.
works.significance: The most corrosive of the Elizabethan revenge plays — a satire of Christian, Jew, and Turk alike that Shakespeare answered in Shylock.
works.meter: Blank verse for Barabas's great soliloquies of gold ('infinite riches in a little room') against the prose of the play's farcical intrigues.
works.context: Performed from 1592, in the aftermath of the Lopez affair and the Marrano anxieties of the 1590s; not printed until 1633, when it was revived with prologues by Heywood.
works.characters: Barabas; Abigail; Ithamore; Ferneze, governor of Malta; Lodowick; Mathias; Calymath; Bellamira; Pilia-Borza; the two Friars (Jacomo and Bernardine); Machevill (the Prologue)
works.structure: A five-act intrigue of escalating double-dealing, alternating the prologue's sardonic commentary with farcical villainy, and ending in the spectacular engine of the cauldron.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Plays

works.title: The Judgement Day I and II
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990 (Judgement Day I); Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (Judgement Day II)
works.description: Two independent eschatological poems on the last judgment. Judgement Day I (119 lines) describes the cosmic terrors of doomsday and the soul's reckoning; Judgement Day II (306 lines), based on Bede's De die iudicii, is a sustained meditation on sin, penance, and the judgment, addressed to the individual soul.
works.plot: Judgement Day I depicts the universal conflagration, the trumpets, and the assembly of all souls before the judge, contrasting the fate of the blessed and the damned. Judgement Day II urges the penitent soul to recall its sins now, while confession is still possible, painting the terrors of judgment in images of fire, darkness, and weeping, and closes with hope for those who repent.
works.significance: The fullest Old English verse treatments of the last judgment, and (in Judgement Day II) an important vernacular witness to the reception of Bede's Latin eschatological poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; Judgement Day II's sustained length and homiletic urgency make it the most ambitious of the Exeter/CCCC 201 eschatological poems.
works.context: The judgment was the master-image of Anglo-Saxon homiletics, from the Blickling and Vercelli homilies to Wulfstan's Sermo Lupi; the poems belong to that culture of penitential fear and are the verse counterpart of the homilists' doomsday rhetoric.
works.structure: Both poems move from description of the cosmic catastrophe to exhortation; Judgement Day II is organized as a sequence of meditations on sin, the hour of death, the judgment, and the possibility of mercy through penance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two poems are independent compositions; Judgement Day II is an adaptation of Bede's De die iudicii, not by Bede himself.
themes: Memory and the growth of the poet's mind
sources: The Edinburgh Edition of Walter Scott's 'Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border' (3 volumes)

works.title: The Judgment of Paris
works.form: Masque or libretto for sung drama in three acts, composed as a competition text for the music prize of 1701.
works.description: A masque written in 1701 for the musical prize contested by the chief composers of the day, and not seen as a stage entertainment until the Haymarket production of 1712. The classical fable of the apple and the three goddesses is recast as an English pastoral contest, in which the rival claims of power, wisdom and beauty are set out for music rather than for dramatic action. The piece is the only considerable dramatic writing of its author's mature years, and it reads as a study in how a poet may build a text to be set.
works.plot: Celestial machinery opens the fable anew, and the three goddesses descend to the shepherd Paris on Ida that he may judge their appeals as of old. Juno offers power and extended empire, Pallas offers wisdom and renown in arms, and Venus offers beauty and the pleasures of love; each claim is urged in set airs and in recitative addressed to the shepherd's judgment. Paris, who is already beloved by the nymph Oenone, awards the prize to Venus, and the desert of the forsaken nymph supplies the tender undercurrent that keeps the allegory from being merely a programme. The several appeals are commented upon by pastoral attendants and by choruses, so that the moral of the choice is delivered in the alternation of musical effects rather than by argument, and the closing matter commends the triumph of beauty to the audience of the day.
works.significance: It preserves the only masque written by the foremost comedy-writer of his generation and is a document of the English effort to make serious musical drama out of an allegorical fable. Its graded lyric lines, adjusted to the composer's convenience, were long cited as a model of the poet's service to music, and the piece marks the late reach of the masque tradition into the competitive concert and opera life of London.
works.meter: Deliberately varied lyric line-lengths, short song-measures set off against longer declamatory lines for recitative, a prosody designed to give the composer distinct musical occasions; the choral and closing matter is in brisk regular rhyme.
works.context: The libretto was written for the musical contest of the spring and summer of 1701, in which several composers set the same English poem, an episode in the attempt to sustain an English musical drama after the generation of the great court composers. The interval of eleven years between the prize and the full stage production at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket in March 1712 measures the small market for such work before the Italian vogue of the following decade changed conditions. The poet had by then abandoned the public stage for other employments, and this text stands alone among his later writings for the theatre.
works.characters: Jupiter; Juno; Pallas; Venus; Paris the shepherd; Oenone the forsaken nymph; the attendants of the goddesses and the pastoral chorus
works.structure: A masque in three acts for singers, machinery and chorus; the dramatic line is subordinated to a sequence of competitive appeals and their musical answers, with an opening invocation and a celebratory close.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Juvenile Miscellany
works.form: Juvenile and educational periodical: the monthly miscellany of instruction and amusement, with the tale, the dialogue lesson and the recitation poem as its characteristic units.
works.description: The first periodical published in the United States specifically for children, begun in Boston in 1826 and edited there through its earliest years. It appeared monthly in small numbers combining stories, natural history, geography, poetry, puzzles and moral tales, and it was written and compiled with a deliberate educational theory: that the child's imagination should be engaged before the conscience is lectured. Its editorship gives it a place in the reform literature of the period as well as in the history of schooling.
works.plot: As a serial it has no single argument but a programme. Its numbers teach through narrative rather than catechism, offering tales of animals and travel, short biographies of worthies, lessons on the temperance and abolition questions, and verse meant to be repeated aloud. Its editorial voice insists that children are rational beings entitled to interest and delight, and it gradually introduces political and moral subjects, including the condition of the enslaved and of Native Americans, into the child's reading room.
works.significance: It is the founding periodical of American literature for children, and an early demonstration that reform argument could be addressed to the young; its editorial practice shaped the juvenile book trade for a generation. Its history is also the history of its editor's developing politics, since the abolition and Native American questions entered her pages before they entered her books.
works.meter: Chiefly simple prose; its verse is in singable ballad and hymn stanzas written for juvenile recitation.
works.context: Launched in the same years as the American Sunday-School Union's mass juvenile publication and as the great reform agitations were beginning, it belongs to the period's new conviction that the child reader could be addressed directly and seriously. Its Boston origins place it at the centre of the unitarian and abolitionist print culture of the 1820s and 1830s.
works.structure: Serial monthly miscellany: undifferentiated succession of tale, lesson, poem, puzzle and answer, with editor's notes to correspondents and young contributors.
works.attributionNotes: The first years were edited by the woman who founded it, and its leading matter is hers; individual contributions are otherwise anonymous or by correspondents, so the serial is a collaborative print object.
