works.title: The Katherine Group
altTitles: The Lives of St Katherine, St Margaret, and St Juliana
works.description: Three prose lives of virgin martyrs — St Katherine of Alexandria, St Margaret of Antioch, and St Juliana of Nicomedia — written in the same West Midlands 'AB language' as Ancrene Wisse for a female religious audience. They are the classic Middle English saints' lives: rhetorically elaborate, vivid in their debates and torments, and fervent in their celebration of virginity.
works.plot: Each saint refuses a pagan suitor and judge, defeats her learned or demonic adversaries in debate, endures spectacular torments, and wins a martyr's crown, with Christ or angels as her comforters.
works.significance: The founding texts of the AB language group and the model for Middle English hagiography in the thirteenth century and after.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative prose with the characteristic AB-language vocabulary and spelling.
works.context: Composed c. 1190–1225 in the same Herefordshire milieu as Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
works.characters: St Katherine; St Margaret; St Juliana; the tyrant-judges (Maxentius, Olibrius, Eleusius); the demons
works.structure: Conventional martyr-act structure (arraignment, debate, torture, death) enriched by long speeches and prayers; Juliana includes the saint's dialogue with a demon.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; grouped with Ancrene Wisse and the Wooing Group by dialect and manuscript kinship.
sources: An Appeal in Favor of That Class of Americans Called Africans

works.title: The Keepsake
altTitles: The Keepsake: An Annual Gift-Book of Poetry, Entertainment, and the Fine Arts
works.form: Literary annual and keepsake verse: a serialized gift-book miscellany of lyrical poems, sentimental tales and engraved plates, sold in decorative bindings at a premium price.
works.description: The first and longest-lived of the fully commercial literary annuals, an embossed and finely bound gift book published each season from 1828 with an engraved steel plate as its centrepiece. It assembled poems, short tales and plates from fashionable contributors and was presented as a New Year's and birthday present. The record covers its foundation volume and the model it established. Together with its competitors it created the gift-book economy that dominated periodical literary production through the 1830s and 1840s.
works.plot: As an anthology it has no plot; its characteristic structure is a frontispiece after a painting, followed by an assortment of occasional verse, prose tales of sentiment and adventure, and contributions of historical or decorative interest. Its editorial programme, announced in its opening numbers, was to combine the fine arts and letters in a form made for giving, so that the plate and the poem were designed as a single presentational unit.
works.significance: It defines the annual as an economic and aesthetic institution: the form that set the price, the plate-and-poem design and the contributor list of Victorian literary culture, and the market in which much of the period's best-known verse by women was published and paid for. Its history is central to accounts of Romantic and early-Victorian authorship, patronage and the literary marketplace.
works.meter: Mixed; its verse is predominantly song-like lyric and short meditative pieces in familiar stanzas and blank verse, written to a small emotional register suited to the plate.
works.context: Founded by an engraver seeking a new market after the boom in illustrated topographical books, and published in London for a seasonally gift-buying readership with money to spend on presents. Its commercial success created a decade of imitation and drove the annuals' characteristic combination of art reproduction and commissioned literary work.
works.structure: Serial annual anthology: undated-in-essence miscellany of verse, prose and engraved plates, each volume built around one or more steel engravings.
works.attributionNotes: Volume editorship changed hands during the long run and the founding volume's editorial responsibility is a matter of scholarly description rather than of single authorship; contents are individually attributed to their contributors.

works.title: The Kentish Hymn
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vespasian D.vi, fol. 69 (tenth century)
works.form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: A 43-line paraphrase of the Gloria in excelsis in the Kentish dialect, the only substantial Old English poem preserved in that dialect. It praises the Trinity, Christ the Lamb, and the Holy Spirit, and prays for the mercy of the Lord.
works.plot: The poem renders the Greater Doxology clause by clause: praise of God the Father, the Lamb of God who takes away sin, the Holy Spirit with Father and Son, and a closing petition for the Lord's mercy and protection.
works.significance: A rare dialectal witness to Old English religious verse and an early example of the Gloria rendered in English verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the Kentish forms of the text are among the few dialectally marked verse survivals outside West Saxon.
works.context: The hymn was added to a manuscript otherwise containing Kentish glosses and documents; it attests the spread of vernacular liturgical paraphrase beyond the West Saxon heartland of the literary standard.
works.structure: A direct liturgical paraphrase following the order of the Gloria; the doxological clauses are expanded with brief devotional glosses.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
sources: The Poems of John Keats

works.title: The Kingis Quair
works.description: The dream vision traditionally attributed to James I of Scotland, written c. 1424 after his eighteen years of captivity in England: the imprisoned narrator, sleepless with love, reads Boethius, sees his lady from the tower window, and is taught by the goddesses of Love, Fortune, and Wisdom in a vision that reconciles him to his fate. The fountainhead of the Scottish Chaucerian tradition.
works.plot: The sleepless captive, turning the pages of Boethius, hears the bell of matins and falls into a dream; guided by the goddesses, he ascends to the sphere of Venus, where his love for the lady seen from the tower is confirmed and fortune's wheel is explained; waking, a dove brings him the message of hope, and he ends his book in praise of love and his lady.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the makars' tradition: the first great poem in the Scottish Chaucerian line and the model for the royal and courtly poetry of the Stewart century.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of Chaucerian fluency, in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1424, on the eve of James's release, celebrating his love for Joan Beaufort, whom he married in February 1424; preserved uniquely in the Selden manuscript (Bodleian Arch. Selden. B.24, c. 1488).
works.characters: the captive narrator (James I); the lady (Joan Beaufort); Venus; Minerva; Fortune; the dove
works.structure: A single dream vision in the Chaucerian-Boethian manner: reading, waking complaint, dream ascent, counsel of the goddesses, and waking resolution.
works.attributionNotes: The attribution to James I rests on the poem's autobiographical frame and manuscript tradition; it is widely but not universally accepted.

editions.title: The Kingis Quair and Other Prison Poems
editions.editor: Linne R. Mooney and Mary-Jo Arn (eds.)

works.title: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
works.description: Beaumont's mock-romance of the citizen audience: a grocer and his wife, watching the play 'The London Merchant', demand that their apprentice Rafe act the part of a knight errant; the 'Knight of the Burning Pestle' then rides his adventures through Waltham Forest and the giant Barbaroso's barber shop, while the merchant play and the citizens' interruptions double and parody each other to the final, multiple endings.
works.plot: The Citizen and his Wife interrupt the Prologue and hijack the play; Rafe's quests — the dainty damsel, the giants, the adventure of the barber — alternate with the merchant comedy of Venturewell, Jasper, and Luce; the plots collide at the mock-death of Rafe ('for the honor of Knights') and the play ends with the citizens' epilogue and the players' revenge on their audience.
works.significance: The first great English theatrical burlesque — the ancestor of Sheridan's Critic and of every later play about the audience's power over the stage.
works.meter: Mixed verse and prose, with the ballad metres of Rafe's adventures and the songs of old Merrythought ('Nose, nose, jolly red nose') as its parodic instruments.
works.context: First performed by the Children of the Revels at Blackfriars about 1607, where it failed; revived by the Queen's Revels boys and printed in 1613; it mocks the citizen taste that The Shoemaker's Holiday had flattered.
works.characters: the Citizen; his Wife; Rafe (the Knight of the Burning Pestle); George (the apprentice); Venturewell; Jasper; Luce; Humphrey; Merrythought; Mistress Merrythought; Barbaroso the barber; the players
works.structure: A play-within-a-play satire in which the audience is on stage from the start — the first burlesque of the English theatre's own conventions, including the romance, the city comedy, and the 'lamentable' death scene.
works.attributionNotes: Generally assigned to Beaumont alone (perhaps with Fletcher's help); the 1613 title page names only Beaumont.

editions.title: The Knight of the Burning Pestle (Revels Plays)

works.title: The Lady of May
works.description: Sidney's pastoral entertainment, written for a royal visit to Wanstead (probably that of 1578 or 1579): a May Lady must choose between the shepherd Espilus and the forester Therion, while the clownish schoolmaster Rombus and the Queen herself referee the debate between the contemplative and active lives.
works.plot: The Lady of May is courted by the shepherd Espilus and the forester Therion; Rombus presents the case for each; the suitors debate in verse and prose, and the Lady — after a comic intervention by Rixus the pedant — gives her hand to one of them, with Elizabeth I invited to judge the dispute.
works.significance: The earliest English pastoral entertainment of the great age and a document of Sidney's courtly politics; it established the genre that Jonson's masques would crown.
works.meter: Mixed prose and verse, including singing parts.
works.context: Performed for Elizabeth I during her progress to Wanstead, probably in 1578 or 1579, when Leicester (Sidney's uncle) was pressing Sidney toward the Anjou marriage policy.
works.characters: the Lady of May; Espilus the shepherd; Therion the forester; Rombus the schoolmaster; Queen Elizabeth (as judge)
works.structure: A short masque-like entertainment in prose and verse, built on the debate form and ending with the Queen's judgment.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; first printed in the 1598 folio of the Arcadia.

works.title: The Lady of Pleasure
works.description: Shirley's most admired comedy, contrasting the extravagant, pleasure-seeking Lady Ariola Bornwell with the prudent and reformed Mistress Constance; it is the sharpest Caroline critique of conspicuous consumption and fashionable vice.
works.plot: Sir Thomas Bornwell, disgusted by his wife's extravagance, pretends to leave her, while the virtuous Lord Lacywoth courts Constance; the Lady is finally shamed into reform and the couples are properly matched.
works.significance: Long regarded as Shirley's masterpiece and the finest comedy of manners before Etherege; its treatment of the extravagant lady anticipates Restoration social comedy.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed at the Cockpit in 1635, at the height of the fashionable London society that Shirley depicts and satirises.
works.characters: Lady Ariola Bornwell; Sir Thomas Bornwell; Constance; Lord Lacywoth; Celestina; Littleworth; Decoy
works.structure: Five acts with two parallel domestic plots of contrasted moral temperaments.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Lady of the Lake
altTitles: The Lady of the Lake: A Poem
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; Highland romance with court intrigue and a disguised monarch plot.
works.description: The third and most popular of the metrical romances, a Highland tale of a royal progress in disguise, a banished lord and a maiden reared in the wilds of the Trossachs. Its rapid octosyllabic movement, its lake, cave and gathering-of-the-clans set pieces, and its elaborate notes on Highland custom made it the best-selling narrative poem of its generation. It was advertised as the work that would decide whether the author's verse should continue.
works.plot: King James the Fifth, touring the south of the Highlands in the summer under the borrowed name of Fitz-James, loses his attendance in a long chase and is guided by a mountaineer to the caves and island recesses of the lake country, where he is harboured by an aged hermit and by the outlawed Douglas, the last of his line. There he sees Ellen, Douglas's daughter, reared among the wilds, whom the young minstrel Malcolm Graeme loves and whom the chieftain Roderick Dhu of Clan Alpine would win. Roderick, at feud with Douglas and slighted in his suit, gathers his clan and joins the enemies of the crown; the king's stranger is drawn into the pursuit, and an illegal arrow almost ends his part. The quarrel is brought to judgement at Stirling, where a champion in unknown arms fights before the king's court for the attainted lord; the royal secret is disclosed, honours are distributed, Roderick dies of his wounds, and Ellen is married to the lover of her youth.
works.significance: The most widely sold and most translated British narrative poem of the second decade of the century, and the chief conduit through which Highland Scotland entered the popular imagination of the nineteenth century. Its scenery, its hilloa gathering and its lake scene became standard equipment for later verse, painting and stage spectacle. Its success hastened the author's decision to abandon verse for prose fiction.
works.meter: Iambic tetrameter couplets in the easy short measure already used in the earlier romances, with ballad stanzas, hymns, a boat-song and an epithalamium interpolated.
works.context: Published in the year of Napoleon's ascendancy in Europe, when the demand for national romance was at its height and when Highland costume and clan history were being simultaneously documented and romanticised. The author's notes draw on the statistical and antiquarian survey of Scotland then in progress. Its dedication and its epistles engage directly with the review controversy about the value of romantic poetry.
works.characters: King James the Fifth; Ellen, the Lady of the Lake; Douglas, the banished lord; Roderick Dhu, chief of Clan Alpine; Malcolm Graeme; the hermit of St. Bride
works.structure: Six cantos of continuous romance narrative with a lyrical opening invocation and a closing epistle to a noble patron, supported by copious antiquarian notes on Highland customs; the set pieces - the boat-song on the lake, the gathering of the clan, the cave, the combat at Stirling - carry the structure.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's own name; no dispute.

works.title: The Lady's Trial
works.description: Ford's last surviving play, a tragicomedy in which Aurelio tests his wife Spinella's chastity, is deceived by the malicious Amoretto, and the trial is resolved by the intervention of Spinella's sister Castanna and the reformed Benatzi.
works.plot: Aurelio's test of Spinella, engineered by the villain Amoretto, appears to confirm her unfaithfulness; the truth emerges when Castanna's own constancy is proved and Amoretto's imposture is exposed.
works.significance: Ford's final play and a mature example of Caroline tragicomedy; its concern with the testing of female chastity connects it to the tradition from Boccaccio to Shakespeare's Cymbeline.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed at the Cockpit in 1636 and published in 1639.
works.characters: Aurelio; Spinella; Castanna; Amoretto; Benatzi; Fulgoso; Adurni
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue with a tragicomic resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1639 title page; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Lamentation of a Sinner
works.description: Catherine Parr's spiritual autobiography and treatise on justification by faith, published posthumously in 1547; the fullest statement of the queen's evangelical faith.
works.plot: Parr confesses her former life 'in superstition and ignorance', recounts her awakening to the doctrine of justification by faith through the reading of scripture, and expounds the gospel of free grace against the reliance on works, ending with a meditation on the passion and an exhortation to trust wholly in Christ's merits.
works.significance: The first spiritual autobiography by an English queen and an important document of the Reformation's inward turn; it shows the queen — the only woman whose books were printed in her lifetime in Tudor England — articulating the doctrine of faith in her own voice.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the last years of Henry VIII's reign, when Parr's evangelical circle faced persecution (Askew was burned in July 1546), and published by William Cecil (later Lord Burghley) in 1547 after the king's death; the book became a manual of Edwardian Protestant piety.
works.characters: Catherine Parr (narrator)
works.structure: A two-part work: a first-person confession and conversion narrative, followed by a doctrinal exposition of faith, grace, and the law.

editions.title: Katherine Parr: Complete Works and Correspondence

works.title: The Land of Cokaygne
works.description: A rollicking satire of some 190 lines on the fantasy land of Cokaygne, a paradise of food, sleep, and license reached by a week in a sow's belly, whose abbey of gluttonous monks is described with anti-monastic glee. It is the earliest English example of the European Cockaigne tradition and a masterpiece of clerical self-satire.
works.plot: The poet describes the geography of Cokaygne — roast geese flying, rivers of oil and wine, the fountain of youth — and dwells lovingly on the abbey where the monks, fattened without labour, fly about at their pleasure with the abbess.
works.significance: The first English Cockaigne poem and the liveliest anti-clerical satire before Langland; a favourite of modern anthologies for its comic invention.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of comic energy, in an Irish-influenced Middle English.
works.context: Composed c. 1300, perhaps in Ireland (the sole manuscript is the Kildare miscellany, BL Harley MS 913, c. 1330), where the Cockaigne tradition flourished among the friars.
works.characters: the monks of Cokaygne; the abbess
works.structure: A catalogue-description of the dream land, closing with the burlesque of the monastic abbey.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: Modern Chivalry: Containing the Adventures of Captain John Farrago, and Teague O'Regan, His Servant

works.title: The Last Essays of Elia
works.form: Familiar essay and character sketch, with a share of topographical and university meditation, in the revived Elizabethan and eighteenth-century manner of the first series.
works.description: The second and last series of the familiar essays, gathered from the periodicals of the later 1820s and published in 1833, with an introductory letter affecting to come from a kinsman of the earlier persona. The voice is the same retired, book-loving and affectionate essayist of the first series, but the pieces are more various and sometimes more occasional, taking in the country, the universities, the pleasures of a day's excursion, and the quarrels and kindnesses of literary society. It contains some of the best of the later papers and the last of the essays written under the assumed name.
works.plot: The volume moves between reminiscence, portrait and travel. Several papers revisit the first series' country of childhood and of relationship, and one of them returns to the sister and to the old houses of the family history with a gravity the earlier essays had held in check. Others are excursions and topographical meditations: a day's journey into the counties about London, a visit to the university towns and their colleges and libraries, with their chapels, gardens and memories of the older writers, and the observations of an inland town and its inns and companies of players. A third group are character papers and arguments about books - the pleasures of reading the old poets, the use of a library, the faults of the current criticism, and the portraits of acquaintances and of the peculiar people of the metropolis. The continuing argument is that a retired and obliging temper, reading and remembering, is a sufficient employment for a life without fortune.
works.significance: Completes the series that defined the English familiar essay of the nineteenth century, and contains papers, among them the university excursion and the later country essays, that are usually placed beside the best of the first series. The two volumes together remain the standard model of the personal essay, and this series is the document of the essayist's old age and of his last quarrels and kindnesses.
works.meter: Prose still more various than that of the first series, passing from the gossiping sentence to the long periodic meditation, with a richer and more continuous texture of quotation and with a slower, more elegiac cadence in the retrospective papers.
works.context: Contributed to the magazines and annuals of the later 1820s and collected in 1833, when the writer had withdrawn from his official employment and had taken a late literary independence; the university and country papers belong to the tour-writing of the 1830s, and the volume appeared in the same years as the first collected editions of the essays in the periodical press.
works.characters: The essayist writing under the assumed name; the kinsman who professes to edit the papers; the sister of the family history; the collegers and the poor relations; the hostler, the player and the odd characters of the country towns
works.structure: A collection of free-standing essays with no imposed scheme, ordered so that the autobiographical, the topographical and the critical papers alternate; the unity is again that of the persona, whose voice and memory connect the subjects, and the prefactory letter supplies a thin frame for the series.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the prefatory letter, which affects to proceed from a relation of the earlier writer, is by the same hand, and the periodicals of first appearance for the several papers are recorded in the collected editions.

works.title: The Last Man
works.form: Apocalyptic and philosophical fiction; a plague romance and elegy in prose with the machinery of forecast.
works.description: A forecast of the end of the human species, set at the close of the twenty-first century, in which a plague out of the East empties England, Europe and finally the world. Its narrator, a mountaineer's son raised into the governing class of a decaying Commonwealth, survives every person he loves and outlasts the species itself. It is the boldest of the period's fictions of historical exhaustion, and it was written in the years of immediate personal loss.
works.plot: England in 2075 has abandoned monarchy for a republic of virtue under a philosopher-statesman, and the last heir of the royal house, beloved and accomplished, lives retired with the friend of the narrator's youth. The two are drawn back to public life, to Parliament, to the Greek war of independence and to the courts of Europe, while a pestilence creeps westward from Asia. The plague reaches England, desolates London, scours the continent, and is spread by the flight of nations; one after another the friend, the wife, the children and the statesman die, and the survivor's attempts to raise an asylum in Greece fail. The last chapters follow him alone through a ruined Europe, to a cave and a Sibyl's prophecy, and home to a landscape from which human voice has departed.
works.significance: The first great English fiction of total extinction and a founding text of science-fictional eschatology; it reframes the Romantic elegy as the mourning of a species rather than of an individual. Its treatment of epidemic, class and the failure of public virtue has made it a central object of recent historicist criticism. Its recovery in the late twentieth century restored a major work to the canon of the period.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a stately, quotation-laden lament, with verse and lyric fragments interspersed and a sustained rhetorical address to Nature.
works.context: Written in the years after the deaths of a child and of a husband by drowning, and after the collapse of the hopes that the post-war European settlement had encouraged; its republic, its war of Greek independence and its fear of social dissolution belong to the politics of the early 1820s. Its plague borrows the records of earlier visitations and the current reports of Asiatic cholera. It sold badly and was not reprinted in the nineteenth century.
works.characters: Lionel Verney, the narrator; Adrian, the last prince of the fallen royal house; Idris, his wife; Ryland, the poet and friend; the Lady Ryland; Evander, their child
works.structure: First-person confession addressed to a series of auditors, in three parts with a prefaced 'Prospectus' and an epigraphic apparatus of quotations; the frame of a manuscript of the year 2100 gives the narrative its double perspective of witness and elegist.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as by the author of an earlier tale of creation; authorship established by the publisher's records and by family memoranda.

works.title: The Last of the Mohicans
altTitles: The Last of the Mohicans: A Narrative of 1757
works.form: Historical romance and frontier adventure narrative, with elegiac frame
works.description: The most widely read American romance of the colonial frontier, set during the French and Indian war in the Hudson Highlands and the wilderness west of Fort William Henry. Pursuit, capture and rescue give it a velocity unusual in the period. Its elegiac treatment of the extinction of the Mohican line makes the narrative of adventure also a narrative of dispossession.
works.plot: Two daughters of a British colonel are conducted through the forest toward their father at Fort William Henry, escorted by a scout and his Mohican companions. An ambuscade by Hurons separates the party, and the sisters are carried off; one is rescued by an Indian runner whose claim to her is rejected, while the other is saved by the scout in a flight to a mountain fastness. After the massacre following the fort's surrender, the captives and fathers are reunited through a succession of escapes, a burning castle and a cave. The novel ends with the death of Cora in the flames, the killing of the Huron chief by the last Mohican, and the funeral of Uncas as the last of his people.
works.significance: It defined the American frontier romance and established the Mohicans and the scout as the central figures of the national past. Its treatment of race, extinction and captive heroines remains the most contested aspect of the author's work. It is the best-known American novel of the 1820s.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1826 in four volumes, built on the campaigns of 1757 and on the author's own knowledge of the country around Lake George. Its appearance coincided with the national debate over Indian removal, and its theme of a people's extinction gave that debate a literary vocabulary. The novel's success was immediate on both sides of the Atlantic.
works.characters: Natty Bumppo; Uncas; Chingachgook; Magua; Cora; Alice; Heyward; David Gamut
works.structure: Linear romance of pursuit and rescue in four-part alternation of scenes; a strong narratorial voice supplies topographical and ethnographic description between episodes.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

works.title: The Law of Freedom in a Platform; or, True Magistracy Restored
works.description: Winstanley's mature political programme, addressed to Cromwell, in which he sets out the constitution of a free commonwealth without buying, selling, or private land, and with an elected magistracy and universal education.
works.plot: Winstanley proposes a commonwealth in which the earth is a common treasury, labour is organised communally, the clergy of the old order are abolished, magistrates are elected annually by the people, and laws are short, plain, and enforced by storehouses and officers.
works.significance: The fullest statement of English Digger communism and one of the most original political documents of the seventeenth century; it anticipates socialist and anarchist thought and has been a touchstone for the radical tradition.
works.meter: Prophetic, plain, biblical prose of the radical sects.
works.context: Published in 1652, three years after the Diggers' experiment on St George's Hill (1649), and dedicated to Cromwell, whose commonwealth Winstanley urged to go further.
works.structure: Six chapters with a dedicatory epistle to Cromwell and a proposed code of laws.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Winstanley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Laws of Cnut
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: The comprehensive law code of King Cnut (r. 1016-1035), drafted by Archbishop Wulfstan: the most elaborate legislation of the Anglo-Saxon period, combining royal law, ecclesiastical regulation, and Wulfstan's characteristic moral exhortation into a grand statement of a Christian commonwealth.
works.plot: The two parts of the code regulate the church (tithes, sanctuary, feast days, the clergy's conduct), the king's peace, legal procedure (ordeals, oaths, hundred courts), the ranks and dues of society, theft, homicide, and the punishment of the faithless; framed by Wulfstan's homiletic prologues exhorting all men to love God and keep the law.
works.significance: The summit of Anglo-Saxon legislation and the last great royal code in English before the Norman period.
works.meter: Old English prose with Wulfstan's rhythmical cadences.
works.context: Promulgated in the councils of 1020-1023 after Cnut's accession; preserved in later eleventh- and twelfth-century legal manuscripts.
works.characters: Cnut (legislator); Wulfstan (draftsman)
works.structure: A systematic code in two parts, with homiletic prologues and perorations.
works.attributionNotes: Drafted by Wulfstan for Cnut; Wulfstan's authorship is established on stylistic grounds.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Christopher Marlowe

works.title: The Laws of Ine
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: The law code of King Ine of Wessex (688-726), preserved as an appendix to Alfred's law book: the earliest West Saxon legislation, covering church dues, theft, the status of the Welsh, land law, and the mutual obligations of lords and men.
works.plot: The code's seventy-six clauses regulate church dues and oaths, theft and its pursuit, the wer and wergild of each rank (including the Welsh), land tenure and the duties of gesiths and ceorls, and the penalties for harbouring fugitives.
works.significance: The earliest surviving West Saxon law and a major source for early English social structure.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued c. 688-694; preserved in the earliest manuscript of Alfred's laws (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 173), to which Alfred appended it.
works.characters: Ine (legislator); his counsellors (the prologue names his father Cenred and bishops Hædde and Eorcenwald)
works.structure: A clause-by-clause royal code.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ine in the code's prologue.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Shakespeare

works.title: The Laws of Æthelberht
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: The law code of King Æthelberht of Kent, the earliest written English law and the oldest surviving document in the English language: a tariff of compensations for injuries, from homicide through wounding to the loss of a toe or a fingernail, with provisions protecting the Church and its property.
works.plot: The code opens with compensations for offences against the Church's property and peace, then proceeds by descending tariff through the body — head, hair, ear, eye, nose, teeth, fingers, nails, feet — assigning a fixed bot (compensation) for each injury according to the victim's rank.
works.significance: The earliest English law and the first extended document in the English language.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued by Æthelberht of Kent c. 602/3, shortly after the arrival of Augustine's mission (597); preserved only in the Textus Roffensis (Rochester, Cathedral Library, MS A.3.5, c. 1120).
works.characters: Æthelberht (legislator)
works.structure: A list of ninety clauses in the Germanic tariff style.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Æthelberht by Bede (Historia II.5) and by the manuscript's rubric.
sources: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: The Lay of the Last Minstrel
altTitles: The Lay of the Last Minstrel: A Poem
works.form: Metrical tale and romance in verse; a border antiquarian poem with framing ballad-singer and learned notes.
works.description: The poem that created the national metrical romance of the Borders, framed as the song of the last of the itinerant minstrels, who sings for hospitality at the house of Branksome and tells of a feud, a love and a raised corpse of the generation before the Union. Its explanatory notes, collected border tradition and deliberate archaism made it the first full-scale application of antiquarian method to original narrative verse. Its success turned a collector of ballads into a poet.
works.plot: The aged minstrel, taken in at the castle, sings of the baron of Branksome, whose death in the burial vault is foretold, and of the love of his daughter Margaret for the English captive Henry, which the feud of the houses of Branksome and Cragside forbids. The champion Deloraine, under bond not to shed Christian blood, is sent to raise the dead from the vault of Melrose by the help of the monk and the goblin page Gilpin Horner, who is begotten and bred of conjuring. The spirit's warning, the page's fatal errand and the marriage that ends the quarrel close the lay; the minstrel's own age and the passing of his order frame the whole.
works.significance: Opened the vogue for the metrical romance that dominated narrative poetry for two decades, and set the standard for the use of border ballad and antiquarian note inside original verse. Its framing device of the last of a dying order supplied the century's most durable image of oral tradition extinguished. The poem's success created the public for which the prose romances were afterwards written.
works.meter: Stanzas of iambic tetrameter in the mixed romantic measure the author took from the old border poets, varied by ballad stanzas and lyric songs.
works.context: Composed in the years when the author was editing the border minstrelsy and when the claims of national and popular poetry were being argued in the reviews; the poem's sixteenth-century setting looks back to the last generation of the free border. Its publication, early in 1805, was timed to a revived demand for romance while the war with France made the past feel lost. Its sale in the first three years established the commercial model for the long poem.
works.characters: The last minstrel; Margaret of Branksome; Henry the English captive; Deloraine, the outlaw champion; Gilpin Horner, the goblin page; the monk of Melrose
works.structure: Six cantos with an 'Introductory Epistle' in which the author accounts for the measure and design; the framing scene of the aged singer gives the poem its meditative onsets and closings, and each canto contains songs and ballad interpolations.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's own name; no dispute.

works.title: The Legend of Good Women
works.description: Chaucer's unfinished collection of exemplary women's legends (some 2,700 lines), framed by the Prologue in which the god of Love arraigns the poet for slandering women and his queen Alceste assigns him the penance of commemorating good women betrayed by men. Its nine completed legends — Cleopatra, Thisbe, Dido, Hypsipyle and Medea, Lucrece, Ariadne, Philomela, Phyllis, and Hypermnestra — are the seedbed of the English legendary tradition.
works.plot: The Prologue stages the daisy-worship of the poet and his dream trial before the god of Love, who condemns him for the Troilus and the Romaunt; Alceste's intercession wins him the commission to write of faithful women and false men. The legends that follow retell the classical stories of love and betrayal in rhyme royal, until the collection breaks off, unfinished, in the legend of Hypermnestra.
works.significance: The founding text of the English 'good women' tradition (Bokenham's Legends, the Tudor mirrors) and a key witness to Chaucer's negotiation with the courtly politics of gender.
works.meter: Rhyme royal, with the prologue in heroic couplets in the G version.
works.context: Composed c. 1386–88, partly at the queen's (Anne of Bohemia's) request, during the period of the Canterbury Tales' beginnings; its Prologue is the richest single document of Chaucer's self-presentation as poet.
works.characters: the Narrator; the god of Love; Alceste; Cleopatra; Thisbe; Dido; Medea; Lucrece; Ariadne; Philomela; Phyllis; Hypermnestra
works.structure: A dream-vision prologue (two versions, F and G) framing a series of Ovidian legends, each structured as betrayal narrative with moral close.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the relationship of the two prologues is editorial.

works.title: The Legend of the Seven Sleepers
altTitles: The Old English Legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Julius E.vii (c. 1100)
works.description: An Old English translation of the legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus: seven Christian youths who fled the persecution of the emperor Decius, were walled up in a cave, and awoke after some two hundred years to find a Christian empire. The legend was read as a proof of the resurrection of the body and was one of the most widespread stories of the Middle Ages.
works.plot: Seven young Christian nobles of Ephesus hide from Decius's persecution in a cave and fall into a miraculous sleep. Two centuries later they wake to find the world changed: the persecutor is dead and the emperor is Christian. One of them, Malchus, ventures into the city to buy bread with old coins and is taken for a treasure-finder; the emperor Theodosius comes to the cave, and the sleepers, after testifying to the resurrection, die in peace.
works.significance: The earliest English version of a legend that became proverbial across medieval Europe, and a document of the Anglo-Saxon church's teaching on resurrection.
works.context: The legend circulated in both eastern and western Christianity as a demonstration of bodily resurrection, and was known in England from at least the time of Aldhelm; this late Old English translation belongs to the vernacular hagiographic wave of the later eleventh century, and the story later reappears in Middle English and in the Anglo-Norman and continental traditions.
works.characters: Malchus and the six sleepers, the emperor Decius, the emperor Theodosius
works.structure: A single narrative arc in three movements — the persecution and concealment, the awakening and the bewildered visit to the city, and the public vindication before the emperor — framed by the theological point that God can raise the dead as easily as he woke the sleepers.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
sources: Self-Control: A Novel (Chawton House Library: Women's Novels, No. 17)

works.title: The Legion Club
works.description: Swift's last great verse satire, directed against a Dublin club of the Whig and court interest and against the Irish legislature it feeds, in which the poet's Muse is pressed into an inventory of the age's knaves and fools.
works.plot: The poet, appealed to by his Muse to name the wickedness of the times, enumerates the members and the purposes of the Legion Club, the lawyers, the informers and the patriots of the kingdom's administration, and discharges his subject in a catalogue of abuse.
works.significance: It is the ferocious close of Swift's satiric career and a permanent record of what verse invective could do to a party, and its suppression made it one of the century's notable cases of the writer against the licensing power.
works.meter: Heroic couplet driven at speed, with the reiterate name and the heaped epithet, the most violently colloquial of Swift's verse.
works.context: Written in the years when the Irish administration and the Whig clubs of Dublin had set Swift against the establishment of the kingdom he had defended in the Drapier's letters, and suppressed on publication when the Dublin printer was prosecuted.
works.characters: the poet; the Muse; the members of the club; the managers of the Irish parliament
works.structure: A dialogue frame with the Muse opening, followed by an accumulating catalogue and a closing dismissal.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Swift's; published without his name, and the copies were largely destroyed by the prosecution.

works.title: The Leiden Riddle
works.manuscriptDate: Leiden, Universiteitsbibliotheek, Voss. Lat. Q. 106, fol. 25v (c. 800, Northumbrian)
works.description: A fourteen-line Old English riddle translating Aldhelm's Latin Enigma 33 on the mail-coat (lorica): the garment made of many small iron rings, woven by no woman's hands, that guards the warrior's breast. It is the earliest surviving English riddle, preserved in a Northumbrian dialect.
works.plot: The riddle-speaker describes itself: a garment whose countless rings are joined without thread, forged of iron by smiths' skill, protecting the breast of the warrior who wears it in battle. The solution is the mail-coat (lorica).
works.significance: The earliest surviving English riddle and the earliest evidence of the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition's translation into the vernacular, bridging Aldhelm and the Exeter Book.
works.meter: Fourteen alliterative long lines translating Aldhelm's hexameters; the poem keeps the riddle's obliquity while adapting it to vernacular alliterative technique.
works.context: Written into the last leaf of a Leiden manuscript of the Latin riddles, the poem documents the translation of Aldhelmian learning into Northumbrian vernacular verse in the age of Bede; it is the direct ancestor of the Exeter Book riddle tradition.
works.structure: A classic first-person riddle in the Aldhelmian manner, moving from the material of the object to its making to its use in war.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation of Aldhelm's Enigma 33 ('Lorica'); the translator is unknown.
sources: Washington Irving: History, Tales, and Sketches (Library of America)

works.title: The Letter of Alexander to Aristotle
works.form: travel and wonders literature in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English translation of the apocryphal letter in which Alexander the Great writes to his teacher Aristotle of the wonders of India — monsters, beasts, and marvels encountered on his campaign — preserved in the Nowell Codex beside Beowulf. A key text of the Alexander legend's early reception in England.
works.plot: Alexander recounts to Aristotle his march into India: the battle with Porus, the encounter with the monstrous beasts (the beast with three horns, the giant crabs, the white lions, the two-headed serpents), the night of terrors in the wilderness, and the wonders of the trees of the sun and moon, concluding with the oracles of his death.
works.significance: The earliest English text of the Alexander legend and a major source for the monstrous imagination of the period.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated from the Latin Epistola Alexandri in the late tenth or early eleventh century; preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv, fols. 107v-131v).
works.characters: Alexander the Great; Aristotle (addressee); Porus
works.structure: An epistolary travel narrative in the first person, framed by the dedication to Aristotle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Time, death, and immortality through verse
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Restoration Drama

works.title: The Liberator
works.form: reform periodical and editorial prose: a four-page weekly combining the polemic editorial, the open letter, the report of testimony and the reprint column, in the tradition of the radical press rather than of the literary review.
works.description: A weekly abolitionist newspaper founded in Boston in January 1831 and continued for thirty-four years. It gave the American immediatist movement its organising vocabulary, its network of readers and its most combative editorials. The record here covers its foundation and first two years, when it moved from a colonisation-compatible position to an unequivocal demand for immediate emancipation without compensation. It printed speeches, letters, testimony of cruelty, reports of slave insurrections and religious controversy alongside its editorials.
works.plot: As a serial the paper has no single argument, but its editorial line is consistent: slavery is a sin and a national crime, immediate emancipation is a present duty, and the movement must be moral, religious and non-political in its first phase. Its prospectus and first issue disclaimed colonisation schemes, and its columns collected evidence of the institution's brutality until that evidence became unanswerable. Later issues covered the founding of the American Anti-Slavery Society, the schisms of the 1840s, the Fugitive Slave Law and the Civil War, ending with a victory number in 1865.
works.significance: It is the central print instrument of American radical Romanticism, the vehicle that converted abolition from a charitable cause into a mass movement, and the model for the sectional literature of the 1830s and 1840s. Historians of the press treat it as the most influential reform periodical published in the antebellum United States.
works.meter: Prose; the paper's signature rhetoric is an accumulated, urgent declarative style with heavy typographic emphasis.
works.context: Founded in the same months as the great pamphlet agitation of 1829-1831 and named after a term already used by earlier British abolition papers, it was funded by Black subscribers and voluntary agents in Boston and elsewhere. Its office was burned by a mob in 1834 and its mail was excluded from Southern post offices, which made its distribution an act of civil disobedience.
works.structure: Serial: weekly numbers, each built from editorial matter, correspondence, extracts from other papers, and notices of meetings; the founding issues establish the programme.
works.attributionNotes: Editorial responsibility is attributed to its founder, but the paper is a collaborative print object: correspondence, agents' reports and reprints from other periodicals form a large part of its text.

works.title: The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey
works.description: George Cavendish's memoir of Cardinal Wolsey, composed in the 1550s from the author's service in Wolsey's household; the first major English biography written by a layman and household servant.
works.plot: Cavendish recounts Wolsey's rise from butcher's son to cardinal and lord chancellor, his magnificence and building, the divorce crisis and the legatine court, his fall from favour, his death at Leicester Abbey in 1530, and the moral of Fortune's wheel; the narrative is thick with eyewitness detail of the cardinal's household, progresses, and final days.
works.significance: A masterpiece of Tudor biographical prose and the great contemporary portrait of Wolsey; its sympathetic account of the cardinal's fall and its influence on Shakespeare's Henry VIII make it a central document of early English biography.
works.meter: Prose with verse interludes
works.context: Written c. 1554–58, partly to vindicate Wolsey against the Protestant chroniclers Hall and Foxe; circulated in manuscript for decades and used by Stow, Holinshed, and Shakespeare, before its first printing in 1641 as The Negotiations of Thomas Wolsey.
works.characters: Cardinal Thomas Wolsey; George Cavendish (narrator); Henry VIII; Anne Boleyn; Thomas Cromwell (in the final scenes)
works.structure: A first-person memoir in chronological order, framed by a prologue on Fortune and divided by the rise, greatness, and fall of its subject; interludes of verse mark the turns of fortune.

works.title: The Life and Death of Mr. Badman
works.description: Bunyan's realistic prose narrative, presented as a dialogue between Mr. Wiseman and Mr. Attentive, of the life and unrepentant death of the wicked tradesman Badman; it is often regarded as the first English novel in prose.
works.plot: Wiseman recounts Badman's apprenticeship, his fraudulent bankruptcy, his mercenary marriage, his debauchery, his illnesses, and his death without repentance, drawing moral and economic lessons from each episode.
works.significance: A pioneering work of English prose realism and a major source for the social and economic history of the Interregnum; its detailed depiction of commercial fraud and domestic misery has no earlier English equivalent.
works.meter: Vivid, colloquial prose of trade, tavern, and household, unusually detailed in its social observation.
works.context: Published in 1658, in the last months of the Protectorate, as a warning against the sins of trade and the false peace of the unregenerate.
works.characters: Mr Badman; Mr Wiseman; Mr Attentive; Badman's first wife; his second wife; his apprentices
works.structure: A dialogue-narrative in which one speaker relates a life-story and the other comments; the episodic structure anticipates the picaresque novel.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bunyan; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy, Gentleman
altTitles: The Life and Opinions of Tristram Shandy
works.form: comic novel; experiment in narrative digression
works.description: A gentleman's life and opinions, begun before his birth and never arriving at it, in which the telling of a life is interrupted by the machinery of telling. Its first two volumes were published together in 1759 and the series ran to nine, with the writing and the reader's impatience forming the true subject.
works.plot: Tristram undertakes to write his life but is driven back to his father's theories of education, his uncle Toby's sieges and the misfortunes of his own naming and circumcising. The events of a Shandean life - the marriages, the wars, the errors of the midwife and of the post - are endlessly displaced by digression, while Yorick, the widow Wadman, Uncle Toby and Trim the horse supply their own episodes. The narrative advances by association and by the reader's expectation, closing in volumes that grow shorter and more reflective.
works.significance: It is the most radical narrative experiment of the century and a founding text of modern self-conscious fiction, anticipated by the readers of postmodernism and central to the history of the novel's idea of time.
works.meter: A prose of extraordinary rhythmic variety, from the aphoristic period of the projects to the broken colloquy of the kitchen, with the silence and the typographic device treated as parts of the style.
works.context: Written by a Yorkshire clergyman and published from 1759 in London after a provincial start, in the season of the new sensibility, the lockean science of ideas and the quarrel over the novel's licence; its publication history is bound up with the author's own delay and revision.
works.characters: Tristram Shandy; Walter Shandy, his father; Uncle Toby; Corporal Trim; Yorick; Dr. Slop; Susannah and the women of the house
works.structure: A digressive and self-referential first-person narration in nine books, with marbled pages, a blank page and a page of arms; the plot is the impossibility of its own chronological telling.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name, with the later volumes withdrawn and revised in issues that include the sermons' material.

works.title: The Life and Pontificate of Leo the Tenth
altTitles: The Life and Pontificate of Leo X
works.form: prose biography and pontifical history; historical narrative with disquisitions and scholarly annotation
works.description: The companion and sequel of the life of the Florentine ruler, a history of the papal pontificate at the moment when the revival of letters and the Reformation met. It rests upon manuscript evidence gathered in the Italian and Roman libraries, and it made its author's reputation as an accurate scholar of the age of the Medici popes.
works.plot: The work opens with the election of the second Medici pope, with the expectations of the cardinals and of the court, and with the pomp of the beginning of the pontificate, when the genius of the age was spent upon the buildings, the festivals, and the patronage of Rome. It then follows the affairs of the state of Europe through the leagues, the wars, and the diplomacy of the Italian powers, and the government of the church through the councils, the dispensations, and the exactions by which the revenue of the court of Rome was sustained. The largest part is the history of the beginning of the Reformation: the indulgence traffic, the appearance and the progress of the great heresiarch of Saxony, the diplomacy of the papal agents, the bull and the burning of the decree, and the interviews and the disputation by which the breach was made incurable, all judged from the side of a liberal Protestant historian who holds the corruption of the court responsible for the loss of the unity of Christendom. The closing volumes survey the literature and the art of the pontificate, the fortunes of the house of Medici, and the death of the pope amid the ruin of Italian affairs.
works.significance: It long held the field as the English history of the pontificate which opened the Reformation, and its combination of recovered manuscript evidence with a liberal judgement of the papal court made it a standard authority and an offence to the Roman censor; the two lives together founded the English historical study of the Renaissance. Its reading of the Reformation as the moral consequence of the corruption of the court, and of the age of Leo as the brilliant and corrupt union of letters and priestcraft, remained a presence in the historical imagination of the following century.
works.meter: Massed, circumstantial, judicial narrative prose: the long period of the balanced character, the accumulated evidence, and a Protestant moderation which keeps its severity within the courtesy of the scholar.
works.context: Published in the year of the author's other historical labours and of the closing of the wars of the revolutionary age, out of the same mass of transcripts gathered in Italy as the former life, and addressed to a British public for which the Reformation, the papacy, and the fate of Italian liberty were live questions. Its author was by then the chief ornament of the learned circle of the great port and a member of the short Parliament of the abolition era.
works.characters: Leo the Tenth; the cardinals and courtiers of the Roman pontificate; the reformers and the agents of the indulgence traffic; the princes of Europe and of Italy
works.structure: Several volumes in continuous annalistic narrative, with the books of the controversy and of the state of Europe divided among the occasions of the pontificate, and with the disquisitions upon the learning and the arts of the age bound into the history.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume of the manuscript materials obtained from the Italian libraries, and the share of the family papers in the later editions got up by the author's son, are recorded in the biographical and bibliographical accounts.

works.title: The Life of Harriot Stuart
altTitles: The Life of Harriot Stuart, Written by Herself
works.form: novel; amatory and autobiographical prose fiction
works.description: A first-person history of a young woman of quality carried by seduction, elopement and war from England to America and back. It was the author's first novel and an immediate success, combining the amatory plot with a self-conscious criticism of the romances its heroine has read.
works.plot: Harriot Stuart, the daughter of a noble family, is courted by designing men, betrayed by one who pretends to honour and pursued through a forced journey to the colonies. Her lover follows her across the Atlantic, the two are caught in the frontier war, and an elopement and a second seduction plot bring them within reach of ruin. Recovery and marriage come only after the exposures, and the narrative closes on the lesson that a woman's judgement must govern her sensibility.
works.significance: It is an important early instance of the novel that both uses and examines the amatory plot, and it established its author as one of the professional women novelists of the mid-century.
works.meter: A fluently emotional prose of the confessional style, with the heightened address of the romantic tradition moderated by ironic self-commentary.
works.context: Published in 1750, in the season of the mid-century vogue for histories written by themselves and of the colonial material drawn from the war in America; its author, a woman of the Bluestocking world, followed it with a series of novels and critical work.
works.characters: Harriot Stuart; the false suitor of her English years; her faithful lover; the officers and settlers of the American sections
works.structure: Continuous first-person retrospect in two volumes, the American sections supplying a picaresque and military interlude inside the amatory design; letters and reported speeches carry the crisis.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and reprinted in the collected editions of her works.

works.title: The Life of Lorenzo de Medici
altTitles: The Life of Lorenzo de' Medici, Called Lorenzo the Magnificent
works.form: prose biography and historical narrative; the life with an introductory survey and scholarly annotation
works.description: The first considerable English history of the Italian Renaissance, built as a life of the Florentine ruler and prefaced by an introductory view of the history of Italy before his age. It rests upon manuscript matter gathered in Italy as well as upon the printed authorities, and it made its author's European reputation with the companion life which followed.
works.plot: The introductory view traces the rise of the communes, the divisions of the guelfs and ghibellines, and the fortune of the house of Medici to the position from which Lorenzo governed; the life then follows his policy, the maintenance of the balance of the Italian states, the league made against the conspiracy of the Pazzi, and the journey to Naples by which, at the height of a crisis, he shifted the fortune of the war by his personal presence and his address. Alongside the narrative runs the history of the revival of letters and of the arts: the Platonist circle, the poetry and the architecture, the collectors and the schools, and the magnificent patronage with which the prince of a republic made Florence the court of Europe. The moral judgement is severe as well as admiring: the genius, the taste, and the political dexterity are allowed their praise, but the corruption of a free constitution under the forms of it, the spending of the public money upon private splendour, and the cultivation of luxury as an instrument of power are handled as the ruin of the country; the book closes with the death of Lorenzo and with the view of the French invasion and of the anarchy that followed his burial.
works.significance: It fixed for English readers the image of the Renaissance and of its most famous patron, and it established the historical method of the English liberal treatment of Italy, the authority against which the later students, from the historians of the age to the travellers of the nineteenth century, measured their own judgments. Its political moral, that a cultivated despotism disguised as a republic destroys the liberty which makes culture possible, was one of the most influential readings of Italian history of the revolutionary decade.
works.meter: Dignified, circumstantial, moralising narrative prose of the Whig historical school, with the full period, the balanced judgement of character, and a constant consciousness of the example to modern times.
works.context: The work of a country-bred lawyer and banker of the great trading community who had retired from practice to letters, made out of years of reading and out of manuscript copies obtained in Italy, and published in the decade in which the French invasion of Italy and the controversy over the French Revolution gave the fall of Italian liberties a direct political bearing. Its author sat afterward for the town of his residence in the short Parliament of the abolition era, and was the centre of a circle of learning and of the arts in the port.
works.characters: Lorenzo de' Medici; Giuliano de' Medici; the conspirators of the Pazzi; the scholars and artists of the Florentine circle; the princes and statesmen of Italy
works.structure: Two parts: the introductory view of Italian history before the age of the Medici, and the life itself in continuous narrative with the historical and literary disquisitions and the notes of the authorities bound in; the whole closes with the fortunes of the immediate successors.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the book's reliance upon the manuscript transcripts obtained from Italian libraries and upon the counsel of an antiquary friend is stated in the work itself and in the correspondence of the author's family.

works.title: The Life of Nelson
altTitles: The Life of Horatio, Viscount Nelson
works.form: Prose biography of the short national type, combining the memoir built on letters with the account of campaigns, and written for a general reader rather than for the navy.
works.description: A short prose biography of Admiral Viscount Nelson, published within months of the subject's death at Trafalgar and written by the poet who had spent the years of the Peninsular War in Portugal and had collected materials there. It was planned as one life in a series of the worthies of the country, and it rapidly became the standard account, passing through many editions and giving the national story of Nelson its permanent shape.
works.plot: The life follows the admiral from his entry as a boy into the service and his apprenticeship in the Arctic and the East Indies, through the losses of his right eye and his right arm, to the Mediterranean command, the battle of the Nile, and the Neapolitan episode, and then to the blockade of Toulon, the pursuit of the enemy fleet across the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, and the battle of Trafalgar, in which he was killed at the moment of victory. The narrative is built on the letters and the journals of the subject, quoted at length, and on the documents of the actions described, and it draws from them a portrait of a commander whose prudence, care for his officers and sailors, and religious faith were as remarkable as his daring. The argument is that a rector's son of Norfolk had made himself the instrument of his country's safety by steady attention, humanity and courage, and that his greatest victories were won before the action that killed him.
works.significance: The most durable English biography of Nelson and one of the most reprinted prose works of the period, fixed in the schools and in the gift-book trade of the nineteenth century as the account of the admiral; it is also the document that showed the Lake poet's later career at its most effective, and its method of building a life out of quoted letters was much imitated.
works.meter: Prose of unusual clearness and compression, in plain periods of narrative and quotation, with a habit of pointed summary at the end of the action; the book is commonly cited as a model of English biographical prose.
works.context: Written in 1813, in the middle of the Peninsular War and after the author's residence in Portugal as secretary to the commander-in-chief, when the nation's need of a hero after the death of Nelson and the fame of Trafalgar made the subject a public claim; the life was part of a plan of national biography and appeared in the same years as the author's appointment to the laurelship.
works.characters: Horatio Viscount Nelson; his father, the rector of Burnham Thorpe, and the kindred of his boyhood; his officers and the seamen of his fleet; the adversaries whom he encountered at the Nile and at Trafalgar
works.structure: A continuous prose life in a single volume, chronological and documentary, with the subject's own letters and the official papers of the actions interwoven, and with brief reflective passages on the character and on the use of biography; there is no dramatic partition of the matter.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested.

works.title: The Life of our Rev. John Wesley
altTitles: The Life of the Rev. John Wesley
works.form: Prose biography and religious history with documentary appendix, in the evangelical life-writing tradition, turned to a church-political argument.
works.description: The author's two-volume biography of the Methodist founder, compiled largely from Wesley's own journals and letters and from documents supplied to him by the Methodist leadership. It presents Wesley as a providential restorer of vital religion in England while insisting that his connexions were schismatic and should be dissolved. The book was a publishing event and an offence, and the quarrel it provoked with the Methodist preachers occupied its author for several years.
works.plot: The narrative follows Wesley from Epworth and Oxford through the Georgia voyage and the Aldersgate experience to the open-air preaching, the building of the connexional system, and the last years. The biographer stresses Wesley's learning, his industry, and his political quietism, and treats the revival as a divine visitation to a slothful church. At the same time he argues that the Methodist itinerants and their chapels are an illegal and unnecessary separation, and that after Wesley's death union with the established church is the duty of Methodists. The volumes reprint long passages of the Journal, of letters, and of doctrinal tracts, annotated critically, so that Wesley's own voice is permitted to answer his critics.
works.significance: The earliest scholarly biography of Wesley and a primary source for the Methodist journal, whose editorial practice - reprinting and commenting on the subject's own papers - made it a model and a warning for later religious biography; it is essential evidence of the romantic-era relation between revival and established religion.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Written when Methodism was negotiating its legal separation from the Church of England and when its author was consolidating his position as a church-and-state writer after the laureateship; it drew replies, pamphlet wars, and a defence in the Quarterly Review, and its text was revised in later editions as the quarrel continued.
works.characters: John Wesley; Charles Wesley; George Whitefield; the Methodist preachers of the connexion
works.structure: Chronological biography interwoven with extensive quotation from the subject's own journals and correspondence, and with argumentative notes and appendices; narrative and polemic alternate by design.

works.title: The Life of Samuel Johnson
altTitles: The Life of Samuel Johnson, LL.D.
works.form: literary biography and memoir, combining chronicle, document transcription and reported conversation
works.description: Boswell's biography of Johnson, the book that fixed the most familiar literary personality in English letters and invented the modern Life as an architecture of documents, conversation and chronology. It gathers letters, notebooks, the recollections of friends and Boswell's own journals into a year-by-year record of Johnson's studies, writings and company. It was advertised by a Prospectus of 1790 and published in 1791, with a revised second edition in 1793.
works.plot: The Life follows Johnson from his birth at Lichfield, through his schooling, marriage, early poverty and labours at the Dictionary, to the years of the Idler, the Tour, the Pension and the last illness, with the conversations of the clubs and the clubs of friends filling the frame. Boswell reports Johnson's arguments on free-will, on death, on Scotland and on the Jacobite past at length, and permits the subject's inconsistencies to stand unharmonised. The result is a biography that is also a record of an age of letters, of the book trade and of opinion.
works.significance: It is the foundational text of modern literary biography and the chief source for Johnson's mind and for the social history of Augustan and late-Augustan letters; its methods of transcription and chronology set the standard for later lives. It also preserves much of the periodical, critical and political writing of the age in a single narrative.
works.meter: Prose; a plain chronological diction framing the reported speech, whose rhythm is carried by Johnson's own sentences as transcribed.
works.context: Composed from materials assembled from Johnson's death in 1784 onward, in the decade when memoir and collected correspondence had become the standard mode of literary monument, and when the Scots and English literary worlds were being renegotiated after the American controversy. The work belongs with the late eighteenth-century efflorescence of biography and of the printed journal.
works.characters: Samuel Johnson; James Boswell; Hester Lynch Thrale; Thomas Tyrwhitt; Joshua Reynolds; the club of the Mitre and the Turk's Head
works.structure: A chronological biography with embedded documents - letters, certificates, earlier journals and the Tour - the largest continuous narrative being the years Boswell knew, and the whole prefaced by a statement of the materials and their provenance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested for the whole, though the Life incorporates the letters and papers of many hands, and the abridgements and re-editings of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries have repeatedly altered its state; the modern standard edition restores the several layers of the text.

works.title: The Life of Sir Thomas More
altTitles: The Lyfe of Sir Thomas Moore, Knighte
works.description: William Roper's intimate biography of his father-in-law Sir Thomas More, written in the 1550s but not printed until 1626; the first biography in English of a private subject written by a close contemporary.
works.plot: Roper recounts More's household and public career from his own memory and family tradition: More's early marriage and life at Chelsea, his rise under Henry VIII, the succession crisis, his resignation of the chancellorship, his imprisonment, trial, and execution, with the celebrated dialogues between More and his wife and daughters and More's reported words to his son-in-law on the king's favour.
works.significance: The founding text of English biographical writing and the principal source for the domestic life of More; its vivid remembered dialogue made it one of the most influential portraits of a Tudor statesman ever written.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written c. 1553–58, probably during Mary's reign, by More's son-in-law who had lived in More's household for sixteen years; circulated in manuscript (the 'Harpsfield' manuscript) and first printed at Saint-Omer in 1626, with the first English printing in 1726.
works.characters: Sir Thomas More; William Roper (narrator); Margaret Roper (More's daughter); Alice More; Henry VIII
works.structure: A continuous first-person memoir in chronological order, emphasizing the domestic and moral More, with set-piece conversations and the famous 'King's servant but God's first' speech.

works.title: The Life of St Katharine
altTitles: Capgrave's Life of Saint Katharine of Alexandria
works.description: John Capgrave's verse life of St Katharine of Alexandria, composed c. 1445: the learned virgin's conversion, her debate with the fifty philosophers, her refusal of the emperor Maxentius, the wheels of her torture, and her mystical marriage to Christ. The most polished saint's life of the fifteenth century, in rhyme royal with an elaborate prologue.
works.plot: Katharine, the learned princess of Alexandria, is converted by a hermit's vision of the Virgin and wedded to Christ; she confounds the emperor's philosophers in public debate, converts them and the empress, endures the wheels and the prison's angelic visits, and is beheaded — her body borne by angels to Sinai, where the milk, not blood, flows from her severed neck.
works.significance: The most accomplished Middle English life of St Katharine — the patron saint of learning — and the summit of fifteenth-century learned hagiography in verse.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of Lydgatean polish, with aureate diction and classical allusion.
works.context: Composed c. 1445 by the Augustinian friar John Capgrave of Lynn, in the learned East Anglian tradition of Lydgate and Bokenham; the prologue places the poem in the line of Chaucer's Legend of Good Women; preserved in Bodleian Rawlinson Poet. 118 and Arundel MS 396.
works.characters: St Katharine; the Emperor Maxentius; the fifty philosophers; the Virgin Mary; the hermit Adrian
works.structure: Five books of hagiographical narrative, from birth and conversion through debate and passion to translation, in the classical five-book scheme.
works.attributionNotes: Capgrave's authorship secure (he names himself in the prologue).
sources: Hope Leslie: Or, Early Times in the Massachusetts (American Women Writers series)

works.title: The Life of Washington
altTitles: The Life of Washington, with Curious Anecdotes, Equally Honourable to Himself, and Exemplary to His Young Countrymen
works.form: Prose biography for juvenile instruction; exemplary life with anecdotic and moral apparatus
works.description: A biography of Washington written for the young by an itinerant book agent and preaching minister, and the most widely circulated American life of the first president. It established the pattern of the exemplary national life built on anecdote and on the reader's feelings. The cherry-tree story of German honesty, added in a later edition, became the founding fable of American juvenile biography.
works.plot: The narrative follows Washington from the anecdotes of his childhood through the surveying and the French-and-Indian war to the command of the Continental army and the presidency. Each stage is illustrated by short stories of honesty, temperance, courage and courtesy, offered as models for imitation. The book dwells on the death at Mount Vernon and on the national mourning, and it urges the young reader to make private virtue the ground of public service. Its final pages bind the character of the man to the character of the republic he left behind.
works.significance: It is the most influential single book in the American culture of character, and the origin of the anecdote tradition in national biography. Its invention of a private Washington for the classroom defined how generations learned the founding. It is the canonical example of the juvenile and educational book of the early republic.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published within a year of the death of Washington in 1799, when the national mourning created an immediate market for his life. Its author was a Methodist preacher turned book canvasser who sold subscriptions in the southern and western country. The expansion of the text through the editions of the 1800s answers the new American demand for a usable founding mythology.
works.characters: George Washington; his mother; the planter and surveyor of the northern neck; the slaves and household of Mount Vernon
works.structure: Chronical biography broken into anecdotal episodes, with moral reflection addressed directly to the juvenile reader; the appendix of maxims and sayings grows with each edition.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the additions that make the book famous belong to later issues rather than to the first text.
