works.title: The Life of William Cowper, Esq.
altTitles: Letters of the Rev. William Cowper
works.form: Prose biography and edited correspondence: a life prefacing collected works, in the evangelical memoir tradition but practised as literary history.
works.description: The author's biography of William Cowper, written as the life prefacing a collected edition of Cowper's works and built on the poet's correspondence and on interviews with survivors. It is a work of editorial as much as of narrative art, and its frank handling of Cowper's madness and of his religious terror made it the most discussed English literary biography of the later 1830s. Its use of private letters also set a precedent, and a warning, for the practice of literary biography.
works.plot: The Life narrates Cowper's school years, his apprenticeship and his first poetry, the friendship with Lady Austen and the years at Olney, the partnership with Mrs. Unwin, and the later settlement at East Dereham and Weston Underwood. It prints and comments on the correspondence with the Rev. Mr. Newton, and gives a clinical and unsentimental account of the poet's depressions, his attempted suicide, and his final evangelical assurance. The biographer draws from the letters a picture of rural and manufacturing England, including Cowper's own condemnation of the way poor parents bound out and ruined their children. The publication of certain letters gave offence to surviving friends and relatives, who objected to what had been made public.
works.significance: The foundation of all later Cowper scholarship and a decisive text in the history of literary biography and of editorial ethics; its documentary passages on eighteenth-century labour and the manufacturing system have been used as social evidence by writers of every politics since.
works.meter: Prose, quoting verse and letters at length.
works.context: Prepared after its author had obtained access to Cowper's papers from the surviving collaterals, and issued in a cheap collected edition of the works in the mid 1830s; the controversy over its use of private letters ran for years and drew replies from those who thought the family betrayed.
works.characters: William Cowper; the Rev. Mr. Newton; Mrs. Unwin; Lady Austen; Mrs. Connard; the curate of Olney
works.structure: Chronological literary biography interwoven with long quoted correspondence and with documentary extract; narrative, letters, and editorial comment alternate, with topographical and social matter folded into the record of the life.

works.title: The Literary Souvenir
altTitles: The Literary Souvenir: A Christmas and New Year's Present
works.form: Literary annual and keepsake verse: the miscellany gift-book of lyric, tale and short criticism, formatted for seasonal presentation with steel engraving.
works.description: One of the two great London literary annuals of the later 1820s, first issued for the season dated 1825 and continued annually under a founding editor who was also a poet and man of letters in his own right. It set itself deliberately against the merely decorative keepsake, claiming to offer literature of durable value as well as a gift-book's plates and bindings. Its volumes assembled poems, tales, historical and topographical papers and criticism from the most fashionable contributors of the day. It is the annual that best documents the editorial self-consciousness of the gift-book trade.
works.plot: The volumes have no continuous argument; their design is an assortment of occasional verse, short prose tales, historical sketches and critical papers grouped around engraved plates. Its editor's prefaces do, however, conduct a running argument about the annual's purpose: that a gift book should keep literature in circulation rather than merely ornament a drawing-room, and that the paying of handsome fees to established writers was the way to secure that.
works.significance: It is the most self-consciously literary of the great annuals and a primary vehicle for the transmission of Romantic and early-Victorian verse into middle-class domestic life. Its editorial statements are the best contemporary account of what an annual was for, and its files preserve poems and papers that entered the canon through gift-book circulation.
works.meter: Occasional and reflective verse in conventional stanzas and the sonnet form, with romantic ballad measures; prose in the familiar essay and tale registers.
works.context: Appearing in the years when the annual boom made the gift book the largest single market for verse and short prose, and when editors competed openly for the same contributions, its early volumes record the trade's circulation figures and its editorial quarrels over originality. It belongs to the later phase of Romantic literary commerce, shaped by new engraving technology and by a reading public that bought presents rather than books.
works.structure: Serial annual anthology: frontispiece plate, editor's preface, then a mixed succession of poem, tale, sketch and critical paper.
works.attributionNotes: The volumes were edited throughout by a single named literary editor, but the annual is a collaborative miscellany whose contents are individually attributable; the record is of the serial as a whole.

works.title: The Little Woodman and his Dog Cæsar
altTitles: The Little Woodman and his Dog Caesar
The History of the Little Woodman and his Dog Cæsar
works.form: juvenile and devotional tale; the domestic narrative of the injured child with the animal fidelity
works.description: A tale for children, first published in 1818 and reprinted without end through the century, of the youngest child of a poor woodman's family, of the cruelty of his elder brothers, and of the fidelity of the dog Cæsar; one of the most widely read of the English books of the exposed child and of the brute that serves the innocent.
works.plot: The tale opens in the hut of a woodman of the forest country, whose family is poor, whose elder sons are hard and envious, and whose youngest, the little William, is a child of gentleness and of the book. Upon the father's death the burden of the household falls upon the brothers, and the wickedness of the elder sons, prompted by the greed of the portion and by hatred of the piety of the little boy, carries him into the forest and leaves him there to perish by hunger and by the beasts. The dog Cæsar, bound to the child by the tenderness of his rearing, watches over him in the woods, defends him against the wolf that stalks him, and becomes the means of the discovery of the guilt; the cruelty is searched out, the guilty brothers come to ruin, and the preserved child is provided for and brought forward in his little education. The argument of the book is the religious argument of the whole class of these tales: that Providence keeps the innocent, that the sin of the household is found out in its own time, and that the reading of the Bible and the duty of gentleness to the young and to the brute are the whole wisdom of the child.
works.significance: The type of the evangelical tale of the exposed child and of the ministering animal, and one of the most permanently remembered of the books of the English nursery: the figure of the faithful dog and the scene of the forest are among the stock images of juvenile writing, and the tale has been read ever since as the exemplar of the method by which terror, pathos, and providential justice were combined for the moral use of children.
works.meter: Plain, urgent, and affecting prose of the evangelical teacher for the young reader, with the little speech of the child, the terror of the forest scene told in short unadorned sentences, and the solemn tenderness of the moral; the pathos of the brute's fidelity is gained by the restraint of the style.
works.context: Published in 1818, the year which gave the world also the religious family history of the same pen, in the season of the cheap and the Sunday-school book, when the tale of the persecuted child and of the faithful animal was the most powerful instrument of the juvenile trade and when the terror and the tenderness of such stories were held necessary to the formation of the conscience of the labouring and middling ranks. Its author, an officer's wife long resident in the company's territories, had already written the Indian child's tale, and the woodman's story became, with her other little books, a standing possession of the nursery and of the circulating juvenile libraries of both countries.
works.characters: The woodman and his wife; the little William, the youngest of the family; the elder brothers, hard, idle, and envious; the faithful dog Cæsar; the neighbours and the people of the forest country who search out the crime
works.structure: A single continuous tale for the young reader, in short chapters of the plain domestic narrative, moving from the hut and the forest to the exposure, the preservation, the discovery, and the religious close, with the direct address of the moral to the child at the turn of the several parts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the title is variously given at length and at abbreviature in the later issues, the name of the dog and the spelling of the title being altered in the reprints, and the tale was also issued in the combined juvenile volumes and in the abridged cheap series, which do not follow the first text.

works.title: The Lord's Prayer I, II, and III
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990 (versions I and II); Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (version III)
works.form: religious lyric (prayer paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: Three independent Old English versifications of the Lord's Prayer. The first (123 lines with its doxology) expands each petition into doctrinal and devotional verse; the second (19 lines) is a close rendering; the third, in a Mercian dialect, survives in Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.plot: Each poem paraphrases the petitions of the Pater Noster — the hallowing of God's name, the coming of the kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil — expanding them with commentary on the soul's needs, the devil's snares, and the last judgment.
works.significance: The fullest surviving Old English treatment of the central Christian prayer, showing how poets turned liturgical texts into vernacular verse of considerable doctrinal ambition.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the first version's expansions use formulaic homiletic diction familiar from the Exeter Book religious poems.
works.context: The Lord's Prayer was among the first texts every Christian learned, and Alfred's preface to the Pastoral Care singles out prayer as a duty of the learned; vernacular versifications made the prayer available for devotion and meditation in the native idiom.
works.structure: The first version works petition by petition through the prayer, ending with an elaborated doxology; the shorter versions render the prayer more directly with brief homiletic expansions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The three versions are independent texts by different poets, grouped here for convenience as in the standard editions.
themes: Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
sources: The Complete Poetical Works of Lord Byron (7 volumes)

works.title: The Loves of the Angels
works.form: Religious narrative poem in the line of sacred and legendary verse, drawing on apocryphal and patristic matter about the angels who transgressed.
works.description: A devotional narrative poem on the antediluvian legend of the Watchers, telling of pure spirits who love the daughters of men, descend into the world of passion and war, and are reclaimed by penitence. It is written in three parts and is expressly a religious poem, intended to assert the possibility of holiness preserved amid temptation. The volume appeared with other shorter pieces and provoked immediate charges of borrowing.
works.plot: Two angels, bound by a friendship that the poem treats as the type of all holy attachment, are drawn down by love of mortal women into the antediluvian world, where they witness and share its wars, its tyranny and its grief. The narrative moves from their fall-like descent through the history of the race towards the coming Deluge, and then to intercession, repentance and restoration. The poem's argument is doctrinal as well as romantic: it claims that created love, rightly ordered, is the means by which even a fallen spirit may return, and it figures the Deluge as both judgement and cleansing. Its closing movements exchange the narrative for address and prayer, so that the legend becomes an image of the soul's education.
works.significance: It is the clearest statement of the poet's religious imagination and one of the more ambitious attempts of the later Romantic generation to write a doctrinal narrative poem. Contemporary controversy over its sources turned it into a case study in the period's anxieties about plagiarism and influence. Its treatment of spiritual friendship and of redeemable fallenness has drawn renewed critical attention in the study of Romantic religious verse.
works.meter: Varied lyric stanza measures with heavy use of refrain, invocation and apostrophe; blank-verse-like meditative passages are interwoven.
works.context: Published in the early 1820s, when biblical and legendary subjects were being treated by poets of every party and when religious poetry had become a field of controversy between evangelicals, Unitarians and infidels. Its appearance was read as a defence of the poet's own piety against sceptical reputation, and its subject was taken up in the reviews alongside questions of originality and of imitation. The Deluge material was familiar both from Milton and from the popular legendary drama.
works.characters: The two loving angels; the mortal beloveds of the antediluvian world; the patriarchal and warrior figures of the pre-Deluge race
works.structure: A continuous narrative in three parts, rising from the descent of the spirits through human history to deliverance, with meditative and apostrophising passages interrupting the story.

works.title: The Loves of the Plants
works.form: Didactic and descriptive verse in heroic couplets with prose scientific notes
works.description: A didactic poem in four cantos which translates the Linnaean sexual system of botany into a pageant of personified flowers, each plant's reproductive organs rendered as the amours of a nymph and her swain. It first appeared in 1789 and was then issued as the second part of The Botanic Garden in 1791, and its brilliance, obscurity and frank eroticism made it at once a bestseller and a scandal. Erasmus Darwin supplies scientific matter in the accompanying notes, where he argues the vegetable kingdom's real structure.
works.plot: The poem passes in sequence through the classes and orders of the Linnaean system, dramatising each as an allegorical courtship or marriage: the polyandrous female fern, the mutual fidelity of the flax, the violent loves of the poppy, the priestly solemnities of the mosses. Beneath the gallantry runs a serious argument about irritability, the contrivances of pollination, and the vegetable physiology revealed by microscopical enquiry. The closing canto turns from the floral court to the great powers of nature and to a deist hymn to universal benevolence, binding vegetable life into a general economy of heat, light and growth.
works.significance: The most influential English poem on botany, it shaped a generation's reading of Linnaeus and supplied the ornamental scientific vocabulary later parodied and admired. Coleridge and Southey acknowledged its example and Wordsworth's protest against personification is partly aimed at it; its mixture of erotic allegory and apparatus of notes is a distinctive late-Augustan solution to the problem of didactic form.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, variably decorated with lyric intercalations, imitation of air-sounds and insect-music
works.context: Written in the Derby-Lichfield circle of erasmian natural philosophy and popular science, it transmits Linnaeus through translation and the sexual politics of the 1780s, amid the Botanical Society vogue, Erasmus Darwin's own zoonomic researches, and the radical Dissenting enthusiasm for progress and abolition.
works.characters: Venus or the presiding goddess of the garden; personified plant-nymphs; sylphs and gnomes of the floral courts
works.structure: Four cantos of linked ekphrastic episodes arranged by Linnaean class and order, with a scientific apparatus of prose notes appended to each.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Erasmus Darwin is established and undisputed.

works.title: The Magnetic Lady; or, Humours Reconciled
works.description: Jonson's last comedy, in which the learned Lady Loadstone acts as a magnet drawing a set of humours characters together and reconciling them through a marriage plot and a discovered heiress.
works.plot: Lady Loadstone's household gathers a soldier, a parson, a courtier, a physician, and others; a concealed heiress, Pleasance, is discovered, the suitors are tested, and the humours are reconciled in marriage.
works.significance: Jonson's farewell to comedy and a final attempt to reconcile the humours tradition with a romantic plot; its induction is a rare piece of Jonsonian meta-theatrical commentary.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in 1632 and published in the 1640 folio.
works.characters: Lady Loadstone; Pleasance; Compass; Bias; Parson Palate; Captain Ironside; Sir Moth Interest; Doctor Rut
works.structure: Five acts with an unusual induction in which two audience figures discuss the play.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Jonson; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Maid of Honour
works.description: Massinger's tragicomedy of Camiola, the 'maid of honour' of Siena, who refuses to ransom the captured noble Bertoldo until he pledges himself to her, and who finally retires to a convent rather than marry a prince's brother.
works.plot: Bertoldo, captured by the King of Tunis, is ransomed by Camiola; he repays her with ingratitude; she brings him to justice, and, her honour vindicated, she takes the veil.
works.significance: An early and influential Massinger tragicomedy, notable for its strong, morally autonomous heroine; it was adapted by Johnson in 1730 as The Successful Pyrate.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men at the Red Bull c. 1622 and published in 1632.
works.characters: Camiola; Bertoldo; Roberto; Ferdinand; Fulgoso; Adorni; Clarinda
works.structure: Five acts with a double plot of court intrigue and moral constancy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Massinger; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Maid's Tragedy
works.description: Beaumont and Fletcher's tragedy of honour: Amintor, commanded by the king, breaks his vow to Aspatia and marries Evadne — who is the king's secret mistress; Evadne's repentance, her murder of the king in the bedchamber, and Amintor's and Aspatia's deaths follow, in the play's double catastrophe of the marriage bed and the wedding night turned funeral.
works.plot: The wedding night reveals Evadne's secret; Amintor's honour forbids revenge on the king; Aspatia, disguised as her own brother, takes the duel's death-blow from Amintor; Evadne, converted by her brother Melantius, kills the king; and the last act's cascade — Evadne's rejection, Aspatia's death, Amintor's suicide — empties the court of its lovers.
works.significance: The strongest of the Beaumont–Fletcher tragedies — the play in which the partnership's courtly polish met the Jacobean taste for blood.
works.meter: The fluent tragic verse of the partnership, with Evadne's and Aspatia's great speeches as its heights.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men about 1610–11 and printed in 1619; its king-killing and bedchamber horrors made it the most talked-of tragedy of its decade.
works.characters: Amintor; Evadne; Aspatia; Melantius; the King; Calianax; Lysippus; Diphilus; the Ladies; the masquers
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of honour in the Senecan manner, with the bedchamber murder and the double suicide as its symmetrical climaxes.
works.attributionNotes: Jointly by Beaumont and Fletcher; the division of scenes is debated.

works.title: The Malcontent
works.description: Marston's tragicomedy of the displaced duke: Altofronto, deposed by his usurping brother Pietro, returns to court disguised as the malcontent Malevole, whose bitter truths scour the court of Genoa; through the intrigues of Mendoza, the play's machiavel, the plots double and reverse until the final scene's masque restores the true duke — and with him the play's satirical license.
works.plot: Malevole haunts the usurper's court with truth-telling; Mendoza, the courtier, plots to seize the duchy, poisoning, banishing, and betraying in turn; the counter-plots of Malevole and the banished Pietro (in disguise) entangle the machiavel; and the final masque, with the deaths staged and revealed, restores Altofronto to his throne and pardons the penitent.
works.significance: The play that named the Jacobean malcontent — the great satire of courtly corruption that Shakespeare answered in Measure for Measure.
works.meter: Marston's snarling, paradoxical verse for Malevole's truths, with prose for the court's baseness.
works.context: Performed by the Children of the Chapel in 1604 and printed the same year; Webster supplied an induction for the King's Men's revival, and the play's 'malcontent' became the decade's signature type.
works.characters: Altofronto (Malevole); Pietro Jacomo; Mendoza; Aurelia; Ferneze; Celso; Bilioso; Maquerelle; Maria; the fools (Passarello)
works.structure: A five-act tragicomedy built on the disguised-duke device, with the malcontent's satiric set pieces and the final masque of revelations.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Man of Mode; or, Sir Fopling Flutter
works.description: Etherege's masterpiece, the greatest comedy of manners of the Restoration, in which the rake Dorimant manipulates a whole fashionable society of lovers, fops, and mothers with effortless wit.
works.plot: Dorimant courts the rich heiress Harriet while abandoning Mrs Loveit; the fop Sir Fopling Flutter is mocked throughout; Dorimant wins Harriet by pretending to be a country gentleman, and the play ends with marriage and the rout of the pretenders.
works.significance: The supreme achievement of Restoration social comedy and the model for Congreve, Sheridan, and Wilde; it created the type of the gentleman-rake and the standard of high-comic dialogue in English.
works.meter: Prose of extraordinary rhythmic precision; the dialogue is the model of Restoration wit.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Garden on 11 March 1676 and dedicated to the Earl of Rochester; Dorimant was widely taken to be Rochester and Sir Fopling to be a caricature of several court fops.
works.characters: Dorimant; Harriet; Mrs Loveit; Bellinda; Sir Fopling Flutter; Young Bellair; Emilia; Lady Woodvill; Medley; Shoat; Orange
works.structure: Five acts of intricate social intrigue with no subplot of consequence, unified by the figure of Dorimant.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Etherege; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
works.form: Illuminated prophetic book and verse-and-prose satire, partly a parody of the devotional table and of the prophetic writing then current, and partly a manifesto of the contrary energies of the soul.
works.description: The most argumentative of the illuminated books, etched and printed by the author in the years following the two collections of songs, and written in a mixed prose and verse manner after the model of a prophetic book and in open parody of the religious tables then current. Its occasion is a memory of a hell where the spirits of the dead are taught by an angel, and its case is that without contraries there is no progression, and that the energies called devilish are the active and creative half of the human soul, while the heaven of patient receiving and the morality of the priesthood are its passive and repressive half.
works.plot: The book opens with the proposition that without contraries there is no progression, and that attraction and repulsion, energy and reason, are necessary to existence, and then reports a memorable fancy in which the author sees in hell an angel sleeping, wakes him, and finds that the angel's religion of patience and of the outward law is undone by the teaching of the place. The voice of the devil follows, arguing that worship is the blessing of the strong to the weak, that the gospel's teacher was a philanthropist and not a priest, and that the true religion is the delight of the senses and the energies of desire. A series of proverbs of Hell then states in short sentences a counter-morality of excess, of the desire that is not executed, of the tigers of wrath being wiser than the horses of instruction, and of the prison and the brothel as built with the stones of law and the bricks of religion. The middle plates give the lights of the six senses, the types of moral character, and a passage on the sacred books of the East, and the book closes with a song of liberty, in which the dragon of the old state is kindled and overthrown and the voices of the morning cry aloud among the nations of the west.
works.significance: The founding text of the poet's own prophetic system and the most widely read of his illuminated books, the source of his most quoted sentences on contraries, on the energies of desire and on the institutions built by the law, and the standing example of the Romantic prose-verse pamphlet. Its closing song of liberty made it a permanent document of revolutionary writing, and its argument supplied the terms in which later readers described the imagination's enmity to the moral system.
works.meter: Chiefly prose of a rapid, gnomic and declamatory kind, with the proverbs in balanced and pointed sentences and the verse passages in short reiterated song lines, the whole varying between the sermon, the aphorism and the air.
works.context: Etched and printed in London in the years immediately after the two collections of songs, in the decade of the English reception of the new religious writings from the Continent and of the controversy about the French Revolution; the book's attack on the priesthood, on the law and on a religion of patience is written out of the radical religious argument of the 1790s.
works.characters: The narrator who records the dream of the sleeping angel; the angel of the book's vision; the voice of the devil, who dictates the book's creed; the daughters of memory and the phantoms of the closed song of liberty
works.structure: A continuous illuminated argument in plates, mixing vision, oration, proverb, catalogue and closing song; the parts are bound by the claim that the book's teaching is the doctrine of contraries, and by the figure of the narrator who reports what the spirits of hell said to him.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of the first issue is fixed by the internal evidence of the plates and by the author's later references rather than by a printed title page.

works.title: The Masque of Anarchy
works.form: Political and revolutionary verse; the allegorical pageant poem and public address, in the ballad measure of the periodical and handbill tradition.
works.description: A political poem of ninety stanzas written within days of the cavalry charge on a peaceful reform meeting in a northern city, and withheld from print for more than a decade. Memory, Murder and Fraud ride in a masque with their following of Plagues, Creeds and Laws, and at their head Power, seated on a throne of skulls, announces that whatever is, is right. The poem then turns to an address to the people of England, urging a resistance of folded arms, and it is the first great statement of non-violent mass protest in modern letters.
works.plot: The dreamer sees a pageant marching through the mist of a northern city, a ghost with a mask of gold crying that God and the king and the people are one with its own interest, and behind it Murder with a bald and shining forehead, Fraud holding a blood-besmeared book, and a procession of Plagues, Hypocrisy and Superstition with their laws and creeds. The mask is broken by the appearance of a figure of Liberty who is trampled down, and the poem's second half passes to an exhortation to the thousands who are starving, to rise with their arms folded and let the sabres fall on nothing but the will. The argument is that a people that refuses to strike, and makes the state's violence visible by its own stillness, is the power that cannot be conquered.
works.significance: It is the founding text of the literature of non-violent resistance and its image of the folded arms was taken up by the labour, chartist and later pacifist movements. Its treatment of a state whose allegorical mask is transparent, and its theory that the governed outnumber the governors in will, remain the most influential Romantic account of popular protest.
works.meter: Four-line ballad quatrains of alternating four- and three-beat anapestic lines, rhyming abab, a measure borrowed from the popular and the school of the earlier political song; the repetition of the refrain gives it its force.
works.context: Written at Leghorn in the September of 1819, within a fortnight of the charge of the yeomanry on the reformers' meeting in the northern city and of the prosecutions and suspensions of public meeting that followed, and offered to a liberal editor who judged it unprintable. It was withheld for more than a decade and published only in 1832, the year of the first reform bill's passage, by the same editor who had declined it, with a prefatory account of its suppression; its delayed circulation among friends influenced the radical poetry of the later century.
works.characters: the dreamer-witness of the pageant; the masked Power at the head of the procession; Murder, Fraud and Hypocrisy as the shapes of the state; Liberty, the trampled woman of the crowd; the assembled people of England
works.structure: Two clearly marked parts, the allegorical pageant seen in a dream of the northern city and the direct political exhortation addressed to the crowd; the whole is in a continuous four-line stanza of ballad measure.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the manuscript was copied and read in the author's circle, and a version altered for the publisher's fears survives, the full text being established from the holograph.

works.title: The Masque of Blackness
works.description: The first of Jonson's great court masques, designed by Inigo Jones and danced by Queen Anne and her ladies: twelve nymphs of Niger, blackened by the sun, voyage to 'Britannia' in a giant sea-shell seeking the land whose sun (King James) can whiten them — the masque of racial transformation that founded the Stuart court's most spectacular genre.
works.plot: Niger, his daughters, and the moon-goddess Aethiopia arrive in a moving shell drawn by sea-monsters; the songs announce that the nymphs must seek 'a land whose name is Britannia'; they dance, and the final song promises their cleansing by the British sun — a transformation deferred to the sequel, The Masque of Beauty (1608).
works.significance: The inauguration of the Jonson–Jones masque, the Stuart court's supreme art form, and a text now central to studies of race in the Renaissance.
works.meter: Songs in varied lyric forms with the speeches in blank verse, the whole scaled to the banqueting house's acoustics and spectacle.
works.context: Performed at Whitehall on Twelfth Night, 6 January 1605, with the Queen herself blackened in body-paint; the masque's racial and political meanings — union, empire, and whiteness — are now the subject of intense critical debate.
works.characters: Niger; Aethiopia; the twelve nymphs (danced by Queen Anne and her ladies); Oceanus
works.structure: A single masque of arrival and prophecy — antimasque, main masque, and revels — with Jones's machinery (the moving shell, the painted waves) as equal partner to Jonson's verse.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the setting and machines are Inigo Jones's designs.

works.title: The Massacre at Paris
works.description: Marlowe's late topical tragedy of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre (1572): the Duke of Guise, with the Queen Mother Catherine de Medici, engineers the slaughter of the Huguenots; the Protestant hero Ramus dies; and the play runs through the assassinations of Guise and of Henry III to the accession of the Protestant Henry of Navarre.
works.plot: Guise murders the Huguenot leadership and the scholar Ramus; Navarre escapes the massacre; the Guise's ambition threatens the crown itself until Henry III has him killed; the friar's dagger avenges Guise by killing the king, and the play ends with Navarre's triumph and England's alliance.
works.significance: The first English play of contemporary European politics — Protestant propaganda raised to tragedy, surviving only in mutilated form.
works.meter: Blank verse with the 'mighty line' audible in the surviving fragments, notably Guise's soliloquies of ambition.
works.context: Performed by Strange's Men in January 1593, in the wake of Henri IV's conversion and English fears of the Catholic League; printed in a poor octavo about 1594.
works.characters: the Duke of Guise; Catherine de Medici; Henry III of France; Henry of Navarre; Ramus; the Duke of Anjou; the Cardinal of Lorraine; Mugeroun; the Friar
works.structure: A compressed chronicle of murder and counter-murder — the surviving text (an octavo of about 1,250 lines) is clearly a cut or memorially reconstructed version of a longer play.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the text is evidently a damaged report of the original.

works.title: The Medal
altTitles: The Medal: A Satire against Sedition
works.description: Dryden's angry direct satire, provoked by the Whig medal struck to honour Shaftesbury after his acquittal on the charge of high treason; it abandons allegory for open invective.
works.plot: The poem denounces Shaftesbury and the City of London as seditious, attacks the doctrine of popular sovereignty, and closes with a prophetic address to the king urging firm government.
works.significance: The most forthright of Dryden's political satires and an important document of Tory argument in the Exclusion Crisis.
works.meter: Heroic couplets.
works.context: Published in March 1682, shortly after Shaftesbury's acquittal by the Old Bailey jury in November 1681; it drew Shadwell's reply The Medal of John Bayes.
works.characters: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury; the 'true-blue Protestant' crowd
works.structure: A three-part invective: the medal and its meaning, the character of the Whig leaders, and the concluding political doctrine.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Menologium
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius B.i (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201), eleventh century
works.description: A metrical calendar of the church year in 231 lines, versifying the fixed feasts and saints' days from Christmas through the year to Advent, with careful attention to the intervals of days between festivals. It is prefixed to the C-text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.plot: The poem proceeds through the liturgical year — Christmas, Epiphany, the spring feasts, Easter's movable cycle, the summer and autumn saints' days, and the return of Advent — computing the days between the major festivals and naming the saints honoured in the English church.
works.significance: The only surviving Old English metrical calendar, and a document of the English church's festal year at the height of the Benedictine Reform.
works.meter: Alliterative long line disciplined to the calendar's enumerative demands; the poet's art lies in varying formulaic phrasing within a rigid frame.
works.context: The poem reflects the English church's calendar as reformed in the tenth century, and its position beside the Chronicle shows the integration of liturgical and historical time in Benedictine Reform culture.
works.structure: A strictly sequential calendar, each feast introduced with its date and interval from the last; the structure is numerical and liturgical rather than narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Gothic confinement and the pursued heroine
sources: The Works of Thomas De Quincey (21 volumes)

works.title: The Merchant of Venice
works.description: Shakespeare's comedy of credit, bonds, and mercy: the merchant Antonio pledges a pound of his own flesh to the Jewish moneylender Shylock to fund his friend Bassanio's courtship of the heiress Portia, who — disguised as a lawyer — saves Antonio in the trial scene and turns the bond against its maker.
works.plot: Bassanio wins Portia by choosing the lead casket; Shylock, his daughter Jessica fled with a Christian and his bond forfeited, claims his pound of flesh; Portia's legal trap — the bond allows flesh but not blood — defeats him, and the play ends with the ring trick and the news of Antonio's restored argosies, leaving Shylock's forced conversion and the play's anti-Semitism to shadow the comedy.
works.significance: One of the most performed and most contested plays in the canon — the 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech and the quality-of-mercy plea are cornerstones of world drama.
works.meter: Blank verse for the trial and courtship, prose for the Venetian streets, with the lyric interludes of 'Tell me where is fancy bred'.
works.context: Written about 1596–97, in the aftermath of the Lopez affair and against the background of the Venetian Ghetto; its Jew is both the period's stock villain and its most human outsider.
works.characters: Antonio; Shylock; Bassanio; Portia; Jessica; Lorenzo; Nerissa; Gratiano; the Duke of Venice; Tubal; Launcelot Gobbo
works.structure: Interlaced Venice and Belmont plots — the bond and the caskets — joined at the trial, with the Jessica–Lorenzo elopement and the ring episode as connecting tissue.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Merry Wives of Windsor
works.description: Shakespeare's only citizen comedy, traditionally said to have been written because Elizabeth I wished to see Falstaff in love: the fat knight courts the wives Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, who turn the tables on him through the buck-basket, the disguise of the fat woman of Brentford, and the final horns of Herne the Hunter in Windsor Forest.
works.plot: Falstaff sends identical love letters to two wives, who conspire to humiliate him; Ford's jealousy supplies a second plot of disguise and misprision; and the play resolves in the midnight masque of the fairies, where Falstaff is pinched and the eloping Anne Page marries the suitor of her choice against her parents' plots.
works.significance: Shakespeare's only comedy of his own England and time — the ancestor of the English sitcom and the later operatic masterpieces it inspired.
works.meter: Over ninety percent prose — the most prosaic of Shakespeare's plays — with the fairy rhymes of the final scene.
works.context: Dated about 1597, possibly for a Garter feast at Windsor; it transplants Falstaff from the history plays into contemporary Windsor life.
works.characters: Sir John Falstaff; Mistress Ford; Mistress Page; Ford; Page; Anne Page; Fenton; Slender; Doctor Caius; Sir Hugh Evans; Mistress Quickly; Pistol; Nym; the Host
works.structure: A three-humiliation comic structure (basket, beating, forest masque) interwoven with the Anne Page marriage intrigue and the Latin lesson of Sir Hugh Evans and William.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Metrical Charms
works.description: A group of verse charms against illness, theft, and misfortune, preserved mainly in eleventh-century medical manuscripts (the Lacnunga and related collections). The charms blend Christian prayer with pre-Christian incantation — most famously the Nine Herbs Charm, invoking Woden as the healer of herbs, and Wið færstice, against a sudden stabbing pain caused by a 'mighty woman's' riding.
works.plot: Each charm prescribes words and actions for a specific ill: the Nine Herbs Charm enumerates the nine sacred herbs and their powers against poison and infection, invoking Woden's victory with nine glory-twigs; Wið færstice fights the elf-shot with a spear-image and a boiled herbal drink; others protect bees from swarming, fields from blight, and travellers from harm.
works.significance: The richest vernacular evidence for Anglo-Saxon folk medicine and for the survival of Germanic ritual in a Christian culture.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, often irregular; incantatory repetition.
works.context: Preserved in London, British Library, Harley MS 585 (the Lacnunga), the Old English Herbarium manuscripts, and other medical compilations; the pre-Christian elements survived within Christian manuscripts.
works.characters: Woden (in the Nine Herbs Charm); the healer; the malevolent powers
works.structure: Prescriptive lyric sequences: invocation, narrative of the ill or its cure, and ritual instruction, often in verse alternating with prose directions.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: William Wordsworth: The Major Works

works.title: The Metrical Psalms of the Paris Psalter
works.description: A verse translation of Psalms 51-150 preserved in the Paris Psalter (Bibliothèque nationale de France, lat. 8824), accompanying the prose translation of Psalms 1-50. Once attributed to King Alfred, the verse psalms are now regarded as anonymous tenth- or eleventh-century work; they constitute the largest single body of Old English psalmody.
works.plot: The psalms are rendered in fluent alliterative verse, expanding the biblical text with traditional poetic diction; the collection provides the fullest surviving example of Old English liturgical translation in verse.
works.significance: The fullest English verse psalter before the late Middle Ages; important for the study of vernacular liturgy.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of a relatively plain, expository kind.
works.context: Preserved in the Paris Psalter (Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, MS lat. 8824), a mid-eleventh-century manuscript with Latin text and Old English translation in parallel columns; the first fifty psalms are in Alfredian prose.
works.characters: David (as psalmist); God
works.structure: A continuous psalter translation, psalm by psalm, in the versified mode.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the older attribution to Alfred is not now accepted, though the prose portion may be Alfredian.
sources: 'Lyrical Ballads,' and Other Poems, 1797-1800

works.title: The Middle English Lyric
works.description: The corpus of short Middle English lyric poems, secular and religious, composed and copied between c. 1200 and 1500: spring songs, love complaints, carols, lullabies, Passion meditations, and Marian praises, preserved in manuscripts and early printed collections. The most widely practised and most elusive of medieval English genres.
works.plot: The corpus's subjects are love and spring, mortality and judgement, the joys and sorrows of the Virgin, and the Passion; many poems are songs, with refrains and burdens, meant for performance.
works.significance: The lyric is the most continuous English poetic tradition of the period, feeding the courtly song of the Ricardians, the carol, and the Tudor songbooks.
works.meter: Every available stanza form, from the tail-rhyme romance stanza to carol form, rhyme royal, and the macaronic hymn.
works.context: Preserved in preaching manuscripts, commonplace books (Harley 2253; the Vernon manuscript), and, at the end of the period, in the printed collections of Wynkyn de Worde and Richard Pynson; the carol flourishes in the fifteenth century.
works.characters: the lovers, mourners, and devotees who speak the lyrics
works.structure: A corpus rather than a single work; individual lyrics are typically stanzaic, with refrain patterns.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous as a corpus; individual poems occasionally attributable (e.g., to Rolle's circle or to Lydgate).
sources: Charlotte Smith in British Romanticism

works.title: The Milesian Chief: A Romance
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's first novel, a Gothic-Irish romance in which O'Donovan, the exiled Milesian chief, attempts to liberate Ireland from English tyranny but is destroyed by betrayal and his own fatal pride. The novel draws on the tradition of the dispossessed Gaelic aristocracy to create a doomed-hero narrative of colonial resistance.
works.plot: O'Donovan, last of an ancient Irish noble line, is driven by messianic conviction to liberate Ireland from English rule. His love for Rosamond De Lacy, daughter of an English official, becomes entangled with political ambition. Betrayed by allies and pursued by agents of the lord-deputy, his rebellion fails; his final retreat and death enact the impossibility of heroic resistance against the modern colonial state.
works.significance: The first of the author's Gothic novels, establishing his themes of doomed heroism, religious guilt, and political exile; a precursor of the Irish Gothic tradition and a significant contribution to the political novel.
works.context: Published in 1812 amid rising Irish nationalism and the post-1798 disillusionment following the Act of Union. The author, an Anglican clergyman of Huguenot descent, explored the tensions of Irish identity and colonial subjection.
works.characters: O'Donovan; Rosamond De Lacy; Clifford; Lady Melbourne; Sir Edward
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative; political intrigue interwoven with romance; a conclusion of failure and exile.

works.title: The Minstrel; or, the Progress of Genius
altTitles: The Minstrel, a Poem, in Two Books
works.form: allegorical didactic poem in two books
works.description: Beattie's allegorical poem of the young bard's education, two books of Spenserian stanzas tracing genius from a wild Hebridean childhood through the discipline of taste to the visions of imagination, melancholy, and Fame. It is at once a pre-Romantic cult of genius and a learned Augustan allegory of the poet's progress.
works.plot: Book I follows the infant minstrel through a 'barren rocky island' of storm and solitude, a nursling of genius who, transplanted to the south, awakens to the beauty of landscape, history, and the arts under the eye of instruction. The poet's education proceeds through contemplation, melancholy meditation, and the society of learning, until the summons of active genius. Book II passes from the school of taste into the realms of Imagination, where the minstrel contemplates the grand, the pathetic, and the terrible, the ghost of Fame and the triumph of the poetical genii over time. The allegory closes on the powers of genius sanctified by virtue, the wild native gift disciplined by art, the century's definition of the poet as at once savage and sage.
works.significance: It ranks with Gray's odes and the poems of the primitive bard as a key document of the pre-Romantic imagination, and it shaped the Victorian reading of poetic education; Wordsworth's boyhood of genius is inconceivable without it.
works.meter: Spenserian stanzas (ababbcbcc), iambic pentameter with the alexandrine, in a diction deliberately coloured by Akenside, Thomson, and the antique.
works.context: Book I appeared in 1765 amid the prize and blank-verse vogue and the Ossian debate; the completed poem of 1771 belongs to the cult of genius and the primitive-bard fervour of the 1760s-70s, and Beattie's Edinburgh-Aberdeen circle of Smith, Reid, and the Fergusson vogue frames its theory of native genius.
works.characters: the Minstrel; Genius; Melancholy; Contemplation; Fancy; the ghost of Fame
works.structure: Two books of Spenserian stanzas, the first the biography and education of the minstrel, the second a procession of personified powers culminating in the vision of Fame.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ
works.description: Nicholas Love's English translation and adaptation of the pseudo-Bonaventuran Meditationes Vitae Christi, completed c. 1410: a life of Christ from the Annunciation to Pentecost, written for the 'simple' reader to make the humanity of Jesus present to the imagination, with meditations, prayers, and passages against Lollard positions. The most widely circulated devotional work of fifteenth-century England.
works.plot: Following the gospel narrative day by day, the Mirror unfolds the life, ministry, Passion, and resurrection of Christ in vivid meditative episodes — the nativity, the sermons, the agony, the crucifixion as witnessed by Mary — each closed with moral application, and supplemented by Love's own anti-Wycliffite 'treatise on the sacrament'.
works.significance: The great bestseller of late medieval English devotion: it fixed the affective image of Christ's humanity for a century of English readers and is the key exhibit in the politics of vernacular theology after Arundel's Constitutions.
works.meter: Plain, warm prose of the Carthusian devotional school.
works.context: Completed c. 1410 by Nicholas Love, Carthusian prior of Mount Grace, with the explicit approval of Archbishop Arundel as an orthodox counter to Lollard vernacular scripture; preserved in more manuscripts than any other Middle English devotional text and printed by Caxton (1484) and his successors.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the disciples
works.structure: A day-by-day meditation on the life of Christ in the Meditationes tradition, with the Passion as its affective centre and devotional prayers appended.
works.attributionNotes: Love's authorship secure (named in the work's memorial note).

works.title: The Mistress
altTitles: The Mistress; or, Several Copies of Love-Verses
works.description: The long sequence of love poems in Cowley's Poems (1656), a display of metaphysical wit and conceit on an idealised, largely fictitious mistress, which Johnson cited for its 'violence' of conceit but which shows Cowley's command of the amorous lyric.
works.plot: The poems court and lament an unnamed mistress through elaborate conceits of love's pain, hope, and constancy, more an exercise of wit than a record of a real attachment.
works.significance: A representative and influential work of metaphysical love poetry, central to Johnson's definition of the 'metaphysical' wit and to later understanding of the school.
works.meter: Varied lyric meters with dense metaphysical conceits and witty argument.
works.context: Published in Poems (1656); Johnson's Life of Cowley famously quoted it as an example of the metaphysical 'violence' of conceit, by which he meant the yoking of heterogeneous ideas.
works.characters: the poet; the mistress
works.structure: A loose sequence of love lyrics united by the conceit of the unattainable mistress.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the identity of 'the mistress' is thought to be largely fictitious.

works.title: The Monk: A Romance
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's scandalous sensation novel about the Hieronymite monk Ambrosio, whose fall from piety into lust, murder, and damnation made it the most notorious Gothic romance of the 1790s. Published anonymously to immediate sales success and vigorous critical condemnation, it combined religious terror with lurid sexual transgression in ways no English novel had previously attempted. The book's notoriety shaped the commercial possibilities of the Gothic and drew down attacks linking sensational fiction to moral dissolution.
works.plot: Ambrosio, a celebrated preacher in Madrid and prior of the Hieronymites, becomes obsessed with the young novice Antonia, whom he has secretly fathered through his own mother's illicit line. Guided by the demon in the guise of the novice Matilda, he passes through a sequence of escalating transgressions: seduction of the innocent Angela, rape, and murder. Meanwhile the parallel plot of Lorenzo and Marguerite involves the ghostly Bleeding Nun and a false marriage. Matilda reveals her true demonic nature and bargains Ambrosio's soul for escape from the Inquisition. After a final act of blasphemy and fratricide against the hermit Serapio, Ambrosio is delivered to eternal torment. The novel ends with his damnation unmitigated.
works.significance: The Monk established the conventions of the English Gothic in the 1790s: fusion of religious terror with sexual transgression, the supernatural as psychological drama, and the lurid anti-Catholic romance. Its commercial success defined the genre's market and its scandal provoked decades of critical debate about fiction's moral influence.
works.context: Written during the 1790s reaction against French Revolutionary violence and amid public anxiety about Catholicism, religious enthusiasm, and the Inquisition. the author drew on Beckford's Vathek and the German horror tradition; it appeared the same year as Godwin's Things Near as Possible and was immediately recognised as a deliberate competitor to Radcliffe's Gothic.
works.characters: Ambrosio; Matilda; Antonia; Jerome; Lorenzo; Marguerite; the Bleeding Nun; Captain Raymondo; Angela; the Devil
works.structure: Linear third-person narrative with two embedded tales (Lorenzo and Marguerite; the Bleeding Nun) and a frame of Inquisition proceedings; the perspective shifts between multiple characters; the conclusion is unrelieved.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; authorship confirmed within months. A heavily expurgated second edition with an altered ending appeared in 1798.

works.title: The Moralists, a Philosophical Rhapsody
authors: Anthony Ashley Cooper, Third Earl of Shaftesbury
works.description: Shaftesbury's platonizing dialogue on natural theology and the happiness of virtue, first printed in the third volume of the Characteristicks and issued separately in the same year. Over a day's walk through the fields near Hampstead, the young Philocles is led by the accomplished Theocles to behold the system of the universe and the interior moral system that mirrors it.
works.plot: Philocles, a youth fresh from reading the moralists, meets Theocles and Crantor in the meadows near Hampstead and asks whether virtue alone is happy. Theocles replies first by an ironical panegyric in the style of the sophists, then seriously, rising through an account of the affections and the moral sense to the 'rhapsody' proper: the visible scene of nature becomes the occasion for the vision of the whole system, its administrative god, and the self-enjoying blessedness of a mind in harmony with it. The dialogue ends with Philocles convinced that virtue, happiness, and the contemplation of the universal system are one.
works.significance: It is the most accomplished piece of Shaftesbury's prose art and a key text of eighteenth-century natural theology and the aesthetics of the sublime system; its rhapsody anticipated the nature-contemplation of Thomson, Akenside, and the Romantic moment.
works.meter: Animated prose dialogue with dramatic description, rising in the closing rhapsody to a deliberately periodic, almost poetic cadence of accumulation and apostrophe.
works.context: Composed in the 1690s from material in Shaftesbury's Journals of the Meridian and printed in 1709, when deistic natural theology was being hotly contested; its vision of the system draws on the Cambridge Platonists and on the new cosmology of the Royal Society age.
works.characters: Philocles; Theocles; Crantor
works.structure: An occasional dialogue framed as a 'rhapsody': reported walk and conversation in a single day, climaxing in an extended inspired passage of natural theology.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Morall Fabillis of Esope the Phrygian
works.description: Robert Henryson's cycle of thirteen beast fables (c. 1480s), translating and transforming Aesopian material into the great vernacular fable collection of the British Middle Ages: the cock and the jasper, the two mice, the lion and the mouse, the fox and the wolf, and the parliament of beasts before King Lion. Its moralitates raise the fable to satiric and philosophical art, with a marked sympathy for the poor and the small.
works.plot: The fables move from the country mouse's visit to the town and back, through the fox's adventures with the wolf and the cock's with the fox, to the lion's parliament, where the beasts' complaints against their rulers and their own natures are heard and judged; each fable closes with its moralitas applying the tale to the estates of men.
works.significance: The summit of the medieval European fable tradition in any vernacular: its moralitates are among the finest medieval poems on justice, poverty, and power.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of supple, colloquial power in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1480s by the Dunfermline schoolmaster Robert Henryson, in the European fable revival of the fifteenth century (Steinhöwel, Caxton's Aesop of 1484); printed in 1570–71, and preserved in the Bannatyne and other manuscripts.
works.characters: the Cock and the Fox; the Town and Country Mice; the Lion; the Wolf; the Sheep; the Swallow; the Toad
works.structure: A prologue and thirteen fables, each bipartite (taill and moralitas), in the medieval Aesopic tradition raised to a coherent cycle.
works.attributionNotes: Henryson's authorship secure (named in the manuscripts).

works.title: The Mourning Bride
works.description: Congreve's only tragedy, a heroic verse play set in a fictionalised Morocco and Granada, which was the most successful tragedy of the 1690s and the source of the proverbial lines on music and on grief.
works.plot: The Moorish king Manuel keeps Almeria, the widow of his murdered enemy, imprisoned and desires her; a series of disguises, a false death, and the return of the true heir lead to the king's downfall and Almeria's deliverance.
works.significance: The most quoted tragedy of the period and the culmination of the she-tragedy tradition; its sententiae passed into proverbial use.
works.meter: Blank verse, with the famous opening 'Music has charms to soothe a savage breast' and 'Heaven has no rage like love to hatred turned'.
works.context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in January 1697 and published in the same year; it ran for thirteen nights, an exceptional success for a tragedy.
works.characters: Almeria; Manuel; Alonzo; Osmyn; Selim; Zara; Heli; Gonzalez
works.structure: Five acts in blank verse with a masque and songs.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Congreve; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Mysteries of Udolpho. A Romance; and Interspersed with Some Pieces of Poetry. In Four Volumes
works.form: Gothic novel and romance of terror, the exemplary form of the explained supernatural, with interspersed songs and pastorals
works.description: The fourth novel of Ann Radcliffe, published in four volumes in May 1794 under her own name, and the masterwork of the Gothic romance of terror. Emily St. Aubert, educated in the Languedoc chateau of Le Blanc by a father whose death on a Pyrenean journey is softened by a monastery funeral and the mourned abbey of St. Clare, falls in love with Valancourt against her aunt Madame Cheron's will; her aunt's runaway second marriage to the Italian Signor Montoni carries Emily into the Apennines and into the castle of Udolpho, where Montoni tyrannises over her person and her hopes of an inheritance. A labyrinth of Italian strongholds follows, of subterranean passages and intercepted letters, of the veiled figure that proves a wax image, of the death of the Signora Montoni and the terrors of banditti, until the mysterious papers, the miniature of the Marchioness de Villeroi found in her father's closet, and the confession of a dying nun make known an old tragedy of enforced vows and jealousy; Emily recovers her fortune, and her constancy is rewarded by the reconciliation of Valancourt.
works.plot: Emily's father St. Aubert dies on the way from the Pyrenees; under her aunt Madame Cheron she is forced into the society of the usurping Montoni, who seizes the castle of Udolpho and would coerce her into signing away her hopes and into a match with a wealthy Italian count; her lover Valancourt, already dismissed by St. Aubert for supposed dissipation, is absent and tried by his own errors. Emily escapes through the castle's secret ways, falls among banditti, is befriended by honest Italians and by the family of Villefort, endures the mysteries of the covered figure, the poisoned draughts and the lady of the papers, and hears at last the Marchioness de Villeroi's whole story: Montoni's imprisonment in the Venetian states and his death leave her wealthy, and her tried love is restored.
works.significance: The Mysteries of Udolpho is the most famous and most imitated of English Gothic novels, the book by which the literature of terror became the dominant prose mode of the 1790s: it defined the pursued-heroine plot, castle and convent scenery, and the ethics of terror regulated by explanation; it was read, praised and parodied across the century, with Catherine Morland's raptures in Northanger Abbey measuring Austen's generation against it, and it remained in print into the Oxford World's Classics and Norton Critical editions.
works.meter: Chiefly prose romance; the interspersed poetry is lyric - songs, pastorals and the Castellan's air, Emily's own verses and the monk's hymn - in regular stanzas, with the great descriptive passages of mountain and lake scenery carrying a poetry of the picturesque within the prose.
works.context: Published in 1794, in the war with Revolutionary France and the height of the Italian picturesque bred of travel and of Ann Radcliffe's own tours, and the year of her Lake District journey; issued in four volumes by G.G. and J. Robinson as by Ann Radcliffe, it was the first of her novels to carry her name, and its success made the sale of her next copyright one of the largest paid a woman writer of the age.
works.characters: Emily St. Aubert; St. Aubert, her father; Madame Cheron, her aunt, later Signora Montoni; the Marchioness de Villeroi, lost to the family history; Valancourt, Emily's lover; Signor Montoni; the Signora Montoni; the Count de Villefort and the Marchioness's story in the papers; Madame Montoni's attendant Annette; Sister St. Agnes of the convent; Du Pont and his brother the Abbot of St. Clare
works.structure: A continuous four-volume romance following a single heroine's experience from the Pyrenees to the Apennines and back toward France, sustained by embedded papers, songs and a concluding expository narrative that resolves every appearance of the supernatural into natural and juridical causes.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's own name, Ann Radcliffe; authorship undisputed. The later prefaces and the Memoir of 1826 document its place as the decisive success of her career.

works.title: The Mysterious Mother
works.form: tragedy in five acts, a closet and private-press drama
works.description: A closet tragedy of a mother's incestuous passion for her son, written for private performance and printed at the author's villa press. It is the most daring of the century's domestic horrors and an experiment in placing an unrepresentable subject at the centre of a regular tragedy.
works.plot: The Countess of Ardenal, whose husband has died and whose son has been kept from her, conceives an unlawful and secret passion for the young count himself. She intercepts his marriage, imprisons his beloved and pursues him with designs that her attendants misread as tenderness. The discoveries arrive too late, the young count learns the truth and kills himself, and the countess's guilt is exposed to the house in a catastrophe of horror rather than of pity.
works.significance: It is the century's most extreme attempt to write the unspeakable family passion as tragedy and a key document of the transmission of Gothic horror from romance into drama.
works.meter: Blank verse of a deliberately old-fashioned and sometimes uneven regularity, with a strong use of the sententious pause and the ominous half-revealed phrase.
works.context: Printed at the villa printing press in 1768 after the author's retirement from active politics, in the season of the domestic tragedy and of the analysis of horror in fiction; its subject was one the public stage could not have carried.
works.characters: the Countess of Ardenal; the young Count her son; his betrothed and her friends; the attendants and officers of the house
works.structure: A regular five-act tragedy of secrets and delayed discovery, with the mother's soliloquies carrying the horror and the final recognition producing the catastrophe; written to be read and privately acted rather than staged.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; printed privately at the author's press with his name withdrawn but never in doubt among his circle.

works.title: The Natural Daughter; with Portraits of the Leadenhead Family
works.form: Novel of Manners and Fashion; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Sentimental and Domestic Novel
works.description: Mary Robinson's last completed novel, published in two volumes in the same year as her Letter to the Women of England, and the most satirical of her fictions. Its subject is the illegitimate daughter of a man of rank, whose natural claim to consideration is set against the artificial morality of a family portrait gallery of the prosperous and the opinionated, the Leadenheads of the title. The book argues in narrative form the case for women's vulnerability that the Letter had argued in prose.
works.plot: The natural daughter, acknowledged by affection but excluded by law and custom, struggles against the interest, pride, and hypocrisy of the families who protect and dispose of her; the Leadenhead portraits supply a comic exposure of genteel prejudice, mercenary marriage, and social ambition, and the heroine's trial ends only when the calculations that governed her are dismantled and her worth is acknowledged on its own terms.
works.significance: The Natural Daughter is valued as the fiction that completes Robinson's attack on the marriage market and on the legal dependence of women, and as one of the most accomplished satires of prosperous family pretension before the Regency novel; it is now read as an important stage in the development of women's social fiction in the 1790s.
works.meter: Prose narrative with pointed satirical description; verse and letter papers are interspersed, and the portraits are drawn in an epigrammatic manner derived from her periodical writing.
works.context: Written in the last years of Robinson's life, when her novels were being bought by the publisher for sums recorded in his accounts and when her own public history as an acknowledged but unprotected woman made the legal position of illegitimacy and of women her natural subject; the novel's pairing in modern editions with the Letter reflects the continuity of their argument.
works.characters: the natural daughter of the title; the Leadenhead family of the satirical portraits; the man of rank whose acknowledgment the law refuses; the marriage-market interests around the heroine
works.structure: A two-volume novel combining a heroine's tale of exclusion with a satirical series of family portraits; the movement is between sentimental analysis and comic exposure, with letters and papers interspersed.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

The Works of Mary Robinson (8 volumes)

works.title: The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne, in the County of Hampshire
works.form: Epistolary natural history and antiquarian survey in familiar letters
works.description: The published form of a long correspondence between the country naturalist Gilbert White and his friends Daines Barrington and Thomas Pennant, The Natural History and Antiquities of Selborne records the seasons, weather, birds, mammals, insects and parish antiquities of one Hampshire village. Its method is patient first-hand observation entered in a memoranda book and then shaped into familiar letters. The result is the founding text of English phenomenological nature-writing and a classic of empirical natural history.
works.plot: White surveys the natural history of Selborne parish under a sequence of heads: the zoology of its vertebrates and invertebrates, the periodical return of migrations, the phenomena of hibernation in bats, the structure of swallows' nests, and the monthly calendar of appearance. Interwoven are antiquarian notices of the parish and its manors, and the weather-journal whose measurements anchor the whole. From these particulars he draws general conclusions about instinct, the economy of nature, and the value of quantitative records kept over many years.
works.significance: It has never been out of print and is read both as a scientific classic, for its accurate records and its early treatment of hibernation and migration, and as a literary model of the observed particular. It set the manner of all later English nature-writing from Richard Jefferies to Laurie Lee, and it is a key document of the empirical, descriptive temper that eighteenth-century natural philosophy bequeathed to Romantic-era writing about the external world.
works.meter: Prose only, in an unadorned, precise, quietly humorous plain style
works.context: The book belongs to the late-eighteenth-century vogue for parish-level natural history, for systematic weather observation, and for correspondence networks among gentleman-naturalists; it also reflects the Linnlean and Buffonian taxonomy then current and the antiquarian culture of the Society of Antiquaries.
works.characters: Gilbert White; Daines Barrington; Thomas Pennant
works.structure: Two parts in the form of letters to two correspondents, arranged topically rather than narratively, with the weather journal and observations woven as enumerated particulars.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Gilbert White is established; the letters were edited for the press by his brother Revd Dr Thomas White, whose editorial hand is documented but does not displace Gilbert's authorship.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Natural History of Religion
altTitles: Of the Natural History of Religion
works.description: Hume's account of how polytheism arose from human fears and hopes and how the human mind tends, through adulation and complaint, back toward a single supreme being: religion explained as a natural history of the mind rather than a truth discovered. First printed among the Four Dissertations of 1757 and composed by 1751-52.
works.plot: Hume argues that the first ideas of the Deity arose not from contemplation of nature's order but from the anxiety and hopes of ordinary life, which clothed unknown causes with human shapes and interests. Because the motives of polytheism are the ordinary interests of men, its gods are limited, sociable, and ludicrous, and its rituals familiar; monotheism, by contrast, lifts God above human comprehension and so inflames priests and fanatics into a jealousy of divine attribute. Polytheism thus proves more gentle and more favourable to civil liberty, while the road from polytheism to monotheism runs through flattery, and the return to superstition through philosophy is via enthusiasm and the pretended reason of natural theology. The closing pages make the whole history of religion a lesson in the uniform passions of the human species.
works.significance: It founded the natural history and psychological explanation of religion, the ancestor of the scientific study of religion from Spencer to contemporary cognitive accounts of religion, and the most quoted religious writing of the Enlightenment.
works.meter: Ironically courteous expository prose, cool generalizations about 'the religious' set against the heated vocabulary of the priesthoods, with a famous dry closing cadence.
works.context: Conceived in the early 1750s, published in London in 1757 in the volume of Four Dissertations that also contained the Dissertation on the Passions and the two historical dissertations, in the season of the French and Indian War's zealotries and of the Church-of England controversy over enthusiasm.
works.structure: A single dissertation in twenty-eight short sections, moving from origins in fear through polytheism's domestic character to monotheism, superstition, and enthusiasm.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Necessity of Atheism
works.form: Polemic and pamphlet prose in the dissenting tradition of the freethinking broadside; the juvenile metaphysical essay with its apparatus of propositions and its appeal to the booksellers' conscience.
works.description: The earliest printed work of its author, a short pamphlet of sixteen pages issued at a seaside town in the first months of his undergraduate career and the occasion of his dismissal from the university. It argues that belief in a creator is not a matter of evidence but of habit, that every chain of reasoning must stop at the limits of sensation, and that the hypothesis of a god explains nothing. Its tone is that of the schoolboy metaphysician, aggressive and compressed, but its premises are those the poet was to hold all his life.
works.plot: The pamphlet begins by refusing the burden of proof, since a negative cannot be demonstrated, and then argues that all human knowledge is built on the relation of sensation and idea, so that no evidence of a first cause is accessible. It presses the impossibility of accounting for the existence of matter and the still greater impossibility of an uncaused creator, and closes that a being all-powerful and all-good would be incompatible with the evils of the world. The concluding pages deny that atheism breeds the moral laxity the apologists assume, and insist that inquiry, however unsettling, is the only ground of a reasonable faith. The argument is throughout a train of short propositions with the manner of a college disputation turned against itself.
works.significance: It is the founding document of a lifelong radicalism and the reason its author's university career ended in dismissal, an event that shaped the whole later biography and the poetry of the outlaw intellect. Its epistemology, that the mind can reason only from the data of sensation, reappears in the mature philosophical prose, and the pamphlet remains the standard case in the history of academic discipline and of the English freethinking tract.
works.meter: Prose; the style is sententious and abrupt, with short declarative sentences, rhetorical questioning and the cadence of the abstract printed for discussion.
works.context: Printed at Worthing in 1811 and offered through the Oxford booksellers who sold the author's earlier joint volume of verse, the tract was the ground on which he was summoned before his college and, refusing to disown it, was dismissed in the March of that year. Its appearance falls in the season of the statutes against blasphemous and seditious writing, when unitarian and deist pamphlets were prosecuted, and the incident made an undergraduate's metaphysics a public scandal.
works.structure: A continuous pamphlet argument in numbered propositions, opening with a plea for the freedom of inquiry, passing to the epistemological case, and ending with a challenge to the reader to disprove the conclusion.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution long contested: the title page carried no name, the author refused to own the tract before his college, and an early biographer and a schoolfellow were credited with a share in it. Modern scholarship accepts the main text as the work of a single undergraduate hand, with the schoolfellow's participation unproven.
