works.title: The New Atalantis
altTitles: The New Atalantis: A Romance. Designed for a Secret History of the Present Juncto
works.form: political romance and secret history in prose
works.description: A political romance and secret history of the Whig Junto, published in August 1709 and prosecuted for libel in the following November. Under the disguise of an Italianate island court it reports the sexual and fiscal intrigues of the ministers, turning the key of romantic fiction into an instrument of party attack.
works.plot: A company of ladies and gallants recounting the histories of the great are led by the goddess Intrepida through the courts and closets of Atalantis. There they see the ministers intrigue for money and for the persons of their female dependants: the snares laid for the yielding, the bribery of the chamber, the ruin of the too frank and the triumph of the crafty. The tales end in exposure and desertion, and the framing discourse claims that Atalantis is a transparent name for England, so that the reader is invited to apply the key herself.
works.significance: It is the most successful of the early key-writing romances and the text that showed how the amatory plot could be turned to party work; it shaped the later secret history and the scandalous novel of the 1720s.
works.meter: The high romantic prose style of the amatory fiction, with elaborate periods, apostrophe and euphemistic detail of the bed-chamber, used to carry identifiable party scandal.
works.context: Published in the last years of the Godolphin ministry and reprinted several times before the Sacheverell season; its libel prosecution in November 1709 was pressed and then dropped with the change of administration, an event central to the history of the press.
works.characters: Intrepida; Delia; Countess de Verruyse; the Duke of Sidonia; the gallants and the betrayed women of the Atalantis court
works.structure: An embedded-tale romance with a framing dialogue, in which reported histories of seduction are stitched together by allegorical presentation; the key is offered openly in the argument and the prefatorial matter.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution established by the contemporary party attacks and by the author's own defence of the design; the first issue was published without the writer's name.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The New Chronicles of England and France
works.description: Robert Fabyan's chronicle of England and France from Brutus to the reign of Henry VII, compiled from the London chronicles and printed by Richard Pynson in 1516 as The New Chronicles of England and France; the first city chronicle of London to reach print.
works.plot: The chronicle narrates the kings of England (with a parallel account of France) reign by reign, drawn from the Brut, the London chronicles, and the work of the French chroniclers, and closes with the accession of Henry VIII; the appended 'Concordance of Histories' aligns the chronicles of England and France.
works.significance: The first printed London chronicle and a major conduit of the English historical tradition from the medieval Brut to the Tudor chroniclers; Shakespeare knew its material (including the story of Lear) through Holinshed and the chronicle tradition.
works.meter: Prose with verse envoys
works.context: Compiled by Fabyan, a London draper and alderman, from the 1490s to c. 1504, with continuations to 1516; printed by Pynson in 1516 and again by William Rastell in 1533, it supplied material to Hall, Holinshed, and the Elizabethan playwrights.
works.structure: Annalistic chronicle in seven parts, each divided by reign; Fabyan's additions include the civic history of London and verse 'Lenvoyes' moralizing each reign.

works.title: The New Law of Righteousness
works.description: Winstanley's principal theological and political manifesto, published in January 1649, which argues that private property is the origin of oppression and that the restoration of the earth as a common treasury is the true law of righteousness.
works.plot: Winstanley identifies the curse of Cain with the enclosure of the earth, argues that Christ's kingdom is a commonwealth of shared labour and property, and calls for the abolition of buying and selling.
works.significance: The founding text of English agrarian communism and an essential document of the radical revolution of 1649.
works.meter: Vigorous, scriptural prose of the radical sects.
works.context: Published in January 1649, days before the execution of Charles I; it prepared the ground for the Digger settlement on St George's Hill in April 1649.
works.structure: A single continuous argument in biblical and prophetic prose.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Winstanley; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The New Testament (Tyndale's translation)
altTitles: The New Testament Translated by William Tyndale
works.description: William Tyndale's translation of the New Testament from the Greek, the first English New Testament translated directly from the original language and the foundation of all later English Bibles, including the King James Version.
works.plot: A complete translation of the Greek New Testament with prefaces and marginal notes; the Cologne fragment (Matthew 1–22) was interrupted by the authorities in 1525, and the first complete edition appeared at Worms in 1526, followed by Tyndale's thorough revisions of 1534 and 1535.
works.significance: The fountainhead of English Bible translation: Tyndale's phrasing survives in as much as 80–90 per cent of the King James New Testament, and his English — 'the powers that be', 'a law unto themselves', 'the spirit is willing' — permanently shaped the language's biblical register.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Tyndale, denied episcopal support in England (the famous rebuke attributed to a Gloucestershire divine — 'we were better to be without God's law than the Pope's'), went to the continent in 1524; the Cologne printing (Quentel, 1525) was raided, and the Worms octavo of 1526 was smuggled into England, where Bishop Tunstall bought up copies for burning. Tyndale's 1534 revision is the text behind the later English versions.
works.structure: Biblical text in the order of the Greek canon, with prologues to the books and expository marginal glosses.

editions.title: Tyndale's New Testament

works.title: The Non-Juror
works.form: Political comedy in five acts in prose dialogue, written for the patent theatre and printed close to performance.
works.description: An anti-Jacobite comedy brought out at Drury Lane in the winter of 1717 and printed with a title page dated 1718, which makes a non-juring clergyman the type of political and religious cant. Passive obedience, the oaths, and the converts of the church are laughed out of doors, and a plain British sea-officer is set against the scheming divine as the voice of national good sense. The play is also remembered for a scene that quoted the national dramatist back at itself, a passage its author withdrew when it was thought to do irreverence to the dead poet.
works.plot: Doctor Wolf, a non-juring clergyman, combines disaffection to the settled succession with greed: he designs upon the fortune of a young Protestant heiress, whom he hopes to win both to his own communion and to his suit, and keeps his son in constraint and in debt. Young Wolf, a rake of the town, runs a course of his own, and the plain-spoken British officer who loves the heiress opposes the divine's arts with open national loyalty. The household dependants, whose interests Wolf professes to serve, are the instruments by which his contrivances are carried on and at last discovered; a disputed obligation pressed with a canting plea of mercy exposes the hypocrisy of the claimant. The father's principles are disavowed by the son, the heiress keeps her fortune and her party, and the comedy ends in the exposure of the divine rather than in a reconciliation.
works.significance: It is the most direct instance of a patent-house comedy written as party warfare, and the one play of its era that made the non-juring clergyman a stock stage character. The history of its suppressed Shakespearean scene is a document in the rising reverence for the bard, and its use of hypocrisy for party ends measures how far the comic treatment of cant had moved since the 1690s.
works.meter: Plain prose dialogue with set speeches of some formality for the party argument; the addresses to the audience are in closed couplets, and the quotation that gave offence is taken from the blank verse of the national stage.
works.context: It was written in the temper of the years after the rising of 1715, when non-juring churchmen were a visible and legally precarious class, and it belongs to the flush of anti-Jacobite stage writing that followed the settlement of the succession. The divine supposed to be satirised complained of a libel and proceeded against the publisher, but the complaint did not prosper. The management that staged it had by then made party business of loyalty on the stage.
works.characters: Doctor Wolf, the non-juring clergyman; Young Wolf, his son; the bluff British sea-officer; the rich Protestant heiress whose fortune is designed upon; the dependants of Wolf's household
works.structure: Five acts of prose comedy organised as a double opposition, the designing hypocrite in the house and the plain British officer against him; the plotting moves through forged claims and overheard counsel to a public unmasking in the final act.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Northern Lass
works.description: Richard Brome's first comedy, and his most popular, in which a young woman from the north of England, Bess Bridewell, is carried to London, falls among thieves and gulls, and is finally matched with her true love.
works.plot: Bess, wronged and dismissed, travels south; mistaken identities, a robbery, and a series of comic adventures in London lead to her reunion with the noble Conrade and the punishment of the false suitors.
works.significance: The play that established Brome's reputation and one of the most frequently reprinted comedies of the Caroline period; its regional dialect comedy is an early landmark.
works.meter: Prose dominant with verse passages and songs; Bess speaks a Yorkshire dialect.
works.context: Performed at the Blackfriars and the Globe in 1629; Brome was Jonson's servant and amanuensis, and Ben Jonson wrote commendatory verses for the 1632 quarto.
works.characters: Bess Bridewell; Conrade; Squelch; Anvil; Trainwell; Lackbeard; the Hostess
works.structure: Five acts of picaresque comic intrigue with songs and dialect humour.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Brome; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Obedience of a Christian Man
altTitles: The Obedience of a Christen Man and How Christen Rulers Ought to Governe
works.description: Tyndale's treatise on the obedience owed by Christians to rulers and on the reading of scripture, printed at Antwerp in 1528; the book that, shown to Henry VIII, drew the king's reported remark that 'this is the book for me and all kings to read'.
works.plot: The book argues that every Christian — ploughman, weaver, or king — must obey his temporal rulers, whom God has ordained; it attacks the pope's claim to absolve subjects of allegiance, defends vernacular scripture against the charge that it breeds heresy, and expounds the duties of fathers, husbands, masters, and kings from the New Testament.
works.significance: The most politically consequential English book of the early Reformation: its doctrine of obedience made the English Reformation conceivable as an act of state, and its defence of vernacular scripture became the platform of the English Bible.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed at Antwerp in 1528 (by Hans Luft's press or its associates); Anne Boleyn's copy reached Henry VIII, and the book's doctrine of royal supremacy over the church made it a cornerstone of Henrician propaganda, feeding directly into the Reformation statutes of the 1530s.
works.structure: A continuous treatise divided into topical sections on the estates and their duties, with a famous preface on the reading of scripture.

editions.title: The Obedience of a Christian Man

works.title: The Odyssey of Homer
works.description: Pope's translation of the Odyssey, published in volumes with the scholarly apparatus and the essay on Homer's genius, and completed largely by under-writers whose share Pope acknowledged in his advertisement.
works.plot: The translation follows the wanderings of Ulysses from Calypso's island, through the Phaeacian court and the cyclops, Circe and the lower world, to the return to Ithaca and the destruction of the suitors.
works.significance: It completed the Augustan Homer and became the standard example of the assisted, commercialised great translation, raising the question of authorial share that the century kept asking about its monument-building poets.
works.meter: Heroic couplet, commonly judged looser, flatter and more mechanical than that of the Iliad, a difference often attributed to the share of the assisting hands.
works.context: Issued after the Iliad and after the Homeric quarrels with the scholars, in the season when subscription was giving way to the booksellers' market; the volume was pirated and its assistant translators later figured among the tribe of the Dunciad.
works.characters: Ulysses; Penelope; Telemachus; the suitors; the gods of the poem
works.structure: A book-by-book verse translation of the twenty-four books of the Odyssey, published in installments with arguments and notes.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative: Pope declared that some books were translated by other hands under his direction, and modern scholarship continues to argue the extent of the assistants' share, of William Brookes's revision and of Pope's own later versification.

editions.title: The Poems of Alexander Pope, Twickenham Edition (11 volumes)

works.title: The Old Bachelor
works.description: Congreve's first comedy, written while he was still in his early twenties and produced at Drury Lane with a cast that included Betterton and Anne Bracegirdle; it ran for an unprecedented fourteen nights.
works.plot: The old bachelor Bellmour is dissuaded from marriage by his friend Heartwell, who is himself undone by his love for the coquette Sylvia; a series of intrigues, a disguised marriage, and a discovery of true parentage resolve in multiple weddings.
works.significance: Announced Congreve as the heir to Etherege and Wycherley and launched the last great phase of Restoration comedy.
works.meter: Prose of precocious brilliance; Dryden remarked that the author was 'but a young man' and supplied corrections.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, in January 1693 and published the same year; it was the most successful first play of the decade.
works.characters: Bellmour; Vainlove; Heartwell; Fondlewife; Laetitia; Araminta; Belinda; Sylvia; Bluffe; Lucy
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy with a strong comic subplot of Fondlewife, Laetitia, and Vainlove.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Congreve; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Old English Baron
altTitles: The Old English Baron: A Gothic Story
works.form: Gothic romance and tale of probability
works.description: A Gothic romance written deliberately as a correction of the excesses of the first tale of terror, in which the supernatural is reduced to a single decent apparition and the passions are kept within probability. It first appeared under another title and was reissued and long known as the story of the old English baron.
works.plot: The infant heir of a castle is put out of his inheritance by a usurping steward, and is fostered in ignorance of his rank by the very family that dispossessed him. He grows up generous and in love with the daughter of the house, while the ghost of his father appears at a banquet to repeat the injuries of the past. The discovery of his birth restores the estate, the fraud of the steward is punished, and the claim of the lovers is allowed.
works.significance: It was the most successful Gothic tale of the 1770s and 1780s and the standard example of the rational reformed romance, and its theory of probability influenced the definition of the Gothic throughout the century.
works.meter: An even, unornamented prose imitating the manner of the old English tales, with the supernatural scenes reported in short and grave sentences.
works.context: Written in the late 1770s in the wake of the first Gothic novel and of the controversy over its machinery, and published in a sequence of issues between 1777 and 1778; its preface and its practice form a deliberate critical answer to its model.
works.characters: the dispossessed young heir; the foster-family of the castle; the daughter he loves; the usurping steward of the estate; the ghost of the former lord
works.structure: A short continuous romance in the manner of the old tale, with the apparition placed at the structural centre and the recognition supplying the close; the sequence is restrained and single-threaded.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published anonymously at the first issue and with the author's name in the later editions and in the critical history she afterwards wrote.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Old English Gospel of Nicodemus
altTitles: The Old English Version of the Gospel of Nicodemus
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, University Library Ii.2.11 (c. 1075); also London, British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.xv (twelfth century)
works.form: apocryphal gospel narrative (Old English prose translation)
works.description: An Old English translation of the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus, comprising the Acts of Pilate and the Harrowing of Hell: the trial, crucifixion, and burial of Christ as recorded by Nicodemus, followed by the testimony of the two sons of Simeon, raised from the dead, on Christ's descent into hell and his liberation of the patriarchs. It is the fullest Old English apocryphal gospel narrative.
works.plot: The first part recounts the trial before Pilate, the miracles that testified for Christ, the crucifixion and burial; the second part is the report of Charinus and Lenthius, the sons of Simeon, who describe how Christ broke the gates of hell, bound Satan, and led Adam and the patriarchs into paradise.
works.significance: The earliest English version of the most influential apocryphal gospel of the Middle Ages, and a principal channel by which the harrowing of hell became a central theme of later English literature.
works.context: The Latin Gospel of Nicodemus was one of the most widely read religious texts of the Middle Ages; its Old English translation belongs to the later eleventh century and stands behind the great Middle English prose and verse versions of the harrowing that culminate in Piers Plowman and the mystery plays.
works.characters: Pilate, Nicodemus, Joseph of Arimathea, Christ, Satan, Adam, Charinus and Lenthius
works.structure: A two-part apocryphon: the Acts of Pilate (a trial narrative dense with dialogue) and the Descensus (a first-person testimony of the harrowing), the second part giving the work its enduring doctrinal importance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
sources: The Monk (Oxford World's Classics)

works.title: The Old English Herbarium
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vitellius C.iii (c. 1050), with two further copies (Harley 585; Harley 6258B)
works.description: An Old English translation of the enlarged Herbarium of Pseudo-Apuleius together with the Medicina de quadrupedibus, the standard late-antique herbal handbook of 185 plants and their medicinal uses. The translation is illustrated with painted plant portraits, making it the earliest illustrated English medical book.
works.plot: The herbal proceeds plant by plant, describing each herb's appearance and habitat and prescribing its preparations and cures — for snakebite, fever, wounds, stomach complaints, and the ailments of women — followed by the quadruped remedies drawn from badger, hare, and other animals.
works.significance: The first illustrated herbal in the English vernacular and a key witness to the transmission of classical pharmacology into early England and thence into the Middle English medical tradition.
works.context: Translated in the late tenth or early eleventh century as part of the vernacular medical programme that produced the Leechbook and Lacnunga; the illustrated Cotton copy shows the book's use in a wealthy late Anglo-Saxon medical household.
works.structure: An alphabetical-sequential catalogue of 185 chapters, each a self-contained plant monograph; the accompanying illustrations follow the antique pictorial tradition transmitted through continental exemplars.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation of the Latin Herbarium of Pseudo-Apuleius; the translator is unknown.
themes: Familiar prose and the essayist's persona
sources: The Edinburgh Review

works.title: The Old English Life of St Christopher (fragment)
altTitles: The Passion of St Christopher (Old English fragment)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.xv, fol. 94 (the Nowell Codex, c. 1000)
works.description: A fragmentary Old English prose passion of St Christopher, the giant cynocephalus (dog-headed) saint of the eastern church, preserved on a single damaged leaf of the Nowell Codex, the manuscript of Beowulf. It is the earliest surviving English version of the Christopher legend.
works.plot: The surviving text narrates Christopher's origin among the man-eating cynocephali and his conversion: granted human speech by divine grace, he receives baptism and the name Christopher ('Christ-bearer') and is sent by the king Dagnus to Alexandria, where he preaches; the fragment breaks off before the martyrdom itself.
works.significance: The earliest English witness to the Christopher legend, and part of the 'marvels' programme of the Beowulf manuscript, illuminating the reception of eastern hagiography in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.context: The text's position in the Nowell Codex, between the prose Wonders of the East and the Letter of Alexander, shows the manuscript's compiler grouping marvels and monsters of the East; the Christopher legend's eastern marvels made it a natural member of that collection.
works.characters: Christopher, King Dagnus
works.structure: A continuous passio narrative of which only the opening survives; the preserved portion stresses the wonder of Christopher's monstrous nature transformed by grace — a thematically apt companion to the Beowulf manuscript's interest in monstrous beings.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
sources: Discipline: A Novel (Chawton House Library: Women's Novels)

works.title: The Old English Life of St Euphrosyne
altTitles: The Old English Legend of St Euphrosyne
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Julius E.vii (c. 1100)
works.description: An Old English translation of the life of St Euphrosyne, the Alexandrian maiden who fled her father's marriage plans and lived disguised as the monk Smaragdus for thirty-eight years, unrecognized by the father who mourned her. The life is the classic transvestite-saint legend of the eastern church.
works.plot: Euphrosyne, the only daughter of the wealthy Paphnutius of Alexandria, secretly takes monastic vows and enters a men's monastery disguised as the eunuch Smaragdus, where her holiness is recognized by the abbot. Her grieving father, visiting the monastery, is consoled by the unknown monk, and only on her deathbed does Euphrosyne reveal herself to him before dying in his arms.
works.significance: The only Old English witness to the transvestite-saint legend, and an early English example of the motif of the disguised woman that recurs through medieval literature.
works.context: Translated in the later eleventh century as part of the wave of vernacular hagiography for monastic and lay readers; the transvestite-saint motif, rooted in eastern monastic legend, held a lasting fascination for medieval English religious writing, reappearing in later legends and romances.
works.characters: Euphrosyne (Smaragdus), Paphnutius, the abbot
works.structure: A single sustained plot unusual in hagiography: disguise, concealment, and deferred recognition generate dramatic irony throughout, culminating in the deathbed revelation scene between father and daughter.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
sources: Melmoth the Wanderer (Oxford World's Classics)

works.title: The Old English Life of St Giles
altTitles: The Old English Legend of St Giles
works.description: An Old English translation of the life of St Giles (Aegidius), the hermit of Provence nourished by a hind and wounded by a king's hunting arrow, whose abbey became a famous pilgrimage shrine. The life combines the eremitical ideal with the romance of the royal hunt.
works.plot: Giles, a Greek nobleman who gives his inheritance to the poor, becomes a hermit in the Provençal wilderness, fed by the milk of a tame hind. When the king's huntsmen wound him with an arrow meant for the hind, the repentant king builds the monastery of Saint-Gilles; Giles heals a possessed man, and his sanctity is confirmed by miracles, including his appearance before Charlemagne to absolve the emperor's secret sin.
works.significance: The earliest English witness to the cult of one of the most popular saints of the medieval West, and a representative of the late Old English eremitic legend.
works.context: Translated in the later eleventh century, when Giles's cult was spreading through England (over 160 English churches were dedicated to him); the life belongs to the same wave of vernacular hagiography as the lives of Margaret and Nicholas in CCCC 303.
works.characters: Giles, the hind, the king (Flavius), Charlemagne
works.structure: A conventional confessor's vita: renunciation, hermitage, the arrow episode, the foundation of the monastery, and a series of healing miracles, climaxing in the Charlemagne episode that made Giles the patron invoked for secret sins.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
sources: The Early Poems of John Clare, 1804-1822 (2 volumes)

works.title: The Old English Life of St Margaret
altTitles: The Old English Legend of St Margaret of Antioch
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 303 (c. 1100); also London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius A.iii
works.description: An Old English prose life of St Margaret of Antioch, the virgin martyr swallowed by a dragon: the most popular female saint's life of the Middle Ages, here translated from the Latin passio of the Mombritius type. The text combines the romance of the dragon-fight with the passio's scenes of torture, making it a favourite of female devotional reading.
works.plot: Margaret, a shepherd's daughter of Antioch, rejects the prefect Olibrius and is tortured for her faith; in prison she overcomes a dragon that swallows her (bursting it from within by the sign of the cross) and a demon in the form of a black man; her final prayer asks that women in childbirth who invoke her be delivered, and she is beheaded, promising her intercession to all who read her passion.
works.significance: The earliest English version of the most influential female saint's legend of the Middle Ages, and a bridge between the Old English hagiographic tradition and the Middle English legendaries.
works.context: Translated in the later eleventh century when vernacular saints' lives multiplied for lay and female audiences; Margaret's cult, with its promise of protection in childbirth, spread through England in the twelfth century and her life became the most copied Middle English saint's legend.
works.characters: Margaret of Antioch, the prefect Olibrius, the dragon, the demon
works.structure: A classic virgin-martyr passio in the Mombritius tradition: courtship-refusal, tortures, the dragon and demon combats in prison, the trial's climax, and a death-scene culminating in the prayer for women in labour that made Margaret the patroness of childbirth.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
sources: Felicia Hemans: Selected Poems, Prose and Letters

works.title: The Old English Life of St Mary of Egypt
altTitles: The Old English Legend of Mary of Egypt
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Julius E.vii (fragmentary) and a Gloucester fragment
works.description: An Old English translation of the life of Mary of Egypt, the penitent harlot of the desert: the story of the sinner who fled to the wilderness and, after forty-seven years of solitary penance, was discovered by the monk Zosimas and found to have attained holiness. One of the great penitential legends of the Middle Ages.
works.plot: Mary, a prostitute of Alexandria, joins a pilgrimage to Jerusalem for wicked ends but is barred from the church by an invisible force; repenting before an icon of the Virgin, she crosses the Jordan and lives as a naked hermit for forty-seven years. The monk Zosimas finds her, hears her confession, gives her communion, and returns a year later to find her dead, with a lion helping him to bury her.
works.significance: The earliest English version of one of the most influential penitential legends of the Middle Ages, notable for its sympathetic treatment of female sin and sanctity.
works.context: Translated in the later eleventh century from the Latin vita, the life circulated among the vernacular devotional texts that multiplied after the Conquest; its themes of sexual sin, penance, and solitary holiness made it a staple of medieval penitential literature, later retold in Middle English.
works.characters: Mary of Egypt, Zosimas, the Virgin Mary (in the icon), the lion
works.structure: A frame narrative: Zosimas's search for a holy man greater than himself encloses Mary's first-person confession of her sins and penance, followed by her death and burial, the whole punctuated by the miracle of the lion and the testimony of the monastery.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
sources: Letitia Elizabeth Landon: Selected Writings

works.title: The Old English Life of St Nicholas
altTitles: The Old English Legend of St Nicholas of Myra
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 303 (c. 1100); also London, British Library, Cotton Caligula A.xiv
works.description: An Old English translation of the life and miracles of St Nicholas, the fourth-century bishop of Myra, patron of sailors, children, and the unjustly condemned: the most popular male saint of the later Middle Ages. The text is the earliest English life of Nicholas and the ancestor of the great Middle English legends of the saint.
works.plot: The life recounts Nicholas's precocious sanctity and election as bishop of Myra; among his miracles are the secret dowering of three impoverished maidens (the origin of his gift-giving legend), the rescue of sailors from a storm, the restoration to life of three murdered scholars, and the deliverance of three unjustly condemned men, together with his death and the translation of his relics to Bari in 1087.
works.significance: The first English life of St Nicholas, source of the medieval English Nicholas legend tradition and of the gift-giving saint's enduring popular image.
works.context: Nicholas's cult swept western Europe after the translation of his relics to Bari in 1087, and this late Old English life shows the cult's arrival in England; the text's miracle stories became the staple of the Middle English Nicholas legends and of the saint's later folklore.
works.characters: Nicholas of Myra, the three maidens, the sailors, the three scholars, the emperor Constantine
works.structure: A conventional episcopal vita followed by a miracle collection, each miracle self-contained; the translation of the relics to Bari is narrated as the crowning vindication of the saint's cult.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
sources: Zofloya: or, The Moor (Oxford World's Classics)

works.title: The Old English Rule of Chrodegang
altTitles: The Old English Version of the Enlarged Rule of Chrodegang
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 191 (eleventh century)
works.form: translation of a canonical rule (Old English prose)
works.description: An Old English translation of the enlarged Rule of Chrodegang of Metz, the eighth-century rule for communities of secular canons, adapted with English material. Made in the Benedictine Reform period, it regulated the communal life of the canons who served the great minsters, prescribing their common meals, dormitory, chapter, and penitential discipline.
works.plot: The rule legislates the canonical life in chapters: the bishop as head of the community, the common refectory and dormitory, the daily chapter and the reading of scripture, confession and penance for faults, and the duties of the canons in the liturgy and the care of the minster.
works.significance: A major document of the reform's extension beyond the monasteries to the secular church, and evidence of the vernacular's role in enforcing ecclesiastical discipline.
works.context: The Benedictine Reform's expulsion of secular clerics from Winchester's minsters in 964 created the need to reform the remaining communities of canons along quasi-monastic lines; the translated rule, together with Æthelwold's Regularis Concordia, extended the reform's discipline to the canonical clergy.
works.structure: A chapter-by-chapter translation of the enlarged rule, with the English material added to the Carolingian original; the text is a working legislative document rather than a narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.
sources: The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner (Oxford World's Classics)

works.title: The Old English Rule of St Benedict
altTitles: Æthelwold's Translation of the Rule of St Benedict
works.manuscriptDate: Five manuscripts including Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 178 and the Wells Cathedral copy (eleventh to thirteenth centuries)
works.description: A complete Old English translation of the Rule of St Benedict, traditionally attributed to Bishop Æthelwold of Winchester, made for the use of reformed monks and nuns whose Latin was limited. The translation is close, clear, and enriched with explanations of difficult terms.
works.plot: The text renders Benedict's rule for monastic life chapter by chapter: the abbot's office, obedience and humility, the daily round of prayer and work, food, sleep, and clothing, the reception of guests, and the discipline of faults, in continuous Old English prose.
works.significance: The first vernacular version of the most influential document of western monasticism, and a foundation text of the reform's vernacular programme of which Ælfric's writings are the culmination.
works.context: The translation belongs to the first years of the Benedictine Reform, when Æthelwold expelled the clerics of Winchester's minsters and replaced them with monks needing vernacular instruction in the rule they were to live by; it is the earliest translation of Benedict's rule into any European vernacular.
works.structure: A chapter-by-chapter translation following the order of the Latin rule, with occasional double glosses (Latin term plus English explanation) for technical vocabulary.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Æthelwold by tradition and by the evidence of his known translation activity; the attribution is widely but not universally accepted. Æthelwold's own preface and the translation are preserved together.
themes: The annual, the keepsake, and the gift-book economy
sources: James Fenimore Cooper: The Leatherstocking Tales (2 volumes, Library of America)

works.title: The Old Manor House
works.form: Prose Fiction and the Early Novel; Sentimental and Domestic Novel; Novel of Manners and Fashion
works.description: Charlotte Smith's most elaborate novel and, by general consent, the greatest of her fictions: the story of Orlando Somerive, disinherited by an eccentric will, and of his love for Monimia, a dependent of the family whose known servitude makes any marriage between them a social scandal. Set between an English manor house, the American war, and the law, the book conducts a sustained analysis of property, entail, primogeniture, depopulation, and the treatment of the poor, and it is now standardly read as a Jacobin novel in the full sense.
works.plot: Orlando, the younger son of the family that ought to be his, is cut off from the estate by his grandfather's will and by his father's compliance; he serves as a volunteer in America, returns to find Monimia, the gentlewoman's dependent he loves, exposed to the designs of other men, and struggles through legal stratagem and social penalty to establish both his right and his marriage. Around that plot the novel gathers portraits of an attorney, a disinherited heir, a decayed manor, and a village emptied by enclosure and by the changes of agricultural property.
works.significance: The Old Manor House is the novel that secured Smith's standing in the history of English fiction, and is valued as the most complete fusion in her work of sentimental plot and economic argument; its treatment of inheritance, service, and class-crossed desire makes it a key text for the study of 1790s radical fiction and for the prehistory of the condition-of-property novel.
works.meter: Prose romance; Smith's narration is interrupted by embedded verse quotations and by set descriptive passages in the rhythms of her topographical poetry.
works.context: Published in the same year as The Emigrants and immediately after Desmond, when Smith was supporting herself and her children entirely by the press and was deep in the Chancery litigation that had already absorbed a generation of her family's inheritance; its treatment of disputed succession, of the law's delay, and of a countryside emptied by enclosure and depopulation is drawn from the disputes over estate property and tenancy that her own suit dramatized.
works.characters: Orlando Somerive; Monimia Morysine; the Somerive family and its attorney and dependants; the American war officers and prisoners of Orlando's episode
works.structure: A multi-volume novel in the third person with a picaresque American-war episode and a legal-plot mechanism, alternating between country-house satire, sentimental courtship, and political narration; the two halves of Orlando's experience at home and abroad are held together by the sustained argument about inheritance.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

editions.title: The Poems of Charlotte Smith
editions.publisher: Oxford University Press, New York and Oxford (Women Writers in English 1350-1850)

editions.title: The Collected Letters of Charlotte Smith
Charlotte Smith in British Romanticism
editions.publisher: Pickering and Chatto, London (The Enlightenment World)

works.title: The Old Wives' Tale
works.description: Peele's folkloric comedy of enchantment: three pages lost in the woods take shelter with the smith Clunch, and the old wife Madge's fireside tale comes alive around them — the brothers seeking their sister Delia, the sorcerer Sacrapant's enchantments, the grateful dead man Jack, and the 'white bear of England's wood' — until the tale's happy ending dissolves back into the night.
works.plot: Madge's rambling tale is staged as she tells it: the wandering knights, the enchanted well that turns heads, the harvesters' song, Huanebango and Corebus's comic quests, and the rescue of Delia from Sacrapant's spells, with the dead man's gratitude and the bear's aid — the whole framed by the pages' bewildered watching.
works.significance: The most delightful of the English enchantment plays — a folk-tale theatre that Milton remembered when he wrote Comus.
works.meter: Mixed verse and prose, with the harvesters' song — 'Whenas the rye reach to the chin' — as its remembered lyric.
works.context: Written about 1591–93 and printed in 1595; it parodies the romances and enchantments of the popular stage (including Greene's and Peele's own) in the manner of a native Arabian Nights.
works.characters: Madge (the old wife); Clunch; the three pages; Sacrapant; Delia; the two brothers; Jack (the grateful dead man); Huanebango; Corebus; the white bear; the harvesters
works.structure: A frame-and-tale structure unique in Elizabethan drama: the story is performed as the old wife invents it, with the boundaries between teller, tale, and audience deliberately porous.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Old Wives' Tale (Revels Plays)

works.title: The Order of the World
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A wisdom poem of some 102 lines in which the poet urges his hearer to contemplate the created order — the sun's course, the stars, the seasons, and the harmony of the world — and to praise the Creator who sustains it all. The poem is an exercise in natural contemplation leading to worship.
works.plot: The poet calls on his audience to observe the wonders of creation: the journey of the sun, the movement of the heavens, the alternation of day and night, the order of the seasons. From the beauty and regularity of the world he turns to its maker, whom all creation serves, and urges man to praise God while he lives.
works.significance: One of the finest Old English poems of natural contemplation, notable for its integration of cosmology and devotion.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the descriptive passages on the heavens and seasons use the formulaic resources of the wisdom tradition with unusual lyrical polish.
works.context: The poem belongs to the Exeter Book wisdom corpus and shares its cosmological interests with the metrical version of Psalm 18 and the creation passages of the Cædmonian poems; it reflects the monastic ideal of contemplating God through his works.
works.structure: An exhortation framed as direct address to a 'wise one', moving from the observation of nature through reflection on the Creator to a closing call to praise; the poem is built of successive contemplations of the cosmic order.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Poetic solitude and the conversation with nature
sources: The Edinburgh Edition of the Waverley Novels

works.title: The Ormulum
works.description: A vast collection of verse homilies on the gospels read in the mass throughout the year, composed by the Augustinian canon Orm c. 1180, of which about a fifth survives (some 10,000 short lines). Its unique, meticulously consistent spelling system makes it a document of the first importance for the history of English.
works.plot: Each homily paraphrases the day's gospel text and expounds it allegorically and morally, with explanations of names and doctrine for the instruction of the English laity.
works.significance: The most ambitious vernacular religious work of the twelfth century and a uniquely valuable witness to early Middle English phonology, orthography, and East Midland dialect.
works.meter: An unrhymed fifteen-syllable septenarius in short couplet lines, strictly syllabic; the spelling system (double consonants after short vowels) is unique and systematic.
works.context: Composed c. 1180 by Orm, an Augustinian canon, probably of Elsham Priory, Lincolnshire, for his brother Walter; preserved in a single authorial or near-authorial manuscript, Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Junius 1.
works.characters: Christ; the evangelists' figures (none dramatically developed)
works.structure: A sequential homiliary following the liturgical year, with each sermon divided between gospel paraphrase, allegorical exposition, and moral application.
works.attributionNotes: Named in the dedication: 'þiss boc iss nemmnedd Orrmulum forrþi þatt Orrm itt wrohhte'.

editions.title: The Ormulum
editions.editor: Robert Meadows White (ed.); rev. Robert Holt

sources: A Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Venture, a Native of Africa: But Resident above Sixty Years in the United States of America. Related by Himself

works.title: The Orphan; or, The Unhappy Marriage
works.description: Thomas Otway's breakthrough tragedy, in which the orphan Monimia is secretly married to the elder brother Castalio and is tricked into his brother Polydore's bed on the wedding night, destroying them all.
works.plot: Castalio secretly marries Monimia; his brother Polydore, disguised, takes his place in the dark; when the truth emerges, Castalio kills himself in a duel with Polydore and Monimia takes poison.
works.significance: The founding work of the 'she-tragedy' mode that dominated Restoration and early eighteenth-century drama, and the play that established Otway's reputation.
works.meter: Blank verse of strong pathos.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Garden in February 1680 and published the same year; Elizabeth Barry's performance as Monimia made her the greatest tragic actress of the age.
works.characters: Monimia; Castalio; Polydore; Acasto; Serina; Chaplain; Ernesto
works.structure: Five acts in blank verse, modelled on the domestic tragedy of a wronged woman.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Otway; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Owl and the Nightingale
works.description: A debate poem of 1,794 lines in octosyllabic couplets in which the Owl and the Nightingale dispute which of them is the more useful and virtuous bird, arguing before a judge (Master Nicholas of Guildford) on matters of song, morality, marriage, and the religious life. It is the masterpiece of early Middle English poetry, combining French courtly wit with native English proverb and invective.
works.plot: The Nightingale accuses the Owl of ugliness and gloom, the Owl the Nightingale of frivolity and seduction; their quarrel ranges over theology, sex, and music, and both appeal to Master Nicholas of Guildford to render judgement — a judgement the poem never records.
works.significance: The outstanding literary achievement of early Middle English and the fountainhead of the English debate tradition that runs through Winner and Waster and the Parliament of Fowls to the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with enjambment and proverbial density; a sophisticated blend of French debate form and native English idiom.
works.context: Probably composed in Dorset or the south-west around 1200 (the text names King Henry as dead, dating it after 1189); preserved in two manuscripts of the mid-thirteenth century (BL Cotton Caligula A.ix and Jesus College, Oxford, MS 29).
works.characters: the Owl; the Nightingale; Master Nicholas of Guildford (named as judge)
works.structure: A continuous debate with prologue and framing judgment scene; the two birds' alternating speeches develop antithetical cases without resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous, but the poem names Master Nicholas of Guildford as its hoped-for judge; the authorship_status reflects scholarly practice in referring the work to its internal speaker.

editions.title: The Owl and the Nightingale: Text and Translation

sources: An Essay on the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, Particularly the African, Translated from a Latin Dissertation, Which Was Honoured with the First Prize in the University of Cambridge, for the Year 1785

works.title: The Palice of Honour
works.description: Douglas's first major poem, a courtly dream vision of prodigious learning: the dreamer, in a wilderness, sees a procession of the courts of Venus, Diana, and Minerva, faints before Venus's pageant, and is led to the Palace of Honour, where he learns the true source of fame and virtue. An answer to Chaucer's House of Fame and the foundation of Douglas's poetic career.
works.plot: The dreamer journeys with a guide from the garden of desire through the courts of Venus and Diana to the Palace of Honour, where the great of all ages sit enthroned; waking, he commits himself to the pursuit of honour through virtue.
works.significance: The most learned poem of the Scottish Renaissance and a central text of the Chaucerians; its allegorical courts prefigure The Faerie Queene.
works.meter: The nine-line stanza (ababbcbcC) inherited from Chaucer; aureate diction and encyclopaedic allusion.
works.context: Written about 1501, when Douglas was provost of St Giles; the poem's learning advertises the Scottish court's claim to the European Renaissance.
works.characters: the dreamer; Venus; Diana; Minerva; Calliope (guide)
works.structure: A dream vision in three movements — desire, instruction, and the vision of honour — modelled on Chaucer's House of Fame.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Panther
works.description: A poem of 74 lines from the Old English Physiologus group: the panther, fairest of beasts with its dappled coat, sleeps for three days and then calls with a sweet breath that draws all animals except the dragon. The poem allegorizes the panther as Christ, whose death, descent, and resurrection draw all souls — and the dragon as the devil who flees his fragrance.
works.plot: The poem describes the panther's beauty and gentleness, its three-day sleep and awakening, and the sweet breath that gathers the beasts; the interpretation identifies the panther with Christ, the dappled coat with his many virtues, and the sweet breath with the call of the gospel, which the old serpent, the devil, cannot endure.
works.significance: Part of the earliest English bestiary and of the allegorical natural-history tradition that culminates in the medieval bestiaries.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book with The Whale and The Partridge; the Physiologus tradition reached England via Latin intermediaries and remained productive through the Middle Ages.
works.characters: the Panther (Christ); the Dragon (the devil)
works.structure: Description followed by explicit allegorical interpretation, the standard Physiologus pattern.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Yale Edition of the Works of Samuel Johnson (21 volumes)

works.title: The Parable of the Wicked Mammon
altTitles: The Parable of the Wycked Mammon
works.description: Tyndale's exposition of the parable of the unjust steward (Luke 16), printed in 1528; his first published work and the classic statement of the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone.
works.plot: The treatise expounds the parable to teach that works do not justify but follow justification: the faithful are justified by faith in Christ's blood, and good works are the fruit of that faith, performed to one's neighbour without thought of merit; Tyndale defends the doctrine against the charge of encouraging licence and attacks the theology of merits, purgatory, and the intercession of saints.
works.significance: The first full English statement of justification by faith and the opening salvo of the English print war between Tyndale and More; its doctrine and its plain style set the terms of the English Reformation debate.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed in 1528 (STC 24454), the year of the Obedience, during Tyndale's exile in the Low Countries; it was among the first English books to state the Lutheran doctrine of justification, and it made Tyndale the prime target of More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies.
works.structure: A continuous doctrinal exposition with a preface 'To the Reader', arguing from scripture in Tyndale's plainest homiletic style.

works.title: The Pardoner and the Friar
works.description: John Heywood's anti-clerical farce of a pardoner and a friar who compete for the offerings of a parish church and come to blows in the pulpit; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
works.plot: A pardoner and a friar each claim the right to preach and collect money in a church; each denounces the other's hypocrisy and greed before the parish priest and his neighbour, until the contest descends into a brawl, the parson attempts to expel them, and both are dragged off toward the secular courts — with the parting promise that the devil will decide between them.
works.significance: The most anticlerical of Heywood's plays and a bridge between medieval estates satire and Reformation polemic; it shows the interlude absorbing the controversies of its moment without ceasing to be entertainment.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Written c. 1519–33 in the climate of lay criticism of clerical abuses that preceded the Reformation; the play draws on Chaucer's Pardoner and the long anticlerical tradition of estates satire, and its printing in 1533 coincided with the height of the campaign against church wealth.
works.characters: The Pardoner; The Friar; The Parson; The Neighbour
works.structure: A single-scene farce of rival harangues escalating into violence, framed by the parson's and neighbour's comments.

works.title: The Parliament of Fowls
works.description: Chaucer's St Valentine's Day dream vision (699 lines in rhyme royal): guided by Scipio's dream and the gate's ambiguous inscription, the dreamer enters the garden of love, where Nature presides over the parliament of birds choosing their mates on the feast of Venus. The debate between the noble eagles and the commons of birds is the great medieval comedy of class, desire, and natural law.
works.plot: After reading Cicero's Somnium Scipionis, the dreamer is led by Africanus through the gate ('through me men go to that blessed place' / 'through me the way to sorrow') into Nature's park, where the goddess holds the parliament of fowls; three aristocratic eagles court the formel on her wrist, their courtly pleas answered by the lower birds' impatient cry 'have done, and let us wende!' — and the formel's request for a year's delay leaves the parliament, and the poem, in unresolved suspension.
works.significance: The classic English poem of Valentine's Day and the finest medieval treatment of the bird parliament; its satire of courtly and common 'commune profyt' is a touchstone of Chaucer's political art.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas, with the lyric roundel ('Now welcom somer') inset.
works.context: Composed c. 1380–82, traditionally read against the marriage negotiations of Richard II (to Anne of Bohemia, 1382); the Valentine convention and the bird parliament derive from French and Italian love vision.
works.characters: the Dreamer; Africanus; Nature; the three eagles; the formel; the goose, cuckoo, turtledove, and other birds
works.structure: A tripartite vision (reading and gate; the garden and temple; the parliament and debate), with the roundel of summer as its lyric centre.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure.

editions.title: The Riverside Chaucer

sources: The History of Mary Prince, a West Indian Slave, Related by Herself

works.title: The Parliament of the Three Ages
altTitles: The Parlement of the Thre Ages
works.description: An alliterative debate vision of the three ages of man: a dreamer watching a deer hunt overhears Youth, Middle Age, and Old Age dispute the values of their lives, in a poem that grafts the morality of the ages onto the romance glamour of the hunt and the nine worthies. Its hunt scene is among the finest descriptive passages of the revival.
works.plot: The dreamer, concealed in the woods, follows the elaborate ritual of the hunt — the harbouring, the chase, the breaking of the deer — and then overhears three debaters: Youth, vaunting love and tournament; Middle Age, priding himself on wealth; and Old Age, who answers with the ubi sunt catalogue of the nine worthies and the lesson of Death the leveller.
works.significance: The most accomplished of the alliterative debate visions after Winner and Waster, and a principal vernacular statement of the ages-of-man topos.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line with stanzaic variation.
works.context: Composed c. 1370–90 in the north or north-west Midlands, drawing on the tradition of the ages of man and the nine worthies; preserved uniquely in BL Additional MS 31042 and (in part) Additional MS 33942.
works.characters: the Dreamer; Youth; Middle Age; Old Age; Death
works.structure: A frame vision enclosing the hunt and the three speeches, in the debate-vision convention.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Selected Writings of Leigh Hunt (6 volumes)

works.title: The Partridge
works.description: A poem of 16 lines, the third of the Exeter Book Physiologus group: the partridge, which steals and broods the eggs of other birds, sees its stolen brood desert it when they hatch and hear their true mother's call. The allegory (imperfectly preserved) contrasts the devil's stolen brood with those who hear the true voice of Christ.
works.plot: The partridge hatches eggs not its own; when the chicks hear their real mother they leave the deceiver. The brief application praises those who turn to their true parent — the text breaks off where the interpretation of the fable is developed.
works.significance: Completes the earliest English bestiary group.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book, immediately after The Whale.
works.characters: the Partridge; the stolen brood
works.structure: Fable followed by a broken-off allegorical application.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Civil War, regicide, and the trial of the king
sources: The Poems of Thomas Gray, William Collins and Oliver Goldsmith

works.title: The Passions: An Ode for Music
works.description: Collins's ode for music, in which the several passions answer the calls of the instruments and the chief among them is given the mastery of the hearer's soul.
works.plot: The passions are summoned in turn by the music, each answering in its own measure, from the plainest to the most heroic and the most melancholy, until the ruling passion closes the concert in the triumph of the mind it has possessed.
works.significance: It is the most accomplished of the century's odes on the powers of music and the passions, and it carries the musical ode from the Dryden manner to the lyric variety of the following generation.
works.meter: A series of contrasting lyric measures, each stanza adapted to the passion and to the air it imitates, in the tradition of the Dryden and Handel ode.
works.context: Written in the decade when the English ode for music was being revived for the London concerts and for the Handel oratorio, and when the theory of the passions supplied the programme of such pieces.
works.characters: the personified Passions; Music as the summoning power; the ruling passion of the close
works.structure: An ode of invocation and succession, the stanzas distributed among the several passions in the manner of the musical entertainment.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Poems of Thomas Gray, William Collins and Oliver Goldsmith

works.title: The Pastime of People
altTitles: The Pastyme of People: The Cronycles of Dyuers Realmys
works.description: John Rastell's chronicle of the kings of England, printed by the author c. 1529 and known principally through the celebrated woodcut portraits of the kings that illustrate it.
works.plot: The chronicle surveys the kings of Britain from the legendary line (Brutus, Arthur) through the Saxon, Norman, and Plantagenet reigns to the author's own day, each reign summarized with a woodcut portrait, the whole prefaced by a prologue on the use of history.
works.significance: A pioneering illustrated chronicle whose woodcut royal portraits influenced the visual tradition of the English kings for centuries; it documents the early Tudor printing industry's combination of history and spectacle.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed c. 1529 by Rastell, More's brother-in-law, printer, and playwright, at his own press; only three copies survive, and the king-portraits became a standard visual source for the Tudor image of English kingship.
works.structure: A compressed annalistic chronicle with full-page woodcut portraits of the kings, arranged by reign.

works.title: The Pastime of Pleasure
altTitles: The Historie of Graunde Amoure and La Bell Pucell
works.form: allegorical romance in rhyme royal and couplets
works.description: Hawes's allegorical romance of the education of the knight Graunde Amoure: his instruction by Lady Fame and the seven liberal arts in the Tower of Doctrine, his courtship of La Belle Pucelle, his combat with a giant, their marriage, and his death, with Time and Eternity closing the poem. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1509, it is the last great allegory of the medieval English tradition.
works.plot: Graunde Amoure, guided by Governance and instructed in the Tower of Doctrine, wins La Belle Pucelle through the arts and arms, marries her, and rules until Age and Death take him; Fame memorializes the lovers.
works.significance: The bridge between the medieval allegorical romance and Tudor poetry; its catalogue of the arts and its ideal of the learned knight were formative for Spenser's Faerie Queene.
works.meter: Rhyme royal handled in the Lydgatian manner, with couplet passages; aureate diction over a clear narrative line.
works.context: Written at the court of Henry VII, to whom the ideal of the educated knight was addressed; printed in 1509, the year of Henry VIII's accession.
works.characters: Graunde Amoure; La Belle Pucelle; Lady Fame; Governance; Godfrey Gobelive (the giant); Time; Eternity
works.structure: An allegorical romance in three movements — instruction, quest, and the fall of the hero — framed by a dream prologue and an epilogue on fame and time.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Pastime of Pleasure

works.title: The Penitential Psalms
works.form: psalm paraphrase in terza rima (prologue) and various stanzas
works.description: Wyatt's paraphrase of the seven penitential psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143), framed by a prologue in which David, the royal lover of Bathsheba, is made the type of the penitent courtier. Based on Aretino's I Sette Salmi, the work turns the psalmist's repentance into a sustained meditation on the dangers of the court and the sovereignty of God.
works.plot: The frame narrative follows David from his sin with Bathsheba through the prophet Nathan's parable to his repentance; each psalm is then paraphrased as David's own speech, with Wyatt's added commentary.
works.significance: The major English religious poem of the Reformation's first generation and the ancestor of Sidney's and Milton's psalm paraphrases; its David is the first great self-portrait of the Tudor courtier in verse.
works.meter: Terza rima in the prologue — the first sustained English use of Dante's metre — and ottava rima in the psalm paraphrases.
works.context: Written after Wyatt's imprisonment of 1536, during the fall of Anne Boleyn; the psalmist's court becomes a mirror of Henry VIII's, and repentance the courtier's only safety.
works.characters: David; Bathsheba; Nathan
works.structure: Prologue narrative (in terza rima) followed by seven paraphrases; each psalm introduced by a stanza of commentary.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Pentateuch (Tyndale's translation)
works.description: Tyndale's translation of the first five books of the Old Testament from the Hebrew, printed at Antwerp in 1530; the first English translation of any part of the Hebrew Bible from the original language.
works.plot: A complete translation of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, with prefaces to each book explaining its sense and typological bearing, and a prologue to the whole ('W. T. to the Reader') setting out Tyndale's principles of translation from the Hebrew.
works.significance: The first English translation from the Hebrew and the origin of the English Old Testament's distinctive phrasing ('let there be light', 'the Lord bless thee and keep thee'); it established the principle that the Bible must be rendered from the original tongues.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Tyndale learned Hebrew on the continent (probably from Jewish scholars), and the Pentateuch of 1530 was printed by Hans Luft at Antwerp (or Marburg) and smuggled into England; it supplied the Old Testament basis for the Matthew Bible (1537) and, through it, for the Great Bible and the King James Version.
works.structure: Biblical text in the Hebrew order, with per-book prefaces and glosses; Genesis and Numbers were printed separately with their own title pages.

works.title: The Phoenix
works.form: allegorical religious narrative in alliterative verse
works.description: An allegorical poem of 677 lines on the legend of the phoenix, which burns itself on its nest of spices and rises renewed: a figure, the poem explains, of the resurrection of the body and the Christian's hope of the heavenly homeland. Based on the Carmen de ave phoenice attributed to Lactantius, it contains one of the finest paradise descriptions in Old English.
works.plot: The poem describes the earthly paradise in the east where the phoenix dwells; after a thousand years the bird flies to Syria, builds a nest of spices, is consumed by fire, and after three days revives from the ashes. The second half interprets the legend allegorically: the phoenix is Christ and the blessed soul, the nest the good works, and the renewal the resurrection at the Last Judgment.
works.significance: The fullest Old English allegory of resurrection and the richest nature-description in the corpus.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the poem is notable for its extended descriptive set-pieces.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; the Latin source (fourth century, attributed to Lactantius) circulated widely in Anglo-Saxon England.
works.characters: the Phoenix (as bird and as allegorical figure)
works.structure: A bipartite structure of literal legend followed by sustained allegorical exposition (the latter an original expansion of the Latin source).
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Spectator, 4 volumes

works.title: The Phoenix and the Turtle
works.description: Shakespeare's 67-line metaphysical elegy, printed in Robert Chester's collection Love's Martyr (1601) alongside poems by Jonson, Chapman, and Marston: the funeral of the phoenix and the turtle dove, whose chaste love united them 'in a mutual flame', leaving reason itself to compose the threne over their urn.
works.plot: The birds assemble for the obsequies; the anthem declares the lovers one in essence, 'two distincts, division none'; reason, confounded, speaks the threne; and the poem closes on the paradoxes of truth and beauty buried with them.
works.significance: The strangest and most debated of Shakespeare's poems — the one place where he joins the metaphysical company of Donne.
works.meter: Trochaic tetrameter with the irregular 'threne' in trimeter — the most deliberately 'metaphysical' verse Shakespeare wrote.
works.context: Published in 1601 as an appendix to Chester's Love's Martyr, dedicated to Sir John Salusbury; its allegorical referents (Salusbury's circle, the Earl of Essex, or pure emblem) remain undetermined.
works.characters: the Phoenix; the Turtle; Reason; the assembled birds
works.structure: A tripartite ceremony — summons, anthem, threne — in the form of a compressed metaphysical emblem poem.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That Which Is to Come (Part I)
works.form: allegory; dream vision; prose fiction; spiritual narrative
works.description: Bunyan's allegorical dream-narrative of the journey of Christian from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City, begun in his second imprisonment and published in 1678; it is the most popular and most translated work of English prose fiction.
works.plot: Christian, burdened with sin, is directed by Evangelist to the Wicket Gate; he passes through the Slough of Despond, the House of the Interpreter, the Cross where his burden falls, the Hill of Difficulty, the Valley of Humiliation where he fights Apollyon, the Valley of the Shadow of Death, Vanity Fair where Faithful is martyred, Doubting Castle where he is imprisoned by Giant Despair, and the Delectable Mountains, until he crosses the river into the Celestial City.
works.significance: The supreme English prose allegory and, with Robinson Crusoe, one of the two founding works of the English novel; it has never been out of print, has been translated into more than two hundred languages, and has shaped the imaginative vocabulary of the English-speaking world ('Vanity Fair', 'the Slough of Despond', 'Doubting Castle').
works.meter: Plain, colloquial prose interwoven with biblical phrase and with short verses at intervals.
works.context: Composed during Bunyan's second imprisonment (1675-6) and published in February 1678 by Nathaniel Ponder, whose shop sign gave the book the nickname 'The Pilgrim's Progress from Ponder's'; it went through ten editions in Bunyan's lifetime.
works.characters: Christian; Evangelist; Pliable; Obstinate; Mr Worldly Wiseman; Faithful; Talkative; Hopeful; Apollyon; Giant Despair; Christiana (Part II); Interpreter; Great-heart
works.structure: A framed dream-vision in two stages of journey, with episodic encounters, embedded verses, and the author's Apology as a preface.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bunyan; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Pilgrim's Progress
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Pilgrim's Progress from This World to That Which Is to Come (Part II)
works.description: The second part of Bunyan's allegory, in which Christian's wife Christiana, with her four sons and the neighbour Mercy, undertakes the same pilgrimage under the protection of the valiant Great-heart.
works.plot: Christiana repents her earlier harshness to Christian and sets out with Mercy and the children; guided by Great-heart, they pass through the same places Christian knew, overcome Giant Grim and the other giants, and reach the Celestial City.
works.significance: Completes the allegory with a domestic and communal pilgrimage that has been widely read as a feminist counterpart to Part I; it is normally printed with Part I in every edition.
works.meter: Plain prose with interpolated verses, gentler and more social in tone than Part I.
works.context: Published in 1684, six years after Part I, in response to its enormous popularity and to the many spurious continuations that had appeared.
works.characters: Christiana; Mercy; Matthew; Samuel; Joseph; James; Great-heart; Mr Prudence; Mr Piety; Giant Grim; Despondency's daughter Much-afraid
works.structure: A framed dream-vision following Part I's itinerary with a female party and a protective escort.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Bunyan; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Pilgrim's Progress
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Pilgrimage
works.form: Devotional-descriptive poem in the Rowley manner, with obsolete diction and gloss; closer to a popular song or carol tradition than to the chronicle-poems of the same series.
works.description: A shorter poem of the Rowley series, in which Chatterton depicts a company of pilgrims making their way to a holy shrine. It belongs to the devotional and descriptive side of the forgeries, and shows Chatterton using the supposed licence of an earlier and simpler age to write religious poetry that no Augustan poet publishing under his own name could have offered.
works.plot: The piece describes the progress of the pilgrimage and the scenes and people it passes: the shrine and its offerings, the devotion of the company, and the rough, homely and unsolemn life of the road. The emphasis falls on the externals of an older popular religion, treated with affection and with a frankness Chatterton thought characteristic of a time before politeness had refined devotion into decorum. There is no dramatic conflict; the interest is pictorial and vocal, sustained by the archaized diction which carries the fiction of date. The underlying argument is that a nation's religion, like its poetry, is most powerful when it is most naive.
works.significance: It is a striking example of the religious imagination available within the forgery: Chatterton invented not only an antique manner but an entire devotional culture, and the poem helped to form the later romantic and antiquarian interest in medieval popular piety. Its frankness about the bodily and homely side of devotion anticipates the romantic recovery of the Middle Ages.
works.meter: Rowley's irregular long measure, with a strong lyric and song-like beat in parts, in deliberately antique spelling; the harshness of the sound is part of the designed effect.
works.context: It is one of the pieces that went out under Rowley's name in the Bristol correspondence of the mid 1760s, at a time when the collecting of old English poetry was becoming a fashionable antiquarian pursuit and when pilgrimage, shrines and popular superstition were being reinterpreted as picturesque national material.
works.characters: The pilgrim company; the shrine and its keepers; the framing poet 'Thomas Rowley'
works.structure: A processional poem: the pilgrimage observed in a sequence of descriptive and apostrophic passages, with invocation and devotional address framing the movement.
works.attributionNotes: Authored by Chatterton though ascribed in the Rowley papers to the fictitious monk; no medieval original exists, and the 'antiquity' of the piece rests on forged manuscripts and glosses. Its place in the series and its date of composition are not fixed with confidence, so the year fields are left null.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Pioneers
altTitles: The Pioneers; or, The Sources of the Susquehanna
works.form: Frontier romance and novel of settlement; social panorama in the manner of the Scottish historical novel
works.description: The first of the series set in the New York backcountry and the earliest American novel to make settlement, law and the destruction of the forest its subject. A declining frontier county in the 1790s supplies a full social survey: judge, lawyer, doctor, Quaker, settler and Indian. Its portrait of an aging scout who prefers the wilderness to the courthouse remains the type of the American frontiersman.
works.plot: In an outpost town on the sources of the Susquehanna, a family of landed English stock is joined by an heiress, and the neighbouring settlers contest game laws, land titles and the right to punish. An old huntsman, the finest woodsman in the county, is fined by the judge for shooting deer out of season and then dispossessed of his cabin by a legal technicality. A disguised prisoner turns out to be a son of the house, and an attempted marriage to a French count reveals the vulnerability of the heiress. The novel ends with the burning of the Indian winter village, the death of the Englishwoman and the huntsman's departure west to die.
works.significance: It created Natty Bumppo, the first permanently American heroic type, and made the conflict between wilderness and institution the masterplot of American fiction. Its legal and ecological conscience anticipated later environmental narrative. It is the foundation text of the American romance of forest and sea.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in January 1823, drawing on the author's childhood in Cooperstown and on the land law, game law and Indian policy of the trans-Allegheny west. The year of its appearance saw the debate over the Indian removal bill, and the novel's dispossession plot answers that debate. Its topographical details were later supplied in a key by the author's family.
works.characters: Natty Bumppo; Judge Marmaduke Temple; Richard Jones; Elizabeth Temple; Oliver Edwards; Chingachgook
works.structure: Third-person panoramic novel of a community, with a central action of legal dispossession and a subsidiary romance; the description of institutions repeatedly interrupts the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed.

editions.publisher: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press
