works.title: The Sceptical Chymist
altTitles: The Sceptical Chymist; or, Chymico-Physical Doubts and Paradoxes
works.description: Robert Boyle's dialogue attacking the Aristotelian and Paracelsian theories of the elements, arguing for a corpuscular (mechanical) account of matter and insisting that chemical claims must be established by experiment.
works.plot: In a dialogue among Carneades, Eleutherius, Philoponus, and Themistius, Boyle argues that neither the four Aristotelian elements nor the three Paracelsian principles can be demonstrated; only experiment can determine the composition of bodies.
works.significance: The work that separated chemistry from alchemy and established it as an experimental science; its sceptical method and its corpuscularianism were decisive for the new philosophy.
works.meter: Argumentative prose with detailed experimental description.
works.context: Published in 1661, a year after the Restoration and the year before the Royal Society's charter; Boyle was a founding fellow and the leading experimental philosopher of the age.
works.characters: Carneades (Boyle's spokesman); Eleutherius; Philoponus; Themistius
works.structure: A dialogue in six parts with an appendix of experiments.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Boyle; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The School for Scandal
altTitles: The School for Scandal: A Comedy
works.form: comedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: The greatest comedy of the late eighteenth century, a play about scandal-mongering and hypocritical virtue in which the surface candour of a fashionable society is dissected by a series of eavesdroppings. Its famous fourth-act screen scene gathers the whole design into one tableau.
works.plot: A house of professed candour is divided against itself: the outwardly moral younger brother supplants his frank and spendthrift elder, and a circle of wits live on the malice of the tea-table. Sir Peter Teazle, newly married to a country girl, is set against his wife by the same tribe, and the wife is taught the ways of the town. The discovery of the hypocrite by the try-all brother and the exposure of the school of scandal in the screen scene restore the elder brother and reform the young couple.
works.significance: It is the final masterpiece of the English comedy of manners and the standard instance of the argument that society's conversation is a form of action; it has never left the repertory.
works.meter: A brilliant prose dialogue of epigram, retort and malaprop-free precision, the high style of the moral sententiae being reserved for parody; the speeches are built to be quoted.
works.context: First performed at Drury Lane in May 1777 after the failure of a rival play on the same design, in the season in which its author became a principal manager of the house; the comedy of sensibility and the comedy of laughter were then openly contending for the stage.
works.characters: Sir Peter Teazle; Lady Teazle; Joseph Surface; Charles Surface; Sir Oliver Surface; Lady Sneerwell; Snake; Maria; the backbiters of the breakfast table
works.structure: Five-act comedy of intrigue and discovery, its turns effected by concealed hearing and the misreport of conversation; the dialogue advances the plot almost entirely by what is overheard.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; published in the author's name and recorded in the manager's own accounts of the season.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The School-Master
works.form: pastoral eclogue in three parts, with argument and annotations
works.description: William Shenstone's earliest considerable poem, a pastoral eclogue in three parts which memorialises his old schoolmaster and turns the village school into an Arcadian scene. The poem honors the learned country usher, sketches his poverty and his patience, and asks what returns a nation makes to the men who form its youth. It is at once a tribute, a pastoral of letters, and a complaint about the treatment of the obscure teacher, and it announced the distinctive Shenstonian mixture of tenderness, rural observation and self-conscious antiquarianism.
works.plot: In the first part the scene of the school is drawn in pastoral disguise, the master's patience and cares mustered, and the poet recalls the benefit he personally received; in the second the ageing master's distresses and his dependence upon a generous eye are set out with a melancholy directness; the third part resolves the poem into an address to the patron and to the Muses, asking that the man who taught others to live should not be left to die neglected. The design is thus tripartite in feeling as well as in form: recollection, complaint, and petition.
works.significance: It gave the century one of its most reprinted poems of gratitude and educational piety, helped to fix the image of the poor country schoolmaster in British feeling, and stands with Shenstone's Leasowes writings as a document of the mid-century culture of retirement, sensibility and rural taste.
works.meter: An uneven pastoral stanza of short iambic lines, in the deliberate archaisms and irregularities of the English eclogue tradition inherited from Spenser and from the seventeenth-century school of the shepheardes calendars; Shenstone's own notes on the stanza's antiquity accompany the poem.
works.context: Published in 1742, when the country retired gentleman and the minor poet of the counties were a recognised figure in the literary geography outside London, and when the school-master was a stock of both charity sermon and satire; Shenstone printed and circulated his poems largely through friends and local presses rather than through the great London houses.
works.characters: the schoolmaster; the pupil-poet; the neighbouring rustics and pupils
works.structure: A pastoral eclogue in three parts, framed by an invocation and a dedicatory address, moving from recalled schoolroom scene to present complaint to closing petition, with the shepherd-poet convention carrying the memoir.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Shenstone's authorship is documented by his own circulation of the poem and by the collected editions of his works.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Schoolmaster
works.description: Ascham's posthumously published treatise on the education of children, especially the teaching of Latin by double translation, with an autobiographical preface on the occasion of its writing.
works.plot: Book I, framed by the preface recalling a 1563 dinner conversation at Windsor on the flogging of schoolboys, advocates gentleness in teaching, criticizes the harsh grammar-school regime, and sketches the ideal education of a gentleman's son. Book II offers a practical method — the 'double translation' of Latin — by which the student imitates classical models, with detailed advice on style, imitation, and the choice of authors.
works.significance: The classic statement of Elizabethan humanist pedagogy; its doctrine of imitation and its advocacy of the vernacular prose style influenced Sidney, Spenser, and the school curriculum for generations.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Begun c. 1563 after the Windsor dinner with Cecil and Sackville (the latter of whom prompted the book), and left unfinished at Ascham's death in December 1568; published in 1570 by his widow Margaret with a dedication to Cecil. Its composition and publication bridge the early Tudor and Elizabethan periods.
works.characters: Roger Ascham (narrator); Sir William Cecil; Sir Richard Sackville
works.structure: Two books; the first is anecdotal and hortatory, the second a systematic method with specimen exercises.

editions.title: The Schoolmaster (1570)
editions.publisher: Cornell University Press (for the Folger Shakespeare Library)

works.title: The Scots Musical Museum
altTitles: The Scots Musical Museum, in Six Volumes
works.form: Anthology, reliques and editorial collection of Scottish song; ballad and popular song, printed with the airs and a vocal part
works.description: The great serial anthology of Scottish song, projected and published by the Edinburgh music-engraver James Johnson and issued in six volumes between 1787 and 1803. It prints traditional and modern Scots songs with their airs, arranged for the voice with simple instrumental accompaniments, and in its later volumes it became the principal printing ground for the songs of Robert Burns, who from about 1788 was its most active contributor and, in effect, its literary editor. The collection is the single most important body of song into which Burns poured his late labour: he revised old texts, recovered fragments from singers and from the printed repertoire, wrote new verses to familiar airs, and supplied the illustrative notes and the historical and critical remarks that carry the volumes. Its six volumes hold the repertory out of which the modern idea of the Scottish song tradition was made, and they document a collaboration between a music publisher and a poet in which the poet's share came to dominate the series.
works.plot: The volumes are not a narrative but a repertory: each number is a song text printed with its air, arranged so that the words and the tune are presented together, with the older traditional pieces beside new or revised lyrics. The scheme broadens from the opening volume's gathering of favourite Scottish songs toward the later volumes' wider historical and comparative range, which includes early pieces, songs in the Scottish dialect, and illustrative prose notes on the texts and their authorities. Burns's contributions fall chiefly in the volumes issued from about 1790 onwards: songs of love, drinking and friendship, comic and pastoral songs, Jacobite and border pieces, and revised versions of traditional texts whose phrasing he restored or re-made. His own account of the work, in letters of the period, describes his method of collating printed and sung versions, keeping the old words where they were best, and writing new stanzas only when the air required them.
works.significance: The Museum is the repository in which Burns's achievement as a songwriter, the largest and most durable part of his work, was first collected and printed, and it changed the status of song within his canon from occasional verse to serious poetic labour. It also fixes the model of the poet at work on traditional texts, revising, restoring and re-creating rather than inventing, a model that bears directly on later accounts of Romantic authorship, orality and cultural property. Its repertory, edited and largely made by Burns, remains the standard record of late-eighteenth-century Scottish song and a central document of the Romantic construction of national tradition.
works.meter: Strophic song verse written to be sung, not read: the texts run mainly in the ballad and song stanzas of the Scottish repertory, common and short measure with alternating four- and three-beat lines, with refrains, tags and the short-tailed stanza forms Burns adapted to individual airs. Because the air governs the line, the metre is disciplined by musical phrase, syncopation and repeat, and Burns's revisions are often measurable as adjustments of syllable count to the notes. Scots dialect spelling, with its own rhyme and assonance habits, carries much of the series' verbal texture.
works.context: Published at Edinburgh by James Johnson, engraver and music-seller, in the same decade as the Kilmarnock and Edinburgh volumes of Burns's poetry, the Museum belonged to the enthusiastic collecting of national song that followed Percy's Reliques and the ballad revivals of the 1780s, and to Edinburgh's competitive music trade, in which Johnson and his rival George Thomson vied for airs, verses and subscribers. Burns, established as a poet after 1786 and settled at Ellisland and then Dumfries from 1788, took up the collection as the work of his later years, believing that the old Scottish songs were a national inheritance worth preserving against the polite dilution of the English stage. His engagement made the series a partnership of a craftsman publisher and a poet-editor; the sixth volume appeared after his death in 1796.
works.characters: the singer-speakers of the songs; the beloveds and false lovers of the lyric texts; the shepherd, hind and ploughboy of the pastoral and labouring numbers; the drunkards and revellers of the tavern songs; the Highland chiefs, border raiders and Jacobites of the historical pieces; James Johnson as projector and publisher and Robert Burns as contributing editor
works.structure: A serial anthology in six octavo volumes, each a numbered sequence of independent songs rather than an ordered argument; the unity is the repertory and the continuing editorial scheme, which passed in practice from Johnson's musical arrangements to Burns's textual judgement as the series reached its middle volumes. The set was completed only after Burns's death, and he interleaved copies of the earlier volumes with his own notes and corrections.
works.attributionNotes: The volumes are Johnson's publication and a joint undertaking: Johnson chose and engraved the airs, contracted the arrangements and holds the title-page credit, while Burns supplied an immense body of lyrics, revisions and notes without ever appearing as author of the work. Burns is named here as a contributing author only, not as the author of the collection. Estimates of his share run in modern accounts to some two hundred songs, but the figure varies between authorities and the attribution of individual numbers between traditional texts, other contributors and Burns has been actively re-opened by recent scholarship, so the record is left at research_status partial.

works.title: The Seafarer
works.description: An elegy of 124 lines spoken by a veteran seafarer who describes the hardship and the irresistible pull of the sea voyage, then allegorizes it as the soul's pilgrimage away from the world toward its heavenly home.
works.plot: The speaker recounts winters of cold watch on the ice-cold sea, hunger, and isolation, yet declares that the sea calls him again; earthly joys, lords, and kingdoms all pass, and the wise man sets his hope on the eternal home where all things endure — the journey of the seafarer becoming a figure for the Christian's exile in the world.
works.significance: Alongside The Wanderer, the great poem of Old English exile; its seascape and spiritual allegory influenced Pound's 'The Seafarer' and much modern poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; vivid winter seascape imagery rare in the corpus.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; influenced by the penitential and pilgrimage traditions (the phrase 'dryhtnes dreamas' has suggested the peregrinus ideal of Irish and Anglo-Saxon monasticism).
works.characters: the Seafarer (speaker)
works.structure: Two movements: a first-person account of seafaring hardship and longing, and a homiletic second half that interprets the voyage allegorically (peregrinatio pro amore Dei); the transition between them is a crux of interpretation.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: A Guide to Old English, 8th edition

works.title: The Series
works.description: Thomas Hoccleve's linked sequence of poems (c. 1419–21), beginning with the Complaint and the Dialogue with a Friend — the first extended account of mental illness in English poetry, describing his 'wylde infirmity' of 1416 — and continuing with the tale of the emperor Jereslaus's wife and the Learn to Die, translated from the Gesta Romanorum and Suso. The founding text of English confessional poetry.
works.plot: The poet, unable to persuade the world of his recovered wits, complains of his illness and its social stigma; a Friend counsels and cajoles him back to writing; the sequence then proceeds through the exemplary tale of the empress and the treatise on dying, the poet's own voice threading the whole.
works.significance: The first extended English poem of mental illness and recovery, and the first secular autobiography in English verse; its frankness has made it a touchstone of disability and confessional studies.
works.meter: Rhyme royal throughout, with the prosimetric flourishes of the translated treatises.
works.context: Composed c. 1419–21, after Hoccleve's breakdown of 1416, for Humphrey Duke of Gloucester among others; preserved in the holograph manuscripts (Durham, Cosin V.iii.9; BL Harley 4866) — the earliest English authorial manuscripts after Orm.
works.characters: Hoccleve; the Friend; the Emperor Jereslaus and his wife (tale)
works.structure: A self-consciously linked series — complaint, dialogue, tale, and treatise — in which the frame of the poet's illness governs the exemplary matter.
works.attributionNotes: Hoccleve's authorship secure; parts survive in his own hand.
sources: Tales of Wonder (Broadview Editions)

works.title: The Sermons before King Edward VI
altTitles: The Seven Sermons before Edward VI
works.description: Hugh Latimer's seven Lenten sermons preached before King Edward VI in the privy garden at Westminster in 1549 and printed the same year; the fullest surviving example of Latimer's court preaching.
works.plot: Preached weekly in Lent 1549, the sermons press the young king and his court with the duties of the magistrate: Latimer denounces the greed of landlords and enclosers, the plunder of church goods, the oppression of the poor, and the corruption of officials, urging the king to be the father of the commonwealth and warning that England's plagues are God's judgement on its sins.
works.significance: The classic example of court preaching in English and a prime source for the social history of Edwardian England; Latimer's plainspoken rebukes of the powerful made him the archetype of the prophetic preacher.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached at Westminster in Lent 1549, the year of the First Prayer Book, the rebellions of 1549, and the fall of Protector Somerset; printed by John Day in 1549, the sermons document the preaching office at the summit of the state and the social crisis of the mid-Tudor years.
works.characters: King Edward VI (addressee)
works.structure: Seven self-contained sermons, each on a set text, in Latimer's direct, colloquial, and anecdotal style, with running rebukes of his courtly audience.

works.title: The Sermons of Mr. Yorick
altTitles: Sermons, by the Late Mr. Yorick
works.description: A collection of parish sermons published under the name of the fictional clergyman whose life the novels also report, and running to several volumes over the middle years of the decade. They are sermons of the conscience and of the passions, on temperance, on the nature of religious consolation, on the duty of mirth and on the danger of a hard heart.
works.plot: The discourses examine the religious emotions of ordinary people, pressing on their hearers the duty of open-heartedness and the sin of the self-flattering hearer. They treat the love of pleasure, the neglect of the afflicted, the temper of a winter evening and the use of religious melancholy. The argument is not doctrinal but diagnostic, aiming to persuade the conscience by the analysis of its own feelings.
works.significance: It supplies the serious underside of the author's reputation and is evidence of how the culture of feeling was worked through in the established church; several of the discourses were separately reprinted and translated.
works.meter: A spoken prose of the pulpit of the day, with the short sentence of application, the rhetorical question and the tender parenthesis; the cadence is deliberately colloquial and moving.
works.context: Published between 1760 and 1767 by a country clergyman who was simultaneously a fashionable writer, in the season of the sensible sermon and of the argument with enthusiasm, and often sold in numbers of the same bookseller as the fiction.
works.characters: Mr. Yorick as the preaching persona; the parish audience; the afflicted and the self-deceived of the instances
works.structure: A serial collection of printed sermons, each a short regular discourse with text, improvement and application, gathered into volumes with the persona of the preacher supplying the frame.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volumes carry the pseudonymous preacher's name and are documented in the author's correspondence, though the persona occasionally disguises the hand.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Seven Penitential Psalms (Fisher's exposition)
altTitles: This treatise concerninge the fruytfull saynges of Davyd the kynge and prophete in the seven penytencyall psalmes
works.description: John Fisher's devotional exposition of the seven penitential psalms, preached as sermons to Margaret Beaufort and published by Wynkyn de Worde in 1508; the first work of the English Catholic humanist reform tradition.
works.plot: The treatise expounds Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143 as a programme of penitence — contrition, confession, and satisfaction — applying each psalm to the life of the Christian penitent and to the passion of Christ as the ground of forgiveness.
works.significance: The finest English devotional prose before the Reformation controversy and a witness to the scriptural piety of the pre-Reformation English Church; its emphasis on preaching and scripture anticipates the reform movements on both sides of the sixteenth-century divide.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached as a Lenten course to the household of Lady Margaret Beaufort, the king's mother, whose confessor Fisher was; printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1508 and reprinted in 1509 and 1525, it belongs to the devotional revival associated with the Charterhouse and the early humanist circle.
works.characters: David (as penitent)
works.structure: Seven sermon-treatises, one per psalm, each structured by the threefold division of the penitential process, with a preface to Margaret Beaufort.

works.title: The Shepheardes Calender
works.description: Spenser's first major work, published anonymously under the signature 'Immerito': twelve eclogues, one for each month, in which shepherds debate love, poetry, and religion in a deliberately archaic diction, with a learned commentary by 'E.K.' and woodcuts for each month.
works.plot: Through the revolving year, the shepherd Colin Clout loves the disdainful Rosalind, sings and despairs, while his fellows Hobbinol, Cuddie, Piers, and Palinode dispute the duties of poets and pastors; the sequence closes with December's elegy for the dying year.
works.significance: The manifesto of the new English poetry: it announced Spenser as the heir of Chaucer and Virgil and launched the Elizabethan pastoral tradition.
works.meter: A bravura display of stanza forms and line lengths — from four-stress couplets to sestinas — in a deliberately archaic 'shepherdly' English.
works.context: Published in the year of the proposed Anjou marriage and the height of the Puritan controversy; its ecclesiastical eclogues (May, July, September) engage the debate over the Elizabethan church.
works.characters: Colin Clout; Hobbinol; Rosalind; Cuddie; Piers; Palinode; E.K. (the commentator)
works.structure: A Virgilian eclogue book of twelve parts arranged by month, with framing apparatus (title page, argument, gloss) supplied by the commentator E.K.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as by 'Immerito'; the authorship was an open secret and is uncontested.

editions.title: The Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser
editions.editor: William A. Oram, Einar Bjorvand, Ronald Bond, Thomas Cain, Alexander Dunlop, and Richard Schell (eds.)

works.title: The Shepherd's Calendar; with Village Stories, and Other Poems
works.form: Pastoral Poetry; Topographical and Descriptive Poetry
works.description: A twelve-part seasonal poem, one number for each calendar month, in which an under-gardener and shepherd's voice records the field labour, weather, birds, and customs of an enclosed midland parish. The month-pieces are followed by village stories and shorter poems. The book is the most sustained attempt in English verse to write the working year itself as a form.
works.plot: Each month presents the tasks pressed upon the labourer at that season, the state of the sky and fields, and the sounds of birds and insects, with an underplot of the shepherd's solitary attendance on the flock. The speaker contrasts the paid day-work of the modern parish with the remembered commons and festivals of his childhood, and moralises on dependence, poverty, and the small economies of the hedge-side. The village stories and accompanying poems extend the same method to incidents of local narrative and to portraits of labouring figures.
works.significance: The work is regarded now as the author's most original achievement, a labouring almanac that anticipates later phenomenologies of seasonal time and that differs from Lake-poet meditation by making paid agricultural work, not retreat, its organising fact. Its publishing history also illustrates how much of the labouring poet's copy was shaped by commercial truncation.
works.meter: The month-pieces run mainly in closed accentual iambic couplets grouped into short stanzas, January for example in tetrameter couplets of six lines, with pentameter and lyric passages among the accompanying village stories; the verse is dense with field, weather, and bird names and avoids rhetorical closure.
works.context: Published after the author's marriage and settlement as an under-gardener in a great park, when his first fame had cooled and his books sold poorly; the volume is dedicated by permission to a noble patron whose family administered the borough and the annuity that supported him. The printed text is shorter than the manuscript, a reduction the author attributed to the publisher's economy.
works.characters: the shepherd-speaker; the flock and its dog; the thatcher, hedge-wright, and day-labourers of the parish; the birds whose note marks each month
works.structure: A cyclical sequence of twelve month-poems in calendar order, without a continuous plot; the unity is the year and the labouring routine, reinforced by framing references to the shepherd's attendance. Later volumes and modern editions restore passages the author complained had been cut by his publishers.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the publisher's abridgement of the manuscript affects length, not authorship.

editions.title: The Early Poems of John Clare, 1804-1822 (2 volumes)

works.title: The Shepherd's Week
altTitles: The Shepherd's Week, in Seven Days
works.description: Gay's burlesque pastoral of the seven days of a labouring week, in which the lovelorn swains of the conventional eclogue are replaced by clowns, ale, the wake, the farthing spit and the spilling of the dish of milk.
works.plot: Pastoral courtship, complaint and banquet are enacted by village swains in their real occupations, and the week closes with the plainest of love matches; the ancient machinery and the fine phrases of the eclogue are retained only to be laughed at.
works.significance: It broke the genteel pastoral and opened the way for the rustic and labouring representation of country life that the later century inherited, and it supplied the burlesque method Gay himself carried to the stage a dozen years later.
works.meter: Varied stanzaic imitation of the old pastoral and of Spenser, in short lines and plain diction, with the deliberate bathos of the closing couplet.
works.context: Published in the year of the quarrel over pastoral diction, when Pope's Pastorals and Philips's own eclogues had made the representation of real shepherds a critical issue; the volume's prose preface and notes are part of the same argument.
works.characters: the clowns and shepherd swains of the week; the shepherdesses of the courtship plots
works.structure: Seven day-poems, each on one pastoral action, with the introductory preface and the explanatory notes defending the low imitation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Ship of Fools
altTitles: The Shyp of Folys of the Worlde
works.description: Barclay's Englishing of Sebastian Brant's Narrenschiff through Locher's Latin version: a fleet of fools — the bookish fool, the covetous, the gluttonous, the lecherous clergy, the negligent bishops — each shipped aboard the vessel of folly in a comprehensive satire of the estates, printed by Richard Pynson in 1509.
works.plot: The narrator gathers the fools of every estate aboard the Ship of Fools; chapter by chapter, each folly is exhibited and moralized, from the pride of scholars to the corruption of Rome.
works.significance: The channel by which the great European estates satire reached England; its catalogue form and its moralizing woodcuts shaped a century of English satirical writing.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of fluent competence; the moralized catalogue form of the continental Renaissance satire.
works.context: Translated in the years before the Reformation, when anticlerical satire was already a licensed genre; printed by Pynson in December 1509.
works.characters: the narrator; the fools (by estate and vice)
works.structure: A catalogue satire in over a hundred sections, each an emblem of a folly with its moral appended; the ship provides the unifying frame.
works.attributionNotes: Barclay's adaptation of Brant (via Locher) is freely made with English additions; recorded as translation-adaptation.

works.title: The Shoemaker's Holiday
works.description: Dekker's comedy of London's craftsmen: the shoemaker Simon Eyre rises from journeyman to Lord Mayor of London, his shop becomes the scene of the play's feasts and jests, and the love-plot of the disguised nobleman Lacy ('Hans the shoemaker') and the Lord Mayor's daughter Rose runs to its happy ending — the play ending with Eyre's feast for all the 'prentices of London and the king's own visit to the shop.
works.plot: Lacy, nephew of the Earl of Lincoln, refuses the arranged marriage and disguises himself as a Dutch shoemaker to serve Eyre and woo Rose; Eyre's fortunes rise through a lucky cargo to the mayoralty; the lovers are discovered and the earl's opposition overcome; and the Shrove Tuesday feast crowns the comedy with the king's blessing on the gentle craft.
works.significance: The classic of the citizen comedy — the play that gave the London trades their theatre, and the ancestor of the sentimental comedy of the next centuries.
works.meter: Prose and blank verse in Dekker's warmest register, with the shoemakers' songs and the feast scenes as its set pieces.
works.context: Performed by the Admiral's Men in 1599 and printed in 1600; its craftsmen's holiday and its king's visit celebrated the civic culture of London on the eve of the century's turn.
works.characters: Simon Eyre; Margery Eyre; Lacy (Hans); Rose Oatley; Sir Roger Oatley; the Earl of Lincoln; Firk; Hodge; Ralph Damport; Jane; Hammon; the King
works.structure: A five-act citizen comedy in the romantic mode, with the shop as its centre and the rise of Eyre as its civic plot.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Shoemaker's Holiday (Revels Plays)
editions.editor: R. L. Smallwood and Stanley Wells (eds.)

works.title: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
altTitles: The Shortest Way with the Dissenters: Or, Proposals for the Establishment of the Church
works.description: A pamphlet written in the voice of a high-flown Church extremist, proposing that the only safe way with the Dissenters is to repeat the severity of the Counter-Reformation and destroy them root and branch. Its ironical impersonation was widely missed, and its writer was pursued for it some years later.
works.plot: A mock-moderate opening complains that the Church has been tamely forbearing, then argues that the sectaries are the real enemies of the constitution and of the settled clergy. It draws the analogy with popery, demands the closing of the meeting-places and the disabling of dissenters from trade and office, and concludes that if the laws will not do the work the people must burn them out. The appended defence explains the design as satire against the extremists of both sides.
works.significance: It is the classical instance of impersonative satire failing and succeeding simultaneously, the mask worn so exactly that it provoked the prosecution it was designed to discredit, and a case study in the law of seditious libel.
works.meter: Prose of the impassioned party harangue, mimicking the cadences and scriptural tags of the extremist pulpit; the irony is carried by an overwrought syntax of peroration.
works.context: Issued in February 1697/8 in the debate over the standing army, the Triennial Act and the toleration settlement; the writer was arrested in 1703 after a renewed issue, tried for a notorious libel and put in the pillory, an event made memorable in the verse of the day. Recorded here in this installment because it anchors an Augustan career, its date falling on the boundary of the period.
works.characters: the impersonated High Church projector; the dissenting minister; the addressers and the zealots of the Church; the legislator addressed by the pamphlet
works.structure: A short impersonative polemic in a single sustained voice, with a self-explaining apparatus of preface and defence attached at the later issues.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the author both acknowledged and defended the design in the follow-up pamphlets, and the prosecution of 1703 establishes responsibility.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Sidney Psalter
authors: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
works.description: A complete metrical translation of the 150 Psalms: Psalms 1–43 by Sir Philip Sidney, the remainder by his sister Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke, who completed the project after his death — 171 poems in a dazzling variety of stanza forms and meters, the most ambitious poetic translation of the English Renaissance.
works.plot: The psalter follows the biblical sequence, rendering each psalm in a distinct verse form chosen to match its mood — penitential, hymnic, or imprecatory — with Mary Sidney's completion deliberately answering her brother's opening.
works.significance: A landmark of English devotional poetry and of women's literary agency; its formal virtuosity influenced Herbert, Vaughan, and the whole seventeenth-century tradition of sacred verse.
works.meter: An encyclopedia of English verse forms: sonnets, terza rima, sapphics, hexameters, and a vast range of stanza shapes, one per psalm.
works.context: Begun by Sidney in the 1580s, continued by his sister after his death in 1586, and completed about 1599; it circulated in manuscript among the godly aristocracy and was not printed in full until 1823.
works.characters: David (the psalmist); God
works.structure: 150 separate psalm paraphrases arranged in biblical order, with the two translators' portions joined at Psalm 43/44.
works.attributionNotes: The division of the psalms between the two Sidneys is established by the manuscripts and uncontested.

editions.title: The Collected Works of Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
editions.editor: Margaret P. Hannay, Michael G. Brennan, and Mary Ellen Lamb (eds.)

works.title: The Siege of Jerusalem
works.description: An alliterative poem of some 1,300 lines on the Roman destruction of Jerusalem by Vespasian and Titus, cast as vengeance for the crucifixion: the siege, the famine, the fall of the city, and the punishment of the Jews who bought and tortured Christ. A poem of notorious violence whose anti-Judaism reflects the worst of its age, and a major witness to the romance of Christian vengeance.
works.plot: Titus, healed by the vernicle, vows vengeance on the Jews; the poem narrates the siege and its horrors — the famine, the mother who eats her child, the crucifixions and selling of Jews — and the city's destruction, framed throughout as the working out of Christ's blood-debt.
works.significance: The most widely copied alliterative poem of its theme and a text of central importance — and difficulty — for the study of medieval Christian anti-Judaism in literature.
works.meter: Alliterative long lines in couplets and stanzaic clusters.
works.context: Composed c. 1390 in the north-west Midlands, from the French Vengeance de Nostre Seigneur and related sources; preserved in nine manuscripts, including the Thornton manuscript and Bodleian Laud Misc. 656.
works.characters: Vespasian; Titus; Pilate; Josephus; Caiaphas
works.structure: A single-movement siege narrative built from the French Vengeance tradition, with the torments of the Jews as its repeated set-pieces.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
sources: The Poetical Works of Thomas Moore

works.title: The Siege of Rhodes
altTitles: The Siege of Rhodes, Made a Representation by the Art of Prospective in Scenes
works.description: Davenant's 'representation by the art of prospective in scenes, and the story sung in recitative music', staged at his house in Rutland during the Commonwealth; it is generally regarded as the first English opera.
works.plot: The Ottoman siege of Rhodes in 1522 is the historical frame; the love story of Alphonso, Ianthe, and Roxolana unfolds across five 'entries' (acts) of sung recitative and spectacular scenery.
works.significance: The first English opera, the first English stage to use painted perspective scenery, the first to employ a professional actress, and the prototype of the Restoration heroic drama.
works.meter: Recitative verse in pentameter couplets and quatrains; the first sustained use of sung drama in English.
works.context: Performed privately at Rutland House in May 1656 and publicly at the Cockpit in 1659, during the Commonwealth ban on public theatres; Davenant's innovations were tolerated because the work was billed as a musical entertainment.
works.characters: Solyman; Alphonso; Ianthe; Roxolana; Mustapha; the Admiral
works.structure: Five entries performed in painted perspective scenes with continuous recitative singing, no spoken dialogue, and a single female performer (Mrs Coleman).
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Davenant; the music was by Matthew Locke, Henry Cooke, Charles Coleman, and George Hudson.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Siege of Thebes
works.form: verse narrative in couplets (framed as Canterbury tale)
works.description: John Lydgate's continuation of the Canterbury Tales (c. 1420–22), presented as the monk of Bury's own tale on the return journey from Canterbury: the story of Thebes from the founding of the city by Cadmus through the tragedy of Oedipus, the war of the Seven, and the deaths of the Theban and Argive heroes. Its frame makes it the first great poem of the Chaucerian succession.
works.plot: Joining the pilgrims at Canterbury, Lydgate's monk tells the Theban story: Oedipus's parricide and incest, the quarrel of his sons Eteocles and Polynices, the expedition of the Seven against Thebes, the duel of the brothers, and the funeral of the heroes — a chain of fortune's falls moralized throughout.
works.significance: The first great act of Chaucerian imitation: by writing himself into the pilgrimage, Lydgate claimed Chaucer's mantle and set the pattern for the fifteenth-century canon of English poetry.
works.meter: Decasyllabic couplets in the Lydgate manner.
works.context: Composed c. 1420–22, in direct response to Chaucer's Knight's Tale (the Theban matter of its background), and copied with the Canterbury Tales in many manuscripts; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1497).
works.characters: the Monk of Bury (narrator); Oedipus; Eteocles; Polynices; Tydeus; Adrastus; Creon
works.structure: A Chaucerian frame (the return-journey tale) enclosing the three-part Theban narrative, with the 'tragedy' of Fortune as its moral armature.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure.
sources: The Whole Disgraceful Truth: Selected Letters of Lady Caroline Lamb

works.title: The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.
works.form: Sketch and character-tale series with familiar essays and legendary romance; the prose tale of the supernatural is folded into essayistic framing
works.description: A series of essays, sketches and legends by a persona who looks at England and at old New York with the same tender irony. It contains the two tales that became national property, a village schoolmaster and a sleeper who wakes a generation later, together with essays on Christmas, on the antiquities of the Inns of Court and on Westminster Abbey. The volume made the American sketch a transatlantic form.
works.plot: The opening English papers, written in the voice of a retired essayist, meditate on lost friendships, on village churches and on the ceremony of old hospitality. The German and Dutch legends transpose European folk material into American settings: a sleepy hunter returns to find his world changed, and a nervous schoolmaster is undone by a headless horseman. Later English papers describe abbey, gallery and coach-roads as places where the past can still be felt. The concluding letters from an English visitor to his friends at home comment on theatre, society and the scenery of the British countryside.
works.significance: It established the literary sketch in America and made the short tale of willed belief a native form. Its two legends entered the schoolroom and the stage, becoming the most widely read American fiction before 1850. Its transatlantic double publication reshaped the terms of the exchange between American and British letters.
works.meter: Prose, with a few verse addresses and songs in familiar stanzaic metres
works.context: Written partly in England and published simultaneously in New York and London between 1819 and 1820, at a moment when American writers were still dependent on British publishing and British approval. Its English subject-matter answers the claim that the young nation had no picturesque past. Its Dutch-New-York legends were devised to give America an inherited legend of its own.
works.characters: Geoffrey Crayon; Rip Van Winkle; Ichabod Crane; Brom Bones; the headless horseman
works.structure: Loose miscellany of some three dozen papers under a unifying persona, with two internal sequences distinguished by setting: English essays and American or German legends.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; published under the persona rather than the author's own name, with the author identified in the advertisements.

editions.publisher: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press

editions.title: The Complete Works of Washington Irving (30 volumes)
editions.editor: Henry A. Pochmann, Herbert L. Kleinfield and Richard D. Rust (general editors)

works.title: The Solitary Reaper
works.form: Nature lyric and song, a lyrical ballad of the later and smoother manner; the poem thematises the relation between untranslated speech, music and memory, and is built as an illustration of the poet's own definition of composition.
works.description: A short lyric of four stanzas, suggested by a scene witnessed during a tour of the Highlands and written in November 1805, in which a peasant girl reaps and sings at the same time in a language the listening speaker cannot understand. The poem's force lies in the withheld meaning: because the sense of the song is unavailable, the speaker invents possible subjects for it, and then surrenders the guess to the sound itself. He carries that sound away as a possession of memory, and the lyric becomes one of the period's plainest demonstrations of what its own theory of recollection claimed for poetry.
works.plot: The speaker tells the valley to be still for one girl's song and watches her single in the field, reaping and singing at once. Since he cannot know what she sings, he asks whether it is some natural sorrow, loss or pain that may be and may be again, or an old, sad and forgotten story of battles long ago, and declares that no nightingale in the forests of the Arabian sand, nor cuckoo-bird in the farthest Hebrides, could have broken the silence of the seas with a happier measure. The girl turns to her labour and the song continues while she binds the sheaves, and the speaker listens motionless until the music stops. In the last stanza he reports that when he had seen and heard no more of it, the music was in his heart and was felt long after it was heard no more, as he lay on a couch in solitude or on a vacant pensive mood - that is, the song is recovered only in memory, and the poem records that recovery.
works.significance: The period's shortest and most quoted illustration of its account of poetry: an uncomprehended sound made permanent by memory, and a demonstration that Romantic lyric can take its subject from a failure of understanding. It was widely imitated and translated in the nineteenth century and remains a standard test case for discussions of lyric address and of the autonomous song.
works.meter: Four quatrains alternating four-beat and three-beat iambic lines with a rhyme scheme that gives the poem an unmistakable song-like regularity; the imperative openings and the repeated question give it the pattern of an air, deliberately unlike the broken stanzaic manner of the 1798 ballads.
works.context: Suggested by an incident on the tour of Scotland taken with his sister in 1803 and composed in November 1805, in the years in which the short lyrics of the 1807 collection were being gathered and the philosophy of the growing mind was being worked out in the long autobiographical poem. The scene of an English listener before a Gaelic song answers the period's vogue for Highland song and its collections of translated airs.
works.characters: The solitary Highland reaper; the travelling listener who remembers her song
works.structure: An occasional lyric moving through a single scene: apostrophe to the landscape, description, a speculative question about the song's meaning, and a retrospective stanza of remembrance, in which the interval between hearing and recalling constitutes the argument.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the author's own note identifies the scene as heard among a solitary Highland valley, and no rival claim has been made.

works.title: The Sophy
works.description: Denham's tragedy, performed and printed in 1642, set at the Persian court of Shah Abbas, in which court intrigue, jealousy, and the machinations of a favourite lead to the death of the prince and a catastrophe of political and personal ruin.
works.plot: At the court of the Sophy (Shah of Persia), envy and intrigue surround the young prince, and the machinations of courtiers bring about his death and the ruin of those who loved him, illustrating the dangers of tyranny and favour.
works.significance: A representative Caroline tragedy of exotic setting and political morality, notable as the dramatic work of the author of Cooper's Hill.
works.meter: Blank verse in a grave, sententious, neoclassical manner.
works.context: Performed in 1642 just before the theatres closed; Waller praised it and it was Denham's early bid for dramatic fame.
works.characters: the Sophy (Shah Abbas); the Prince; Mirza; the courtiers
works.structure: A five-act neoclassical tragedy in blank verse with an exotic Persian setting.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Sorrows of Rosalie: A Tale, with Other Poems
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Literary Annual and Keepsake Verse
works.description: The first volume of a young married woman poet, published in 1829 and containing a long narrative tale of a seduced and abandoned girl together with lyric pieces, translations from the Spanish, and a rendering of the cow-herd's song. The volume announced a feminine Byronic manner, and it was praised in a leading Scottish periodical in the years when that review shaped Romantic taste. Its title poem made the author's reputation and started a connection with the annual and gift-book market that became her livelihood.
works.plot: Rosalie, a poor and beautiful peasant girl, is won and deserted by a man of rank; the poem follows her from the first flattering attention to the loss of her child, the public shame of the village, and the death of her hopes, with the lover's return insufficient to repair what has been done. The tale is told in a continuous meditative address to the sufferer, and the surrounding pieces give the same situation in shorter form, including a fragment on Elvira, the young crusader, Linda Albaya, and the lyric The One you loved the best. Translations and imitations from the Spanish supply the volume's secondary music.
works.significance: The volume is a key document of the woman poet's appropriation of the Byronic tale of outcast guilt for the specifically feminine subject of seduction and deserted motherhood. It established the author as a professional contributor to the annuals and anticipated the protest against the legal disability of married mothers that she later conducted in prose and in the press.
works.meter: The tale runs in measured rhymed stanzas of the popular sentimental line, with frequent apostrophe and refrain; the lyrics use common measure and the song translations keep the stave and burden of the original Spanish and Provençal forms.
works.context: Published in 1829 by a London house then supplying the fashionable annuals, dedicated to a noble patron of letters, at the moment when the gift-book economy was creating paid work for women writers. The author's own position, a marriage already known to be unhappy and a separation shortly to produce a public legal struggle over the custody of a child, gave the seduction subject its biographical edge for later readers.
works.characters: Rosalie; the lover of higher rank who deserts her; her child; the villagers who witness her shame; Elvira; Linda Albaya
works.structure: A single long narrative poem of seduction and death, framed by a section of shorter lyrics and translations, with no organising frame across the volume; the tale moves by stages of feeling rather than by incident.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the volume carries the author's name on the title page and no piece in it has been reassigned.

works.title: The South English Legendary
works.description: The earliest great collection of verse saints' lives in Middle English, compiled in the south-west (probably Gloucestershire) c. 1270–85: a cycle of some 300 poems following the church year, from St Michael through the apostles and martyrs to All Souls. Its rollicking couplets and marvel-filled narratives made it the most popular legendary in medieval England.
works.plot: Each entry narrates a saint's life, martyrdom, or feast — with dragons, tortures, and miracles — and draws the moral for the hearers; the collection includes the famous account of St Brendan's voyage and lives of English saints such as Thomas Becket.
works.significance: The foundational text of popular English hagiography and a principal source for Mirk's Festial and the later legendary tradition.
works.meter: Septenary (fourteener) couplets, loose and lively, designed for public reading.
works.context: Compiled in the 1270s–1280s in the diocese of Worcester or Hereford, for parish and household reading; copied and expanded in some sixty manuscripts into the fifteenth century.
works.characters: the saints of the calendar (Thomas Becket, Brendan, Edmund, Cecilia, and many others)
works.structure: A calendrical cycle of independent verse legends, ordered by the liturgical year, in a frame of prologue and epilogue.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; compilational authorship by one or more clerical redactors.
sources: The Poems of Charlotte Smith

works.title: The Spanish Tragedy
works.description: Kyd's revenge tragedy, the most popular play of its generation: the ghost of Don Andrea and the personified Revenge watch from above as Hieronimo, Knight Marshal of Spain, discovers that his son Horatio has been murdered by the prince Balthazar and Lorenzo, and — after his wife Isabella's suicide — avenges him by staging a play in which the murderers die, biting out his own tongue before stabbing himself.
works.plot: Andrea's ghost, slain in battle by Balthazar, returns with Revenge to see justice done; Horatio is hanged in the arbour by Balthazar and Lorenzo; Hieronimo's madness, his laments, and the discovery of the murderers fill the middle acts; the play-within-the-play 'Soliman and Perseda' becomes the engine of revenge, and the survivors' blood ends the tragedy.
works.significance: The fountainhead of Elizabethan revenge tragedy — the play that taught the English stage the ghost, the delay, and the play-within-the-play.
works.meter: Blank verse of strong rhetorical set pieces — Hieronimo's laments and the additions of 1602 (probably by Jonson) — with the famous 'in a word' tableaux.
works.context: Performed from about 1587 and printed in 1592; revived with additions in 1602; it established the revenge formula that Hamlet, Titus Andronicus, and the Jacobean revenge school all answer.
works.characters: Hieronimo; Bel-Imperia; Horatio; Lorenzo; Balthazar; Isabella; the Ghost of Andrea; Revenge; Pedringano; Serberine; the Viceroy of Portugal
works.structure: A revenge tragedy framed by the choric ghost-and-Revenge, built on the discovery-and-delay pattern, and climaxing in the play within the play.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Sparagus Garden
works.description: Brome's comedy of London society set in the fashionable asparagus gardens of Lambeth Marsh, in which two country women come to London to better themselves and are drawn into the intrigues of the city and the garden.
works.plot: Martha and Rebecca travel to London; Martha is seduced into a false marriage by the gallant Touchwood, Rebecca is courted by the honest Striker; the Sparagus Garden provides the social arena where the deceptions are exposed.
works.significance: One of the sharpest Caroline comedies of urban topography and social mobility, and Brome's fullest treatment of the theme of the country woman in the city.
works.meter: Prose dominant with verse.
works.context: Performed at the Salisbury Court Theatre in 1635 and published in 1640; the Lambeth Marsh asparagus gardens were a notorious resort of fashionable London.
works.characters: Martha; Rebecca; Touchwood; Striker; Annabel; Samuel; Lady Annabel; Snoop; the Host
works.structure: Five acts with a strong topographical unity around the garden.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Brome; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Spectator and Tatler Papers (Addison)
works.description: Addison's contribution to the daily and weekly essay papers he conducted with Steele: the club and character papers, the imagination essays, the Milton criticism, the pastoral series and the oriental tales, which together made the polite essay the century's instrument of everyday moral judgment.
works.plot: Mr. Spectator, who has resolved neither to laugh nor to be serious, presents himself and the club of which he is the silent censor, then reports the speeches, projects and follies of its members and of the citizens, families and readers whose letters arrive at his desk.
works.significance: Addison's papers gave English prose its most widely taught model, invented the character-based periodical essay, and with the imagination and Milton essays installed a criticism of taste and genius inside neoclassical rules.
works.meter: Prose in the balanced middle style Addison theorised, with periodic sentences, tagged couplet quotations from the poets, and the rhythmically clause-balanced close; the papers on verse discuss the couplet and blank verse explicitly.
works.context: The daily Spectator ran from March 1711 to December 1712 and was revived weekly in 1714, exploiting coffee-house and tea-table reading, the provincial postal network and the lapse of the licensing Act; the Addison-Steele partnership divided the papers unevenly and ended in public coolness.
works.characters: Mr. Spectator; Sir Roger de Coverley; Sir Andrew Freeport; Will Honeycomb; Captain Sentry; the club of the Spectator; the letter-writing public
works.structure: A serial miscellany of short unsigned-to-signed papers, framed by a recurring persona and an intermittently advancing club narrative, with inset tales, letters to the editor and critical dissertations.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative by formation: the papers were produced by Addison and Steele together, with contributions from Hughes, Berkeley, Miss Manley and others; individual ascriptions in the early numbers remain partly conjectural, and this record covers the Addisonian share.

works.title: The Spirit of Prayer
altTitles: The Spirit of Prayer, or the Soul rising out of the Vanity of Time
The Spirit of Prayer in Three Parts
works.description: Law's mystical treatise on prayer as the breath of the inward soul, opposing the formal 'prayers of the mouth' to the ceaseless spirit of devotion. Part I appeared in 1733 and Parts II and III followed in 1734, extending the argument into a theology of the believer's constant intercourse with God.
works.plot: Law argues that the Christian life is essentially a spirit and disposition, of which vocal prayers are only the shell; true prayer is the soul's ascending sense of dependence and love. He shows from Scripture and the Lord's Prayer why a form of words is nothing without the wants, humours, and temper it expresses. The later parts work out the practice: the universal, unceasing offering of common life, prayer as the soul rising out of the vanity of time into eternity, and the believer's participation in the intercession of Christ. Formal religion and the love of the world are thus exposed as the same failure of spirit.
works.significance: It transmitted the language of seventeenth-century mysticism into eighteenth-century popular devotion and shaped, among others, the inward-prayer tradition that Methodism and the Oxford Movement both inherited.
works.meter: Incantatory, paratactic prose of long accumulating sentences, borrowing the rhythms of law and the Psalms; the argument advances almost by cadence.
works.context: Written after Law's secession from the Hanoverian establishment and under the influence of his reading of Jacob Boehme and the German mystical tradition, and published in 1733-34 when the blasphemy and Convocation controversies made inward religion a polemical subject.
works.structure: Three progressive parts, each a devotional argument from Scripture followed by practical direction and spiritual anatomy.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Spirit of the Age
altTitles: The Spirit of the Age; or, Contemporary Portraits
works.form: Familiar essay and character sketch in the revived Theophrastan manner, combined with critical review and political character-writing.
works.description: A series of contemporary portraits published in 1825 and usually taken to be its author's best book, which gives the name of the age to a collection of critical and political characters. Its plan is to read the mind of the time through a series of individuals, poets, essayists, critics, advocates, statesmen and men of science and of the church, each essay treating its subject as the exponent of a habit of mind rather than as a private person. The book is at once the most acute record of English literature in the 1820s and a specimen of the character-writing revived by the Romantic essayists.
works.plot: The preface argues that a great age of literature may be recognised by its dominant habits of mind, and that the present is an age of discussion, of personality and of transition. The portraits of the poets of the northern lakes, of the poet of abstraction and of the writer of romantic tales are drawn so as to show a poetry of feeling and a poetry of ideas parted from the passion of the public, and the younger and more revolutionary singers are placed under the head of a poetry of motion and of hope. The men of the bar, of the banks, of the church and of the great quarterly journal are given as the characters of an age of enquiry and of party, and the closing papers pass from letters to the arts, with the portrait of the first actor of the London stage and of the one great living painter. Through the whole series the argument is that the age is divided between the spirit of party and the love of the ideal, and that the truest criticism reports the mind of its writer with the same sympathy with which the dramatist reported the minds of his characters.
works.significance: The most quoted book of contemporary portraits in English and the standard account of the literary and intellectual temper of the 1820s, from which most later histories of the period still take their phrases for its poets and its critics. Its method of treating a living writer as the exponent of a habit of mind became the model of the character essay, and its sentences on poetry and on the age are a permanent part of the vocabulary of criticism.
works.meter: Prose of the author's most concentrated kind, built of balanced antithesis, of the short sentence of verdict and of the long period of accumulation, with a constant use of the epigrammatic turn and of the summarising clause.
works.context: Published in London in 1825, several of the papers having appeared during the two preceding years in the magazines, in a season of intellectual and political expectation before the changes in the representation and in the press that followed; the author's own fortunes were at their lowest point, and the portraits of living writers were read as the criticism of a rival and a former friend.
works.characters: The living writers, critics, pleaders, bankers, statesmen and men of the church and of the stage whose portraits make the series; the essayist himself, who comments on the temper of his own age and on the trade of the literary profession
works.structure: A series of some twenty-four independent character-essays, with a general preface on the age and no continuous argument; the unity is that of the method, each paper taking one public figure as the exponent of a habit of mind, and the order being loosely arranged by the divisions of letters, of public affairs and of the arts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; a second series of portraits, contributed to another journal, appeared some years later and is printed separately in the collected editions.

works.title: The Spleen
works.description: Anne Finch's Pindaric ode on melancholy, depression, and the 'spleen' — a condition she herself suffered — which explores its physical, psychological, and gendered dimensions and defends the imagination and poetry against its deadening effects.
works.plot: The ode describes the many forms and causes of the spleen (vapours, grief, the body's disorder), its particular burden on women, and the consolation of friendship, verse, and faith.
works.significance: An important early poem on depression and on the woman writer's condition, admired for its candour and its Pindaric form, and central to Finch's recovered reputation.
works.meter: The irregular Pindaric form on Cowley's model, with varied and expressive line lengths.
works.context: Written in the 1690s and printed in a 1701 miscellany (attributed to 'Ardelia'); it reflects Finch's own lifelong depression and the period's discourse on the spleen and melancholy.
works.characters: the poet; the Spleen (personified)
works.structure: A Pindaric ode in varied line lengths and stanzas, moving through description, lament, and consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Published under Finch's pastoral name 'Ardelia'; attribution uncontested.

works.title: The Spy
altTitles: The Spy: A Tale of the Neutral Ground
works.form: Historical novel and romance of the Revolutionary war, with picaresque disguise plot and topographical description
works.description: The first important American historical novel and the book that created a native romance of the Revolution. Set in the neutral ground between the British lines and the American army in Westchester County, it makes espionage, disguise and neighbour-against-neighbour violence the substance of national history. Its pedlar of small wares, who turns out to be a spy of many identities, is the founding American figure of the disguised hero.
works.plot: In the neutral ground of Westchester County, between the British lines in New York and the American army, the daughters of a Loyalist colonel are repeatedly thrown into the power of British officers, partisan leaders and the lawless skinners who infest the border. A pedlar of small wares, treated by both sides now as a simpleton and now as a knave, carries intelligence for the American command under a studied disguise. Hospitality, neutrality and betrayal alternate in a country where neighbour hunts neighbour, and where an old Whig widow's house becomes a refuge. The novel closes with the condemnation of a British officer taken as a spy and with the disclosure of the pedlar's real service to the American cause.
works.significance: It gave American fiction its first historical romance and its first national hero of concealment. Its neutral ground became the model for the American frontier as a moral borderland. It made the historical novel the dominant American narrative form for a generation.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1821-1822 from Westchester tradition, the author's childhood recollections and the histories of the war then current. It appeared in the same season as the Scottish historical romance and adapted its methods to republican material. Its treatment of Tory persecution reflects the nationalist reconciliation of the 1820s.
works.characters: Harvey Birch the pedlar; Colonel Wharton; the Wharton sisters; Sarah the young Quaker; Kirkwood the deserter
works.structure: Third-person historical novel with a choric neutral community at its centre; the plot of espionage is delayed by disguises and revealed at the close, in the manner of a discovered identity romance.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the author later added a preface and notes defending his use of documentary sources.

works.title: The Squire of Alsatia
works.description: Shadwell's late comedy, set in the Whitefriars district known as Alsatia, a sanctuary for debtors and criminals, in which the innocent young Belfond senior is corrupted by the cheats of the place.
works.plot: Two brothers are raised in strict ignorance by their father; the elder is taken into Alsatia and ruined by its rogues, while the younger, Shamwell, survives; the plot exposes a whole gallery of swindlers.
works.significance: Shadwell's most ambitious late comedy and his fullest study of London criminal topography; 'Alsatia' entered the language as a word for a lawless district.
works.meter: Prose dominant.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1688, shortly before the Revolution; Shadwell was Poet Laureate and Historiographer Royal from 1689 until his death in 1692.
works.characters: Belfond senior; Belfond junior (Shamwell); Sir William Belfond; Cheatly; Captain Teresia; Abraham Cow; Mrs Termagant; Laure
works.structure: Five acts with a strongly topographical Jonsonian comic method.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shadwell; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Staple of News
works.description: Ben Jonson's late satirical comedy on the new business of news-gathering, in which a 'Staple of News' is established to supply the gulls of London with fabricated intelligence and young Pecunia is courted by fortune hunters.
works.plot: Thomas Barber opens an office that manufactures news for the town; the young heir Pennyboy junior squanders his fortune chasing novelty; the Censure and Prologue figures comment throughout, and the play ends with the Staple's collapse.
works.significance: Jonson's most explicit commentary on the new print culture and journalism, and an important document in the history of the news; it was long considered one of his weaker late plays.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in February 1626 and published in the first folio of Jonson's works in 1631; it attacks the newly emerging news-sheet industry.
works.characters: Thomas Barber; Pennyboy junior; Pennyboy senior; Pecunia junior; the Censure; the Prologue; the Register; Fitton
works.structure: Five acts with intermeans in which a Censure and a Prologue debate the play's own merits.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Jonson; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Steel Glass
works.description: Gascoigne's satirical mirror poem: renouncing the flattering crystal of courtly verse, the poet holds up the 'steel glass' of truth to every estate — kings, knights, clergy, lawyers, merchants, and ploughmen — in the first original English poem in blank verse, its plain style answering its plain purpose.
works.plot: The poet's glass shows each estate its vices: the king's flatterers, the soldier's greed, the lawyer's delays, the merchant's falsehood, and the farmer's honest toil praised last and most; the poem ends with the satirist's defence of his plain dealing and his glass's unflattering truth.
works.significance: The first original blank-verse poem in English and the bridge between medieval estates satire and Elizabethan satire proper.
works.meter: Blank verse — the first original English poem in the form — in the plain style its argument demands.
works.context: Published in 1576, in Gascoigne's final year, with the woodcut frontispiece of the author; it answered the court's demand for moral counsel in the decade of the Northern Rebellion's aftermath.
works.characters: the poet; the estates personified (kings, knights, clergy, lawyers, merchants, ploughmen)
works.structure: A single continuous satire in the estates tradition, ordered by rank from court to country, with the glass as its governing emblem.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Story of Rimini: A Poem
works.form: A narrative or romantic poem in the market for Italian tale-in-verse that Byron's tales had made profitable, but deliberately turned against that fashion's declamation. It is a story poem of ordinary feeling rather than a romance of adventure: no marvels, no contests, no supernatural machinery except the closing Dantean scene. The conventions it works with are those of the colloquial romantic narrative, and its form is that of a plain recital, closer in spirit to a novel reduced to verse than to the epics its reviewers expected of heroic couplets.
works.description: Hunt's only sustained verse narrative, a romantic tale in rhymed couplets that retells and sympathetically modernises the episode of Paolo and Francesca which Dante set in the second circle of Hell in Inferno V. Where Dante judges the lovers, Hunt dwells on the ill-matched marriage, the slow growth of the attachment and the force of circumstance, treating his subject as human rather than exemplary. Published in 1816 and dedicated to Byron, it was the book that brought the full force of the sectional reviewing of the period down on its author, and it remains the central document of what his enemies called the Cockney school of poetry. Its colloquial diction, its homely domestic detail and its insistence that tenderness could be the matter of a serious poem made it a byword and a battleground in Romantic literary politics.
works.plot: The poem takes from Dante its situation and its persons: Francesca, given in marriage to the lord of Rimini for reasons of policy and not of affection, finds in his brother Paolo the companion her marriage has denied her. Hunt builds his argument not on the crime but on the slow preparation for it, on the dulness of the husband, the loneliness of the wife and the civilities of the court in which their friendship grows. The lovers are at last surprised together and slain, and the poem closes on the fate that Dante assigned to them, the pair still bound in the love that was their condemnation. Throughout, Hunt keeps the reader's sympathy with the actors rather than with the moralist, and treats the famous reading of the tale of Lancelot as the decisive incident in two ordinary lives.
works.significance: The Story of Rimini is the fullest statement of Hunt's belief that poetry should be written in the language of felt experience and that a subject once judged damnable might be rendered entirely in terms of human tenderness. It gave the Romantic period its clearest instance of criticism as personal and sectional war, and it helped define the party lines of Regency verse, with the Lakers, the Edinburgh reviewers and the Cockney school each defining themselves against the others. Later readers have valued it as a link between Byron's Italian tales and the sensual narrative impulse of Keats, and as proof that Hunt's theory of familiar verse could carry a subject of real weight.
works.meter: Heroic couplets: rhymed pairs of decasyllabic iambic lines, the ordinary English verse of narrative and of polite speech since Pope, and here used with a studied ease and a run-on syntax that many contemporary reviewers thought a violation of the form. Hunt's couplets are continually enjambed, their diction familiar and their imagery domestic, so that the closed mechanical pair becomes the vehicle of a flowing uncourtly narrative voice. The prosody was the poem's most contested feature: its defenders heard naturalness, its attackers heard the absence of verse at all.
works.context: The poem appeared in the first peace years, when Hunt had just left prison for the sedition committed in the Examiner, when Byron was in exile and when the Edinburgh and Quarterly reviewers were policing the limits of English verse. Its subject belonged to the early nineteenth-century revival of interest in Dante and in Italian story, and its politics belonged to Hunt's liberal London circle, which included Shelley, Keats and Hazlitt. The attacks that followed it in the Edinburgh and Quarterlies, personal as much as literary, were part of the same campaign that degraded Hunt's verse as a Cockney product and made his nose as famous as his poem.
works.characters: Paolo; Francesca; Francesca's husband, the lord of Rimini
works.structure: A single continuous romantic narrative told in order, without frame, allegory or editorial commentary, and organised by the growth of the relationship rather than by incident. Hunt moves slowly through domestic and conversational scenes, so that the poem's action is mostly psychological: the marriage, the acquaintance, the attachment, the discovery and the killing, followed by the brief infernal closing vision taken from Dante. There are no digressive tales within the tale and no competing plots; the machinery of romance is reduced to the few situations needed to make the readers' sympathy inevitable.
works.attributionNotes: The poem is undisputedly Hunt's and appeared with his name on its title page; no part of it has been claimed for another hand and no serious question of apocryphality attaches to it. Complications are bibliographical rather than attributive: the volume was reissued in revised form, later editions were printed for other publishers, and the text is therefore not identical across its first issues. Its dedication to Byron is on the face of the 1816 volume and has been taken as evidence of the friendship the two poets later fell out over, but it raises no question about who wrote the poem.
