works.title: The Supplication of Souls
works.description: More's defence of purgatory, written as the answer of the souls in purgatory to Simon Fish's Supplication for the Beggars (1529), which had demanded the dissolution of the monasteries and denounced purgatory as a clerical fiction.
works.plot: The souls of the dead speak in their own persons, showing from scripture and reason that purgatory exists, that prayers and masses for the dead avail them, and that those who deny purgatory rob both the dead and the living poor who depend on clerical charity.
works.significance: The most rhetorically inventive of More's early controversial works — using the fiction of the speaking dead — and a key document of the pre-Reformation debate on purgatory and monastic wealth.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed late in 1529 as a direct reply to Fish's Supplication for the Beggars, which Henry VIII is said to have shown to More; the exchange belongs to the parliamentary debates of the Reformation Parliament and the campaign against church wealth.
works.characters: The Souls in Purgatory
works.structure: A continuous oration in two books, framed as a supplication addressed to the king, lords, and commons, with the dead themselves as the petitioners.

works.title: The Tale of Old Mortality
altTitles: Tales of My Landlord, First Series
works.form: Historical novel of religious war and persecution; a tragedy-plot in prose with a framed antiquarian apparatus.
works.description: The first of the Covenanted series, a novel of the Scottish CAMERONIAN persecutions of the 1670s presented as the transcription of an aged tradition-keeper's papers. Its young hero, drawn equally to the disciplined field-preachers of the south-west and to the disciplined cavalry of the Crown, learns that both causes can consume a private conscience. It is the most unsmiling of the series and the one that most openly interrogates fanaticism and its victims.
works.plot: Henry Morton, the son of a deceased Presbyterian minister and a ward of a Jacobite uncle, is apprenticed to a Covenanting elder and becomes entangled in the armed conventions of the south-west. He loves Edith, the sister of the Cavalier Lord Evandale, and is threatened by John Graham of Claverhouse, the dragoon commander who is at once his patron and his enemy; Morton's capture, sentence and reprieve follow the failure of the rising and the murder of Edith's father. Morton finally takes up arms at Bothwell Brig, is condemned, and is saved by an irregular act of the king's soldier, while Evandale falls in the field on the other side. The aged woman of the title, who keeps the memory of the persecuted, supplies the tale's moral register and its material.
works.significance: The period's greatest novel of religious fanaticism and of the violence done in the name of conscience, and the model for later treatments of Scottish covenanting history. Its frame, in which the past is preserved by an old woman and edited by an idler, is a founding statement of the historical novel's theory of evidence. Its portraits of Claverhouse and of the field-preachers entered the permanent debate about the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; Covenanting psalm-tags and field-preaching cadences are quoted and parodied; ballad and psalm verse punctuate the narrative.
works.context: Drawn from the Cameronian records of the Killing Time after the Restoration, from the conventions and the battles of 1679-80, and from the family traditions of the author's South-Lowland childhood. The introduction records the pleasure a nineteenth-century reader took in religious controversy now dead. Its publication completed the transition from ballad editorship to prose fiction that the war years had made profitable.
works.characters: Henry Morton; Edith Balfour; Lord Evandale; John Graham of Claverhouse; the Old Mortality; Cuddie Headrigg
works.structure: Framed fiction: the tale is dug out of the papers of an aged traditionary 'Old Mortality' and transcribed by a fictitious idle country gentleman, introduced in a letter from the parish minister; the interior narrative is third-person, with heavy use of sermon, covenant and examination documents.
works.attributionNotes: Published as by the Author of Waverley, the tale being edited by the fictitious 'Landlord'; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Tales of the O'Hara Family, First Series
altTitles: Tales of the O'Hara Family; by the Author of 'Damon and Pythias'. First Series
works.form: The Sketch and Character Tale; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
works.description: The first series of the national tales of a Kilkenny peasant family, published in 1825 and written in collaboration between two brothers, one of whom supplied the historical and topographical groundwork and both of whom share the narrative voice. The numbers give the cabin, the faction fight, the agrarian combination, and the phantom of the fetch in an Irish speech and at Irish length. The series founded the vogue of the Irish peasant tale and long stood as the standard account of the country people before the Famine.
works.plot: The Fetches tells of the double or phantom seen before a death, of a murdered man whose fetch appears to his kin, and of the country rules by which such an appearance is read, making the supernatural a matter of evidence and of neighbourhood testimony. John Doe; or, The Peep o' Day gives the agrarian war of the secret combinations, the cottier's hatred of the middleman and of the tithe, the midnight burning and the broken contract, and the fate of a family caught in the faction. Crohoore of the Bill-hook follows a woman of the out-lawed countryside who leads the boys in the agrarian rising and is hunted to her end. The series is held together by the O'Hara household and its neighbours, whose talk and genealogy frame the tales.
works.significance: The first series of the O'Hara tales established the Irish peasant narrative as the dominant mode of the 1820s and supplied much of the vocabulary in which the fetch, the combination, and the cottier's grievance were discussed in English. Its collaborative authorship also makes it a standard instance of joint production in the national tale.
works.context: Written in the years after the Act of Union and before the agitation for emancipation reached its crisis, out of the Kilkenny world of the hedge-school, the faction fight, and the agrarian association, and published at the moment when the national tale was the most prestigious form in British fiction. The brothers' earlier training as artists accounts for the series' emphasis on costume, cabin interior, and local scene, and one of them had been a pupil of the national drawing academy.
works.characters: the O'Hara household and its dependants; the murdered man whose fetch is seen; the cottier families of the agrarian combination; Crohoore of the Bill-hook, the woman leader of the boys; the middlemen and the rural police
works.structure: A framed series of independent tales told by and about one family, with a narratorial voice that reports Irish speech and supplies the historical and agrarian explanation inside the story; the series is not a continuous novel.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative: the two brothers share the series, with one of them understood to have written the woman-led agrarian tale and to have supplied the historical and topographical matter; early reviews and later biographies divided the numbers unequally between them.

works.title: The Talisman
works.form: Prose fiction; historical novel and romance of the Crusades
works.description: A romance of the Third Crusade which sets a fanatical and magnanimous English king beside a generous and sceptical Saradin leader, and makes the mutual respect of the two warriors the moral centre of the book. An English knight of disowned Saxon lineage, whose vows and his mistress's commands bring him to the East, serves unknowingly under the very king who despises him, while a talisman of supposed protection becomes the instrument by which reason and tolerance are shown to work. The book is the most deliberate of its author's apologies for civility across the line of faith. It was published with a companion tale of the same period in one series.
works.plot: A Christian knight of an injured Saxon house, bound by his mistress's command to wear a relic and to forbear battle, attaches himself to the English host in Palestine and is taken into the service of the great commander of the opposite faith. The two chiefs meet, are saved and instruct each other, and are brought into conflict by the jealous ambition of the knight's own patron and by an injured lady's suit for protection. The relic proves in the event to be an innocent object whose supposed virtue worked only by the courage and courtesy it taught, and the tale ends with reconciliation between the enemies and the knight's restoration to his mistress and his line.
works.significance: The clearest statement in the series of the romance of toleration and of the exemplary meeting of enemies, and a much-anthologised source for nineteenth-century ideas of chivalry and of the East. Its treatment of a false relic as an instrument of moral teaching makes it a central text for study of the author's handling of superstition and enlightenment.
works.meter: Prose, no metre, with quoted lyric and dramatic epigraphs in ballad and song measures at the head of chapters
works.context: Published in 1825 with a companion tale of the Crusading period, it belongs to the vogue for Crusade romance revived by the antiquaries and by travelled knowledge of the nearer east. Its plea for courtesy across religious difference reflects the liberal moment of the Catholic and civil-relief controversies then in progress in the British parliament, and the book's oriental chivalry draws on the contemporary translation of Arabic history and poetry.
works.characters: The English king of the Crusade host; the great commander of the Saracen camp; Kenneth, a Saxon knight in disguise; the lady of an English house whose suit he defends; an ambitious courtier patron of the hero
works.structure: Third-person romance in three volumes with a continuous single hero's career, framed by chapter epigraphs from older plays and ballads; the argument is carried by set-piece interviews between the two great captains rather than by intrigue.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name now disclosed in the general title of the series; no dispute over authorship.

works.title: The Taming of the Shrew
works.description: Shakespeare's farcical comedy of courtship and domestication: the fortune-hunter Petruchio 'tames' the headstrong Katherine of Padua by a regime of contradiction and deprivation, while her sister Bianca is courted by a crowd of disguised suitors — all framed by the Induction, in which the drunken tinker Christopher Sly is tricked into believing himself a lord for whom the play is performed.
works.plot: Sly is gulled into watching a play: Lucentio disguises himself to woo Bianca, his servant Tranio impersonates him, and Petruchio marries Katherine and breaks her will — or teaches her the game — until she delivers the play's closing speech on wives' obedience, its irony a matter of perennial dispute.
works.significance: Shakespeare's most durable farce, endlessly revived and argued over — a test case for every generation's view of marriage, gender, and power.
works.meter: Mostly prose and doggerel in the farcical scenes, with blank verse for the courtship of Kate and Petruchio.
works.context: Written about 1590–92, in dialogue with the anonymous play The Taming of a Shrew (1594); its debate over wifely subjection has made it the most contested of the comedies in modern performance and criticism.
works.characters: Christopher Sly; Petruchio; Katherine; Bianca; Lucentio; Tranio; Baptista Minola; Grumio; Hortensio; Gremio
works.structure: An Induction framing a two-plot comedy (the Bianca courtship intrigue and the Petruchio–Kate duel), in the manner of Italian commedia-derived farce.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the relation to the anonymous A Shrew remains debated.

works.title: The Task: A Poem
works.form: meditative and didactic long poem in blank verse, in the Thomson-Ossian tradition of the reflective essay-poem
works.description: Cowper's principal poem, a blank-verse meditation in six books that begins as an occasional exercise on a sofa and becomes a survey of retirement, of the times, of the world and of the winter year. Its movement from domestic ease to public prophecy, and its account of the Christian's dependence on providence, made it one of the most read long poems of the last third of the century. It contains the century's most quoted plea for solitary escape and some of its earliest verse protest against the slave trade.
works.plot: Book I excuses the trivial occasion of the poem and commences the praise of soft retirement; Book II, the Time-Piece, moralises the hours of the day and the vanity of fashionable occupations; Book III considers the world and its corruption; Book IV the winter evening with its lamp, its tea and its news; Book V the winter morning walk in the country; and Book VI the winter walk at noon, ending in the wish for a lodge in some vast wilderness and in a religious conclusion on the faith that sustains the solitary soul. Throughout, the poem argues that true happiness is found in dependence on providence rather than in the noise of the age.
works.significance: The Task was a bestseller and the model for a generation of reflective and topographical verse, admired by Wordsworth and the younger romantics for its command of blank verse and its treatment of ordinary domestic life. Its abolitionist passage and its 'time and tide' morality made it a site of both moral and literary authority in the 1790s.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of unusual smoothness and variety, with the famous 'O for a lodge in some vast wilderness' lines in a mixed and more prosaic measure; the couplet is used only occasionally and the sentence-periods are long.
works.context: Written at the Olney and Weston Underwood retirements in 1783-84 on a wager or request that he should make a poem in blank verse on an unfashionable subject, and published in 1785; its reflections on the times respond to the American war's aftermath, to enthusiasm in religion, and to the growth of luxury, commerce and colonial exploitation.
works.characters: The retired poet; the friends and patroness of the Unwin household; the world and its votaries; the personified Times and Solitude
works.structure: A long poem in six books of unequal length, each opening with an address and proceeding by reflection, description and digression; the design is associational, with the winter sequence of the last three books giving the strongest local unity.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Cowper's own letters and memoranda record the commission and the books' composition, and the several revisions of the text across editions are documented in the standard edition.

works.title: The Tatler Papers
works.description: Richard Steele's three-times-weekly paper, conducted under the mask of Isaac Bickerstaff Esq., which turned the newsbook, the coffee-room gossip and the character sketch into a morally reformed periodical and created the English essay paper.
works.plot: Mr. Speculator and his correspondents report the clubs, the play-house, the opera, the town and the country, alternating manners, marriage and duelling stories with party politics and with praise of Addison's Cato and of private virtue.
works.significance: It made periodical moral commentary a profession and a literary form, and its account of the affective, tearful reform of manners prepared sentimental comedy and the novel of character.
works.meter: A looser, more colloquial and syntactically broken style than Addison's, full of ellipsis, exclamation and half-unfinished sentences, which Steele's imitators took for the natural tone of feeling.
works.context: Launched in April 1709 and running to the beginning of 1711, the Tatler exploited the new cheap journalism after the lapse of licensing, the party pressure of the Sacheverell trial years, and Steele's continuing interest in the reformation of the stage.
works.characters: Isaac Bickerstaff Esq.; the Speculator; cousin Jenny; Will Honeycomb; the Whig and Tory clubs; the readers who write to the editor
works.structure: Serial papers distributed among fixed stations of observation (the coffee-house, the theatre, Kit-Cat, the opera, the country), with a lightly advancing fictional biography of the editor and of his correspondents.
works.attributionNotes: Principally Steele's, with a substantial early contribution from Addison and papers from Hughes, Berkeley, Prior and others; the joint numbers are still disputed by bibliographers.

works.title: The Tempest
works.description: Shakespeare's farewell to the stage: Prospero, the deposed Duke of Milan, has raised the storm that wrecks his enemies on his island; with his spirit Ariel and the enslaved Caliban, he conducts the shipwrecked court through the play's ordeals to repentance, wins the betrothal of his daughter Miranda to Ferdinand, breaks his staff, and sails for Milan — 'our revels now are ended'.
works.plot: The tempest delivers Alonso's court to Prospero's island; Ferdinand and Miranda meet and are tested; Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo plot their drunken coup; Ariel's banquet harrows the 'three men of sin'; and the final scene forgives all — with Caliban left to 'seek for grace' and Prospero to drown his book.
works.significance: Shakespeare's valediction — the play that has served every later age as a fable of art, empire, and forgiveness, and the most reinterpreted text in the canon.
works.meter: The late verse at its most musical — Ariel's songs, the masque, the 'cloud-capped towers' speech — with Caliban's prose and the sailors' comedy as counterpoint.
works.context: Performed at court, 1 November 1611, and for the wedding of Princess Elizabeth in 1613; its New World echoes draw on the Virginia pamphlets and the wreck of the Sea Venture (1609).
works.characters: Prospero; Miranda; Ariel; Caliban; Ferdinand; Alonso; Antonio; Sebastian; Gonzalo; Stephano; Trinculo; Sycorax (reported); Juno, Ceres, and Iris (in the masque)
works.structure: The most classical of the plays — a single island, a single day, a masque at its centre — shaped as Prospero's design from storm to pardon.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Tempest; or, The Enchanted Island
altTitles: The Tempest or The Inchanted Island
works.description: The Davenant-Dryden adaptation of Shakespeare's The Tempest, adding a second island inhabitant, Hippolito, a sister for Miranda, and extensive musical and spectacular material; it held the stage for over a century.
works.plot: Prospero, exiled to the island, raises a tempest that wrecks the Neapolitans; the new plot gives Miranda a sister and adds Hippolito, a young man who has never seen a woman, with whom both sisters fall in love.
works.significance: The dominant version of The Tempest on the English stage from 1667 until the nineteenth century and a crucial document of Restoration Shakespeare adaptation; it inspired Purcell's semi-opera The Fairy-Queen tradition and Shadwell's operatic version of 1674.
works.meter: Mixed blank verse, rhyme, and song.
works.context: First performed by the Duke's Company at Lincoln's Inn Fields on 7 November 1667; Davenant died in 1668 before publication, and Dryden wrote the preface.
works.characters: Prospero; Miranda; Hippolito; Ariel; Ferdinand; Dorinda; Caliban; Trinculo; Stephano; Sycorax
works.structure: Five acts with songs, dances, and machinery; about half Shakespeare's text is retained and the rest newly written.
works.attributionNotes: The 1674 quarto names Davenant and Dryden; the extent of each contribution is disputed, but Dryden's preface claims the greater part of the new material as Davenant's design.

works.title: The Temple
altTitles: The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations
works.description: George Herbert's posthumous collection of 160 English religious poems, arranged in three parts — 'The Church-Porch', 'The Church', and 'The Church Militant' — which renders the life of the soul and the parish in an extraordinary variety of forms, from pattern poems to hymns and dramatic soliloquies.
works.plot: 'The Church-Porch' gives moral precepts to a young man; 'The Church' traces the soul's struggles with God through poems of sin, affliction, love, and consolation ('The Collar', 'The Pulley', 'Love III'); 'The Church Militant' is a prophetic vision of the church's corruption and the spread of true religion westward.
works.significance: The Temple is the supreme work of English devotional verse, fusing metaphysical wit with Anglican humility; it shaped religious poetry from Vaughan and Crashaw to Coleridge, Eliot, and Heaney.
works.meter: A prodigious variety of stanza forms, shaped and pattern poems ('Easter Wings', 'The Altar'), concrete imagery, and colloquial rhythm in the service of devotion.
works.context: Herbert sent the manuscript to Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding shortly before his death in 1633, asking him to publish it if he thought it might 'turn to the advantage of any dejected poor soul'; it was printed at Cambridge in 1633 and became a devotional best-seller.
works.characters: the poet-priest; God; the soul; the Church
works.structure: A tripartite collection with the shape of a spiritual autobiography, moving from moral instruction through the drama of devotion to eschatological prophecy.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Temple of Glas
works.description: John Lydgate's early dream vision (1,403 lines in rhyme royal, c. 1400–05): the dreamer, enclosed in a glass temple of Venus, overhears the complaint of a lady bound by an unwanted marriage and the answering lament of her true lover, until the goddess unites them. The most accomplished of Lydgate's courtly poems and the first printed by Caxton.
works.plot: The dreamer finds himself before a temple of glass whose walls depict famous lovers; within, the lady laments her forced betrothal and the knight his despair; Venus, appealed to by both, grants them one another, and the dreamer wakes to write his vision for his own lady.
works.significance: The finest of Lydgate's courtly visions and a key text of the early Chaucerian tradition; its printing history marks the beginning of the English poetry market.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas with the early Lydgate line's characteristic fluency.
works.context: Composed c. 1400–05, early in Lydgate's career, perhaps for a marriage occasion; widely copied and printed — it was among the first poems Caxton printed at Westminster (1477).
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Lady; her Lover; Venus
works.structure: A courtly dream vision in the Chaucerian manner (House of Fame, Parliament of Fowls), with the double complaint as its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure (named in the envoy).
sources: Macaulay: Prose and Poetry

works.title: The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America
works.description: Anne Bradstreet's first collection, published in London in 1650 without her knowledge by her brother-in-law, containing learned 'quaternions' on the four elements, humours, seasons, and the four monarchies, as well as poems on public events — the first volume of poetry published by a woman in the English colonies.
works.plot: The long poems survey natural philosophy and world history in the Du Bartas tradition, while shorter verses address family, faith, and public events, all framed by prefatory modesty topos.
works.significance: The Tenth Muse is the founding work of American poetry and a landmark of women's writing, documenting Puritan learning and a woman's ambitious but humble voice.
works.meter: Formal verse in the tradition of Du Bartas and Sidney, with learned allusion and occasional homely warmth.
works.context: Written in New England and carried to London by Bradstreet's brother-in-law, who published it in 1650; it made Bradstreet the first American and the first colonial woman to publish a volume of verse.
works.structure: A collection of long didactic 'quaternions' and shorter occasional poems in the Renaissance encyclopaedic manner.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published without Bradstreet's knowledge, signed 'A.B.' in some issues.

works.title: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates
altTitles: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates: Proving That It Is Lawful ... to Call to Account a Tyrant, King or Magistrate
works.description: Milton's republican tract, published weeks after the execution of Charles I, arguing that sovereignty originates in the people, that kings are the people's servants, and that it is lawful to depose and execute a tyrant — a defence of regicide and popular sovereignty.
works.plot: Milton argues from scripture, classical authority, and the law of nations that magistrates hold power by the people's trust, that a tyrant forfeits it, and that the people may judge and punish him, defending the Army's act against Presbyterian critics.
works.significance: A foundational text of republican political theory and resistance doctrine, influencing later Whig and revolutionary thought in England and America.
works.meter: Forceful, learned, argumentative prose with a fierce polemical edge.
works.context: Written in February 1649 immediately after Charles I's execution, partly to answer Presbyterians who had supported the war but recoiled from regicide; it secured Milton his post as Latin Secretary to the Commonwealth.
works.structure: A polemical prose treatise of sustained argument, moving from political theory to the immediate justification of the regicide.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name.

works.title: The Testament of Cresseid
works.description: Robert Henryson's great continuation of Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde (616 lines, c. 1475–90): the abandoned Cresseid, stricken with leprosy as judgement on her blasphemy against Venus and Cupid, meets the leper troop at the roadside and is recognized, too late, by Troilus, who cannot name her but casts her alms; she dies repentant, her testament a warning against the falsehood of love and fortune. The most powerful 'continuation' in English literature.
works.plot: The narrator, taking up 'ane uther quair' on the fate of Cresseid, tells how Diomede abandoned her; in her complaint she blasphemes Venus and Cupid, and the planetary court, convened by Saturn and Cynthia, condemns her to leprosy; in the lazar house she meets Troilus, who pities the unknown leper; learning the truth from the leper woman, she makes her testament, dies, and is buried under a tomb inscribed with her tragedy.
works.significance: Universally ranked among the great short tragedies of English literature; its compassion for Cresseid and its cosmic judgement scene make it the supreme Scottish response to Chaucer.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of austere, compassionate power in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1475–90 in the Chaucerian tradition of the Scottish makars, answering Chaucer's Troilus with a Scottish judgement on its heroine; printed with Chaucer's works by Thynne (1532), where it long passed as Chaucer's own.
works.characters: Cresseid; Troilus; Diomede; Saturn; Cynthia; Venus; Cupid; the leper woman
works.structure: A five-movement tragedy (abandonment; blasphemy and judgement; leprosy; the roadside meeting; testament and death), closed by the narrator's warning to the women of the audience.
works.attributionNotes: Henryson's authorship secure (named in the manuscripts).

works.title: The Testament of the Papyngo
altTitles: The Testament and Complaynt of Our Soverane Lordis Papyngo
works.form: verse satire in the testament tradition
works.description: Lindsay's satire of court and church: the king's parrot, dying after a fall from the palace wall, makes her testament — leaving her heart to the king, her body to the courtiers, and her counsel to the clergy — and delivers a dying bird's-eye satire of the bishops, the court, and the vices of the age.
works.plot: The Papyngo, perched high on the palace wall, falls and dies; before death she disposes of her estate in a testament that satirizes each legatee in turn, closing with an epistle to the bishops on their duties.
works.significance: The wittiest of Lindsay's satires and a classic of the Scots complaint; its parrot looks back to Skelton's Speke Parrot and forward to the beast satires of the later century.
works.meter: Scots couplets and stanzas; the mock-legal diction of the testament handled with satirical point.
works.context: Written in 1530 as the Scottish church's wealth and the court's corruption became the subjects of Reformation debate; the parrot speaks with the licence of the dying.
works.characters: the Papyngo; James V (legatee); the courtiers; the bishops
works.structure: The testament form — the dying bird's will and last counsel — used as a vehicle for estates satire; mock-legal framework, satirical legacies, and a closing sermon.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
works.description: Adam Smith's first great work, the fullest elaboration of the moral-sense tradition through the mechanism of sympathy and the impartial spectator. It explains how fellow-feeling, admiration, and the desire for praiseworthiness generate moral judgment, duty, and virtue, and it remains the century's most comprehensive treatise on the social psychology of ethics.
works.plot: Part I shows that we judge the propriety of another's feelings by imagining ourselves in his situation, sympathy being the imaginary transposition of spectator and agent, and that the senses of propriety and justice arise from this exchange of perspectives. Part II traces the feelings of merit and demerit, the rules of justice and beneficence, and the influence of custom and fashion on moral sentiment. Part III introduces the impartial spectator as the internal judge and the desire for praiseworthiness as the mature moral motive. Parts IV and V analyse the corruption of the moral sentiments by the love of riches and rank, and survey the rival systems of ethics from the ancients to the moderns. Part VI completes the taxonomy of the virtues of prudence, justice, beneficence, and self-command. The whole grounds society not on contract but on the mutual mirror of sympathetic sentiments.
works.significance: It supplied the moral psychology for commercial society's self-understanding, is the necessary companion to the Wealth of Nations, and anchors the modern revival of sympathy-based ethics and the study of the Scottish Enlightenment.
works.meter: An expansive, illustrative lecture prose dense with social observation, its famous generalizations stated in balanced declaratives, addressed alike to polite and philosophical readers.
works.context: Grown from Smith's Glasgow lectures begun in the early 1750s and published in London in 1759 with Hume's encouragement, it appeared in the season of the Edinburgh and Glasgow debates on scepticism and the French materialists and was revised by Smith through five later editions.
works.structure: Six parts of graduated argument, from the analysis of sympathy through the general rules and the impartial spectator to the history of ethical systems and the taxonomy of the virtues.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: The Thorn
works.form: Lyrical ballad and early form of the dramatic monologue; a poem that treats the popular tale as something made by the mind that tells it, and that places the psychology of belief in the foreground.
works.description: The most radical experiment of the anonymous 1798 volume: a long dramatic ballad narrated by a garrulous old man who reports what he thinks he has seen and heard on a hill where a thorn, a heap of moss and a nameless woman in a scarlet hood have gathered a local legend. The poem's interest is not the story but the mind of the teller - his superstition, his vanity, his need for a pathetic tale and his uneasy awareness that the simple truth would not serve him. A prose note explaining the narrator's character was appended in the edition of 1800, and the poem became the test case for the theory of poetic language defended in the Preface.
works.plot: The narrator bids his listener open his eyes wide and observe the thorn, which looks older than it is, and the mound of moss, which looks like a grave though none lies there. He then reports the gossip of the neighbourhood: a woman named Martha Ray met her lover by that thorn, was deserted, and has ever since sat there with her hood about her face, calling on the name Edward in a voice that has frightened those who pass at night. He alternately insists on and disowns the tale, offering natural explanations, then abandoning them for the pleasure of the wonderful, and the poem ends on the repeated cry as it sounds in his own superstitious ear. The subject is thus the growth of a legend and the creative power of an uneducated and sorrowful mind, together with the pleasure a tale of woe can give when it is badly told.
works.significance: Taken by later critics as the clearest demonstration of Romantic interest in the unreliable imaginative narrator and in the psychology of belief, and an ancestor of the Victorian dramatic monologue. It is also the poem against which the co-author of the volume later weighed the success of the Preface's theory, praising in it the power of an excited and credulous voice.
works.meter: A mixture of four- and three-beat ballad lines in stanzas of uneven length, marked by heavy punctuation, exclamatory emphasis and the repetition of words and half-lines, designed to imitate an excited and untrained voice rather than to sound poetical.
works.context: Written in the period of the western collaboration, when the two poets were experimenting with the speech of persons whose language is less refined than that of the class of readers to whom it is addressed. The explanatory prose note of 1800, in which the narrator is accounted for by decayed fortune and superstitious habits rather than by rustic charm, is one of the first applications of the new theory to a particular text.
works.characters: The aged, decayed and superstitious narrator; Martha Ray; the lost lover, Edward; the villagers whose gossip forms the legend
works.structure: A dramatic monologue addressed to an overhearer, in stanzas of unequal length: description of the site, report of the local story, self-correction and protestation of honesty, and a final reversion to the repeated cry. The narrator's unreliability is the structure, since each stanza qualifies the one before it.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the prose note of 1800, which explains the character of the speaker, is by the same hand and is printed with the poem in scholarly editions.

works.title: The Three Perils of Woman; or, Love, Jealousy, and Disobedience of Parents
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
works.description: the author's collection of three prose tales warning women against the three perils of romantic love, jealousy, and disobedience to parents, written in the years before his great novel Confessions of a Justified Sinner. It is his most sustained fictional prose before the 1824 novel and combines Gothic, border, and domestic modes.
works.plot: The three tales each demonstrate the ruin that follows one peril: the first, centred on a passionate elopement, shows the disaster of love mistaken for marriage; the second explores a jealous husband's destruction of his innocent wife; the third narrates a daughter's refusal of a suitable match for a dangerous stranger and her consequent suffering. The tales are set variously in Scotland, the Borders, and the Continent, and draw on ballad and Gothic conventions to make their moral case. the author's frame voice is urbane, digressive, and self-aware.
works.significance: The Three Perils of Woman is a major precursor of Confessions of a Justified Sinner and shows the author's development as a prose fiction writer; its Gothic and domestic tales illustrate the range of Scottish fiction in the 1820s.
works.context: Published in 1823, just before the author's masterpiece; the moral framework of the 'three perils' belongs to the conduct tradition, while the settings and plots use Gothic and ballad materials widely popular in the Waverley period.
works.characters: The various heroines of the three tales; their lovers and husbands; the author's frame narrator
works.structure: Three independent tales within a frame; each has its own setting and narrative voice; the moral frame gives coherence to the three very different plots.

works.title: The Tomb
works.form: Meditative blank-verse poem, a planned sequel or pendant to 'The Grave', surviving among the manuscripts Blair left and printed posthumously; short in relation to its companion and incomplete in the sense that its author left it.
works.description: Robert Blair's projected companion to 'The Grave', left in manuscript at his death and printed among his posthumous poems. It pursues the same subject in the same measure, but narrows the focus to the sepulchre itself and to the monuments and inscriptions by which the living attempt to keep the dead in mind.
works.plot: Like 'The Grave', the poem is an exercise of thought rather than a narrative. It meditates upon the tomb as a structure, an inscription and a hope: the masonry and the heraldry of memorial are surveyed and found insufficient, while the Christian tomb is read as the pledge of a resurrection. The turn from the vanity of monumental fame to the faith of the buried believer is the argument, and the piece supplies a closing reflection to the open-ended contemplation of its predecessor.
works.significance: It completes the conception of 'The Grave' and shows how far the graveyard meditation had become, in Blair's hands, a structured sequence rather than a single performance. It is a minor but authentic document of the preromantic contemplation of death.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter in the same weighty, Latinate manner as 'The Grave'; the diction is funerary and lapidary, with the compressed phrasing of an epitaph.
works.context: It was written in the same period as 'The Grave', when Blair was assembling a sequence of poems on the last things, and it stands within the 1740s fashion for churchyard, tomb and resurrection meditation. Its survival in manuscript and its posthumous printing are part of the history of that fashion, since the editors of Blair's papers were also the editors of his reputation.
works.structure: A continuous meditation addressed to the tomb, in the same sectional, associative movement as 'The Grave', with apostrophe and epitaph-like reflection taking the place of events.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Blair is not contested; the difficulty lies in its publication history. Because it was not printed in the poet's lifetime and because the several posthumous collections and reissues of Blair's poems are differently dated, no first-print year is asserted here and the publication field is left null rather than guessed.

works.title: The Tournament
works.form: Antiquarian romance in verse among the Rowley poems; long, irregular and catalogue-driven, in the archaic orthography Chatterton supplied, with glosses of the obsolete words attached in the manuscripts and collections.
works.description: One of the longest and most ambitious of the poems Thomas Chatterton put into the name of the fifteenth-century Bristol monk Thomas Rowley, and a centrepiece of the forgeries he sent to Horace Walpole in 1764. It presents itself as an antiquarian account of a medieval tournament, complete with lists of champions, devices and heraldic blazon, in a deliberately archaized spelling and diction. Its interest is double: as an early achievement of the primitive-genius vogue, and as a document of a Bristol apprentice's furious self-education in the literature of the past.
works.plot: The poem narrates the summoning, the gathering and the running of a great tournament, and dwells on the heraldry, the armour, the ladies' favours and the encounters of the champions with a minuteness meant to look like a period chronicler's rather than a modern poet's imagination. Chivalric honour, religious invocation and the pomp of the field are combined without any neoclassical sense of proportion, so that the piece reads as a series of illuminated tableaux. Its frame is the more important fiction: Rowley is made to be an eyewitness and recorder of the scene, an authority older than any modern antiquary. The result is the most complete of Chatterton's impersonations, in which the medieval is not described from outside but re-enacted in a language the eighteenth century was willing to believe.
works.significance: It is the largest single exercise in the Rowley impersonation and an important text in the history of literary forgery, of medievalism, and of the cult of the primitive genius; its mixture of heraldic learning and genuine imaginative power is what later readers from the Romantics onwards remembered. It also helped to establish the vogue for an invented national antiquity which the same decade received from Macpherson and from Percy.
works.meter: Rowley's supposed measures: long lines with medial caesura and mixed rhyme formations, imitating fifteenth-century verse rather than any Elizabethan or Augustan practice.
works.context: It belongs to the Rowley correspondence of 1764, when Chatterton, a clerk in Bristol, supplied Walpole with parchment 'originals' and letters in a fabricated antiquarian persona, at the moment when the taste for chivalry and for national origins was being formed by Walpole's own circle at Strawberry Hill. The forgery was detected within a few years, but the poems continued to be read as poetry.
works.characters: The framing chronicler 'Thomas Rowley'; the knights and champions of the listed tournament; the ladies whose favours are proclaimed
works.structure: A chronicle-poem in the supposed voice and hand of Rowley: annalistic opening, catalogue of champions and devices, narrative of the field, and devotional and heraldic digression, without regular stanzaic closure.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship is recorded as single because Chatterton, not any medieval monk, wrote the poem. The ascription in the manuscripts is to 'Thomas Rowley', a fictitious fifteenth-century Bristol priest and chronicler whose parchment 'originals' and glosses Chatterton supplied; the deception imposed upon Walpole and other antiquaries before it was seen through. The year 1764 refers to the Rowley correspondence in which the piece was produced.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Tragedy of Tragedies; or, The Life and Death of Tom Thumb the Great
works.form: burlesque tragedy in five acts, written for the stage
works.description: A burlesque tragedy on heroic subjects, in which the tiny hero of the old ballad is placed inside an exact parody of heroic verse, with its declamation, its mono-syllabic names and its catastrophes of absurd magnitude. It is the most sustained English exercise in tragicomical burlesque of the century and was revised into a two-act form with a dedication that became a manifesto.
works.plot: Tom Thumb, in miniature and married to the queen, discovers his beloved's intrigue with a courtier and sends his rival on errands that end in death. King Arthur's court supplies the dignity, the giants and the fathers the ceremony, and the accumulating duels and poisonings grow past all probability. The finale buries nearly the whole cast, the survivors being left to moralise on the fragility of heroic design.
works.significance: It is the classic English parody of heroic tragedy and a key document of the quarrel between the legitimate theatre and the little houses; its preface and dedication are primary statements of the comic theory later applied in the novels.
works.meter: Heroic couplets and the inflated blank verse of tragedy used exactly for nonsense, with the famous mono-syllabic names and the tautological similes of the high style.
works.context: First played at the Haymarket in 1731 and revived in altered form at Drury Lane in 1737 with a prose dedication to the reader and a preface critical of contemporary tragedy; the season was one of heroic revival and of managerial dispute.
works.characters: Tom Thumb; King Arthur; Queen Huncamunca; Doodle; Grumio; Glumdalca; Meridanta
works.structure: A regular five-act burlesque tragedy in the heroic manner, reduced later to two acts, with the parody sustained scene by scene against the conventions of tragic structure; the deaths are stacked for cumulative effect.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the revised edition of the late 1730s carries the author's name, prefatory matter and a dedication much debated as criticism.

works.title: The Traitor
works.description: Shirley's most successful tragedy, a political play on the assassination of the Duke of Florence by his favourite Sciarrha, loosely based on the murder of the Florentine Duke Alessandro de' Medici in 1537.
works.plot: The Duke's favourite Sciarrha, ambitious and jealous, conspires with the Duke's rival to assassinate him; the conspiracy succeeds, but Sciarrha's sister Amidea refuses the Duke and the murder destroys both plotters.
works.significance: The finest Caroline political tragedy and a principal influence on later plays of tyrannicide, including the Restoration heroic drama.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit in 1631 and read at court by Charles I, who is said to have remarked that it was 'a tragedy'.
works.characters: the Duke of Florence; Sciarrha; Amidea; Cosmo; Lorenzo; Depazzi
works.structure: Five acts following the rise, execution, and ruin of the conspiracy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Shirley; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Traveller; or, A Prospect of Society
works.form: Philosophical-reflection poem in the tradition of Pope's 'Essay on Man', cast as a verse epistle to a friend and organised as a comparative survey of nations; issued as a separate pamphlet in quarto.
works.description: Goldsmith's first published poem and the work that established him as a poet: a reflection in heroic couplets on the forms of society and on the place each gives to human happiness, written in the manner of the Augustan philosophical essay in verse and addressed to his friend the painter Sir Joshua Reynolds. It takes the traveller's survey of the nations of Europe as the frame for an argument about happiness, government and contentment.
works.plot: The poem opens with the traveller's farewell to his family and his retirement from the world's noise, and proceeds as a survey of the chief states of Europe, each examined for the kind of happiness its institutions secure or refuse. The commercial states of Flanders, the hardy independence of the Swiss cantons, Italy under priestcraft, smiling but servitude-prone Gaul, proud and darkly policed Spain, and England with its liberty, its commerce and its unequal distribution of enjoyments, are each allowed their plea and then judged. The argument is that happiness does not follow from any single form of policy or condition of life, since every state has its own peculiar miseries and every rank its own discontents, and that felicity depends rather on the mind and on the balance of the whole. The close withdraws from the prospect of society to the poet's own retired lot, content to have failed in the world if he has kept his integrity.
works.significance: It made Goldsmith's poetical reputation at the moment when the couplet tradition was beginning to be questioned, and it remains the best example of the Augustan philosophical survey in verse written in the 1760s. Its doctrine that forms of society do not determine happiness, and its portraits of national character, were much quoted, and it prepared the moral manner of 'The Deserted Village'.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, iambic pentameter, in the polished Augustan manner with balanced antithesis, sententious closure and a good deal of the epigrammatic turn Goldsmith took from Pope.
works.context: It was composed largely during a country retirement in the English midlands and published at the height of the debate about commercial society, national character and the comparative history of government, in which the Scottish and English moral philosophers were then engaged. Its survey of Europe drew on the Grand Tour and on the travelling literature of the age, and on the post-war confidence and anxiety about British commerce.
works.characters: The traveller-poet and his own family left behind; the nations of Europe as collectively personified conditions of society
works.structure: A single sustained argument in the epistle-reflection form: opening retirement and apostrophe, a sequence of national portraits each with its own balance sheet of good and evil, general conclusion on the dependence of happiness on the mind, and personal peroration of retirement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was published anonymously at first but was known and acknowledged as Goldsmith's, and its history is documented in his letters and in the contemporary accounts of its subscription publication.

works.title: The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo
altTitles: The Treatise of the Two Married Women and the Widow
works.description: William Dunbar's scandalous Midsummer Eve debate (c. 1500–07, 530 lines): the eavesdropping poet overhears three women — two wives and a widow — exchanging frank confidences on marriage, their husbands' inadequacies, and the arts of deceiving them, in the most sustained exhibition of female licence (and male ventriloquism) in medieval English verse. The most brilliant of Dunbar's alliterative poems.
works.plot: Hidden in the hedge on a June night, the narrator hears the first wife anatomize her husband's age, impotence, and jealousy, the second mock hers as a coward and braggart, and the widow — dismissing both as amateurs — advise on choosing, managing, and surviving husbands, until the dawn and the lark's song end the colloquy.
works.significance: The supreme comic-satiric poem of the Scottish tradition: its frankness and metrical brilliance made it a scandal in its own day and a touchstone of medieval misogyny debate in ours.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line in Dunbar's hands — colloquial, obscene, and metrically audacious.
works.context: Composed c. 1500–07 at the court of James IV, in the makars' revival of alliterative verse; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508) and preserved in the Bannatyne manuscript.
works.characters: the narrator (Dunbar); the two married women; the widow
works.structure: A debate-frame of three long monologues, each more outrageous than the last, in the tradition of the débat and the Wife of Bath's prologue.
works.attributionNotes: Dunbar's authorship secure.

editions.title: The Poems of William Dunbar

works.title: The True Intellectual System of the Universe
works.description: Ralph Cudworth's massive learned work against atheism, in which he argues that the ancient philosophers were not atheists and that a rational theism is the true intellectual system of the universe.
works.plot: Book I sets out the various forms of atheism and refutes them; the work argues for the existence of plastic natures, for the immateriality of the soul, and for the eternity of moral truths against Hobbesian materialism.
works.significance: The most learned philosophical work of the seventeenth-century English Platonists; its concept of 'plastic nature' influenced Leibniz and later vitalist philosophy, and its refutation of atheism was a standard reference.
works.meter: Dense, heavily cited scholarly prose of the Cambridge Platonists.
works.context: Published in 1678, the year of the Popish Plot, and licensed by Samuel Parker; Cudworth was Master of Christ's College, Cambridge.
works.structure: A single vast treatise in four books (only the first volume was published), with enormous learned apparatus.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Cudworth; authorship undisputed.

works.title: The Tryal: A Comedy
works.description: The comic play of the first volume of the series delineating the stronger passions, assigned by its author's introductory discourse to the passion of love and laid in the English bathing city of Bath. It is a comedy of mercy and of Scotch-English difference, written in the manner of the older sentimental comedy but built on a hard legal and financial plot. Modern editors have found it the liveliest piece in the volume and the best adjusted for the stage.
works.plot: Withrington, a Scottish officer who has been ruined and imprisoned by the false evidence of the English merchant Harwood, comes to Bath with his daughter Agnes, poor and dependent. Harwood is now prosperous, engaged in a suit of debt in which Withrington, as a witness, holds the power to destroy him, and his son is in love with Agnes. At the trial Withrington withholds the testimony that would have ruined his enemy, and the disclosure of who the injured party has all along been turns the legal victory into forgiveness. The younger lovers are free to marry, and the comedy ends on mercy rather than on punishment, with the passion of love working through a father's power to revenge himself.
works.significance: The Tryal is the clearest illustration in the series of the theory that a comedy may be built on a single passion as rigorously as a tragedy, and its movement from the right to punish to the choice to forgive has made it the most frequently revived of the author's comic numbers. It is now a standard text for the study of women's drama and of the Romantic-period sentimental comedy.
works.meter: Written in dialogue of the closed heroic-couplet school used by the eighteenth-century comedy, with a brisk prosaic interchange in the lower scenes and more sustained rhetorical passages in the scenes of disclosure.
works.context: Published anonymously with the first volume of the series of plays in the last years of the eighteenth century, when the anti-theatrical debate and the licensed patent theatres made a closet series of analytic plays a practical form, and when the union of Scotland and England supplied a stock of national-character comedy. The legal and mercantile business of the plot reflects the small-bath society of the 1790s, where debts, evidence, and imprisonment for debt were familiar.
works.characters: Withrington, the injured Scottish officer; Harwood, the English merchant he could ruin; Agnes, Withrington's daughter; Mariane; Sir Loftus Prettyman; Miss Eston
works.structure: A regular five-act comedy of single design, opening on the master's concealed identity and closing on public disclosure and reconciliation; the courtroom scene forms the structural and moral hinge of the plot.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in the first volume, 1798, and reissued under the author's name in the collected dramas; no dispute attaches to the play.

works.title: The Tunning of Elinour Rumming
works.description: Skelton's carnivalesque masterpiece: a Skeltonic account of the alewife Elinour Rumming of Leatherhead and the procession of women who come to drink her noxious ale, a low-life gallery from drunken Alice to the beggarly Maud Ruggy — ugliness, appetite, and disorder rendered with gleeful verbal energy.
works.plot: The poem describes Elinour's brewing and her customers in turn — their poverty, their lechery, their brawling — as the alehouse degenerates into a riot of appetite without plot or moral.
works.significance: The most vivid low-life poem in English before the eighteenth century; its catalogue form and demotic energy made it a model for later satire.
works.meter: The Skeltonic at its most anarchic — breathless rhymes, macaronic puns, and tavern speech.
works.context: Set at Leatherhead in Surrey; the poem belongs to the alehouse satire of the early sixteenth century and reflects the moralists' anxieties about disorderly women.
works.characters: Elinour Rumming; her customers (drunken Alice, Maud Ruggy, and others)
works.structure: A catalogue or procession of drinkers, framed by the description of the brewing; no plot, but a mounting carnival intensity.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Turkish Embassy Letters
altTitles: Letters Written During the Turkish Embassy
works.description: The correspondence of the ambassador's wife at Constantinople and Adrianople, describing the seraglios, the baths, the Greek church and the women's society of the Turkish capital, and reporting the inoculation practice she afterwards brought to England. It is the most vivacious of the century's travel writing and the classic account of the East seen by a woman.
works.plot: The letters follow the party from Vienna through the Hungarian and Bulgarian roads to Adrianople and Constantinople, giving an account of the way of travelling, of the houses and of the ceremonies of the embassy. They describe the women's baths and the seraglio, the Greek ladies and their usages, and the cathedral of the Phanar, with the writer's own freedom of access to a society closed to other travellers. The later letters from the embassy report the smallpox operation, and the correspondence closes with the return into Poland and Germany.
works.significance: It created the literary image of the Turkish women's world for English readers and is a foundational text of the travel letter and of the female account of the East, its evidence on inoculation being of the history of medicine as well as of letters.
works.meter: An animated epistolary prose of the quick phrase, the parenthesis and the indignant comparison, its sentences built on the sudden turn of observation rather than on the balanced period.
works.context: Written during the embassy of 1717-18 at the time of the Turkish war and the settlement of the Passarowitz season, in the current of the correspondence of the diplomatic corps, and returned to by the writer's own account of inoculation in the English medical press.
works.characters: the writing lady of the embassy; the friend at home to whom the letters are addressed; the begum or lady of the seraglio and her attendants; the Greek ladies of Constantinople; the ambassador and his household
works.structure: A continuous family correspondence, chiefly to a single friend, ordered by the route and the stay, and rising to the set descriptions of the baths and the seraglio; there is no plot beyond the journey and the observation.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the letters remained in manuscript and were given to the press after the writer's death, so that no publication year in her lifetime can be asserted here.

works.title: The Twa Dogs
works.form: beast fable and debate poem in the Scottish vernacular, in the tradition of Ramsay's and Dryden's dialogues of creatures
works.description: Burns's animal fable of the two dogs - Luath the farmer's working stock-dog and Caesar the gentleman's pampered spaniel - who meet at a tavern door and compare the conditions of their lives. Under the covering of the beasts the poem delivers a searching social analysis of rank, idleness, hire and hunger in the agricultural west of Scotland, and one of the sharpest indictments of the privileges of great families in the century. It is among Burns's earliest considerable poems and the first open declaration of his egalitarian creed.
works.plot: Caesar, kept warm and idle by his laird, and Luath, the working dog of a farmer, meet and dispute their respective happiness. Caesar reports the luxuries and the boredom of the hall, the squire's dogs, horses and flatterers, and the uselessness of his own life, while Luath describes the labour, the weather, the hunger and the honest dependence of the poor. The dialogue arrives at the poem's famous conclusion that the rank of the creature makes no difference in its worth, and that the poor dog and the poor man have at least the merit of usefulness.
works.significance: It established Burns's characteristic politics of the worth of the common creature and supplied the imaginative ground of his later songs on rank and equality. As a dialect fable it is the most successful modern descendant of the Scots 'Makkar' tradition of talk between beasts, and it remains a standard text for the literature of the nations and for social analysis in verse.
works.meter: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie), four long and two short Scots lines with the a-a-a-b-a-b rhyme, used for sustained dialogue.
works.context: Begun about 1784 and revised for the Kilmarnock volume, in a decade of enclosure, of improving agriculture and of depressed rural wages in Ayrshire; the poem's comparison of the idle and the useful draws on a long native tradition of estates criticism and on the contemporary debate about the condition of the labouring poor.
works.characters: Luath; Caesar; the poor laird; the farmer and his bailiff; the tavern company
works.structure: A framed tavern scene followed by a matched dialogue of the two dogs, each speech elaborating the conditions of its master, closing with the moral of the fable.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; Burns dated the poem in his own memoranda as an early attempt, and the standard editions record his successive revisions of the text.

works.title: The Two Gentlemen of Verona
works.description: Shakespeare's early romantic comedy of friendship and betrayal: Valentine and Proteus, the 'two gentlemen' of Verona, both fall in love with Silvia; Proteus betrays his friend and his own beloved Julia, and the play moves through disguise, forest outlawry, and attempted rape to a reconciliation whose abruptness has troubled audiences ever since.
works.plot: Proteus, sent to Milan, falls in love with Valentine's Silvia and betrays him to the Duke; Valentine joins the outlaws, Silvia flees to the forest, and Proteus's assault on her is stopped by Valentine's intervention, leading to the double reconciliation and the play's famously compressed ending.
works.significance: The first of Shakespeare's romantic comedies and the seedbed of themes — friendship versus love, the heroine in disguise, the green world — he would develop for a decade.
works.meter: Blank verse and prose, with songs; among Shakespeare's earliest surviving verse.
works.context: An early play, probably written about 1590–91 from the Spanish romance Diana Enamorada (via its French and English versions); not printed until the 1623 First Folio.
works.characters: Valentine; Proteus; Silvia; Julia; the Duke of Milan; Launce; Speed; Crab the dog
works.structure: Five acts of alternating Milan and forest scenes, built on the paired lovers plot with the comic servants Speed and Launce (and his dog Crab) as counterpoint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Two Noble Kinsmen
works.description: Shakespeare's last play, written with John Fletcher from Chaucer's Knight's Tale: the cousins Palamon and Arcite, kinsmen and friends, both fall in love with Emilia from their prison window; their rivalry is settled by the tournament for her hand — Arcite wins and dies in a riding accident, and Palamon marries her, while the Jailer's Daughter's mad sub-plot runs its course.
works.plot: The cousins swear eternal friendship, then break it over Emilia; Arcite is released, Palamon escapes; the tournament appoints the winner; Arcite's victory is followed by his fatal fall from the horse; the dying Arcite bequeaths Emilia to Palamon; Theseus closes the play on the riddle of fortune, while the Jailer's Daughter is cured by the doctor's masque of her wooer.
works.significance: The closing chord of the Shakespeare canon — a return to Chaucer, and to the question of friendship and love with which his career began.
works.meter: The collaboration's two styles are audibly joined — Shakespeare's ceremonial verse (the prayers at the altars) with Fletcher's supple fluency.
works.context: First performed about 1614, after the Globe fire, probably at Blackfriars; printed in quarto in 1634 as 'by the memorable worthies... Mr John Fletcher and Mr William Shakespeare'; omitted from the First Folio.
works.characters: Palamon; Arcite; Emilia; Theseus; Hippolyta; the Jailer; the Jailer's Daughter; the Wooer; Pirithous; the Doctor
works.structure: A tragicomedy of friendship and fortune in five acts, with the Jailer's Daughter's madness as a tragic sub-plot and the Morris dance and tournament as spectacle.
works.attributionNotes: Joint authorship with John Fletcher is established on title-page and stylistic evidence and is universally accepted; the division of scenes is broadly agreed.

works.title: The Two Ways
altTitles: The Boke of the Two Ways
works.description: Sir John Clanvowe's devotional prose tract on the two ways of life and death — the narrow way of virtue and the broad way of the world — a Lollard-leaning meditation written in the circle of the 'Lollard knights' of Richard II's court, probably in 1391. It is the earliest prose work of the English reforming tradition by a lay courtier.
works.plot: The tract expounds Christ's teaching of the two ways, contrasts the few who walk the narrow path with the many on the broad road to perdition, and anatomizes the sins of the world — pride, avarice, gluttony — with a particular Lollard sharpness against clerical wealth and display.
works.significance: A principal document of the Lollard sensibility among the courtly elite and the earliest lay devotional prose of the Ricardian court.
works.meter: Plain, earnest prose with scriptural quotation.
works.context: Composed c. 1391 by the courtier-knight Clanvowe (d. October 1391), in the company of the Lollard knights at the court of Richard II; preserved in Bodleian MS Eng. th. c. 39 and later copies.
works.characters: the writer (as penitent teacher)
works.structure: A single homiletic meditation organized by the scriptural image of the two ways, with catalogue of sins and exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Clanvowe in the manuscripts.

works.title: The Undying One, and Other Poems
works.form: Metrical Tale and Romance in Verse; Literary Annual and Keepsake Verse
works.description: The second volume of the same hand, built on a long poem in four cantos treating the legend of the Wandering Jew, whom the author calls the Undying One. The poem makes the outcast of Christian legend a figure for the eternally repentant and homeless soul, and the accompanying miscellaneous poems print some of the lyrics most often reprinted in the gift-books of the decade. The book confirmed the author's standing in the annual market.
works.plot: The Undying One passes through four cantos in which the Shoeman of Jerusalem, condemned to walk until the last day, meets at intervals the mortals whose lives his own length makes tragic; his penance, his memory of the crucifixion, and his inability to die form the poem's sustained subject. The miscellaneous section that follows prints short poems on friendship, childhood, the bride, and loss, including The Careless Word, They Loved one Another, My Heart is like a Withered Nut, My Childhood's Home, Old Friends, and The Bride. The volume's argument thus moves from an immortal's guilt to the mortal affections he watches.
works.significance: The poem is the most substantial treatment in English by a woman Romantic poet of the Ahasuerus legend as a figure of unforgiven guilt and homelessness, and its combination of the supernatural tale with short domestic lyric is typical of the keepsake volume at its best. Several of the miscellaneous pieces became standard anthology items and were reprinted in America.
works.meter: The four cantos use a sustained measured rhymed stanza with apostrophe and lament, the notes append ballad and song stanzas, and the miscellaneous poems are in common and long measure with refrain; the whole is rhetorical and vocal rather than narrative in rhythm.
works.context: Published in 1830 by the London firm that issued the fashionable popular books of the season and inscribed by permission to a princess of the blood, at the height of the gift-book economy and of the vogue for legends of penance and exile. The Wandering Jew subject belonged to a stock of continental legends then being rewritten by women poets, and the volume's economics depended on the annuals that bought such pieces.
works.characters: the Undying One, the Wandering Jew; the mortals he successively meets; the speaker of the miscellaneous lyrics; the bride and the old friends of that section
works.structure: A four-canto narrative-lyric in which episodic meetings replace continuous plot, prefaced and followed by notes and by an unordered section of miscellaneous poems.
works.attributionNotes: Single authorship; the volume is signed and dated and the several contents have not been disputed.

works.title: The Unfortunate Traveller
works.description: Nashe's picaresque novel: the page Jack Wilton travels through the wars and cities of Europe — tricking the camp at Tergou, fleeing the sweating sickness and the plague, witnessing the massacre of the Anabaptists at Münster, courting in Italy, and escaping the rape-and-execution plot of the Jew Zadoch and the courtesan Juliana — in the first English novel of adventure and the grotesque.
works.plot: Jack's tricks in the army, his travels with the Earl of Surrey (and the Italian Diamante in boy's disguise), the horrors of Münster and of plague-struck Rome, the anatomies and executions, and the final escape through the villain's own engines carry the narrative to its abrupt, comic close.
works.significance: The first English picaresque novel — the ancestor of Defoe, Smollett, and the English novel's roguish line.
works.meter: Prose of Nashe's most violent invention — the grotesque, the comic, and the lyrical in rapid succession.
works.context: Published 1594; its continental horrors answered the decade's appetite for travel lies and martyrdom pamphlets, and its Italian scenes the anti-Catholic mood.
works.characters: Jack Wilton; the Earl of Surrey; Diamante; Zadoch; Zachary; Juliana; the Pope; Heraclide; the Anabaptists
works.structure: A first-person travel narrative in the manner of Lazarillo de Tormes, episodic and sensational, with the set pieces of horror (the anatomies, the executions) as its climaxes.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancaster and York
altTitles: The Union of the Two Noble and Illustre Families of Lancastre and Yorke
works.description: Edward Hall's chronicle of the Wars of the Roses and the triumph of the house of Tudor, from the deposition of Richard II to the death of Henry VIII; printed posthumously by Richard Grafton in 1548 and continued by Grafton in later editions.
works.plot: Hall narrates the dynastic strife between Lancaster and York as a providential drama culminating in the union of the two houses in Henry VIII, with long set-piece speeches and a moralizing emphasis on the ruin brought by ambition, faction, and rebellion; the reign of Henry VIII occupies the final section ('The Triumphant Reign of King Henry the VIII').
works.significance: The principal source of Shakespeare's English history plays (the second tetralogy follows Hall closely) and the classic statement of the Tudor myth of union and providential kingship; its dramatic speeches made it the most literary of the Tudor chronicles.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled over the 1530s and 1540s by Hall, a lawyer and MP, drawing on More's Richard III, Polydore Vergil, and Fabyan; the 1548 edition was supervised by Grafton, who added continuations in the editions of 1550.
works.characters: Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI; Edward IV; Richard III; Henry VII; Henry VIII; Cardinal Wolsey
works.structure: Chronicle divided by reigns, from Richard II through Henry VIII, framed by a preface on the theme of union and enriched with speeches invented in the manner of classical historiography.

works.title: The Unnatural Combat
works.description: Massinger's dark tragedy in which the Marseilles admiral Malefort, under pressure from his son, kills him in single combat, and the son's ghost returns to expose the father's crimes.
works.plot: The young Malefort, corrupted by the villain Beauford junior, demands a combat with his father; the father kills him; the ghost reveals the unnatural deed and the father's earlier crime, and Malefort dies in madness.
works.significance: One of Massinger's most powerful tragedies, notable for its psychological intensity and its treatment of paternal guilt; it was long thought to have influenced later Jacobean and Caroline revenge drama.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Globe c. 1624-26 and published in 1639.
works.characters: Malefort senior; Malefort junior; Beauford; Theocrine; Montrevile; Rochefort
works.structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a ghost and a catastrophic recognition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Massinger; authorship undisputed.
