works.title: Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of Caleb Williams
works.form: Philosophical and anarchist fiction; picaresque pursuit novel and domestic gothic of lawless power.
works.description: The founding novel of philosophical anarchy and of the pursuit plot, written to dramatise the argument that private virtue is destroyed by law, rank and the arbitrary power of a benefactor. Its hero, a curious clerk who forces out of his patron the secret of an old murder, becomes the victim of an inexorable persecution that carries him from a country house to a London prison. The novel's machinery of spies, forgery, false arrest and flight supplied the gothic and sensation plotting of the next half-century.
works.plot: Caleb Williams, the son of an old dependant of the country gentleman Falkland, is educated, made secretary and admired, and by an unlucky question extracts from his benefactor the confession that years before he killed a low and malignant rival in the fight over an estate. Falkland's pride turns to alarm and then to systematic persecution: Caleb is dismissed, falsely suspected of theft, pursued through the country and driven to London, where, poor and unknown, he is befriended by an alderman and by a man of ruined reputation, and is at last trapped by an artifice of friendship into a spunging-house and a marshal's custody. Escape, disguise and a project of revenge put weapons in his hands; he returns to England, extorts from Falkland a public confession, and stands by while his persecutor is prosecuted, convicted and sent into exile, where he dies. Caleb, the victor, has spent his patron's fortune and ruined his own prospects, and the tale closes with the writing of his confession.
works.significance: The most influential English novel of persecution and of the psychology of a tyrant and his victim, and the work that gave the pursued-hero plot its secular, legal form. Its treatment of class power, of the spectacle of punishment and of the failure of revenge makes it a founding text of political fiction. Later gothic, sensation and detective fiction inherited its apparatus of spies, forgeries and prisons.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; rapid first-person argumentative narrative with long analytical passages and colloquial dialogue of clubs, prisons and the road.
works.context: Written in the train of a systematic treatise on justice published the year before, and in the atmosphere of the 1790s controversies over law, aristocratic privilege and the efficacy of punishment. Its legal machinery reflects the actual procedures of civil arrest, spunging-houses and criminal trial at the close of the century. Its publication was followed by denunciation in the ministerial press as a school of Jacobinism, and a table of the contents of the argument was prefixed to the first edition.
works.characters: Caleb Williams; Falkland, the patron who becomes his persecutor; Mr. Bailey, the London alderman who befriends him; Julian, the friend who is ruined by his kindness to the hero
works.structure: First-person confession written by the hero and addressed to the public; three volumes of continuous pursuit, with an inserted narrative told by another sufferer; a conclusion that reports the deaths of both principals.
works.attributionNotes: Published with the author's name; no dispute. Early copies are dated 1793 or 1794 according to the issue of the last volume.

works.title: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil and Wicked Traffic of the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species, Humbly Submitted to the Justice of Great Britain by the Africans
altTitles: Thoughts and Sentiments on the Evil of Slavery
works.form: Polemical essay in natural-law, scriptural and legal argument
works.description: An abolitionist polemic by Ottobah Cugoano, a Fante man kidnapped and sold in 1769, who by the 1780s was a literate servant in the London household of the artist Richard Cosway. The book argues from natural law, scripture and British law that the slave trade and West Indian slavery are crimes against God and humanity, and it demands immediate remedy rather than gradual relief. A short abridgement for wider circulation followed in the same year, and a second edition with an appendix on the slave insurrection in Jamaica appeared in 1788.
works.plot: Cugoano first states the natural right of every human being to liberty, so that enslavement is a violation of the law of God written on the conscience. He then examines the scriptural evidence and shows that neither Hebraic servitude nor the New Testament's household codes sanction the modern traffic, and he presses the legal argument that a Christian cannot lawfully hold a fellow Christian in perpetual slavery. Turning to practice, he denounces the planters' plea of necessity and property, refutes the political arithmetic that counts colonial wealth as national strength, and proposes remedies: the recall of British subjects from the colonies, the education of the enslaved, and the establishment of lawful commerce in Africa in place of the trade in persons. The conclusion warns that Britain's national guilt for the trade will draw national judgment.
works.significance: It is the first published abolitionist argument written by an African in England to confront the slave trade as a national crime and to claim the authority of reason and scripture against the planters' case. Its insistence that liberty is a divine and natural right, and its refusal of gradualist compromise, make it a foundational text of black Atlantic political writing and a necessary companion to Equiano's narrative.
works.meter: Prose only, in an urgent, latinate, sermon-like style marked by biblical cadence
works.context: Written between the Somersett decision of 1772 and the first parliamentary abolitionist campaign of 1788, it joins the printed output of the Committee for Abolishing the Slave Trade and the black London community of Equiano, Sharp and Ramsay, and reflects the evangelical moral-language of natural rights then current.
works.structure: Continuous argumentative treatise in short numbered sections, moving from first principles to scriptural, legal and commercial refutation and then to proposals for remedy.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship by Cugoano is accepted; the extent of assistance from friends and patrons in a household of artists and literati is discussed but does not displace his authorship, which the text signs as an African speaking for Africans.

works.title: Thoughts on African Slave-Trade
works.form: Polemic and pamphlet; applied moral and political philosophy addressed to a public question
works.description: A short polemic against the slave trade and against the argument that commerce in human beings can be regulated or excused. Its reasoning is applied philosophy rather than feeling: the trade is shown to rest on the same violation of private judgement and of person which the writer's political theory had condemned, and the pleas of property, of climate and of gradual amendment are answered one by one. It belongs to the renewed abolition campaign of the 1820s and is the writer's most direct intervention in a live parliamentary question. The pamphlet is argumentative, lucid and unhedged in its conclusion.
works.plot: The trade in enslaved people is examined as a system of law and interest rather than as a scene of private cruelty, and the writer contends that no regulation can alter the nature of a claim to property in a person. The apologies offered for the trade - that it is sanctioned by long usage, that the condition of the enslaved is improved by service, that abolition would ruin commerce and endanger the colonies - are each tested against the principle that judgement and the person are not transferable. The argument closes with the claim that emancipation, not amendment, is the only consequence consistent with the principles of justice, and with an appeal to the public and to the legislature to act on that principle.
works.significance: A significant document of the abolition campaign of the 1820s and of the application of philosophical anarchism to a live political question. It is read now as part of the literature of slavery and emancipation, and as the late political writing of the circle out of which the period's radical fiction came.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; a plain, closely argued style of the philosophical pamphlet, free of invective
works.context: Published in 1823, when the renewed abolition movement was pressing the question of the colonial slave populations before parliament and when the writer's own political reputation had lasted a generation. It answers the amelioration argument of the period's colonial writing and draws on the reports and speeches of the renewed campaign. It belongs to the literature of emancipation between the abolition of the trade and the acts of the 1830s.
works.structure: Continuous short argument in a single pamphlet compass: statement of the question, examination of the defences offered for the trade, and a positive conclusion addressed to the legislature and the public.
works.attributionNotes: Published as the work of a named author of the philosophy of political justice, whose identity was indicated on the title page; the attribution is undisputed.

works.title: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters
altTitles: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, in the Early Part of Life
Thoughts on the Education of Daughters. In the Early Part of Life; with Remarks on the Management of Children, from Birth to the Age of Ten Years
works.form: conduct and educational treatise in prose
works.description: A conduct and educational treatise for the management of girls from earliest childhood, drawn from the author's experience as a governess and a schoolmistress. It argues for the cultivation of reason, truthfulness and independence in girls, and for the reform of the needlework and accomplishments curriculum of the day.
works.plot: The work sets out the duties of the mother and the governess in the first years of a girl's life, treating the government of the temper, the formation of habits of veracity and the dangers of false modesty. It criticises the female academies and their round of accomplishments, recommends the study of religion and of reason, and gives directions on health, amusement and the choice of company. Its conclusion is that a woman's virtue depends on her understanding being taught to act for itself.
works.significance: It is the first published work of the century's most influential advocate of women's rational education and supplies the practical ground of the later argument about the rights and the cultivation of women's minds.
works.meter: A clear, earnest and direct prose of instruction, with the occasional apostrophe to mothers and the sententious summation of the section.
works.context: Published in 1787 after the author's keeping of a school for girls and her service as a governess, in the season of the public debate on female academies and on women's rational education, the same debate that occupied the Bluestocking writers of the day.
works.structure: A continuous didactic essay in numbered heads and reflections, with the instance and the practical direction alternating; the argument is orderly rather than systematic.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the volume was issued without the writer's name in the first edition, its authorship being established by her correspondence and by the later issues.

works.title: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous
altTitles: Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous, in Three Parts
works.description: Berkeley's immaterialism restated in dialogue form, his most readable and most-quoted philosophical performance. Over three consecutive conversations on a walk, the sceptical materialist Hylas is led to concede that matter is unintelligible and that only spirits and their ideas exist, to the vindication of common sense and religion.
works.plot: In the first dialogue Philonous drives Hylas from the dispute about secondary qualities to the concession that no sensible thing can exist unperceived. In the second, the doctrines of absolute space, time, and motion, and of matter as an inert occasion or unknown cause of ideas, are dismantled, and the real is redefined as what is perceived by minds. The third dialogue answers the charge that immaterialism breeds scepticism, solipsism, and atheism: the stability of things is secured by the divine perception, the senses give real knowledge of a world, and God is nearer to us than matter ever was. Hylas ends convinced, Philonous having shown that the paradox destroys only a philosophical fiction and leaves the garden, the table, and the body exactly as they were.
works.significance: It supplied the century's model of dialogue as philosophical argument and remains the standard entry to immaterialism; its Hylas-Philonous exchange shaped later philosophical dialogues from Hume to the Victorians.
works.meter: Lucid dramatic prose of question and retort, with the courtesy, warmth, and scene-painting of the Platonizing dialogue tradition.
works.context: Published in London in 1713 as a popular companion and corrective to the difficult Treatise of 1710, after the furor over the Principles had made Berkeley a marked man in Dublin and London intellectual society.
works.characters: Hylas; Philonous
works.structure: Three consecutive dialogues framed by a brief narrative introduction of the speakers and their walk, rising from sensation to substance to theology.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, with no competing claim and no spurious edition reported.

works.title: Threnodia Augustalis
works.description: Dryden's funeral ode on the death of Charles II in February 1685, a public lament that mourns the king and welcomes the accession of James II.
works.plot: The poem opens with an ominous vision of a bleeding comet, narrates the king's last illness and death, laments the nation's loss, and turns to consolation in the new reign.
works.significance: A significant example of the Restoration public ode and of Dryden's adaptation of Cowley's Pindaric form to serious occasion.
works.meter: Irregular Pindaric stanzas with varying line lengths and rhyme schemes.
works.context: Written within weeks of Charles II's death on 6 February 1685 and printed in the same year.
works.characters: Charles II; James II; the mourning nation
works.structure: A Pindaric sequence of irregular stanzas moving from omen through narrative to consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Timon of Athens
works.description: Shakespeare's (with Thomas Middleton's) unfinished-seeming tragedy of misanthropy: the prodigal Timon of Athens bankrupts himself in bounty, is abandoned by his flatterers, and retires to the woods to curse Athens and mankind — digging for roots and finding gold, which he flings to the whores, thieves, and the general Alcibiades, whose sack of Athens the play leaves hanging.
works.plot: Timon's feasts and gifts draw the parasites; his creditors call; his friends refuse him; at his last banquet he serves them warm water and curses them; in the woods his gold draws a new parade of leeches; Alcibiades marches on Athens; and the play ends with Timon's epitaph and the city's submission, its loose ends never fully tied.
works.significance: The most extreme of the tragedies — a play of pure negation that has found its moment in every age of financial crisis.
works.meter: A verse of savage curses — Timon's tirades against gold and mankind are its glory — with the prose of the flatterers' scenes.
works.context: Probably written about 1605–08, in the phase of Lear and Coriolanus; its satire of the Jacobean credit economy has made it a favourite of economic criticism.
works.characters: Timon; Flavius; Apemantus; Alcibiades; the Poet; the Painter; Lucullus; Lucius; Sempronius; Phrynia; Timandra; the Fool
works.structure: A two-movement structure — Athens and the woods — with the masque of the false banquet as hinge; the play's rough edges suggest an abandoned draft revised for the press.
works.attributionNotes: Thomas Middleton's share (the banquet scene and parts of the middle acts) is generally accepted on stylistic evidence.

works.title: Tirocinium
altTitles: Tirocinium; or, Advice to Parents on the Point of Sending Their Sons to Public Schools
works.form: didactic poem and conduct piece in blank verse, belonging to the century's writing on education and domestic duty
works.description: Cowper's poem of advice to parents on the education of their children, urging home and day-school teaching against the boarding public school. It sets the school-boy's loneliness, the tyranny of his seniors and the hardness of classical drudgery against the supervision of a father and the example of a Christian household, and extends its argument to the education of daughters. The poem is the most vigorous poetical statement of the eighteenth-century attack on the boarding-school.
works.plot: The speaker urges parents to keep their sons at home, arguing that the public boarding school exposes childhood to fear, vice and an idle learning of words rather than of sense. He describes the boy's first day at school, the austerities of the seminary, the return home with its spoiled affections, and the mischief of friendships formed under such confinement. The close passes to the education of girls and to the plea that the domestic and religious instruction of the family is the true seminary of the mind.
works.significance: It is the strongest poetical intervention in the eighteenth-century quarrel over boarding, and its appeal to the domestic and imaginative life of childhood belongs with the growing cult of the child that leads to the Romantic poets. Its influence on later conduct and educational writing was considerable, and it remains a primary document for the social history of schooling.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter of the Task's school, more abrupt and hortatory than Cowper's meditative verse, with pointed sententious closures.
works.context: Written in 1784, when the boarding public school was already a target of moral and educational writers and when the debate over classical curriculum, parental authority and the religious training of children was active in Evangelical and dissenting households; Cowper's own schooling and its hardships lie behind the picture.
works.characters: The advising speaker; the parent addressed; the school-boy of the description; the masters and ushers of the seminary
works.structure: A continuous didactic argument in several thematic sections, opening with the direct advice to parents, proceeding through the picture of school life, and closing with the extension to female education and the commendation of home.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is given in Cowper's own account, while the year of first separate impression has been variously reported, so publication_date is left null with the uncertainty stated.

works.title: Titus Andronicus
works.description: Shakespeare's first tragedy, written in collaboration with George Peele: the Roman general Titus returns from the Goths with the captive queen Tamora, whose revenge — the rape and mutilation of Titus's daughter Lavinia, the deaths of his sons — drives the play to its banquet of horrors, where Titus serves Tamora her own sons baked in a pie.
works.plot: Titus sacrifices Tamora's son and refuses the empire; Tamora, empress through Saturninus, avenges herself through her lover Aaron and her sons Chiron and Demetrius; Titus feigns madness, discovers the rapists, and executes his revenge in the cannibal banquet that ends the play.
works.significance: The most performed of the early tragedies and a laboratory of Shakespeare's tragic art — revenge, madness, and the stage as charnel house.
works.meter: Early verse of rhetorical set pieces — Lavinia's mute testimony, Titus's mad wordplay — with Ovid's Metamorphoses as the play's internal book of horrors.
works.context: Performed from 1594 and printed the same year; its extreme violence answered the vogue for Senecan blood inaugurated by Kyd's Spanish Tragedy.
works.characters: Titus Andronicus; Tamora; Aaron the Moor; Lavinia; Saturninus; Bassianus; Marcus Andronicus; Lucius; Chiron; Demetrius; young Lucius
works.structure: A Senecan revenge tragedy of symmetrical atrocity and counter-atrocity, with Aaron the Moor as its gleeful vice-figure.
works.attributionNotes: George Peele's co-authorship of Act 1 (and possibly other scenes) is now widely accepted on stylistic evidence.

works.title: To a Mouse
altTitles: To a Mouse, On Turning Her up in Her Nest with the Plough, November, 1785
works.form: occasional meditative lyric and address, in the tradition of the 'To a' poems of the Scottish vernacular
works.description: The shortest and most quoted of Burns's ploughman poems, addressed to a field mouse whose nest has been laid bare by the poet's plough in November 1785. Pity for the small creature turns into a meditation on provision, fear and the human lot, since the mouse at least lives in the present while mankind is tormented by memory and forecast. It is the classic lyric instance of the eighteenth-century cult of sympathy extended to the lower creation.
works.plot: The speaker apologises to the frightened mouse for the destruction of its winter house, and reflects that its pains in storing for the winter have been laid aside by an accident it could not foresee. He then envies it, because its troubles are but of the moment, whereas man looks backward and forward and is wretched. The poem ends in a prayer that the mouse may be spared the cruel human remembrances, and that its fate may teach the poet himself to bear his own disappointments of hope.
works.significance: Its lines on the best laid schemes of mice and men passing often ago became among the most familiar proverbs in English, and the poem is a standard example of the preromantic lyric that reasons outward from a small accident of feeling. It also fixed the figure of the thinking ploughman as a poet of sensibility and of providential anxiety.
works.meter: The six-line Burns stanza (Standard Habbie): four four-beat Scots lines and two short trimming lines, with the rhyming pattern a-a-a-b-a-b and an insistent colloquial rhythm.
works.context: Written at Mossgiel in the autumn of 1785, when Burns's farming prospects were failing and his poems were being prepared for the press; the mood of disappointed hope and of dependence on the weather of a small farm belongs exactly to that season, and the poem's ethic of pity for animals draws on the contemporary debate about sympathy and the moral sense.
works.characters: The mouse; the ploughman-speaker
works.structure: Six short stanzas moving from the immediate incident to apology, comparison and general conclusion, the argument of the meditation rising steadily out of a single act of ploughing.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the date of composition is Burns's own, entered in his memorandum of the poem, and the printed title carries that date.

works.title: To a Skylark
works.form: Romantic ode and elemental hymn; the invisible-voice lyric of the school of the greater odes, with the simile catalogue of the devotional hymn.
works.description: The period's most quoted hymn to an invisible bird, addressed to a skylark rising out of the English meadow into the unfelt air and singing as it ascends. The poem reasons from the bird's joy to the condition of the human mind, which can only imagine pleasure it cannot feel and which forebodes pain even in its mirth. Its structure of twenty-one stanzas with a recurring short closing line gives it the character of an incantation, and it was written, by the poet's own account, from a walk on the shore near the Tuscan city where he then lived.
works.plot: The bird, hailed as a spirit rather than a bird, hides in the blue deep of the sky and is known only by the sound that falls like hail, like moonlight, like a glow-worm in the grass. The poem then runs through a series of comparisons, a poet new to his thoughts, a noble damsel in a palace of hushed sorrow, a glow-worm, a rose hidden by its own leaves, rain waking the flowers, and every sweet and joyful sight, before granting that no simile reaches the bird's happiness. The human condition is then set against it, we look before and after and mourn before our mirth is gone, and the poem ends with the prayer that if the bird's spirit were known, the poet's words would not fall dead upon the world. The argument is that the unembodied song measures the distance between nature's joy and human self-consciousness.
works.significance: It is the best-known of the period's lyrics and became a schoolroom and anthological test of pure rapture in verse, much imitated in the short measures of the later nineteenth century. Its analysis of human consciousness as a creature that looks before and after gave the century one of its most portable definitions of melancholy, and the stanza's structure has been much discussed as a model of the lyric line's upward figure.
works.meter: Stanzas of four iambic pentameter lines followed by a single trimmed tetrameter line, rhyming ababb with the short fifth line repeated as a refrain; the abbreviations of the measure, all but two lines being of fewer syllables, give the stanza its upward momentum.
works.context: Written in the summer of 1820, in the season the poet spent on the coast of Tuscany after the birth of a son and in the months of the Neapolitan and Piedmontese risings and their suppression, and published in the London volume of that year's shorter poems. Its companion volume of the same season contained the titan drama and the wind ode, and its treatment of inspiration as something granted rather than achieved answered the era's account of the poet's faculty.
works.characters: the skylark, addressed as a star of heaven and as a spirit of joy; the poet who would be taught the measure of its thoughts
works.structure: Twenty-one stanzas of continuous address, moving from the ascent to the catalogue of similes, to the reflection on human sorrow and to the closing prayer; there is no story but a single sustained act of attention.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; an early prose note on the circumstances of composition was written out by the poet, and the text varies only in small readings between the first issue and the posthumous collections.

works.title: To a Waterfowl
works.form: Nature lyric and conversation poem addressed to a bird
works.description: The shortest and best-known of the author's nature lyrics, in which a single bird flying across an evening sky becomes a lesson in providential guidance. The poem's argument is that the same power which directs the bird also orders the wanderer's steps. It is the central text of the American conversation with nature.
works.plot: The speaker watches a waterfowl flying alone across the twilight, seeking its resting place on the marsh or the lake. He asks what guide directs the bird over pathless waters, and answers that no eye watches it in vain. The second movement draws the moral: the same power that teaches the bird his way will teach the poet, wandering alone, his path too. The poem closes with an act of trust, committing the wanderer's steps to that guidance.
works.significance: It is the model of the American lyric of single perception and moral inference, imitated for a generation. Its trust in a guidance revealed by nature rather than by scripture defines the author's religious imagination. It is the poem most often cited as the native counterpart of Wordsworth's shorter lyrics.
works.meter: Alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter in the common-metre hymn stanza, with regular rhyme
works.context: Composed in 1811 on a solitary ride and long kept among the author's papers before appearing in print; the collected volume of 1821 gave it its permanent text. Its providential consolation belongs to the decline of Calvinist election in New England. The poem's currency in school recitation made it a national property by mid-century.
works.structure: Two-stanza lyric of observation and application, the first stanza picturing the flight, the second drawing the consoling inference.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the date of the poem's first periodical appearance is reported differently in the biographical literature and is not asserted here.

works.title: To Autumn
works.form: Romantic ode and nature lyric of the school of the great odes; the seasonal meditation and the hymn of the year's departure, in the most concentrated form the period reached.
works.description: The last of the great short poems and the closing piece of the volume of 1820, a lyric of three eleven-line stanzas which presents the season not as the prelude to death but as a condition of ripeness and of its own music. It personifies autumn as the close friend of the maturing sun, as the harvester resting by the half-reaped furrow and as the gatherer of the last gleanings, and answers the questions of the spring with the sounds of the day of departure. Its stillness, its freedom from argument and its handling of the transience of the year have made it the most admired short poem of the period.
works.plot: The first stanza presents autumn as the neighbour of the sun that ripens the fruit and fills the gourd and the hazel shells with kernel, and as the season that makes the swags bulge and the cyder press drop the last oozings. The second finds the season itself at rest, sitting on a half-reaped furrow, winnowing on the floor, and sleeping by the harvest cider-house while the last gleanings cross the brook, and the third asks where are the songs of spring, and answers that the listener has his own music in the wailful choir of the small gnats, the bleating lambs, the crickets and the swallow. The argument is that the season of decay has its own completeness and that the music of departure is not an absence but an instrument.
works.significance: It is the most complete and most quoted of the period's short poems, and the standing example of a lyric that presents a process without a moral and a death without lamentation. Its handling of the personified season gave the later nature lyric one of its permanent registers, and the sequence of the three odes and this poem forms the schoolroom definition of the Romantic lyric at its limit.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter in three stanzas of eleven lines, the rhyme abab and the remainder varied, with the closing line of each stanza used as a caesura of rest; the poem is almost free of metaphor of the violent kind and depends on the verb and on the article of detail.
works.context: Composed on a Sunday in the September of 1819, on a walk in the fields near the town where the poet was staying with a friend, in the season of his last effort at the titan poem and of the beginning of his illness, and printed in the volume of July 1820 as one of the closing pieces. Its date, after the abandonment of the larger work, made it the symbol in later biography of a short career's harvest, and its freedom from the argument of the greater odes was widely imitated in the seasonal lyric of the later century.
works.characters: autumn personified as the close friend of the maturing sun, as the reaper, the winnower and the gleaner, and as the hearer of the season's own choir
works.structure: Three stanzas of eleven lines, the first of ripening, the second of the season at rest in the harvest field, the third of the sounds of the evening of the year; there is no development but a change of aspect.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution uncontested; the poem is in the transcript of the volume and is dated by the poet's own letters of the season.

works.title: To Helen
works.form: Romantic lyric of idealized beauty; address-poem in the Horatian and classical manner
works.description: A short lyric of classical beauty addressed to a woman whose loveliness is figured as a ship arriving from a warm sea into a harbour of the soul. It is the poem that made beauty, and not desire, the author's enduring subject. Its three stanzas move from simile to arrival to a scene of the beloved as a torch-bearer of the antique world.
works.plot: The beloved's beauty is compared to the barks that, wind-laid upon a perfumed sea, bear weary wayfarers to their native country. The poem then asks what the tired wanderer would give to reach the casements of that shore and the Niche where the Faun stands, half-embowered in the fragrant lilies of the stream. In the last stanza the beloved comes across the night with shining feet, and the region of the poem is disclosed as a home to which the wanderer belongs.
works.significance: It is the earliest of the author's lyrics to enter the permanent anthologies and the source of his reputation for the poetry of beauty. Its treatment of the beloved as a vessel of homecoming set a pattern for later American lyric addresses. It marks the moment at which his verse left cosmological ambition for the short perfect form.
works.meter: Iambic trimeter and tetrameter stanzas of nine lines with an intricate rhyme scheme
works.context: First printed in the collected volume of 1831, where it stands among the poems the author's later editors classed with his verse of youth. Its classical furniture belongs to the schoolroom Hellenism of American colleges in the 1820s. The lyric was revised and reissued through the following decade.
works.characters: Helen; the weary wayfarer
works.structure: Three-stanza lyric, each stanza developing one figure: the arriving ship, the shore and its shrine, the beloved's approach by night.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the title under which the poem is known was settled in the author's lifetime.

works.title: To His Coy Mistress
works.description: Marvell's most famous lyric, a carpe diem argument to a reluctant mistress: had we world enough and time, coyness were no crime, but time's winged chariot hurries near, so let us rather devour time than languish — a brilliant fusion of logic, wit, and urgency.
works.plot: A three-part syllogistic argument ('Had we but world enough and time ... But at my back I always hear / Time's winged chariot ... Therefore ...'), urging physical love against the pressure of mortality.
works.significance: One of the most anthologised and admired English lyrics, a supreme example of metaphysical wit applied to the carpe diem theme.
works.meter: Iambic tetrameter couplets with metaphysical conceits and a witty, urgent tone.
works.context: Composed probably in the 1650s, unpublished in Marvell's lifetime and printed in Miscellaneous Poems (1681); it draws on the classical carpe diem tradition of Horace and Ovid.
works.characters: the speaker; his coy mistress
works.structure: A dramatic monologue structured as a logical argument in three movements, in iambic tetrameter couplets.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: To the Ladies
works.form: ironic address in verse; poem of the women question
works.description: A short ironic poem addressed to women, remonstrating against the conditions of marriage and against the education that makes a wife a dependent. It is one of the most anthologised lyrics of the debate about women, and its couplets turn the commonplaces of gallantry against the law and custom that they conceal.
works.plot: The poet addresses her sex with a complaint of their treatment, showing that they are educated only to please and are then governed by the men they have pleased. Marriage is represented as a condition in which the wife's person and estate pass into another's keeping, and the language of superiority used against women is turned back upon it. The poem closes on the advice that the ladies improve their minds and their use of them.
works.significance: It is a landmark of early feminist verse and one of the most quoted of the period's poems on marriage and women's condition, much used in the modern recovery of the writing of women before the eighteenth century.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of the plain Augustan manner, the point of the argument closing on the rhyme; the idiom is that of the conversation poem of the debate about the sexes.
works.context: Written in the circles of learned women of the south-west in the last years of the seventeenth century, circulating in manuscript, and appearing in print among her poems in 1703, in the season of the pamphlet and stage war about women's abilities that produced the essays and the verse poems of the question.
works.structure: A single continuous address in closed couplets, moving from complaint to argument to counsel; there is no narrative, the argument being carried by the sequence of the retorts.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to the poet is settled by the manuscript tradition and by the printed collections that carry her name; the poem existed in more than one state, so the year recorded here is that of the printed collection and not of composition.

works.title: To the Memory of Mr. Oldham
works.description: Dryden's elegy for the young satirist John Oldham, who died of smallpox in December 1683; a short masterpiece of restrained praise that compares Oldham's early death to that of Marcellus and Nisus.
works.plot: The poem laments the loss of a kindred wit, concedes the difference in style between the two poets, and consoles with the thought that Oldham's early death spared him the decay of age and dulness.
works.significance: Often judged the finest short elegy in English between Lycidas and In Memoriam, and a canonical instance of Dryden's capacity for personal warmth.
works.meter: Heroic couplets with frequent enjambment and a deliberately unpolished, masculine roughness suited to the subject.
works.context: Written in the winter of 1683-4 and prefixed to the 1684 edition of Oldham's Works.
works.characters: John Oldham; the speaker; Marcellus (alluded to)
works.structure: A single continuous elegiac meditation of twenty-seven lines.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Tottel's Miscellany
altTitles: Songes and Sonettes, written by the ryght honorable Lorde Henry Haward late Earle of Surrey, and other
works.form: anthology of sonnets, lyrics, and epigrams
works.description: The first great printed anthology of English poetry: 271 poems by Surrey, Wyatt, Nicholas Grimald, and other courtly poets, published by Richard Tottel on 5 June 1557 under the title Songes and Sonettes. It fixed the public canon of the Henrician lyric and went through nine editions by 1587.
works.plot: An anthology without narrative frame: sonnets, songs, elegies, and epigrams arranged by author, beginning with Surrey, whose name gave the volume its selling title.
works.significance: The founding anthology of English poetry: it created the reading public for the lyric, fixed the reputations of Wyatt and Surrey, and supplied the Elizabethan poets with their metre and manner.
works.meter: The full range of the early Tudor lyric: sonnets, poulter's measure, short-line songs; the anthology standardized the decasyllabic line for a public audience.
works.context: Printed two years after the Marian restoration began; the miscellany carried the Henrician court's poetry into the Elizabethan age and made the court lyric a national possession.
works.characters: the courtly poets (Surrey, Wyatt, Grimald, and others)
works.structure: Miscellany organized by poet, with the Earl of Surrey's poems first; the arrangement itself constitutes the first printed history of the English lyric.
works.attributionNotes: Compiled by Richard Tottel (publisher); the authorship of the 'uncertain authors' poems remains largely unknown. Recorded as collaborative with no author links, per the validator's anonymity rule.

works.title: Towneley Plays
works.description: The Towneley (Wakefield) cycle of thirty-two plays, from the Creation to the Last Judgement, preserved in the Towneley manuscript (c. 1500) and long associated with Wakefield: famous above all for the six plays in the nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' attributed to the Wakefield Master — including the Second Shepherds' Play, the comic masterpiece of the English cycles, with its sheep-stealing Mak and its nativity of the stolen lamb.
works.plot: The cycle retells salvation history from Lucifer's fall through the patriarchs to Christ's Passion and the Judgement; the Master's plays — Noah and his scolding wife, the two Shepherds' plays, Herod, and the Buffeting — transform the biblical matter with a vernacular comedy of Yorkshire shepherds, shrews, and ranting tyrants unmatched in the other cycles.
works.significance: The Second Shepherds' Play is the most famous English medieval drama: the cycle's blend of farce and nativity embodies the mystery tradition at its theatrical summit.
works.meter: The unique nine-line 'Wakefield stanza' (aabcccbddb with internal rhyme) in the Master's plays; thirteen-line stanza and couplets elsewhere.
works.context: Composed and compiled c. 1400–1500, probably at Wakefield, where the plays were performed on Corpus Christi day; the manuscript (Huntington Library, MS HM 1) belonged to the Towneley family of Lancashire, from which the cycle takes its name.
works.characters: Mak the sheep-stealer; Gill; the shepherds (Coll, Gib, Daw); Noah and his wife; Herod; Christ; Pilate
works.structure: A pageant cycle of thirty-two plays, partially dependent on York but transformed by the Wakefield Master's comic and homiletic genius.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative; the 'Wakefield Master' is a scholarly construct for the author of the six stanza-linked plays.

works.title: Toxophilus
works.description: Ascham's dialogue on the art of archery, presented to Henry VIII as both a practical treatise and a model of English prose style — the first book on a sport written in the English language.
works.plot: Two speakers, Toxophilus ('lover of the bow') and Philologus ('lover of learning'), debate whether study or shooting better befits a gentleman; Toxophilus vindicates archery as recreation, describes the bow, its parts, and the craft of shooting, and argues for the health and military value of the sport, while the dialogue itself demonstrates the eloquence the English tongue can achieve.
works.significance: The first English treatise on a sport and a deliberate demonstration of the capacities of English prose for learned subjects; together with The Schoolmaster it established Ascham's reputation as a stylist and educational theorist.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written 1544–45 when Ascham was reader in Greek at St John's College, Cambridge, and presented to Henry VIII in 1545 in the royal library at Westminster, for which Ascham received a pension; archery's military role had been reaffirmed by statute in 1541.
works.characters: Toxophilus; Philologus
works.structure: Two-book dialogue framed by a preface to 'all gentle men and yeomen of England', with a systematic technical exposition embedded in the conversational form.

works.title: Translation of Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (Hutchinson)
works.description: Lucy Hutchinson's complete verse translation of Lucretius's De Rerum Natura, the first ever into English, undertaken in the 1650s and dedicated to the Earl of Anglesey; she later wrote a preface condemning the Epicurean philosophy she had so brilliantly rendered.
works.plot: The translation renders all six books of Lucretius's didactic epic on Epicurean physics, the nature of the soul, the origin of society, and the fear of death.
works.significance: A landmark of Restoration translation and of women's classical learning; its preface is a striking document of a devout Puritan woman negotiating with Epicurean materialism.
works.meter: Heroic couplets; Hutchinson's version is the first complete English Lucretius.
works.context: Composed in the 1650s and revised up to the 1670s; the manuscript was dedicated to Arthur Annesley, Earl of Anglesey, and remained unpublished until 1996.
works.characters: Venus; Epicurus (alluded to); Memmius
works.structure: Six books in heroic couplets, following Lucretius's own structure.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lucy Hutchinson; the manuscript is in her hand with her prefatory address to the Earl of Anglesey.

works.title: Translations of the Letters of a Hindoo Rajah
works.form: Prose fiction; epistolary and travel satire with an oriental framing device; fiction of the India question
works.description: A satirical epistolary fiction presented as the letters of an Indian envoy and his attendants, translated by their interpreter, observing English society, its politics, its literature and its religions on a tour from Bengal through London and Scotland. The oriental point of view exposes the arrogance, inconstancy and self-interest of the British in India, and the ridicule of Anglo-Indian nabob wealth and of fashionable exotic taste is double-edged, since the observer's own superstition is also laid bare. The book was an immediate success and established the writer's reputation. It is the most accomplished of the 1790s vogue of oriental-mirror satire.
works.plot: A Hindoo rajah's embassy, accompanied by his interpreter and his family, travels to England on the business of a disputed succession and a claim for redress against company officials. In letters home the party describes the English constitution, its parties and its pulpit, its theatres, its manners and its treatment of women, while the interpreter's own narrative of an injury in India reveals the mechanism of corruption and ruined families behind the civilising spectacle. The succession claim miscarries, the embassy disperses, and the closing letters report the observer's return and his confirmed contempt for a nation that talks of liberty while oppressing dependants.
works.significance: The ablest of the woman-written oriental satires of the 1790s and an important text for study of British writing about India before and after the impeachment, of the epistolary travel-satire tradition, and of the conservative answer to philosophical fiction. Its framing of translation and interpretation has made it a frequent object of later critical attention.
works.meter: Prose, no metre; the style imitates formal translated correspondence, with sententious moral reflection and sustained ironic understatement
works.context: Published in 1796, after the India debates, the impeachment trial of a company governor-general and the regency settlement had made oriental dependency a subject of daily parliamentary and print controversy. The book also answers the decade's fashion for pretend oriental tales and for imitations of a famous Persian translation, and its Edinburgh and London scenes draw on the debate over Jacobin novels and political enthusiasm after the French Revolution.
works.characters: The interpreter-narrator and his family; a young rajah and his counsellors; English acquaintances in London and Edinburgh, including a man of letters and a political orator; a nabob's family in Bengal
works.structure: Epistolary satire in two volumes with an embedded narrative by the interpreter; the letters progress from description to argument and are framed by a translator's preface and notes, which allow the joke to be sustained at several levels of narration.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name, with the translation device as a fictional persona; no dispute over authorship.

works.title: Travels in New-England and New-York
works.form: Travel narrative and local guide; topographical and statistical survey with moral argument
works.description: A survey of the country and the people of the northern states, written from journal matter and printed after the author's death. It combines topographical description, agricultural observation, statistical tables and moral and religious argument. It is the fullest early American example of the traveller's national survey.
works.plot: The narrative moves through Connecticut, Massachusetts and the eastern and western parts of New York, describing towns, soils, manufactures, schools and churches as it goes. It reports conversations with farmers, clergymen and lawyers, and it argues that the prosperity of the country depends on its religious and educational institutions. Its accounts of the Dutch settlements and of the western districts give a picture of a nation in motion. The work closes with reflections on the destiny of a Christian and lettered commonwealth.
works.significance: It is the most systematic American portrait of the northern states before Tocqueville and a central document of the clerical survey of the republic. Its fusion of topographical detail with religious argument shows the didactic descriptive tradition continuing into the 1820s. It supplies the social map against which the native fiction of the same decade was written.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published from the author's papers in 1821, with an enlarged four-volume issue shortly afterwards, and composed from tours taken in the last years of the eighteenth century and after the peace of 1815. Its attention to canals, schools and denominations reflects the internal-improvement moment of the era. Its author had been president of Yale since 1795.
works.structure: Travels arranged by route and district, with journal narrative, descriptive survey, tables of numbers and inserted disquisition; posthumously edited from memoranda.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the volume was edited and issued after the author's death from his journals.

works.title: Treatise on the Astrolabe
works.description: Chaucer's prose treatise on the construction and use of the astrolabe, written in 1391 for his ten-year-old son Lewis: the first technical treatise in English prose, and the earliest English work on a scientific instrument. Its precision, clarity, and fatherly address make it unique in the medieval English canon.
works.plot: In five planned parts — of which the first two and a supplement survive — the treatise describes the astrolabe and its parts, teaches the child to take altitudes and tell the time, and promises the tables and theories that would complete the work; the famous prologue addresses 'Lyte Lowys my sone' with pedagogical tenderness.
works.significance: The first scientific prose in English and the classic of its kind: the treatise's plain style is a landmark in the development of English as a language of learning.
works.meter: Prose: plain, exact, and carefully ordered, in the tradition of the practical manual.
works.context: Dated 1391 in the prologue, written for Lewis Chaucer, then about ten years old, in London; it draws on the Latin tradition of Messahala and the practical astronomy of the universities; preserved in some thirty manuscripts.
works.characters: the author (as father-teacher); Lewis (addressee)
works.structure: A didactic treatise of definitions, propositions, and conclusions, each numbered for the child's use, with worked examples from the Oxford latitude.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure (named in the prologue).

works.title: Trivia
altTitles: Trivia; or, the Art of Walking the Streets of London
works.description: Gay's mock-didactic guide to the sights, shows, coaches, clothes and night entertainments of London, written as an art of town-walking in the manner of the classical didactic poem.
works.plot: The Muse of Trivia instructs the citizen and the country visitor where to look and how to dress, what to see by day in the parks, the exchange and the shops, and what to seek by night in the tavern, the box at the theatre and the masquerade, with an antiquarian appendix on the town's own history.
works.significance: It is the century's most charming urban descriptive poem and the complement to the country prospect of Windsor-Forest, preserving the topology of Augustan London for later readers.
works.meter: Heroic couplet of easy narrative breadth, with the rapid list and the colloquial tag.
works.context: Published in the season of the Spectator's town-painting essays and of the new London guide books, when the coach, the pawn and the opera made the street a subject of moral and commercial description.
works.characters: the poet and his Muse of Trivia; the town of London and its shows
works.structure: Three books of didactic argument after the manner of the art poem, with the catalogue of places and the closing historical inquiry.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the poem appeared among the pieces of a periodical miscellany conducted by Gay and his friends, which has encouraged occasional mis-division of the volume's parts.

works.title: Troilus and Cressida
works.description: Shakespeare's bitter anatomy of the Trojan War: the lovers Troilus and Cressida are separated by her exchange to the Greeks, and her infidelity with Diomedes poisons their romance, while the Greek camp degenerates into a satire of its own heroes — Achilles sulking, Ajax a blockhead, and the cynical Thersites commentating on the whole — and Hector's chivalry dies under Achilles' Myrmidons.
works.plot: The war stalls; Cressida is traded for a Trojan prisoner and betrays Troilus with Diomedes before his eyes; the debate over Helen, Ulysses' speech on degree, the gulling of Ajax, and the duel of Hector and Ajax fill the middle acts; the play ends with Hector's murder and Pandarus's epilogue bequeathing the audience his diseases.
works.significance: The great Elizabethan debunking of the heroic ideal — the play in which the Renaissance turned its scepticism on its own founding myth.
works.meter: A harsh, debate-driven verse, with Thersites' prose invective as the play's running commentary.
works.context: Written about 1602, in the wake of the 'war of the theatres' and Essex's fall; printed in 1609 with an epistle hailing it as a play never clapper-clawed by the vulgar.
works.characters: Troilus; Cressida; Pandarus; Hector; Achilles; Ulysses; Agamemnon; Nestor; Ajax; Diomedes; Thersites; Helen; Priam; Cassandra
works.structure: A double plot — the love story and the war council — that refuses tragic or comic closure, ending in anti-climax and epilogue.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Troilus and Criseyde
works.description: Chaucer's great poem of love and loss, some 8,200 lines in rhyme royal, translating and transforming Boccaccio's Il Filostrato: the Trojan prince Troilus, aided by Pandarus, wins the love of Criseyde, loses her to the Greek camp in an exchange of prisoners, and learns of her betrayal with Diomede before his death in battle — all concluded by the narrator's Boethian repudiation of worldly love. The greatest love poem in Middle English.
works.plot: Troilus, scorning love, is struck by Criseyde's beauty in the temple; his friend and uncle Pandarus engineers their union through letters and stratagems, and the lovers enjoy a secret happiness — until Criseyde is exchanged for the prisoner Antenor and sent to the Greek camp, where Diomede courts her and she yields; Troilus, after ominous dreams and the sight of the brooch he gave her on Diomede's armour, seeks death in battle, and his soul ascends to the eighth sphere, laughing at the woe of the world below.
works.significance: The greatest narrative poem of the English Middle Ages after the Canterbury Tales; its psychological depth and tragic irony made it the model for Henryson's Testament of Cresseid and the ancestor of Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas (seven-line, ababbcc) handled with supreme flexibility; the first sustained masterpiece of the English decasyllabic line.
works.context: Composed c. 1382–86 in London, after Chaucer's Italian journeys, adapting Boccaccio's Filostrato with additions from Boethius, Dante, and the Trojan romances; dedicated to 'moral Gower and philosophical Strode'; preserved in sixteen manuscripts and printed by Caxton (c. 1483).
works.characters: Troilus; Criseyde; Pandarus; Diomede; Hector; the Narrator
works.structure: Five books moving from courtship through consummation to betrayal and death, framed by the narrator's ironic service to the servants of love and closed by the palinode commending the love of God.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the work is the first he names in the Retraction.

works.title: Troy Book
works.description: John Lydgate's vast verse translation (over 30,000 lines) of Guido delle Colonne's Historia destructionis Troiae, commissioned by Henry V in 1412 and completed in 1420: the full Trojan story retold as a mirror of chivalry, kingship, and tragedy. The most ambitious poem of the fifteenth century and the foundation of Lydgate's fame.
works.plot: From Jason and the golden fleece through the rape of Helen and the ten years' war to the fall of Troy and the wanderings of the Greeks, the poem recounts the Trojan matter at length, moralizing throughout on pride, treason, and the fickleness of fortune, with Hector as its pattern of knighthood.
works.significance: The fullest English Troy narrative and the great monument of Lancastrian literary patronage; it made Lydgate the laureate of the fifteenth century and fed the Tudor cult of Troy.
works.meter: Decasyllabic couplets in the 'Lydgate line', frequently headless, with aureate diction.
works.context: Commissioned by Henry, Prince of Wales, in 1412, completed in 1420, and dedicated to the king after Agincourt; its Troy matter spoke to Lancastrian imperial ambition; printed by Pynson (1513) and widely read into the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Hector; Achilles; Priam; Paris; Helen; Troilus; Ulysses; Agamemnon
works.structure: Five books following Guido's divisions, with prologue and envoy to Henry V; set-piece descriptions, speeches, and moral digressions throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Lydgate's authorship secure.

works.title: Twelfth Night
altTitles: Twelfth Night, or What You Will
works.description: Shakespeare's comedy of disguise and desire: Viola, shipwrecked in Illyria, serves Duke Orsino disguised as the boy Cesario and carries his love-suit to Olivia — who falls in love with Cesario — while the Puritan steward Malvolio is gulled into yellow stockings by the forged letter, and the revels of Sir Toby and the clown roll on to the reunion of the twins.
works.plot: Orsino loves Olivia; Olivia loves Cesario (Viola); Viola loves Orsino; the triangle dissolves when Sebastian, Viola's twin, appears and marries Olivia; Malvolio's humiliation darkens the last scene with his promise of revenge — 'I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you'.
works.significance: The crowning achievement of Shakespearean comedy — the subtlest study of erotic fluidity before modern drama — and the seed of a thousand later plots.
works.meter: A flexible mix of blank verse, prose, and song, with Feste's 'Come away, come away, death' and the closing rain-song.
works.context: Performed 1601–02 (the Middle Temple performance of 2 February 1602 is recorded); the title marks the Feast of Epiphany and the licence of holiday misrule.
works.characters: Viola (Cesario); Orsino; Olivia; Sebastian; Malvolio; Sir Toby Belch; Sir Andrew Aguecheek; Maria; Feste; Antonio; Fabian
works.structure: Two households — Orsino's and Olivia's — with the sub-plot of Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, Maria, and Feste against Malvolio, all resolved by the twins' reunion.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Twelve Conclusions of the Lollards
works.description: The Lollard manifesto of 1395, presented to parliament and nailed to the doors of Westminster Hall and St Paul's during its session: twelve conclusions denouncing the church's temporal lordship, clerical celibacy, transubstantiation, blessing of material things, clerical exemption, and the wars, crafts, and oaths by which the clergy sustain their power. The most famous document of English medieval dissent.
works.plot: The conclusions move from the church's worldly dominion and the clergy's unworthy estate through the 'false miracle of the sacrament' to the 'unnecessary trades' (goldsmiths, armourers) that serve the church's pride, closing with the demand for a poor, preaching clergy and the renunciation of war and oaths.
works.significance: The founding manifesto of English religious dissent: its arguments against images, pilgrimage, and transubstantiation anticipate the Reformation by a century and a quarter.
works.meter: Plain, forceful English with Latin tags, in the Lollard plain style.
works.context: Presented to parliament and posted at Westminster and St Paul's in 1395, in the political crisis of Richard II's reign; it provoked the orthodox counter-writings of Roger Dymmok and others and fixed the public image of Lollardy.
works.characters: none (collective manifesto)
works.structure: Twelve numbered propositions, each with its brief scriptural and logical support, in the petitionary form of a parliamentary bill.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous (collective authorship in the Wycliffite movement).
sources: Modern Chivalry (American Fiction Series)

works.title: Two Treatises of Government
altTitles: Two Treatises of Government: In the Latter, the False Principles and Foundation of Sir Robert Filmer and His Followers are Detected and Overthrown
works.description: Locke's classic of liberal political theory, published anonymously in 1689, which refutes Filmer's divine-right absolutism and sets out a theory of government founded on natural rights, consent, property, and the right of resistance.
works.plot: The First Treatise demolishes Filmer's Patriarcha chapter by chapter; the Second Treatise argues that political power derives from the consent of free and equal individuals who form a society to protect their natural rights to life, liberty, and estate.
works.significance: The foundational text of modern liberalism and of the theory of limited constitutional government; it directly influenced the American Declaration of Independence and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man.
works.meter: Vigorous argumentative prose with biblical and legal citation.
works.context: Composed during the Exclusion Crisis of 1679-81, revised in Holland, and published anonymously in December 1689 (dated 1690) as a justification of the Revolution that brought William and Mary to the throne; Locke never acknowledged authorship.
works.structure: Two treatises: the first a detailed refutation, the second a positive theory in 19 chapters.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; Locke's authorship was not publicly acknowledged in his lifetime but is established from his correspondence and papers.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Ulysses
altTitles: The Tragedy of Ulysses, King of Ithaca
works.description: Rowe's last completed tragedy, taking the return of Ulysses to a court and a household invaded by suitors, and making the trial of recognition and of constancy the moral centre of the play.
works.plot: The disguised king of Ithaca watches the insolence of the suitors and the trial of his wife's fidelity, and the recognition of Ulysses by his son and his household issues in the destruction of the invaders and the restoration of order.
works.significance: It closes the line of regular Augustan classical tragedy that Rowe had helped to establish, and its handling of fidelity and of the invaded household shows the moral drama of the Fair Penitent transferred to the Homerick subject.
works.meter: Blank verse of the later Rowe, plainer and more argumentative than that of The Fair Penitent, with the formal recitative of the recognitions.
works.context: Acted at Drury Lane in the last season of Rowe's official connection with the theatre, in the years when the classical and Homerick subjects were being reworked for a public that was turning to the opera and the pantomime.
works.characters: Ulysses; Penelope; Telemachus; the suitors of Ithaca
works.structure: Regular tragedy in five acts on the Homelian argument, organised as a progression from disguise and observation to recognition and judgment.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Unitarian Christianity
works.form: Homily or sermon with polemical argument; the party sermon of a religious movement
works.description: The sermon that gave American Unitarianism its public statement of faith and its reply to the charge of unbelief. It distinguishes the doctrinal and practical articles of the Unitarians, claims the authority of reason in religion, and refuses to make the creeds of other parties its own. Its plain, deliberate style became the manner of a movement.
works.plot: The sermon first separates the doctrines on which its party is defined from the practices for which it is censured, and grants that some charges are just. It then states the Unitarian belief in one God and in the moral authority of Christ, and argues that a unitarian creed is simpler and therefore more fit for a reasonable creature. It answers the accusation that its party denies the scriptural scheme of atonement and of innate depravity. It closes by commending charity of judgment and by claiming for the conscience the duty of thinking.
works.significance: It is the founding document of American Unitarianism as a self-conscious party and one of the most influential religious statements of the early republic. Its defence of reason in religion shaped the preaching, the criticism and the social reform of the next generation. It supplies the intellectual context for the religious conscience of the literature of New England in this period.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached at Baltimore in May 1819, at the moment when the Unitarian controversy had divided the standing congregations of eastern Massachusetts and when the party was organizing its churches, its periodicals and its divinity school. The occasion was an ordination service, and the sermon was soon read as the public statement of a body of ministers who had not yet taken an institutional name. Its plain rhetoric was itself a claim about the relation of reason to faith in a republican country.
works.structure: Occasional sermon in the discursive New England manner, divided between statement of doctrine, answer to objections and practical application.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution undisputed; the sermon was printed from the pulpit notes and reissued in the author's collected discourses.

works.title: Upon Appleton House
altTitles: Upon Appleton House, to My Lord Fairfax
works.description: Marvell's long country-house poem written while he was tutor to Mary Fairfax at Nun Appleton during the Civil Wars: a topographical and meditative tour of the estate that allegorises the Fairfax family's retirement, the turmoil of the times, and the ideal of a well-ordered natural and social world.
works.plot: The poem moves through the house, gardens, meadows, river, and woods of the estate, reflecting on the modest architecture against the vanity of great buildings, on Fairfax's withdrawal from public life, and on the mowing of the meadows as an emblem of the Civil Wars, before turning to the young Mary Fairfax as the estate's hope.
works.significance: The great English country-house poem, it combines topography, politics, natural history, and allegory and has been central to modern readings of Marvell, of landscape poetry, and of the literature of the Interregnum.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with a witty, glancing, associative movement.
works.context: Written c. 1651 during Fairfax's retirement from Parliament's command, amid the Civil Wars and the Scottish campaign; it is the fullest English estate poem and a subtle reflection on the political moment.
works.characters: Lord Fairfax; the poet; Mary Fairfax; the estate
works.structure: A country-house poem in octosyllabic couplets, structured as a progress through the landscape with meditative digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested.

works.title: Utopia
altTitles: Libellus vere aureus, nec minus salutaris quam festivus, de optimo rei publicae statu deque nova insula Utopia
works.description: A humanist dialogue in two books describing the imaginary island commonwealth of Utopia, where property is held in common, religious toleration prevails, and the social and economic abuses of early sixteenth-century Europe are criticized by contrast.
works.plot: Book I frames the work as a report of a conversation in Antwerp among More himself, his friend Peter Giles, and the fictional traveller Raphael Hythlodaeus, who denounces the social evils of Europe — enclosure, penal severity, court flattery — and debates whether a philosopher should serve princes. Book II contains Hythlodaeus's full description of Utopia: its geography, magistrates, working day, communal property, marriage customs, education, religion, and warfare.
works.significance: The founding text of the utopian genre and one of the masterpieces of northern humanism; its punning title (ou-topia 'no place' / eu-topia 'good place') and its fusion of satire, political theory, and fiction made it the most influential secular prose work of the English Renaissance, directly shaping works from Bacon's New Atlantis to modern dystopian fiction.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Composed in 1515–16 during More's embassy to the Netherlands for the wool trade negotiations, at the height of his humanist circle's activities; printed at Louvain by Thierry Martens under the supervision of Erasmus, Giles, and others, and translated into English by Ralph Robinson in 1551.
works.characters: Thomas More; Peter Giles; Raphael Hythlodaeus; Cardinal John Morton (recalled in the dialogue)
works.structure: Two-part dialogue framed by a prefatory letter to Peter Giles and paratexts (maps, Utopian alphabet and quatrain); Book I is a debate on counsel, Book II a systematic description of the island, with the whole enclosed in the fiction of Hythlodaeus's eyewitness report.

works.title: Vainglory
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A moralizing poem of 84 lines contrasting the boastful man, puffed up with wine and pride in the hall, with the wise man who walks humbly before God. The poem analyses the psychology of vainglory and warns that pride corrupts the soul and courts the devil.
works.plot: The poet describes the vainglorious man at the feast, eloquent in self-praise but hollow within, deceived by the devil's arrows of pride; against him is set the wise man of measured speech and right counsel, whom God rewards. The poem closes with the warning that the proud man's fall is certain.
works.significance: A penetrating psychological study of pride that fuses the wisdom and homiletic traditions, and a vivid picture of the moral dangers of the Anglo-Saxon feast-hall.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic diction of the Exeter religious poems; the hall setting is evoked in the heroic vocabulary of feasting and treasure.
works.context: Pride was the sin of the heroic hall culture, and the poem turns the imagery of the feast and the boast against its own social setting, in the manner of the homilists' attacks on drunkenness and vainglory.
works.structure: A diptych structure: parallel portraits of the proud man and the wise man, developed through antithesis, followed by a homiletic conclusion on the wages of pride.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous.
themes: Nature, landscape, and the shaping mind
sources: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Jane Austen

works.title: Vancenza; or, The Dangers of Credulity
works.form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror; Epistolary Fiction
works.description: Mary Robinson's first novel, a two-volume gothic romance written in letters and published by subscription the year after her first volume of poetry. Its heroine, Vancenza, is a girl formed by the extravagant reading of romance and of the marvellous, and the plot subjects her credulity to real persecution, so that the book at once exploits and criticizes the machinery of the novel of terror. Its large subscription list shows how quickly Robinson translated poetical fame into novel-reading capital.
works.plot: Vancenza, an imaginative young woman brought up on tales of the marvellous and persuaded of preternatural intimations, is drawn into a succession of real dangers engineered by interested and tyrannical men; the narrative of her trials, told in letters, converts the expectations formed by romance into evidence of the vulnerability of women left uninstructed, and resolves her sufferings by the exposure of the fraud and violence that produced them.
works.significance: Vancenza is an early and instructive instance of a woman writer using gothic machinery to argue against the credulity that gothic feeds, and it marks the start of Robinson's remarkable sequence of eight novels, of which Walsingham and The Natural Daughter are the most considered; its subscription success is a fact of the first importance for the economic history of women's writing in the 1790s.
works.meter: Prose correspondence; the novel's heightened situations are phrased in the diction of Robinson's descriptive and elegiac verse, and verse is quoted as sententious comment on the action.
works.context: Published in the same years as the most productive phase of the English gothic, and immediately after Robinson had begun her public career as a poet and performer dependent on subscriptions and on her own credit; its title-page promise of a moral against credulity belongs to the 1790s debate about the dangers of novel-reading, in which women's fiction was simultaneously a commercial and an educational risk.
works.characters: Vancenza; the tyrannical and interested men who persecute her; the female companions and protectors to whom she writes
works.structure: An epistolary gothic novel in two volumes, the story delivered in letters from the heroine and her companions, with romance-style suspense and explanation used in the service of an argument about reading and belief.
works.attributionNotes: Published under the author's name; attribution is undisputed.

works.title: Vathek
altTitles: The History of the Caliph Vathek
works.description: An Arabian tale of a curious and voluptuous caliph who pursues knowledge and power until he is carried down into the palace of Eblis. It was composed in French by its author and issued in English in 1786, and its magnificence of description and its philosophy of despair made it at once notorious and influential.
works.plot: Vathek, caliph of Samarah, abandons the duties and the pleasures of his throne for the search after intellectual power, and is tempted by a sorcerer's project of an underground palace. He abandons the worship of his fathers for the star-worship of his cousin Carathis, and with her and the genii penetrates the cavernous halls of Eblis. He is sealed there in the company of the Petrified Worshippers of the Stars, doomed to an eternity of unsatisfied desire, while the tale reports his former splendour and his mother's prophecy.
works.significance: It is the most splendid of the century's literary arabesques and a central text of the Gothic-Oriental imagination, its palace of Eblis being one of the great visions of despair in English prose.
works.meter: A prose of superb and accumulated description, translated and revised from the author's French, with the long period of the catalogue and the terrible closure of the sentence as its characteristic effects.
works.context: Composed in French during the author's villa years in the early 1780s and published in English translation in 1786, with the French original printed soon afterwards; it stands in the line of the Arabian tales and of the Gothic romance of the same decade.
works.characters: Vathek the caliph of Samarah; Carathis his cousin and temptress; the old sorcerer Holgher; the rebellious genii and the prince of the palace of Eblis; the mother and the prophetess of the opening
works.structure: A single continuous oriental tale with the frame of prophecy and the descent as its climax, arranged as a sequence of spectacular tableaux; the interpolated stories of the palace of Eblis are set within the last movement.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution of the design uncontested, the English first edition being a translation from the author's French manuscript made with his knowledge and revised by him, the translator's share being traditionally assigned to a scholar of the day; the record is here held under the author's name alone.
